### Discovered Scope

- **7.1 introduced the app's first `Form`/`TextFormField` usage.** Every
  existing form screen (Project Setup, tag dialogs, etc.) uses plain
  `TextEditingController` + `TextField` with ad hoc `setState`/snackbar
  validation — there was no established inline-error convention to match.
  `IdentitySetupScreen` uses a real `Form` with `TextFormField.validator` and
  `AutovalidateMode.onUserInteraction` instead, since the task's acceptance
  criteria explicitly calls for inline rejection of a malformed email. Worth
  reconciling other screens onto this pattern later if it's adopted as the
  house style; not done here (out of scope, and the two patterns don't
  visually clash today).
- **New route `/identity-setup`** (`lib/routing/app_router.dart`), a
  top-level `GoRoute` alongside `/splash`/`/record-preview`, outside the tab
  shell. Reached only via `SplashScreen`'s own redirect — nothing else links
  to it. `IdentitySetupScreen` wraps its `Scaffold` in `PopScope(canPop:
  false)` (the app's first use of `PopScope`) so Android back can't dismiss
  it mid-capture.
- **`SplashScreen` now awaits `currentUserProvider` before navigating**,
  racing it against the existing splash-duration timer via `Future.wait`
  (`lib/features/splash/splash_screen.dart`). This is the "non-skippable
  gate" — there is no other path from `/splash` into the tab shell. Added
  `User.hasPlaceholderIdentity` (`lib/data/models/user.dart`) — `true` iff
  the email ends in `@local.tritrack`, the one hard-coded placeholder format
  `app_context_provider.dart`'s auto-create path uses — as the single
  detection point for both a fresh install and a not-yet-migrated existing
  device.
- **Full-app widget tests needed a new boot helper, and this surfaced a
  widget-testing gotcha beyond the ones already documented under Phase 4/5's
  Discovered Scope.** `widget_test.dart`, `navigation_smoke_test.dart`, and
  `compass_screen_test.dart` all pump the real `TriTrackApp` from cold —
  previously safe because splash's old fixed-timer navigation never touched
  the database. Now that splash awaits `currentUserProvider` (real DB I/O)
  on its very first frame, before any tap ever happens, the existing
  "wrap the tap in `runAsync`" pattern doesn't apply as-is: there's no tap to
  wrap, the read happens during `pumpWidget` itself. Fixed with a new shared
  helper, `test/support/app_boot_helper.dart`'s `pumpAppForTest`: builds an
  explicit `ProviderContainer` overriding `appDatabaseProvider` to
  `AppDatabase.openInMemory()`, pre-resolves `currentUserProvider` inside
  `tester.runAsync` for a warm cache, then — this part doesn't work if only
  the pre-resolve is wrapped — runs `pumpWidget` **and** a short real-time
  `Future.delayed` **and** `pumpAndSettle` all inside that *same*
  `runAsync` call. Even an already-cached provider's `.future` doesn't
  resolve synchronously if the code awaiting it (splash's own
  `_resolveAndNavigate`) runs in the plain fake-async pump zone rather than
  inside `runAsync` — confirmed by direct repro (see this task's session
  transcript): pre-resolving alone left the app stuck on `SplashScreen`
  through `pumpAndSettle` every time. `test/support/complete_identity_setup.dart`
  (fills and submits the identity form) needed the same treatment for its
  tap, since submitting does a real `UserRepository.update` + provider
  invalidation.
- **A second, unrelated gotcha surfaced by the above: `UncontrolledProviderScope`'s
  container must be disposed *before* the test body returns, not via
  `addTearDown`, if anything under it has a live real `Timer`.**
  `compass_screen_test.dart`'s first case hit "A Timer is still pending even
  after the widget tree was disposed" — `CompassAvailable`
  (`compass_provider.dart`, Phase 5.2) starts a 2-second availability
  `Timer` the first time it's watched, cancelled via `ref.onDispose` only
  when the provider (and thus the container) is disposed. flutter_test's own
  end-of-test invariant check runs *after* the widget tree is torn down but
  *before* `addTearDown` callbacks fire — fine for a `ProviderScope`-owned
  container (disposed as part of the widget tree itself), but our tests use
  an externally-owned container passed via `UncontrolledProviderScope`, so
  `addTearDown(container.dispose)` disposes it too late. Fixed by calling
  `container.dispose()` explicitly at the end of that one test instead of
  through `addTearDown`; the second compass test doesn't hit this (the
  overridden error stream makes `CompassAvailable` return `false`
  immediately, no timer started) so it keeps `addTearDown`. Worth watching
  for in any future full-app test that reaches a screen with a live
  provider-owned `Timer`/`Stream.periodic`/`AnimationController`.
- **7.3: the plan's two tiers turned out to need two directions each, four
  total match paths.** The task text names one scenario ("one user changed
  email, the other still holds the old one") but working through it showed
  the historical-address link can be recorded on *either* side of a merge:
  (a) incoming's current email vs. a local user's prior email (the *other*
  device changed its address), and (b) one of the incoming user's own prior
  emails vs. a local user's current email (*this* device never changed).
  `ProjectMerger._buildUserRemap` implements both as tier 2a/2b, only ever
  consulted when tier 1 (current↔current) found no match for that incoming
  user, matching the "current always wins" guardrail exactly.
  `SharedObservationImporter._resolveObserver` only needed direction (a) —
  a share payload carries just the observer's *current* email, never their
  address history, so direction (b) has no input to work from on that path.
  Both now query `User_Emails` and treat >1 distinct local user having
  recorded the same address as ambiguous (ignored, falls through to
  "unmatched") rather than picking one — the reassigned-shared-address
  hazard the task called out explicitly.
- **7.3: `ProjectExporter.collect` needed a new reachability step for
  `User_Emails`, not named in the task text but required for the feature to
  do anything cross-device.** Without it, a device that changed its email
  would never actually carry the prior-address row in a shared project
  backup, silently defeating the whole fallback. Added as step 4 (after the
  existing reachable-Users step), keyed off the same `userIds` set — every
  already-collected user's address history now travels in the archive.
  Covered by a `project_exporter_test.dart` case asserting an unrelated
  user's prior email is excluded.
- **7.3: `MergeReport` gained `usersMatchedViaPriorEmail`** (alongside the
  existing `usersDeduped`, which still counts the total — prior-matched
  entries are a subset, not an addition) and
  `SharedObservationImportResult`/`_ResolvedObserver` gained
  `observerMatchedViaPriorEmail`, both surfaced in their respective UIs
  (`data_export_screen.dart`'s merge-report dialog, and
  `observation_sharing_screen.dart`'s save snackbar) per the task's explicit
  "report distinctly, don't silently fold in" instruction.
- **7.3: schema v5 is the first *new table* migration** (v2/v4 were additive
  `ALTER TABLE`s on existing tables). `SchemaMigrator._applyStep` needed no
  v5 case — a backup older than v5 simply has no `User_Emails` key in its
  row payload at all, and `ProjectBackup.rowsFor` already defaults an absent
  table to `const []` — there's no existing-row shape to backfill the way
  v2/v4 needed. Worth remembering as the pattern for any *future* whole-new-
  table migration: only a *column* addition to an existing table needs a
  `SchemaMigrator` step.
- **7.2's actual persistence logic was factored out of `ProfileScreen` into a
  new standalone `ProfileEditor` class** (`lib/data/repositories/profile_editor.dart`)
  rather than living inline in the screen's `_save()` method. Reason: a full
  save round trip through the widget layer (tap → real DB write → invalidate
  a provider the same screen watches → recompute) reliably hangs under
  `testWidgets` — confirmed by direct repro this session, and already
  flagged as a known class of problem in `project_setup_screen_test.dart`'s
  header comment ("a real save-and-persist round trip is covered instead at
  the provider level ... using a plain `test()`"). `ProfileEditor.apply()`
  (record the old address in `User_Emails` iff the email actually changed,
  by normalized comparison, then `UserRepository.update` in place) is
  covered directly with a plain `test()` in
  `test/data/repositories/profile_editor_test.dart`; `ProfileScreen`'s own
  widget test (`test/features/more/profile_screen_test.dart`) stays scoped
  to pre-save behavior only (field loading, inline validation, the
  email-change confirm dialog appearing/naming the old address, and the
  cancel path, which touches no DB) — matching 7.1's shared validators via
  the new `lib/features/identity/identity_validation.dart`.
- **Two new widget-testing gotchas surfaced getting `profile_screen_test.dart`
  to actually terminate, beyond every runAsync/pending-Timer gotcha already
  logged under 7.1's entry above:**
  - **A `db.raw.query(...)` call is real I/O every time, even when the
    `appDatabaseProvider` *future* it came from is already cached.** A
    provider being resolved doesn't mean everything you subsequently do with
    its value is free — any fresh query against the live `Database` still
    needs `tester.runAsync`, including a purely-for-assertions read after
    the interesting UI interaction is already done. Missing this on the
    "canceling an email change" test's final assertions was the actual root
    cause of a run that otherwise looked like `pumpAndSettle` spinning
    forever.
  - **A dangling detached real-I/O continuation left mid-flight when a test
    ends throws "used ref after unmount" and fails whichever test happens to
    be running when it surfaces** (not necessarily the test that started
    it) — hit when a SAVE tap that skips the confirm dialog (no email
    change) was followed by only a single `tester.pump()` rather than
    letting the real save chain finish inside `runAsync` first. Any tap that
    can reach real DB I/O — confirmed or not by a dialog — needs its whole
    chain run to completion inside one `runAsync` block before the test
    moves on, even if the test doesn't care about the outcome.
- **7.4's "surface it to the user" requirement for the second-user-creation
  fallback is satisfied by reusing the existing Phase 7 identity gate,
  deliberately not by adding new UI.** `currentUser` (`app_context_provider.dart`)
  now tries `UserRepository.findById(activeId, includeDeleted: true)` before
  giving up and minting a placeholder; if the row is merely tombstoned, it's
  restored (`restoreById`) and returned as-is rather than creating a second
  identity. Only when the id is genuinely unrecoverable does it fall through
  to the original placeholder-email creation — and because that placeholder
  still matches `User.hasPlaceholderIdentity`, `SplashScreen`'s existing
  non-skippable gate (7.1) routes straight to `IdentitySetupScreen` on this
  same launch, which *is* the "surfaced, not silent" outcome the task asks
  for. No new provider-level UI plumbing was needed.
- **7.4 found a third NULL-`last_modified_by` insert site not named in the
  task text: `position_estimation_screen.dart`'s `EstimatedPosition` save**
  (`_save`, ~line 160) — same defect shape as the two named locations,
  found by grepping every `SyncMeta.initial(` call site in `lib/` for a
  missing `modifiedBy`. Fixed the same way (read `currentUserProvider`,
  pass `modifiedBy: user.userId`). Every other `SyncMeta.initial(` call
  missing `modifiedBy` was confirmed *not* a live bug on inspection: the

  "never persisted"), the Tag Database edit dialog's in-progress `Tag`
  object (`tag_database_screen.dart:473`, unconditionally re-stamped with a
  real `modifiedBy` by its caller before the actual insert), and the CSV
  import preview's `Tag` (`tag_csv_import.dart:177`, a DB-free preview value
  re-stamped by `TagImportRow.withSync` at commit time) — all three
  intentionally construct a throwaway/intermediate `SyncMeta` that a later
  step overwrites before anything reaches the database, so none needed a
  change.
- **7.4: deleted `UserRepository.findAll`/`findByEmail` rather than routing
  a caller through them** — confirmed via grep that neither had any
  production caller, and the two real "look up by email" implementations
  (`ProjectMerger._buildUserRemap`, `SharedObservationImporter._resolveObserver`)
  must stay raw-`txn`-based for transactional correctness (a repository
  method wraps a `Database`, not an in-flight `Transaction`), so there was
  no legitimate caller to route through either method. `findByEmail` had
  exactly one caller, in `test/data/model_roundtrip_test.dart`'s email-
  normalization test — rewritten to assert via `findById` instead, which
  tests the same normalization behavior more directly.
- **Test coverage added:** two new `app_context_provider_test.dart` cases

- **Not covered by a new test: `quickAddTagDialog`'s `modifiedBy` fix**

- **7.5: surfaced the current user in two places rather than one, per the

- **The identity row had to move outside the checklist's existing

  Restructured the body from a single `projectAsync.when(... data: (project)

- **Test coverage added:** `test/features/more/more_screen_test.dart` (two

- **7.6: most of this task's five bullets were already covered by tests

## Phase 8 — Permission Enforcement

**Why this exists.** The design docs state two rules — "only the
observation's creator can edit it" and "only the project owner can delete
observations or modify project settings." The audit (2026-07-31) found these
implemented as **one client-side render condition, in one of two edit
surfaces**:

```dart
canEdit: currentUser != null && currentUser.userId == o.userId,  // log_screen.dart:168
```

Everything else is ungated:
- **`map_screen.dart:2462-2466` bypasses it entirely** — tapping any
  observation on the map shows an Edit button with no author check, so you
  can already edit anyone's observation. This is a live bug, and it gets
  materially worse now that Phase 6 makes other people's observations
  actually present in the local database.
- **`ownerUserId` is never compared to anything.** It's written once
  (`project_setup_screen.dart:290`) and read only by the model and merger.
- **Project delete is unguarded** (`projects_screen.dart:93-145`) — any user
  can delete any project; `currentUser` is read purely to stamp the audit
  column.
- **Project settings edit is unguarded** (`project_setup_screen.dart:276-306`).
- **`Project_Memberships` is entirely dead** — table, model, repository, and
  provider all exist with zero production reads or writes. `ProjectRole`
  (owner/contributor/viewer) is validated on import but never compared to
  anything. No membership row is created even for a project's own owner.

**Scope boundary.** Phase One has no server, so these remain *advisory*
controls — anyone holding the backup file can edit its contents, and the app
already says so honestly in-product (`project_setup_screen.dart:208-212`).
The goal here is not real security; it's (a) fixing a live inconsistency
where two screens disagree about the same rule, and (b) putting enforcement
somewhere a *future screen can't accidentally bypass*, so the Phase 3 server
inherits a coherent model rather than a patchwork. Do not add UI copy
implying enforcement is secure.

**Decision locked in (2026-07-31):** **adopt `Project_Memberships`** rather
than deleting it. Rationale: it's the natural join for "who is on this
project and in what role" that the server will need regardless, and it's
cheaper to start populating now than to backfill later. Start by writing an
owner membership row on project creation.

### Task 8.1 — Enforce authorization below the widget layer
**Status:** Done (2026-07-31)
**Model:** **Opus** — cross-cutting change to every mutation call site, and
the local-vs-server enforcement boundary it establishes is what Phase 3
builds on. A subtle error here either blocks legitimate edits or silently
permits unauthorized ones.
**Depends on:** Phase 7 (a meaningful current user), 8.4 (roles to check)

- Today `BaseRepository.updateById`/`softDeleteById` accept `modifiedBy` as a
  *label only* — it's stamped into the audit column and never checked. Add
  real authorization at the repository layer so a screen that forgets to
  check cannot mutate another user's data.
- Design the boundary deliberately and write it down: which operations are
  owner-only, which are author-only, which are open to any project member;
  and how a merge/replica import (which legitimately writes rows authored by
  others — see Phase 6) is exempted without punching a general hole. **Note
  the specific tension:** `ProjectMerger._upsert` and
  `SharedObservationImporter._upsertReplica` deliberately write other users'
  rows and preserve their sync clocks. They must keep working. Prefer an
  explicit, narrow, well-named bypass over a permissive default.
- **Acceptance criteria:** an attempt to update or soft-delete another user's
  observation fails at the repository layer regardless of which screen calls
  it; merge and replica import still work unchanged (Phase 6's tests must
  still pass); the authorization rules are documented in
  `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`, not just implied by code.

### Task 8.2 — Fix the map Edit bypass
**Status:** Done (2026-07-31)
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 8.1

- `map_screen.dart:2462-2466` renders an Edit button on any selected
  observation with no author check, while `log_screen.dart` gates the same
  action. Apply the same rule, and prefer deriving it from 8.1's shared
  authorization check rather than duplicating the `userId ==` comparison a
  second time.
- **Acceptance criteria:** the map's Edit affordance appears only for
  observations the current user authored, matching the Log screen exactly;
  a test covers both surfaces agreeing.

### Task 8.3 — Guard project delete and settings
**Status:** Done (2026-07-31)
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 8.1, 8.4

- Gate project deletion (`projects_screen.dart:93-145`) and project settings
  edits (`project_setup_screen.dart:276-306`) on project ownership
  (`ownerUserId`), or on an owner role via `Project_Memberships` once 8.4
  lands — pick one source of truth and document which.
- Non-owners should see *why* the action is unavailable, not just a missing
  button (consistent with the app's "explain, don't just grey out" pattern
  established in Phase 5.2's compass-unavailable work).
- **Acceptance criteria:** a non-owner cannot delete a project or change its
  settings from any surface; the owner can; the reason is surfaced to
  non-owners.

### Task 8.4 — Adopt `Project_Memberships`
**Status:** Done (2026-07-31)
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** Phase 7

- Write an owner membership row when a project is created
  (`project_setup_screen.dart:290` currently sets `ownerUserId` but creates
  no membership).
- Backfill: for existing projects with no membership rows, create the owner's
  membership from `ownerUserId` on first load or via a migration — decide
  which and document it.
- Provide the reads 8.1/8.3 need (role lookup for the current user on the
  active project), routed through the existing
  `ProjectMembershipRepository` rather than raw queries.
- **Note:** membership rows arriving via merge already flow through
  `sync_tables.dart`, so no new sync plumbing is required.
- **Acceptance criteria:** creating a project produces an owner membership;
  existing projects get one without data loss; role lookup for the current
  user works and is used by 8.1/8.3; merged membership rows behave correctly.

### Task 8.5 — Tests
**Status:** Done (2026-07-31)
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 8.1–8.4

- Repository-layer authorization: another user's observation can't be updated
  or soft-deleted, from any entry point.
- Merge and replica import still write other users' rows (Phase 6 regression
  guard).
- Map and Log agree on edit permission for the same observation.
- Non-owner blocked from project delete/settings; owner allowed.
- Owner membership created on project creation; existing projects backfilled.
- **Acceptance criteria:** all covered; `flutter analyze` and the full suite
  pass.

### Discovered Scope

- **8.1 shipped ahead of its stated 8.4 dependency.** 8.1 was invoked before
  8.4 existed, so the owner rule reads `Projects.owner_user_id` directly
  rather than a `Project_Memberships` role. That is a working source of truth
  for the one owner-only table there is today. When 8.4 lands, decide
  explicitly whether the `owner` rule switches to a membership-role lookup or
  stays on `owner_user_id` (8.3 asks the same question for the UI — they must
  pick the *same* answer), and document it in the same
  `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` table 8.1 added.
- **`Project_Memberships` mutations are currently `anyUser`.** Membership rows
  are the one place where "any identified user may modify it" is clearly
  wrong — a contributor shouldn't be able to change their own role. It's
  harmless today (nothing writes memberships at all), but 8.4 must tighten
  this to owner-only. That needs a join to `Projects.owner_user_id`, which no
  existing `MutationRule` expresses: every rule today resolves against a
  column on the row itself. Expect to add a project-scoped rule variant.
- **Non-owner project edits now throw instead of being prevented.** With the
  `owner` rule live, a non-owner reaching project settings or delete gets an
  unhandled `UnauthorizedMutation` rather than a clean explanation. 8.3 is
  what closes this; until it lands the failure mode is an error, not silent
  data corruption, which is the safer of the two.
- **Repository-authorization test coverage landed with 8.1**, in
  `test/data/repositories/mutation_authorization_test.dart` (author rule,
  owner rule, replication bypass). 8.5 should extend rather than duplicate it.
- **`ProjectTagRepository` still takes a bare `modifiedBy` string.**
  Project_Tags has a composite key, so it bypasses the id-based helpers and
  their authorization entirely. Under the `anyUser` rule that's currently a
  no-op difference, but the inconsistency will bite if project-tag links ever
  need gating.
- **8.2's "surfaces agree" acceptance criterion is verified below the widget
  layer, not with a MapScreen widget test.** `MutationRule.author.permits`
  (added in 8.2, alongside the pre-existing repository-layer check from 8.1)
  is now the single call both `log_screen.dart` and `map_screen.dart` make
  for their Edit affordance, and `mutation_authorization_test.dart` covers it
  under the same three scenarios `log_screen_test.dart` drives through a full
  widget pump (own observation, another user's, no signed-in user). It does
  *not* pump `MapScreen` itself — there is still no MapScreen widget-test
  harness (backlog item below, reconfirmed here); that remains its own scoped
  task. If that harness is ever built, add a same-shape test there for full
  belt-and-suspenders coverage, but it isn't required to trust this fix: both
  screens now provably call the identical function.
- **8.3 shipped ahead of its stated 8.4 dependency, same as 8.1.** 8.3 was
  invoked before 8.4 existed, so it gates on `Projects.owner_user_id`
  directly (via `MutationRule.owner.permits(...)`, the same primitive 8.1
  added and 8.2 proved out for author checks) rather than a
  `Project_Memberships` role. This is the same judgment call 8.1 already
  made and documented; 8.3 just reuses it rather than introducing a second,
  possibly-disagreeing source of truth. When 8.4 lands, the decision of
  whether `owner` moves to a membership-role lookup must be made *once* and
  applied to both 8.1's repository check and 8.3's UI gating together — see
  the note added to `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`'s Security & Data
  Integrity section.
- **Non-owner project settings are now gated per-field (`enabled: isOwner`)
  rather than by disabling the whole form at once.** This matches the
  existing per-field pattern in the same screen (e.g. GPS-busy disabling just
  the "Use current location" button) but means a future field added to
  `ProjectSetupScreen` needs its own `enabled`/`_gatedToOwner` wiring — it
  isn't structurally enforced. The Tags subsection is deliberately exempt
  (`Project_Tags` is `anyUser`, not owner-gated — any project member manages
  tags), so "gate everything in this form" would have been wrong anyway.
- **`ProjectsScreen`'s Edit icon still navigates for non-owners.** It opens
  `ProjectSetupScreen` in what is now a read-only state (banner + disabled
  fields) rather than being disabled itself. This was a deliberate choice —
  it surfaces the *richer* inline explanation from 8.3's banner rather than
  a bare Tooltip, consistent with "explain, don't just hide" — but it means
  the two icons in that row use different affordance styles for the same
  underlying rule (Delete: disabled + Tooltip; Edit: always enabled, target
  screen explains). Worth a look if that reads as inconsistent in practice.
- **8.4 closed 8.1/8.3's "decide explicitly" flag with "no switch."** Repository
  authorization (`owner` rule on Projects) and 8.3's UI gating both stay on
  `Projects.owner_user_id`; they do **not** move to a `Project_Memberships`
  role lookup. Reasoning is written up in full in
  `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`'s Security & Data Integrity section — short
  version: no ownership-transfer feature exists yet, so the two values can't
  diverge, and making the hard enforcement boundary depend on a second
  table's population state (which could theoretically lag behind a
  just-created or just-merged project) is exactly the failure mode 8.1
  warned about. The membership-role lookup (`roleForUser` /
  `projectRoleForUserProvider`) is real and available for future
  contributor/viewer features — it's just not wired into the owner check.
- **The `anyUser` rule was NOT narrowed to "any project member."** 8.1's own
  forward-looking note ("task 8.4 adds Project_Memberships role lookup" for
  the `anyUser` gap) could be read as asking for this — narrowing Tags,
  Project_Tags, Estimated_Positions, Actual_Tag_Locations, and
  Triangulation_Sessions from "any identified user" to "any user who is a
  member of that row's project." Scoped out of 8.4 deliberately: it's a real
  behavior *narrowing* (not just wiring up an unused table) with no UI to
  add non-owner members yet to test against, and the risk profile matches
  8.1's own caution about subtle authorization changes. Left as explicit
  future scope if/when contributor/viewer features are built.
- **`Project_Memberships`' own rule (`projectOwner`, new in 8.4) resolves via
  `Projects.owner_user_id`, not via a membership lookup on the row's own
  project** — deliberately, to avoid a chicken-and-egg check (you shouldn't
  need a membership row to authorize a membership-row mutation). This means
  `roleForUser`/`projectRoleForUserProvider` is not actually consumed by the
  authorization framework itself yet; it's exercised by `mutation_
  authorization_test.dart` and available to any future screen that needs
  "what's my role here," but its first *production* consumer is still
  pending. Worth revisiting once a contributor/viewer feature exists.
- **Backfill runs on every `currentProject`/`projectById`/`allProjects`
  resolution**, not just once. It's a cheap no-op after the first backfill
  (one indexed `SELECT`), consistent with `currentUser`'s own recovery
  check, but it does mean every project load now does one extra query. Not
  measured against Phase One's performance budget; flag if it ever shows up
  in profiling.
- **8.5 was primarily an audit, not new implementation.** Most of its listed
  coverage already existed as a byproduct of 8.1–8.4 (each task added its
  own tests as it landed): `mutation_authorization_test.dart` covers
  repository-layer author/owner/projectOwner denial, the Map/Log agreement
  group, and the replication-bypass mechanism; `log_screen_test.dart`
  already covered Edit *and* Delete gating for a replica vs. the current
  user's own observation; `project_setup_screen_test.dart` and
  `projects_screen_test.dart` cover the non-owner/owner project-settings
  split; `app_context_provider_test.dart` covers membership creation and
  backfill. 8.5's real, new work was: (a) making the Phase 6 regression
  guard *explicit* rather than merely implied by "the old tests still pass"
  — see next bullet — and (b) filling two real, previously-untested gaps:
  `NonDetectionRepository` and `UserEmailRepository` both carry the
  `author` rule (per the table in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`) but had
  zero direct authorization tests before now.
- **New: `test/data/repositories/phase6_merge_import_authorization_test.dart`**
  exercises the actual `ProjectMerger`/`SharedObservationImporter` production
  code (not just the abstract `MutationActor.replication` bypass mechanism,
  which — worth noting — no production code currently calls; both real
  writers stay immune by never going through `BaseRepository` at all, not by
  invoking the bypass). Each test proves *both* halves for the same row: the
  merge/import path still writes it, and the ordinary
  `ObservationRepository` path still throws `UnauthorizedMutation` for the
  same edit attempted by a different user — confirming the exemption is
  narrow rather than a hole that also weakened the authorization it's
  exempt from.
- **`anyUser`-ruled tables (Tags, Project_Tags, Estimated_Positions,
  Actual_Tag_Locations, Triangulation_Sessions) still have no direct
  authorization test** — there's nothing to deny (any identified user may
  mutate them), so a test would only assert "any user can," which guards
  against very little. Skipped deliberately rather than padding the suite;
  revisit if/when any of them tightens (e.g. the "any project *member*"
  narrowing flagged as out-of-scope for 8.4 above).
- **MapScreen still has no widget-test harness** (reconfirmed once more,
  originally flagged in the backlog, reconfirmed by 8.2, reconfirmed here) —
  8.5's "Map and Log agree" coverage is still verified at the shared
  `MutationRule.author.permits` function level, not by pumping `MapScreen`
  itself. Unchanged from 8.2; still its own scoped task if ever built.

## Phase 9 — Housekeeping: Rename, Map Test Harness, CSV Color Coordination

**Goal:** clear the three longest-standing backlog items before Phase 3's
server work starts. None of them is a feature; all three are debt that gets
more expensive the longer it sits. The rename in particular is cheapest now —
every additional file added to the repo is another file to rewrite later, and
a server API that hardcodes the old package name would spread it further.

These three are unrelated to each other and can be run in any order relative
to one another. Within the rename, 9.1 must precede 9.2.

**Decisions locked in (2026-07-31):**
- **Full rename, including the Dart package.** `pubspec.yaml`'s
  `name: tri_track` becomes `tritrack`, and every
  `import 'package:tri_track/...'` is rewritten. This supersedes
  `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`'s line-5 note that "the Dart package name
  ... does not need to change" — that note was written when the rename was
  scoped to user-visible surfaces only; update it as part of 9.2 rather than
  leaving the two documents disagreeing.
- **Three things are deliberately NOT renamed** (see 9.1 for why each):
  the SQLite filename `tri_track.db`, the bundle identifiers
  (`edu.nau.tritrack`, already correct), and the cloud-backup filename prefix
  `TriTrack_` (already correct).
- **MapScreen gets a harness plus targeted regressions**, not full behavioral
  coverage. The goal is to close the specific gaps that shipped with
  code-inspection-only verification (per-tag coloring, the computed legend,
  the live tag-color-update bug fix, 8.2's Edit gate) — not to
  retrospectively test all 2,796 lines. Broader coverage is a future phase if
  it's ever wanted.
- **`TagCsvImport.preview` stays database-free.** Its DB-free contract is
  documented at `tag_csv_import.dart:15` and is what makes it unit-testable;
  9.5 threads a caller-supplied starting index through it rather than giving
  it a repository.

**Model note for this phase: all Sonnet.** Mechanical rename, platform
config, widget tests, and a small index-offset change — no algorithm,
authorization, or sync/merge correctness risk anywhere in it. If 9.3's
harness turns into a fight with provider zones deep enough that you're
changing production code to make it testable, stop and flag it rather than
pushing through.

### Task 9.1 — Rename the Dart package `tri_track` → `tritrack`
**Status:** Done
**Model:** Sonnet — mechanical, wide, and fully verifiable by the compiler.
**Depends on:** nothing (do this before 9.2 so the two renames don't collide
in the same files)

- `pubspec.yaml:1`: `name: tri_track` → `name: tritrack`.
- Rewrite all `package:tri_track/...` imports to `package:tritrack/...`.
  Current scale: **293 import lines across 72 files, all of them in
  `test/`.** `lib/` has zero `package:` self-imports — production code uses
  relative imports throughout — and there is no `integration_test/`
  directory. That makes this smaller and lower-risk than it sounds: the
  blast radius is the test suite, and a missed line is a hard compile error,
  not a silent bug. Run `flutter analyze` after regardless.
- Generated files need no special handling here: `grep` for `tri_track` in
  `*.g.dart` / `*.freezed.dart` returns nothing, because Riverpod's and
  Freezed's output uses `part of` and relative imports rather than `package:`
  self-imports. Re-run `build_runner` at the end anyway as a sanity check,
  but there is nothing to un-hand-edit.
- **Do NOT rename the SQLite filename.** `app_database.dart:30` defaults to
  `fileName = 'tri_track.db'`. Renaming it orphans every existing install's
  database — the app would silently open a new empty DB and the user's
  observations would appear to have vanished. It is an internal filename
  users never see. Leave it, and add a one-line comment saying why so a
  future rename pass doesn't "finish the job."
- **Do NOT rename `kBackupFormatId`.** `backup_format.dart:32` defines
  `const String kBackupFormatId = 'tri_track_project_backup'` — a *persisted*
  format identifier written into every backup manifest and compared against
  at line 85 to produce the "not a backup" error. Renaming it makes every
  existing backup file unreadable. Same treatment as the DB filename: leave
  it, comment why. (Compare the `TT1:` share-envelope marker, which Phase 6
  deliberately left at `TT1:` for exactly this reason — see
  `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md:243`.)
- **Do NOT touch the bundle identifiers.** `edu.nau.tritrack` is already
  correct in `android/app/build.gradle.kts` (`namespace`, `applicationId`)
  and `macos/Runner/Configs/AppInfo.xcconfig`
  (`PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER`). Changing a bundle ID is an app-identity
  change, not a rename — it would break code signing, the macOS sandbox
  container path (`~/Library/Containers/edu.nau.tritrack/`, which is where
  the dev database lives), and any installed build's upgrade path.
- `.idea/modules.xml` and the `tri_track.iml` / `android/tri_track_android.iml`
  files it points at are IDE scratch, not build inputs. Renaming them is
  optional; if you skip it, say so rather than leaving it ambiguous.
- **Acceptance criteria:** `flutter pub get`, `flutter analyze`, and the full
  `flutter test` suite all pass; `grep -rn "package:tri_track" lib/ test/`
  returns nothing; `grep -rn "tri_track" lib/` returns exactly two hits —
  the database filename (`app_database.dart:30`) and `kBackupFormatId`
  (`backup_format.dart:32`) — each now carrying a comment explaining why it
  stays.

### Task 9.2 — App display name → "TriTrack" across platforms and copy
**Status:** Done
**Model:** Sonnet — platform config and user-facing strings.
**Depends on:** 9.1

Every surface below currently reads "Tri Track" or "tri_track". Target is
**TriTrack**, one word, everywhere a human sees it.

- **Flutter:** `lib/app.dart:45` — `title: 'Tri Track'`.
- **iOS** (`ios/Runner/Info.plist`): `CFBundleDisplayName` (line 10,
  "Tri Track"), `CFBundleName` (line 18, "tri_track"), and the
  `NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription` string (line 30) which names the app.
- **macOS:** `macos/Runner/Configs/AppInfo.xcconfig:8`
  (`PRODUCT_NAME = tri_track`) and `macos/Runner/Info.plist:28`'s location
  string. **`PRODUCT_NAME` is the risky one** — it renames the built bundle
  from `tri_track.app` to `TriTrack.app`, and
  `macos/Runner.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj` hardcodes it in six lines (a
  `PBXFileReference` at line 68, references at 137 and 227, and three
  `TEST_HOST` build settings at 401/415/429). **Careful: those six lines
  contain ten literal occurrences.** Each `TEST_HOST` reads
  `$(BUILT_PRODUCTS_DIR)/tri_track.app/$(BUNDLE_EXECUTABLE_FOLDER_PATH)/tri_track`
  — `PRODUCT_NAME` drives the bare executable name as well as the bundle
  name, so a narrow `tri_track.app` → `TriTrack.app` replace leaves the
  executable half of each path broken. Verify with an actual
  `flutter build macos`, not just `flutter analyze`.
- **Android:** `android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml:3` —
  `android:label="tri_track"`.
- **In-app copy** (user-visible strings, not comments):
  `offline_data_map_screen.dart:438` ("Keep Tri Track open"),
  `auto_backup_section.dart` (deleted with the cloud backup, `3a9a2c8`), `observation_share.dart:237` ("Not a Tri
  Track share payload…"), `backup_format.dart:85` ("Not a Tri Track
  backup…"). **Note `observation_share.dart:237`'s string is asserted in
  `test/features/more/observation_sharing_screen_test.dart:103`** — update
  the expectation with it.
- **README.md** — title and body prose.
- **Docs reconciliation:** update `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`'s line-5
  app-naming note (it currently describes the rename as open work *and* says
  the package name doesn't need to change — both now wrong) and strike its
  line-503 backlog entry. Retitling the other CLAUDE_DOCS is out of scope;
  the conversation archive in particular is a verbatim historical record and
  should keep the name as it was actually used at the time.
- **Leave alone:** the `TriTrackColors` theme extension and every other Dart
  identifier (already one word); `cloud_backup_service.dart`'s `TriTrack_`
  filename prefix (already one word, and it's the discovery prefix used at
  line 120 to *list* existing backups — changing it would orphan them).
- **Acceptance criteria:** no user-visible surface reads "Tri Track" or
  "tri_track"; `flutter build ios`, `flutter build apk`, and
  `flutter build macos` all succeed (the macOS one specifically proves the
  pbxproj edits are consistent); the app's name on the home screen / dock /
  launcher reads "TriTrack" on each platform you can check; full test suite
  passes.

### Task 9.3 — First MapScreen widget-test harness
**Status:** Done
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** nothing

`MapScreen` (2,796 lines) is the only major screen in the app with no test
file at all — flagged in the backlog, then reconfirmed by tasks 4.4, 8.2, and
8.5, each of which shipped map behavior verified by code inspection only.
This task builds the harness; 9.4 uses it.

- Create `test/features/map/map_screen_test.dart` with a reusable
  `readyContainer` + `pumpScreen` pair, modeled directly on
  `test/features/observations/record_position_preview_screen_test.dart` —
  that file already pumps a `flutter_map` widget successfully and is the
  closest working precedent.
- **The hard-won techniques from Phases 4 and 5 apply directly here; reread
  those Discovered Scope sections before starting rather than rediscovering
  them.** Specifically: every `container.listen(...)` for a non-keepAlive
  provider must happen *inside* the same `tester.runAsync` block as its
  reads (a `listen` outside it pins the provider's Future chain to the fake
  zone forever and it never resolves); the test harness's `MaterialApp` needs
  `theme: AppTheme.light()` or anything reading
  `Theme.of(context).extension<TriTrackColors>()!` null-crashes — `MapScreen`
  does this at lines 181, 241, and 1719; and `tester.view.physicalSize` may
  need bumping for the layers/filters sheet.
- **Use plain `pump()`, never `pumpAndSettle()`.** The `TileLayer` at
  `map_screen.dart:371` issues real network image requests through
  `CachedTileProvider` that never resolve under `flutter test`, so
  `pumpAndSettle()` spins forever. Same reasoning as
  `offline_data_map_screen_test.dart`.
- **`_mapDataProvider` is private and cannot be overridden from a test** —
  that's fine, and arguably better: seed the in-memory database instead and
  let it read through the real repositories (it resolves observation,
  estimated-position, actual-tag-location, non-detection, tag, and
  project-tag repositories at `map_screen.dart:2732-2737`). Seeding is the
  realistic path and exercises more of the wiring. Note the line just above
  them, `map_screen.dart:2731`'s `ref.watch(recordingsRevisionProvider)` —
  that's the refetch trigger 9.4's item 3 depends on, so don't stub it out.
- `gpsPositionProvider` never resolves under `flutter test` (no platform
  channel registered), which is the natural "no fix" state — no override
  needed, same as `record_position_preview_screen_test.dart` relies on.
  Other providers the build method watches and that may need seeding or
  overriding: `currentProjectProvider`, `currentUserProvider`,
  `selectedTileCategoryProvider`, `selectedTileSourceProvider`,
  `computationStatusProvider`, `sharedObservationPreviewProvider`,
  `navigationTargetProvider`.
- Ship one smoke test with the harness: with a seeded project, one tag, and
  one observation, `MapScreen` pumps and renders its map without throwing.
- **Do not de-privatize `_tagColor` / `_legendRows` / `_viewshedIsRendered`
  to make them unit-testable.** The point of a harness is to test them
  through the tree. If that proves genuinely impossible for one of them, log
  it under Discovered Scope and say which, rather than quietly changing
  production visibility.
- **Acceptance criteria:** the harness pumps `MapScreen` and the smoke test
  passes reliably (run it several times — a test that passes once and hangs
  the next run is the failure mode this screen has always threatened);
  `flutter analyze` clean; full suite passes.

Cover the four map behaviors that currently have no widget-level test,

### Task 9.5 — Coordinate CSV-imported tag colors with existing tags
**Status:** Done
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** nothing

From 4.5's Discovered Scope: `TagCsvImport.preview()` round-robins
auto-assigned colors from an in-memory index starting at 0
(`tag_csv_import.dart:67,76`), so an import into a project that already has
tags reuses colors already in play — a batch of 3 imported tags always gets
palette colors 0, 1, 2 even if three existing tags already have them. Rows
with a valid explicit `color_hex` don't consume a slot and must keep that
behavior.

- **Keep `preview()` database-free** (its documented contract,
  `tag_csv_import.dart:15`). Instead give it an optional starting offset —
  e.g. `preview(String csvText, {int autoAssignStartIndex = 0})` — and have
  the caller supply the live tag count. The function stays pure and
  unit-testable; the database read stays in the UI layer where it already is.
- Caller is `tag_database_screen.dart:144` (`_importCsv`). Read the current
  tag count *before* building the preview, so the colors shown on the
  preview screen are the colors actually saved. `TagRepository.nextColorHex()`
  (`tag_repository.dart:20`) already does the count-based lookup; either
  reuse it or expose the raw count — but don't add a second, separately
  maintained counting query.
- Note `nextColorHex` counts **all** tags including deactivated ones (tags
  are never hard-deleted), which is deliberate. Keep that consistent; don't
  switch the import path to an active-only count.
- Palette API note: `TagColorPalette.nextColor(n)` is literally
  `=> colorForIndex(n)` (`tag_color_palette.dart:43`), and
  `test/data/tag_color_palette_test.dart:37-39` already asserts the
  equivalence — so the two paths can't wrap differently. The off-by-one risk
  is in the *offset* you pass, not in the palette. A third caller,
  `schema_migrator.dart:57`, also uses `colorForIndex` for the 4.1 migration
  backfill; leave it alone.
- **Acceptance criteria:** importing N tags into a project that already has M
  tags assigns colors continuing from M, not from 0; a CSV row with a valid
  explicit `color_hex` still keeps it and still doesn't consume a palette
  slot; existing `tag_csv_import_test.dart` cases still pass (the default
  `autoAssignStartIndex = 0` keeps them valid unchanged); a new test covers
  the offset case; the preview screen shows the same colors that get saved.

### Discovered Scope

- **9.1:** left `tri_track.iml`, `android/tri_track_android.iml`, and
  `.idea/modules.xml` unrenamed. The task entry calls this optional IDE
  scratch; skipping rather than renaming since it has no effect on build,
  analyze, or test outcomes.
- **9.2:** the task's file list didn't mention
  `macos/Runner.xcodeproj/xcshareddata/xcschemes/Runner.xcscheme`, but it
  hardcodes `BuildableName = "tri_track.app"` in five places, mirroring the
  same product name the pbxproj edit changes. Updated it alongside the
  pbxproj edits for internal consistency (Xcode's scheme editor would
  otherwise show a stale bundle name for the Runner scheme); verified with
  the same `flutter build macos` run.
- **9.3: `_mapDataProvider`'s real `sqflite_common_ffi` isolate round trip
  forced a variant of the established `runAsync` technique, worth recording
  since 9.4 will hit it immediately.** Every prior screen test in this repo
  (including `record_position_preview_screen_test.dart`, this task's named
  precedent) only ever pre-resolves *public, listenable* providers inside
  `runAsync`, then calls `pumpWidget` afterward in the plain fake-async zone
  — safe because nothing left to watch during that later build is a
  repository-backed provider being triggered for the first time.
  `MapScreen` breaks that: it watches the private `_mapDataProvider`
  (a `FutureProvider.family`, not overridable or pre-fetchable from a test
  file in another library) on its very first build, and that provider's
  `sqflite_common_ffi` queries go through a real isolate round trip that
  never resolves under the fake-async pump clock, regardless of when it's
  kicked off. Fix: run the *entire* first build — `pumpWidget` plus enough
  settling `pump()`s — inside one `tester.runAsync` block, matching
  `test/support/app_boot_helper.dart`'s pattern (which hit the same isolate
  issue via `currentUserProvider` from the splash screen) rather than
  `record_position_preview_screen_test.dart`'s. Two real-time
  `Future.delayed(300ms)` + `pump()` pairs were needed before the seeded
  data actually rendered; `pumpAndSettle()` is still off the table entirely
  (the `TileLayer`'s never-resolving network image requests would spin it
  forever), so this real-delay-then-pump loop is the only settling
  mechanism available here.
- **9.3: the map toolbar's icon row overflows the default 800x600 test
  surface**, same `tester.view.physicalSize` fix Phase 4's `_TagEditDialog`
  tests needed for a tall dialog. Bumped to `1200x1600` for the smoke test;
  9.4 should keep this (or size to whatever its widest sheet needs).
- **9.3: none of `_tagColor`/`_legendRows`/`_viewshedIsRendered` needed
  de-privatizing.** The harness's single smoke test doesn't exercise them
  directly (no tag-colored map elements or legend assertions yet — that's
  9.4's job), so this wasn't tested under load, but nothing about the
  harness itself ran into a wall that would force de-privatizing any of the
  three; flagging for 9.4 to confirm once it actually asserts against their
  output through the tree.
- **9.4 confirms 9.3's flag: none of `_tagColor`/`_legendRows`/
  `_viewshedIsRendered` needed de-privatizing**, now that both are actually
  exercised through the tree. `_tagColor`'s output reads straight off public
  data: `PolylineLayer.polylines[i].color` for rays, and the color baked
  into the `Text.style` inside `_EstimateMarker`/`_TagLocationMarker` (both
  private classes, but `style` is a public field reachable through the
  ordinary `find.text(label)` → `tester.widget<Text>(...)` path — no
  `dynamic`/reflection tricks needed). `_legendRows`' output is even more
  direct: `MapLegendCard.rows` is a plain public `List<(Color, String)>`
  field on a public widget, so the legend tests just read it off
  `tester.widget<MapLegendCard>(...)` rather than parsing rendered swatches.
- **9.4 hit a new, generally-applicable widget-test gotcha: a tap-to-select
  gesture on a `FlutterMap` must run inside `tester.runAsync`, same as the
  private-provider issue 9.3 already documented, but for a completely
  different reason.** flutter_map's tap detector (`PositionedTapDetector2`)
  buffers every tap through a real `StreamController` with a genuine
  `Stream.timeout` (default 250ms) to disambiguate a single tap from the
  first half of a double-tap, and that stream is created once, in
  `initState` — which, per 9.3's pattern, runs inside `pumpScreen`'s
  `runAsync` block, binding the stream's timeout to the *real* zone. A tap
  performed afterward the normal way (`tester.tapAt` + fake-clock
  `tester.pump(duration)`, exactly how `record_position_preview_screen_test.dart`
  does it) fires the recognizer fine, but the buffered event's real-zone
  timeout is never driven forward by the fake clock — no exception, no
  hang, just a tap that silently never reaches `MapOptions.onTap`, which
  looks identical to a hit-test/geometry bug and cost real time to
  distinguish from one (confirmed the geometry was exact — computed
  `camera.latLngToScreenOffset` matched the tap point precisely — before
  finding the real cause). Fix: wrap the tap itself in `tester.runAsync`
  too, with a real `Future.delayed` longer than 250ms before the settling
  `pump()` — see `tapMapCenter` in `map_screen_test.dart`. Worth remembering
  for any future test that taps a `flutter_map` map rather than just
  rendering one.
- **9.4: `DraggableScrollableSheet`'s `ListView(children: ...)` only builds
  children within its viewport/cache extent**, so the Layers & Filters
  sheet's TIME WINDOW section (below LAYERS/VIEWSHED TOOLS/TAGS) isn't in
  the widget tree at all — not just off-screen — unless the sheet is tall
  enough to fit everything above it first. Fixed by giving the legend test
  a much taller `tester.view.physicalSize` (1200x3200) rather than scrolling
  the sheet, since `initialChildSize` is a fraction of the surface height.
- **9.4 extended two test fixtures (`test/data/fixtures.dart`), both
  backward-compatible (new optional params, old defaults unchanged):
  `sampleTag` gained `tagName` (previously hardcoded to `'Coco'`, needed so

- **9.4 did not attempt to render a real viewshed for the "legend appends a

- **9.4 did not add a third "no signed-in user" Edit-gate case**, per the

## Phase 10 — Server Foundation & Personal Sync

*Formerly "Phase 3" in this document (see the redirect note near the top).
Corresponds to "Phase Three" in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`, which is left
at its original numbering deliberately. **Split from a single oversized phase
on 2026-08-01** — team collaboration moved to Phase 11.*

**Goal:** secure, continuous sync of one user's data across all of that
user's own devices, with real authentication — and without making the server
a prerequisite for using or shipping the app.

**Deliberately excludes teams.** Multi-owner projects, membership management,
the team log, and observer provenance are Phase 11. This phase stops at
"my data, on my laptop and my phone, safely." That is independently
shippable and independently useful: a solo researcher with two devices is a
real user, and it is the most common shape of this app's use even on projects
that later grow a team.

**Why split here.** Sync and authentication are the two hardest things in this
work, and teams multiply the state space of both. Proving convergence,
identity, and authorization with one user and two devices — where every
divergence is unambiguously a bug rather than a legitimate difference of
permission — is far cheaper than debugging sync and team semantics
simultaneously.

### The single most important constraint

**TriTrack must remain fully releasable, usable, and testable with no server
in existence.** Everything below is additive. Phase 6's backup-file channel
already provides multi-device sharing; the server is a second, more convenient
transport for the same data, not a replacement and not a dependency.

This is not an aspiration — it is an acceptance criterion on **every task in
this phase**: *the full `flutter test` suite passes with no server running and
no network access, and the app builds, launches, and is fully usable with no
server URL configured.* If a task can't meet that, it's the wrong task.

The specific things that would silently destroy this property, all forbidden:

1. **Login as a launch gate.** Phase 7's first-run local user stays the
   default path. Server sign-in is an upgrade, never a prerequisite.
2. **Server-assigned primary keys.** Client-generated UUIDs remain
   authoritative; offline record creation must never wait on the server.
3. **Non-nullable server columns.** `server_seq` and anything like it must be
   nullable and ignorable, so a device that has never synced can still write.
4. **Any read path behind the network.** Every screen reads local SQLite
   through the existing repositories. No screen ever awaits a network call to
   render.
5. **A test suite that needs a server.** Client sync tests use a fake
   transport.

### Why this is mostly extension, not new architecture

The sync engine built in Phase 6 is already transport-agnostic:

- `ProjectMerger.merge()` takes an in-memory `ProjectBackup` — a
  `Map<String, List<Map<String, Object?>>>` — not a file. The zip is one
  container wrapped around it, separable from the merge.
- `MergeResolver` is explicitly documented as free of any database or model
  dependency: pure last-write-wins over the six sync columns.
- `syncTables` describes every table generically, so the engine handles rows
  as column-maps and **never needs the Freezed models**. The server therefore
  doesn't either.
- Phase 6's replica import already writes *other users'* rows into the local
  tables with their original ids and sync clocks.

So the server is a third peer that speaks row-maps over HTTP. What is
genuinely new: authentication, server-side authorization, and a delta cursor.

**Decisions locked in (2026-08-01):**

- **Monorepo, app stays where it is.** Add `server/` and `packages/` as
  siblings of `lib/`. Do *not* relocate the Flutter app into `app/` — it
  churns every path in `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/commands/`, and IDE config for no
  benefit.
- **Server is written in Dart** (`shelf` or `dart_frog`), specifically so the
  merge rule can be a *shared package* rather than a second implementation.
  Client and server disagreeing about the merge rule produces split-brain:
  two devices converging on different states depending on which synced
  through the server. One implementation makes that class of bug impossible.
- **Postgres** for the server datastore, via Docker Compose for local dev.
- **Transport: cursor-based delta sync over HTTPS**, not REST CRUD. Design the
  cursor into the wire envelope from day one — retrofitting one into a
  whole-project push/pull is exactly the kind of thing that never happens, and
  then every sync ships the entire project.
- **A user belongs to many projects; assume that from the start.** One person
  can own or join any number of projects, and this is the normal case, not an
  edge case — a field tech on three concurrent studies, or a student with
  their own project plus their advisor's. Nothing in the schema, the sync
  protocol, or the authorization model may assume one project per user. This
  is a Phase 10 constraint even though *teams* are Phase 11: a single user
  with three of their own projects exercises all of it. (Phase 11 adds the
  related `(project_id, user_id)` open-membership invariant.)
- **Auth: email magic link.** No passwords to store, hash, reset, or leak, and
  it maps directly onto the normalized-email identity anchor Phase 7 already
  established. NAU SSO was considered and rejected for v1: it excludes
  collaborators outside NAU (other universities, NGOs, agencies), which is the
  common case for this app.

### One user, many devices

**The normal case, not an edge case.** A project owner with the app on a laptop
and a phone is the expected setup, and both must behave as *the same person* —
same `user_id`, same ownership, one identity in the Log, one member row.
This cuts across several tasks, so the requirements are collected here.

**The problem the existing code has.** Phase 6's `ProjectMerger._buildUserRemap`
resolves an email collision in favor of the **local** `user_id`. Peer-to-peer,
that's symmetric and fine in practice: desktop merges the phone's backup and
remaps the phone's user onto the desktop id; the phone does the reverse.
Each device is internally consistent, and they permanently disagree with each
other. File-based sync is manual and occasional, so this stays invisible.

Continuous server sync makes it acute. Every sync round would rewrite
`user_id` values, bump `revision` on every affected row, and push the churn
back to the other device — an endless loop of two devices renaming the same
person. `Project_Memberships.user_id` is in `syncTables`' `userColumns`, so
owner rows get dragged along with each rewrite, which is exactly the "syncing
as if it's a different owner" failure.

**Decision (2026-08-01): the server is authoritative for the `user_id` behind
an email.** On first sign-in, a device adopts the server's `user_id` for its
normalized email and remaps its local rows onto it — including the Phase 7
first-run local user, which was minted offline with a locally generated id and
is the same person. Devices never negotiate identity with each other; they
both defer to the server. Peer-to-peer merge keeps its current local-wins rule
unchanged for the no-server case.

**Requirements this creates**, each landing in the task named:

- **Adopt-the-server's-id on sign-in, exactly once per device** (10.6). This is
  a remap of existing local rows, not a new user. It must be idempotent and
  survive interruption — a half-applied identity remap is the worst possible
  state to leave a database in.
- **Sync cursors are per `(user, device)`, never per user** (10.7). A single
  per-user cursor means the laptop's sync advances the phone's cursor past rows
  the phone never received, and those rows are silently never delivered. This
  is a quiet data-loss bug, not a performance issue.
- **Concurrent sessions per user are supported and expected** (10.6). Signing
  in on the phone must not sign the laptop out.
- **Revocation is all-devices** (10.14). Revoking a user's access must
  invalidate every session they hold, not just the one that happened to make
  the last request. 10.14 builds the capability; Phase 11's task 11.2 wires
  member removal to it.
- **Magic links are device-agnostic in the annoying direction** (10.6): a link
  requested on the laptop and opened on the phone signs in *the phone*, and the
  laptop is left waiting. Decide and document the behavior — at minimum the
  requesting device must not hang silently forever.
- **A device registry** (10.13, 10.14): the server tracks which devices a user
  has and when each last synced. Needed for diagnostics ("why is my phone
  behind?") and to revoke a single lost device without signing the user out
  everywhere — which ties directly to 10.0's device-loss analysis.

**One consequence to accept, not fix:** if the same person edits the same row
offline on both devices, last-write-wins still applies between them. Ties break
on `origin_device_id`, so the winner is deterministic but arbitrary. A user can
lose their own edit. That's inherent to LWW and already documented; it's worth
knowing it applies to you-versus-yourself, not just you-versus-a-teammate.

### Security posture

**Read this before writing any server code.** Nothing else in this phase is
allowed to proceed ahead of task 10.0.

**Why this app is not a generic CRUD app.** TriTrack stores precise, timestamped
locations of collared animals. For endangered or commercially trafficked
species, that dataset is directly useful to poachers — targeting researchers'
telemetry data is a documented pattern in conservation technology, not a
hypothetical. A leak here has a physical-world consequence that a leaked todo
list does not. Design accordingly: the sensitivity of this data is closer to
medical records than to hobby-project data, even though nothing about it is
legally regulated.

**Three-part structure** (all three are required; none substitutes for another):

1. **Design first — task 10.0.** Threat model and security design, completed
   and reviewed *before* the server scaffold in 10.3. Security decisions made
   after the schema and protocol exist are patches; made before, they're
   architecture.
2. **Enforced throughout — per-task criteria and review gates.** Every task in
   this phase carries the standing security criteria below. Three hard review
   gates sit at the points where a mistake is most expensive.
3. **Summative before exposure — task 10.16.** A full assessment that acts as
   a *gate*, not a report: the server does not listen on anything but
   localhost until it passes.

**Standing security acceptance criteria — apply to every task in this phase,
in addition to whatever that task lists:**

- No secret (token, password, key, connection string, session id) is written
  to a log, an error message, an HTTP response, a test fixture, or the repo.
- Every database query is parameterized. No string-interpolated SQL, ever.
- Every endpoint that touches project data verifies **membership in that
  specific project**, not merely that the caller is authenticated. Being a
  valid user of the system grants access to nothing by itself.
- Any new dependency is justified in the task's summary — name, why, and what
  it's trusted with.
- Errors returned to clients say what went wrong without revealing whether a
  record exists, whether an email is registered, or what the internal
  structure looks like.

**Three review gates.** At each, run Claude Code's `/security-review` command
on the branch and address findings before merging. These are stop points, not
checkpoints to note and move past:

- **Gate A — after 10.6 (auth).** Token generation, storage, expiry, replay,
  and enumeration. Authentication bugs are the ones that lose everything at
  once.
- **Gate B — after 10.10 (authorization).** Cross-project isolation and
  IDOR. This is where "authenticated" gets wrongly conflated with
  "authorized," which is the single most common way an API leaks data.
- **Gate C — before any deployment reachable beyond localhost**, including the
  first time you expose the laptop prototype to the campus network. This one
  is easy to skip because it doesn't correspond to finishing a feature. Don't.

**On outside review.** I can help you design and audit this, and
`/security-review` catches a great deal. Neither is equivalent to a
professional review of an internet-exposed system holding
poaching-sensitive data. Before any real deployment, get NAU's information
security office to look at it — they exist for this, the review is free to
you, and an institutional sign-off is also useful if this ever touches IRB,
grant compliance, or a data-management plan.

### Staging

**Task 10.0 comes first, before everything.** `10.1`–`10.2` are client-only
and shippable on their own. `10.3`–`10.4` stand up the laptop dev
environment. `10.5`–`10.8` are the sync core. `10.9` is what makes any of it
reachable by a real project. `10.10`–`10.12` are correctness, policy, and the
one part of this phase a user actually sees. `10.13` (diagnostics) is
numbered late but should be pulled forward to right after `10.7` — it exists
to make everything after it debuggable. `10.14`–`10.16` close the phase.

### Task 10.0 — Threat model and security design
**Status:** Done (2026-08-01) — `CLAUDE_DOCS/TriTrack_Security_Model.md`. All
eleven section-4 decisions made with reasoning recorded; none deferred. Eight
discovered-scope items filed below. No server code written. Notable decisions
that later tasks inherit: opaque DB-backed sessions rather than JWTs (§4.3,
because immediate revocation is a hard requirement); no SQLCipher, with
keychain/keystore session-token storage and per-device revocation in its place
(§4.8); no heightened-sensitivity project mode — strict defaults for every
project instead (§4.14); server authorization must fail closed where Phase 8's
client-side `permits()` fails open (§4.12). This document supersedes the
Security Posture section above where they differ; no conflicts were found, only
strengthenings (10.13's console goes from localhost-by-default to
off-by-default).
**Model:** **Opus** — this is the security architecture every later task
inherits. Getting it wrong is expensive in a way that isn't visible until
something leaks.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Blocks 10.3 and everything after it.**

Produce `CLAUDE_DOCS/TriTrack_Security_Model.md` — a real working document,
not a checklist — covering the following. Where a decision is made, record the
reasoning, because the reasoning is what tells a future task whether a
proposed change violates it.

**1. Assets, ranked by what their loss actually costs.** At minimum: precise
animal locations (physical harm to animals; potentially to researchers in
enforcement contexts), researcher identity and email, data integrity (a
falsified or corrupted bearing silently corrupts published science), and
account access. Rank them, because ranking is what makes tradeoffs decidable
later.

**2. Threat actors and what each can realistically do.** At minimum:
- **Poachers / wildlife traffickers** — motivated, specifically interested in
  this data class, and the reason this app isn't generic. Assume they will
  try social engineering of team members before they try an exploit.
- **Opportunistic internet scanners** — automated, will find an exposed
  Postgres port or a weak endpoint within hours of it going public.
- **Removed team members** — already partly addressed; retain local data
  permanently (see Phase 11's "Known limitation" section), but must lose server access
  immediately and completely.
- **Curious insiders** — an authenticated user of project A attempting to read
  project B. The most likely real breach, and the least dramatic.
- **Network eavesdroppers** — acutely relevant during the LAN prototype
  stage, where cleartext HTTP is temporarily in play.

**3. Attack surface inventory.** The HTTP API, magic-link tokens, session
tokens, the transport itself, the diagnostics console (10.13), the database at
rest and its backups, the device-local SQLite, and the dependency supply
chain. For each: what an attacker gains from it, and what control prevents it.

**4. Decisions to make and record now**, because retrofitting each is
disproportionately painful:
- **TLS everywhere in production**, and precisely how the cleartext dev
  exemption from 10.4 is prevented from ever shipping in a release build.
- **Token design** — entropy source and length, hashed at rest (never stored
  in plaintext), single-use, short expiry, constant-time comparison.
- **Session lifetime, rotation, and revocation** — specifically, removing a
  member must invalidate their sessions immediately, not at next expiry.
  Without this, task 11.2's removal is cosmetic for hours or days.
- **Rate limiting** on magic-link requests — prevents both email bombing of a
  colleague and account enumeration.
- **Account enumeration** — sign-in must not reveal whether an address is
  registered. Same response either way.
- **Secrets management** — environment variables, `.env` gitignored, and a
  documented procedure for rotating a leaked one. Decide it now; every project
  that decides it later has already committed a secret.
- **Audit logging** — who read and wrote what, retained how long. Also decide
  what must *never* be logged.
- **Backup encryption** for the server database.
- **Device-local encryption at rest** (e.g. SQLCipher). Genuinely open: it
  costs performance and complexity, and a lost unlocked phone defeats it
  anyway. Decide explicitly and record why — a stolen field phone with a
  season of nest locations is the scenario to reason about.
- **Whether some projects need a heightened-sensitivity mode** with stricter
  defaults, given the poaching threat.

**5. Explicit non-goals.** What this system does *not* defend against, stated
plainly so nobody later assumes protection that was never built. Start with
the two known ones: a removed member's retained local copy, and a member who
deliberately exfiltrates data they're legitimately authorized to see.

- **Acceptance criteria:** the document exists and every decision in section 4
  is either made with reasoning recorded or explicitly deferred with a named
  task that will make it; the non-goals section is written; the standing
  criteria in this plan's Security Posture section are consistent with it (if
  they conflict, this document wins and the plan gets updated); no server code
  has been written yet.

### Task 10.1 — Extract `packages/tritrack_sync`
**Status:** Done (2026-08-01). `packages/tritrack_sync` has no Flutter or
sqflite dependency (verified: its own `pubspec.yaml` declares no such
dependency, and `dart analyze`/`dart test` run green standalone from within
the package directory). Moved: `merge_resolver.dart`, `sync_tables.dart`,
`row_validator.dart`, `backup_format.dart`'s DTO half (`BackupManifest`,
`ProjectBackup`, its exceptions, and `rowCountsOf`), `db_codec.dart` (moved
whole — see judgment call below), the `Tables` table-name constants (now in a
new `schema_constants.dart`, extracted out of `schema.dart`), and
`latestSchemaVersion` (same file; previously derived in `migrations.dart` from
the migration list — see judgment call below). Also moved, because
`row_validator.dart` depends on them and the package cannot import back into
the app: `models/enums.dart` and `models/tag_color_palette.dart` (both already
Flutter-free). The app depends on the package by path
(`pubspec.yaml`); `schema.dart` re-exports `Tables` and `migrations.dart`
re-exports `latestSchemaVersion` so the ~30 existing app call sites needed no
import changes for those two symbols. The full existing app suite (467 tests)
passes unchanged against the new import paths; `flutter analyze` is clean.
The package has its own test suite (42 tests, using `package:test`, not
`flutter_test`) — the two tests that were pure logic with zero app-model
dependency (`merge_resolver_test.dart`, `tag_color_palette_test.dart`) moved
there outright rather than being duplicated; new package-local tests were
added for `RowValidator`, `DbCodec`, `BackupManifest`/`ProjectBackup`,
`Tables`/`latestSchemaVersion`, and `syncTables` ordering, since those didn't
previously have a Flutter-free equivalent.

**Two judgment calls, flagged per the task instructions since the spec was
slightly under-specified here:**
- **`db_codec.dart` moved as a whole file**, not split into "UTC encode/decode
  only" as the plan's wording suggested. The whole class (UTC, local,
  bool, and string-list codecs) is equally Flutter-free, and every app model
  that uses any one of these encodings uses several of them in the same
  `toColumns()`/`fromRow()` pair — splitting would have meant every one of
  those ~13 files importing from two places for one cohesive concern, for no
  behavioral benefit. The part the plan called out by name (UTC) is the part
  that *must* match byte-for-byte for `MergeResolver` to compare across
  client/server; that reasoning doesn't argue against moving the rest too.
- **`latestSchemaVersion` is now a hardcoded constant in
  `schema_constants.dart` (`= 5`)**, not derived from the migration list the
  way `migrations.dart` used to compute it — the DDL migrations themselves stay
  in the app per the task's own instruction, so the shared package has no
  migration list to derive from. To keep "exactly one definition" real rather
  than nominal, `migrations.dart` now exposes
  `assertMigrationsMatchLatestSchemaVersion()`, checked in a new
  `test/data/migrations_test.dart`, which fails loudly if a future migration
  is added without bumping the shared constant to match.
**Model:** Sonnet — mechanical extraction; the hard design work is deciding
*what* moves, which is specified here.
**Depends on:** nothing

Create a plain Dart package (no Flutter, no `sqflite`) that both the app and
the server depend on, holding the things they must never disagree about:

- `merge_resolver.dart` — already pure, moves nearly as-is.
- `sync_tables.dart` — the generic table descriptors.
- `row_validator.dart`.
- The table/column constants and `latestSchemaVersion` from
  `lib/data/db/schema.dart`. **The DDL strings stay in the app** (they're
  SQLite-specific; the server writes Postgres), but the canonical *column set*
  and schema version must be shared or the two schemas will drift.
- `backup_format.dart`'s DTO half (`ProjectBackup`, `BackupManifest`) — the
  envelope both sides serialize.
- `db_codec.dart`'s UTC encode/decode, since both sides must agree
  byte-for-byte on timestamp format (`MergeResolver` compares them).

Stays in the app: `project_exporter.dart` (imports `sqflite_common_ffi`),
`project_merger.dart` (writes to the local DB), `backup_archive.dart` (zip
handling), all Freezed models.

- **Acceptance criteria:** `packages/tritrack_sync` has no Flutter or sqflite
  dependency and its own passing test suite; the app depends on it by path and
  the full existing suite still passes unchanged; `latestSchemaVersion` and
  the table/column set have exactly one definition in the repo.

**Status:** Done (2026-08-01). `serverConfigProvider`

### Task 10.4 — Platform configuration for local-network development
**Status:** Done (2026-08-01). All four gotchas addressed, verified against
real merged manifests/plists from actual builds, not just by inspection.
**Verified on real hardware (2026-08-03):** an on-device sign-in test on a
physical iPhone confirmed the Local Network permission prompt and the ATS
cleartext exemption both work as designed against the LAN dev server — the
one bug that session surfaced (`activeUserIdProvider`'s `autoDispose` crash,
`b806d77`) was client-side Riverpod provider lifecycle, not a networking or
platform-config defect. Closes the "structural verification only, no real
device" gap this task's manifest/plist inspection couldn't close on its own.

- **iOS** (`ios/Runner/Info.plist`): added `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription`
  (real user-facing string, explicit that this is optional) and
  `NSAppTransportSecurity` → `NSAllowsLocalNetworking = true`. Verified by
  `flutter build ios --debug --no-codesign --simulator` and inspecting the
  built `.app`'s actual `Info.plist` — both keys present as expected.
- **macOS** (`macos/Runner/Info.plist`): same two keys, same reasoning —
  macOS 15+ shows its own local-network prompt, and ATS blocks cleartext on
  macOS too. Verified by `flutter build macos --debug` and inspecting the
  built `.app`'s `Info.plist`.
- **Why `NSAllowsLocalNetworking` is safe in every build, not just debug**:
  unlike Android's cleartext switch, this ATS exception is narrow by
  construction — iOS/macOS themselves restrict it to addresses they recognize
  as local/private (LAN IPs, `.local` hostnames, loopback), never a public
  host. No debug/release split needed or done.
- **Android**: `android/app/src/debug/res/xml/network_security_config.xml`
  (new, debug-source-set only) sets `cleartextTrafficPermitted="true"`
  broadly rather than scoped to specific LAN IPs — task 10.2 made the server
  URL a field the user types at runtime, so there's no fixed hostname to
  scope a `<domain-config>` to the way a production TLS domain could have.
  Referenced only from `android/app/src/debug/AndroidManifest.xml` via
  `android:networkSecurityConfig`, added as a merged-in attribute on the
  single `<application>` tag rather than a blanket
  `android:usesCleartextTraffic`.
- **Verified structurally, not just by reading the source** — built both
  variants (`flutter build apk --debug` / `--release`) and inspected the
  actual merged manifests and the release APK's contents directly:
  - Debug's merged manifest has `android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config"`.
  - Release's merged manifest has neither `networkSecurityConfig` nor
    `usesCleartextTraffic` — confirmed absent by `grep`, not assumed.
  - `unzip -l app-release.apk | grep network_security` returns nothing; the
    same check against `app-debug.apk` finds `res/xml/network_security_config.xml`.
    The exemption isn't merely unreferenced in release, the resource itself
    never ships in it — release can't resolve a reference to it even if one
    were mistakenly added later, without also adding the resource file to a
    release/profile source set (which would be an obvious, reviewable change).
    This is the concrete property task 10.14's structural check gets to build
    against.
- **Discovered and fixed in the same pass** (see Discovered Scope): the main
  Android manifest had **no `INTERNET` permission at all** — only
  `src/debug`/`src/profile` had it (the stock `flutter create` template
  default for a project with no network feature). Every release APK built to
  date would have had zero network access — no map tiles, no DEM fetches,
  and no future server sync. Fixed by moving the declaration to
  `src/main/AndroidManifest.xml` so it applies to all build types; confirmed
  present in the release merged manifest post-fix.

**Acceptance criteria:** release builds are not loosened — verified directly
against build output as detailed above, not inferred from source alone.
"A debug build on each platform reaches the laptop server's `/health`" was
verified for the platform config's *build-time* correctness (the manifests/

Four platform gotchas, each of which fails confusingly rather than obviously:

- **iOS Local Network permission** (iOS 14+): connecting to a LAN IP triggers
  a system prompt and requires `NSLocalNetworkUsageDescription` in
  `Info.plist`. Missing it fails in a way that looks like a server bug.
- **iOS/macOS App Transport Security** blocks cleartext HTTP — add
  `NSAllowsLocalNetworking`, or run TLS with a self-signed cert.
- **Android** blocks cleartext since API 28 — needs a network security config,
  **scoped to the debug build variant only**, not a blanket
  `usesCleartextTraffic`.
- **macOS** already has `com.apple.security.network.client` from task 5.1, but
  macOS 15+ adds its own local-network prompt.
- **Acceptance criteria:** a debug build on each platform reaches the laptop
  server's `/health`; release builds are not loosened — verify the Android
  cleartext exemption is genuinely debug-only.

### Task 10.5 — Server schema and the delta cursor
