  means `createHandler` never mounts the router at all, so the routes 404
  exactly like any nonexistent path (`router.dart`); a `_requireLocalUnless
  Allowed` middleware refuses anything whose *real TCP peer address*
  (`shelf.io.connection_info`, not a spoofable header) isn't loopback, unless
  `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ALLOW_REMOTE=true`; `DiagnosticsRepository` issues
  `SELECT` only, and its own doc comment says so explicitly, since it is the
  layer any future route is built on.
- **No per-user login — a single shared token instead, checked in constant
  time (`Tokens.constantTimeEquals`), by design.** The console reads across
  every project and every user; building a second authorization system for a
  tool with one intended caller (a developer who already has shell access to
  set the token) would be a second thing to get wrong for no real gain.
  Recorded as a deliberate decision in `DiagnosticsConfig`'s doc comment, not
  an oversight.
- **Never selects a token column, enforced structurally, not just by
  convention.** `recentRows` only ever queries tables in `syncTablesByName`
  — the sync protocol's own table list — so it cannot become a way to probe
  `auth_sessions`/`auth_magic_links`/`auth_link_requests` by name.
  `identities`/`devices` use explicit column lists precisely because they
  *do* join against `auth_accounts`/`auth_sessions`; neither ever selects
  `token_hash`, verified by a test that asserts the hash value itself never
  appears anywhere in a response.
- **Tests:** `diagnostics_config_test.dart` (the four env-var states),
  `diagnostics_routes_test.dart` (the gating middleware, using a fake
  `HttpConnectionInfo` to simulate a remote peer without a real second host —
  no Postgres needed since `/diagnostics/health` never touches the
  repository), `diagnostics_repository_test.dart` and `sync_traffic_log_test.
  dart` (Postgres-tagged, the actual queries), and a real-HTTP-socket
  `test/integration/diagnostics_test.dart` proving a row that loses LWW over
  actual `/sync/push` calls shows up in `/diagnostics/traffic?lost_only=true`
  end to end, and that the console is genuinely absent (404) when not
  enabled. `dart analyze` clean; full suite passes (109 Postgres-tagged + 101
  non-Postgres). `.env.example`, `docker-compose.yml`, and the root `README.md`
  document the three new env vars.

### Task 10.14 — Cross-cutting security hardening
**Status:** Done (2026-08-07)
**Model:** **Opus** — security controls.
**Depends on:** 10.0 (design), 10.7, 10.10

The controls from 10.0 that belong to no single feature task and would
otherwise be smeared across six of them, each half-done. Implement them once,
centrally, where they can be tested and audited as a unit.

- **TLS termination** for production, plus the mechanism that makes 10.4's
  cleartext dev exemption structurally impossible to ship — a build-time
  assertion or release-config check, not a code comment asking nicely.
- **Rate limiting** on magic-link requests and sign-in attempts, per address
  and per source.
- **All-devices session revocation**, built here as a capability: revoking a
  user invalidates every session they hold, not just the one that made the
  most recent request. Phase 11's task 11.2 wires member removal to it —
  revoking only the latest session would leave a removed member's other
  devices syncing normally, which is the same as not revoking at all. Build
  the mechanism now so 11.2 is a call site, not a redesign.
- **Per-device revocation** as a separate capability: sign out one lost or
  stolen device without signing the user out everywhere. Depends on the device
  registry (see "One user, many devices") and is the practical mitigation for
  10.0's device-loss scenario.
- **Security headers** and a restrictive CORS policy. The API has no browser
  origin that needs broad access; the diagnostics console is same-origin.
- **Secrets management** as decided in 10.0: environment variables, `.env`
  gitignored, documented rotation procedure, and a check that no secret is
  committed.
- **Audit log** of authentication events and project-data access, with the
  retention and never-log rules from 10.0.
- **Dependency policy** — pinned versions, and a documented command to audit
  for known advisories.
- **Uniform error responses** that don't leak existence, structure, or
  registration status.
- **Acceptance criteria:** each control has a test that fails when the control
  is removed — a security control with no failing-path test is decoration;
  rate limits verified by exceeding them; revoking a user mid-session
  invalidates that user's sessions on every device, verified with two active
  sessions; a release build cannot be produced with cleartext permitted;
  `/security-review` run on the branch with findings addressed.

**Implementation (2026-08-07).** All new code is under `server/lib/src/security/`
plus a client half; every control has at least one test that fails if the control
is removed, which was the acceptance bar. **203 new tests** (server: 80
non-Postgres + 18 Postgres; app: 32).

- **TLS / non-shippable cleartext.** `TransportSecurityConfig` replaces
  `bin/server.dart`'s unconditional `anyIPv4` bind with §4.1's decision table.
  **The default is now loopback-only** — through 10.13 a server that configured
  nothing published tokens and coordinates to whatever network it landed on.
  Cleartext beyond loopback needs `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN=1`, which is
  *refused at startup* under `TRITRACK_ENV=production`; half-configured TLS
  refuses rather than silently falling back to cleartext. `docker-compose.yml`
  sets the flag explicitly, because serving a phone over plain HTTP is what that
  harness is for.
- **The platform half needed only its test.** 10.4 had already done the config
  correctly (debug-variant-only `network_security_config.xml`, no
  `usesCleartextTraffic` anywhere, `NSAllowsLocalNetworking` rather than
  `NSAllowsArbitraryLoads`) — and that file's own comment names 10.14 as where
  the check gets built. `test/security/platform_cleartext_test.dart` asserts the
  property that actually makes release safe: the cleartext config exists *only*
  under `src/debug/` and is referenced *only* from the debug manifest, so the
  resource reference cannot resolve outside a debug build. Static inspection
  rather than a real merged manifest, deliberately: a Gradle release assembly
  cannot run in `flutter test`, which would make the control conditional on
  infrastructure and therefore usually skipped.
- **Client release-mode refusal.** `validateServerUrl` rejects `http://` when
  `kReleaseMode`. Exposed as a defaulted parameter so it is testable at all — a
  test binary is never a release build, so a bare constant read would be
  permanently unexercised.
- **Rate limiting, and its one genuinely subtle requirement.** §4.4's table,
  keyed per-email *and* per-source simultaneously. The per-email limit returns
  the **byte-identical 202** a success returns and silently does not send — a 429
  keyed on an address tells the caller somebody recently requested links for it,
  which is a real oracle about a third party and would undo §4.5. The per-source
  limit returns an honest 429. Source comes from the real TCP peer, never
  `X-Forwarded-For`; a test rotates a forged header and confirms it changes
  nothing. Counters are in-process, which §4.4 calls a prototype-only shortcut —
  written up as a deployment precondition in the new `server/README.md` rather
  than "fixed" with Redis.
- **Revocation: the mechanism existed but was unreachable.**
  `revokeAllSessionsForUser`/`revokeDeviceSessions` had no HTTP route and no
  production caller. Added `POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all` and
  `/revoke-device`, both self-service — the `user_id` comes from the validated
  session, never the body (§4.11 applied to a destructive route). **No cross-user
  route**, deliberately: 11.2 calls the service method server-side inside a flow
  that already established ownership, so an endpoint now would be an attack
  surface for a capability nothing calls. A test asserts those paths 404.
  The acceptance criterion — two real sessions on two devices, both dead after
  one revoke — is `revocation_test.dart` against real SQL.
- **The client half of revocation, which was the gap that made it illegible.**
  A 401 and a 403 were indistinguishable (`isTerminal` covers both), so a
  revoked session stopped the schedule and rendered as generic "sync isn't
  working" with no actionable text — exactly what 10.12 warned trains people to
  ignore the indicator. Added `isSessionEnded`, client-authored copy ("sign in
  again"), a `SyncHealth.sessionEnded` state, and **dropping the dead token**.
  The message deliberately does not say *why*: expired/revoked/reinstalled are
  indistinguishable by design, and "you were removed" is the project owner's
  message to deliver, not the app's.
- **Security headers + no CORS — a decision this task had to author.** The
  security model had no §4.x for it and no mention of CORS anywhere, so per that
  doc's standing clause this is now **§4.16**, not just middleware. No
  `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` ever (nothing that legitimately calls this API is
  a browser), preflight refused explicitly rather than 404ing by accident, and
  CORS headers *stripped* rather than merely not written. HSTS only under real
  TLS — over cleartext it is meaningless and on the LAN dev path it bricks the
  browser for that host:port. The one HTML page gets a **per-response nonce**
  rather than `'unsafe-inline'`, since that page renders a live magic-link token.
- **Audit log.** New `auth_audit_log` (1 year) beside 10.13's `sync_traffic_log`
  (180 days) — §4.7's two logs, one recording mechanism, both read by the
  console via a new `/diagnostics/auth-events`. The never-log rules are
  **structural**: there is no token column and no coordinate column, so a caller
  cannot record one, and tests assert the schema itself. Audit writes are
  best-effort and swallow their own failures — a full disk must not stop anyone
  signing in.
- **Retention, which closes 10.13's own Discovered Scope item.**
  `AuditRetentionService` prunes both logs; §4.7's `Violated by:` list names
  "retention that quietly grows without bound", which is what both did.
  `bin/purge_audit_logs.dart` makes it schedulable — without an entrypoint the
  service would be unreachable in production and the control would be decoration.
- **Uniform errors.** There was **no error handler at all**, so an unhandled
  exception reached shelf's default, which answers with the exception's
  `toString()` — for a Postgres error that is the SQL, the constraint, the table,
  and often the offending *value*, which on an `Observations` write is a
  coordinate. So the old behaviour violated §4.13 *and* §4.7 rule 6 in one
  response. Now: an opaque 500, a `trace_id` on every response, and server-side
  logging of the exception *type* only. Named `trace_id` rather than
  `request_id` because `/auth/magic-link`'s 202 already uses that key for
  "poll this for the link's outcome".
- **Secrets.** `.gitignore` patterns and `pubspec.lock` were already right (10.3
  did them). Added placeholder rejection — §4.6 requires refusing a *placeholder*,
  not just a missing value, because `changeme` passes every "is it set?" check.
  `test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart` runs in the default app suite:
  no tracked `.env`, no key material, no PEM block under an innocuous filename,
  `.env.example` values all empty.
  - **A near-miss worth recording.** The first draft of the placeholder list
    included the value this machine's gitignored `.env` uses. That would have
    *committed a real local password to the repository* as part of a control
    whose purpose is preventing exactly that, and broken the dev stack and every
    Postgres test. The list now holds only strings that are already public, with
    the reasoning written into the code.
- **Dependencies.** Server pins moved from caret ranges to exact versions (§3.8);
  a test fails on any `^`, `>`, `<`, or `any` constraint, so loosening one is a
  visible act. Audit commands documented next to the pins and in the README.
- **§4.9 (encrypted DB backups) is NOT implemented, and that is the recorded
  decision.** The security model's Appendix assigns it to 10.14 while the plan's
  bullets omit it — a real doc/plan disagreement. Resolved as **open**, because
  its own precondition is unmet: §6 item 8 requires a key custody arrangement
  before the first backup that matters, and encrypting to a key with no custody
  story makes recovery risk worse rather than better. There is also no deployed
  server to back up. §4.9 now carries a status note and the Appendix marks it
  open; 10.16 must not treat it as satisfied.

**Not done here:** `/security-review` on the branch (the last acceptance
criterion) — see Discovered Scope.

### Task 10.15 — Tests and release-without-server verification
**Status:** Done
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 10.1–10.14

- Server test suite: auth token lifecycle, authorization denial paths,
  `server_seq` monotonicity, merge parity with the client resolver.
- Three-peer convergence (two clients + server), including sync interrupted
  mid-transfer.
- **Cross-project isolation, single user:** one user owning two of their own
  projects — no row of project A ever appears in project B's sync payload, in
  either direction. This is the Phase 10 half of what Security Gate B checks;
  Phase 11's task 11.8 adds the multi-user version.
- Version skew and tombstone retention policies from 10.11/10.18 behave as
  documented: a minor-version-behind client syncs with no data loss, a
  major-version mismatch is refused with the correct side named, and a
  deliberately stale client past the tombstone window is refused.
- Durability invariants from 10.19: no failure path deletes local data
  (failed sync, refused version, failed migration, revoked session), and a
  migration cannot run without a backup written first.
- First-sync chunking (10.7): a large project syncs completely to a fresh
  device, and an interruption mid-way resumes rather than restarting.
- **One user, two devices** — the case this phase is most likely to get subtly
  wrong. All of the following, as explicit tests:
  - Two devices sign in to the same email and converge on the **same**
    `user_id`, matching the server's, from two *different* locally minted
    starting ids.
  - The owner's membership row follows the remap, so both devices see
    themselves as owner — no phantom second owner, and the project does not
    briefly appear to have two owners mid-sync.
  - Sync converges with **no identity churn**: after both devices are synced,
    a further sync round rewrites no `user_id` and bumps no `revision`. Assert
    on revision stability directly; this is what catches the rename loop.
  - Two independent cursors: rows pulled by the laptop are still delivered to
    the phone. Drive this by syncing the laptop twice before the phone syncs
    at all — the per-user-cursor bug passes a naive alternating test.
  - The identity remap is idempotent, and interrupting it mid-transaction
    leaves no rows stranded on the old id.
  - Signing in on a second device leaves the first device's session valid.
  - Revoking that user's access invalidates sessions on **both** devices
    (10.14's capability; Phase 11 adds the member-removal flow that calls it).
  - An observation created on the phone appears in the Log attributed to one
    person, not two.
- Diagnostics console (10.13): read-only enforcement, no token values in any
  response, unreachable off-host without the explicit opt-in.
- Security regression suite (from 10.14): every control has a test that fails
  if the control is removed. These live alongside the functional tests and run
  on every change — a security control that isn't continuously tested quietly
  stops working the first time someone refactors around it.
- **The headline test: a full run of the app's suite with the server stack down
  and network disabled.** This is the phase's central promise; it gets an
  explicit, named test run, not an assumption.
- Verify a release build with no server URL configured is fully functional.
- **Acceptance criteria:** all of the above pass; `flutter analyze` clean;
  server suite green in Docker from a clean checkout.

**Implementation (2026-08-07).** Most of this checklist was already
satisfied by the test suites 10.6–10.14 built along the way (three-peer
convergence and chunking/resume in `packages/tritrack_sync`, identity
idempotency/crash-safety in `server_identity_adopter_test.dart`,
both-devices revocation in `server/test/security/revocation_test.dart`,
merge parity in `server/test/sync/row_merge_test.dart`, a
security-regression test per control in `server/test/security/`). What this
task added:

- `server/test/authz/authorization_test.dart`'s new "cross-project
  isolation, single user" group — one user owning two of their own
  projects, no bleed-through either direction.
- Explicit revision-stability ("no `user_id` rewritten, no `revision`
  bumped") and single-attribution assertions added to
  `test/e2e/two_device_convergence_e2e_test.dart`.
- The headline test, as a real named run rather than an inference:
  `scripts/run_offline_suite.sh` brings the server down and runs the full
  `flutter test` suite; `test/headline_offline_suite_test.dart` drives a
  full first-run boot to the tab shell inside that run (also covering "a
  release build with no server URL configured is fully functional," since
  `ServerConfig` is unconfigured by default and nothing in that test ever
  sets it).
- `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` + a new `docker-compose.server-test
  .yml` overlay — a loopback-only Postgres port, kept out of the base
  compose file on purpose (see that file's own comment on why Postgres has
  no `ports:` there) — for "server suite green in Docker from a clean
  checkout." Run for real against a throwaway container during this task:
  309 tests green.
- Both `flutter analyze` and `dart analyze` (server) are clean.

### Task 10.16 — Summative security assessment (deployment gate)
**Status:** Done as an assessment (2026-08-07) — **and the gate FAILED.** The
server does not listen beyond localhost. Five blocking findings, filed under
this phase's Discovered Scope as C-1…C-5; four of the five were reproduced
against a live server over raw HTTP, not argued from code. Full record —
verdict table for every §2 actor and §3 surface, every adversarial attempt and
its result, the git-history verdict, the §4.15 backup verdict, and the
plain-language residual-risk summary — is `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §7.
**This task is not closed:** it must be re-run once C-1…C-5 are fixed, and the
NAU review (below) has not happened yet. Do not lift the localhost restriction.

**The one result worth carrying forward:** the important finding is not any
single bug but that `RowAuthorizer` reasons about *who owns the row being
written* and never about *who the row names*. C-1's four instances are that one
omission in four columns. Gate B closed two instances of the same class by
name; the reasoning was right and was applied per-column instead of derived as
a rule. Fix it as one invariant.

**Second result, about process:** Gates A and B were both genuinely run and
their findings genuinely closed — verified in the record, not assumed, and
neither was wrong about what it examined. C-1 is not a regression of a Gate B
fix; it is an adjacent column Gate B never looked at. That is the argument for
keeping a summative gate: A and B each verified their own scope correctly, and
the class-level pattern was only visible from outside both. It also argues for
running the adversarial pass against a live server rather than reading code —
309 passing tests, two prior gates, and two `/security-review` runs did not
surface C-1, and a single crafted `curl` did.

**Also confirmed while attacking, and worth keeping:** the shared `RowValidator`
genuinely stops a hand-crafted request inserting what the client's forms would
reject (a bad enum value came back `invalid`); a foreign-key violation produced
an opaque 500 that logged the exception *type* only, which is §4.13 and §4.7
rule 6 working on a path nobody wrote a test for; and the diagnostics console
refused this machine's real LAN address with and without the correct token
while `/health` answered 200 from that same address.

**Model:** **Opus**
**Depends on:** 10.0–10.15 — everything.

**This is a gate, not a report.** The server does not listen on any interface
beyond localhost until it passes. Failing items block exposure; they don't get
noted as future work.

- Re-run the 10.0 threat model against what was actually built. Every threat
  actor and attack surface gets a current verdict: mitigated (how), accepted
  (why), or open (blocking). Drift between the design and the build is the
  expected finding, not a surprise.
- Verify every standing security criterion from the Security Posture section
  holds across the whole phase's output, not just where it was convenient.
- Confirm all three review gates (A, B, C) were actually run and their
  findings closed — check the record, don't assume.
- Full `/security-review` on the complete diff for the phase.
- **Adversarial pass, done as an attacker rather than as a reviewer:** attempt
  cross-project data access using a session scoped to a different project of
  the same user's; attempt to reuse a consumed magic link; attempt to act on
  a session that has been explicitly revoked; attempt to reach the
  diagnostics console
  off-host; attempt to enumerate registered addresses; attempt to mutate
  another user's observation over raw HTTP, bypassing the client entirely.
  Each attempt gets a recorded result.
- Verify no secret exists anywhere in git history — the whole history, not
  just the working tree.
- **Confirm 10.19's cloud-backup default was decided explicitly**, not
  defaulted into. Backup archives contain precise animal locations — the
  asset 10.0 ranks highest — so a default-on egress of them needs a recorded
  decision, and the archives' own protection (encryption at rest, retention,
  what a compromised cloud account exposes) needs a verdict here.
- Produce a written summary of residual risk in plain language, suitable for
  showing NAU's information security office, and **do that.** An institutional
  review before internet exposure is the last item on this gate.
- **Acceptance criteria:** every adversarial attempt above fails, with results
  recorded in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`; no unresolved blocking finding; the
  residual-risk summary is written; the localhost-only restriction is lifted
  only after all of the above.

### Task 10.17 — End-to-end client/server integration suite
**Status:** Done (2026-08-02). No protocol mismatch found — the escalation
trigger did not fire.

Built `test/e2e/` (`@Tags(['e2e'])`, opt-in via `TRITRACK_E2E_BASE_URL` +
`TRITRACK_E2E_MAGIC_LINK_DIR` — same presence-gated pattern as the server's
`DatabaseConfig.fromEnvironment`) and `docker-compose.e2e.yml`, a layered
override adding `TRITRACK_DEV_MAGIC_LINK_DIR` and a bind mount so the suite
can read a real magic-link token off the host filesystem — the base compose
file deliberately has no way to retrieve one, and stays that way. Full
walkthrough in the README's new "End-to-end integration suite" section.

Seven files, twenty tests, all driving the actual client classes
(`HttpSyncTransport`, `SyncEngine`, `AuthClient`, `ServerIdentityAdopter`,
`ProjectPublisher`/`ProjectJoiner`) against a live `docker compose up`
server — no mocks, no in-process shortcuts:

- **Serialization fidelity** (the task's own "start here" priority): every
  column kind on `Observations` and `Tags` — negative/high-precision
  doubles, explicit nulls, all six sync columns, a sub-second UTC
  timestamp — compared value-for-value after a real push/pull round trip,
  plus confirms an unauthenticated request is refused before any row is
  read.
- **`HttpSyncTransport` + `SyncEngine`**: a full push-then-pull merging
  through the real `ProjectMerger`, and an interrupted pull (a
  `_FlakyTransport` decorator that lets everything through until a
  configured pull call, then drops the connection) resuming from the
  stored cursor with no loss and no duplication.
- **Magic-link sign-in + identity adoption**: a fresh device adopting the
  server's `user_id`, two devices converging on one identity, a second
  sign-in on the same device being a true no-op, and an unknown token
  being refused.
- **Two devices, one person, over real HTTP**: re-runs 10.15's
  same-user-two-device scenarios (independent `(user, device)` cursors, no
  further churn once settled) through the actual network path rather than
  `FakeSyncTransport`.
- **Publish and join over the wire** (10.9), including the idempotent
  re-publish and a joined project dropping out of
  `listAvailableToJoin`.
- **Authorization denial over real HTTP** (10.10): a stranger's push and
  pull are both refused with a real 403 at the project boundary, and an
  attempted overwrite of a row they don't own never reaches the server's
  copy.

**Every failure encountered was a test-harness bug, not a product defect —
verified by first confirming each was reproducible, then fixing it, never by
patching the server or client to match a wrong assumption:**

- Every raw, hand-crafted push (the fidelity and authorization-denial
  suites bypass `ProjectPublisher`/`ProjectExporter` on purpose, to test the
  wire directly) needs its own `Users` row pushed first, or a referencing
  `Projects`/`Observations` row fails Postgres's foreign key — exactly the
  fixture bug task 10.9's own tests hit for the same reason. Fixed with
  `E2eDevice.pushOwnUserRow`/`pushOwnUserAndProject` harness helpers.
- The test harness's `seedLocalProject` initially created only a `Projects`
  row, on a misreading of a comment about how ownership is *resolved*
  (`Projects.owner_user_id`, never a membership row's claimed role) as
  meaning no membership row is ever *created*. The real app creates one at
  project-creation time regardless (task 8.4), and `/projects/mine`
  (`ProjectDirectoryService`) is driven entirely off that table — a project
  with no membership row publishes fine but never appears in its own
  owner's join-from-a-second-device list. Fixed by having
  `seedLocalProject` create both rows, matching the real app.
- A fixed historical `DateTime` for seeded rows, used alongside `signIn()`'s
  real-wall-clock-stamped `Users` row, can sit *before* the push watermark
  that row establishes — new rows written "in the past" relative to that
  watermark are then silently never offered by `SyncEngine`'s
  `updated_at >= watermark` selection. This is the watermark scheme's own
  documented weakness (task 10.8: "a device whose clock jumps backwards"),
  triggered here by test setup rather than a real clock jump. Fixed by
  capturing `now` as `DateTime.now().toUtc()` *after* sign-in wherever a
  test does more than one `SyncEngine` round.
- A copy-paste bug in one test's own helper closed over the wrong device's
  database/state regardless of which device's transport was passed in,
  silently testing device A twice instead of A and a joining device B.
  Fixed by parameterizing the helper on the device.
- Two rounds of legitimate, expected last-write-wins settling (two
  devices each independently minting their own local `Users` row copy for
  the same freshly-adopted identity, on their first two sync rounds) were
  mistaken for "no further churn" in a test that checked too early — not a
  defect, since each device's row content was identical, and it resolves in
  one round via ordinary LWW comparison, not the repeated `user_id`
  rewriting task 10.6 actually warns against. Fixed by moving the assertion
  to *after* that one-time settling completes.
- `PostgresMigrations._hasMigrationsTable`'s `public.` schema qualifier
  (found and fixed during the earlier Docker verification catch-up) held;
  not rediscovered here.

**Verified, not merely reasoned about:** `docker compose up --build`,
`curl /health`, both compose files together, all twenty tests passing
against a live server, twice in a row for stability, and — the acceptance
criterion this task states explicitly — `flutter test` (no tags, no server,
no network configured) confirmed to still pass with the e2e suite loading
and skipping cleanly (603 passed, 20 skipped, same 603 as before this task).
`flutter analyze` clean throughout.

**Model:** Sonnet — writing tests against a contract that already exists on
both sides. **Escalate to Opus and stop if** the suite uncovers an actual
client/server contract mismatch: fixing that is protocol work (10.7's
territory), not test work, and patching one side to match the other without
deciding which is correct is how a wire format quietly becomes whatever the
first bug made it.
**Depends on:** 10.8, 10.9, 10.10.
**Run this before 10.11** — numbered late only because it was added after the
phase was laid out. Same pattern as 10.13.

**Why this exists.** As of 2026-08-02 both halves of the system are well
tested and the seam between them is entirely unproven. The server has 79
passing tests against real Postgres; `SyncEngine` has full coverage against
`FakeSyncTransport`. Three separate task status notes (10.6, 10.7, 10.8)
independently record the same gap: nothing has ever spoken this protocol over
real HTTP from the actual client. The characteristic failure is a
serialization mismatch — the client writes a timestamp, null, or numeric one
way and the server reads it another — which leaves **both** suites green and
the product broken.

The Docker catch-up already made the case for closing gaps early rather than
at 10.15: it surfaced two real bugs (non-idempotent migrations outside the
`public` schema, a missing `Users` row in the publish fixture) that analysis
alone had missed across five tasks. The wire seam is a larger surface than
either.

**This does not weaken Phase 10 invariant 5.** That invariant governs the
*app's default suite* — `flutter test` must pass with no server and no
network — not whether an integration test may exist at all. Put this suite
behind a tag, exactly as the server does with `@Tags(['postgres'])`, so it is
opt-in and excluded from the default run. `SyncEngine`'s existing
fake-transport tests stay exactly as they are; this is additive.

Coverage:

- **Serialization fidelity first.** Round-trip every column type through the
  real wire: UTC timestamps, nulls, doubles, booleans, and all six sync
  columns. Assert values come back byte-identical, not merely present. This is
  the most likely defect and the cheapest to find.
- **`HttpSyncTransport` push/pull round trip** against a live server, with the
  client merging what comes back through `ProjectMerger`.
- **Magic-link sign-in from the client** against a live server, including the
  identity adoption path — the device adopts the server's `user_id` and remaps
  local rows (10.6). A UI-driven flow needs a simulator; driving the client's
  auth layer directly is sufficient here and a device pass can come later.
- **Two client instances converging over real HTTP.** The two-device scenarios
  10.15 specifies against a fake transport, re-run through the actual network
  path: same `user_id` from two different locally minted ids, independent
  `(user, device)` cursors, and no identity churn (no `user_id` rewritten, no
  `revision` bumped on a further round).
- **Publish and join over the wire** (10.9), including the idempotent
  re-publish.
- **Authorization denial over real HTTP** (10.10): a client attempting to
  mutate a row it doesn't own is refused by the server, not merely by the
  client's own check.
- **Interrupted sync** resumes without loss and without advancing the cursor
  past unmerged rows.

- **Acceptance criteria:** the suite runs against `docker compose up` and
  passes; it is tagged and excluded from the default `flutter test` run, and
  `flutter test` still passes with no server and no network (verify, don't
  assume); every defect found is fixed or logged under Discovered Scope with
  a named owner task; 10.15 later extends this suite rather than duplicating
  it.

### Task 10.18 — Additive schema compatibility
**Status:** Done (2026-08-06). Two-part version, unknown-value preservation,
generic promotion, and the five standing rules are all in place; the rules are in
`TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` under "Version skew: same major syncs, different
major refuses", which replaces 10.11's exact-equality section.

**`schemaMajorVersion = 1` is now the compatibility floor.** It sits next to
`latestSchemaVersion` in `schema_constants.dart`, rides the envelope as
`schema_major`, and is the only thing `SyncEnvelope.fromJson` refuses on. The
minor is carried for reporting and may differ freely. The minor deliberately
stays monotonic across a future major bump, because it is also the migration
counter and migration numbers can never be reused or reset — which is why
`senderIsOlder` decides direction on the major, not the minor.

**The holding area is a client-only table, not a schema bump.** `Unknown_Columns`
(`table_name`, `row_key`, `column_name`, `value_json`, composite PK) is outside
`Tables`/`tableSpecs`/`syncTables` and therefore outside `latestSchemaVersion`,
and is created `IF NOT EXISTS` on every open. That is 10.11's own precedent for
server-only tables applied to the client, and it kept this task from bumping the
shared version — which would have forced the server's Postgres migrations to gain
an incremental-`ALTER TABLE` path they do not have, for a table the server has no
use for. Values are stored as their JSON encoding, which is the form they arrive
and leave in, so byte-identity is a property of the storage rather than something
the tests hope for.

**The one design decision worth recording: holding is an upsert, never a
delete.** A column absent from a *winning* incoming row leaves any held value
alone. The tempting alternative — the winning row is authoritative for the whole
row, so replace the held set — looked more consistent with last-write-wins and is
wrong. `txn.update` writes only the columns the row carried, so a build that
*did* know the column would leave it untouched too. The rule is parity: an older
build must behave exactly like a newer one, not more destructively and not more
cautiously. Replace-on-win would have reintroduced the destruction this task
exists to remove, via any peer that legitimately never saw the column.

Preservation is wired at all four boundaries, not just the sync path:
`ProjectMerger._upsert` splits and holds on the way in (so backup restore, join,
and share get it too), `SyncEngine._collectChangedRows` and
`ProjectExporter.collect` re-attach on the way out. `SchemaMigrator` no longer
treats a newer *minor* as too new — it leaves those rows' extra columns in place
for the merger to hold. A newer *major* is still `SchemaTooNewException`; an older
major is `BackupFormatException`, since there is no step that migrates across a
major and "too new" would be the wrong word for it. `BackupManifest` gained
`schema_major`, defaulted rather than required so a manifest written before the
field existed still parses.

**Found and fixed: unknown tables really could wedge the cursor** — the task
asked to confirm this and it was not fine. `decodeRows` drops rows for unknown
tables, and `SyncEngine._pull` broke out of its loop on `rowCount == 0`. A page
containing only rows from a table a newer server had added therefore decoded to
nothing, and the loop exited *without advancing the cursor* — parking it on that
page forever. Sync dead, no error, nothing to notice, and not fixable by
retrying. The loop now decides exhaustion on the server's `next_cursor` (an
exhausted stream is the one where the server hands back the cursor it was given)
and skips the merge rather than the advance when a page decodes empty.

**Server-side preservation remains out of scope, with its condition recorded** in
the technical context: standing rule 5 upgrades the server first, so the app is
never ahead, and the server writes only what `tableSpecs` declares. If the
release order changes or anyone else self-hosts, the server needs a holding area
too.

**Tests:** 12 shared-package (`version_skew_test.dart`, rewritten — minor skew
accepted both directions, major refused both directions, a missing major is a
protocol error, and the major decides direction even when the minor disagrees), 9
client (`schema_compatibility_test.dart` — the byte-identical pull→edit→push
round trip, held values in backups, LWW over held values, absent-column parity,
promotion including across two bumps and the no-op rerun, the client-only
assertions, and the cursor-wedge case), 4 e2e
(`schema_compatibility_e2e_test.dart` — minor skew both directions and major
refusal both directions against a live server, asserting the right party is
named), plus `schema_migrator_test.dart` updated for the new major/minor
boundary. Suites: `tritrack_sync` 106, app 626 / 20 skipped, server 175 against
real Postgres, e2e 24 green against a live `docker compose` server.
`flutter analyze` / `dart analyze` clean.
**Model:** **Opus** — this is the compatibility boundary. It protects only
versions that ship with it, so a mistake here is unfixable for every device
already in the field.
**Depends on:** 10.11. **Run before 10.12**, which surfaces the refusal
messages this task's vocabulary defines.

**Revises task 10.11's exact-equality decision** (2026-08-05). 10.11 was
right that a naive relaxation destroys data — an older app that pulls a row,
drops a column it can't store, and pushes the row back wipes a value another
device contributed. It was also right that column-level merge is a different
engine. But there is a third option 10.11 didn't consider: **the older app
never drops what it doesn't recognize.** It stores the unknown value verbatim
and hands it back untouched on the next push. The destruction scenario
disappears without changing the merge model at all. Protocol Buffers have
worked this way for twenty years.

**Why now and not later.** This protection works by the *older* side knowing
how to preserve unknown values. An app released without it can never be
protected retroactively — bumping the schema still strands it. Whatever
version first ships this becomes the permanent compatibility floor. Nothing
is deployed yet, so the cost today is near zero; after release, the gap is
permanent for everyone already in the field.

**Case analysis (2026-08-05).** With preservation in place, of nine change
types, three become compatible and six remain breaking:

| Change | Old app still works | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Add optional column | **Yes** | Preserved verbatim, echoed back intact |
| Add column with default | **Yes** | Rows it creates take the default |
| Add a table | **Yes** | Ignores it; server keeps its own copy |
| Delete a column | No | Keeps showing and re-sending something retired |
| Rename a column | No | Both versions maintain the same fact separately |
| Change a column's type | No | Sends the wrong type |
| Same name, new meaning | No | **Undetectable** — both sides accept it |
| Delete a table | No | Re-uploads removed rows |
| Tighten a validation rule | No | Previously-legal rows rejected unexplained |

Scope:

- **Two-part schema version.** Same major = compatible, different major =
  refuse. Safe changes bump minor, breaking changes bump major. Replaces the
  single-integer exact match at `sync_protocol.dart:171`. Keep 10.11's
  which-side-is-behind reporting and its client-side refusal vocabulary —
  both were correct and are unaffected.
- **Unknown-value preservation in the app.** A holding area for columns the
  running version doesn't recognize, round-tripped byte-identical on push.
  Assert byte-identity in tests, not merely presence.
- **Generic promotion on upgrade.** When the app updates and a held value's
  column now exists, a migration step moves it into place. Write this once,
  generically, so every future addition is covered without new code.
- **Server-side preservation is out of scope.** The release rule below makes
  the server always upgrade first, so the app is never ahead. Record this as
  a deliberate omission with its condition: if that release order ever
  changes, or if anyone else ever self-hosts, the server needs it too.
- **Unknown tables:** confirm an unrecognized table cannot stall cursor
  advancement. Data safety is fine (the app never had those rows); the risk
  is a wedged sync.

**Standing rules — write these into `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`. They are
worth more than the machinery above.**

1. **Prefer adding to changing.** To retire a column: add the replacement,
   stop writing the old one, leave it in place. An unused nullable column
   costs a few bytes; a major version bump strands every device in the field.
2. **Never reuse a column name for a different meaning.** This is the only
   change no software can detect — both versions accept every value and the
   data is silently wrong. If the meaning changes, the name changes.
3. **A major bump is a last resort and requires written justification** in
   the plan doc naming what was tried instead.
4. **Never edit a shipped migration** (already documented in
   `migrations.dart`; restated here because it belongs with the others).
5. **Release order: server first, app second.** Always. Schedule any major
   bump for a quiet period — noting that field seasons vary by species and
   hemisphere, so "quiet" is not universal and shrinks as the user base grows.

- **Acceptance criteria:** an app one minor version behind syncs with no data
  loss, proven by asserting an unknown column's value survives a full
  pull-edit-push round trip byte-identical; a major mismatch still refuses
  with the correct side named; promotion moves held values into real columns
  on upgrade, including values held across two minor bumps; the five standing
  rules are in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`; 10.17's e2e suite gains an
  old-client-against-new-server case.

### Task 10.19 — Data durability guarantees
**Status:** Done (2026-08-06). All six items implemented; the security tension
was resolved in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.15 before any default changed.

**Security decision made first, per the task's own instruction.** §4.15 records
why cloud auto-backup defaulting to on is still the right call despite §3.7
naming it the largest existing disclosure surface in the app: it is a default-
*setting* change, not a default-*effect* one — `enabled` does nothing until a
folder is linked, and linking one is still a single deliberate OS-level action.
The destination is storage the user already owns and trusts with other field
data, not a new channel. Archive encryption stays explicitly out of scope
(recorded as a residual, not a permanent, gap) and the in-flow disclosure text
now names what leaves the device — names, emails, precise coordinates — rather
than saying "a backup file." Discovered Scope item 4 in the security doc is
updated to reflect what's resolved and what's still open.

**Pre-migration backup: a raw file copy, not a row-level export.**
`PreMigrationBackup.ensureBackedUpBeforeMigration` (new,
`lib/data/db/pre_migration_backup.dart`) opens a throwaway, versionless
connection to peek at the on-disk `PRAGMA user_version`, closes it, and — only
if a migration is actually about to run — copies the file into
`pre_migration_backups/` before `AppDatabase.open` ever passes `version:` to
sqflite. Deliberately not `ProjectExporter`/`BackupArchive`: a row-level export
needs working knowledge of the schema that's about to change (the very thing in
question) and would have to iterate every project one at a time, where a file
copy needs neither and is fast enough to run on every launch unconditionally
were that ever necessary. Retention keeps the newest 3 snapshots, mirroring
`CloudBackupService`'s own pattern.

**Verified, not assumed: sqflite already makes a multi-step migration atomic.**
Read the vendored `sqflite_common` source rather than trusting a comment: `db.
batch().commit()` runs inside `database.transaction(...)`, and the entire
`onCreate`/`onUpgrade` callback is itself wrapped in one outer exclusive
transaction by `doOpen` before `PRAGMA user_version` is ever updated. A
standalone test (`migration_failure_test.dart`) proves this empirically — a
migration that runs a real `ALTER TABLE` and then throws leaves the file
un-altered and at its old version on reopen. This means the pre-migration file
backup is not the *only* thing standing between a failed migration and data
loss — sqflite's own transaction is the first line, the file copy is the second,
for the case that first line can't cover (a crash or force-quit truly mid-write,
which no application-level transaction protects against on its own).

**Cloud backup wiring.** `CloudBackupSettings` defaults changed to `enabled:
true, frequency: dailyOnForeground`. Fixed a latent display bug while at it:
the settings toggle previously showed "on" from the stored `enabled` flag alone,
which — combined with the new default — would have shown a checked switch with
no folder linked and nothing actually happening; it now reads `enabled &&
isLinked`.

**A new persistent, non-dismissible indicator**, not confined to Data
Export/Backup: `BackupHealthBanner` (`lib/widgets/backup_health_banner.dart`)
renders in `_TabShell` (`app_router.dart`), above every tab, whenever
`backupHealthProvider` reports anything other than `healthy`/`notApplicable` —
no folder linked, linked but never run, last attempt failed, or stale beyond 7
days. The status computation (`backupHealthFrom`) is a pure function taking
`CloudBackupSettings` and `now`, kept separate from the platform-gated provider
wrapper specifically so it has a test seam — `Platform.isIOS`/`isAndroid` has
none anywhere else in this codebase (`AutoBackupSection` gates on it directly
too), so the thin wrapper stays deliberately untested, consistent with that
existing pattern, rather than inventing a new one just for this file.

**No-deletion invariant: proven for the paths that weren't already covered.**
10.8's suite already proves an unreachable server changes nothing locally;
`durability_test.dart` adds the two refusal shapes that isn't the same
claim — a *terminal* schema-version refusal and a 403 authorization denial (what
a removed membership looks like from the client) — plus the two paths that
don't go through `SyncEngine` at all: a locally-expired session
(`CurrentSession.build`) and `signOut()`. Both already documented themselves as
not touching local data (`signOut`'s own doc comment says so); the tests exist
so a future change that adds a `DELETE` to either path fails loudly rather than
shipping.

**Manual export confirmed to need neither a server nor a cloud folder** —
`manual_export_offline_test.dart` drives `ProjectExporter.collect` →
`BackupArchive.encode` → `.decode` → `ProjectMerger.merge` end to end without
configuring `serverConfigProvider` or touching `CloudFolderChannel` at all,
onto a second, unrelated database standing in for the receiving device.

**Tests:** `pre_migration_backup_test.dart` (7 — no-op cases, version-tagged
copy, data survives in the copy, retention), `migration_failure_test.dart` (1,
against real sqflite semantics, no app code involved), `backup_health_provider_
test.dart` (8, every status transition plus the boundary at exactly the
staleness window), `durability_test.dart` (4), `manual_export_offline_test.dart`
(1). Suite: app 647 / 24 skipped (e2e, unaffected by this task).
`flutter analyze` clean.
**Model:** Sonnet — the machinery mostly exists; this is wiring, defaults, and
visibility. **Escalate to Opus** if the pre-migration backup turns out to need
transactional coordination with the migration itself.
**Depends on:** 10.18 (for the pre-migration backup hook)

**Field data is irreplaceable.** An observation is a person standing in a
specific place at a specific time with a receiver; it cannot be recreated. This
task is separate from versioning because the actual risk has little to do with
versions: **the everyday condition of this app is that a phone holds the only
copy.** A tech with no signal for two weeks has the same exposure as one
stranded by a version mismatch.

Worth stating plainly, because it shapes the work: a version mismatch does
**not** delete anything. It refuses to sync; the data sits on the phone intact.
What actually loses field data is a lost, broken, drowned or wiped phone, or a
migration that fails partway. Version skew only lengthens the window in which
the phone is the sole copy.

- **Back up automatically before every migration.** Non-negotiable, invisible,
  cheap. This is the one place the app itself could destroy data, so it is the
  one place a guaranteed backup matters most.
- **Turn cloud backup on by default.** `CloudBackupService` already packages a
  project, writes a timestamped archive to a linked folder, verifies the
  written size, and prunes old copies — solid work that currently defaults to
  `enabled = false, frequency = manualOnly`, so most users would never switch
  it on. **See the security note below before implementing.**
- **Make "not backed up in N days" persistently visible**, not a dismissible
  toast. Silence is what loses data.
- **No failure path may delete local data** — state as an invariant and test
  it: failed sync, refused version, failed migration, revoked session, removed
  membership. Believed true today; make it provable.
- **A manual export that always works**, even with sync broken and no cloud
  folder linked.
- **Do not block recording on backup configuration.** Strongly encourage,
  make declining visible and persistent, but never lock someone out — a tech
  who can't record falls back to paper, which loses more data than it saves.

**Security tension to resolve, not assume (flagged 2026-08-05).** Task 10.0
ranks precise animal locations as the highest-value asset in the system, with
poachers as a named threat actor. Turning cloud backup on by default means
that data leaves the device by default, into a user-chosen third-party folder.
That is defensible — it is the user's own storage, and losing the data is also
a real harm — but it is a default-on egress of the most sensitive data the app
holds, and it deserves an explicit decision rather than being slipped in as a
usability improvement. **Resolve it in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` before
implementing**, and consider whether a heightened-sensitivity project (already
an open question in 10.0) should default differently.

- **Acceptance criteria:** a migration cannot run without a backup written
  first, proven by a test that fails when the backup step is removed; cloud
  backup is on by default with the security decision recorded; the
  not-backed-up state is visible without navigating to settings; every failure
  path listed above has a test asserting local data survives; manual export
  works with no server configured and no cloud folder linked.

### Task 10.20 — C-1: row-naming authorization invariant
**Status:** Done (2026-08-09)
**Model:** **Opus** — authorization architecture; the severest finding.
**Depends on:** 10.16

Fix as **one invariant, not four patches**: an incoming row may not name a user
other than the caller, on any table, insert or update, unless real replication
provenance backs it. `RowAuthorizer` today reasons only about who *owns* the
row, never who it *names*.

- Every one of C-1's four instances needs a **failing test before the fix**.
- Preserve legitimate first-publish replication. The seam noted by the gate:
  disclosure is only possible when the named `Users` row already exists on the
  server.
- Gate B closed this class for `last_modified_by` and `Project_Memberships`
  per-column. Derive the rule those two were instances of; don't add a fifth
  and sixth special case.
- **Acceptance:** all four live reproductions from `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`
  §7.3 fail; the fabricated-attribution case (attacker creates a row, rewrites
  `user_id` to a victim) is impossible; replication and publish still pass.

**Done 2026-08-09.** The invariant is `RowAuthorizer._authorizeNaming`, iterating
`SyncTable.userColumns` on every table: a name must be the caller; on update it
may otherwise only be what the stored row already said; on insert it may
otherwise only be someone this project already reaches or someone the server has
never heard of (no `Users` row *and* no `auth_accounts` row). Rows governed by
`owner`/`projectOwner` get no insert exemption at all, which is what makes Gate
B's hand-written `Project_Memberships` check unnecessary — it is deleted, and
the test that pinned it still passes. Gate B's other instance is derived too:
the `last_modified_by` exclusion is now `SyncTable.identityUserColumns` in the
shared package, and reachability moved into `ProjectReachability` so the write
check and pull's read filter cannot drift apart. Decision recorded as §4.17.

Ten failing tests were written first (`server/test/authz/authorization_test.dart`,
group "Gate C — the row-naming invariant"), seven of which failed before the fix.
Verified beyond that at the level the gate itself used —
`scripts/verify_c1_row_naming.py` runs all four reproductions over raw HTTP
against a live `docker compose` stack, and was **checked against a build with the
invariant removed**, where all four succeed and B1d writes the fabricated record
verbatim. Server suite 319/319 green against Postgres; every e2e file green
against a live server, including publish/join.

Three existing tests asserted the vulnerable behaviour and were corrected, not
relaxed: the "replication exemption stays narrow" group used Bob — a registered
user of the server — as its imported colleague, which is finding C-1's own
disclosure path rather than replication. It now uses a colleague the server has
never seen, pushed with the `Users` row the foreign key requires, which is what
the app actually sends.

### Task 10.21 — C-2: close the project existence oracle
**Status:** Done (2026-08-09)
**Model:** **Opus** — the fix interacts with publish, which needs `absent`
permitted.
**Depends on:** 10.16

Nonexistent project returns 200-empty; existing-but-forbidden returns 403 — on
pull, push and ack. Make the two indistinguishable without breaking
first-publish.

- **Acceptance:** an attacker cannot distinguish a real project id from a
  fabricated one on any sync route; publish of a genuinely new project still
  works; §4.13's named failure mode is retested.

**Done 2026-08-09.** `ProjectAccess.absent` no longer permits sync — that
permission *was* the oracle. Publish is permitted by the shape of the request
instead: `createSyncRouter` lets through a push carrying no rows of that project
(the publisher's first two requests are global rows only) and the push that
**establishes** it with a valid `Projects` row naming the caller as owner.
Everything else — pull, ack, any push of a project's own rows — is refused
identically whether the project is forbidden or fictional. Mechanism and the one
irreducible residual are recorded in §4.13.

Two consequences were not in the task's framing and are load-bearing. First, once
a global-only push is permitted against *any* id, a project the caller has no
relationship to must vouch for nothing, or the outcome map answers what the
status code no longer does: `RowAuthorizer` now gates both §4.17's
already-reachable clause and the tag-ownership check on real access. That also
closed a **write** hole the same permission opened — naming a stranger's project
in the envelope would have made its tags writable, defeating Gate B's "a stranger
cannot overwrite a tag belonging to another project". Second, a *failed* first
publish had to stop being a `500`: a deliberately malformed establishing row
answered `500` for a free id and `403` for a taken one, so the attempt runs in a
savepoint with `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE` (deferred FKs would otherwise not
raise until COMMIT, past the savepoint) and any failure becomes the ordinary
refusal.

Seven failing tests written first, five of which failed before the fix
(`server/test/integration/publish_and_join_test.dart`, group "the project
existence oracle (C-2)" — real socket, real auth, comparing the two responses to
each other rather than to expected text). Verified again at the gate's own level
by `scripts/verify_c2_existence_oracle.py`, over raw HTTP against a live stack,
**checked against a build with the seam removed**, where all five comparisons
diverge — two of them through a `500` rather than the recorded `200`. Server
suite 326/326; every e2e file green against a live server.

Three tests asserted behaviour that only worked because of the oracle, and were
corrected rather than relaxed: `ProjectAccess.absent.permitsSync` was pinned as
`true`, and two e2e suites seeded a project locally and then synced it without
ever publishing — which answered 200-empty. The app cannot do that: `SyncEngine`
runs only for a project already marked linked, and only publish or join marks
one.

### Task 10.22 — C-3: cleartext exemption and shipped defaults
**Status:** Done (2026-08-09)
**Model:** **Opus** — transport security posture.
**Depends on:** 10.16

`security_config.dart` has **no private-range check**, so cleartext on a public
interface is warned about rather than refused. `docker-compose.yml:54-55` then
defaults `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN=1` and `TRITRACK_ENV=development` behind
a `0.0.0.0` publish.

- Implement the private-range check and **refuse**, not warn.
- Fix the shipped compose defaults. §4.10's own reasoning — *the default is
  what gets deployed* — was applied to the diagnostics console and not here;
  apply it consistently and check for a third place it was missed.
- **Acceptance:** cleartext on a non-private address is refused at startup; a
  clean checkout cannot serve cleartext beyond the LAN without a deliberate,
  documented override.

**The third place existed, and so did a fourth.** The private-range half of
§4.1's condition was missing from the *client* too — `validateServerUrl` gated
only on `kReleaseMode`, so a debug build accepted `http://tracker.example.edu`.
Same sentence, same missing half, second enforcement point; fixed here, since
leaving it would have made "apply it consistently" untrue on the side users
touch. Both now call one `isPrivateNetworkAddress` in `packages/tritrack_sync`
rather than two hand-rolled range lists. The fourth is `SslMode.disable`
hardcoded on every Postgres connection — logged under Discovered Scope, not
fixed here, because changing the database transport is a deployment-topology
decision and not this task's.

`isPrivateNetworkAddress` is a closed list — anything unrecognised is public,
so an unconsidered range fails toward refusing. Accepts RFC 1918, loopback,
link-local, IPv6 ULA/link-local, IPv4-mapped IPv6, and 100.64/10 (CGNAT and
Tailscale — a mesh VPN address is a *safer* deployment than the LAN one §4.1
was written around, so refusing it would punish the better setup).

Compose now publishes `${SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}` and no longer
defaults `TRITRACK_ENV=development`. `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN` is fixed at
`1` there and deliberately not overridable: inside the container "all
interfaces" means the private Docker bridge, and Docker's port proxy cannot
reach a process bound to the container's loopback, so binding narrower would
break the harness without making anything safer. The exposure decision is the
publish address, and the reasoning sits between the two lines in the file.

**Verification.** `scripts/verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py` reproduces the
finding rather than asserting against a mock: it runs the real server image on
a Docker network with subnet `203.0.113.0/24`, so the container genuinely holds
a public address, and requires exit `78` with a readable refusal naming it —
observed. It reads the defaults back out of `docker compose config` (Docker's
own resolution, `.env` applied), and against a live stack confirmed
`127.0.0.1:8080` answers `200` while `192.168.0.88:8080` refuses. Restoring
`SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` re-opened the LAN path, which is the evidence
the override works and that the check is not passing vacuously.

Server suite 340/340 (was 326; +14). `packages/tritrack_sync` 116/116. Flutter
suite green except one pre-existing failure unrelated to this task — see
Discovered Scope. All seven e2e files green against a live server, run one file
per rate-limit window; see Discovered Scope for why the suite can no longer be
run in one pass.

The startup warning was reworded: it said "readable by anyone on this network",
which under the corrected publish default is false on every ordinary dev boot.
A security warning that overstates on every start is one people learn to scroll
past, which costs the boot where it is true.

### Task 10.23 — C-5: authorization-denied audit events
**Status:** Done (2026-08-09)
**Model:** Sonnet — a transaction-scoping bug with a clear cause.
**Depends on:** 10.16

`auditDenial` runs `AuthAuditLog` on the raw `Connection` while the sync
handler's `db.runTx` is open; `postgres` refuses it and `record`'s catch
swallows the exception. Verified: **zero** rows after many 403s.

- Run the write on the correct executor.
- **Stop swallowing.** A silent catch is why this survived to a live gate.
- `grep authorizationDenied server/test` returns nothing — add coverage.
- **Acceptance:** a denied request writes an audit row, proven against
  Postgres; removing the fix fails a test; no audit write silently discards an
  exception.

**Done 2026-08-09.** The bug was the executor, confirmed against the
`postgres` 3.5.12 source: `_verifyStateBeforeQuery` throws "Attempting to
execute query on connection while inside a `runTx` call" the instant a
statement runs on a connection whose own transaction is open — deterministic,
not a race, which is why `authorization_denied` was zero every time while the
other audit events (recorded after their own transaction closed) mostly
survived. `bin/server.dart` now opens a second, dedicated `auditDb` connection
at startup — never handed to any `runTx` — and both `withAuditLog` and the
diagnostics console's `AuthAuditLog` use it instead of the sync connection.
Either connection failing at startup is now treated as no database at all,
rather than serving with the audit half missing.

Separately, `AuthAuditLog.onError` moved from optional to a required
constructor argument. The "must never fail a request" design stands — a full
disk still must not stop anyone signing in — but the old shape let a caller
construct the class with no failure path at all (nothing did, but nothing
stopped it either); now every call site has to decide what happens when a
write is lost, in the open, at compile time.

`server/test/security/audit_log_test.dart` gained a test that reproduces the
original collision directly against Postgres — writing on a connection while
its own `runTx` is open loses the row and calls `onError`; a second, dedicated
connection used inside that same open transaction does not. `server/test/
integration/sync_audit_test.dart` is new: a stranger's denied push, over a
real bound HTTP socket wired exactly like `bin/server.dart` (two connections),
now leaves one real `authorization_denied` row naming the caller and the
project. Reverting the test's `withAuditLog` closure to reuse the sync
connection was checked by hand: the push still returns `403`, but the
denial-row assertion drops to zero and fails — the exact zero from §7.3 B5.

Server suite 342/342 against Postgres (was 340; +2 — the two tests above).
Full suite otherwise unchanged from `main`; the 11 pre-existing
`tombstone_retention_test.dart` failures when Postgres is unavailable predate
this task (confirmed via `git stash`) and are unrelated to it — see Discovered
Scope below.

### Task 10.24 — C-4: encrypted server backups and key custody
**Status:** Done (2026-08-09)
**Model:** **Opus** — key custody is a design decision with no undo.
**Depends on:** 10.16

Recorded open by 10.14 for a sound reason: no key custody arrangement exists.
Still blocking, because §2.1 names it against the actor this whole model is
organised around.

- Decide custody **first**: who holds the key, where, what happens when it is
  lost, and who can decrypt a backup. Record in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`.
- Then implement.
- **Acceptance:** custody arrangement written down and workable by one person
  running a single server; backups encrypted at rest; a restore proven end to
  end, because an untested restore is not a backup.

**Custody first, and it changed the code.** `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.9.1
answers the four questions the task asked, before any pipeline existed: **two
holders, each with their own `age` identity**, so every archive is encrypted to
both recipients and no private key is ever copied between people — the
alternative (one key, two copies) multiplies the places it can leak and the
second copy is always the untracked one. Each key lives in exactly two places:
the holder's own machine at mode `0600`, and one **paper** offline copy stored
physically apart from it, an `age` identity being one line of text. The public
recipients are not secret and live in `.env`. Blast radius is written out
rather than left to be discovered mid-incident: one key lost is *nothing* lost;
**all** keys lost means every archive is permanently unreadable, with no escrow
and no vendor — but the live database is untouched, so it is loss of history,
not of data, and the response is rotate-and-delete. There is deliberately **no
break-glass copy on the server**, since that reinstates exactly the property
§4.9 exists to prevent. Only the two holders can decrypt: not the server, the
job, the container, the Postgres password holder, or anyone with the storage
the archives are synced to.

That decision is what forced the implementation shape. `server/backup/` is one
image carrying both `pg_dump` and `age` so the pipeline runs **inside a single
container** — splitting it across two would route plaintext through the host,
which §4.9 forbids. The job refuses to run with no recipients rather than
falling back to anything (there is no unencrypted path to fall back to), and
builds each archive under a `.part` name renamed only after *both* halves
succeed. That last part is not defensive decoration: without `pipefail`, a
`pg_dump` that dies halfway leaves `age` exiting 0 and a well-formed archive of
a truncated database — a backup that restores silently missing rows, which is
this section's own failure mode wearing a control's clothing. `docker-compose
.yml` gains a `backup` service behind `profiles: ["backup"]`, so `docker compose
up` does not start a long-lived container holding a mount of every historical
snapshot.

**The restore is proven, not asserted.** `scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh` is
self-contained and destroys everything it creates: its own compose project,
volumes, and throwaway key pair. It stands up a real server so the **server's
own migration code** builds the schema (21 tables — a hand-written DDL could
drift from it), seeds an observation carrying coordinates, and runs nine checks.
From the run of 2026-08-09, all nine green: refuses with no recipients and
writes nothing; archive carries an `age` header and **none** of the seeded
coordinate, email, project name or note appears in it in the clear; an unrelated
private key is refused (`no identity matched any of the recipients`); the
correct key restores into a fresh database whose every column of every table
matches the original by name and type, with the seeded observation returned
identically, coordinates included; a `pg_dump` against a nonexistent database
leaves **no** archive and no `.part` behind; and `TRITRACK_BACKUP_KEEP=2` prunes
the *oldest* archives and their checksums rather than the newest. Two real bugs
surfaced while getting there, both caught by the drill rather than by review:
the seed omitted `Projects.coordinate_format`/`triangulation_window_minutes`
(schema v2 columns declared after the sync columns), and the base image's
`docker-entrypoint.sh` had to be cleared or it wrapped every invocation.

`test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart` gains a detector for the `age`
private-key prefix, because this task created a class of key material the
repository did not previously have and an `age` identity has no PEM armour for
the existing check to catch. It passes — and it caught this paragraph on the
first run, when the prefix was written out here literally. That is the same
docs-quote-the-pattern shape as the one pre-existing failure in that file (a
compose required-secret marker quoted in §4.6's prose), which is task 10.26's,
confirmed present at `HEAD` and untouched here. Both say something about the
detector: a scanner that cannot tell prose from a value will keep finding the
documentation that describes it, so 10.26 should fix the *detector*, not the
sentences.

**Deliberately not closed:** holder 2 is unnamed, because no server holding real
data exists yet and inventing a name would be the paper control §4.9 refuses.
§4.9.1 makes filling it in the trigger for the first real backup, and the job
warns on every run while a single recipient is configured.

is `exported="true"`, `FlutterActivity.getInitialRoute()` returns the caller's
`route` extra unconditionally, and go_router prefers it over `initialLocation`,
so `splash_screen.dart:44-45`'s "non-skippable gate" is false on Android
(reproduced at hops 2–3 with a negative control; bounded by §5.4). **K-4**,
`ServerIdentityAdopter` writes an unvalidated server-chosen `user_id` into 11
tables and hard-deletes the superseded `Users` row with no capture. **K-5**,
`UnknownColumnStore.promote` writes stashed values from `onOpen` with no
validation, no bound and no conflict record — latent until the next additive
schema bump, and one of its outcomes is a database that never opens again.
**K-6**, a malformed `rows` *container* is still accepted silently — J-5's shape
one level up, found immediately below the pass that closed J-5. **K-7**, two
instrument notes. **K-8**, §4.19 rule 4's consent gate writes a clock-only
payload with no dialog while the UI says *"replaced as you confirmed — 0 values
were changed"* (reproduced; `origin_device_id` is the LWW tiebreaker). **K-9**,
10.69's `CREATE ROLE` race reintroduced in `backup.sh` by the same commit that
adopted 10.66's rule. **K-10**, `throwsA(anything)` on the test guarding J-3.
**K-11**, the new unchecked-return detector never reads the file the class was
named after, and 10.67's sweep table omits `lib/data/sync/`.

**The lesson, and it is a different one this time.** Task 10.66's rule worked —
§4.19.1 is that rule applied honestly and is how K-1 came to be written down at
all. What failed is the step after: **three import paths were recorded "Open"
and none was given a task**, and six weeks later a written "Open" reads exactly
like a written "Closed." §12.4 did the same with K-2. So §12.11's practice needs
one cheap clause: **a finding recorded as open must leave the session with a
task number, or it has not been recorded — it has been described.** Both
blocking items this round were described, both accurately, and neither was
scheduled.

**Fifth re-run (2026-08-15) — record below, superseded in part.** **All nine scheduled remediations
landed and every one holds where it was aimed.** I-2 is genuinely closed — a
renamed copy of a genuine signed pair now draws a loud `RETENTION REFUSED` and
no genuine archive is pruned, proven by the drill's new step 10c rather than by
reading `backup.sh`. I-4 through I-11 hold. C-1…C-5, D-1 and I-4 refuse again.
**All four suites green in one pass — 792 client / 420 server / 32 e2e /
offline — and all ten instruments ran against a live server**, the second
consecutive gate where the tools worked first time. The adversarial pass held
36 of 40, and the four failures are the same four §10 and §11 recorded, with no
new ones.

**One thing proved that no previous gate had proved.** §11.6 warned that a proxy
forwarding a caller's own header "lets the caller pick their own rate-limit
bucket," and no gate had ever tested that against the proxy this repo ships. A
forged `X-Forwarded-For` through the shipped Caddy — five variants, including
one naming the proxy and one naming `127.0.0.1` — reached the origin as nothing
at all: every audit row named the real client, and rotating forged addresses did
not lift a `429`. 10.52's one load-bearing assumption about a component this
repo does not author is now measured rather than asserted (§12.3).

**Three blocking items — two new, one carried for the fifth consecutive gate.**
Both new findings are the same failure twice: **a fix that was correct for the
configuration it was written against, in a project that ships two.**

- **J-1 — a pasted `TT1:` share payload silently overwrites an observation the
  device already holds (§12.2).** Reproduced end to end. It moves the
  coordinates, reassigns `user_id` to the attacker, forges `last_modified_by` to
  the victim, inserts an attacker-chosen `Users` row, and **NULLs the nine
  fields that make the bearing reconstructible** — sweep endpoints, declination,
  WMM model version, capture method, antenna, gain. One row survives; the
  original is not kept. The app reports *"You already had this observation —
  updated it to the newer version."* No server involved, no authorization step
  by construction, no `RowValidator` on this path, and the merge clock is
  attacker-chosen (`revision` any `int >= 0`, `updated_at` unbounded). Live in
  the app **as shipped**, and the forged row propagates to the server and every
  other device on the next push. This is silent loss of irreplaceable field
  data — the highest-ranked concern in this project.
- **J-2 — I-1 is live in the base deployment (§12.4).** 10.52 closed it behind
  the proxy; `README.md`'s LAN walkthrough has no proxy. Reproduced: two
  genuinely distinct callers recorded **one** `source_address`, and twelve
  requests from one returned `429` to an unrelated caller. `RequestSource.direct`
  is assumed distinguishing unconditionally, so 10.52's real fail-safe cannot
  fire where it is most needed. **The collapse is described accurately inside the
  remediation's own file** (`rate_limiter.dart:62-79`) — as the justification for
  a test escape hatch — and was never connected to the deployment it also
  describes.
- **The NAU review — carried ×5, and the only item engineering cannot close.**
  `NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is byte-for-byte unchanged since `3333cb0`,
  recipient still blank, "Still not sent."

**The lesson, sharpened.** §10's was "the fix was never run in the configuration
it ships in"; §11's was "the control was never run in the configuration it ships
in, and the configuration changed underneath it." This round: **this project
ships more than one configuration, and a remediation aimed at one of them is not
a remediation.** J-1 is the same shape one level out — five gates have attacked
the server and then the topology around it, and the `TT1:` import path is
neither. It is the one place a string chosen by somebody else is parsed straight
into the field record, and no gate had looked at it because it is not the server.

**Non-blocking findings (§12.5–§12.7).** **J-3:** the server's own database
connection is a Postgres superuser — `COPY … FROM PROGRAM` demonstrated live,
running `id; hostname` on the database container. 10.59 closed exactly this on
the once-a-year restore path and left it on the always-on one; the same role can
also `DELETE FROM auth_audit_log`, so C-5's record is erasable by whatever
compromises the process that writes it. Not reachable today (static identifiers,
bound parameters), so rated as I-10 was. **J-4:** untyped `500`s on
attacker-typed input — `cursor` and `batch_size` wrongly typed (four variants
each) and a NUL byte in `device_id`/`project_id` — H-4's class on the fields
beside the one H-4 named, from any account. **J-5:** a non-Map row entry inside
a *known* table vanishes with `applied: 0, outcomes: {}`; 10.46 fixed that
silence for unknown table *names* and left the per-row case, so the `invalid`
outcome the protocol defines is still emitted by nothing. Harm bounded on the
client by 10.28's rule 2 — that design working against a defect nobody had
found. **J-6:** three instrument defects, each demonstrated rather than read —
`verify_tls_termination.sh:189-192` cannot fail (`|| true`, empty output passes;
shown against a down project and a nonexistent compose file), which is `Cf`'s
defect **reintroduced by 10.54 in the step it rewrote**; `gate_smoke_test.sh`'s
self-test cannot detect a *missing* instrument, which is precisely the
`verify_h3` omission 10.54 existed to fix — it added the name and not the check;
and `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py` now honestly prints "C-3 is NOT confirmed
closed by this run" while still exiting 0.

**Two claims chased and not reproduced, recorded because a gate that reports
only its hits is not a measurement:** an 8 MB body is *not* read and parsed
before authentication (`401` in 0.06 s with no credentials), and a wrongly-typed
`user_id` on a pushed row does *not* reach the unchecked cast — project
authorization refuses first, on all four type variants.

**Secrets clean across the whole history, 116 commits** — and by a committed
test now (`no_committed_secrets_test.dart` walks `git rev-list --all`, I-7
closed) rather than by hand. Gates A and B re-confirmed genuinely run and
closed, in the record.
