**Fourth re-run (2026-08-15) — record below, superseded in part.** **Nine of the ten scheduled
remediations hold, and the two that mattered most for the gate's own machinery
are genuinely closed.** H-1: `flutter test` is **779 passed, 9 skipped, exit
0** on a clean checkout. H-2: all seven instruments ran against a live server
and reported real results — **the first gate in four where the tools worked on
the first attempt**. G-1/G-2/G-3, H-4, H-5, F13 and ATS all hold under
re-attack; the reverse proxy three gates asked for exists and
`verify_tls_termination.sh` passes 7 checks, with `ports: !override []`
confirmed by re-rendering the merged compose rather than by trusting the drill.
C-1…C-5 and D-1 refuse again; the adversarial pass held 36 of 40, and **the
four failures are the same four §10 recorded, with no new ones**.

**Three blocking items — two new, one carried for the fourth consecutive
gate.** Both new findings came from attacking ground no previous round touched:
not the server, but **the configuration the server is deployed in**.

- **I-1 — §4.4's per-source rate limit is one global bucket, and every audit row
  records a constant address (§11.3).** Reproduced live in **both** the shipped
  `docker compose` and the mandated TLS/Caddy deployment: **ten unauthenticated
  requests deny magic-link sign-in to every user**, and all events recorded the
  proxy's container IP. C-5's forensic content is void with it. The 2026-08-07
  filing from 10.14 said whoever fronts the server with a proxy must either
  refuse `/diagnostics/*` there and accept the rate-limit merge, or add a
  trusted-proxy header. **10.49 shipped the proxy and did neither**, and
  recorded no acceptance.
- **I-2 — H-7 is not closed: retention verifies bytes, not names (§11.4).**
  Reproduced live on the current build with the remediation fully configured.
  10.44's signature predicate is structurally sound, but a minisign signature
  covers contents, not filenames: **30 copies of one genuine `(archive,
  .minisig)` pair renamed to 2999 all verify**, retention does not refuse, and
  the next legitimate backup run **deleted the entire genuine history**. The
  survivors are valid, signed and restorable, so a later restore silently rolls
  the database back to a stale snapshot, with no alarm at any point.
- **The NAU review — carried ×4, and the only item engineering cannot close.**
  The residual-risk summary it needs is written and current (**§11.10**,
  superseding §7.7) and the cover note is revised for the third time. What
  remains is a human sending an email.

**The lesson, and it is one lesson twice.** Neither new finding is a bug in a
piece of code. `rate_limiter.dart` is correct and its own doc comment predicts
I-1 exactly; `minisign` verifies precisely what it claims to. Both are
properties of the **seam between a correct control and the topology it runs
in** — and a seam is nobody's file. §10's lesson was "the fix was never run in
the configuration it ships in." This round: **the control was never run in the
configuration it ships in, and the configuration changed underneath it without
the control being re-measured.**

**And the reason I-1 survived four gates is the gate's own stack.**
`docker-compose.e2e.yml` sets `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED=1`, so
**no adversarial pass has ever observed the per-source limiter doing
anything.** The one control claiming to cover it, `Cf`, is a negative `grep`
over `docker compose config` stdout **whose return code is never checked** —
demonstrated to report HELD when the command fails outright.

**Instruments, again (§11.5).** Four more vacuous-pass paths, each confirmed by
demonstration rather than by reading: `verify_tls_termination.sh`'s
origin-reachability check is unscoped to its own compose project and **false-
alarmed live on this very run** (it failed while the override worked perfectly,
because an unrelated stack held 8080); its "no trust anchor" control cannot
fail (exit 7 with nothing listening); `Cf` as above; and
**`verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` never writes a `.minisig`**, so both of its
"with and without a verifying key" arms take the identical unsigned path and
`minisign -V` is reached by no instrument at all. Separately,
`verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` is run by **nothing** — absent from
`gate_smoke_test.sh` and its self-test, though both landed in the same commit.

**Decisions taken here, as the Opus 10.45 deferred them to (§11.7).**
`User_Emails` and `Tags` key oracles: **accept both**, and amend §4.13 to state
the exception rather than restate a rule the build knowingly violates in three
places. Both keys are random 122-bit client UUIDs, not enumerable, and the
structural fix is unavailable — `sync_tables.dart:78-80` records that these
tables cannot take a project column without breaking pull's reachability
filter.

**Also re-verdicted (§11.9): 10.19's cloud-backup default.** Confirmed explicit
and confirmed in code — `enabled = true`, plain `ZipEncoder()`, no encryption.
But §4.15's single-user justification was falsified by 10.9's publish/join in
§7.5, and **four gates have carried the decision without re-making it.** It is
now the largest accepted risk in the product that is not tracked as an open
finding.

**Secrets clean across the whole history, 107 commits.** Gates A and B
re-confirmed genuinely run and closed, in the record.

**Third re-run (2026-08-14) — record below, superseded in part.** **G-1, G-2 and G-3 are all genuinely
closed**, each verified the way it was found rather than the way it was
reported: `!override` rendered through `docker compose config` with the LAN
opt-in taken, the e2e guard exercised unconfigured *and* with a test file
deliberately removed, and the restore drill now typing
`TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE=I_UNDERSTAND` against a live database with the server
stopped, in four destructive cases. C-1…C-5 and D-1 refuse again. The
adversarial pass is the largest it has been: **40 checks, 33 held**, with a new
group E on ground no previous group covered.

**Seven blocking items — four new, three carried for the third consecutive
gate.** The two most serious are new ground: **nothing had ever adversarially
probed the backup path.** C-4 closed it at the first gate and three tasks
(10.24, 10.36, 10.37) have worked on it since, each correctly — and all three
were reasoning about accidents (corruption, truncation, a wrong key, a
destructive ordering). Nobody asked what someone who can write a file into the
archive directory can do, and §4.9's decision that the public recipients need
not be secret makes that person cheap.

- **H-6 — a forged backup archive is accepted, executed as superuser, and
  promoted over the live database (§10.5.1).** Reproduced live. The attacker
  needs the **public** recipient string and write access to the archive
  directory — the off-site copy §4.9 chose to trust with ciphertext. Asset 2
  integrity plus code execution, in the control C-4 created. 10.37's
  rename-aside means the real database is recoverable.
- **H-7 — retention deletes by filename, so write-only access to that same
  directory destroys every genuine backup (§10.5.2).** 30 planted files dated
  2999 and the next legitimate backup run deletes the whole history. No key, no
  read access.

- **H-1 — 10.39's guard turns the default `flutter test` run red.** The new
  `test/e2e/e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart` is tagged `e2e`, and there is no
  `dart_test.yaml` anywhere in this repo, so nothing excludes that tag from a
  plain `flutter test`. **772 passed, 30 skipped, 1 failed, exit 1** on a clean
  checkout — the suite Phase 10 invariant 5 and the README both promise stays
  green with no server and no network. G-1 is closed; it was closed by breaking
  the guarantee beside it. The fix is a tag exclusion, not a change to the
  guard: making the guard skip is G-1 reopened. New.
- **H-2 — 10.40's new self-check disabled all five wire-speaking instruments.**
  `gate_wire.preflight()` asserts `200` on a `/sync/pull` whose designed answer
  is `403` (§4.13's uniform denial — the thing C-2's remediation created).
  `verify_c1`, `verify_c2`, `verify_c5`, `verify_d1` and the adversarial pass
  all aborted before running a single control, against a healthy server. The
  gate repaired its own tools to take the measurement (§9.1.1's precedent) and
  records the finding; the one-line correction and its reasoning are in
  `scripts/gate_wire.py`, and the repaired check was re-verified by forcing a
  stale major and confirming it still aborts. New.
- **F13, TLS termination, and the NAU review** — all three carried, all three
  unchanged in every particular, all three now rated blocking at three
  consecutive gates. `server_http_client_provider.dart` still contains no
  scheme check and `cupertino_http` is still absent; a fresh sweep finds no
  reverse-proxy configuration of any kind in the repository;
  `NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is untouched since `831a269` and still reads
  "not sent", recipient blank.

**The lesson, and it is one lesson twice: the fix was never run in the
configuration it ships in.** 10.39 verified its guard under `--tags e2e` and
never ran plain `flutter test`. 10.40 wired a self-check into five tools and
never ran one against a live server. Both wrote accurate completion notes —
10.39's even says a live run "was not re-verified here" — and both notes were
passed over. Neither is a reasoning error.

**New non-blocking findings (§10.7).** **H-3:** `Tags` is a global-key
existence oracle (`lost_to_server` for a taken `tag_id` vs `inserted` for a
free one) — the table §9.5 named as *covered* by 10.29's reachability rule,
which governs referencing a tag, not claiming its key. Fourth instance of
fixing the reproductions and writing the sentence as a derived rule; §4.13 has
been corrected again and now carries a standing warning about its own
provenance. **H-4:** `schema_major` sent as a string answers `500`, on the
version check 10.35 put in front of authorization on every sync route. **H-5:**
a table name this server does not know is dropped silently (`200`, `applied: 0`,
`outcomes: {}`) — the `invalid` outcome the protocol defines and never emits,
G-5's gap from the other side.

**And two findings about the record's own reliability.** **H-8:** 10.40's
weak-assertion sweep reported "zero new instances beyond the five known ones";
an independent sweep of 206 sites found **six**, five of them in the gate's own
instruments — including `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:341` reading an empty
`outcomes` map as "every table refused the forged row", a vacuous pass on
**C-1** (fixed this run; `Ca` still holds under the strict form), and
`verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py:150-152` exiting 0 with "C-3 closed" when the
stack is down. **H-9:** three unproven edges left around 10.37's restore
ordering, one of them certified by a text-grep detector rather than tested. Both
under Discovered Scope. The compose merge sweep 10.38 asked for is also now done
(§10.7.3): two latent instances, one Compose-version residual, and a comment in
`docker-compose.e2e.yml` that now contradicts the line below it.

**Also re-checked rather than assumed:** D-2's row-count arm still open (40
denials → 44 audit rows; §4.7's retention still implemented by nothing, while
tombstones have a service); D-4 unchanged (three project-level call sites);
D-5 unchanged (shipped default answers `404`); secrets clean across 96 commits;
§9.7's device residual still owed.

**Two of group E's own checks were wrong in their first draft, in opposite
directions** — one reported a disclosure that was only a `trace_id`, the other
reported a finding against a server that had ignored every attempt. Both were
caught by reading the detail lines rather than the verdicts, both are fixed in
the repository, and that habit has now caught something at four consecutive
gates.

**Second re-run (2026-08-13) — record below, superseded in part.** The previous round's remediation holds
where it was checked: **D-1, D-2's size arm, D-3 and E-1 are genuinely closed**,
all re-verified live rather than taken on trust, and C-1…C-5 refuse again. Three
suites green in one pass — **764 client / 357 server / 30 e2e** — the last
including a new live check (§9.7) that closes most of the device instruction
three tasks had deferred.

**Six blocking items, three of them places where the record and the code
disagree:**

- **G-1 — the e2e suite reports success when it runs nothing.** `flutter test
  test/e2e --tags e2e` with the environment unset prints "All tests skipped" and
  exits `0`. E-1's exact shape on the one suite that exercises the wire
  protocol, the schema-major boundary and the refused-row path against a real
  server; 10.31's guard was built for the server only. New.
- **G-2 — E-2 is not closed.** Compose *merges* `ports:` rather than replacing
  it, so with the LAN opt-in taken the base file's `0.0.0.0:8080` still renders
  alongside 10.32's loopback mapping. The stack fails to start rather than
  exposing — Docker's bind ordering, not a control — and the natural repair
  leads straight back to C-3. Verified fix (`ports: !override`) tested and
  reverted; a gate does not repair its own findings.
- **G-3 — E-3, reproduced destructively.** The documented in-place restore
  dropped a live database holding the only copy of an observation, then failed
  to decrypt the archive. Recorded as must-fix-before-this-gate at the last run
  and **never given a task**. Asset 2.
- **F13, TLS termination, and the NAU review** — all three carried, all three
  unchanged in every particular.

**Non-blocking but the record must be corrected: G-4.** §4.13 and §8.4 both
state that D-1's arm (c) was "fully closed" by 10.35's project-scoped keys.
`Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` are still keyed globally; `Users` and `Tags`
are covered by other rules, **`User_Emails` is covered by neither** and answers
`unauthorized` for a key another user holds against `inserted` for a free one.
Disclosure is negligible (guessing a 122-bit UUID), which is why it is not
blocking — but it is the third instance of *fixing the instances that had
reproductions and describing it as a derived rule*, and §4.13 has been corrected.

**Also recorded:** D-2's row-count arm is still open (size arm closed;
11 MB/s → **122 KB/s**, and §4.7's retention sweep is still implemented by
nothing); D-5 is worse than recorded — the only configuration that can read the
audit log is the one §4.10's network gate exists to prevent; D-4 unchanged; a
malformed row from an authorized caller fails the whole push with `500` (G-5);
and `revision` pinning at `2^63-1` is now reproduced live rather than read.

**The instruments had rotted before the gate could use them** (§9.1.1). Four of
five `verify_*.py` scripts plus the adversarial pass still sent
`schema_major: 1` one day after 10.35 moved the server to 2 — every request
`409`, every check reading `None` from an empty outcomes map, which for a
"is this refused?" check is indistinguishable from the control holding. This is
10.35's own filed Discovered Scope item arriving a year early. Fixed at the
level of the finding: `scripts/gate_wire.py` **parses** the envelope and every
table's primary key out of the Dart source that defines them, so a bump updates
the tools by definition. Doing it surfaced that
`verify_c1_row_naming.py`'s regression section had been asserting the *opposite*
of current behaviour since 10.29 landed.

New reusable evidence in the repository: `scripts/gate_wire.py`,
`scripts/verify_e3_restore_replace.sh` (G-3's live reproduction), group D of

**First re-run (2026-08-12) — record below, superseded in part.**

**C-1 through C-5 are genuinely closed** — all five re-run live and refused,
three of them additionally checked against a build with the fix reverted, where
each reproduces the original finding verbatim. C-5 had no live verification
script and now does (`scripts/verify_c5_denial_audit.py`); reverting
`bin/server.dart`'s dedicated audit connection reproduces the gate's original
`zero rows` evidence exactly. All three suites are green in one pass for the
first time (703 / 347 / 26), which is task 10.26's contribution and the
precondition for this gate being able to read its own instruments.

**Seven independent blocking items.** Four new, three carried:

- **D-1 — C-2 was closed one level too high.** The status code is uniform now
  (verified, including by timing), but the per-row `outcomes` map answers the
  same question: a three-way read of whether a stranger has an account and has
  published a profile, plus tag-id and row-key existence, from an ordinary
  session with no project and no relationship to anything asked about. 10.20
  *added* the user arm; the tag and row-key arms predate the remediation and
  were missed by Gates B and C both. Same class as C-2, which was blocking.
- **D-2 — the C-5 fix is an unbounded attacker-controlled write.** The
  caller's `project_id` lands in `auth_audit_log.outcome` untruncated, the sync
  body limit is 8 MB, and `/sync/pull` has no rate limit. Measured: 10 denied
  requests, 0.9 s, 10 MB on disk. §4.7 retention is still unscheduled.
- **D-3 — a refused row is silently lost and the app says "Synced."** The case
  this task named in advance, failing the way it predicted. `SyncEngine._push`
  keeps only `lostToServer` outcomes and discards `unauthorized`; the watermark
  advances anyway; a replica's preserved sender clock puts it below the new
  watermark, so it is never re-offered and never counted as pending. Asset 2.
- **E-2 — the e2e override reopens C-3 through two documented steps.**
  `docker-compose.e2e.yml` declares no `ports:`, so it inherits
  `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS`. An operator who followed the README's LAN
  walkthrough and then runs the e2e suite gets cleartext on every interface,
  §4.4's per-source limits raised to `1<<30`, and a mount of live magic-link
  tokens. Verified with `docker compose config`. One line.
- **F13 — carried, and §7.6 already called it "blocking before any real
  deployment."** Still a form validator, not transport enforcement, and its
  compensating control is weaker than recorded: no `cupertino_http`, so
  `http.Client()` is `IOClient` over `dart:io` and iOS/macOS ATS probably never
  applies. Needs a device check.
- **TLS termination — unverifiable.** No reverse proxy, no certificates, no
  deployment of any kind exists. The gate cannot confirm a control nobody has
  built. Whatever topology is eventually proposed, the proxy is in scope for
  the gate that approves it.
- **The NAU review still has not happened.** Drafted 2026-08-07, unsent,
  recipient line still blank. §7.8's terms are unchanged and this is a human
  action; independently of everything above, the gate cannot pass until it
  happens.

**Two more that do not block exposure but block the next re-run's ability to
claim anything**, filed under their own Discovered Scope heading: **E-1**, the
C-1/C-2/C-5 regression tests default to inert without a database (and the
obvious fix to the 11 failures currently exposing that would make the suite
green with ~150 silent skips), and **E-3**, the documented in-place restore
drops the live database before it knows the archive can be decrypted.

**The result worth carrying forward:** all three new blocking findings were
introduced by, or left visible by, the remediation of the previous gate's
findings — and a pass that only re-ran C-1…C-5 would have found none of them.
This task's insistence on repeating the whole adversarial pass rather than
spot-checking the five was right twice over: the scoped thing to check was the
five findings, and the five findings were all fine. **Repairing a security
control is a change to the attack surface and has to be attacked as one.**

Reusable evidence now in the repository: `scripts/gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`
(24 attempts, 20 held) and `scripts/verify_c5_denial_audit.py`, alongside
10.20–10.22's existing verification scripts.

**Model:** **Opus**, high effort.
**Depends on:** 10.20–10.24 (and 10.26, run first)

Re-run task 10.16 in full. **Not a spot-check of the five findings** — the
gate's own most important conclusion was that the class-level pattern behind
C-1 was invisible to two prior scoped reviews and 309 passing tests, and only
appeared under a live adversarial pass. Repeat the whole pass.

- Every C-1…C-5 reproduction from §7.3, re-run live, must fail.
- Full adversarial pass again, not just the known five.
- **Verify TLS actually terminates in front of the server on the real host.**
  Task 10.22 closed C-3 but recorded a residual it cannot close: a container
  cannot see its host's addresses, so inside Docker every interface looks
  private and the startup refusal can never fire on a public VPS. The
  `127.0.0.1` publish default stands in for it, and a default is not a
  control. On a real deployment the actual protection is the reverse proxy,
  so confirm it exists and works — do not rely on the app's own check, which
  is structurally blind there.
- **Check the user-facing surfaces the fixes touched, on a device — not just
  the API.** 10.20's invariant denies a case Phase 6's observation-sharing
  flow can legitimately hit: saving a `TT1:` payload from a colleague who has
  a server account but isn't on your project. Confirm that fails *visibly*
  and says something useful. This is a code-review blind spot by construction
  — the server behaviour is correct and tested, and the app can still present
  it as a silent nothing. That is exactly how the sign-in bug reached a real
  phone with 700+ tests passing. Do the same for 10.22's startup refusal and
  10.23's audit path: a correct refusal nobody can see is a support call.
- Then the NAU information-security review, which has still not happened.
- **Acceptance:** no blocking finding; §7 updated; only then does the
  localhost restriction lift.

### Task 10.27 — F15: stop the gate run destroying the dev database
**Status:** Done (2026-08-12)
**Model:** Sonnet — a missing flag.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Do this first.**

The 10.25 gate run destroyed `tritrack_postgres_data`. One `-p` flag. It has
already cost real local data once and will again on every future gate run.

- **Acceptance:** a full gate/verification run cannot remove or reuse the
  developer's data volume; proven by running it with data present and
  confirming the data survives.

`scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` built its `COMPOSE` command with no `-p`,
so its project name defaulted to the checkout's directory name — the same
default project name a plain `docker compose up` uses for the real dev stack.
Its `cleanup()` trap runs `$COMPOSE down -v`, which removes the named volume
under that project, so a test run and a live dev stack collided on the same
`tritrack_postgres_data` volume and the test run's teardown deleted it.
Fixed by giving it its own project name (`-p tritrack-server-test`), the same
pattern `scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh` already used correctly. Docker
namespaces named volumes by project, so this isolates the test stack's volume
from the dev stack's without touching `docker-compose.server-test.yml`.
`scripts/run_offline_suite.sh`'s bare `docker compose down` (no `-v`, no `-p`)
was checked too — it targets the same default project name but never removes
volumes, so it was not at risk.

### Task 10.28 — D-3: a refused row must never be silently lost
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13)
**Model:** **Opus** — silent data loss on the sync path.
**Depends on:** 10.20

`sync_engine.dart:201-202` discards a row the server refused, advances the
watermark past it, never retries, and reports "Synced." **This is silent loss
of irreplaceable field data** — the highest-ranked concern in this project —
and it was predicted in advance by 10.25's own checklist before it fired.

- A refused row must be retained locally, excluded from watermark advancement,
  and surfaced. Nothing may report success while a row was dropped.
- The legitimate case that produces it: 10.20's invariant refusing an imported
  observation from a registered colleague who isn't on the project (see 11.2).
  So the right outcome is "held and explained," not "retried forever."
- Ties to 10.12's three-state distinction — offline, refused, broken.
- **Acceptance:** a refused row survives locally; the watermark does not pass
  it; the user is told, in the app, that something did not sync and why; a
  test fails if any path can advance past a refusal.

**What was built.** A new client-only table, `Sync_Held_Rows`
(`lib/data/sync/sync_held_rows.dart`), is the memory that was missing: one row
per refused row — never one per refusal, which would be an unbounded local write
driven by a remote decision, the mistake 10.30 had to undo server-side. It
records the row's identity, the reason, and the `updated_at` it carried when it
was refused, and it stores **no copy of the row's data** (the record is already
in SQLite, and a second copy would be a second thing to keep current and a
second place for field data to sit).

`SyncEngine._push` was rewritten around four rules, in this order:

1. Every outcome is classified by `HeldRowReason.forOutcome`, an **exhaustive
   switch with no `default`** — adding a `SyncRowOutcome` is now a compile error
   rather than a row falling through the accepted branch, which is exactly how
   `unauthorized` and `invalid` came to be handled by a `continue` written for
   `lostToServer`.
2. **Every offered row is checked for an outcome, and silence is a refusal**
   (`HeldRowReason.unaccounted`). Reachable under version skew — the server
   drops rows for tables it does not know — and the case where quietly assuming
   success would be worst.
3. Refusals are written to the store **before the watermark moves**, so a
   failure between the two re-offers the row instead of forgetting it.
4. The watermark is then **clamped to the earliest refusal**, replacing the
   unconditional "highest row offered."

**One deliberate deviation from the acceptance wording, because the acceptance
criteria contain a genuine tension.** "The watermark does not pass it" and "held
and explained, not retried forever" cannot both hold forever: the refusal is
permanent until somebody changes the project's membership, so a watermark pinned
below it re-offers every row written *after* it on every sync, forever, growing
without bound as the season goes on — and pinning it also wedges any project
larger than one batch. So the clamp holds for the round that learns of the
refusal, and from then on the **held record, not the watermark**, is what keeps
the row from being forgotten: it is counted, surfaced, and excluded from
selection only while it is unchanged. Edit the row and it goes back on the wire
automatically; tap "Try again" and it goes immediately; and until the server
takes it, nothing in the app may say it synced. The invariant actually enforced
is therefore **"no path advances past a refusal that has not been durably
recorded and counted,"** which is the version that survives contact with a
permanent refusal. Tests assert both halves, including that the round *after* a
refusal — which refuses nothing new and used to look perfectly clean — still
reports `heldCount: 1`.

**`ProjectPublisher.publish` had the same hole, reached earlier.** It ignored
per-row outcomes entirely, marked the project linked, set the watermark to *now*
(past every refusal), and returned a count of rows *sent* labelled
`rowsUploaded`. It now applies the same three rules and reports `refused`;
publishing still links the project, deliberately — refusing to link would leave
the accepted rows unable to sync and the refused one unable to be retried.

**The user-facing half**, which §7 was right to insist on separately:
`SyncHealth.rowsRefused` is the third of 10.12's three states (offline / refused
/ broken), ranked above `offline` and unreachable from `healthy`, so the banner
can no longer read "Synced" while a record is held — it reads "1 record isn't on
the server. Tap to see why." in red. The status screen gains a "Not synced to
the server" section above "Overwritten edits" (a different situation: those rows
*are* on the server), with a client-authored explanation per reason and a "Try
again" per row. Publish and join confirmations are qualified the same way.
`pendingCount` now **subtracts** held rows: "waiting to sync" and "refused" are
different statements with different remedies and one row must not be in both.

**Tests.** `FakeSyncTransport` can now deny rows and ignore rows — before this
it could not, which is the mechanical reason a suite of 700+ tests never saw
D-3. 17 new store/retry cases, 15 new engine cases (including the refused-`Users`
row, which is the case the real workflow actually produces), 4 new publisher
cases, and the **first widget tests for `SyncStatusBanner` and
`SyncStatusScreen`** — the surfaces §8 noted had none at all. 751 client tests
green.

**Fixed in passing, because this change would have amplified it:** every
re-offered identical row was recorded as "an edit you made was superseded."
The server answers `lost_to_server` for any row it did not apply, including one
identical to its stored copy, and the `>=` watermark bias re-offers the boundary
row every round — so the user's review list was collecting entries where nothing
was superseded, and the clamp would have added a batch of them per refusal.
`_recordConflicts` now skips a loss where the authoritative row equals the one
offered.

### Task 10.29 — D-1: close the per-row existence oracle
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13)
**Model:** **Opus** — same class as C-2, one level down.
**Depends on:** 10.21

C-2 was closed at the HTTP status code — that part holds, including against
timing. The per-row `outcomes` map still answers the same question, in three
arms reproducible from an ordinary session with no project: a stranger's
registration status (three-way), tag-id existence, and row-key existence.

- Two of the three predate the remediation and were missed by Gate B and the
  first Gate C. **The current test suite asserts the oracle as correct
  behaviour** — those tests need correcting, exactly as 10.20 had to.
- Fix at the level the answer leaks, not the level it was reported at. That
  is the lesson of C-2 → D-1.
- **Acceptance:** all three arms refuse; no per-row outcome distinguishes
  "absent" from "forbidden"; legitimate publish and sync are unaffected;
  every corrected test is checked as corrected, not relaxed.

Fixed inside `RowAuthorizer`, at the three points where an answer forks on
hidden state — deliberately not in the `outcomes` map, since patching what is
*reported* is the mistake the finding is about. The rule it now enforces is
written once in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.13: **no per-row outcome may
depend on server state the caller has no other way to observe, and where
authorization must consult such state both branches answer the refusal** —
because the permissive branch performs a write, and a write cannot be concealed
by what comes back.

**Arm (a) — a stranger's registration status — closed, and it cost the seam the
finding predicted it would.** §4.17's third naming clause ("the server has never
heard of them") is deleted, along with the `Users`/`auth_accounts` lookup behind
it. A row may name only the caller or someone the project already reaches.
Converging the *other* way was not available: it is finding C-1 verbatim, the
permissive branch writes a row regardless of how the answer is worded, and —
the argument that actually settles it — naming someone is **attribution** as
well as disclosure, so stamping a stranger's name on a telemetry record is
fabrication of the primary scientific record whether or not this server has
heard of them. That harm is the same in both branches, which is why the
disclosure-only justification could not survive being asked about.

The third value in that arm, `lost_to_server` for a stale copy of a real user's
row, needed its own fix: a no-op push used to skip authorization entirely
("nothing is mutated, so nothing needs permission"), and "the server already
holds that" is a statement about the stored row. A no-op now checks whether the
caller may be told the row exists, at the **reachability** bar rather than the
authorship one — a row an ordinary pull would deliver anyway — so the re-offer
every sync round performs is untouched. `RowAuthorizer`'s own doc comment
already made this argument for cross-project rows and had not generalised it,
which is C-1's pattern for the third time.

**Arm (b) — tag existence — closed.** The old test asked "does any *other*
project reference this tag?", which permitted orphans and refused claimed ones:
the fork. It now asks `ProjectReachability` — the same computation pull's read
filter uses — so a tag may be referenced exactly where a pull would already
deliver it. `Project_Tags` is the one row allowed to widen a project's reach,
and there a tag id that names nothing and one another project holds are a single
refusal. Two mechanisms keep the ordinary flow working: a tag the push has
itself been allowed to establish vouches for later rows of the *same* push (the
`SyncEngine` shape, where a whole batch is judged against one pre-push snapshot),
and an orphaned tag row already on the server can still be claimed (the
`ProjectPublisher` shape, one table per request). Both are covered by tests and
by the verification script.

**Arm (c) is the residual, and it is general.** Pushing a row under a primary
key lifted from someone else's export is the create-if-absent collision inherent
to **client-chosen primary keys** — the same signal §4.13 already stated and
bounded for `Projects`, which turns out to be a property of every table. §4.13
now says so, with the bound *checked* rather than asserted: existence escapes,
the victim's row does not move, change, or come back. Closing it means scoping
primary keys to their project — see Discovered Scope.

**Found while reproducing it, and not in the write-up:** where the "server does
not hold it" branch left a dangling foreign key, the push answered **`500`**
while the held id answered `200`. That is a status-code-level oracle on the
routes C-2 was supposed to have made uniform, and it is closed by the same
change, because the reference is refused before any write is attempted.

**The corrected tests were checked as corrected, twice over.** The two
assertions §8.4 names were flipped to the refusal, with the test bodies now
saying that their old expectations *were* the oracle. Seven new cases are
written as **equivalences** — two pushes differing only in a fact about the
server's contents must come back the same — because pinning each answer
separately is exactly what let this survive two gates. Reverting
`row_authorizer.dart` fails four of them; the two "a new tag still syncs" cases
pass either way by design, since they guard against the fix rather than the bug.
New `scripts/verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py` applies `verify_c2_existence_oracle.py`'s
method one level down over raw HTTP against a live stack: **six distinguishable
pairs against the pre-fix build, none after**, with arm (c) reported as
RESIDUAL and its bound verified. 357 server tests green, 752 client tests green,
e2e suite green, analyzer clean.

**The accepted cost, stated plainly because it is a product decision and not
only a security one:** an imported colleague's observations no longer replicate
to the server until that colleague is on the project — not merely once they
register here, which was the pre-existing cost. In Phase 10 there is no way to
*be* a collaborator, so in practice a project syncs only rows naming its owner,
and §4.17's clause 2 has no reachable instance yet (it is modelled and tested
against seeded state, as `ProjectAccess.member` is). Task 11.2's invitation
record is what reopens it. **Nothing is lost meanwhile** — task 10.28's
`SyncHeldRowStore` keeps every refused row, counts it against "everything is
synced", and explains it; that machinery landing first is what made this trade
payable at all.

### Task 10.30 — D-2: bound the denial audit write
**Status:** Done (2026-08-12)
**Model:** Sonnet — add a limit to a route that has none.
**Depends on:** 10.23

The C-5 fix made denial auditing an unbounded attacker-controlled write: 10
requests, 0.9 s, 10 MB on disk, no rate limit on that route.

- Bound it — rate limit, size cap, or aggregation of repeated denials.
- Keep C-5's guarantee intact: denials must still be recorded, and failures
  must still not be swallowed. A cap that silently drops events recreates C-5.
- **Acceptance:** a flood cannot grow the audit store without bound; genuine
  denials are still recorded; removing the bound fails a test.

Fixed with a size cap (the option the plan itself lists first), applied at the
API's write boundary rather than at `sync_routes.dart`'s call site: `AuthAuditLog.record`
(`server/lib/src/security/audit_log.dart`) now truncates every free-text
parameter — `outcome` (where the caller-controlled `project_id` lands),
`reason`, `email`, `deviceId`, `sourceAddress`, `userId`, `requestId` — to
`maxAuditFieldLength` (500 chars) before the insert. Chosen over rate-limiting
`/sync/pull` because the measured amplification (10 requests → 10 MB) came
from *payload size per request*, not request volume, and every real id/email/
trace-id value already sits far under 500 chars, so the cap costs nothing on
the genuine-denial path C-5 exists to protect. Doing it inside `record()`
rather than only at the one known call site means a future caller that puts
caller-controlled text in a different field doesn't reopen the same hole
(same "fix at the level the answer leaks" lesson C-2 → D-1 already established).
Two new cases added to `test/security/audit_log_test.dart`: an oversized field
is truncated (not dropped, not stored in full — proven by asserting the
row exists at exactly `maxAuditFieldLength`), and an ordinary-sized value
round-trips untouched. Full suite (350 tests) green against Docker Postgres.

### Task 10.31 — E-1: tests must not pass by skipping
**Status:** Done (2026-08-12)
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** nothing. **Run before the next gate.**

139 server tests silently skip without a database. Eleven are unguarded, so
the suite currently fails — but the obvious fix to those eleven would make it
**green with ~150 silent skips and zero coverage of C-1, C-2 and C-5.**

- **Order matters: land the guard first**, then fix the eleven. Reversed, the
  suite goes green while covering nothing, and nobody looks again.
- A run with no database must fail loudly, not report success.
- Third instance of this pattern in Phase 10 (the swallowed sign-in exception,
  10.26's red detector, this). Worth a standing rule in
  `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`: a test that cannot run must not look like a
  test that passed.
- **Acceptance:** no database means a loud failure; the skip count is asserted
  against an expected number so a future silent jump breaks the build; the
  C-findings' coverage is proven to actually execute.

### Task 10.32 — E-2: the e2e override reopens C-3
**Status:** Done (2026-08-12)
**Model:** Sonnet — a compose default.
**Depends on:** 10.22

`docker-compose.e2e.yml` declares no `ports:`, so two documented steps
recreate the condition C-3 closed. Same lesson as C-3 itself: the default is
what gets deployed.

- Fix the override, then check every other compose file and documented command
  for the same shape.
- **Acceptance:** no documented sequence in the repo produces a cleartext
  listener beyond localhost; the e2e suite still runs in one pass (10.26).

`docker-compose.e2e.yml`'s `server` service had no `ports:` of its own, so it
fell through to the base file's `${SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}`. An
operator who had followed the README's LAN walkthrough (`SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0`
in `.env`, for a phone on the Wi-Fi) and then brought up the e2e override for
the integration suite got that same `0.0.0.0` publish back — combined with
this same file's `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED: "1"` and a live
magic-link token mount. That is a worse posture than plain C-3, on a file
whose own reasoning never mentions `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS` at all. Fixed by
hardcoding `ports: ["127.0.0.1:${SERVER_PORT:-8080}:8080"]` in the override,
deliberately not reading `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS`, so no `.env` value can
change it — the e2e suite only ever needs `localhost`, per its own
documented run command.

Checked every other compose file and documented command for the same shape:
`docker-compose.server-test.yml` already hardcodes `127.0.0.1` for Postgres
(fixed at 10.15); the base `docker-compose.yml` is the one file where
`SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS` is supposed to be honored. The e2e teardown command
documented in the root README (`docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f
docker-compose.e2e.yml down -v`) shares the dev stack's project name and
volume by design — the surrounding text says the suite intentionally runs
against "the *same* persistent database across runs" — so that is not this
bug's shape (contrast task 10.27's `run_server_tests_docker.sh`, which shared
that name *by accident* for a stack meant to be throwaway).

### Task 10.33 — Batch limit can strand rows below the watermark
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13)
**Model:** **Opus** — a second silent-loss path on the sync engine, same class
as D-3.
**Depends on:** 10.28

Found by a regression test written for 10.28, pre-existing and not fixed there.

`_collectChangedRows` walks tables in FK order under a **shared** batch limit,
then the watermark advances to the highest row offered. Rows in later tables
that the limit never reached therefore sit *below* the new watermark and are
never selected again.

**The rows it strands are precisely older-clock replicas** — task 6.3
deliberately preserves the sender's clock on a shared observation, so an
imported colleague's record carries an older `updated_at` and sorts late. That
is the same workflow as D-3, and the same asset: a colleague's field
observation, silently never uploaded, with the app reporting success.

- 10.28 established the invariant that no path advances past a row that wasn't
  durably recorded. This is a path that does exactly that, by omission rather
  than by misclassification.
- **10.28's note explains why the obvious interim patch is worse** — it stalls
  the push instead of stranding rows, which trades silent loss for a wedged
  sync on any project bigger than one batch. Read that before choosing an
  approach; the fix needs per-table progress, not a clamped shared limit.
- **Acceptance:** a push whose batch limit is exhausted mid-walk cannot
  advance the watermark past any unoffered row; an imported older-clock
  replica in a late table is eventually uploaded; a test reproduces the
  stranding on the pre-fix code; no project size wedges the push.

**The task entry understates the bug, and that decided the approach.** The
finding attributes the stranding to the batch limit — "on any device holding
more than `defaultSyncBatchSize` rows newer than it." It is worse than that.
The watermark is a single per-project timestamp set to the highest `updated_at`
*offered*, so an imported replica carrying its sender's older clock (task 6.3)
is below it the moment it is written, on **any device that has ever pushed
anything newer** — no batch limit involved, no truncated walk, just the ordinary
result of saving a colleague's shared observation on a device that syncs. A
per-table watermark, which is what "the fix needs per-table progress" suggests,
closes the truncated-walk arm and leaves that one wide open: `Observations` has
its own watermark, and on a device that has been syncing all season that
watermark is already past last week. Since the whole subject of this task is a
colleague's field record silently never uploaded, a fix that closes one route to
it and not the other is not a fix. **So this took the pending-set option the
Discovered Scope note names as the real answer** ("a dirty flag or local change
sequence, so selection is 'rows not yet accepted' rather than a clock
comparison"), rather than the narrower reading of the task entry. Flagged here
rather than done quietly because it is a bigger change than the entry asks for.

**What was built: `Sync_Row_Receipts`** (`lib/data/sync/sync_row_receipts.dart`),
one durable receipt per row the server has confirmed, recording the `updated_at`
it confirmed. **A row is pending when no receipt matches its current
`updated_at`.** The pending set is now exact rather than inferred, and the push
watermark is gone — `SyncStateStore.pushWatermark`/`setPushWatermark`/
`resetPushWatermark` are deleted, not deprecated, so nothing can quietly keep
using an approximation that loses rows. It is a client-only table created with
`IF NOT EXISTS` on use, following `SyncHeldRowStore` exactly: not project data,
never synced, out of `tableSpecs` and out of `latestSchemaVersion`.

The **direction of failure is the design**. A receipt is written only for an
outcome that means the row is on the server, so anything the table does not know
about is pending: a row a batch never reached, a round that died between the
server's answer and the receipt, a row written by a path nobody thought of, a
clock that jumped backwards, a restore from backup. Over-pushing costs
bandwidth; under-pushing loses an observation. Every ambiguity resolves toward
the cheap one.

**Four consequences worth naming:**

1. **`_collectChangedRows` selects by join, not by comparison** — one
   `_pendingClause` written once and used by *both* the push selection and
   `pendingRowCount`, so "3 records waiting to sync" is now, by construction,
   the set of rows the next push will offer. They were previously two
   hand-written predicates that agreed by convention.
2. **Held rows are excluded in SQL rather than post-filtered**, which retires
   task 10.28's over-fetch compensation and the stall it existed to prevent.
3. **The `>=` boundary re-offer is gone**, and with it the starvation case the
   Discovered Scope note filed alongside this one: rows sharing one timestamp
   used to be re-offered every round and could consume every batch forever. A
   bulk import writes exactly that shape — many rows carrying one sender's
   clock — so it was reachable, not theoretical. There is a test for it.
4. **Task 10.28's watermark clamp is deleted from both `SyncEngine._push` and
   `ProjectPublisher.publish`.** That clamp was the most a watermark could do
   about a permanent refusal, and it came with a documented cost (a batch of
   accepted rows dragged back onto the wire after every refusal). With per-row
   receipts the tension it was managing does not exist: the refused row is
   pending because it has no receipt, and nothing else comes with it. The
   "Try again" action loses its watermark-rewind half for the same reason.

**The pull writes receipts too**, for every row a committed page delivered —
against the *delivered* `updated_at`, not against whatever the merger left
behind. Without it a device joining a project would pull a season of data and
then immediately re-upload all of it. Recording the delivered timestamp is also
what keeps last-write-wins honest: when the merger keeps a newer local edit, the
local row no longer matches the receipt, so it stays pending and goes up.

**Tests.** A new `task 10.33` group with five cases: a row a full batch never
reached, an imported older-clock replica on an already-synced device, the
stranded row counted as pending, a loop asserting no project size wedges the
push, and an interrupted round losing nothing. **All three that could be
expressed against the pre-fix API were run against the pre-fix code in a
worktree at HEAD and fail there** — including the replica case, which fails with
no batch limit involved at all, confirming the wider reading above. Every
watermark assertion in the existing suite was rewritten as the receipt-level
statement it was standing in for, checked as corrected rather than relaxed: "the
watermark does not pass the refused row" became "the refused row has no receipt
and the accepted row beside it does," and the pending count in the held-row test
went from 2 to **0** — the old 2 were rows already on the server that the `>=`
bias re-offered every round. 757 client tests green, and the full e2e suite
green against a live server over real HTTP.

### Task 10.34 — Held-row copy and audit volume after D-1's narrowing
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13)
**Model:** Sonnet — copy and a threshold review; no new mechanism.
**Depends on:** 10.28, 10.29, 10.30

Task 10.29 converged the authorization branches correctly, but it moved two
things from *corner case* to *common case*, and neither was sized for that.

**Held-row explanation is now the normal outcome, not an edge.** An imported
colleague's observation cannot reach the server until that colleague is on the
project, and in Phase 10 nobody can be. So every shared observation saved from
a `TT1:` payload is now held. 10.28 keeps and counts these correctly — the
gap is wording. A user seeing a generic refusal on the common path will read
it as a bug.

- The message must name the actual condition in plain language: waiting until
  that person joins this project, not "unauthorized" or "refused."
- It must be clear the record is **safe and kept**, not lost — that is the
  single most important thing this screen says, given the data involved.
- Sits with 10.12's three-state distinction (offline / refused / broken); this
  is the refused state's dominant instance.
- **Also affects Phase 10's own promise.** "My data on all my devices" now has
  a documented exception: imported rows stay on the device that imported them.
  Record it as a stated limitation rather than letting it read as a bug, and
  note 11.2 as the closing task.

**The denial audit bound was sized for rare events.** 10.30 capped the denial
audit write to stop an attacker filling the disk, on the assumption that
denials were unusual. 10.29 made them routine.

- Check the bound does not now clip legitimate traffic. A cap that silently
  drops real denial records recreates C-5's silent-success shape.
- Re-weigh **D-4** (row-level denials still unaudited), filed as non-blocking
  when it was a corner. If most denials now flow through the unaudited path,
  that judgment no longer holds — say so explicitly either way.
- **Acceptance:** held-row copy names the condition and reassures the record
  is kept, verified on a device; the Phase 10 limitation is written down; the
  audit bound is re-derived against realistic denial volume with the reasoning
  recorded; D-4's non-blocking classification is re-confirmed or withdrawn.

**What was built.** `HeldRowReason.notPermitted.explanation`
(`lib/data/sync/sync_held_rows.dart`) was reworded from "The server will not
accept this record..." — accurate, but shaped like a rejection — to lead with
"This record is safe on this device and nothing has been lost" and name the
actual condition: it is waiting because it names a person, or uses a tag, that
is not yet part of this project, and it resolves once whoever owns the project
adds them. `SyncStatusScreen`'s `_HeldRowsSection` (heading "Waiting to sync",
was "Not synced to the server") and the status card's held-count line got the
same treatment, kept short and distinct from the per-row explanation to avoid
restating it. `sync_status_screen_test.dart` was updated to the new copy — one
of the two failures it caught doing so was real: the first, longer draft of
the section subtitle pushed the "Try again" button below the test viewport's
fold, which is exactly the "held row nobody can reach" bug shape 10.28 already
fixed once for the retry wiring itself. Trimmed back down; both tests pass.
Full client suite (751+ tests) green.

**Phase 10's own promise, written down as a limitation.**
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.17 now states explicitly, next to the decision
that produces it: "my data on all my devices" has a real exception in Phase
10 — an imported colleague's shared observation stays on the device that
imported it until that colleague is a project member, which nothing in Phase
10 lets them become — and names task 11.2 as the closing task, per the
existing "Accepted cost" paragraph it sits beside.

**Audit bound re-derived, not changed.** Traced `auditDenial`'s three call
sites (`sync_routes.dart:199, 487, 551`) and confirmed they are all
project-level `403`s — a caller with *no* relationship to the project at all.
10.29's row-level `unauthorized` outcome never reaches `auditDenial` (that is
D-4's own complaint); its only server-side trace is the fixed-width
`rows_rejected` integer on `sync_traffic_log`. So 10.29 did not raise the
volume the one-year auth log's `maxAuditFieldLength` bound was sized against —
importing an unlinked colleague still requires the *caller* to be a real
project member, only the *named* person or tag is outside it. 10.30's bound
holds unchanged. Reasoning recorded in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.7.

**D-4 re-weighed: non-blocking confirmed, priority and fix shape both
changed.** No new disclosure risk — D-1 already made the row-level probe teach
an attacker nothing regardless of whether it's audited, which is what actually
settles the "probe indefinitely" half of B5's original complaint. But the
console gap now hides the single most common authorization outcome the server
produces in ordinary operation, not just attack traffic, which raises the
operational cost of leaving it unfixed. And whoever implements it must budget
for volume from the first commit: unlike the project-level channel (rare by
construction — it needs a caller with zero project relationship), the
row-level channel has no such rarity to lean on, so an append-only event per
denial would recreate D-2's growth curve without an attacker required to
trigger it. Recommended default: aggregate one row per held identity, updated
on repeat refusal, the same shape `SyncHeldRowStore` already uses client-side.
Full reasoning in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §8.4, D-4.

**Not done: live device verification.** The acceptance criterion calls for
verifying the held-row copy on a device rather than only in a test. Producing
a genuine server-refused row end-to-end needs a running server, a published
project, and a second identity the project doesn't reach — feasible with this
repo's `docker-compose.yml` and the app's own import flow, but driving the
macOS/iOS UI through that flow needs interactive GUI control this session did
not have available. What *was* verified is the exact rendered widget tree
(`sync_status_screen_test.dart`), which is strong enough to catch layout
regressions (see above) but not strong enough to claim "verified on a device."
Filed under Discovered Scope below so it isn't silently dropped; folding it
into 10.25's next device checklist, alongside D-3's own still-open "real
server, real phone" item, is the natural place for it.

### Task 10.35 — Project-scoped primary keys (schemaMajor)
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13) — **decision: proceed.**
**Model:** **Opus** — a breaking schema change touching every table's identity.
**Depends on:** 10.29

D-1's arm (c) residual: create-if-absent on client-chosen primary keys lets a
caller learn whether a row id exists by attempting to claim it. 10.29 bounded
it and stated it as a property of every table; the real close is
project-scoped keys.

**This is a `schemaMajor` bump under 10.18's rules**, which means every device
in the field is refused until it updates. That cost is **near zero today** —
nothing is deployed — and permanent afterwards. The decision is therefore not
"is this worth fixing" but "if ever, then now."

- Decide first, and record the decision either way in
  `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`. Declining is a legitimate answer; leaving it
  undecided until after release is not.
- If proceeding: this is the schema bump to bundle any other breaking change
  into, since you only get one cheaply.
- Migration must carry existing data forward (see `migrations.dart`); the
  local database and every existing backup archive have to remain readable.
- **Acceptance:** the oracle is closed rather than bounded; existing local
  data and backup archives migrate without loss; the major-version refusal
  path from 10.18 is exercised deliberately at least once, since this is the
  first real use of it.

**Decision: proceed — and the deciding argument was not the oracle.** Recorded
in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.13. The oracle was genuinely bounded, and on
its own would not have justified a major bump under §4.16 rule 3. What settled
it is that the same global-key assumption was a **silent permanent data loss in
an ordinary intended workflow** — asset 2, and the same shape as D-3, which had
already been paid for once:

- Phase 6.3's replicas keep the sender's `observation_id`, and the `TT1:`
  payload carries **no project id**, so the importer always writes into its own
  current project. **Cross-project is the default for shared observations, not
  the exception** — landing in the same project requires both devices to hold
  the identical `project_id`, which only publish/join produces.
- The server looked the key up globally, found the original in the source
  project, and refused with `crossProjectCapture` — check 2 of 6 in
  `authorizeWrite`, returning before the replication exemption at check 6.
  **Task 11.2 could not have fixed it**: the denial never reads membership.
- The lockout is **symmetric and first-writer-wins**: if the receiver syncs
  first, the *original author's own field data* becomes permanently unsyncable.
- 10.34's held-row copy told the user "once whoever owns the project adds them,
  tap Try again" — a remedy that could never work for this denial.

**What was built.** `project_id` joined the primary key of the six
project-scoped data tables (`Project_Memberships`, `Triangulation_Sessions`,
`Observations`, `Non_Detections`, `Estimated_Positions`,
`Actual_Tag_Locations`). `Projects` keeps a bare key because its id *is* the
scope; `Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` are global and have no project column
to add. `Project_Tags` was already composite. `schemaMajorVersion` 1→2,
`latestSchemaVersion` 5→6.

**The id leads and the scope follows** — `(observation_id, project_id)`, not the
reverse. The leading key column is the one an index can be searched on alone,
and by-id lookup is the query this schema runs most; `project_id`-first would
turn every by-id repository read into a scan, and the reverse lookup is already
served by the `(project_id, server_seq)` indexes. Uniqueness is identical.

**The server needed no change to close the oracle.** `SyncService._findRow`
builds its predicate from `SyncTable.primaryKey`, so it became project-scoped
for free — which is also why `crossProjectCapture` is now unreachable. It was
**kept rather than deleted**, with its comment rewritten: it states the
invariant, and `_findRow` is generic enough that a future edit there could
reopen the hole silently.

**Migrations.** SQLite v6 rebuilds the six tables (v3's create-copy-drop-rename,
parent-first so `Observations` follows `Triangulation_Sessions`), and
`Observations` gains a **composite foreign key** `(session_id, project_id)` —
a single-column reference into a composite key is a foreign-key mismatch
Postgres rejects and SQLite reports at first write. `PRAGMA foreign_keys` moved
from `onConfigure` to `onOpen` so migrations run with enforcement off, which is
SQLite's own prescribed rebuild procedure; `runMigrations` now runs `PRAGMA
foreign_key_check` afterwards so that window cannot hide a violation. **The
server gained its first real migration** — `PostgresMigrations.run` previously
threw on any version beyond the bootstrap, with a note that the next schema
change would need one. `schemaV6Statements` is deliberately hardcoded rather
than derived from `tableSpecs`: a spec-derived migration silently becomes a
different migration the next time the specs move.

**No data moves, which is what made the archive decision available.**
`project_id` was already `NOT NULL` on all six tables, so every row's new key is
derived from what it already held. `SchemaMigrator` therefore **migrates a
major-1 archive forward instead of refusing it** — deliberately asymmetric with
the wire, which still refuses any major mismatch. The wire refusal exists
because two live peers must agree on a shape neither controls; reading an
archive is one-way and the reader knows strictly more. Refusing would have made
every backup written before the bump — including 10.19's default-on cloud
backups — unreadable, a larger loss than the bump was paid for.
`_lowestMigratableMajor` is an explicit constant so a future major that *cannot*
cross losslessly has to say so rather than inherit this.

**Client-only stores.** `Sync_Held_Rows`, `Sync_Row_Receipts` and
`Sync_Conflicts` store keys in the protocol's format and sit outside the
versioned schema, so no migration could reach them; `RowKeyMigration` rewrites
them from the `project_id` each already carries — a rename, not a
reconstruction. `Unknown_Columns` is purged instead, because it has no
`project_id` and its held values came from a peer this build can no longer talk
to at all. Idempotent by construction rather than gated on a flag.

**Repositories.** `BaseRepository.pk` became a `List<String>` and every helper
builds its `WHERE` from the whole key. Two latent bugs fell out of doing this
properly rather than minimally: `_authorize` under `MutationRule.projectOwner`
would have resolved *another project's* owner for a colliding id (a
privilege-escalation path, invisible in any call-site count because
`_authorize` is private), and `updateById` stripped only the id, so it would
have emitted `SET project_id = ?` on a key column. `ProjectTagRepository`
declared `pk: 'project_id'` — half a key, harmless while nothing read it, now
corrected. `SharedObservationImporter`'s two raw-SQL sites were the highest-risk
of all and no repository change reached them: its existence check and its
verbatim replica update both matched on `observation_id` alone, so a replica
could have compared against and overwritten a *different project's* row.

**Verification.**
- `scripts/verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py` now reports **arm (c) as an
  equivalence check that passes** rather than a bounded residual — all three
  arms indistinguishable against a live server over raw HTTP, with the victim's
  row still verified untouched. The script itself needed its envelope bumped to
  major 2, which is worth noting: any out-of-tree tool that speaks the wire is
  refused until updated.
- `test/data/schema_v6_migration_test.dart` — a v5 database built by running the
  real migrations, seeded across all six tables, upgraded, then checked
  column-for-column (not just "a row is there": `INSERT … SELECT *` is only
  correct while column order matches, and a mismatch shifts values rather than
  failing). Plus: FK integrity intact, the same id now coexisting in two
  projects, a duplicate *within* one project still conflicting, and the
  composite FK refusing an observation that references another project's
  session.
- **The major-refusal path, exercised deliberately against a real server** —
  `schema_compatibility_e2e_test.dart` gained a test pinning major **1** as a
  literal rather than `schemaMajorVersion - 1`, so a second bump cannot silently
  retarget it, and one asserting a refused major-1 push writes nothing (the
  refusal has to be ahead of the write, not merely reported after it).
- Suites: 764 client, 357 server in Docker, 119 shared package, **28 e2e green
  in a single pass** against a live server.

**Two tests were asserting bugs as correct behaviour, and both were inverted.**
This is the part worth reading:

- `identity_round_trip_test.dart`'s "two devices independently saving one shared
  observation converge to a single row" merged Bob's and Carol's **separate
  projects** and asserted `hasLength(1)`. Under global keys the second merge
  overwrote the first, so **one of the two projects silently lost its
  observation entirely** — and the assertion never checked which `project_id`
  survived, so the loss was invisible to it. Split into two tests: different
  projects keep one row each, and a new same-project case covers the real Phase
  6 convergence guarantee, which is the only scope in which convergence means
  anything.
- `authorization_test.dart`'s "project C's own row cannot be captured by
  relabelling it into project A" was byte-for-byte the benign replica push — one
  user, two projects they legitimately write to, one shared id — labelled as a
  capture control. The passing test *was* the bug. Both it and its sibling now
  assert the insert succeeds **and** the other project's row is untouched, which
  is the real invariant and is now structural rather than checked.

**Guard added for the hazard this task kept hitting.** `RowValidator` hand-copies
the primary keys rather than importing `syncTables`, and nothing asserted the
two agreed; `tableSpecs` and `syncTables` were likewise two independent
declarations of one fact. Both are now pinned to each other by tests, along with
"a primary key column is never nullable" — the property that made this migration
a pure re-key with nothing to backfill.

### Task 10.36 — Schema-version marker on encrypted backups
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13)
**Model:** Sonnet — a header field and a read path.
**Depends on:** 10.24, 10.35

Encrypted server backups carry no schema-version marker, so an operator cannot
tell which schema major an archive holds before committing to a restore.

Filed by 10.35, and **10.35 is what made it real**: that was the first major
bump, so from now on an archive can be from either side of a boundary the wire
refuses to cross. It fails loudly rather than corrupting, so this is not a
loss risk — but "restore is guesswork" undercuts 10.19 and 10.24, which exist
precisely so an irreplaceable dataset can be recovered under pressure.

- Record `schemaMajor` (and minor) in the archive header, readable **without
  decrypting the payload** — an operator choosing between archives shouldn't
  need the key just to see what's in them.
- On restore, refuse a major this build cannot read, naming both versions —
  the same which-side-is-behind reporting 10.11 established for the wire.
- Mind 10.35's asymmetry: the wire refuses any mismatch, but `SchemaMigrator`
  may carry an older major forward where the crossing is lossless. Honour
  `_lowestMigratableMajor` rather than duplicating the rule.
- Existing archives predate the marker — treat a missing marker as the last
  major before this task, not as unknown-and-refuse, or you strand every
  backup taken so far.
- **Acceptance:** an archive's schema version is readable without the
  decryption key; restoring an unreadable major refuses and names both
  versions; a pre-marker archive still restores; a round trip across a major
  boundary is proven end to end, because an untested restore is not a backup.

**Implementation.** `server/backup/backup.sh` queries `schema_migrations` for
the max applied minor version, maps it to a major via a threshold mirroring
`schema_constants.dart` (major 2 begins at v6, per 10.35), and writes a plain
`<archive>.schema` sidecar (`schema_major=`/`schema_version=`) beside the
`.age` file — untouched by encryption, so `cat` reads it. `server/backup/
restore.sh` reads the sidecar before touching the key; a missing sidecar
defaults to major 1 (`_lowestMigratableMajor`'s value, "the last major before
this task"); a major outside `[1, schemaMajorVersion]` refuses, naming both
the archive's major and the build's supported range. Retention now prunes the
sidecar alongside its archive and checksum.

`scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh` gained three checks (now 11 total, run
2026-08-13): the sidecar is readable and correct without the key (5b), a
copy of the real archive with its sidecar removed still restores as major 1
(7b), and a copy with a forged `schema_major=99` sidecar refuses, naming both
99 and the supported range (7c). `server/README.md` documents the sidecar and
records the drill run.
### Task 10.37 — G-3: the restore path destroys data and does not restore
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13)
**Model:** **Opus** — a failed restore is a durability failure, not a script bug.
**Depends on:** 10.24, 10.36. **Do this first.**

`scripts/verify_e3_restore_replace.sh` dropped a live database holding the
**only copy of an observation**, then failed to decrypt the archive. Recorded
as must-fix before the last gate and never given a task — that omission is
itself addressed in 10.40.

Two separate failures, and the second is the serious one:

- **The script destroys before verifying.** Nothing may drop a live database
  until the replacement archive has been decrypted, read, and confirmed to
  contain what it claims. Verify, then swap — never swap, then hope.
- **The archive would not decrypt.** Encrypted backups that cannot be restored
  are not backups. Everything 10.19 and 10.24 promise rests on this working,
  and it demonstrably did not. Find the actual cause; do not paper over it by
  making the script more careful.
- **Acceptance:** a restore drill runs end to end on a database holding real
  data and that data survives regardless of outcome; an archive that cannot be
  decrypted is detected **before** anything destructive happens; the decryption
  failure's root cause is identified and fixed, with a test that fails if it
  returns; the drill is re-runnable so it can be repeated at every future gate.

**Correction to this entry's second bullet.** The archive at the gate did not
fail to decrypt because of a defect in the backup pipeline. It failed because
`verify_e3_restore_replace.sh` had deliberately truncated it (12656 of 37969
bytes) to manufacture an unreadable archive — `age` refusing a truncated
STREAM is the correct behaviour, and §9.4's own wording is precise about this
("destroys live data *before it knows* the archive can be decrypted"). Verified
before changing anything: a good archive decrypts and restores cleanly on both
the fresh-name and in-place paths, canary intact. **Encrypted backups do
decrypt.** So there is no separate "backups are not backups" defect to root
cause, and inventing one would have been the paper-over.

The real defect underneath, and the actual answer to "how did an unreadable
archive reach a `DROP DATABASE`": **the integrity check lived on the wrong
path.** `backup.sh` has always written a `.sha256`, and the only thing that
verified it was `scripts/restore_db.sh` — the wrapper that *cannot* perform an
in-place replace, because it never sets `TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE`. The single
path capable of destroying live data was the single path with no integrity
check on the archive it was trusting, and `server/README.md` credited the check
anyway. Same shape as §8.4's `TRITRACK_ENV` comment: a control described in
prose that is not on the path being described.

**Implementation.** `server/backup/restore.sh` is restructured around one
invariant — nothing destructive happens until the archive has been read.
Pre-flight now verifies the recorded checksum (moved onto this path, a note
rather than a refusal when absent), then the schema sidecar, then decrypts the
**whole** stream and requires pg_dump's own `-- PostgreSQL database dump` /
`… complete` markers, which proves the plaintext reached its end independently
of age's framing. The restore then lands in a `<target>_restore_<stamp>`
database under `--single-transaction`, and only a restore that produced tables
reaches the swap. The swap **renames** the existing database to
`<target>_replaced_<stamp>` rather than dropping it, and rolls that rename back
if promotion fails; the displaced copy is left for the operator to drop by hand.
Taking over a name needs the server stopped (Postgres will not rename a
database with sessions attached), which is checked up front rather than after a
full decrypt. Derived names are length-guarded against Postgres's 63-byte
identifier truncation, and the target name is restricted to `[A-Za-z0-9_]`
since two more names are derived from it.

`scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh` gained steps 7d–7g, which are the first
thing in the repo ever to type `TRITRACK_RESTORE_REPLACE=I_UNDERSTAND`: with
the server stopped and the live database holding the only copy of the seeded
observation, a checksum-mismatched archive, a truncated one and a wrong-key one
must each leave it untouched, and a good archive must still replace in place
with the displaced database preserved. Step 6 was also strengthened — it
accepted any non-zero exit as "the wrong key was refused", so a missing archive
or an unmountable key would have passed it. The drill now prints its own check
count (20, run 2026-08-13) instead of trusting a number in the README, which
had already drifted twice.

`test/security/restore_ordering_test.dart` is the cheap half that runs without
Docker on every checkout: it reads `restore.sh` structurally and fails if the
decrypt verification moves after the swap, if anything but the staging database
is dropped, if `--single-transaction` or the checksum check disappears, or if
the drill stops exercising the replace path. Both regressions were
mutation-tested — reintroducing G-3's `DROP` and deleting the verify block each
turn it red. `scripts/verify_e3_restore_replace.sh` is removed: it was written
to *fail* once the bug was fixed, and its cases now live in the drill, which is
the re-runnable instrument the gate should use.

### Task 10.38 — G-2: compose still renders the public port
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13)
**Model:** Sonnet — the fix is known and was tested.
**Depends on:** 10.32

Compose **merges** `ports:` rather than replacing it, so with the LAN opt-in
taken, the base file's `0.0.0.0:8080` still renders beside 10.32's loopback
mapping. The stack currently fails to start rather than exposing — that is
Docker's bind ordering, not a control, and the obvious repair leads straight
back to C-3.

- `ports: !override` was verified working during the gate and deliberately
  reverted so the gate wasn't grading its own fix. Re-apply it.
- **Then check every other compose key that merges rather than replaces** —
  this class of mistake is not unique to `ports`.
- **Acceptance:** no documented sequence renders a non-loopback binding; the
  stack starts cleanly with and without the LAN opt-in; verified by inspecting
  the merged config, not the source files.

### Task 10.39 — G-1: the e2e suite passes by skipping
**Status:** Done (2026-08-13)
**Model:** Sonnet — 10.31's guard, applied to the suite it missed.
**Depends on:** 10.31

`flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` with no environment set prints "All tests
skipped" and exits 0. That is E-1's exact shape on **the one suite that

- Apply the same rule: a suite that cannot run must fail loudly, not report

- Assert the expected test count so a future silent drop breaks the build.
- Fourth instance of this pattern in Phase 10. The standing rule 10.31 added

- **Acceptance:** an unconfigured e2e run exits non-zero with a clear reason;
  a configured run still passes in one pass; the count assertion catches a
  deliberately removed test.

**Closed.** Added `test/e2e/e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart`, mirroring
`server/test/support/database_coverage_guard_test.dart`'s shape exactly: one
test that `fail()`s (never skips) when `E2eEnv.isConfigured` is false, tagged
`@Tags(['e2e'])` so it actually runs under `--tags e2e` instead of being
filtered out like the guarded groups. A second test in the same file counts

`_expectedE2eTestFileCount` (8), so a deliberately or accidentally removed
file breaks the build instead of just lowering the skip count silently.
Verified: `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` with no environment set now
exits 1 ("Some tests failed") instead of 0. A configured run against a live
server was not re-verified here (no server was brought up in this session);
the guard test itself only inspects `E2eEnv.isConfigured` and the file
