#### From task 10.62 — the brief's premise was false (2026-08-16)

**The task file said "10.52's fix is correct and holds behind the proxy — the
gate confirmed it." Measured directly, it does not hold for the callers the
README is about.** The gate confirmed that forged `X-Forwarded-For` headers do
not reach the origin. That is a different claim from "the proxy resolves distinct
callers distinctly," and the second one is false wherever the host's publish path
rewrites source addresses. Evidence, on this host (macOS, Docker Desktop 29.6.2),
through the real `header_up X-Forwarded-For {remote_host}` directive:

```
direct        (published port)            remote=192.168.65.1  x3 callers
proxied       (Caddy, published port)     xff=192.168.65.1     x3 callers
proxied-onnet (Caddy, on compose network) xff=172.31.246.60 / .61
```

`verify_i1_source_identity.sh` only ever exercises the third line — its client
containers sit on the compose network and reach Caddy directly, crossing no
publish path. So J-2's own remediation reproduces J-2's structure one layer out:
a control verified in the configuration the instrument could reach, then
described as verified generally. Recorded in §4.4.2's verdict table and at the
end of §12.4 rather than folded in silently.

- **Open, and it needs its own task: source identity through the TLS overlay's
  own publish path.** Not closed here because the server cannot see its proxy's
  publish path, and refusing on a guess is the guess §4.4.1 says not to make.
  The honest options are (a) document `docker-compose.tls.yml` as a Linux-host
  deployment and make the probe a required pre-flight step with a recorded
  verdict, or (b) find a proxy arrangement that preserves identity across a
  Docker Desktop publish path — my measurement says there isn't one, so (a) is
  probably the answer, but that should be decided rather than inherited.
  **`verify_i1_source_identity.sh` should also grow the off-host caller case**,
  so the instrument stops implying a coverage it does not have.
- **10.66's rule, applied here, is what found it.** The class is "a control
  whose correctness depends on an unmeasured property of the host" — §11.0's own
  sentence, quoted in §12.4 and never turned into a check. Sites enumerated with
  a verdict each: rate-limit keying (this task); `auditValue`'s
  `source_address` (same collapse, same fix — the shape is refused); the
  diagnostics console's loopback gate (**verified unaffected** — it reads the raw
  TCP peer, and the publish path rewrites to a bridge gateway rather than to
  loopback, so it stays closed; `verify_i1` step 4 remains its guard);
  `assertExposureIsPrivate` (**partially improved** — `TRITRACK_PUBLISH_ADDRESS`
  now closes for source identity the same blind spot §4.1 documents for
  exposure, and §4.1 could use it too, which is a small follow-up worth doing).
- **The escape-hatch comment is now linked rather than merely accurate.**
  `rate_limiter.dart`'s justification for `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED`
  described this exact collapse and drew "so the e2e suite needs a hatch" from
  it. It now says, in the same comment, that the paragraph above it is a
  security finding. `server/README.md`'s copy of the same paragraph got the same
  treatment. **Worth generalising into 10.66's rule: a comment that explains why
  a control cannot work in some configuration is a finding about that
  configuration, and should be required to name it.**
- **Stale docs fixed in passing** (found by 10.62's exploration, all in
  `server/README.md`): the rate-limit table omitted `GET /auth/link-status/<id>`
  (30/min, added by 10.56); "those two rules" said two where the flag now raises
  three; and the prose still referenced `peerAddressOf`, the accessor 10.52
  deleted as finding I-1.

#### From task 10.61 — the rest of the untrusted-import class (2026-08-16)

10.61 wrote §4.19 (what an untrusted import may do to a record this device
already holds) and closed J-1 against the share-payload path. Per 10.66's rule
the same five questions were then asked of **every** path in the app where
external data is parsed into a row; §4.19.1 is the table. Two answers needed no
work — tag CSV import is already safe (validated, identity re-stamped locally),
and **there are no deep-link, URL-scheme, file-open or share-extension handlers
at all**, verified across the three platform manifests and `pubspec.yaml`.
One was fixed inside 10.61 because it is the same pasted string on the same
screen: `_createTag` wrote a `Tag` from payload-supplied frequency and pulse
rate with no `RowValidator`, which the strictly-less-exposed CSV path has had
since Phase 4.

Three remain open. None is a variant of J-1 to be patched by analogy — each
needs §4.19's questions answered on its own terms.

- **Client backup restore (`ProjectMerger` ← a picked `.zip`) is the widest
  instance of this class.** It can update rows in *every* table; it takes
  `user_id`, `owner_user_id`, `last_modified_by`, `revision` and `updated_at`
  verbatim from the file; `MergeStrategy.preferIncoming` is offered in the
  import UI and makes the file win regardless of clock; `RowValidator` is an
  opt-out parameter (`merge({bool validate = true})`) rather than an invariant;
  and no prior version is captured. It differs from J-1 in *exposure*, not in
  shape — a restore is a deliberate whole-project act on a file the user chose,
  not a casual paste — which is the only reason it was not folded in here.
  Deserves its own task, and should decide explicitly whether `preferIncoming`
  survives §4.19 clause 4 at all.
- **`ServerIdentityAdopter` runs no `RowValidator` and hard-`DELETE`s.** On a
  server-supplied `user_id` it rewrites the user columns of every table and
  deletes superseded `Users` rows, constrained only by the redemption-time
  email equality check. Clause 5 does not reach it and clause 4 was never asked.
- **`UnknownColumnStore.promote` writes held values into real columns on a
  later upgrade**, after the validation opportunity has passed — raw SQL, no
  repository, no validation, and it updates existing rows.

Also from 10.61, and deliberately *not* done there:

- **Share payloads are unauthenticated, and §4.19 says so rather than implying
  otherwise.** Clause 2's author check resolves the observer by email, so a
  forger who knows the victim's address and an `observation_id` can still
  present as the author; what stops harm is then clauses 1, 4 and 5 —
  visibility and recoverability, not prevention. Closing the residual means
  signing payloads with a key the sender holds and the receiver trusts, which
  is Phase 11 identity work and not a patch to the importer.
- **`MutationAuthorization`'s docstring is now out of date in a way worth
  fixing.** It names `ProjectMerger` and `SharedObservationImporter` as the two
  documented replication bypasses; the sweep found `ServerIdentityAdopter` and
  `UnknownColumnStore.promote` also write raw SQL outside `BaseRepository`, and
  every path that can update or delete an existing row bypasses the rule table
  entirely. The comment reads as an exhaustive list and is not one.

#### BLOCKING — Security Gate C, fifth re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-15)

Full evidence in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §12. Both new blocking findings
are the same failure twice: **a fix correct for the configuration it was written
against, in a project that ships two configurations.**

- **J-1 — a pasted `TT1:` share payload silently overwrites an existing
  observation and destroys the bearing reconstruction (§12.2).** Reproduced end
  to end against a real database. `SharedObservationImporter._upsertReplica`
  (`lib/data/sharing/shared_observation_importer.dart:190-235`) updates **every
  non-key column** when the incoming clock wins, and the replica is built from
  only the ~20 fields the wire format carries — so `magnetic_bearing_start/end`,
  `true_north_bearing_start/end`, `magnetic_declination`, `wmm_model_version`,
  `bearing_capture_method`, `bearing_method`, `antenna_type`, `receiver_gain`
  and `altitude_agl` are written `NULL` over live data. The merge clock is
  attacker-chosen (`revision` any `int >= 0`, `updated_at` unbounded —
  `observation_share.dart:370-381`), so winning is free. `user_id` becomes the
  attacker's, `last_modified_by` becomes whatever the payload says, and an
  attacker-chosen `Users` row is inserted as a side effect (`:301-313`). The
  app reports *"You already had this observation — updated it to the newer
  version."* No authorization runs (documented repository bypass,
  `mutation_authorization.dart:34-45`) and `RowValidator` never runs on this
  path — the only write path in the app that skips it.
  **This is live for users of the app as shipped, independent of any server, and
  it is silent loss of irreplaceable field data.** Needs: a bound on the payload
  clock; a merge that cannot null columns the payload does not carry; the
  refusal surfaced honestly rather than as "updated"; `RowValidator` on this
  path; and a decision about whether an unauthenticated string may create a
  `Users` row at all. The §12.2 reproduction should land as a regression test.
  **Model: Opus** — data-loss path plus a trust decision.

- **J-2 — I-1 is still live in the base/LAN deployment (§12.4).** 10.52 closed
  it behind the proxy; `README.md`'s LAN walkthrough has no proxy, so there is
  no header for §4.4.1's scheme to read and `TrustedProxies.fromEnvironment`
  does not refuse (that deployment is not `TRITRACK_ENV=production`).
  Reproduced: two genuinely distinct callers recorded **one** `source_address`
  (`192.168.65.1`), and twelve requests from one returned `429` to an unrelated
  caller. **`RequestSource.direct` is assumed distinguishing unconditionally**
  (`request_identity.dart:111-114`), so 10.52's fail-safe — suspend the
  per-source rule when the key cannot tell callers apart — cannot fire in the
  one case where the server has not been told. The collapse is described
  accurately in `rate_limiter.dart:62-79` as the justification for the e2e
  escape hatch. Severity is host-dependent (Docker Desktop rewrites the source;
  Linux DNAT usually does not) and **nothing in the deployment measures which
  case it is in** — that is the finding as much as the collapse is. Needs either
  a way for the server to detect a degenerate `direct` key, or a documented,
  measured deployment posture for the LAN walkthrough. **Model: Opus** — same
  decision surface as 10.52.

- **The NAU information-security review — carried ×5.** Unchanged, unsent,
  recipient blank. Not an engineering item. The residual-risk summary it points
  at is now §12.9 and the cover note needs that one-line repoint.

#### Non-blocking, from the fifth re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-15)

- **J-3 — the server's own database connection is a Postgres superuser
  (§12.5).** Demonstrated live: `COPY … FROM PROGRAM 'id; hostname'` ran as
  `uid=70(postgres)` on the database container, from the credentials the
  network-facing process holds. The same role can `DELETE FROM auth_audit_log`,
  so C-5's forensic record is erasable by whatever compromises the process that
  writes it. Task 10.59 closed exactly this on the once-a-year restore path with
  a `NOSUPERUSER` role and a correct explanation of why `NOSUPERUSER` and not a
  `GRANT` is what removes the capability — the same reasoning, unapplied to the
  connection that is open all day. Not reachable today (static identifiers,
  bound parameters, unknown tables never reach SQL), so rated as I-10 was, and
  it should get I-10's treatment: a restricted role for the server's own
  connection. **Model: Sonnet.**

- **J-4 — untyped `500`s on attacker-typed input (§12.6).** From any account:
  `/sync/pull` with `cursor` as a string, float, object or bool → `500`; same
  for `batch_size`; a NUL byte in `device_id` or `project_id` on `/sync/push` →
  `500`. `schema_major: "2"` correctly answers `400 malformed_envelope`, which
  is 10.46's fix working on the one field H-4 named. This is H-4's class on the
  fields beside it, on a route 10.56 said it had swept. Low severity (no write,
  no growth, transaction rolls back); it matters as evidence about the sweep.
  Bound and type-check the whole envelope from one place, not field by field.
  **Model: Sonnet.**

- **J-5 — a non-Map row entry inside a *known* table vanishes (§12.6).**
  `{"rows": {"Observations": ["hello", 1, null]}}` answers `200`, `applied: 0`,
  `outcomes: {}`. 10.46 fixed this silence for unknown table *names* and left
  the per-row case, so the `invalid` outcome the protocol defines is still
  emitted by nothing. Harm is bounded on the client by 10.28's rule 2 (silence
  on an offered row is a refusal and is held) — that design working against a
  defect nobody had found. **Model: Sonnet.**

- **J-6 — three instrument defects, each demonstrated (§12.7).**
  (a) `verify_tls_termination.sh:189-192` **cannot fail**: `PUBLISHED="$(… ||
  true)"` discards the return code and empty output passes — shown against a
  project that is not up and against a nonexistent compose file, both printing
  nothing while the step reports "the proxy is the only way in." This is `Cf`'s
  defect **reintroduced by 10.54 in the very step it rewrote to fix a different
  defect in the same check.**
  (b) `gate_smoke_test.sh`'s self-test **cannot detect a missing instrument** —
  it asks whether each instrument that ran is in `WIRE_INSTRUMENTS`, never
  whether each `WIRE_INSTRUMENT` ran. Demonstrated with the loop lifted verbatim
  and `verify_h3` absent: prints `SELFTEST PASSED`. `verify_h3` being absent is
  precisely the omission §11.5 reported and 10.54 was written to fix; it added
  the name and not the check. (`:188` also still says "all five" for a list of
  seven.)
  (c) `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py` now honestly SKIPs and prints "C-3 is
  NOT confirmed closed by this run" — §10.7.1's finding is genuinely fixed — but
  **still exits 0**, which is the only thing any harness reads.
  **Model: Sonnet.**

- **Add the forged-header arm to `verify_i1_source_identity.sh` (§12.3).** The
  drill attacks with honest clients only; the gate had to write its own probe to
  measure the assumption the whole trusted-proxy scheme rests on. It held —
  five forged `X-Forwarded-For` variants through the shipped Caddy reached the
  origin as nothing, and rotating forged addresses did not lift a `429` — and
  that result should be a committed control rather than a one-off gate run.
  **Model: Sonnet.**

- **A standing practice, not a task (§12.11).** Six recorded instances now of
  fixing a finding where it was reproduced and writing the sentence as though
  the class had been closed (§9.5 `User_Emails`, §10.7 `Tags`, §11.5 the
  instrument sweep, J-4's typed fields, J-6's self-test, J-2's second
  deployment). Worth adopting explicitly: **when a finding is fixed, the
  acceptance criterion names the other places the same shape could be, and the
  instrument measures one of them.**
#### BLOCKING — Security Gate C, fourth re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-15)

***These block any exposure beyond localhost.** The ten scheduled remediations
(10.41–10.50) all landed and nine hold — H-1, H-2, H-4, H-5, H-6's refusal,
F13, ATS and TLS termination are closed and re-verified live, and the
adversarial pass found no new failures. These are what the fourth re-run found
instead. Full evidence is `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` **§11**. Each needs its
own task, and the gate has to be run a fifth time once they are closed.*

- **I-1 — §4.4's per-source rate limit is a single global bucket, and every
  audit row records one constant source address (§11.3).** **Reproduced live in
  both the shipped `docker compose` and the mandated TLS/Caddy deployment.**
  Ten unauthenticated magic-link requests exhaust the per-source budget and
  **deny sign-in to every user of the deployment** for 15 minutes (60 sustains
  it for an hour); the eleventh attacker request and an unrelated innocent
  user's request both answer `429`. All events recorded `source_address` =
  `172.19.0.1` (base) / `172.20.0.4` (behind Caddy) — the Docker gateway and
  the proxy container. C-5's whole forensic contribution goes with it: 158
  events in the gate database, one distinct source address between them.
  - **The design decision comes first, and it is Opus's.** The 2026-08-07
    filing from 10.14 already framed it: either **refuse `/diagnostics/*` at
    the proxy and record the rate-limit merge as accepted**, or **introduce a
    trusted-proxy header** with all the care that needs. 10.49 shipped the
    proxy and made neither choice. Note the server's refusal to read
    `X-Forwarded-For` (`request_identity.dart:26-31`) is **correct and must
    stay** as an unconditional rule — any trusted-proxy scheme has to be an
    explicit allowlist of proxy peer addresses, not a header read.
  - Whichever way it goes, **the per-source limiter must be observed working in
    a stack the gate attacks.** It never has been (see I-3 below).
  - Consider a per-email-only fallback that fails safe when the source key is
    known-degenerate, so a collapsed key cannot become a global lockout.
  - **Acceptance:** with the TLS overlay up, ten requests from one source do
    not refuse an unrelated address; audit rows carry distinguishable sources
    or the merge is explicitly recorded as accepted in §4.4 with the DoS
    consequence named.
  - **Model:** **Opus** for the trusted-proxy decision, then Sonnet for wiring.
  - **Note the diagnostics console fails *closed* here** — Caddy reaches the
    origin from a bridge address, not `127.0.0.1`, so the loopback gate still
    refuses. Verified, not assumed. Do not "fix" that in passing.

- **I-2 — H-7 is not closed: backup retention authenticates bytes, not names
  (§11.4).** **Reproduced live on the current build with signing and verifying
  keys fully configured.** 10.44's structure is sound — `backup.sh:250-263`
  refuses to prune unless every archive verifies — but a minisign signature
  covers contents, not filenames. Thirty copies of **one genuine `(archive,
  .minisig)` pair** renamed to dates in 2999 all verify, no `RETENTION
  REFUSED` is printed, and the next legitimate backup run **deleted both real
  archives**, leaving 30 planted copies of one stale snapshot — every one of
  them valid, signed and restorable, so a later restore succeeds and silently
  rolls the database back.
  - **The fix is already latent in the data.** `backup.sh:197` writes
    `archive=<basename>` into the signed trusted comment and retention never
    reads it back. Require the signed comment's `archive=` to equal the actual
    basename, and a renamed copy stops verifying.
  - The attacker is write access to the archive directory **plus one genuine
    pair** — a narrowing of H-7's write-only attacker, and an exact description
    of the off-site copy destination §4.9 chose to trust with ciphertext.
  - `backup_restore_drill.sh` plants only an **unsigned** file, so this variant
    is untested. Add the renamed-genuine-copy case.
  - **Acceptance:** 30 renamed genuine copies cause a loud refusal and no
    deletion; ordinary retention still prunes oldest-first; the drill covers it.
  - **Model:** Sonnet — the predicate is one comparison.

- **I-3 — the gate has never observed the per-source limiter working, and the
  control that claims otherwise is vacuous.** `docker-compose.e2e.yml:24` sets
  `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED=1`, and every adversarial pass runs
  against that stack. `Cf` (`gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:473-476`) is a negative
  substring test over `docker compose config` **stdout whose return code is
  never checked** — demonstrated to report HELD with a non-existent compose
  file (`returncode=1`, empty stdout). This is why I-1 survived four gates.
  - Fix `Cf` to check the return code and to assert the limiter's **behaviour**
    against a stack where it is enabled, not the absence of a string.
  - **Blocking** because it is the measurement failure that hid a blocking
    finding, not merely a weak assertion. **Model:** Sonnet.

- **The NAU information-security review — carried ×4, blocking, and the only
  item on this gate engineering cannot close.** The residual-risk summary is
  written and current: **§11.10**, superseding §7.7, plain-language and
  self-contained. `NAU_infosec_review_request.md` is revised for the third time
  and is accurate as of this gate — the two items it previously listed as open
  (client cleartext enforcement, ATS on hardware) are now closed, and it now
  asks specifically about the two new findings and about the cloud-backup
  default. **What remains is a human sending an email**: find the address for
  NAU's Information Security Office, attach §11.10, send. Roughly twenty
  minutes. Two gates have now revised this letter without being able to send
  it.

#### Non-blocking, from the fourth re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-15)

- **I-4 — a latent identity-forgery path that Phase 11 will arm (§11.8).** The
  server never compares a pushed `Users.email` to the authenticated account's
  address; **live, an attacker's push claiming another user's email returned
  `200 'updated'`**. The client merger then treats a matching current email as
  proof of identity — `project_merger.dart:184-190`, *"tier 1 always wins
  outright"* — and `_applyUserRemap` rewrites `user_id`, `owner_user_id` and
  `last_modified_by` on every row of the page. That is C-1's harm exactly
  (an attacker's observations attributed to a colleague), through the email
  column instead of the id column. **Not reachable today** — cross-user project
  membership does not exist in Phase 10, so the row is never delivered, and a
  self-granted membership is still refused. **Phase 11's stated purpose is to
  open that door.** Fix server-side before then: refuse a `Users.email` that
  does not match the authenticated account, or that another `user_id` holds.
  **This must be a precondition on Phase 11, not a Phase 11 task.**
- **I-5 — an oversized `device_id` answers `500` (§11.8).** 2 MB `device_id` on
  `/sync/push` → `internal_error`. Nothing landed in `sync_traffic_log`
  (widest stored value 26 chars), so this is *not* an unbounded-growth vector —
  but it is H-4's class on a field 10.46's envelope sweep did not cover.
  `/sync/ack` bounds it; push and pull do not.
- **I-6 — `/auth/link-status/<id>` is unauthenticated and rate-limited by
  nothing.** 60 requests, 60 × `200`, no `429`, no audit row. §3.1 claims rate
  limits on the unauthenticated routes; this is one and has none.
- **I-7 — the committed secrets test scans the working tree, not history.**
  Every check in `no_committed_secrets_test.dart` runs over `git ls-files`
  (`:35`). The gate criterion is the whole history; the gate does that by hand
  each round (clean again, 107 commits), but nothing between gates would catch
  a secret committed and later removed.
- **I-8 — profile builds still permit cleartext.** §3.4 and §4.1 both say
  "a debug build"; the code says `kReleaseMode`
  (`server_config_provider.dart:105,114,151`), and profile is neither. F13 is
  genuinely closed for release and at the seam; the gap is the
  internal-distribution build. One-word fix: gate on `!kDebugMode`.
- **I-9 — `docker-compose.server-test.yml` re-renders the base publish
  mapping.** With `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` the merged config renders
  `server: 0.0.0.0:8080:8080` — G-2's shape in the third compose file, and the
  one instance 10.47's sweep did not tag. Latent only: the harness starts
  `postgres` alone.
- **I-10 — the restore path executes archive SQL as a Postgres superuser.**
  10.43's containment is on the database *name* and it holds; it does not
  contain what the SQL may do (`COPY … FROM PROGRAM`) once an operator has
  accepted an unsigned archive via `TRITRACK_RESTORE_UNSIGNED`. Bounded by a
  deliberate override with a loud name; a restricted restore role would close
  it properly.
- **I-11 — retention is inert in the shipped configuration.**
  `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY` defaults empty, so retention prints a NOTE and
  prunes nothing, forever. Fail-safe and correct as a default — but it means
  the shipped path never exercises retention, which is how I-2 went unnoticed.
- **More instrument defects (§11.5), all confirmed by demonstration.**
  `verify_tls_termination.sh`'s origin-reachability check is unscoped to its own
  compose project (**false-alarmed live on this run** when an unrelated stack
  held 8080; false-clears with a non-default `SERVER_PORT`; and probes `http://`
  against a TLS-only listener); its "no trust anchor" control cannot fail (exit
  7 with nothing listening); and **`verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` never writes a
  `.minisig`**, so both its arms take the identical unsigned path and
  `minisign -V` is exercised by no instrument at all — the
  present-but-invalid-signature branch is the heart of 10.43 and is untested.
  `verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` is run by nothing.
- **The `User_Emails` / `Tags` accept-or-scope decision is settled: ACCEPT
  (§11.7).** Both keys are random 122-bit client UUIDs, not enumerable, and the
  structural fix is unavailable — `sync_tables.dart:78-80` records that these
  tables cannot take a project column without breaking pull's reachability
  filter. **The deliverable is an amendment to §4.13**, which is wider than
  this design can deliver and has now been "corrected" three times while the
  build kept violating it in the same three places. Scope the rule; stop
  restating it.
- **10.19's cloud-backup default needs re-deciding, not re-confirming
  (§11.9).** Confirmed explicit and confirmed in code — `enabled = true`, plain
  `ZipEncoder()`, no encryption, an unencrypted copy of asset 1 egressing to
  consumer cloud by default. §4.15's single-user justification was falsified by
  10.9's publish/join in §7.5 and four gates have carried it unchanged. Largest
  accepted risk in the product not tracked as an open finding. It is now an
  explicit question in the NAU letter.

#### From task 10.60 (2026-08-15) — what the re-decision accepted, and what it owes

*§4.15.1 records the three decisions: default stays on, payload stays an
unencrypted zip under a **time-bounded** acceptance, disclosure copy rewritten
to name other people's data. These are the pieces that decision deliberately
did not close.*

- **Archive encryption with a key-custody design — required before the beta
  team puts a field season into this, and needs its own task.** §4.15.1 accepts
  the unencrypted payload on one ground only: the key-custody design does not
  exist yet, and shipping ciphertext before it does converts a confidentiality
  gap into unrecoverable data loss in exactly the scenario auto-backup serves.
  **The constraint the task must satisfy: restore has to survive total device
  loss.** That rules out a keychain-held key outright (the phone in the river
  took it), and it means a user passphrase needs a real recovery affordance —
  §4.9.1's named-offline-holder arrangement is the server's answer and has no
  client analogue. Design first, then ship; do not take this on as a "just add
  `age` to the zip" ticket. Sequence it so it lands with time to test a restore
  before March, not against it. **Model: Opus** for the custody design.
- **A colleague still has no notification and no revocation.** The disclosure
  tells the *backing-up* user what they are doing on someone else's behalf; it
  tells the someone else nothing. The two things that would change that are
  §4.14's deferred per-project backup policy (a project owner restricting
  whether members may auto-back-up), and not carrying foreign identity rows in
  a *backup* archive at all. The second is not free: `ProjectExporter` steps 3
  and 4 exist so a restore is mergeable on a device that has never seen those
  users, and dropping them breaks `ProjectMerger`'s prior-email fallback on the
  restore path. Neither is a copy change; both are open.
- **The disclosure is guarded by a source scan, not by a device.**
  `test/security/backup_disclosure_test.dart` reads
  `auto_backup_section.dart` as text, because the section is
  `Platform.isIOS`/`isAndroid`-gated via `dart:io` and renders nothing in a
  host-run widget test. Same shape as task 10.34's copy gap — the words are
  verified, their appearance on a real screen is not. Worth folding into
  whatever on-device copy pass 10.34 gets.
- **§7.5's dating was wrong and is corrected in §4.15.1.** It attributed the
  widened trust boundary to 10.9's publish/join — a server feature never
  exposed. The live path is Phase 6 share import (`project_merger.dart:226`,
  `:216`), so this has been true of the shipped app for far longer than the
  gate notes imply. Worth a glance at whether any *other* finding was scoped as
  server-only on the same assumption.
- **The NAU letter's cloud-backup question now has an answer to include.**
  `NAU_infosec_review_request.md` asks about the default as an open question;
  §4.15.1 is the reasoning to attach when it is finally sent. Update the letter
  on the next revision rather than leaving the reviewer to infer a decision was
  never made.

#### From task 10.55 (2026-08-15) — a client assumption, a stated cost, and six instruments that assumed a fixture

- **Changing your profile email while signed in now stops your own `Users` row
  syncing.** §4.18 requires the address on the row to be the one the account
  authenticated with, and `ProfileEditor` lets a user type a new one at any
  time. The row is held and explained (task 10.28), not lost, and the remedy —
  sign in with the new address — is the right one. But the held-row copy is
  generic ("the server refused this row"), so the user is told *that* it was
  refused, not that they need to re-authenticate. **Phase 11's account UI should
  either say so or take the edit off the table while signed in**; either is a
  product decision, not a security one. Small, and worth doing before a beta
  team meets it.
- **A colleague met twice — once from a shared file, once from the server — now
  appears twice.** Falls out of `IdentityTrust.serverAssignsIdentity`: an
  imported colleague has a file-assigned local id, the same person arriving over
  sync has the server's id, and nothing folds them together any more because
  the only thing that could was the email trust we just removed on that path.
  Not a regression of anything that worked (§4.17 already refuses a colleague's
  rows until they are a project member), and not resolvable by trusting an
  address. **Phase 11 wants server-backed reconciliation** — an invitation or
  membership record naming an authenticated address is the provenance that can
  do it properly.
- **Six gate instruments built their fixture `Users` row with an invented
  address, and all six aborted the moment §4.18 landed.** Fixed in the same
  pass. Two of them needed more than a fixture edit: `Dc` in
  `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py` and the `User_Emails` arm of
  `verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` probe whether a *key* another user holds
  is distinguishable from a free one, and with an invented address both probes
  are refused for the address — so the equivalence would have passed for a
  reason it was not written for. Both now push the pusher's own authenticated
  address. **This is the §10.5 weak-assertion class arriving through a fixture
  rather than through an assertion**, and it is worth remembering for the next
  control that narrows what a fixture may say: a tightened rule can turn a
  probe green without the probe noticing it stopped probing.

#### From task 10.59 (2026-08-16) — `SET ROLE` over a second login, and a step the drill never ran

- **I-10's fix used `SET ROLE`, not a second credential.** The obvious shape
  for "run this SQL as a restricted role" is a new login role with its own
  password — which then needs a `pg_hba.conf` entry, a credential to manage,
  and a decision about whether the backup container mounts it or generates it
  per run. All of that is unnecessary: `restore.sh` is already connected as
  `$POSTGRES_USER`, a superuser, and Postgres lets a superuser `SET ROLE` to
  *any* role with no prior `GRANT` — only a non-superuser needs to already be
  a member. One statement, prepended to the same stream that pipes the
  decrypted dump into `psql`, demotes every statement after it in that same
  `--single-transaction` to a `NOSUPERUSER` role that can only create objects
  in the one disposable `$STAGING` database. No new auth path, no new secret.
- **Verified live, not just read.** `scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh` (its
  own compose project, `tritrack-backup-drill`, isolated from any other
  stack) ran the full sequence twice: once at 37 checks before the I-11 step
  was added, once at 38 after. Both runs replayed a real 21-table dump
  through the demoted role and confirmed every row byte-identical — the
  restricted role is not a change nothing exercises. One run's step 7d–7g
  (`a truncated archive is stopped at the decrypt`) failed on its first
  attempt with `'tritrack' has 1 open connection(s)` — a `docker compose stop`
  timing race in code this task did not touch, not a regression — and passed
  cleanly on immediate re-run, confirming it was transient.
- **I-11's fix is a drill step plus documentation, deliberately not a default
  change.** The fail-safe "print a NOTE and prune nothing" behaviour is
  correct and stays; what was missing was (a) any instrument that runs a
  backup in the exact configuration `docker-compose.yml`/`.env.example` ship
  — every existing drill step deliberately sets `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY`,
  because the rest of the drill needs a signature to check things against —
  and (b) documentation that says plainly, next to the variable, that leaving
  it unset disables retention entirely and not merely in-place restore. Both
  now exist: `backup_restore_drill.sh` step 8b, and matching notes in
  `.env.example` and `server/README.md`.
- **Not done: making the shipped default louder over time.** An operator who
  never sets `TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY` still gets only a log-line NOTE on
  every run, forever — nothing escalates if `backups/` has been growing
  unbounded for a year. Considered and set aside: the fail-safe default's own
  reasoning (§4.9, §10.5.2) is that retention refusing to guess is correct
  behaviour, not a fault to alarm on, and this phase already has a
  documentation fix for the "nobody knew this was the tradeoff" half of the
  gap. An operational alert (disk-usage monitoring, a scheduled check that
  counts archives against `TRITRACK_BACKUP_KEEP`) is a deployment-operations
  concern outside a Sonnet-scoped code fix, not a security finding — named
  here rather than silently out of scope.

#### From task 10.58 (2026-08-15) — proving the detector, and one thing it found doing so

- **Performance decided the implementation, not just correctness.** The
  naive translation of "scan every historical blob" — one `git cat-file -p
  <sha>` process per blob — measured at 31 seconds for this repository's
  ~1,650 historical blobs (113 commits). A single `git rev-list --objects
  --all | git cat-file --batch` call does the same read in well under a
  second; the Dart side parses the batched wire format (`<sha> <type>
  <size>\n<content>\n`, byte-offset-driven because content can itself
  contain `\n`) rather than shelling out per object. Whole suite,
  working-tree checks plus the new history pass: about two seconds. Worth
  recording because the slow version would have been correct too, and would
  have been the version that got the history scan quietly excluded from the
  default suite the first time someone complained `flutter test` got slow —
  which is the H-1 failure mode this phase already spent a task fixing.
- **Proof discipline, per the task's own instruction:** planted a real
  `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<value>` string on a throwaway branch (`git checkout -b
  tmp-secret-proof-10-58`, deliberately isolated from this session's other
  pending changes via `git stash` first — a "prove the detector" commit must
  not also smuggle in unrelated work), confirmed both checks failed,
  removed it in a second commit, confirmed the working-tree check went
  green while the history check kept failing on the exact commit sha, then
  deleted the branch and confirmed both checks green again with the planted
  commits unreachable from `git rev-list --all`. A detector nobody has seen
  fail is not a detector, and this specific detector's whole reason for
  existing is the case where the working-tree check goes green and the
  history check must not.
- **The scan found a real gap in its own detector, live, on the first run**
  — not a hypothetical. Six historical revisions of this document contain
  `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=... dart test --tags postgres` (a worked shell
  example's ellipsis placeholder), which the value-exemption list had no
  entry for. Confirms the task's framing: the working-tree scan had never
  seen this, because the line was reworded before this task ran, so a
  detector that only ever sees the tip cannot even be wrong about it.
  Fixed with one exemption (`value == '...'`) and a regression test using
  the exact historical string.
- **Not extended to `.env.example`'s historical content.** §7.4's manual
  review also confirmed every historical `.env.example` shipped with empty
  values; this task's automated pass only re-runs the *secret-detector*
  checks (PEM, age key, assignment, key/cert paths, `.env` tracking) across
  history, not the "every value empty" check specifically. Low-value gap —
  a filled-in `.env.example` value would itself be caught by the
  assignment-pattern history scan if the variable is one of
  `_secretVariables`, and the three tracked variables are — but naming it
  rather than letting the coverage claim silently round up.

#### From task 10.57 (2026-08-15) — a decision paragraph that never matched its own implementation

Both fixes were one line each; what took the time was confirming which
artifact was actually wrong, since for I-7 the docs, the code, and the
shipped Android config all disagreed with each other pairwise:

- **§4.1's own "Decision" paragraph said "the client build is debug or
  profile," which matched *nothing else in the phase*.** §3.4's summary
  already said "debug builds only." The shipped Android
  `network_security_config.xml` was scoped to the debug variant only, and
  `platform_cleartext_test.dart` already had a test pinning that ("Profile
  is a release-mode build. §4.1's exemption is debug-only.") — so Android's
  implementation was never the bug; only the Dart validator's `kReleaseMode`
  read agreed with the paragraph, and both moved to `!kDebugMode`/"debug
  only" together. Fixing the code alone would have left the doc newly
  contradicting the Android side it had never actually described correctly.
- **The build-mode difference cannot be exercised from `flutter test`
  at all** — a test binary is neither release nor profile, so `kReleaseMode`
  and `!kDebugMode` are indistinguishable by calling the function under
  test; both evaluate `false` there. Regression cover for I-7 is therefore a
  source-text assertion (`release_mode_transport_test.dart`) that the live
  code no longer reads `kReleaseMode`, in the same spirit as
  `platform_cleartext_test.dart`'s file-placement checks for Android/iOS —
  proving a build-mode property structurally rather than by building three
  separate binaries in CI.
- **I-8's fix was verified by rendering the merged compose config, not by
  reading the file**, per the task's own instruction — `docker compose -f
  docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.server-test.yml config` with
  `SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` set. Reverting the fix and re-rendering
  reproduces `host_ip: 0.0.0.0` exactly, confirming the render — not a
  source read — is what would have caught this the first time (10.47's own
  gap, named in the finding).
- Checked and found clean: `docker-compose.tls.yml`'s `server.ports` is
  already `!override []` (task 10.47), and its `proxy` service's `0.0.0.0`
  publish is the deliberate, documented reverse-proxy decision, not an
  instance of the same class. No other `kReleaseMode`/`kDebugMode` read
  exists anywhere in `lib/` outside a debug-only log gate in
  `server_config_screen.dart` unrelated to transport security. The server
  binary (Dart, not Flutter) has no debug/release/profile concept at all —
  its own environment-gating (`TRITRACK_ENV=production`) is a single
  boolean with no equivalent third state to fall through.

#### From task 10.56 (2026-08-15) — the field-bound rule, generalized past the envelope

Both I-4 and I-5 came from probing one field each (`device_id` on `/sync/push`,
the `link-status` path parameter); the task's actual scope was sweeping every
route for the same class rather than patching the two reproductions. The
sweep surfaced instances neither finding named:

- **Every table's primary-key column(s) had no length bound at all**, not
  just `device_id`/`project_id` in the envelope. A primary key is a Postgres
  btree index entry exactly like the envelope fields, so an oversized
  `tag_id`, `observation_id`, etc. arriving inside `rows` would have thrown
  the identical uncaught `500` mid-`INSERT`, on any of the eleven synced
  tables, entirely inside `RowValidator`'s blind spot (it range-checks
  numeric columns and enums but never checked a string's length). Closed
  generically: `RowValidator.maxPrimaryKeyLength` checks every table's PK
  columns from one shared map, so a table added later inherits the bound
  rather than needing someone to remember it.
- **`Users.email` / `User_Emails.email` are btree-indexed for cross-device
  dedup and had no length bound either**, despite not being primary keys —
  the same crash class on a column §11.8's I-4 never mentioned.
  `RowValidator.maxEmailLength` (320, matching `/auth/magic-link`'s existing
  bound) closes it.
- `project_id` was unbounded on `/sync/push` and `/sync/pull` (only
  `/sync/ack`'s `device_id` had a cap before this task); both are now bounded
  identically in `sync_routes.dart`'s shared `handle()`, one check instead of
  three duplicated ones.
- **The two documents disagree about finding numbers past I-3.**
  `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §11.8 calls these findings I-4 (`device_id`)
  and I-5 (`link-status`); this plan's own task titles call the same pair
  I-5 and I-6, and every later task in the phase (10.57 "I-8, I-9", 10.58
  "I-7", 10.59 "I-10, I-11") carries the same one-off drift forward. Neither
  document is self-inconsistent — each counts consistently within itself —
  but a search for "I-7" finds a different finding depending on which file
  answers. Not fixed here (renumbering one document mid-phase risks a worse
  mismatch than the one it fixes); flagged so the next phase's planning
  session picks one counter before Phase 11 adds more findings to it.
- Diagnostics console path/query parameters (`/diagnostics/projects/<id>`,
  `.../rows/<table>`, `?user_id=`, `?email=`) remain unbounded strings.
  Deliberately not touched: every value there reaches only a parameterized
  `SELECT`, never an `INSERT`, so none can trigger I-4's crash class, and the
  route is already local-only-by-default plus shared-token-authenticated
  (10.13). Worth a hygiene pass if the console is ever opened beyond that.
- `GET /auth/redeem`'s query-string `token` is still bounded only by the
  underlying HTTP server's request-line limit, not an explicit application
  check — it performs no write and echoes back only what the caller sent, so
  it is outside I-4's crash class, but it is the one unauthenticated route
  this sweep did not add an explicit bound to. Named rather than silently
  skipped.

#### BLOCKING — Security Gate C, third re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-14)

***These block any exposure beyond localhost.** The previous round's three
scheduled findings — G-1, G-2, G-3 — are all **closed and verified live**, as is
10.40's findings audit. These are what the third re-run found instead. Full
evidence is `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` **§10**. Each needs its own task, and
the gate has to be run a fourth time once they are closed.*

- **H-6 — the restore path authenticates integrity, not origin (§10.5.1).**
  **Reproduced live**, `scripts/verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh`, new this run. An
  archive forged with nothing but the **public** age recipient — which §4.9 says
  may appear "in documentation, tickets, or a commit" — passes all three gates
  `restore.sh` applies (a checksum file the attacker writes, a cleartext schema
  marker the attacker writes, and a decrypt that succeeds because anyone holding
  the public half can encrypt to it, plus a content test that is two literal
  `pg_dump` comment lines). The forged SQL is then piped into `psql` as
  `POSTGRES_USER`, which the `postgres:16-alpine` entrypoint makes a
  **superuser**, and renamed into the live database name. 10.37's rename-aside
  saves the real database; nothing else intervenes.
  - **The design question comes first, and it is Opus's.** `age` has no signing
    mode, so this is a signature scheme (`minisign`/`signify`, or an SSH-key
    signature) over the archive *and* its sidecars, with the verifying public
    key living with the restore procedure rather than beside the archive — which
    is a change to §4.9's custody arrangement, not a patch to a script.
  - Then correct `restore.sh:98` and `:200-202`, whose comments assert the
    property that does not hold ("the decrypt below authenticates the bytes
    regardless"; the header "proves this is a database dump at all, and not some
    other file that happens to be encrypted to the same key"). Both are true
    against an accident and false against an adversary, and they are why three
    tasks read this path and nobody asked the question.
  - Add the forged-but-decryptable case to `backup_restore_drill.sh`. Every
    existing case is an accident (corruption, truncation, wrong key); none is an
    adversary. The reproduction script can be folded in rather than re-authored.
  - **Acceptance:** `verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` refuses and the live row
    survives; a genuine archive still restores on both paths; the drill covers
    the forged case.
  - **Model:** **Opus** for the custody decision, then Sonnet for the wiring.
  - **CLOSED by task 10.43 (2026-08-14).** Custody arrangement first, as
    **§4.9.2**; `minisign` pinned beside `age`; one signature binds the
    ciphertext, the checksum and the schema marker via the signed trusted
    comment; verifying key configured with the restore procedure. The rule that
    closes it is *an archive of unverified origin is never promoted over an
    existing database*, under any flag combination — legacy archives still
    restore into a new name. Reproduction extended to run **with and without a
    verifying key configured** and refuses in both; drill green at 33 checks;
    **confirmed load-bearing by a negative control** that neutralised the origin
    gate alone and watched H-6 reproduce.

- **H-7 — retention deletes by filename, so write access to the archive
  directory destroys every real backup (§10.5.2).** `backup.sh:150-155` keeps
  the `KEEP` lexically-highest `tritrack-*.age` names and deletes the rest, on
  the comment "Timestamps are ISO basic UTC, so lexical order is chronological
  order" — true only for names this script wrote. Plant 30 files dated 2999 and
  the next legitimate backup run deletes the entire genuine history, checksums
  and sidecars included. No key, no read access, and the deletion is performed
  by the backup job itself.
  - Prune only what the run can account for — a manifest the backup box keeps,
    or names validated against the archive's own decryptable content — and treat
    an unexpected name as a reason to **refuse to prune**, not as an instruction
    to delete something else.
  - Note `backup.sh:85` already refuses to overwrite an archive it would write.
    The asymmetry (careful about its own names, trusting of everyone else's) is
    the whole finding.
  - **Acceptance:** planted future-dated files cause a loud refusal and no
    deletion of genuine archives; ordinary retention still prunes oldest-first
    (the drill's existing check must still pass).
  - **Model:** Sonnet, once H-6's decision fixes what a "genuine archive" is
    provably identified by. **Do H-6 first** — a signature makes this a
    one-line predicate.

- **H-1 — 10.39's guard turns the default `flutter test` run red (§10.4).**
  `test/e2e/e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart` carries `@Tags(['e2e'])`, and there is
  **no `dart_test.yaml` anywhere in this repository**, so no tag is excluded
  from anything: a plain `flutter test` loads the guard, `E2eEnv.isConfigured`
  is false, and the run exits 1 (772 passed / 30 skipped / 1 failed). That
  contradicts Phase 10 invariant 5 and the root README's explicit promise that
  the default suite stays green with no server and no network.
  - **The fix is a tag exclusion, not a change to the guard.** Add a
    `dart_test.yaml` that keeps `e2e`-tagged tests out of the default run, so
    `--tags e2e` is the only way to load them and the guard can only fire on a
    run that meant to be an e2e run. **Do not make the guard skip** — that is
    G-1 reopened, and it is the same repair path that made G-2 worse.
  - Check the same question for the server suite deliberately rather than by
    analogy: `database_coverage_guard_test.dart` has the identical structure and
    no tag exclusion either, but there a no-database `dart test` failing is
    *intended* (10.31). Say which is which in the file, so the next person does
    not "fix" the server's on the strength of this one.
  - **Acceptance:** plain `flutter test` is green on a clean checkout with no
    server and no network; `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` unconfigured still
    exits non-zero; a deliberately removed e2e test file still breaks the count
    assertion. All three checked in one session.
  - **Model:** Sonnet — the fix is one config file. **Run before the next gate.**
  - **Closed (10.41, 2026-08-14) — with a deviation from the acceptance
    wording, flagged here.** `exclude_tags: e2e` in `dart_test.yaml` was tried
    first and makes `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` fail non-zero exactly as
    written above — but it does so by making `--tags e2e` **permanently
    unsatisfiable** (`package:test` unions config-level `exclude_tags` with the
    CLI's tag selectors rather than letting the CLI override them), so a
    *configured* e2e run would report "no tests match tag selectors" forever
    too, not just the unconfigured guard. That silently deletes the e2e suite's
    ability to ever run — worse than the red tree this task exists to fix.
    `paths:` was tried second and doesn't work at all: `flutter test` always
    hands `dart test` an explicit file list, so it never falls back to
    `paths`' default-when-no-path-given behavior.
    Shipped instead: `tags: e2e: skip: <reason>`, which skips e2e-tagged tests
    by default (bare `flutter test` is green) without touching the
    include/exclude selectors. The cost is that an explicit e2e run now needs
    `--run-skipped` too — `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` *alone* now exits
    **0** ("all tests skipped"), not non-zero as the acceptance line above
    literally says; `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e --run-skipped` is what
    exits non-zero, both for the unconfigured guard and for the file-count
    check. README.md and `e2e_coverage_guard_test.dart`'s doc comment were
    updated to the `--run-skipped` form. `run_offline_suite.sh` needed no code
    change — it only ever ran plain `flutter test`, which is green again.
    `database_coverage_guard_test.dart` got a doc comment explaining why it
    deliberately gets no `dart_test.yaml` exclusion (a no-database `dart test`
    failing is intended there, task 10.31).

- **H-2 — 10.40's self-check disabled all five wire-speaking instruments
  (§10.5).** `gate_wire.preflight()` asserts `200` on a `/sync/pull` for a fresh
  account against a random project id; the designed answer is `403`. Every
  instrument aborted before running a control. **The gate applied the one-line
  correction itself** (a `403` proves the envelope was understood, because
  10.35's major check runs in front of authorization) and re-verified that a
  stale major still aborts, so the tools work now — but the task-level work is
  the thing that would have caught it:
  - **Give the instruments a smoke run that a human does not have to remember.**
    One script that brings up the gate stack, runs all five instruments plus the
    drill, and reports pass/fail per instrument — so "the tools work" is a
    command, not a belief. This is the third consecutive gate to lose a cycle to
    instrument rot (§8.2, §9.1.1, §10.5); a wrapper is cheaper than a fourth.
  - Two of group E's new checks were wrong in their first draft in opposite
    directions (a `trace_id` read as a disclosure; a non-`200` demanded where
    "nothing was written" was the real bar). Both are fixed in the repo. The
    standing rule stays as 10.40 stated it: **a check that cannot distinguish
    success from its own failure is not a check** — and note that it applies to
    checks that are too strict as well as too loose.
  - **Acceptance:** a single documented command runs every gate instrument
    against a freshly brought-up stack and fails loudly per instrument; run it
    once with a deliberately stale constant to prove it catches that.
  - **Model:** Sonnet. **Run before the next gate.**
  - **Closed (10.42, 2026-08-14).** `scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh` brings the
    e2e stack up, runs the five wire-speaking instruments plus
    `backup_restore_drill.sh`, and prints a PASS/FAIL line per instrument
    plus a per-instrument log path — "the tools work" is now
    `scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh`, not a belief between gates. Its own exit
    code reflects each instrument's own exit code verbatim: a wire-speaking
    instrument that finds a genuine open finding (several still do — Ce2,
    Ch, Dc, Dh, Ea2, Eb, Ec2, tracked in their own tasks) reports FAIL
    correctly, because that is the instrument doing its job, not the
    instrument being broken. Self-proof lives in the same script:
    `GATE_SMOKE_SELFTEST=1` patches a copy of `scripts/gate_wire.py` with
    `SCHEMA_MAJOR + 1000` for the duration of the run (the real file is
    restored via an `EXIT` trap even on failure), and asserts all five
    wire-speaking instruments abort with `PREFLIGHT ABORT` while the drill
    — which doesn't speak the sync wire — is unaffected. Verified live: a
    normal run correctly reports `gate_c_adversarial_pass` FAIL for the
    known-open findings above and five PASS plus the drill PASS elsewhere;
    the selftest run correctly reports all five wire-speaking instruments
    FAIL on `PREFLIGHT ABORT` and the drill still PASS.

- **F13, TLS termination, and the NAU review — carried, and now blocking at
  three consecutive gates.** All three already have Discovered Scope entries
  from 10.40's findings audit; nothing about any of them changed this round.
  Two are human actions nobody has taken in seven days and one is a single
  client seam. **They are now the only reason the gate cannot pass on
  technical grounds**, and no adversarial pass can close any of them.

#### Non-blocking, from the third re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-14)

- **H-3 — `Tags` is a global-key existence oracle, and §4.13 said it was
  covered (§10.7).** A `tag_id` another project holds answers `lost_to_server`;
  a free one answers `inserted`. §9.5 named `Tags` as covered by 10.29's
  reachability rule, which governs *referencing* an unreachable tag and says
  nothing about *claiming its primary key*. The victim's row is untouched, so
  this is disclosure only, and probing means guessing a 122-bit UUIDv4 — the
  same negligible-disclosure judgement G-4 got, and the reason it is not
  blocking. §4.13 has been corrected and now carries a warning about its own
  provenance.
  - **The work is the sweep, not the patch.** This is the fourth instance of
    fixing the tables that had reproductions and writing the result as a derived
    rule. Every table in `sync_tables.dart` needs a probe that claims a key
    another caller holds and compares the answer to a free key — including the
    ones currently believed covered. Then §4.13's list is evidence rather than
    argument.
  - **Model:** Sonnet for the probes; the accept-or-scope decision on
    `User_Emails` and `Tags` is Opus's if anyone reopens it.

- **H-4 — a wrongly-typed envelope field answers `500` (§10.7).**
  `schema_major: "2"` as a string draws `500 internal_error` where the absent
  field and the future major draw `400` and `409`. Uniform across project
  existence, discloses nothing, applies no rows — F10's and G-5's family, on the
  check 10.35 put in front of authorization on every sync route. Worth folding
  into whatever task finally closes F10, rather than its own.

- **H-5 — an unknown table name is dropped silently (§10.7).** `rows: {"NotATable": [...]}`
  answers `200`, `applied: 0`, `outcomes: {}`. 10.18 decided unknown *columns*
  are preserved; an unknown *table* vanishes without a word, and the protocol's
  per-row `invalid` outcome (`HeldRowReason.forOutcome`) is never emitted on
  this path. The app cannot reach it today and 10.28's rule 2 means the client
  holds rather than loses the rows; the case that reaches it is a newer client
  against an older server, which is what schema-major compatibility is for.
  Same owner as G-5.

- **H-8 — the weak-assertion sweep missed six, five of them in the gate's own
  instruments (§10.7.1).** 10.40 reported "zero new instances found beyond the
  five known ones" after sweeping for this shape. An independent sweep of 206
  candidate sites found six, each confirmed by reading the code and the first by
  running it: W-1 is H-1 (and it also breaks `scripts/run_offline_suite.sh`,
  task 10.15's headline claim); **W-2**, `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:341`, read
  an empty `outcomes` map as "every table refused the forged row" — a vacuous
  pass on **C-1** — *fixed this run*, and `Ca` still holds under the strict
  form; **W-3**, `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py:150-152`, prints `SKIP` when
  the stack is down, appends nothing to `failures`, and exits 0 claiming C-3
  closed; **W-4** counts an untested control as HELD; **W-5** is vacuous on an
  empty audit log, i.e. on C-5 regressing; **W-6** is `|| true` under a `PASS`
  claim. Full table, and the specific list of what was cleared and why, in
  §10.7.1.
  - **Fix W-3 first** — it is the one that can print a false pass on a blocking
    finding — then W-4, W-5, W-6.
  - **The class-level item is worth more than the six:**
    `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py:75` returns `(0, repr(e))` on a connection
    failure, so every *negative* assertion in the file ("the secret is not in
    the body", "the victim's id is not in the response") is satisfied by a
    server that stopped answering. `preflight()` guards the start of a run; add
    a liveness re-check at the **end**, so a mid-run crash cannot convert the
    remainder into HELDs.
  - **Acceptance:** each of the six either fails when its input is absent, or
    carries a recorded reason why it cannot; the end-of-run liveness check is
    proved by killing the server mid-pass and confirming the run fails rather
    than reporting HELDs.
  - **Model:** Sonnet. Pair with H-2's instrument smoke run.
  - **Closed (10.42, 2026-08-14).** W-1 was 10.41; W-2 was already fixed.
    W-3 (`verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py`): the stack-down branch is now
    `skip()`, tracked apart from `failures`, and the script exits non-zero
    and prints "NOT confirmed closed" rather than "C-3 closed" when it
    never checked the LAN. W-4 (`gate_c_adversarial_pass.py` A4): a
    `skipped_check()` helper keeps an untested control out of the `held`
    total instead of `held_check(..., True, "skipped")`. W-5 (Cd's event
    check): `bool(events) and all(...)` instead of a bare `all(...)`, so an
    empty `auth_audit_log` (C-5 regressing) no longer reads as "still holds
    only the closed enum". W-6 (`run_offline_suite.sh`): after `docker
    compose down ... || true`, the script now `curl`s `/health` and aborts
    if anything still answers, instead of asserting "no server running"
    unchecked — verified live by leaving the server up and confirming the
    script refuses to claim the offline suite passed.
    **Class-level liveness re-check:** `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py` now
    hits `/health` once after every group finishes and fails the whole run
    if the server stopped answering, regardless of what the checks above it
    reported. Verified live by starting a run, `docker compose stop server`
    partway through, and confirming the run exits non-zero on "LIVENESS
    RE-CHECK FAILED" rather than reporting the remainder as HELD (the
    degenerate-paging group that ran during the outage did read its dead
    connections as HELD, which is exactly the failure mode this exists to
    catch downstream of — the end-of-run check is what stops that from
    being the reported result).

- **H-9 — three unproven edges in the restore path, and a detector that
  blesses one of them (§10.7.2).** G-3 is closed; these are the edges. The
  staging `DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS` in the EXIT trap is the one drop nothing
  checks (`$TARGET` gets a `pg_database` lookup and a `REPLACE` gate; `$STAGING`
  gets neither), reachable only by a same-second name collision or a clock
  stepped back — but `restore.sh:79-82` asserts the property, so enforce it with
  one `SELECT`. The trap stays armed across the swap, so the worst-case swap
  failure (rename-aside succeeds, promote fails, rollback fails) drops the
  verified restored copy without saying so, as does Ctrl-C inside that window
  (`INT`/`TERM` are not trapped). And the rollback itself has never run: no
  drill case forces a rename to fail. Meanwhile
  `test/security/restore_ordering_test.dart:80-95` is a text grep that the
  unguarded staging drop *satisfies*, so it currently certifies the drop worth
  questioning. **Model:** Sonnet. Fold into H-6's task if that one is opened
  first — same file, same drill.
  - **CLOSED by task 10.43 (2026-08-14)**, folded into H-6's task as suggested.
    Staging guarded by a `pg_database` check *before* the `CREATE`, with the
    trap armed only afterwards — the previous order meant a `CREATE` that
    collided ran a trap that dropped what it had collided with, which is worse
    than the finding as filed. Trap disarmed *before* the swap rather than
    after, so no swap failure can discard the verified restore; `INT`/`TERM`
    covered for the window before it. Rollback forced by a drill-only
    `TRITRACK_RESTORE_FAULT` seam (single failure and the double failure), and
    the staging collision forced deterministically at drill step 7m by
    pre-creating the next five second-stamps inside the container that then runs
    the restore — all five survive. The detector now asserts the *guard* and
    carries a comment naming what a grep cannot prove, plus an `isNotEmpty`
    assertion, since a grep over zero matching lines passes.

- **The compose merge sweep 10.38 asked for is now done (§10.7.3), with two
  latent instances and one residual.** `docker-compose.e2e.yml:47-48`'s
  `volumes:` merges and is harmless only because the base `server` has no

  **Residual:** `!override` needs Compose ≥ 2.24 and nothing in the repo records

places where a fix was recorded as landed and the thing it was supposed to close

running the artifact would have missed all three.*

#### Non-blocking, from the second re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-13)

*Evidence for all of these is §9. None blocks exposure; the first is the one
that needs a decision rather than a patch.*

- **G-4. `User_Emails` is still a global-key existence oracle, and §4.13 said
  otherwise.** 10.35 project-scoped the six project-scoped data tables.
  `Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` remain keyed globally. `Users` is covered by
  §4.17's naming invariant and `Tags` by 10.29's reachability rule — both
  re-verified indistinguishable live — but `User_Emails` is covered by neither:
  a caller naming *themselves* satisfies the naming invariant, there is no edge
  to consult, and the key collision is the whole answer. Live: a
  `user_email_id` another user holds → `unauthorized`, a free one → `inserted`.
  **The disclosure is negligible** — a client-generated UUIDv4 that appears in
  no share payload, so probing means guessing 122 bits — which is why this is
  not blocking and why a second major bump to key it `(user_email_id, user_id)`
  is probably the wrong trade. **What was not negligible is that §4.13 and §8.4
  both claimed arm (c) was closed outright.** Both have been corrected in place;
  the decision left for planning is whether to accept the residual as now stated
  or spend the bump. Third instance of *fix the instances with reproductions,
  describe it as a derived rule.*
- **D-2's row-count arm, still open.** 10.30's size cap is real and works —
  measured, the widest storable field is exactly 500 chars and the amplification
  fell from ~11 MB/s to **~122 KB/s** for 200 denied requests. But
  `/sync/pull` still has no rate limit, the row count still grows 1:1 with
  requests, and **§4.7's 1-year retention is implemented by nothing**, which is
  §4.7's own `Violated by:` clause. Not blocking under §5.6 (DoS is an explicit
  non-goal, and 10.28/10.33 mean the client loses nothing when the server is
  unavailable). The remaining work is the purge schedule, not another cap.
- **D-5, sharpened and now verified live.** With the console enabled *and* the
  correct bearer token, `/diagnostics/auth-events` still answers `403
  diagnostics_console_local_only` from the host — under Docker every host
  request arrives from the bridge gateway, never loopback. It answers `200` only
  with `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ALLOW_REMOTE=true`. **The only configuration that
  can read the audit rows C-5 exists to create is the one §4.10's network gate
  was built to prevent.** The shipped default now returns `404` rather than the
  `403` §8.4 recorded (better — a disabled route should not announce itself),
  but the README's documented `curl` still yields nothing and no explanation,
  and the working alternative (`docker compose exec postgres psql`) is
  documented nowhere. §7.6's owed README note now has two things to say.
- **G-5. One malformed row fails the whole push with `500`.** Live, as an
  authorized caller on their own project: a missing `NOT NULL` column or a
  wrong-typed value returns `500 internal_error`, and a valid row batched
  alongside it does not land either. The protocol has a per-row `invalid`
  outcome — `HeldRowReason.forOutcome` handles it explicitly — and this path
  never produces one. Low severity: not an oracle (requires being authorized),
  discloses nothing beyond a trace id, unreachable through the app's own
  serializer, and 10.28's rule 2 means the client holds rather than loses.
  Recorded because it is §7.6 F10's family on the routes every fix has
  rewritten, and because "one bad row and this device can never sync again" is a
  support call with a `500` at the end of it.
- **`revision` pinning, now reproduced rather than read.** A row inserted at
  `revision = 2^63-1` is accepted, and a later legitimate edit at revision 2
  does not apply. Recorded non-blocking at the last gate from code reading; the
  live reproduction is now check `Dh` in the adversarial pass.
- **`server/backup/restore.sh`'s schema bounds are hand-maintained.** Task 10.36
  added `SCHEMA_MIN=1` / `SCHEMA_MAX=2` as shell literals with a comment saying
  to update them whenever `schemaMajorVersion` moves — the same coupling that
  had just silently invalidated five gate scripts (§9.1.1). One bump from
  refusing a restorable archive or accepting an unrestorable one, and
  `backup_restore_drill.sh` asserts the sidecar's value without ever comparing
  it to the constant. Cheap to fix alongside G-3, which touches the same file.
- **The last mile of the device check.** §9.7 closed most of 10.25's device
  instruction with a live check driving the real `SyncEngine` against a real
  server refusal
  (`test/e2e/refused_row_visibility_e2e_test.dart`). What still needs a human
  with a phone: that the held-row sentence reads correctly at a glance in the
  actual workflow on a small screen (10.34's residual), and F13's ATS question,
  which needs an iOS build.

#### BLOCKING — Security Gate C re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-12)

> **Superseded in part by the 2026-08-13 section above.** D-1, D-2's size arm
> and D-3 are closed and re-verified live. **E-2 is not** — see G-2. F13, TLS
> and NAU are carried forward unchanged.

***These block any exposure beyond localhost.** C-1…C-5 are all closed and
verified live — these are what the re-run found instead. Full evidence,
including live reproductions and the reverted-build controls, is in
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` **§8**. Each needs its own task, and the gate must
be re-run a second time once they are closed. Model: **Opus** for D-1 and D-3 —
D-1 is an authorization-protocol design question with no patch-shaped answer,
and D-3 is a sync-engine correctness question, not UI wiring.*

- **D-1. The per-row `outcomes` map is a general existence oracle.** Task 10.21
  closed C-2 at the HTTP status code, and that holds — pull, push and ack answer
  a real foreign project and a fabricated id identically, by response and by
  timing. But a push returns per-row outcomes inside every `200`, and those
  answer the same question one level down. Three arms, all reproduced live from
  an ordinary session with **no project and no relationship** to what is being
  asked about: a stranger's `user_id` returns `lost_to_server` if they have a
  published profile, `unauthorized` if they have an account only, and
  `inserted` if the server has never seen them — a three-way read of
  registration status; a `tag_id` returns `unauthorized` if any project
  references it and `inserted` otherwise; and an `observation_id` returns
  `unauthorized` if that key exists anywhere on the server, including in
  someone else's project. No content leaks — the victim's row was verified
  unchanged afterwards — and none of it is audited, because every probe returns
  `200` and never reaches `auditDenial`.
  **The user arm is new and 10.20 created it**: before the row-naming
  invariant, naming a known foreign user was permitted (that was C-1's
  disclosure), so both cases answered `inserted`. The tag and row-key arms
  predate the remediation and were missed by Gate B, Gate C, and by 10.21 —
  which found this exact channel, patched the instance in front of it, and
  wrote in §4.13 that "the outcome map answered the question the status code no
  longer did." **That is C-1's pattern again: right reasoning, applied to the
  instance instead of derived as the rule.**
  **Fix as one rule, and expect it not to be a patch.** Making the unknown case
  answer `unauthorized` closes the user arm and breaks the first-publish
  replication seam C-1's fix depends on; the two branches have to converge and
  choosing the answer is a design decision. If it is irreducible without
  breaking publish, it must be **stated and bounded in §4.13 and §4.17** the way
  the publish-collision residual already is. Note that the current suite asserts
  the oracle as correct behaviour (`authorization_test.dart:642-653` and
  `:1007-1030`) — those tests need revisiting with the rule, not around it.
  **Closed by task 10.29 (2026-08-13)** for the user and tag arms — see that
  task's entry for the rule, and for the design decision the finding said had to
  be made: the branches converge on the **refusal**, and the first-publish
  replication seam is the price, paid rather than worked around because naming
  someone is attribution as well as disclosure and that harm is identical either
  way. The row-key arm is the create-if-absent collision inherent to
  client-chosen primary keys; it is now **stated and bounded in §4.13 as a
  property of every table** rather than of `Projects` alone, with the real close
  (project-scoped keys, a `schemaMajor` change) filed below for the planning
  session. Both cited tests were flipped to the refusal and the whole area is
  now written as equivalence tests; `scripts/verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py` finds
  six distinguishable pairs against the pre-fix build and none after. Reproducing
  it turned up **a fourth shape the write-up did not name** — a dangling
  reference answered `500` for an id the server did not hold and `200` for one it
  did, a status-code oracle on the routes C-2 had made uniform — closed by the
  same change. **Still open next to it: none of this is audited (D-4)**, and the
  refusals are now the common answer rather than a corner.
- **D-2. C-5's fix made denial auditing an unbounded attacker-controlled
  write.** `auditDenial` records the caller's `project_id` in
  `auth_audit_log.outcome` — correct, an operator needs to know which project
  was refused — but nothing truncates it, the column is unbounded `TEXT`, the
  sync body limit is 8 MB, and `/sync/pull` carries no rate limit (§4.4 limits
  magic links and redemptions only). Measured live with incompressible content:
  **10 denied requests, 0.9 s, 10 MB on disk**, ~11 MB/s from one ordinary
  registered user while the server answers `403` throughout. §4.7's retention
  sweep is still a mechanism nothing schedules, so nothing removes it either.
  Asset 5. This exists *because* the control was repaired — before 10.23 every
  one of these writes was silently discarded.
  Fix is small (bound the stored value; the trace id already correlates to the
  full request) but **should land with the §4.7 purge schedule**, which this
  makes urgent rather than tidy.
- **D-3. A refused row is silently lost, and the app reports "Synced."** Task
  10.25 named this case in advance and it fails exactly as predicted. A user
  saves a colleague's `TT1:` payload; the importer writes a faithful replica
  including a local `Users` row; the app says "Observation saved, attributed to
  the original observer." On the next sync the server refuses the row —
  correctly, that is 10.20's invariant — with a per-row `unauthorized` inside a
  `200`. `SyncEngine._push` keeps only `lostToServer` outcomes and `continue`s
  past the rest (`sync_engine.dart:201-202`); `SyncRunReport` has no field for
  them; the push watermark has already advanced unconditionally (`:195-197`);
  and because a replica preserves the sender's clock verbatim by design (task
  6.3), its `updated_at` sits below the new watermark, so
  `_collectChangedRows`' `updated_at >= watermark` predicate never selects it
  again (`:396-399`). **The row is never retried and never counted as
  pending.** The user sees "Synced just now.", a green "Synced" headline, no
  pending count, and "No overwritten edits."
  This is a silent permanent loss of a primary scientific record through an
  ordinary intended workflow — asset 2, and the exact shape of the sign-in bug
  that reached a real phone with 700+ tests green. The report already carries
  enough to detect it (`pushed - applied - lostToServer.length`); nothing
  consumes it and there is no surface to show it on. **No test covers it** —
  the fake transport never denies a row, and there is no widget test for
  `SyncStatusScreen` or `SyncStatusBanner` at all. Both gaps are part of the
  fix, not follow-ups to it.
  **Closed by task 10.28 (2026-08-13)** — see that task's entry for what was
  built, the one deliberate deviation from the acceptance wording (a watermark
  pinned below a *permanent* refusal re-offers everything after it forever, so
  the durable held-row record carries the guarantee once the clamp's round is
  over), and the four residuals filed below. Both named gaps were closed as part
  of it: `FakeSyncTransport` can now deny and ignore rows, and
  `SyncStatusBanner`/`SyncStatusScreen` have widget tests for the first time.
  **Still to be checked live, not against a fake**: 10.25's device instruction
  for this case stands — a real server refusing a real replica, and a real phone
  showing the banner.
  **Mostly closed at the 2026-08-13 gate re-run (§9.7).**
  `test/e2e/refused_row_visibility_e2e_test.dart` drives the real `SyncEngine`
  against the real server, produces the refusal through the ordinary import
  workflow, and asserts the row survives, is held, is counted, is explained, is
  not counted as applied, is not re-offered until released, and is re-offered
  when it is. What is left is the phone: whether the sentence reads right at a
  glance on a small screen.
- **E-2. The e2e override reopens C-3 through two documented steps.**
  `docker-compose.e2e.yml` declares no `ports:` of its own, so it inherits
  `${SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}` from the base file. Follow the
  README's LAN walkthrough (`SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0`, the deliberate
  one-line opt-in 10.22 built), then follow `README.md:387` to run the e2e
  suite, and you get — verified with `docker compose config` — `host_ip:
  0.0.0.0` **plus** `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED=1` **plus** a
  bind-mounted directory of live magic-link tokens. Cleartext on every
  interface with §4.4's per-source magic-link and redemption limits raised to
  `1<<30`. That is C-3's own condition, recreated by 10.26, which is why it is
  rated as C-3 was. `docker-compose.server-test.yml:18` already shows the fix:
  hardcode `127.0.0.1:` rather than deriving from `.env`. **One line.**
  **NOT closed by task 10.32 (found 2026-08-13, G-2 above).** That one line was
  added, and it does not replace the base file's mapping — Compose *merges*
  `ports:` — so with the LAN opt-in taken both `0.0.0.0:8080` and
  `127.0.0.1:8080` still render. The stack now fails to start rather than
  exposing, which is Docker's bind ordering and not a control. G-2 has the
  verified one-token fix and why the task's own verification missed it.
- **F13 (carried, was already recorded blocking).** §7.6 rated it "Blocking
  before any real deployment" and it is unchanged — `validateServerUrl` has one

#### Must fix before the NEXT gate re-run (task 10.25, 2026-08-12)

*Neither blocks exposure. Both block the next gate being able to claim
anything, so they are not ordinary follow-ups. Evidence in §8.4.*

- **E-1. The regression tests for C-1, C-2 and C-5 default to inert.** `dart

  failed.** The 11 are `LateInitializationError` from
