  The finding this project's own record calls "invisible to two scoped reviews
  and 309 passing tests" would then be guarded on the default path by nothing,
  in green. **The fix is a guard test that fails when the database-backed suite
  did not run**, plus the missing `skip:` — in that order, because the second
  without the first is a regression.
  This also means task 10.26's acceptance criterion is not met for the server
  half: green there requires `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`, which is
  exactly the special knowledge the criterion said should not be needed.
  Recorded here rather than reopening 10.26, since the fix is new work.
  **Closed by task 10.31 (2026-08-12).** Guard landed first:
  `server/test/support/database_coverage_guard_test.dart` fails (never
  skips) when no database is configured, so `dart test` with no `POSTGRES_*`
  now exits non-zero instead of reporting "197 passed, 139 skipped" as
  green. Then the missing `skip:` was added to
  `tombstone_retention_test.dart`'s four groups, using a new shared helper
  (`server/test/support/database_test_config.dart`) that the other eleven
  Postgres-backed files were also migrated onto, replacing eleven
  copy-pasted `_config`/`_skipReason` pairs (one of which had a wording
  variant, one a differently-named variant) with a single definition. With
  no database: `dart test` now fails loudly at exactly 150 skips (139 + the
  11 newly-guarded). Against a real database
  (`scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`): all 348 tests pass, zero skips,
  including the C-1/C-2/C-5 coverage this was blocking. Standing rule
  recorded in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` under "Test Signal Integrity."
- **E-3. The documented in-place restore drops the live database before it
  knows the archive can be decrypted.** ***Never given a task, still open, and
  now reproduced destructively — see G-3 above, which supersedes this entry.*** `server/backup/restore.sh:59-84` runs
  `DROP DATABASE` → `CREATE DATABASE` → *then* `age --decrypt | psql`, with no
  prior validation of the identity or the archive header. The scenario is the
  one §4.9.1 exists for: an incident, the documented replace path, and either
  the wrong holder's identity mounted or an archive truncated in transit —
  live data gone, backup unreadable. No `--single-transaction` either, and
  since `age` authenticates per STREAM chunk, a truncated archive commits a
  valid prefix and then aborts, producing precisely the "exists, answers
  queries, missing rows" outcome the script's own comment claims
  `ON_ERROR_STOP` prevents (true for SQL errors, not for a decrypt abort).
  **The drill does not catch this**: its wrong-key check targets
  `drill_wrongkey`, a database that does not exist, so the drop path is never
  exercised with a bad key — which is how nine green checks and this coexist.
  Fix: verify the decrypt before dropping, restore into a temporary name and
  rename, add `--single-transaction`, and extend the drill to cover the
  replace path. Asset 2.

*Also from the re-run, non-blocking but recorded in §8.4 with evidence: D-4
(C-5's audit covers project-level denials only — every row-level `unauthorized`,
which is where C-1's exploits and D-1's probe live, writes nothing); D-5 (the
audit rows are unreadable as shipped — the console is off by default,
unreachable from the host under Docker even when on, and both READMEs document
a `curl` that returns 403; §7.6's owed README note is still owed and now
matters more); `revision` is unbounded so any writable row can be pinned at
`2^63-1`; the failed-first-publish path is distinguishable by timing; the
private-range check runs only at startup; `docker-compose.yml`'s `TRITRACK_ENV`
comment credits a behavioural no-op as a control; and two backup operational
defects — the SSH-recipient branch is dead code from a word-split, and the
restore identity mount sits on the shared service so a left-set variable binds
the private key into every backup run.*

*And still live from earlier gates, re-confirmed: **F15**, which fired during
this gate run and destroyed `tritrack_tritrack_postgres_data`. One `-p` flag.
Fix it regardless of the gate.*

#### From task 10.37 (2026-08-13) — G-3's second failure was not real, and what that says

***The finding's "two failures" framing was half wrong, and the half that was
wrong is instructive.** G-3 was written up as (a) the restore destroys before
verifying and (b) the archive would not decrypt, "which means encrypted backups
currently are not backups". (a) was real, reproduced, and is now fixed. (b) was
the harness reading its own setup as a result: `verify_e3_restore_replace.sh`
truncated the archive to 12656 of 37969 bytes **on purpose**, to manufacture an
unreadable one, and `age` refusing a truncated STREAM is the control working.
Confirmed before touching anything — a good archive decrypts and restores on
both paths, canary intact. §9.4's prose is actually careful ("before it knows
the archive can be decrypted"); the summary row and the task brief compressed it
into a decryption defect that does not exist.*

*Worth a task or an explicit acceptance, because this is a **reporting** failure
in the same family as the ones §9 catalogues: a gate instrument's deliberate
fault injection was carried forward as a finding, and the next reader was asked
to root-cause correct behaviour. **Recommend: gate instruments must distinguish
injected faults from observed ones in their own output** — the harness printed
`age: error: failed to decrypt…` with nothing marking it as the fault the
harness itself had just introduced. Belongs with 10.40's instrument self-check
work; if 10.40 is already in flight, fold it in there rather than opening a
task.*

*Also from this task, both closed here rather than deferred: the recorded
checksum was verified only by `scripts/restore_db.sh`, which cannot do an
in-place replace — so the one destructive path had no integrity check while
`server/README.md` said it did; and drill step 6 ("a different private key must
not decrypt it") accepted **any** non-zero exit, so a missing archive or an
unmountable identity would have passed it. That last one is the E-1 shape again
— a check that reports a pass without the control it names having run — now
seen in the backup drill as well as the server and e2e suites. **It strengthens
the case that 10.39's standing rule should be stated over every instrument, not
every test suite.***

*One consequence to be aware of rather than fix: a successful in-place restore
now leaves a `<target>_replaced_<stamp>` database behind on purpose, and nothing
prunes it. That is deliberate — the alternative is the failure mode this task
exists to remove — but an operator who restores repeatedly will accumulate them.
Documented in `server/README.md`; no scheduled cleanup, same gap §4.7's
retention and the backup cron already have.* **Resolved by 10.40: the retention
rule is "never automatic"** — a `_replaced_` database can be the only proof a
bad restore is recoverable, so auto-pruning it reintroduces G-3's shape one
layer up. `restore.sh` now prints a `NOTE` listing any other `_replaced_`
databases still present every time it creates a new one, so the count is
visible at the moment an operator is already looking; dropping them stays a
manual, deliberate act. Documented in `server/README.md`.

#### From task 10.28 (2026-08-13) — a second silent-loss path, needs its own task

***This is D-3's failure mode reached by a different route, and it predates the
refusal path entirely.** Found because a 10.28 regression test tripped over it:
the test seeded observations older than the device's own `Users`/`Projects` rows
and pushed with a small batch, and the observations were never offered — not on
that round, and not on the four rounds after it. Not a refusal, not a conflict,
not counted as pending: **rows that exist only on the device while the app
reports a clean sync.** Model: **Opus** — it is a selection-and-cursor design
question, and the plan's own note says over-pushing is cheap and under-pushing
loses an observation.*

- **The push watermark advances past rows the batch limit never offered.**
  `_collectChangedRows` walks `syncTables` in FK order, taking `limit - count`
  rows from each with `ORDER BY updated_at ASC`, and `_push` then sets the
  watermark to the highest `updated_at` **offered**. When the limit is reached in
  an early table, later tables are never queried — and their rows can be *older*
  than what was offered, so the new watermark is above them and
  `updated_at >= watermark` never selects them again. The per-table ordering is
  local; the watermark is global; nothing reconciles the two.
  **The realistic trigger is the same workflow as D-3.** A replica preserves the
  sender's clock verbatim (task 6.3), so an imported observation is *older* than
  almost everything else on the device — exactly the row this strands, on any
  device holding more than `defaultSyncBatchSize` rows newer than it.
  `pendingRowCount` uses the same predicate, so it does not count the stranded
  row either.
- **Related, same root: boundary rows can starve a small batch indefinitely.**
  The deliberate `>=` bias re-offers every row sharing the watermark timestamp,
  and those re-offers consume batch slots before anything new is reached. With
  enough rows on the boundary and a small enough batch, no new row is ever
  offered. Only a problem at small batch sizes today, but it is the same
  "per-table selection under a global limit" defect and should be fixed with it.
- **The fix is the exact pending-set `_collectChangedRows`' own doc comment
  already files as follow-up** — a dirty flag or local change sequence, so
  selection is "rows not yet accepted" rather than a clock comparison. This is
  the second, sharper reason to want it: the first was a device whose clock jumps
  backwards, which is speculative; this one is reachable with a correct clock and
  ordinary data. An interim narrowing (clamp the watermark to the truncation
  point rather than the highest offered) was considered and rejected as a
  drive-by: done naively it stalls the push instead, which is worse. **Do not
  patch it inside another task.**

  **All three closed by task 10.33 (2026-08-13)**, by the pending-set route the
  third bullet names: `Sync_Row_Receipts` replaced the push watermark outright,
  so selection is "rows the server has not confirmed" and the batch limit can no
  longer strand anything, the `>=` boundary re-offer that caused the starvation
  is gone, and `pendingRowCount` shares the push's own predicate rather than
  re-deriving it. See that task's entry — in particular for **why the first
  bullet understates the bug**: the imported replica is stranded on any device
  that has ever pushed anything newer, with no batch limit involved, which is
  what ruled out the narrower per-table-watermark fix.

#### From task 10.33 (2026-08-13) — the receipt table's own edges

*None of these is a loss path — the receipt scheme fails toward re-offering —
but each is a place where the new table is less tidy than the data it describes.*

- **Nothing ever removes an orphan receipt.** A receipt outlives the row it
  describes if that row is hard-deleted. There is exactly one such path today,
  `ServerIdentityAdopter._deleteOldUserRows` (the documented exception to the
  no-hard-deletes rule), so the leak is a handful of rows per identity
  adoption — and task 10.11's tombstone retention will add a second if it ever
  purges locally. Harmless (an orphan is never joined against) and bounded, but
  it means the table is not exactly "one row per row this device holds," which
  is what its own doc comment claims. A vacuum pass, or a delete alongside that
  one call site, closes it.
- **The push selection now scans a project's rows rather than a range.** Once
  everything is synced the old `updated_at >= watermark` query touched roughly
  one row; the join touches every row of every table for the project, per push,
  probing a unique index for each. Measured against a season of field data this
  is milliseconds and it buys an exact pending set, which is the trade the plan
  asks for — but it is a real change in shape, and it is worth an actual
  measurement on a full season before the first long field deployment rather
  than an estimate.
- **A merge that only remaps a `user_id` is invisible to the receipt.**
  `ProjectMerger`'s cross-device user dedup rewrites FK columns on rows it
  merges; where it does so without touching `updated_at`, the row still matches
  its receipt and is not re-offered, so this device's remap is not propagated.
  Pre-existing — the watermark did not catch it either, and
  `ServerIdentityAdopter`'s own rewrite *does* bump `updated_at`/`revision`, so
  the main identity path is fine. Recorded because the receipt scheme makes
  "what does the server actually hold" a question with a precise answer for the
  first time, and this is the one place the answer can be wrong.
- **`SyncStateStore.clear` deliberately leaves receipts alone.** A receipt
  states what the server holds, which does not stop being true at sign-out, and
  dropping them would make the next sign-in re-upload the whole project. If a
  future decision says a different identity on the same device must not inherit
  them, that is a policy change with a real cost, not an oversight to patch.

#### From task 10.29 (2026-08-13) — what closing D-1 could not close, and what it narrowed

*The first item is the one that needs a planning decision; it is the only real
close for D-1's third arm and it is a schema change, so it is deliberately not
attempted inside a remediation task. The rest are consequences of the fix.*

- **Project-scoped primary keys — the actual close for the create-if-absent
  residual (§4.13).** Every table is keyed by a client-chosen UUID that is unique
  *across the server*, so "create a row under this id" answers differently
  depending on whether some other project already holds it. That is the whole of
  what D-1's arm (c) is, and it is also the `Projects` publish-collision residual
  §4.13 has carried since 10.21 — one property, recorded twice. Keying rows by
  `(project_id, row_id)` removes it outright: a key another project holds no
  longer collides, so there is nothing to answer. It would also make Phase 6.3's
  faithful replicas importable into a *different* project, which
  `crossProjectCapture` currently refuses. **Cost: composite primary keys and
  composite foreign keys on every table, on both schemas, i.e. a `schemaMajor`
  bump and a migration on real field data.** Needs its own task and the planning
  session's call on whether the residual is worth that; recorded so the choice is
  made rather than inherited. Model: **Opus**.
  **Done by task 10.35 (2026-08-13) — decision: proceed.** See that task's entry.
  The residual alone would not have justified the bump; what settled it was the
  parenthetical above about Phase 6.3's replicas, which turned out to be not a
  bonus but the actual case: shared observations land in a different project
  than they came from *by default* (the payload carries no project id), so
  `crossProjectCapture` was permanently refusing an ordinary intended workflow,
  symmetrically, in a way task 11.2 could not have fixed.
- **Row-level denials are still unaudited (D-4), and D-1's fix makes more of
  them.** Every probe closed above returns `200` with an `unauthorized` outcome
  and never reaches `auditDenial`, which is wired only to the three project-level
  `403` paths. §7.3 B5's complaint — "an attacker can probe indefinitely and
  `/diagnostics/auth-events` shows a clean history" — is still literally true for
  exactly these requests, and the refusals are now the *common* answer rather
  than a corner. D-4 already exists as a recorded non-blocking finding; this is
  the second reason to give it a task, and it must be done with 10.30's bound in
  hand or it recreates D-2 on a route an attacker controls the volume of.
- **A tag used by a project but never linked to it will now be held.** The tag
  check asks whether the project *reaches* the tag, and in practice that edge is
  the `Project_Tags` row every tag-creation path writes
  (`ProjectTagRepository.linkOrReactivate`). A tag reachable only through an
  observation that is itself being pushed for the first time is fine — the push's
  own established-tag set covers it — but a legacy database holding an
  observation whose tag was never linked would have that observation held rather
  than synced. Held, explained and retryable (10.28), not lost, and no code path
  in the app produces it today. Worth a one-off local integrity check before the
  first real deployment rather than a code change.
- **`TagCsvImport` creates tags with a null `last_modified_by`.**
  `SyncMeta.initial(now: DateTime.now())` with no `modifiedBy`, unlike every
  other creation path in the app. Noticed while looking for server-verifiable tag
  provenance — the fix above does not depend on it, which is why it is filed
  rather than patched here. It is the same class as task 7.4's NULL-modifiedBy
  work and should be swept up with anything else in that family.

#### From task 10.28 (2026-08-13) — the refused-row fix's own edges

*None blocking. All are residuals of the D-3 fix rather than of the finding, and
the first two are the ones that will look like bugs to a user first.*

- **The importer still tells the user their import succeeded with no hint it may
  never sync.** `SharedObservationImporter` says "Observation saved, attributed
  to the original observer" the moment it writes the replica, and everything
  10.28 built only speaks after the *next* sync round refuses it. The
  information needed to warn at import time already exists locally — whether the
  named user is a member of this project — so the import flow could say "this
  will not sync until Ada is added to the project" immediately instead of
  reporting a refusal minutes later on a different screen. Belongs with **task
  11.2**, which owns membership and invitations and is what makes the refusal
  fixable at all; filed here so 11.2 inherits the requirement rather than the
  surprise.
- **`SyncStatus.pendingCount` overstates by design, and the clamp nudges it.**
  The `>=` watermark bias means rows sharing the boundary timestamp count as
  "waiting to sync" on every round even though the server already has them, and
  a refusal's clamp widens that window to a batch for one round. Held rows are
  now subtracted, so the number is no longer wrong about *those* — but it is
  still "rows in the push window," not "rows the server lacks." Fixing it
  properly is the exact-pending-set item `_collectChangedRows`' own doc comment
  already files (a dirty flag or local change sequence instead of a clock
  comparison); this is one more reason to want it.
- **`SyncRunReport.lostToServer` still counts no-op losses.** The durable
  conflict record now skips a "loss" where nothing was superseded, but the
  report's tally is raw protocol outcomes, so a round that re-offers accepted
  rows still reports them as lost. Nothing user-facing reads it that way
  (the reviewable list is read from the store), so this is a naming/telemetry
  wart rather than a defect — but a future consumer of that list would inherit
  the wrong meaning.
- **An unkeyable refusal cannot be clamped or automatically retried.** If the
  server refuses a row it could not key (`Table/?`), there is no timestamp to
  clamp the watermark against and no identity to suppress on, so the guarantee
  reduces to the durable held record plus a generic entry on the status screen.
  Pathological — every sync table's primary key is a non-empty UUID `TEXT` — and
  the fail-safe direction, but worth knowing when reading `_earliestRefusedUpdatedAt`.
- **Neither `Sync_Held_Rows` nor `Sync_Conflicts` is cleaned up when a project
  is deleted or unlinked.** `SyncStateStore.clear` drops the prefs keys; both
  client-only tables keep their rows keyed by a `project_id` that no longer
  exists. Harmless today (every read is project-scoped, so an orphaned row is
  simply never selected) and it is the same shape for both tables, so it wants
  one fix, not two.

#### From task 10.35 (2026-08-13) — the major bump's loose ends

*None blocking. The first two are real gaps the bump created or exposed; the
third is a carried item this task could have closed and did not.*

- **Encrypted server backups still carry no schema-version marker, and now it
  matters.** `server/backup/backup.sh` writes `tritrack-<timestamp>.age` with a
  `.sha256` sidecar and nothing else — no manifest, no version in the filename,
  no grep hit for `schema_version` anywhere in the backup or restore scripts.
  The version exists only inside the dump, as `schema_migrations` rows,
  discoverable only *after* a full decrypt and restore. Before task 10.35 this
  cost nothing because there was only ever one schema. Now a pre-bump archive
  restored under a post-bump binary hits `PostgresMigrations.run`, which
  applies v6 and succeeds — the right outcome — but an archive from a *future*
  major would fail with a `StateError` after the restore has already happened.
  Loud, not silent, so it is not a data-loss risk; the cost is that an operator
  cannot tell which major an archive holds before committing to restoring it.
  Fix is small (version in the filename, or a plaintext sidecar next to the
  `.sha256`). **`scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh` should assert it**, since its
  own header already says to re-run it after any schema change and it currently
  knows nothing about versions.
- **Any out-of-tree tool that speaks the wire is refused until it is updated,
  and nothing lists them.** `scripts/verify_d1_per_row_oracle.py` hardcoded
  `schema_major: 1` and started failing with a `409` the moment the server
  moved — correct behaviour, and it was caught immediately because the script
  is run as evidence. But the other `verify_*.py` gate scripts have the same
  shape, and a major bump silently invalidates every one of them that is not
  exercised in the same session. Worth either centralising the envelope
  constant across `scripts/`, or listing the wire-speaking tools somewhere the
  next bump will look. Cheap now, confusing in a year.
- **The e2e serialization-fidelity fix is analyzer-verified only.**
  `test/e2e/serialization_fidelity_e2e_test.dart` built a push outcome key as
  `Observations/<observation_id>` and was corrected to use `syncRowKey`. The
  full e2e suite subsequently ran green in one pass against a live server, so
  this is very likely fine — but that file's assertion was not individually
  traced, and it is the kind of change that can pass by no longer asserting
  anything. Worth one look during the next real-server session.
- **Carried, not closed: the live-device verification from 10.34.** This task
  ran everything against a real server over HTTP, including the refused-row and
  major-refusal paths, but still nothing against a real *phone*. 10.34's
  held-row copy and D-3's banner both remain verified only at the widget-tree
  level. Unchanged and still folded into 10.25's next device checklist — noted
  here only so the "verified live" language above is not mistaken for having
  covered it.

#### From task 10.52 (2026-08-15) — what the trusted-proxy scheme newly assumes

*None blocking. Each is a consequence of the fix rather than a gap in it, and
each is the kind of assumption that becomes wrong quietly.*

- **The e2e stack still disables the per-source limit, and that is now the only
  place the control is unmeasured.** `docker-compose.e2e.yml` still sets
  `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED=1`, deliberately untouched here —
  that is **task 10.54's I-3**, and 10.52 had no business changing the stack
  the gate attacks out from under it. Worth saying explicitly for 10.54: the
  reason the flag exists (Docker's port proxy collapsing every e2e client onto
  one address) is *the same collapse this task just built the machinery to
  resolve*, and it is now fixable rather than only suppressible — put the e2e
  stack behind the same proxy, or teach the suite to declare the bridge
  gateway. Either turns a disabled control into an exercised one. Not done
  here because it changes what every other instrument runs against.
- **The in-process counter shortcut is load-bearing in a second way now.** §4.4
  already flags per-instance counters as prototype-only because they multiply
  the effective limit. With per-client keys they also multiply the *memory*:
  the key space was previously bounded by the number of peers that could reach
  the origin — behind a proxy, exactly one — and is now bounded by the number
  of distinct client addresses on the internet. `evictExpired` and the fixed
  windows keep this bounded in time rather than in count, which is the same
  posture as before but with a much larger constant. Fine at TriTrack's scale;
  it belongs in the Redis/Postgres migration's brief, not deferred silently.
- **`172.31.242.0/24` is now a fixed assumption of the TLS overlay.** Pinning
  the proxy's address is what makes it nameable in the allowlist, and pinning
  the address requires pinning the subnet. It is overridable
  (`TRITRACK_TLS_PROXY_SUBNET` / `_ADDRESS`, documented together in
  `.env.example`), but a host that already uses that range gets a compose
  failure at `up` rather than a hint. Acceptable — it fails loudly and the fix
  is one line — but it is a new way for a clean checkout to not come up on
  somebody's machine, and the first such failure will not obviously be about
  rate limiting.
- **A second proxy hop is parsed but never tested against a real one.** The
  right-to-left walk that skips trusted hops has unit coverage
  (`trusted_proxies_test.dart`) and no live coverage, because this repository
  ships one proxy. If a deployment ever fronts Caddy with something else, that
  path becomes real and is currently believed rather than observed — which is
  precisely the shape of the failure this whole task was about.

#### BLOCKING — Security Gate C (task 10.16, 2026-08-07)

***All five are CLOSED as of task 10.25 (2026-08-12)** — re-run live against a
running stack and all five refused, with C-1, C-2, C-3 and C-5 additionally
checked against builds with their own fixes reverted, where each reproduces the
original finding verbatim. Evidence: §8.2, and `scripts/verify_c1_row_naming.py`,
`verify_c2_existence_oracle.py`, `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults.py`,
`verify_c5_denial_audit.py`, `backup_restore_drill.sh`. **The gate still fails**
— on the items filed above this block, not on these. Kept as written for the
record.*

***These block any exposure beyond localhost.** Gate C failed on all five. Full
evidence, including live reproductions, is in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §7.3.
Each needs its own task; the gate must be re-run once they are closed. Model:
**Opus** for C-1 through C-3 — these are authorization and transport
architecture, not wiring.*

- **C-1. `RowAuthorizer` never checks who a row *names*, only who owns it.**
  One omission, four confirmed-live instances: an `Observations.user_id` insert
  and a `Non_Detections.user_id` insert both disclose an arbitrary victim's
  `Users` row *and* their full `User_Emails` history to the attacker's own
  project; a `Projects.owner_user_id` **update** does the same while the
  attacker keeps access through their own membership row; and — the severest —
  an attacker can create a row they legitimately author, rewrite its `user_id`
  to a victim, and be **locked out of the row they fabricated**, leaving the
  server's authoritative record saying the victim made an observation they
  never made. That last one is asset 2 and directly contradicts
  `RowAuthorizer`'s own class doc ("updating a row attributed to someone else …
  Always denied, with no exemption").
  **Fix as one invariant, not four patches:** an incoming row may not name a
  user other than the caller, on any table, on insert or update, unless real
  replication provenance backs it. Note the seam that probably preserves
  legitimate first-publish replication: disclosure is only possible when the
  named `Users` row **already exists on the server**. Gate B closed this exact
  class for `last_modified_by` and `Project_Memberships` — the reasoning was
  right and was applied to two columns instead of derived as a rule. Every
  instance needs a failing test before the fix lands.
- **C-2. Project existence oracle — violates §4.13.** `ProjectAccess.absent`
  permits sync (correctly, for publish), so a nonexistent `project_id` returns
  **200 empty** while an existing-but-forbidden one returns **403**, on pull,
  push, and ack. §4.13's `Violated by:` list names this failure mode first, and
  task 10.10 rejected the row-level version of it by name. Existence only, no
  content; ids are v4 UUIDs but they travel in `TT1:` payloads and CSV exports.
- **C-3. §4.1's cleartext exemption was half-built, and the shipped compose
  file defaults it on.** `security_config.dart` implements the `TRITRACK_ENV`
  check and has **no private-range check at all**, so cleartext on a public
  interface is permitted with a warning rather than refused. `docker-compose
  .yml:54-55` then defaults `TRITRACK_ALLOW_CLEARTEXT_LAN=1` and
  `TRITRACK_ENV=development` behind a `0.0.0.0` publish. §4.10's own reasoning
  — "the default is what gets deployed" — was applied to the diagnostics
  console and not to this file.
- **C-4. §4.9 encrypted server backups remain unimplemented.** Already recorded
  as open by 10.14 with a sound reason (§6 item 8: no key custody arrangement).
  10.16 did not treat it as satisfied. Still blocking for a deployment holding
  real data, because §2.1's control list names it against the actor this whole
  model is organised around. Needs the custody arrangement first.
- **C-5. `authorization_denied` audit events are never written.** `auditDenial`
  runs `AuthAuditLog` on the raw `Connection` while the sync handler's
  `db.runTx` is open; `postgres` refuses it and `record`'s catch swallows the
  exception. Verified against the database: **zero** such rows after this gate
  generated many 403s, while every other event type recorded normally. An
  attacker can probe indefinitely and `/diagnostics/auth-events` shows a clean
  history. `grep authorizationDenied server/test` returns nothing — no test
  covers it. Same root cause affects `DiagnosticsRepository`/`SyncTrafficLogStore`
  sharing that one `Connection`, where it surfaces as an opaque 500 instead.

#### From task 10.20 (2026-08-09)

*The first two are not caused by 10.20 — they were found by running the suites
it needed. Both matter to task 10.25, which has to run everything.*

- **`flutter test` is red on `main`, and has been since the Gate C commit.**
  `test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart` flags
  `CLAUDE_DOCS/TriTrack_Security_Model.md` for `POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?...}` — a
  shell parameter-expansion fragment quoted inside §4.6's own prose, not a
  credential. The test is right to be blunt about this class, so the fix is
  probably to make the scanner recognise `${VAR:?...}` / `${VAR:-...}` as
  expansions rather than assignments, not to reword the doc. Verify against the
  whole doc set, since the same shape will recur. **One test, one file, but it
  means nobody can currently tell a real secret leak from this.**
- **The e2e suite cannot be run in one shot, and never could.** `flutter test
  test/e2e --tags e2e` fails ~18 of 22 with `429` from `/auth/magic-link`: §4.4
  allows 10 sign-ins per source per 15 minutes and the suite mints a fresh
  identity per test — `two_device_convergence_e2e_test.dart` alone spends 12, so
  it cannot pass even alone. Every file passes with a server restart between
  files (in-process limiter, so a restart resets it), which is how 10.20 ran it.
  The rate limit is behaving exactly as designed; the *suite* is the thing that
  needs fixing — a test-only policy override or a documented per-file loop. As
  it stands the README's documented command cannot succeed, which is how a real
  e2e regression would get mistaken for the usual 429s.
- **Phase 11 must reopen replication for colleagues who have accounts here.**
  The invariant refuses an insert naming a user the server already holds, which
  is right in Phase 10 (there is no way to *be* a collaborator) but means a
  genuine teammate's imported observations stop replicating the moment that
  teammate registers. Task 11.2's invitation record is the provenance that
  should reopen it — deliberately, as an explicit clause in `_authorizeNaming`,
  rather than by widening the exemption. Fold into 11.2 alongside its existing
  `Project_Memberships` relaxation.
- **A membership row that already names someone else becomes updatable by the
  project owner.** Deleting Gate B's per-table check means `projectOwner` alone
  governs an update whose `user_id` is unchanged — i.e. an owner could end-date
  or re-role an existing member. Unreachable in Phase 10, because the invariant
  makes such a row impossible to create in the first place, and it is plausibly
  the behaviour 11.2 wants. Flagged so 11.2 decides it rather than inherits it.
- **Residual, recorded not closed: the "server has never heard of them" seam is
  evaluated at insert time.** An attacker who plants a naming edge to an id the
  server does not yet hold keeps that edge if the id later *becomes* held —
  which would disclose that person's `Users` row on a later pull. It cannot be
  aimed at an account (`auth_accounts.user_id` is server-generated at redemption
  and unpredictable), so it requires a third party to publish that exact id from
  a `TT1:` payload the attacker already has — meaning the attacker already held
  the identity. Closing it properly means recording naming provenance per edge
  and filtering at pull, which is a Phase 11 shape. Re-check under 11.3's
  multi-member reachability.

#### From task 10.21 (2026-08-09)

- **Phase 11 must re-examine what "no relationship" means, in both directions.**
  10.21 made a project the caller has no relationship to contribute nothing to
  row authorization — no reachability, no tag vouching. That is right while
  `permitsSync` means owner-or-member, but 11.1 widens membership and 11.2 adds
  invitations, and both change *when* a caller has a relationship without
  touching the code that assumes it. The gate to re-run is the one in
  `verify_c2_existence_oracle.py`: it compares responses, so it stays valid.
- **The residual create-collision signal should be rate-limited, not just
  audited.** A first publish still distinguishes a free id from a taken one
  (§4.13), and nothing bounds how often a session may attempt one. §4.4's
  limiter covers the unauthenticated auth routes only. A per-session cap on
  *failed* establishing pushes would make the residual expensive as well as
  attributable. Not blocking — the probe already costs a well-formed project row
  and leaves the prober owning a project — but it is the obvious next turn of
  the screw, and it belongs with 11.2's invitation work where publish stops
  being the only way a project appears.
- **`ProjectAccess.member` is still unreachable, and now load-bearing.** It was
  modelled ahead of Phase 11 (task 10.10) and never occurs, because every
  project has exactly one member. 10.21 put it in `permitsSync` alongside
  `owner`, so the first time 11.1 creates a real non-owner member it will also
  be the first time that branch executes — including the two vouching checks
  above. Worth an explicit test in 11.1 rather than discovering it in a gate.
- **The savepoint is the only one in the codebase.** `attemptPublish` opens
  `SAVEPOINT tritrack_publish` inside the request transaction and rolls back to
  it on any failure. Nothing else nests a transaction, so if a second call site
  ever wants one, the savepoint name needs to stop being a single constant.
  Noted because a name collision here fails silently in the worst way — an inner
  rollback undoing an outer one's work.

#### From task 10.22 (2026-08-09)

- **`SslMode.disable` is a hardcoded cleartext default on every Postgres
  connection** — `bin/server.dart`, `bin/purge_audit_logs.dart`, and eleven test
  files, as a `const`. This is the *third* place §4.10's "the default is what
  gets deployed" was missed, found while checking for one; already recorded as
  an observation in §7.6, but 10.22's own finding is that it is worse than a
  default — there is no override at all, so a deployment moving Postgres to a
  managed host cannot enable TLS without a code change and will ship every row
  of asset 1 in cleartext between hosts. Not fixed here: it is a
  deployment-topology decision (which sslMode, verify-full or not, and what CA),
  and doing it properly means resolving `POSTGRES_HOST` and refusing `disable`
  when it is not private — the same predicate 10.22 added, applied to the other
  socket. Correct today only because the base compose keeps Postgres on the
  Docker-internal network with no `ports:`. **Should land before any deployment
  that does not, and before 10.25 signs off a topology that could.**
- **The e2e suite can no longer be run in one pass, and this is not new.**
  §4.4's magic-link limiter allows 10 per 15 minutes per source, and behind
  Docker's port publish every client presents as the bridge gateway — one shared
  bucket for the whole suite (already recorded in §7.6). The suite mints more
  than 10 sign-ins, so `flutter test test/e2e` fails ~18 tests with 429
  regardless of `-j`. Confirmed pre-existing: reproduced identically with the
  old `0.0.0.0` publish restored. All seven files pass one at a time with a
  `docker compose restart server` between them, which is the procedure until
  §4.4's per-source bucket stops collapsing — but "green e2e" currently depends
  on knowing that, and the README does not say it. Either document the
  procedure or exempt a private-range source from the limiter in dev.
  **Resolved by task 10.26**: `RateLimitPolicy.fromEnvironment` reads
  `TRITRACK_RATE_LIMIT_PER_SOURCE_DISABLED` (set only in
  `docker-compose.e2e.yml`, refused under `TRITRACK_ENV=production`) to raise
  the per-source magic-link/redemption ceilings for the e2e environment only.
  `flutter test test/e2e --tags e2e` passes in one pass now; verified twice
  live against the compose stack.
- **`test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart` has been failing on `main`
  since before this task.** It flags `CLAUDE_DOCS/DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md` and
  `CLAUDE_DOCS/TriTrack_Security_Model.md` where prose *quotes* compose's
  required-secret marker — the variable name, a colon, then `?` and the error
  text — and the assignment regex reads that as a literal value. Verified
  pre-existing by stashing all of 10.22's changes. Nothing is leaked; the cost
  is that a security test is red in the tree, and a red security test is one
  people stop reading. Note the trap while fixing it: the regex matches from the
  variable *name*, so its `value.startsWith(r'$')` escape never fires for a
  `${...}` interpolation — the compose file itself is exempt only because it is
  in `_selfDocumentingPaths`, which is why this reads as a docs-only problem
  when it is really a detector one. Small, and worth doing before 10.25 rather
  than during it.
  **Resolved by task 10.26**: the regex now captures the separator character
  and skips bash parameter-expansion operators (`:-`, `:=`, `:+`, `:?`) that
  reuse `:`, rather than treating every `NAME:` as a YAML-style assignment.
  Covered by four new unit tests against the detector logic directly,
  including one that plants a real-looking assignment and confirms it is
  still caught.

#### From task 10.23 (2026-08-09)

- **`server/test/sync/tombstone_retention_test.dart` fails instead of skipping
  when Postgres is unavailable.** Every other Postgres-tagged file in
  `server/test` passes `skip: _skipReason` (or checks `_config == null` before
  doing anything) on each `group(...)`, so a `dart test` run with no database
  configured shows those as skipped. This file's four `group(...)` calls
  (`the resurrection case`, `the guard does not strand devices...`, `the
  upgrade path`, `what purging does and does not remove`) never take
  `skip:`, so instead of skipping cleanly the tests run, hit
  `LateInitializationError: Local 'connection' has not been initialized` in
  the shared `pushAs` helper, and report as **failed** — 11 failures on a
  clean `dart test` with no Postgres configured. Confirmed pre-existing on
  `main` before this task via `git stash`; not caused by this task's changes,
  and this task did not touch this file. Cosmetic in that Postgres-backed CI
  is unaffected (`dart test --tags postgres` is green, 342/342), but it is
  exactly 10.26's failure mode — a red signal nobody can act on trains people
  to stop reading it — and 10.25 will see these 11 failures on any pass that
  doesn't already have Postgres up. Fix: add `skip: _skipReason` to all four
  groups, matching every sibling file.

#### From task 10.24 (2026-08-09)

- **Nothing schedules the backup, and nothing schedules the drill.** Exactly
  the gap §4.7's retention already has (`AuditRetentionService.purge()` is a
  working mechanism nobody runs), now duplicated for the control §2.1's own
  list names. `scripts/backup_db.sh` is a cron line and `scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh`
  is a quarterly calendar entry, and both currently exist only as sentences in
  `server/README.md`. A backup job that was never scheduled and an audit purge
  that was never scheduled fail the same way: the mechanism passes review, the
  deployment has neither. Worth one task that decides *where* periodic work
  runs for this server — cron in the container, a host timer, or a scheduler
  service — and wires all three (purge, backup, drill reminder) to it, rather
  than three more README paragraphs. **Should land before 10.25 signs off a
  deployment posture**, since "backups exist" and "backups are being taken" are
  different claims.
- **Holder 2 of the backup key is unnamed, and that is the last unmet half of
  §6 item 8.** Deliberate — see the task entry — but it means the shipped
  arrangement is one-recipient-plus-paper until a real deployment exists. The
  trigger is written into §4.9.1 (before the first backup of real data) and the
  job warns on every run, which is a warning and not a control. Whoever stands
  the server up owns this; it is an arrangement between two people, not code.
- **A departing holder requires archive re-encryption, and nothing tooling-side
  supports it.** §4.9.1 records the obligation — their key still decrypts every
  archive written during their tenure, so rotating recipients is not sufficient
  and those archives must be deleted or re-encrypted — but there is no
  `rotate_backup_recipients.sh`. Today the honest answer is "delete them and let
  retention be the exposure bound", which is acceptable for a 30-archive window
  and would not be for a longer one. This is §2.1's departing-student case
  applied to the backup key itself; revisit if retention ever lengthens.
- **Archives are second-resolution and refuse to overwrite, so two backups
  within the same second fail the second one.** Correct behaviour (never
  clobber an archive) with a slightly rough edge (a confusing failure if
  someone loops the script). Only reachable by running backups back to back;
  recorded rather than fixed because the fix — a counter suffix — adds a
  filename shape the retention sort would have to learn about.

#### Non-blocking, from Security Gate C (2026-08-07)

*Recorded in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §7.6 with evidence. Several become
blocking the moment the server is exposed or Phase 11 adds a second member —
each says which.*

- **Blocking before any real deployment: the client's release-mode `https`
  requirement is form validation, not transport enforcement.**
  `validateServerUrl` is only called by the settings screen's validator;
  `setUrl` persists whatever it is given and `build()` reads it back unchecked,
  so an `http://` URL stored by a debug build carries the 90-day bearer token
  in cleartext from a release build. Android fails closed; iOS/macOS do not.
  Fix at client construction, not at form submit. *(Narrowed by 10.22, not
  closed: the validator now also refuses a non-private `http://` target in
  every build, so the stored URL can at least only be a LAN one. The bypass is
  unchanged — `setUrl` still persists whatever it is handed, and `build()`
  still reads it back unchecked.)*
- **Blocking for Phase 11 (fold into task 11.3 alongside §5.9):** orphan `Tags`
  are readable *and* overwritable cross-user, which widens §5.9(a) — that item
  recorded the write half only, and the read half is new. A `User_Emails` row
  for your *own* `user_id` may carry someone *else's* address, which is a staged
  identity-collision primitive that 11.2's invitation flow supplies the delivery
  path for. And `Users` row pre-emption lets an attacker permanently win
  last-write-wins against a victim's genuine profile push.
- **§4.15 needs re-deciding against a multi-member population.** Its central
  argument — "the destination is storage the user already owns" — is falsified
  by 10.9's publish/join: one member's default-on, unencrypted cloud backup now
  carries their colleagues' names, prior email history, and coordinates into
  that member's personal cloud account, without those colleagues' knowledge.
  The decision itself was properly explicit (10.16 confirmed that); the trust
  boundary it reasoned about has since widened.
- **Controls specified but never built, none of them recorded as deferred until
  now:** §4.12 requirement 1 (a NULL governing value must be a server-side
  rejection — currently substituted for by NOT NULL constraints, which a future
  nullable column silently removes); §4.8 control 2 (detect whether the device
  has a passcode and warn once — §4.8's entire case for skipping SQLCipher rests
  on platform disk encryption, which is void without one); §4.10's "never
  enabled in production" refusal; §4.7's retention *schedule* (the mechanism
  works, nothing runs it).
- **Smaller, each a one-file fix:** the diagnostics router is mounted as a
  catch-all, so with the console enabled *every* unmatched path returns a
  branded diagnostics error (verified: `/nope`, `/admin`, `/wp-login.php`);
  unchecked casts run before authentication on all three sync routes, so an
  unauthenticated malformed body returns 500 rather than 401;
  `/auth/link-status` distinguishes an email-rate-limited request from a
  delivered one (extends Gate A finding 6, which was explicitly deferred here);
  `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_TOKEN` is exempt from the §4.6 placeholder check;
  `EmailSender.sendMagicLink` returns `void`, making §4.5's async requirement
  unexpressible before an SMTP sender exists; Postgres `SslMode.disable` is a
  hard-coded constant rather than configuration.
- **`scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` destroys the developer's Postgres
  volume.** No `-p`, so it resolves to the same `tritrack_postgres_data` the dev
  stack uses, and `trap cleanup EXIT` runs `down -v` on success, failure, and
  Ctrl-C alike. Untracked working-tree file, never reviewed. Give the test stack
  its own project name and drop `-v` from an EXIT trap. Durability, not
  confidentiality — but it silently deletes every published project and audit
  row in whatever local stack was running.
- **Worth a README note before someone reaches for it:** inside Docker the
  server sees the bridge gateway as the peer, never `127.0.0.1`, so the
  diagnostics console is unreachable through the published port even from the
  host. That is the right failure direction, but it means the console as shipped
  cannot be used at all — which someone will eventually "fix" with
  `TRITRACK_DIAGNOSTICS_ALLOW_REMOTE=true`. Combined with C-3 that puts every
  project's coordinates in a browser over cleartext, with the console token in a
  readable header.

*From task 10.0 (2026-08-01). Section references are to
`CLAUDE_DOCS/TriTrack_Security_Model.md`. None of these blocked 10.0.*

- **`.gitignore` has no secret patterns** — no `.env`, no `*.key`, no
  `secrets*`. §4.6 requires them and they must land **before 10.3**, which
  creates the first file that could hold a credential. Smallest possible change;
  fold into 10.3.
- **Task 10.6 needs to name secure storage.** §4.8 makes keychain/keystore
  storage of the session token mandatory — it is the highest-value control in
  that decision, and the app currently has no secure-storage dependency at all
  (`device_id` sits in plaintext SharedPreferences). 10.6 needs the dependency
  (`flutter_secure_storage` or equivalent, justified per the standing criteria)
  and an acceptance criterion that the token is never written to
  SharedPreferences or the SQLite DB.
- **Task 10.1's spec is slightly off on `latestSchemaVersion`.** It is not a
  constant in `lib/data/db/schema.dart` — it is derived as the max of the
  migration list in `lib/data/db/migrations.dart` (currently 5). The
  "exactly one definition in the repo" criterion still holds; the extraction is
  just a different mechanism than the plan describes.
- **The auto cloud backup path is the largest existing disclosure surface in
  the app, and it predates the server entirely.** `CloudBackupService` writes
  unencrypted zips containing every user's name and email plus every
  full-precision coordinate for a project, on a schedule, into a user-linked
  third-party cloud folder. Outside every control in the security model
  (§3.7, §5.7). Needs its own task: at minimum an in-flow statement of what
  leaves the device, plausibly optional archive encryption. **Not a Phase 10
  task** — it is a client-side data-handling task with no server dependency, so
  it wants a home rather than being wedged in here.
- **`TT1:` share payloads are unauthenticated** (§3.7, §4.12). No signature or
  MAC, so a pasted payload's claimed `user_id`, `origin_device_id`, and
  `revision` are attacker-controlled inputs to last-write-wins ordering.
  Bounded server-side by §4.11 (a pushed row only lands in a project the
  session already has) but real client-side, and it touches Phase 6's payload
  format. Needs a task to decide whether to sign them.
- **`device_id` is forgeable and is the final LWW tiebreaker** (§3.7, §4.12) —
  a `Uuid().v4()` in plaintext SharedPreferences, so a chosen value wins ties
  deterministically. Probably acceptable; the point is to record the acceptance
  explicitly rather than leave it unexamined. Fold the decision into 10.16's
  residual-risk summary if no earlier task claims it.
- **Rate-limit storage must move out of process before any multi-instance
  deployment** (§4.4). In-process counters silently multiply the effective
  limit by the instance count, which looks like the control working. A
  deployment precondition rather than a code task, but it needs to be written
  down where someone checks it — 10.14's README section.
- **The backup private key needs a custody arrangement** (§4.9) — an offline
  copy and a second holder — before the first backup that matters. Operational,
  not code. Same failure mode §4.8 refused on devices: an encrypted backup
  nobody can decrypt is a data-loss event wearing a control's clothing.
- **From task 10.1 (2026-08-01):** `latestSchemaVersion` now lives in
  `packages/tritrack_sync` as a hardcoded constant rather than being derived
  from the app's migration list (the DDL migrations stay app-side by design, so
  there's nothing in the shared package to derive it from). A future migration
  (schema v6+) must bump `packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/schema_constants.dart`
  by hand alongside adding the new `Migration` entry in
  `lib/data/db/migrations.dart` — `assertMigrationsMatchLatestSchemaVersion()`
  (checked in `test/data/migrations_test.dart`) catches a mismatch, but nothing
  currently calls it outside that one test, so a contributor who doesn't run
  the full suite before committing a schema change could still land the drift
  locally for a while. Worth deciding in 10.5 (which touches the server's own
  schema-version story) whether this needs a stronger guarantee — e.g. a
  build-time check — or whether the test is sufficient.
- **From task 10.2 (2026-08-01):** `flutter_test`'s `find.text`/
  `find.textContaining` match `EditableText` contents as well as `Text`
  widgets — a widget test asserting on a banner string that happens to
  contain the same substring as a nearby form field's current value will
  double-count and fail with "too many" rather than the intended match. Hit
  in `server_config_screen_test.dart`; worth remembering for any future
  screen-under-test with both a status banner and a text field showing the
  same value. Also: a plain `ListView(children: [...])` in a widget test does
  not build/mount items outside the viewport + cache extent — a `ListTile`
  appended near the end of a long `ListView` (as the new Server Connection
  row is on `MoreScreen`) needs `tester.scrollUntilVisible(...)` before
  `find.text(...)` will see it at all, not just before it's "visible."
  Neither is a code defect, both are easy to lose an hour to next time.
- **Resolved (2026-08-02): `docker compose up` was verified for the first
  time.** Docker became available in this execution environment. `docker
  compose up --build` from the existing `.env` built and started both
  containers cleanly (Postgres healthy, server up behind it), and
  `curl http://localhost:8080/health` returned `{"status":"ok"}`. The literal
  acceptance criterion's first half is now genuinely confirmed rather than
  only code-reviewed. **The phone-on-LAN half remains unverified** — no
  physical device was available in this pass; still wants a real check on
  actual hardware when one is available. See task 10.3's own status note for
  full detail.
- **From task 10.3 (2026-08-01):** `shelf_io.serve` adds an `X-Powered-By`
  header by default, which is exactly the kind of dependency-fingerprinting
  leak the security model warns about for *every* route, not just `/health`
  — worth checking for on any other bare `shelf_io.serve` call site a later
  task adds (10.5+), not just the one this task fixed. A `Handler`-level unit
  test can't see it (the header is added by `shelf_io.serve` itself, outside
  the handler); only a real bound-socket test catches it, which is why
  `server/test/server_io_test.dart` exists as a second, slower test alongside
  the cheap in-process ones rather than being redundant with them.
- **Resolved (2026-08-02): the build-stage/runtime-stage glibc compatibility
  concern was verified — `docker compose build` (and the subsequent `up`)
  succeeded cleanly.** `dart compile exe`'s AOT binary ran without an "exec
  format" or missing-library error at container startup, confirming
  `dart:stable`'s Debian bookworm base and `debian:bookworm-slim`'s runtime
  do in fact match glibc versions as assumed.
- **From task 10.4 (2026-08-01):** the main Android manifest
  (`android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`) had no `INTERNET` permission
  at all before this task — only `src/debug` and `src/profile` declared it
  (the stock `flutter create` template's default, correct only for a project
  with no network feature). Every release APK built before this fix would
  have had **zero network access**: no map tiles, no DEM fetches. Fixed as
  part of this task since it was directly encountered while editing the same
  manifest for the local-network config, and is a one-line, low-risk,
  clearly-correct addition — flagging it here rather than leaving it as a
  silent side effect. Worth double-checking release-build screenshots/QA
  going forward actually show map tiles, since this may have been masked
  until now if release testing mostly happened via `flutter run --release`
  from a machine where a debug-signed install lingered, or via `--debug`/
  `--profile` builds that already had the permission.
- **From task 10.4 (2026-08-01):** Android's `network-security-config`
  `<domain>` element does not support CIDR ranges — only exact hostnames or
  IP literals. This is why the debug-only cleartext exemption uses a broad
  `<base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="true">` rather than an enumerated
  list of private-IP ranges: task 10.2's server URL is a field the developer
  types in at runtime, so the exact LAN IP can't be known ahead of time the
  way a fixed hostname could be domain-scoped. Worth revisiting if this ever
  needs to be narrower than "all cleartext, debug builds only" — e.g. if
  10.14's structural check ends up wanting something tighter, the options are
  a small enumerated list of common private ranges as literal IPs (lossy —
  misses uncommon subnets) or accepting the current broad-but-debug-scoped
  approach as the deliberate tradeoff it is.
- **From task 10.5 (2026-08-01): task 10.1 shipped a narrower "shared column
  set" than its spec described** — table names and `latestSchemaVersion`, but
  not the columns, which lived only inside the app's SQLite DDL strings. 10.5
  had to add `tableSpecs` before it could mirror anything. Now closed, and
  both schemas are tested against it, but worth noting as a pattern: 10.1's
  status note recorded what moved accurately, and the gap was still only
  caught when a downstream task tried to use it. Later tasks depending on
  "shared X" should check what's actually in the package rather than trusting
  the plan's wording.
- **Resolved (2026-08-02): the Postgres DDL has now actually been executed.**
  Docker became available in this execution environment; all twelve of this
  task's `postgres`-tagged integration tests ran against real Postgres for
  the first time and passed (see task 10.5's own status note for the full
  list). The generated `CREATE TABLE` statements are confirmed syntactically
  and semantically correct against a real database, not just string-level
  tested.
- **From task 10.5 (2026-08-01): `server_seq` allocation serialises all
  accepted writes** by design (the locked counter row — see the task note and
  `postgres_schema.dart` for why a bare sequence silently loses rows). Fine at
  this app's scale and deliberately chosen, but it *is* a known scaling limit
  rather than an oversight, so it belongs somewhere visible: if push latency
  ever becomes a real complaint, the fix is a commit-ordered redesign
  (`pg_current_snapshot()`-based cursors) with its own correctness tests, not
  swapping in `BIGSERIAL`. A test blocks the naive swap.
- **From task 10.6 (2026-08-01): `/auth/link-status/<id>` is a third-party
  behaviour oracle** (Gate A finding 6, Low). Whoever calls
  `POST /auth/magic-link` gets the `request_id` and can poll it unauthenticated,
  so triggering links to a list of guessed colleague addresses reveals which
  addresses are live and whose owners act on TriTrack sign-in mail —
  reconnaissance for §2.1's phishing path. It does **not** reveal prior
  registration (an unregistered address that clicks also reports `consumed`).
  Left in place because the endpoint is what stops the requesting device
  waiting forever, and any fix that doesn't bound *request volume* just moves
  the oracle — 10.14's rate limits are the real control. Needs an explicit
  acceptance in 10.16's residual-risk summary.
- **From task 10.6 (2026-08-01): sign-in needs a deep link.** Today the user
  copies a code from the browser landing page and pastes it into the app.
  That is deliberate and secure (the device that redeems is the device signed
  in, and a prefetching mail scanner cannot consume anything), but it is clumsy
  — three steps where one tap should do. A custom URL scheme / universal link
  would hand the token to the app directly and changes only *how the token
  reaches the app*, not who redeems it, so it is additive rather than a
  redesign. Platform config of the same shape as tasks 5.1/10.4.
- **From task 10.8 (2026-08-01): the push watermark is clock-based, not exact.**
  `updated_at >= watermark` cannot select rows written by a device whose clock
  jumped backwards. Mitigated by 10.5's skew flagging, by
  `SyncStateStore.resetPushWatermark`, and by the `>=` bias toward re-sending —
  but an exact pending-set (a trigger-maintained local table, or a local-only
  change-sequence column) would remove the failure mode entirely. Worth doing
  if a real device ever exhibits it, or in 10.15 if the test matrix wants
  certainty. Note a local-only table would still bump the client schema
  version, which the server also tracks — decide whether the shared version
  should cover client-only tables at that point.
- **From task 10.8 (2026-08-01): automatic sync can spend cellular data.** No
  connectivity plugin is used (they report the interface, not whether it
  works), so there is no "unmetered only" option — only "automatic on/off" plus
  the manual button. Acceptable given the 15-minute floor and small steady-state
  payloads, but a user on satellite billing has a coarser control than they
  deserve. A real implementation needs interface detection plus a user setting;
  worth pairing with 10.12's sync-status UI so the control lives next to the
  state it governs.
- **From task 10.8 (2026-08-01): a device pulls back its own just-pushed rows.**
  The server returns everything above the cursor including rows this device
  authored, so a round trip re-downloads what was just uploaded. Correct (the
  device must learn the server's authoritative copy, which may have won a merge
  and differ) and harmless (they merge to no-ops), but it doubles first-sync
  traffic. If that matters on metered links, the fix is a server-side
  "exclude rows whose `server_seq` came from this device's push" filter — which
  needs care, because it must NOT exclude rows the server modified.
- **From task 10.7 (2026-08-01): the client's push watermark is unsolved and
  belongs to 10.8.** *(Resolved by 10.8 — see above.)* The protocol defines what a push *contains*; it does not
  define how a client decides which local rows are new since its last successful
  push. Nothing in the schema marks a row as pushed — there is no dirty flag and
  no local change sequence. The options each have a real cost: a per-row
  side table (heavy), a new column (touches the shared schema and every
  migration), or selecting on `updated_at >= watermark` (needs `>=` and
  tolerates re-pushing, which is safe because the server's merge is idempotent
  and a re-push resolves to `lost_to_server` — but a device whose clock jumps
  backwards would under-select, which is the one unsafe direction). Worth
  deciding deliberately in 10.8 rather than defaulting; note that over-pushing
  is harmless and under-pushing is silent data loss, so the bias should be
  obvious.
- **From task 10.7 (2026-08-01): sync routes are built but not mounted.**
  `createSyncRouter` needs a `withSyncContext` that resolves an authenticated
  session *and* opens a transaction, and `bin/server.dart` does not yet supply
  one — session validation on sync requests is 10.10's authorization work. So
  the routes exist and are unit-testable but are not reachable over HTTP yet.
  Deliberate (wiring them before authorization exists would mean an
  unauthenticated sync endpoint) but worth stating plainly so it is not
  mistaken for done.
- **From task 10.6 (2026-08-01): `dart format` on the whole repo is a trap.**
  Running `dart format lib test` reformatted 184 files this task never touched
  and introduced `curly_braces_in_flow_control_structures` lints in unrelated
  code, burying the real diff. Reverted. Format only the files a task actually
  edits; the repo is not uniformly formatted and making it so should be its own
  deliberate commit, not a side effect.
- **From task 10.5 (2026-08-01):** `ClockSkew.plausibleFloor` is a hardcoded
  `2020-01-01`. Defensible (TriTrack didn't exist then, and it's well below the
  app's real history so a legitimate old import is never mistaken for a fault)
  but it is a magic date that will look arbitrary in five years. If a
  configuration surface for server policy appears in 10.14, this and
  `ClockSkew.tolerance` are the two values that should move onto it.
- **Resolved by task 10.9 (2026-08-01): the "sync routes built but not
  mounted" item above is no longer accurate.** `bin/server.dart` now supplies
  a real `withSyncContext` (bearer-token session resolution) and both
  `/sync/*` and `/projects/mine` are mounted and reachable over HTTP, guarded
  by `ProjectAccessGuard` (see below) rather than being unauthenticated.
- **From task 10.9 (2026-08-01): `ProjectAccessGuard` is a narrow, explicitly
  temporary stand-in for 10.10, not a preview of it.** It permits exactly
  three cases — project doesn't exist yet (publish/creation), requester is
  `Projects.owner_user_id`, or requester has an open `Project_Memberships`
  row — because mounting `/sync/push`/`/sync/pull` for the first time (which
  10.9 must do to make publish/join reachable) meant the Security Model's
  "every project-data endpoint verifies membership" criterion now applied
  where nothing enforced it before. **Task 10.10 must replace this call site
  in `sync_routes.dart` and `project_routes.dart`, not extend
  `ProjectAccessGuard` itself** — it exists only to make 10.9 testable
  end-to-end without pulling 10.10's full authorization rule table forward.
- **From task 10.9 (2026-08-01): a retried publish re-uploads the whole
  project from scratch rather than resuming a partial upload.** Safe (every
  row is upserted by primary key, so nothing duplicates) but not efficient —
  a publish interrupted after chunk 40 of 50 re-sends all 50 on retry. Fine at
  today's typical project sizes; worth a resumable-from-last-acked-chunk
  follow-up if a season's worth of data makes a from-scratch retry
  expensive on a marginal connection.
- **From task 10.9 (2026-08-01): the new Postgres-tagged tests
  (`project_access_guard_test.dart`, `publish_and_join_test.dart`) have never
  actually run against a database.** Same standing caveat as every
  Postgres-tagged test since 10.3 — Docker is unavailable in this execution
  environment. They are structurally sound and skip cleanly, but "verified"
  here means "typechecks and would run," not "has run."
- **Resolved by task 10.10 (2026-08-02): Docker became available in this
  execution environment, and every Postgres-tagged test across the server —
  10.3 through 10.10's, `publish_and_join_test.dart` included — ran for real
  for the first time.** Two pre-existing bugs surfaced immediately: a
  hardcoded `public.` schema qualifier in `PostgresMigrations` that made
  migrations non-idempotent outside the default schema (fixed), and 10.9's
  own publish test pushing a `Projects` row without the `Users` row its
  foreign key requires (fixed, plus the assertion it was masking). If Docker
  becomes unavailable again in a later session, treat any *new* Postgres test
  as unverified until it actually runs — passing structurally is not the same
  claim as having executed.
- **From task 10.10 (2026-08-02): the replication exemption's author-column
  reachability is a real, unclosed disclosure path, and closing it needs
  message-level provenance that doesn't exist yet.** Any project owner can
  insert a fabricated `Observations`/`Non_Detections` row naming an arbitrary
  `user_id` they already know (the `author`-rule insert exemption exists
  precisely so a genuinely replicated row can carry someone else's id), which
  makes that id "reachable" and discloses the named user's real name and
  full email history on the next pull. Verified with a live repro against
  Postgres, not just reasoned about: pushing one throwaway observation
  naming a victim's `user_id` was enough to have their `Users` row appear in
  an unrelated project's pull response. Bounded — it requires already
  knowing the target's opaque UUID, not an enumeration of the whole
  directory, and the same `user_id` cannot exist server-side at all unless
  its owner has already published or joined some project of their own — but
  real: a UUID that leaks once (a shared backup file, a screenshot, a
  compromised device) becomes a permanent, repeatable identity-disclosure
  key against that person, from anyone who ever sees it.
  **Not fixed here, deliberately**, because every mitigation tried either
  reopens the hole (dropping `user_id` from reachability breaks the FK the
  receiving client needs to merge a legitimately imported observation) or
  is vacuous (gating on "the named user already has a project relationship"
  is always true, since a `Users` row cannot reach the server at all except
  by way of one). This is the sync-endpoint-shaped instance of the risk
  §4.12/10.0's Discovered Scope already named and deliberately deferred —
  "`TT1:` share payloads are unauthenticated," "a pushed row's claimed
  `user_id` is an attacker-controlled input" — and the real fix is the same
  one that risk was left waiting on: cryptographic authorship provenance for
  replicated rows, not another authorization rule. Needs its own task,
  scoped together with that one rather than solved piecemeal here.
- **From task 10.10 (2026-08-02): `RowAuthorizer._isForeignTag`'s query does
  not exclude tombstoned references.** A project that once linked a tag via
  `Project_Tags` and later soft-deletes that link keeps "owning" the tag for
  authorization purposes forever after — over-conservative (it can block a
  legitimate second project of the *same* user from reusing that physical
  tag once the first project releases it) but never permissive, so it is a
  usability rough edge rather than a security gap. Worth revisiting if
  physical-tag reuse across a user's own projects turns out to be a real
  workflow.
- **From task 10.10 (2026-08-02): `Project_Memberships` writes are now
  restricted to rows naming the caller themselves, which is correct for
  Phase 10 (no invitation flow exists) but will need to be deliberately
  relaxed by task 11.2.** The check lives in `RowAuthorizer.authorizeWrite`
  — 11.2 should replace it with real invitation semantics (a pending-invite
  record an invitee accepts into their own membership row) rather than simply
  deleting the restriction, or an owner could push a membership row directly
  granting someone else access with no consent step.
- **From task 10.17 (2026-08-02): `/projects/mine` is entirely
  `Project_Memberships`-driven, with no fallback to `Projects.owner_user_id` —
  a project that is genuinely owned but has no membership row is invisible to
  join from a second device, even though it publishes and syncs completely
  normally.** Not a defect today: task 8.4 already makes the app's own
  project-creation screen create the owner's membership row every time, so
  this never happens through the real UI. Recorded because this task's e2e
  test harness reconstructed a project by hand and initially skipped that row
  (on a misreading of a comment about how *ownership* is resolved —
  `owner_user_id`, never a membership role — as meaning no membership row is
  ever created), and the failure mode was silent: publish succeeded, the
  project just never appeared in `listAvailableToJoin`. Worth a line in
  `ProjectDirectoryService`'s own doc comment, and worth remembering for any
  future code path that creates a `Projects` row without going through
  `project_setup_screen.dart` (a bulk import, an admin tool, a future
  restore-from-backup-as-new-project flow) — it must also create the
  membership row, or `/projects/mine` will silently omit it.
- **From task 10.17 (2026-08-02): the client's `HttpSyncTransport` has never
  been exercised from the actual Flutter UI, only from this suite's bare
  harness driving the same classes directly.** This closes the *protocol* gap
  10.6/10.7/10.8 each recorded (nothing had ever spoken the wire over real
  HTTP from real client code) but not the *UI* gap — a simulator- or
  device-driven pass through the actual sign-in screen, server-connection
  screen, and sync-status UI once 10.12 builds it is still unverified. Same
  standing note as task 10.3's "phone on a real LAN" gap: needs physical or
  simulator hardware this environment doesn't have.
- **For task 10.12: `completeSignIn` consumes the magic-link token before
  comparing `expectedEmail`, so a mismatched or empty email field burns the
  token — every retry with the correct address then fails too, with a
  different, more confusing error (`RedemptionRejected`, "already used"-shaped,
  not "you typed the wrong email").** Single-use redemption is correct and
  deliberate (§4.3, task 10.6); the gap was that nothing told the user their
  code was now dead and they needed a fresh one. **Partially resolved
  (2026-08-02):** `server_config_screen.dart`'s `IdentityMismatch` message now
  says "The code is now used up — request a new one," fixed incidentally
  while addressing feedback-visibility issues on the same screen (below). The
  underlying `completeSignIn`/redemption ordering is unchanged — still
  consumes-then-compares — so this is a copy fix, not a protocol fix; 10.12
  should still decide whether that ordering itself is worth revisiting.
- **Real-device bug (2026-08-03), found by task 10.4's on-device iPhone
  check: `completeSignIn` (`auth_provider.dart:129`) crashed with "Cannot use
  the Ref of activeUserIdProvider after it has been disposed."** `ActiveUserId`
  and `ActiveProjectId` (`active_selection_provider.dart`) were plain
  `@riverpod` (`autoDispose`), and every real call site — `completeSignIn`
  included — mutates them via a bare `ref.read(...).notifier).set(...)` with
  no active watcher. An `autoDispose` notifier with no listener can be torn
  down the instant its refcount hits zero; if that lands while `set()` is
  suspended on `await _prefs.setString(...)`, the `state = AsyncData(...)`
  line after it throws. **Fixed:** both are now `@Riverpod(keepAlive: true)`
  (the same precedent task 10.2 set for `ServerConfigNotifier` — this is
  app-global selection state, not a screen-scoped value), plus a defensive
  `ref.mounted` guard in `set()` on both. Notably, this did **not** reproduce
  in a plain `ProviderContainer` unit test even with a real `Future.delayed`
  standing in for the network round trip — a bare container schedules
  disposal off a zero-duration `Timer`, while the real app's widget-bound
  `ProviderScope` schedules it off a `Vsync` (frame callbacks), so the two
  don't race identically. The fix holds regardless of that difference; see
  `active_selection_provider.dart`'s own doc comment for the full account.
- **Atomicity assessment arising from the same bug (2026-08-03):
  `completeSignIn` is five sequential steps (redeem, adopt, store session, set
  active user, update in-memory state) with no cross-step transaction, and
  this crash proved a partial completion is reachable — a real gap against
  10.6's own acceptance criterion that the identity remap be "crash-safe."**
  Traced the actual risk: `ServerIdentityAdopter.adopt()` **hard-deletes** the
  old local `Users` row inside its own transaction (a documented, deliberate
  exception to the no-hard-deletes rule — the person still exists, under the
  new id), but `ActiveUserId` — a separate, non-transactional
  `SharedPreferences` value — isn't repointed at the new id until later in the
  same method. An interruption in that window leaves `ActiveUserId` naming a
  row that is now permanently gone, and unlike the tombstone case
  `app_context_provider.dart`'s `currentUser` already recovers, there was no
  recovery path at all — the next launch would silently mint a **third**
  identity, while the real data sits correctly attributed under the server's
  id. **Partially fixed:** `currentUser` now falls back to the stored session
  (`sessionStoreProvider`) when the active id is neither present nor
  tombstoned — if a valid session names a user id that does exist locally,
  it adopts that instead of minting a phantom, and repoints `ActiveUserId`
  accordingly. This closes the practical case the crash actually hit
  (interruption after the session was stored but before `ActiveUserId` was
  set). **Not fixed, and escalated rather than patched further:** a narrower
  window remains — an interruption between `adopt()` committing and the
  session being written — where no persisted signal of the just-adopted id
  exists yet, and a phantom is still minted (self-healing on the user's next
  successful sign-in, since `adopt()` is idempotent and folds the phantom's
  placeholder identity in too, but not before). Fully closing that would mean
  either moving the active-user pointer into the same SQLite transaction
  `adopt()` uses, or adding a persisted breadcrumb `currentUser` can resume
  from — a real storage/session-persistence design decision, not a bug fix,
  and squarely the kind of correctness-critical call task 10.6's own model
  guidance already routes to Opus. Flagged here for that review rather than
  guessed at.
- **Coverage gap closed (2026-08-03): task 10.17's e2e suite drives
  `AuthClient`/`ServerIdentityAdopter` directly, so it never exercised the
  Riverpod provider layer — which is exactly where the bug above lived.**
  Added `test/core/providers/auth_provider_test.dart`: drives
  `CurrentSession.completeSignIn` through a real `ProviderContainer` against a
  faked HTTP transport, with no listener on `activeUserIdProvider` (mirroring
  `completeSignIn`'s own bare `ref.read` — the condition that must not crash).
  Covers the success path end-to-end (session, active user, and
  `currentUser` all converge), `IdentityMismatch`, and `RedemptionRejected`.
  This does not reproduce the disposal race itself (see above) — its value is
  in exercising `completeSignIn`'s full provider-graph path at all, which
  previously had zero coverage at any level. A device- or simulator-driven
  pass through the actual sign-in screen remains the still-open gap the
  2026-08-02 10.17 entry above already names.
- **From task 10.11 (2026-08-05): a device refused by the tombstone-retention
  guard has no recovery path, and building one is a real design task.** The
  guard is deliberately terminal — it refuses push and incremental pull, and
  does not auto-reset the cursor, because the obvious automatic recovery is
  precisely the resurrection it exists to prevent (a full re-pull leaves the
  purged row sitting locally, since `ProjectMerger` never deletes rows the
  server merely omitted, and the next push revives it). What is missing is the
  deliberate act the user is told to perform. The shape it probably wants:
  show which local records the server no longer has, distinguish "you created
  this offline and it has never synced" from "this was deleted elsewhere while
  you were away", and let the user keep or discard each — i.e. a reconciliation
  screen, not a button. Needs its own task; a natural companion to 10.12's
  conflict-visibility work, which has the same "show the user what
  last-write-wins did" shape. **Rare by construction** (purge is held back by
  every device that synced inside the 24-month window, so only genuinely
  abandoned devices reach it), which is why it was acceptable to ship the guard
  without it — but "rare" is not "never", and the current UX for it is a
  sentence explaining the device is stuck.
- **From task 10.11 (2026-08-05): global tables are not tombstone-purged.**
  `Users`, `User_Emails` and `Tags` have no `project_id`, so neither the
  per-project purge floor nor a per-project cursor applies to them, and the
  whole guard is built on that comparison. Their tombstone volume is negligible
