  today (tens of tags, not thousands of observations) so this is not urgent,
  but it means the "grows without bound" problem the task set out to solve is
  only solved for project-scoped tables. Purging them safely needs a different
  scheme — plausibly a global floor compared against every device's *lowest*
  cursor across all projects, which is a stricter and less useful bound, or
  reachability-based purging that mirrors how those tables are pulled.
- **From task 10.11 (2026-08-05): `latestSchemaVersion` is described in a few
  places as "derived from the migration list" and it is not.** It is a
  hand-written `const int` in
  `packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/schema_constants.dart`, and the migration
  list is checked *against* it by `assertMigrationsMatchLatestSchemaVersion` —
  the dependency runs the opposite way from how this task's own entry described
  it. The single-source-of-truth property still holds, so nothing is broken;
  the descriptions are just backwards. Worth correcting wherever it appears so
  a future task does not go looking for a derivation that does not exist.
  Note the assertion is only invoked from a test, never at startup.
- **From task 10.18 (2026-08-06): the server has no incremental Postgres
  migration path, so a minor bump that adds a column cannot actually be
  deployed yet.** `PostgresMigrations.run` bootstraps the whole current schema in
  one step on an empty database, then on an already-bootstrapped one only ensures
  the server-only tables and throws `StateError` if `targetVersion` is not in
  `schema_migrations`. There is no branch that alters an existing table. 10.18
  did not need one (its holding table is client-only and outside
  `latestSchemaVersion`), so this was avoided rather than solved — but the first
  real additive column will hit it, and 10.18's entire premise is that additive
  columns are now the normal way to evolve. **Needs a task before any minor bump
  ships.** The generic shape is a reconcile pass that adds columns declared in
  `tableSpecs` but absent from the live table, then records the new version; the
  one real design question is what to do about a column the spec marks NOT NULL,
  since `ColumnSpec` carries no default and `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN NOT NULL`
  cannot succeed on a non-empty table without one. Adding a default to
  `ColumnSpec` is probably the answer and is not a decision to make in passing.
- **From task 10.18 (2026-08-06): held values are never garbage-collected.**
  `Unknown_Columns` entries are removed only by promotion. Rows are soft-deleted
  rather than hard-deleted, so nothing orphans today and the volume is bounded by
  how many columns a newer version added — kilobytes at this scale. But if any
  path ever hard-deletes a row (a purge, a project removal, a reconciliation
  flow), its held values become permanent orphans keyed to an identity nothing
  will ever attach to again. Cheap to fix whenever such a path is built; not
  worth a table scan on open before then.
- **From task 10.18 (2026-08-06): the app's own local database, unlike the
  server's, is never checked for schema drift on open.** `assertMigrationsMatch
  LatestSchemaVersion` runs only in a test, and promotion silently skips any held
  column whose table or spec it cannot resolve. That is the right behaviour for
  promotion, but it means a genuinely corrupt or partially-migrated local schema
  produces no signal at open — it surfaces later as a failed query in whatever
  screen touches it first. Related to the 10.11 note above about the assertion
  never running at startup; worth resolving together.
- **From task 10.18 (2026-08-06): 10.12 should surface a minor skew, not just a
  refusal.** With minor skew now *accepted*, a device can sync happily for months
  while unable to display fields the rest of the team is filling in — no error,
  no refusal, nothing in the UI. The sync status surface 10.12 builds is the
  natural place to say "this app is a version behind; some fields recorded by
  other devices are being kept but not shown." That is a materially different
  message from the version *refusal* 10.12's spec already anticipates, and it is
  the more common one. **Resolved by task 10.12 (2026-08-07):**
  `SyncStatus.hasUnrecognizedFields` (backed by `SyncEngine.
  hasHeldUnknownColumns`) surfaces this on the Sync Status detail screen — see
  10.12's own entry and the new Discovered Scope item on its project-scoping
  limitation below.
- **Process lesson (2026-08-03): a real-device pass should happen at the end
  of each remaining phase, not saved up for the final 10.16 gate.** This
  session's on-device iPhone sign-in test found a sign-in-breaking crash
  (`activeUserIdProvider`'s `autoDispose` race) that 79 server tests, 20 e2e
  tests, and the full ~600-test Flutter suite had all missed — none of them
  exercise the Riverpod provider layer against real, timed I/O the way an
  actual device does. Waiting until 10.16 to run real hardware for the first
  time means any bug of this shape is found only after every remaining Phase
  10 task has already been built on top of the same untested assumption.
  Recommend: a short on-device smoke pass (sign in, sync, basic navigation)
  after each of the remaining tasks that touch the client provider layer, not
  just once at the end.
- **From task 10.19 (2026-08-06): auto-backup is scoped to the single
  "current project," not every project on the device.** `CloudBackupSettings`
  is one global blob (one folder, one enabled flag) and
  `maybeRunDueAutoBackup` only ever backs up `currentProjectProvider`. A user
  who works across multiple projects gets automatic protection for whichever
  one is active *right now*; switching away from a project does not stop its
  data from aging, it just stops it from being the one that gets backed up.
  This was already true before 10.19 — defaulting the feature to on makes the
  gap matter more, since more people will now be relying on it. Needs a task
  to decide whether settings become per-project, or whether
  `maybeRunDueAutoBackup` should iterate every project with local data instead
  of only the active one.
- **From task 10.19 (2026-08-06): desktop has no equivalent nudge.** The
  persistent `BackupHealthBanner` and the auto-backup feature it reports on are
  both iOS/Android-only (a security-scoped bookmark / SAF tree URI has no
  desktop analogue), so a macOS/Linux/Windows user gets no reminder of any
  kind beyond remembering to tap "Export project backup" manually. Given the
  actual durability risk (§1 asset 2) is platform-independent, desktop needs
  its own visibility mechanism — plausibly "days since last manual export,"
  tracked the way `lastBackupAtUtc` already is for the cloud path, surfaced
  the same way.
- **From task 10.19 (2026-08-06): the pre-migration backup has no restore
  UI.** `PreMigrationBackup` writes a real, openable SQLite file to
  `pre_migration_backups/` before every migration, but nothing in the app
  reads it back — a corrupted post-migration database today would need someone
  to find that directory manually (e.g. via a support request) and swap the
  file in by hand. `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.9 names the same gap for
  server backups as a real requirement ("a backup that has never been restored
  is not a backup"); the same reasoning applies here at smaller stakes. Needs a
  task if a real migration failure in the field ever makes this urgent, but
  worth deciding deliberately rather than only in a crisis.
- **From task 10.19 (2026-08-06): `retentionCount` note for a future
  reader.** `CloudBackupService`'s own retention and `PreMigrationBackup`'s are
  two independent, differently-scoped mechanisms with similar-looking code —
  intentionally not shared, since one prunes per-project cloud files by
  filename prefix and the other prunes a device-wide local directory with no
  project concept at all. Not a defect; recorded so nobody "deduplicates" them
  into a shared helper that would have to reintroduce a project scope the
  local one doesn't need.
- **From task 10.12 (2026-08-07): `hasHeldUnknownColumns` is not project-scoped.**
  `Unknown_Columns` (task 10.18) carries no project id, so a device working on
  more than one server project cannot tell *which* project a held value
  belongs to — the minor-skew note on the Sync Status screen is a device-wide
  signal, not a per-project one. Harmless today (Phase 10 is one user, and
  most users have one active project at a time), but worth fixing before
  Phase 11 makes multi-project, multi-person use routine. The fix is adding a
  `project_id` column to `Unknown_Columns` and scoping `hold`/`attach`/
  `promote` by it — not attempted here to avoid touching 10.18's holding-table
  format without its own review.
- **From task 10.12 (2026-08-07): pending-row count is a live query, not a
  maintained counter.** `SyncEngine.pendingRowCount` re-scans every sync table
  with the same `updated_at >= watermark` predicate `_collectChangedRows`
  pushes by, run fresh on every status rebuild. Fine at field-study data
  volumes (hundreds to low thousands of rows per project); would want an
  actual dirty-count mechanism if a project's row counts ever grow enough to
  make an unindexed per-table `COUNT(*)` noticeable on a status-screen open.
- **From task 10.12 (2026-08-07): no reconciliation path for a tombstone-
  retention refusal.** 10.11's Discovered Scope already named this as a
  natural companion to 10.12's conflict-visibility work — a device refused for
  falling behind the tombstone-purge window has no equivalent "here's what
  changed while you were away" screen, only the refusal message. Still true
  after this task: the conflict log built here only covers last-write-wins
  losses during an otherwise-successful sync, not the terminal
  `cursor_too_old` case, which needs its own reconciliation flow entirely.
- **From task 10.13 (2026-08-07): `sync_traffic_log` has no retention policy.**
  Unlike every other server-only table (a cursor row per device, an account
  row per user — bounded by how many devices/users actually exist),
  `sync_traffic_log` grows by one row per sync request forever. Fine at
  Phase 10's scale; the right answer (age-based purge, a row cap, shipping it
  to an external log sink instead of Postgres) is a product decision someone
  should make deliberately before this runs against real traffic for months,
  not an implementation detail to guess at here.
- **From task 10.13 (2026-08-07): the localhost-only gate trusts the real TCP
  peer address, which stops being trustworthy behind a same-host reverse
  proxy.** `_requireLocalUnlessAllowed` checks `shelf.io.connection_info`'s
  `remoteAddress` — correct and unspoofable *today*, since the server is
  reached directly. Task 10.14 adds TLS termination, and a common way to get
  that in front of a bare Dart process is a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy) on
  the same host forwarding to `127.0.0.1`. If that ever happens, every real
  request's peer address becomes the proxy's own loopback connection, and
  this gate would wave through traffic from anywhere the proxy accepts it
  from — silently defeating the control this task built. Needs revisiting
  specifically when 10.14 picks a TLS-termination strategy: either the proxy
  must be configured to refuse forwarding `/diagnostics/*` at all, or this
  middleware needs to understand a trusted-proxy header (with all the care
  that requires — an untrusted `X-Forwarded-For` is exactly the spoofing
  vector this design avoided in the first place).
- **From task 10.14 (2026-08-07): `/security-review` has not been run on this
  work.** It is the last of 10.14's own acceptance criteria and the one thing the
  task did not deliver — the nine controls plus their tests were the session's
  budget. This is the highest-value follow-up in Phase 10 right now: the whole
  point of implementing the controls centrally was to make them auditable as a
  unit, and they have never been audited. Should run before 10.16's gate, not as
  part of it, so findings have somewhere to be fixed.
- **From task 10.14 (2026-08-07): rate-limit counters must leave process memory
  before any second instance.** §4.4's own prototype-shortcut admission, now with
  code behind it. Per-instance counters multiply the effective limit by the
  instance count — the failure mode that looks like the control is working, since
  every instance dutifully enforces "3 per 15 minutes" while the user gets one
  email per instance. Written up in `server/README.md` as a deployment
  precondition; §6 item 7 in the security model tracks it. Not a code task until
  a second instance is actually on the table.
- **From task 10.14 (2026-08-07): the audit-log purge is schedulable but not
  scheduled.** `bin/purge_audit_logs.dart` exists and is documented, and nothing
  runs it. Until a deployment adds a cron entry, retention is a capability rather
  than a fact — which is a weaker claim than §4.7's `Violated by:` list wants.
  Needs a line in whatever deployment configuration ends up existing, plus a way
  to notice when it stops running.
- **From task 10.14 (2026-08-07): §4.9 (encrypted server DB backups) remains
  open, with its precondition named.** The security model assigns it to 10.14;
  10.14 deliberately did not implement it because §6 item 8's key custody
  arrangement — an offline copy and a second holder — does not exist, and
  encrypting to a key nobody can be sure of is worse than not automating backups
  at all. Needs an *operational* task owned by whoever stands up a real server:
  custody first, then `pg_dump | age` with plaintext never on disk, bounded
  retention, and a restore actually performed once.
- **From task 10.14 (2026-08-07): the reverse-proxy peer-address problem is now
  load-bearing in two places, and still unresolved.** 10.13 filed it for the
  diagnostics console's loopback gate; 10.14's per-source rate limiting keys on
  the same `shelf.io.connection_info` peer address. Both are correct while the
  server is reached directly, and both silently degrade behind a same-host
  reverse proxy — every request's peer becomes `127.0.0.1`, so the console gate
  waves everything through and per-source limits collapse into one shared bucket.
  10.14 chose in-process TLS partly to avoid this, but a real deployment may
  still front the server with nginx/Caddy for certificate management. Whoever
  decides that must either refuse `/diagnostics/*` at the proxy and accept the
  rate-limit merge, or introduce a trusted-proxy header with all the care that
  needs — an untrusted `X-Forwarded-For` is the spoofing vector both designs
  deliberately avoided.
- **From task 10.14 (2026-08-07): a revoked session leaves the client's local
  sync state stopped until something clears it.** Dropping the dead token and
  reporting `SyncHealth.sessionEnded` is now correct, but `SyncSchedule`'s
  `stoppedReason` is only cleared by `SyncSchedule.resumed()`, and nothing calls
  it on a fresh sign-in. So signing back in produces a valid session whose
  schedule still refuses to attempt. Small and clearly a bug; not fixed here
  because the sign-in flow is 10.6's surface and the fix wants a test that drives
  sign-out → sign-in → sync, which is an e2e shape rather than a unit one.
- **From task 10.14 (2026-08-07): `auth_link_requests.token_hash` is unindexed
  despite being an UPDATE predicate**, and expired `auth_magic_links` /
  `auth_link_requests` rows are never swept. Both are performance/growth rather
  than security, both are trivial, and neither is worth a schema change on its
  own — fold into whatever next touches the auth schema.
- **From task 10.12 (2026-08-07): the conflict log is per-device, not
  per-project-membership.** `Sync_Conflicts` records only what *this* device's
  own pushes lost — by design, since that is the only loss a user can act on
  locally — but it means a project owner reviewing "what got overwritten" has
  no way to see conflicts detected on a teammate's device. Fine for Phase 10
  (one user, multiple devices); Phase 11's multi-person case may want a
  server-side or shared view of the same information.
- **From task 10.15 (2026-08-07): most of 10.15's checklist was already
  covered by the diligence in 10.6–10.14's own test suites** (three-peer
  convergence, chunking/resume, identity idempotency/crash-safety,
  revocation of both devices, merge parity, a security-regression test per
  control). The genuinely missing pieces this task added: single-user
  cross-project isolation (`server/test/authz/authorization_test.dart`'s new
  "cross-project isolation, single user" group); explicit revision-stability
  and single-attribution assertions on the two-device identity path
  (`test/e2e/two_device_convergence_e2e_test.dart`); the headline
  network-disabled run as an actual named script
  (`scripts/run_offline_suite.sh` + `test/headline_offline_suite_test.dart`,
  which also covers "release build, no server configured, fully
  functional"); and a real clean-checkout Docker script for the server suite
  (`scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`, using a new loopback-only
  `docker-compose.server-test.yml` overlay — the base compose file
  deliberately never exposes Postgres's port, so this needed its own file).
  Both new scripts were run for real against a throwaway Postgres container
  during this task and are green.
- **From task 10.46 (2026-08-14): a dangling foreign key at `COMMIT` may be a
  gap G-5's fix does not close, self-inflicted by a caller naming themselves
  before their own `Users` row exists — flagged, not reproduced.**
  `SyncService._tryWrite`'s per-row `SAVEPOINT` catches an immediate
  constraint violation (a missing `NOT NULL` column, a type mismatch) because
  those fail at the `INSERT`/`UPDATE` statement itself. Foreign keys on every
  synced table are `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED` (task 10.5), so a
  dangling one is not caught until `COMMIT` — outside every row's savepoint,
  since each is released the moment its own `INSERT`/`UPDATE` statement
  returns without error, long before the constraint is actually checked.
  Traced (not yet reproduced) one specific path: `RowAuthorizer._authorizeNaming`
  (`row_authorizer.dart:413`) skips its reachability check entirely when a
  row names **the caller themselves** (`if (named == userId) continue;`) —
  no check that a `Users` row for that id exists anywhere. F5 (§7.6) already
  records that sign-in creates an `auth_accounts` row, **not** a `Users`
  row, so a freshly authenticated caller can push before ever publishing
  their own profile. If such a caller's first-ever push is a lone
  `Observations` (or `Non_Detections`) row naming themselves, with no
  `Users` row in that same push and none stored from before, does the
  deferred FK on `user_id` fire at `COMMIT` and turn that single row into a
  `500` — G-5's shape, one layer further out, for a row that named nobody
  but the pusher? The naming path for a *foreign* colleague looks already
  closed for this: `_projectAlreadyNames` requires the reachability query to
  find them, which only a prior, separately-committed push can satisfy, so
  the ordinary two-request publish shape (`Users` first, then anything that
  names them) never reaches `COMMIT` with a dangling reference. Self-naming
  is the one branch that skips the check.

  **Narrowed on tracing further — the *establishing* push is already safe.**
  `sync_routes.dart`'s `attemptPublish` runs `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE`
  inside its own savepoint before checking the result, specifically so "a
  dangling foreign key, a missing NOT NULL column" (its own comment) becomes
  a clean refusal rather than a `500` — so a first publish that names itself
  without its own `Users` row is already caught. What is untraced is the
  *ordinary, non-establishing* push: a caller who already has project access
  (an existing `Project_Memberships` row) but has never pushed their own
  `Users` row, pushing a lone `Observations` row naming themselves into a
  project that already exists. That path does not go through
  `attemptPublish` at all — only `SyncService.applyPush`'s per-row savepoints,
  which do not force immediate constraints. Not clearly reachable from
  today's single-owner app (Phase 10 has no real second-member flow yet;
  Phase 11 does), which is why this was not chased into a live repro here —
  but the wire protocol accepts it today. Needs a live probe: get a second
  session real project access without ever letting it push its own `Users`
  row, then push one `Observations` row naming that session's own `user_id`,
  and see what `COMMIT` does with it.
- **From task 10.47 (2026-08-14): `scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh` needed the
  same `-p tritrack-gate` fix as the two scripts it invokes, not named in the
  task's own bullet list.** Giving `verify_c5_denial_audit.py` and
  `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py` an explicit default project name (rather than
  none) only fixes the ambiguity if whatever brings the stack up agrees with
  it. `gate_smoke_test.sh` brings the e2e stack up itself and then invokes
  both scripts without setting `COMPOSE`, so its own default had to change to
  match, or the smoke test would have started failing them with a
  container-not-found error the moment this task's other fix landed — the
  same class of "fixed the named instance, missed the caller" this whole
  section exists to catch. Caught here because the smoke test was run for
  real after the change, not assumed correct from reading the diff.
- **From task 10.50 (2026-08-15): two genuine `flutter drive`/`integration_test`
  tooling constraints, worth knowing before any future task builds another
  on-device test.** (1) `flutter drive` refuses `--release` outright for
  every non-web target ("Flutter Driver (non-web) does not support running
  in release mode") — there is no way to drive an `integration_test` against
  a true Xcode/Gradle Release build with this tooling, full stop. `--profile`
  is the closest available mode, and whether it is *equivalent* evidence
  depends entirely on whether the thing under test is gated by build mode —
  it was for ATS here (Info.plist is shared across configurations) but will
  not always be; check before assuming to the next time. (2) AOT
  (`--profile`/`--release`) builds are not buildable for the iOS **Simulator**
  at all ("release/profile builds are only supported for physical devices")
  — only Debug works there, unconditionally. Neither constraint is
  TriTrack-specific; both are worth a line in whatever future task adds the
  next on-device integration test (task 10.51's readiness check, or a
  future device-dependent verification) so nobody re-discovers them by
  watching a build fail for ten minutes first.
- **From task 10.50 (2026-08-15): the physical-device run was completed for
  the half that matters, and its remaining gap is a device-deployment
  reliability issue, not a networking or ATS one — traced across seven
  attempts, two sessions.** Michael connected his iPhone (first wireless,
  then USB) mid-task. Requests #1/#2 — the ATS refusal itself — passed on
  the device twice, independently (separated by a `flutter clean`). Request
  #3 (local-network reachability) never completed, for three distinct
  reasons found in sequence:
  1. `verify_ats_transport_security.sh` pointed request #3 at `127.0.0.1` for
     every device, which is correct for macOS/Simulator (same network stack
     as this Mac) but wrong for a physical device (its `127.0.0.1` is
     itself). **Fixed**: the script now detects a physical Apple device via
     `flutter devices --machine`'s `emulator: false` and targets this
     machine's real LAN address (`ipconfig getifaddr en0`) instead.
  2. The address the fix computed was independently confirmed correct by
     Michael (not inferred), Wi-Fi confirmed on the same network — and the
     phone still could not reach it (`NSURLErrorDomain` code `-1009`).
     **Not diagnosed further**; a plausible next step is a packet capture or
     confirming no client-isolation/AP-isolation setting on whatever network
     this actually was, but that is genuinely open.
  3. Xcode's install/launch handshake ("Xcode is taking longer than expected
     to start debugging the app") stalled three of the seven attempts before
     the test ever ran — a device-deployment reliability issue that did not
     reproduce on macOS or the Simulator once. **Not diagnosed further**;
     candidates are a stale device pairing/trust state or an Xcode/device
     communication issue unrelated to this codebase.
  Optional next step for Michael; not required for F13's closure, whose own
  acceptance criteria scoped to macOS + iOS (simulator counts) and which the
  physical-device ATS passes now exceed rather than merely meet.

*Split out of Phase 10 on 2026-08-01. Phase 10 delivers secure sync for one
user across their own devices; this phase adds everyone else.*

**Goal:** multiple people on one project, with real roles, a managed
membership lifecycle, and team data that is visible, attributable, and usable
for triangulation — without letting anyone silently rewrite anyone else's
field records.

**Depends on all of Phase 10.** Every invariant Phase 10 establishes still
holds here, verbatim: the app remains fully usable and shippable with no
server, no read path goes behind the network, and the standing security
criteria and review gates from Phase 10's Security Posture section apply to
every task below.

**Decisions carried over from the original combined phase:**

- **Co-equal owners via `Project_Memberships`, plus transfer.** Any number of
  `role='owner'` rows, all with identical rights. This revises task 8.4's
  decision to gate on `Projects.owner_user_id` — see task 11.1.
- **Rejoining creates a new membership row, it does not null `end_date`.**
  Nulling would erase the record of the prior stint, which is the whole point
  of keeping it. The schema already supports this: `Project_Memberships` has
  no unique constraint on `(project_id, user_id)`, and 8.4's `findForUser`
  already filters `end_date IS NULL`, so a closed stint correctly doesn't
  count. Invariant to enforce: **for any single (project, user) *pair*, at
  most one row with `end_date IS NULL`.**
- **Users belong to many projects; this is a first-class case, not an edge
  case.** The invariant above constrains the *pair*, not the user — someone
  with open memberships in ten projects has ten distinct pairs and violates
  nothing. A field tech working three concurrent studies, or a grad student
  on their own project plus their advisor's, is the normal shape of this app's
  user base. Nothing in the schema, the sync protocol, or the authorization
  model may assume one project per user. The reason the pair invariant matters
  at all is narrow: 8.4's `findForUser` takes `rows.first`, so two open rows
  for the *same* pair would make role lookup silently arbitrary.
- **Teammates' bearings stay included in position estimates by default**
  (today's behavior — `findByProjectAndTag` has no author filter), but become
  visually attributable and sortable. The gap is provenance visibility, not
  the inclusion rule.
- **Team observations get their own tab**, not a merged list.

### Known limitation, to be surfaced in-product

**Removing a member cannot revoke data already on their device.** Setting
`end_date` stops future syncs and blocks server access; it cannot delete the
copy in their local SQLite. This is inherent to offline-first, not a gap to
close later.

Accepted as a tradeoff (2026-08-01), **conditional on disclosure**: the owner
must be told this at the moment they add a member, not buried in
documentation. For projects tracking endangered or poaching-target species,
precise historical locations in a departed member's offline copy are a real
disclosure surface, and the person adding them should know that before they
do it. See task 11.2.

### A standing rule for any task that ever computes an accuracy figure

**Settled by Michael 2026-08-31 and placed here rather than inside one task's entry,
because the task it constrains has not been written yet.** Task 11.92 asked for exactly
this and was right to: a decision that lives only in a completed task's entry is a decision
nobody will find.

> **When anything reports "the estimates were accurate to within X metres", that figure
> counts animal-and-collar truth points only by default.** The other kinds are includable
> deliberately, **and the screen must say which kinds the figure counted.**

**The reason, which is the part that must survive:** a collar-only point may be where the
collar was **shed days earlier**, so scoring a bearing estimate against it reports the app
as wrong when it was right. **No task may compute such a number without carrying this rule
in its acceptance.** The rule is already written into `ActualTagLocationCsv`'s class
documentation and `ActualTagLocation.foundKind`, so somebody meets it in the code as well
as here, and the CSV exports `found_kind` verbatim so the split can also be made in R.

### What must land before a beta ships — the division, 2026-08-29

**Why this exists.** The queue had grown to the point where Michael said he would
never reach the end of it, and he is right that he never will: **running the app is
what finds work, so the list grows as fast as it is worked.** The answer is not a
shorter list, it is a line. Everything below the line is real and none of it is
abandoned; it simply does not gate a beta.

**Task 11.40 has run, and `CLAUDE_DOCS/RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` (2026-08-30) is now the
authority.** This block stays because it ranks the *tasks*, which is what a command
table needs; the checklist adds the hardware, field and deployment items a task list
cannot carry. **They do not conflict — where they ever do, the checklist wins.**

| Must land before a beta | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **11.57** | A beta tester leaves a project in their first week, and today that can leave their device holding a project it belongs to and cannot reach |
