### Beta scope, and the decisions taken 2026-08-17

**Phase 11 is the March beta's feature set.** A single-team beta with no
membership, no invitations and no team view is a beta of nothing, so scope
discipline matters more here than in Phase 10 — that work was defensive and
open-ended by nature; this has a date.

**Built for March:** 11.1, 11.2, 11.3, 11.4, 11.5, 11.7, 11.9.
**Deferred:** 11.6 (view modes) — 11.4 gives Team with filters and 11.2 gives a
management screen, so the three-mode toggle across Log *and* Map is duplication
until a real team has been watched using it.
**Dissolved:** 11.8 (tests). Every task below carries its own tests. A
tests-at-the-end task is how seven tasks ship untested, which Phase 10 taught
repeatedly.

**Roles are a gradient** (decided 2026-08-17):

| Role | Can |
| --- | --- |
| `viewer` | read the project; record nothing, change nothing |
| `contributor` | record observations, edit and delete **their own** |
| `owner` | everything, plus manage membership, roles, and data quality |

**Editing stays author-only.** A teammate cannot edit your observation. That is
Phase 8's rule and it survives teams: observations are primary scientific
records, and an owner rewriting what a colleague wrote in the field breaks
provenance in a way that matters to a publication, a permit or an enforcement
action. **The correction mechanism is supersede** (11.7) — the new row points at
the one it replaces, the original survives with its author intact, and position
estimation counts only the superseding row. That last clause is what stops a
correction being double-counted as independent evidence and falsely tightening
the confidence ellipse.

**Invitations travel out of band** (decided 2026-08-17). The owner generates a
code in the app and sends it however they like — text, email, in person, read
over the radio. **The server never sends mail to a non-member**, which keeps
deliverability and abuse out of the project entirely. Not a link: task 10.77
closed deep-link route injection, iOS is safe today only because no URL type is
registered, and a join link registers one.

**Removal governs future access only.** A departed member's observations stay in
the project, attributed to them. Scientifically they must, and the record of who
collected what is the point. Combined with the known limitation below: removal
stops future sync and blocks server access, and reaches nothing already on their
device or already synced to teammates.

### Task 11.1 — Co-equal project owners and ownership transfer
**Status:** Done (2026-08-20)
**Model:** **Opus** — revises an enforcement boundary.
**Depends on:** 10.5, 10.10

Task 8.4 decided the `owner` rule reads `Projects.owner_user_id`, explicitly
because no ownership-transfer feature existed so the column and the membership
table could not diverge. Both halves of that premise now change.

- Enforcement moves to **`role='owner'` rows in `Project_Memberships` with
  `end_date IS NULL`**. Any number, all with identical rights.
- `Projects.owner_user_id` is **retained as a creator/audit record** but is no
  longer the authorization source. Do not drop the column — it is populated in
  every existing project and backup.
- Backfill: 8.4 already writes an owner membership on project creation and
  backfills existing projects, so the rows exist. **Verify before relying on
  it** — that is a claim about the past, and this phase has learned what those
  are worth.
- Ownership transfer: grant `owner` to another member, then optionally end your
  own owner membership.
- **Guard the last-owner case:** a project must never reach zero open owner
  memberships. Refuse with an explanation rather than leaving an unmanageable
  project — a realistic failure mode when someone leaves a lab.
- Update `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`'s Security & Data Integrity section,
  which documents the opposite decision, and note that 8.1/8.3's "decide once,
  apply to both" flag is now resolved the other way.
- **Tests:** two owners each perform every owner action; transfer works; the
  last owner cannot remove themselves; client and server agree on who is an
  owner; **Phase 8's existing authorization tests are updated, not bypassed.**

### Task 11.2 — Membership lifecycle, invite tokens, and the owner's dashboard
**Status:** Done (2026-08-20)
**Model:** **Opus** for the token design; the lifecycle and UI are specified.
**Depends on:** 11.1

**Carries an accepted cost from task 10.20 (C-1) — this task is the fix.**
10.20's row-naming invariant permits naming a user unknown to the server, or
already reachable from the project being written to, and denies naming someone
who has an account but is *not* in that project. That closes a disclosure path
and blocks a legitimate case: saving a shared observation authored by a
colleague who has registered but is not on your project. **An accepted
invitation is the provenance the invariant lacks** — the server's own evidence
that this person belongs here.

**The invite token, which is the security-carrying part:**

- **Bound to the invitee's email address.** The owner enters it when creating
  the invite; the code redeems only for an account authenticated as that
  address. A forwarded or shoulder-surfed code is then worthless. Given what
  this data is, that is the right default and it costs almost nothing.
- **Short and human-typeable.** Roughly 8 characters from an alphabet with no
  `0/O` or `1/I/l`. It has to survive being written on a whiteboard, read over
  a radio, and typed with cold hands. **Do not use a UUID.**
- Single-use, expiring, and revocable. Pending invites are visible to owners.
- Redemption requires an authenticated session — sign in first, then join.
- **Joining needs connectivity, and the flow must say so** rather than letting
  someone discover it at a trailhead. This is the one part of the app that
  cannot work offline, and that is inherent, not a gap.

**Lifecycle:**

- **Rejoining creates a new membership row; it does not null `end_date`.**
  Nulling erases the record of the prior stint, which is the whole point of
  keeping it. `Project_Memberships` has no unique constraint on
  `(project_id, user_id)` and 8.4's `findForUser` filters `end_date IS NULL`,
  so a closed stint correctly does not count. **Invariant: for any single
  (project, user) pair, at most one row with `end_date IS NULL`.**
- **Users belong to many projects — first-class, not an edge case.** The
  invariant constrains the *pair*, not the user. A field tech on three
  concurrent studies, or a student on their own project plus an advisor's, is
  the normal shape of this user base. Nothing in the schema, protocol or
  authorization model may assume one project per user. The pair invariant
  matters narrowly: 8.4's `findForUser` takes `rows.first`, so two open rows
  for the same pair would make role lookup silently arbitrary.
- **Removal disclosure is a condition of this feature, not a nice-to-have.**
  The owner must be told, at the moment they add someone, that removal cannot
  reach data already on that person's device. See the known limitation above.
  For projects tracking poaching-target species that is a real disclosure
  surface and the person adding a member should know before they do it.

**Inserts are not covered by Phase 8's rule table — this table is the
exception, and it is 11.1's discovered scope.** Phase 8 checks edits and deletes
and deliberately does not check inserts, because creating a row is normally
adding your own data and harms nobody. **In `Project_Memberships` the insert
*is* the grant.** 11.1's `grantOwner` therefore checks the actor itself rather
than relying on the rule table, and **invite redemption is a second insert into
that same table and needs its own check for the same reason.** The rule table
will not supply one, and nothing will fail loudly if you forget.

A client-side check only stops honest paths. **The check that matters is 11.3's,
server-side** — a hostile device can insert a membership row locally and sync
it. Both are required: this task's for the app's own correctness, 11.3's for
security. Add a test that a redemption with a valid session but no valid token
inserts nothing.

**The owner's dashboard** (decided 2026-08-17): one screen listing members with
their role, joined date, and past stints, where changing someone's role is
obvious and takes one interaction. Pending and revoked invites live here too.
This is the surface an owner uses under time pressure — make it boring and
legible rather than clever.

**Tests:** a token redeems once and only for its bound address; an expired,
revoked, or wrong-address code is refused with no information about which;
rejoining produces a second row and the pair invariant holds; a removed member's
**next request for that project is refused, while their
other projects keep working** (the earlier wording here said "session is revoked
immediately", which was wrong: sessions are per user, so revoking one would cut
someone off from every project they belong to — a planning error corrected
2026-08-17 on 11.2's report); the disclosure is present in the add-member flow
and a test asserts it.

**Done 2026-08-20.** All of it, plus the C-1 closure the framing promised — and
that closure is the part worth reading first.

**The invariant was not touched.** §4.17 refuses a row naming somebody the
project does not already reach. What changed is that a project can now reach
somebody other than its owner: an accepted invitation writes a
`Project_Memberships` row, `user_id` on that table is in
`SyncTable.identityUserColumns`, and `ProjectReachability` — the same
computation pull uses — therefore names them. Pinned over a real socket in
`server/test/integration/membership_and_invites_test.dart`: the *same*
observation row naming a colleague answers `unauthorized` before redemption and
`inserted` after, with the invitation the only thing that changed. A second case
pins that the widening is per project.

**The token** (`invite_code.dart`, `invite_service.dart`; design recorded as
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §5.1.1): 8 characters of Crockford Base32 — digits
and letters minus `I`, `L`, `O`, `U`, with `I`/`L`→`1` and `O`→`0` folded on
input so a misread character still lands on the printed code. SHA-256 at rest,
single-use via one atomic conditional `UPDATE`, 14-day expiry, revocable, and
**bound to the address the server authenticated for the redeeming session**
(`auth_accounts.email`, never anything from the request). 40 bits rather than
§4.2's 256, reasoned in §5.1.1: a correct guess is useful only to somebody who
has already been invited, so the binding is the control and the entropy bounds
nuisance. Rate-limited per authenticated user rather than per source — the only
authenticated route limited here, because a session's `user_id` cannot collapse
the way §4.4.1's source key does.

**Redemption is server-side, and the server writes the membership row itself**
from the invitation's own `project_id` and `role`. The client never proposes
one. The alternative — let the joining device push it and teach `RowAuthorizer`
to permit a row backed by a redeemed invitation — hands the attacker the pen, so
**the push path needed no exemption and still refuses every membership insert
from a non-owner.** That is 11.3's job made simpler, not harder; two tests here
already pin it (a stranger, and a contributor who is genuinely on the project).
The one seam is `SyncService.insertServerAuthoredRow`: one call site, named so a
second one shows up in a grep.

**The insert check became a rule rather than a second hand-check.** 11.1 flagged
that `grantOwner` checks its actor by hand because Phase 8 does not authorize
inserts and in this table the insert *is* the grant. Every insert into
`Project_Memberships` now names a `MembershipInsertAuthority` —
`bootstrapOwner` (no open owner yet, and names the recorded creator),
`byOwner(actor)`, or `replication(reason)` — and the repository verifies it.
There is deliberately **no** door for accepting an invitation, because the
client never writes that row. Phase 8's own test that asserted "inserts are
never authorized" was corrected rather than bypassed, and three new cases were
possible only after the change: the bootstrap door cannot name anyone but the
creator, cannot be replayed once an owner exists, and a non-owner cannot add a
member.

**The disclosure is a control.** `removalDisclosure` gates the "Create invite
code" button — disabled with a valid address entered, enabled only after
acknowledgement — and is repeated on the removal confirmation. Asserted in
`test/features/more/project_members_screen_test.dart`.

**Lifecycle.** Rejoining writes a new row and never nulls `end_date`; the pair
invariant (at most one open row per (project, user)) is checked at redemption
and tested, including that one person holds open memberships in two projects at
once. Role changes and removal travel by ordinary sync — both are *updates* the
rule table already governs on both sides, last-owner guard included — rather
than through endpoints that would be a third place for the same decision.

Server 544 green against Postgres (24 new in `test/projects/`, 17 new in
`test/integration/`); app 989 green with no server (12 in
`packages/tritrack_sync/test/invite_code_test.dart`, 6 in
`test/data/sync/invite_redemption_test.dart`, 5 in the screen test, plus the
corrected Phase 8 cases). The e2e suite was **not** run — it compiles and its
one hand-written transport was extended, but no live-stack run was made.

### Task 11.3 — Server-side member authorization and the role gradient
**Status:** Done (2026-08-20)
**Model:** **Opus** — security boundary.
**Depends on:** 11.1, 11.2, and Phase 10's task 10.10

Phase 10's task 10.10 enforced the rules that need no membership table.
This completes the model now that real membership exists.

- Narrow `anyUser` from "any identified user" to **"any current member of that
  row's project."** Task 8.4 deferred this for lack of any way to add non-owner
  members; 11.2 creates that, so it lands here. Affected tables: `Tags`,
  `Project_Tags`, `Estimated_Positions`, `Actual_Tag_Locations`,
  `Triangulation_Sessions`.
- **Enforce the role gradient server-side:** `viewer` writes nothing;
  `contributor` writes its own and nothing else; `owner` per 11.1. The client's
  counterpart must agree, and the server is the authority.
- **Membership inserts need an explicit server-side rule, and the rule table
  has no insert coverage.** Phase 8 checks edits and deletes only, on the
  reasoning that creating a row harms nobody — false for `Project_Memberships`,
  where the insert is the grant. 11.1 hand-checked `grantOwner`; 11.2
  hand-checks redemption. **Neither client check binds a hostile device**, which
  can insert the row locally and sync it. So: the sync push path and the
  membership endpoints must both refuse a membership row the caller is not
  entitled to create. **Test it by pushing one directly, not through the UI.**
  While here, ask whether any *other* table has the same property — a row whose
  existence is itself a permission.
- **Re-deliver newly-reachable `Tags` rows when `Project_Tags` widens a
  project's reach.** 11.2 fixed this for people — someone joining a project has
  to receive rows that were already there before they arrived. The same gap is
  still open for tags: attaching a tag to a project makes that tag reachable to
  everyone in it, and nothing currently re-sends it. Recorded in a code comment
  by 11.2 as a Phase 11 problem; scheduled here so a gate does not rediscover it.
- **Cross-project isolation on every endpoint.** Membership in project A grants
  nothing in project B. **This is the most likely real breach in the whole
  system** — not a dramatic exploit, just one endpoint that checks
  *authenticated* and forgets *authorized for this project*. Enumerate every
  endpoint; a verdict per endpoint, per the standing rule.
- **Re-evaluate two `RowAuthorizer` judgment calls accepted under Phase 10's
  single-member assumption** (`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §5.9): an orphan
  `Tags` row is currently writable by anyone who knows its id — re-derive
  "referenced by no project" against real multi-member reachability; and
  `Non_Detections.tag_ids_listened_for` and
  `Estimated_Positions.observation_ids_used` are unvalidated delimited-id-list
  columns with no foreign-key check, currently harmless only because neither
  feeds `_reachable`. Decide whether they need a real check **before** any
  future feature folds them into reachability. Both go on 11.9's list
  explicitly rather than waiting to be rediscovered.
- **Tests:** an authenticated member of project A cannot read or mutate any row
  of project B by any endpoint including sync; a `viewer` cannot write; a
  `contributor` cannot touch another member's row; **Security Gate B is re-run
  against these surfaces.**

**Done 2026-08-20.** All of it, plus one thing the task did not ask for and one
the gate found in this task's own work — read the second one first.

**Security Gate B was re-run and it failed the first pass, on a bug this task
introduced.** Making a no-op `Tags` row skip the write checks was right: a
device re-offers unchanged rows whenever a sync receipt is missing, so a viewer
would otherwise have accumulated a permanent refusal for every tag in their
project — a held row is a claim that something is unwritten, and these were not.
What it missed is where that row then landed. The no-op branch recorded the tag
id as *established by this push*, which is the bookkeeping that lets a tag
created and first used in one round be referenced by the rows using it. So: two
rows for one tag id in one push, the first losing last-write-wins and therefore
needing no permission — and vouching; the second carrying a winning revision and
short-circuiting the role gradient, the claimed-by-another-project refusal and
the orphan author check alike. A `Project_Tags` row in the same batch rode the
same vouching to link a stranger's tag into the attacker's project, after which
`ProjectReachability` delivered its frequency and deployment notes on the next
pull. **Any signed-in user holding a tag's id could rename, retune or tombstone
another team's transmitter record, and read it.** Reproduced as a failing test
against Postgres first, then closed — the fix is not to stop skipping the checks
but to stop the no-op vouching: *vouching is a claim that this push established
the row, so only a row that passed authorization **and wrote something** may make
it.* Recorded as `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.21.3, because the rule
generalises past tags.

**How the fix was verified, and what was not machine-checked.** The regression
test was watched go red against the broken code and green against the fix —
that direction matters more than a passing test, and it is the check the gate's
own instruments have been caught skipping. The adversarial re-run then refused
every variation put to it (a poison row as an insert that loses, as an
`invalid` row, ordered after the payload, split across `Tags` and
`Project_Tags`, and with the payload aimed at each of the four other tables
carrying a `tag_id`) — but the re-run **stalled before finishing**, so the last
three checks were completed by hand instead: every remaining
`_noteEstablishedTag` call site sits on a path that writes; the legitimate
flows the fix must not break are covered by four existing tests that still pass
("a new tag still syncs" in both its one-push and one-request-per-table forms,
an unlinked tag between one author's devices, and an unchanged row re-offered
without permission); and the disclosure half of the finding is asserted end to
end by the new test, which pushes the link *and then pulls* to prove the tag is
not delivered.

**The gradient.** `ProjectAccess` splits Phase 10's single `member` into
`contributor` and `viewer`, resolved through one shared `resolveProjectRole`
(`packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/project_roles.dart`) so the app and the server
cannot disagree — the same move 11.1 made for ownership. `viewer` counts for
`permitsSync`, because reading is the whole of what a viewer was granted; the
gradient applies to writes, through `permitsProjectWrite`. A viewer's push is
refused **per row**, not with a transport-level 403: a 403 would refuse the one
push a viewer legitimately makes — their own `Users` profile, which is theirs
and not the project's — and would turn every locally-recorded row into a failed
sync rather than a held, counted, explained refusal (task 10.28's rule).

**This is also `anyUser`'s narrowing**, and the narrowing is deliberately not
written into the enum. Membership and role are properties of the caller and the
project, not of the row, and answering them needs a database — the shape 11.1
had to give the two ownership rules, and which it made `permits` throw for
rather than answer wrongly. The tables `anyUser` governs (tags, sessions,
estimates, recovered locations, tag links) were exactly the half with no author
column to stop a viewer, which is why "read-only" was a word on an invitation
and nothing else until now.

**"Contributor writes its own and nothing else" needed a reading, and the
strict one is wrong.** Recording one observation also writes a
`Triangulation_Sessions` row and may link a `Project_Tags` row, and neither
table has an author column to be "your own" by. Reading the rule as *no shared
row either* would leave the role unable to do the one thing it exists for. So:
a contributor passes the gradient and is still held to their own observations by
`MutationRule.author`. Recorded in §4.21 as a decision rather than left implicit.

**Membership inserts, proved by pushing one rather than through the UI.** Every
table now declares `SyncTable.insertIsAGrant` — **required, not defaulted**, so
a new table cannot join the permissive branch by omission, the same discipline
`tableMutationRules` gets from having no default entry. Three answer yes, and
the class question the brief asked has an answer: `Project_Memberships` (the
insert *is* the membership), `Projects` (creating one makes you its owner) and
`Project_Tags` (linking a global tag makes it readable by everyone in the
project — a read grant issued by creating a row, which is the one nobody had
named before). The switch that authorizes them is exhaustive and its unhandled
branch **denies**, so flagging a table without deciding what may create its rows
fails closed and loudly. Exactly one membership insert survives on the push
path: a project's own creator bootstrapping their owner row, or backfilling it
on a project that predates 8.4. The pair invariant is enforced against stored
rows *and* against what the same push has already been cleared to create —
without that second half two rows in one batch would each see a snapshot
containing neither, which is the shape 11.1's `_ownershipsRemovedThisPush`
already had. Seven cases pin it over a real socket: a contributor promoting
themselves, a contributor adding a second row, a viewer, an owner adding
somebody else, an owner adding a second row for themselves, a stranger, and two
rows in one push.

**Cross-project isolation: a verdict per endpoint**, all 24 routes, in
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.21.2 — including the ones with no project-scoped
identifier, since silence about an endpoint is not a verdict. Each of the eight
that takes one is tested against a **fabricated** project id rather than against
a hard-coded status, so a test cannot pass by both branches matching one
constant. One route family gets a verdict rather than a pass: the diagnostics
console takes a `project_id` on two routes and runs no per-project
authorization, because it has no user session at all — it is gated on a real
loopback peer plus an operator token and exists so the person running the server
can read their own database. Stated rather than assumed, with the consequence
written down: **the day the console grows a per-user session, this becomes a
live gap.** On 11.9's list.

**§5.9's two deferred items, re-derived.** (a) The orphan-`Tags` entry ran two
worries together and only one was ever about orphans. The *viewer* arm was real
and is closed by the gradient. The *removed member* arm does not apply: every
tag id a departed member holds is one their old project references, which makes
it claimed rather than orphaned, and the existing refusal already stops them.
The orphan case itself is unchanged by Phase 11 and is **kept open on purpose**,
because an unlinked tag is a supported product state — the tag dialog offers
"None (unlinked)" outright — so refusing to sync one would hold somebody's own
tag hostage on their own device. Narrowed anyway, for free: only the user the
stored row already names may maintain an orphan, which drops "anyone who knows
the id" to "the person who last wrote it". What stays open is that an orphan can
still be *linked* into a project by anyone holding its id; that has to stay
open, it is how a tag becomes a project's at all. (b) The two unvalidated
id-list columns stay accepted, and the reason that survives the change of
population is the second one, not the first: neither feeds reachability, so a
foreign id in them is a dangling reference and not a disclosure. Not given a
foreign-key check, and the cost is real rather than laziness — a position
estimate and the observations it cites arrive in one batch and are all
authorized against a snapshot in which none of them is written yet, so the
within-push bookkeeping that solves this for tags would have to be built twice
more, to close a gap that discloses nothing. **The acceptance's condition is now
enforced instead of merely written**: a test fails if either column is ever
declared in the sets reachability walks, with a positive control that fires in
the same run. Both items are on 11.9's list by name.

**Newly-reachable `Tags` rows are re-delivered.** 11.2 fixed this for people and
recorded the tag half as still open. A `Project_Tags` insert now re-stamps the
tag it claims, so a teammate whose cursor is already past it receives it instead
of pulling a page their own foreign key refuses — which would have stopped that
device syncing entirely, not just that row. Only on insert: a link's creation is
what widens reach, and re-stamping on every no-op re-offer would redeliver an
unchanged row forever.

**One thing beyond the brief, and why.** Task 11.11 states that a `viewer` may
not create a tag. A viewer could, because `Tags` is global and the gradient runs
on project-scoped tables. Closed here rather than left for 11.11, because §4.21
claims a viewer writes nothing and a claimed control that does not quite fire is
the §4 B4 shape this project keeps finding at gates. 11.11 still owns the
product side — the near-duplicate warning, and narrowing tag *editing* to owners
— and the seam it should tighten is named in §4.21.

**The app agrees, and deliberately less strictly.** `BaseRepository` refuses on
an explicit `viewer` and on nothing else, where the server also refuses a caller
with no role. The two are answering in different situations: a local database
legitimately holds projects this device has no membership row for — a restored
backup, a colleague's import, one created offline and never published — and
refusing those would make the app read-only on data it is the only holder of.
Inserts are gated too, which Phase 8 does not do, by reading the acting user off
the row's `last_modified_by`; nothing replicates other people's rows through a
repository, so the column is sound on an insert specifically, and a null one
permits.

Server 579 green against Postgres (35 new in
`test/integration/member_authorization_test.dart`); app 1001 green with no
server (12 in `test/data/repositories/role_gradient_test.dart`); the shared
package 219 green (13 in `test/project_roles_test.dart`, 3 in
`sync_tables_test.dart`). **The e2e suite was run and passed** — 33 tests
against a live Docker stack, which 11.1 and 11.2 both skipped; its
`authorization_denial_e2e_test.dart` and `refused_row_visibility_e2e_test.dart`
are the two cases that most directly exercise what changed here.

### Task 11.4 — Team log tab
**Status:** Done
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** nothing structural — teammates' rows already land in
`Observations` via Phase 6 replica import, so this is testable by seeding the
database with no server present.

- Second tab alongside the existing Log: the whole project's observations with
  observer attribution. **The personal Log stays personal.**
- Sortable by **member, tag, time, and distance**. The observer filter chip
  already exists in `log_screen.dart` (`_HistoryFilters.userId`) — extend it
  rather than building a parallel filtering path.
- **Distance means distance from the user's current GPS position.** With no fix
  — desktop, or indoors — the distance sort must present as *unavailable*,
  disabled with a reason, and **never silently fall back to another ordering.**
  A sort that quietly reorders by something else is worse than one greyed out.
- **Tests:** teammates' observations appear with attribution; all four sorts
  work; the personal Log's existing behaviour and tests are unchanged; the tab
  is correct with data seeded locally and no server configured.

### Task 11.5 — Observer provenance in position estimation
**Status:** Done — implemented member/time/distance sorts, not tag/member/distance
as originally scoped; see the Discovered Scope note below for why.
**Model:** Sonnet — UI and sorting over an existing solver. **Do not touch the
Lenth MLE or the geometry guards.** If it turns out you must, stop and flag it.
**Depends on:** nothing structural (same reasoning as 11.4)

Position estimation already gathers every observation for a tag regardless of
author, already supports per-ray include/exclude, and already records
`observationIdsUsed`. What is missing is that **a teammate's ray is visually
identical to your own** — and since teammates' bearings are included by
default, that invisibility is a data-quality hazard rather than a cosmetic gap.

- Distinguish rays by observer — badge or styling on the ray and its list row.
  Colour already carries tag identity, so **this must not be a colour-only
  cue** (the project's standing redundant-cue rule).
- Sort the bearing selector by **tag, user, and distance**, so including or
  excluding a subset is quick rather than a hunt. Distance uses 11.4's
  definition and its no-fix behaviour.
- **Default inclusion is unchanged** — everything in, tap to exclude.
- **Tests:** every ray's observer is identifiable without relying on colour;
  all three sorts work; **the solver's inputs and outputs are byte-identical to
  before for any given included set**, proven by the existing localization
  tests passing untouched.

### Task 11.6 — View modes: Mine / Team / Manage
**Status:** **Deferred past the March beta** (decided 2026-08-17). Numbered so
it is tracked, not scheduled.
**Model:** Sonnet when it runs.
**Depends on:** 11.4, 11.5

A Mine / Team / Manage toggle applied consistently across Log and Map. Deferred
because 11.4 delivers Team with filters and 11.2 delivers a management screen,
so this is largely duplication until a real team has been observed using them.

The design decision from 2026-08-01 stands and should be honoured whenever it
does run: **a mode toggle available to every user, not a role-forked UI.** The
field-versus-desk distinction is about *context*, not role — a contributor
reviewing data at a desk wants the full picture, an owner standing in a drainage
wants three things on screen. Role-forked views get it wrong in both directions
and mean an owner can never reproduce what a member sees when troubleshooting.
Manage mode visible to all, its controls rendered only for owners, disabled with
a reason rather than hidden. Remembered per device, not per account.

### Task 11.7 — Supersede and exclude
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-21).** Built as a new synced table,
`Observation_Exclusions` (schema v7, additive; schema major stays 2), rather
than as columns on `Observations` — the observation is never written by either
action, which is the strongest available form of this task's own "may not
rewrite the original" rule, and the only design that survives sync. See the
completion note below. Superseding is contributor-level on anyone's
observation; excluding is owner-only. Both controls render disabled with a
reason, closing the item task 11.12 left open.
**Model:** **Opus** — touches the provenance guarantees Phases 6 and 8 exist to
protect.
**Depends on:** 11.1, 11.3

**Scope narrowed 2026-08-17: supersede and exclude. `flag` is dropped** — it is
a third state nobody had a use for, and a status field with no consumer is a
future migration for nothing.

Recorded because a future task will otherwise "simplify" this into plain edit
access: observations are primary scientific records. Phase 6 went to deliberate
trouble to preserve original authorship on replicated rows and Phase 8 made
mutation author-only on purpose. The need behind the request — bad data must not
corrupt analysis — is fully met without destroying the original.

- **Supersede** is also the answer to the two-people-one-observation case. A
  corrected row points at the row it replaces; the original survives with its
  author and values intact; **position estimation counts only the superseding
  row.** Get that last part right — the solver treats each bearing as
  independent evidence, so counting both would tighten the confidence ellipse
  on evidence that does not exist. A wrong answer that looks more precise is
  the worst outcome available here.
- **Exclude** removes a row from analysis without altering or hiding it. It must
  be visible and reversible, and the excluded row must remain in the Team log
  with its state shown.
- Neither action may rewrite `user_id`, `last_modified_by`, or any measurement
  column of the original row. **A test must assert that**, not a comment.
- **Tests:** a superseded row is excluded from the solver and its replacement
  included, proven by a position estimate that changes when expected and does
  not when not; an excluded row stays visible and its exclusion reverses; a
  round trip through export and re-import preserves both relationships.

**Completion note (2026-08-21).**

- **Columns on `Observations` were tried first and do not work.** That table is
  governed by `MutationRule.author` — only the person who recorded an
  observation may write its row — and sync authorizes *whole rows*, so the
  server cannot tell "an owner touched only the exclusion columns" from "an
  owner rewrote the bearing." A mark stored on the observation could never
  leave the device that made it. The argument is written into
  `Tables.observationExclusions`, `schema.dart` and
  `ObservationExclusionRepository` precisely because this task predicted a
  future attempt to simplify it into edit access.
- **The pointer direction follows from the same constraint.** In the
  two-people-one-observation case the record you must retire is the *other*
  person's, so a `supersedes` column on the replacement row would be
  unwritable by the person making the correction. A mark row authored by that
  person works in every case.
- **Reversal is a tombstone on the mark**, so the undo merges between devices
  instead of resurrecting on the next sync.
- **The solver claim was measured, not assumed.** With four or fewer perfectly
  consistent bearings the Lenth estimator reports *no* uncertainty ellipse at
  all (no residuals to estimate a spread from), so the double-count effect is
  invisible at that scale. At a realistic eight-bearing set with ordinary
  compass scatter, counting one bearing twice shrinks the reported ellipse from
  430 m to 386 m — a 10% false gain in precision on evidence that does not
  exist. That is the number the test asserts.
- Tests: app 1082 green, 9 skipped (25 new across
  `test/data/analysis/analysis_eligibility_test.dart`,
  `test/data/repositories/observation_exclusion_repository_test.dart`,
  `test/data/sync/observation_exclusion_round_trip_test.dart` and
  `test/features/more/log_screen_test.dart`); shared package 219 green; server
  586 green **against real Postgres in Docker**, including four new cases in
  `member_authorization_test.dart` over a bound socket.

### Discovered Scope — from task 11.7 (2026-08-21)

- **The role split diverges from what task 11.12 predicted, deliberately.**
  11.12's note guessed that "a contributor sees it only on their own
  observations, consistent with `authorEditVerdict`." Built the other way:
  **a contributor may supersede anyone's observation.** Holding supersede to
  your own rows would leave the feature unable to do the job the Beta-scope
  preamble gives it — "a teammate cannot edit your observation; the correction
  mechanism is supersede" — and would leave the two-people-one-observation
  case with no answer at all. Excluding *is* owner-only, matching the
  gradient's "data quality" rung. **No action needed**; recorded so the
  divergence is a decision on the record rather than a drift.
- **An owner cannot withdraw a contributor's supersede mark.** The mark is
  governed by `MutationRule.author`, so its creator withdraws it and nobody
  else. In practice a contributor who superseded wrongly can undo it, and an
  owner can exclude the replacement — but there is no owner override on a
  mark, which is a gap if a member leaves the project with a bad mark in
  place. **Action: ask the planning session whether this needs its own task**;
  it is a real hole but a narrow one, and closing it needs a rule the rule
  table cannot currently express (author-or-owner).
- **The share payload (`TT1:` text sharing) does not carry marks.** Sharing a
  single observation to a colleague transmits the observation and nothing
  about whether it has been superseded or excluded, so a recipient who imports
  it as a replica will count it. The backup/restore and server sync paths both
  carry marks correctly (round-trip tested). **Action: ask the planning
  session whether the share payload should carry the receiving side's mark
  state** — arguably it should not, since a mark is a judgment made inside one
  project and the payload lands in a different one by default, but that is a
  product call rather than mine.
- **The v7 server migration has not been run against an existing database.**
  `schemaV7Statements` is exercised only as part of a fresh bootstrap in the
  test suite, because the server's v6 migration was never given migration-path
  coverage either and nothing is deployed. **Action: ask the planning session
  whether server migration-path coverage deserves a task** — it is cheap to add
  now and expensive to discover missing the first time a real server upgrades.

### Task 11.8 — (dissolved)
**Status:** **Dissolved into 11.1–11.7** (decided 2026-08-17). Each task above
carries its own tests, in the same task, verified by running them.

A tests-at-the-end task is how a phase ships seven untested features and
discovers it at a gate. Phase 10 produced that shape repeatedly — most
expensively when a suite reported 261 tests green while a third of it never ran
for want of a database. Tests belong to the change that needs them.

### Task 11.10 — A database constraint for the one-open-membership rule
**Status:** Done, 2026-08-21. A partial unique index,
`idx_memberships_one_open`, on `Project_Memberships(project_id, user_id)
WHERE end_date IS NULL AND deleted_at IS NULL` — schema v8 on both sides
(v7 was already spent by 11.7's `Observation_Exclusions`, so this is v8, not
the v7 the brief guessed before that task landed). App: `schemaV8Statements`
in `lib/data/db/schema.dart`, wired into `lib/data/db/migrations.dart`.
Server: `schemaV8Statements` in `server/lib/src/schema/postgres_schema.dart`,
wired into `serverMigrations` **and appended directly to `schemaStatements`**
— a fresh bootstrap never replays `serverMigrations`, so the index needed
its own line there too, or every new server would silently lack it while
every upgraded one had it (caught by a test before it shipped, not in the
field). The existing code check stays as the readable-error path;
`InviteService.redeem` now opens a `SAVEPOINT` around the consuming write
and the membership insert, and on a `23505` (unique_violation) from the
index, rolls back to it and returns `RedemptionRefused(alreadyMember)` —
plain `try/catch` around the insert alone does not work with
`package:postgres`, which rethrows a transaction's recorded error from
`runTx` regardless of any local `catch`; only a `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT`
clears that. The rollback undoes the consuming `UPDATE` too, so a lost race
leaves the code unconsumed, matching the ordinary (non-racing)
`alreadyMember` path. Tested against a **real** race: two acceptances on two
independent `Connection`s (the suite's one shared connection provably cannot
race itself — `package:postgres` serializes all `runTx` calls on one
connection through an internal `Pool(1)`, confirmed by first writing the
test against the shared connection and watching it pass with the fix
reverted). `server/test/projects/invite_service_test.dart` and
`test/data/schema_v8_migration_test.dart`; `server/test/schema/postgres_schema_test.dart`
gained the fresh-bootstrap regression test above. One pre-existing bug
found and fixed along the way: `_ensureOwnerMembership` (task 8.4/11.1's
"repair a project with no open owner" backfill,
`lib/core/providers/app_context_provider.dart`) inserted a brand-new owner
row unconditionally, which — for a creator who already held an open row of
some other role (e.g. demoted to contributor) — created a second open row
for the same person and violated the very invariant this task exists to
enforce; the index turned that from silent to a hard failure and an
existing test (`app_context_provider_test.dart`) caught it immediately. Fix:
centralized into `ProjectMembershipRepository.ensureOwnerMembership`, which
promotes the creator's existing open row in place instead of duplicating it.
**Model:** Sonnet — a schema migration and an index.
**Depends on:** 11.2

**Raised by 11.2, 2026-08-17.** The rule that a person has at most one *open*
membership per project is currently enforced by a check in code. That covers
every path the app actually has — but not two invitations for the same person
being accepted at the same instant, on two devices or two requests. A check
reads, then writes; between those two steps the other one can slip in.

The consequence is not dramatic and is worth stating plainly: two open rows for
one person in one project would make role lookup arbitrary, because 8.4's
`findForUser` takes the first row it finds. Someone could silently end up with
the wrong permissions.

- Add a **partial unique index on `(project_id, user_id)` where the membership
  is open**, at **schema version 7**, on both the app's SQLite and the server's
  Postgres. Both, because either side can be the one that accepts.
- Keep the code check. The index is the backstop that holds when two writes
  race; the check is what produces a sensible error message.
- **Test the race, not just the index.** Two concurrent accepts for the same
  person and project: one succeeds, one is refused, and the refusal is legible
  rather than a raw constraint violation surfacing in the UI.

### Task 11.11 — Who may create a tag, and warning before a duplicate
**Status:** **Done, 2026-08-21.** Both halves landed. Tag *editing and retiring*
is now owner-only on both sides of the wire — the server at the reachable-tag
branch of `RowAuthorizer._authorizeTagReferences` (`access != ProjectAccess.owner`,
where it was `!access.permitsProjectWrite`), the app at
`TagRepository.assertMayEdit`, which `Tags` needs a seam of its own for because
it is a global table with no `project_id` for `BaseRepository.assertRoleMayWrite`
to resolve a role against. Creation stays open to contributors, per the reasoning
below. The near-duplicate warning is `lib/data/tags/near_duplicate_tags.dart`
plus `confirmTagIsNotADuplicate`, wired into all four places a person can create
a tag by hand; it names the matched tag and what matched, and its affirmative
button creates the tag. Tests: `test/data/tags/near_duplicate_tags_test.dart`,
`test/data/repositories/tag_authorization_test.dart`, four widget tests in
`test/features/more/tag_database_screen_test.dart`, and four in
`server/test/integration/member_authorization_test.dart` — one of which inverts
what that file previously asserted ("a contributor can" rename a tag), which is
this task's decision landing.
Security Model §4.21 and §5.9(a) updated to match.
**Prior status, for the record:** half landed by 11.3 (2026-08-17) — the "a
viewer may not create a tag" rule was closed there, because leaving it open would
have made a claim in the security document untrue.
**Model:** **Opus** — a permission decision with a field-blocking failure mode.
**Depends on:** 11.3

**Raised 2026-08-17. The proposal was owner-only tag creation; the
recommendation is against it, and the reasoning matters more than the verdict.**

**Owner-only does not solve the problem it aims at.** Two owners, each offline,
each creating "F12" for the same collar, collide exactly as an owner and a
contributor would. The duplicate arises from *offline-first*, not from *who is
allowed to write*. So the restriction pays a real cost and buys nothing.

**And the cost is severe.** A field tech on a transect with no signal who hears
an unlisted collar and cannot create a tag **cannot record the observation at
all.** That trades a tidiness problem for a data-loss problem, on the app's
primary use case, in the one place where nothing can be fixed later. Losing a
bearing is worse than carrying a duplicate tag.

**Decision to implement:**

- **`contributor` and `owner` may create tags. `viewer` may not.** This follows
  11.3's gradient with no exception.
- **Editing and retiring a tag is owner-only.** Creation is additive and
  recoverable; changing what an existing tag *means* is not, because
  observations already reference it.
- **Warn before creating a near-duplicate, and let the user proceed.** Check the
  project's existing tags on:
  - **frequency** — the one that matters. Two tags on one frequency in one
    project will confuse triangulation and is usually a duplicate.
  - **name** — softer. `F12` beside `F12b` is often legitimate.
**Decision 2026-08-17 — unlinking a tag from a project is OWNER-ONLY, and here
is the line it draws.** 11.11's implementation left it contributor-level, which
was a defensible reading: it is reversible, it has UNDO, and it touches neither
the tag nor its observations. Overruled, because the distinction that matters is
not *how reversible* a write is but *whose data it changes*:

> **Additive writes that unblock field work are contributor-level. Subtractive
> writes that change what the whole team sees are owner-level.**

Creating a tag is additive and unblocking — a contributor who cannot create one
cannot record the animal in front of them, which is why 11.11 refused to make
creation owner-only. Unlinking is subtractive and it edits shared project
configuration: it removes a tag from *every* member's list, including someone
mid-transect whose quick-add just lost it. UNDO helps the person who did it, in
that session; a teammate who synced in between sees churn they cannot explain.

And the costs are asymmetric. A contributor who wants a tag gone asks an owner —
one message, nothing blocked. An owner whose tag was unlinked has to *notice*
first, and mid-season they may not.

**Apply the same rule to the rest of the gradient rather than re-deciding each
case**, and record it in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` so the next twelve
questions of this shape answer themselves.

- **Warn, never refuse.** Two collars can legitimately share a nominal
  frequency if they are never in range together — uncommon but real. A refusal
  here blocks honest field data to prevent a tidiness problem, which is the same
  trade this task exists to avoid.
- The warning must say *what* it matched and *which* existing tag, not just
  "possible duplicate". A warning the user cannot evaluate gets dismissed.

- **Tests:** a `viewer` cannot create a tag; a `contributor` can; a contributor
  cannot edit or retire one; a frequency collision warns and names the existing
  tag; the user can proceed and the tag is created; no warning fires for a
  genuinely distinct tag.

### Task 11.12 — Role-aware controls in the app's screens
**Status:** Done (2026-08-21). Every control named in this task's own sweep is
now disabled with a reason for a role that may not use it, matching task
11.1's pattern. The `ProjectTagRepository.setStatus` permission-layer bypass
is closed, and — since this landed the same day as the "unlinking is
owner-only" decision below — `setStatus` enforces that split directly:
deactivating (unlinking) requires ownership via a new
`assertMayUnlink`, activating (linking, or re-adding a previously-removed
tag) stays contributor-level. Two controls found along the way (the map's and
the Log/Team tabs' Edit/Delete, and the Members screen's "Add member" FAB)
were hidden rather than disabled and are now brought into the same pattern,
since they are the same class of finding this task exists to fix. Widget
tests per role added throughout. **11.7's supersede/exclude was not swept —
that feature has not been built yet (still "Not started")** — see Discovered
Scope below.
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 11.3. **Beta-blocking — this is a viewer's first five minutes.**

**Raised by 11.3, 2026-08-17, and it is a usability problem rather than a
security one.** The boundary holds: a `viewer` cannot write anything, anywhere,
and 11.3 proved it. But **no screen in the app knows about roles yet.** So a
viewer still sees a "Record" button, walks a transect, takes a bearing, fills
the form, taps save — and gets a raw error.

That is somebody's first experience of being added to a colleague's project, and
it teaches them the app is broken.

- Every control that writes must know the current user's role in the current
  project and **render disabled with a reason**, not hidden. Task 11.1 already
  did this for project settings — follow that pattern rather than inventing a
  second one.
- "Explain, don't just hide" is the project's standing rule (Phase 5.2, 8.3). A
  greyed control that says *"viewers cannot record observations — ask an owner
  to change your role"* teaches; a missing button confuses.
- **Sweep for the whole set, do not fix the Record button and stop.** Recording
  an observation, editing one, deleting one, creating a tag, editing a tag,
  editing project settings, membership actions, and 11.7's supersede and exclude.
  A verdict per control, per the standing rule.
- **`ProjectTagRepository.setStatus` bypasses the app's permission layer
  entirely** — it writes with a raw SQL statement. So a viewer who removes a tag
  from a project watches it appear to work, and the change is refused on the next
  sync instead. **The server refuses it correctly, so nothing unsafe gets
  through** (11.11 verified this over a real socket); it is a confusing-UI
  problem. Route it through the permission layer like everything else.
- **The specific tag controls to cover**, named by 11.11 so this task does not
  have to hunt: the Tag Database screen's `+` button and its list rows, project
  setup's "+ New tag", and Observation Logging's quick-add.
- **The client is not the boundary and must not be treated as one.** These
  controls are courtesy; 11.3's server-side refusal is the security. Do not
  weaken anything server-side because the UI now prevents it.
- **Tests:** for each role, every write control is either enabled or disabled
  with a reason, and no control is silently absent; a widget test per role
  rather than a manual pass.

### Decision 2026-08-21 — the `TT1:` text share does not carry supersede or exclude

**Raised by 11.7. Confirmed: it should not, and there is a technical reason that
settles it beyond taste.**

**Supersede is a relationship between two rows.** It says "this observation
replaces that one." A `TT1:` share hands over a *single* observation, so the row
at the other end of the relationship is not in the payload and does not exist on
the recipient's device. The mark would point at nothing. Carrying it would mean
either shipping both rows — a different feature — or writing a dangling
reference, which is the kind of thing this project spends gates finding.

**Exclude is a judgment made inside your project's analysis**, and it travels
without its reason. A colleague who pastes in a bearing marked excluded would
have it silently not counted, with nothing on screen explaining why. That is
worse than counting it: an unexplained omission in someone else's dataset is
harder to notice than an extra ray they can evaluate.

Backup files and server sync **do** carry both, correctly and round-trip tested,
because both move the whole project — the other end of the relationship comes
with it, and the recipient is inside the same analysis.

**One thing worth adding, and it is the real risk in the other direction.** The
person *sending* should be told when they are about to share an observation they
have themselves excluded or superseded — "you are sharing a bearing you have
marked as replaced." Handing a colleague something you had discarded, without
noticing, is the harm here, and it is cheap to prevent. **Fold this into task
11.14's sweep**, which is already touching the sharing screen's controls.

### Task 11.15 — An owner must be able to withdraw a contributor's supersede
**Status:** Done
**Model:** **Opus** — it adds a permission shape the rule table does not have.
**Depends on:** 11.3, 11.7.

**Raised by 11.7 as a hole it deliberately left open, and it is a real one.** A
supersede or exclude mark belongs to whoever made it, so only they can withdraw
it. **If a contributor marks a bearing as replaced by mistake and then leaves the
project, that mark is permanent.** Nobody can undo it — not the owner, not the
observation's own author.

For a project whose data supports a publication or a permit, a wrongly-discarded
bearing that cannot be restored is a real loss, and the person who could explain
it is gone.

- The fix is an **`author-or-owner`** rule: the person who made the mark, or any
  current project owner, may withdraw it.
- **Add it to the rule table, do not hand-code it at the call site.** Every
  existing rule is a single condition — `author`, `owner`, `projectOwner`,
  `anyUser`. This is the first disjunction, and if it is written inline here the
  next feature that needs it writes its own copy, which is how this project
  arrives at six instances of one shape.
- Withdrawing an owner's own mark is already covered; do not regress it.
- **Tests:** a contributor's mark is withdrawn by an owner; by the mark's author;
  and **not** by an unrelated contributor. Plus the case that motivates it — the
  author's membership has ended and an owner can still withdraw.

### Task 11.16 — Test the server's database upgrade path, not just a fresh build
**Status:** Done, 2026-08-21. Server:
`server/test/schema/postgres_migration_upgrade_test.dart` (new file, real
Postgres) builds a database at v6 shape (the current v8 bootstrap with v7's
table and v8's index stripped back off — `tableSpecs` only knows the
*current* schema, so this is the only way to reach an older shape), seeds a
representative row in every table a migration shouldn't touch, runs
`schemaV7Statements()` directly, and asserts every existing row is
unchanged column-for-column, plus that the new `Observation_Exclusions`
table actually works. Same pattern for v7→v8 with `schemaV8Statements()`,
plus a check that the new index actually refuses a second open membership
once real data is present (a fresh-bootstrap test can't tell "the index
works" from "the index was never exercised against data that had a reason
to violate it"). Verified the harness itself: temporarily added a
corrupting `UPDATE` inside each migration function, confirmed the
"byte-for-byte" tests fail, reverted.

**v6 (task 10.35's primary-key rekey) deliberately not reconstructed as an
upgrade-from-scratch here** — its pre-migration shape (single-column
primary keys) has no source of truth left in the current codebase to build
from without hand-writing historical DDL, and that migration's own doc
comment already records why the risk was accepted: it ran "while nothing
was deployed," so no server has ever upgraded through it with real data and
none ever will now that it has shipped. Flagged rather than silently
skipped — see "What you need to do" below.

**Client SQLite migrations had the identical gap, checked rather than
assumed:** v4 (`schema_v4_migration_test.dart`) and v5
(`schema_v5_migration_test.dart`) already had upgrade-with-data tests; v6
(`schema_v6_migration_test.dart`) is thorough. **v2, v3, and v7 had none at
all** — added `schema_v2_migration_test.dart`,
`schema_v3_migration_test.dart` (the highest-value addition: v3 is a
create-copy-drop-rename table rebuild on `Observations`, the same risk
class as v6, and had never been tested against an existing row before this),
and `schema_v7_migration_test.dart`. All three verified against deliberately
corrupted migration output the same way the server tests were, then
reverted. 599 server tests pass (up from 595), 1151 app tests pass (up from
1146), both `analyze` runs clean.
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 11.10. **Before the beta — see why.**

**Raised by 11.7, which correctly noted it did not introduce the gap.** The
server's schema migrations are only ever exercised by **building a database from
scratch**. No test upgrades an existing database with data in it from one schema
version to the next. That was already true before 11.7's new table and before
11.10's new index.

**Why this is beta-blocking rather than merely cheap.** The beta server will hold
one team's real field season. It will also be upgraded during the beta — 11.10
adds schema 7 and Phase 12 will add more. **The first time an upgrade path runs
against real data will be against their data**, and an upgrade that fails halfway
on a live database is the failure mode with no good recovery.

- Test each version step as an *upgrade*: build at version N with representative
  rows, migrate to N+1, and assert the rows survived with the right values — not
  merely that the migration returned without error.
- Include the client's SQLite migrations in the same sweep if they have the same
  gap. Ask rather than assume.
- **A migration that runs to completion and silently drops or blanks a column is
  the case worth writing the test for.** "It did not throw" is not the check.
