### Task 11.18 — Show that a mark was withdrawn, rather than notifying
**Status:** Done, 2026-08-22.
**Model:** Sonnet — **not beta-blocking.** Numbered so it is tracked.
**Depends on:** 11.15.

**Raised by 11.15 as a fairness gap, and it is real.** An owner can now withdraw
a contributor's supersede or exclude — that is the point of 11.15 — but **the
contributor is never told.** Their judgment about a scientific record can be
reversed and they may never know.

**The answer is visibility, not a notification system.** There are no
notifications anywhere in this app, and building the first one for this single
case is disproportionate. But the information already exists: 11.15 tombstones
the withdrawal rather than deleting it, and the tombstone syncs. It is simply not
shown.

- Surface it where someone would look — the observation's detail or history view:
  *"Exclusion withdrawn by Sam Kelly, 14 March."*
- Show the original mark too, not only its withdrawal. "This was excluded and
  then un-excluded" is the useful sentence; either half alone is misleading.
- **Not beta-blocking:** one team of a few people who talk to each other will
  notice. It matters more as teams grow and as owners and contributors stop
  sharing a truck.

**Outcome (2026-08-22).** No new screen — `log_screen.dart`'s Log and Team
tabs are the only place an observation's state was already shown (there is no
separate observation detail/history view), so this landed there, in the row
that already announces a *live* exclusion.

- **New repository read**:
  `ObservationExclusionRepository.withdrawnByObservation(projectId)` — the
  most recently withdrawn mark per observation, keyed the same way
  `activeByObservation` keys the live ones. It reads columns that were already
  there: `ObservationExclusion.userId` (the original marker; untouched by
  withdrawal) and `sync.lastModifiedBy`/`sync.deletedAt` (overwritten to the
  withdrawer and the withdrawal time by `BaseRepository.softDeleteByKey`).
  Nothing needed adding to the schema or to 11.15's write path.
- **Both halves, one sentence, on the row**: *"Excluded by Casey Marker, then
  withdrawn by Alex Owner on 2026-03-14 09:15"* — the marker's name, the
  reason if one was given, and the withdrawer's name and date, following the
  project's existing redundant-cue rule (state spelled out in words, not
  color/strikethrough alone) that the live-exclusion line next to it already
  uses. Rendered independent of whether the observation currently has a new,
  different live mark — an observation can carry both a current exclusion and
  a past excluded-then-withdrawn episode at once, and both are shown.
- **Scope decision: newest withdrawn episode only, not a full timeline.**
  Mirrors `activeByObservation`'s existing "newest wins" convention for live
  marks rather than introducing a new one. An observation withdrawn, marked,
  and withdrawn again shows only the latest withdrawal; not judged worth a
  timeline UI for a not-beta-blocking fairness note.
- **Tests, both red-then-green.** Repository:
  `test/data/repositories/observation_exclusion_repository_test.dart`'s new
  `'withdrawn-mark history for display (task 11.18)'` group (4 tests) —
  a withdrawn mark is returned naming both people; a live mark that was never
  withdrawn is absent; both a live and a withdrawn entry for the same
  observation coexist; the most recently withdrawn of several wins. Widget:
  `test/features/more/log_screen_test.dart`'s new
  `'withdrawn-mark visibility (task 11.18)'` group — seeds a tombstoned mark
  naming two distinct people (`Casey Marker`, `Alex Owner`) and asserts both
  names render and that no live-exclusion text does. Confirmed failing before
  the `_ObservationTile` change (temporarily reverted the widget file, ran the
  test, watched it fail on the missing text, then restored it) and passing
  after — the same demonstrate-the-red discipline task 11.17 established.
- Full suite: 1158 app tests pass (9 pre-existing skips, unrelated to this
  task), `flutter analyze` clean.

### Task 11.19 — Authorize the share-import write path
**Status:** Done, 2026-08-21. §4.19 gained a sixth clause — *an import is a
write, and the person doing it must be allowed to write here* — expressed as
`UntrustedImportRules.receiverMayImport` and checked once at the top of
`SharedObservationImporter._save`, above all three of its write branches
(fresh replica insert, `_upsertReplica` update, and the v1 receiver-owned copy
the task did not name). A viewer's save is now refused on the device with a new
`refusedNotPermitted` outcome; `wrote` is false, nothing is written, and
because the check runs before the observer is resolved a refused import leaves
no `Users` row behind either.

**The actor question, answered:** the **receiver** is checked and the
**payload's observer** is not, and both halves are decisions. The receiver is
performing a write, so §4.21's gradient governs them exactly as it governs every
other write. The observer is not acting — their name is being transcribed onto a
record made elsewhere, which is §4.17's row-naming question and is already
clause 2 on this path. Applying the gradient to the observer would refuse every
genuine share from a colleague not yet invited, converting §4.17's *recorded*
replication delay into local data loss. Written up in full in §4.19 clause 6 and
on `UntrustedImportRules.receiverMayImport`.

The role is resolved through `readProjectRole`, hoisted out of
`BaseRepository.projectRoleFor` so the importer, the repository layer and the
screens answer from the same rows by the same rule. A role this device cannot
resolve permits, identically to `assertRoleMayWrite` — a device legitimately
holds projects its user has no membership in. Guarded by
`test/security/share_import_authorization_test.dart` (16 tests); neutralizing
the predicate turns 7 red and leaves the 9 permitting tests green, and
substituting the observer for the receiver turns a different 7 red.

**Model:** **Opus** — an identity/authorization interaction, not a missing check.
**Depends on:** 11.3, 11.14. **Run before 11.9.**

**Found by 11.14, which correctly refused to fix it inside a UI sweep.**
`SharedObservationImporter.save` writes an `Observations` row with a direct SQL
statement, bypassing the repository layer that authorizes every other write this
app makes — the same shape `ProjectTagRepository.setStatus` was in before 11.12.

**Not a security hole today**, for exactly the reason 11.12 gave: a row a viewer
had no right to create is refused when it reaches the server, so nothing survives
into a colleague's copy. **But it leaves this one control weaker than every
other.** The "Save observation" gate 11.14 added is courtesy only; everywhere
else the repository is a second, independent backstop if the UI gate is bypassed
or races a role change. That asymmetry is the finding.

**The reason this is Opus, and the question to answer before writing code:**
**who is the actor?** For a replica import, the payload's resolved *observer* is
the person the row is attributed to — not the user of the receiving device. So
"is the actor allowed to write this?" has two candidate answers, and they differ:

- the **receiving user**, who must have rights in this project to save anything
  at all, and
- the **payload's observer**, whose identity the row claims and whom Phase 6
  went to deliberate trouble to preserve.

They are both relevant and they check different things. Get the relationship
between them explicit and written down, because this is precisely the interaction
Phase 6's replica-import design and Phase 10's C-1 row-naming work exist to hold
— and improvising it is how J-1 happened on this same file.

- Cover **both branches**: the fresh insert and `_upsertReplica`'s update.
- **This is the third time this file has come up** — J-1 (a pasted payload
  overwriting a field record), 11.2's note that client-layer inserts are
  unauthorized by design, and now this. It is the app's single most
  security-relevant client file. Treat it accordingly.
- Reuse §4.19's `UntrustedImportRules` rather than adding a parallel notion of
  what an import may do. A second rule set on this path is how the first one
  became unreachable.
- **Acceptance:** a viewer's local save is refused **on the device**, not only at
  the server; a genuine share still imports; the actor question is answered in
  writing with the reasoning; both branches tested.

### Task 11.20 — Authorize the backup-restore path
**Status:** Done (2026-08-21)
**Model:** **Opus** — the hard part is a design question, not a missing check.
**Depends on:** 11.3, 11.19. **Run before 11.9. Not gate-blocking — see below.**

**Found by 11.19: the same missing check on a wider surface.** Full evidence is
in Phase 11's Discovered Scope and `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.19.1. Today a
person with read-only access to a project can restore a backup file over it on
their own device. Their changes are refused the moment they sync, so no
teammate's data is at risk; the exposure is that their device shows them
something the project does not agree with until they find out.

**The trap, and it is why a role check alone cannot work.** Membership is
*server-derived*. A device that has just been reinstalled, or a new phone
restoring last season's archive, **has no membership rows yet** — that is
precisely the case restore exists for, and it must keep working with no server,
per Phase 10's invariant 1. So "refuse unless the user is a contributor or owner"
breaks the most important use of the feature while closing a minor one.

**The design question this task exists to answer:** what should happen when a
restore creates or overwrites a project the device has no membership for? Some
candidates, none pre-chosen:

- Allow it, and treat the restored project as local until sync confirms
  membership — closest to today's behaviour, made explicit.
- Allow it, and tell the user plainly that these records may be refused when
  they sync, so the divergence is expected rather than discovered.
- Refuse only when membership *is* known and says read-only — a check that
  applies when the answer exists and abstains when it does not.

The third looks most promising and is not a decision to take from a plan entry
without reading the code. **Whatever is chosen, write down why**, because the
next person to touch this path will otherwise reach for the role check that
cannot work.

- Reuse §4.19's `UntrustedImportRules` rather than adding a parallel rule set.
  Same instruction as 11.19, same reason.
- **Why this is scheduled but not gate-blocking:** it does not meet §4's bar. No
  silent loss — K-1's consent gate still shows the user what a restore will
  change. No disclosure, no authorization bypass affecting anyone else, and no
  control the security model claims exists and does not fire. It is scheduled
  because 10.72's rule says an open finding gets an owner, and **it runs before
  11.9 so the review confirms an owned item rather than discovering an unowned
  one** — which is the whole reason 10.72 exists.

**Outcome (2026-08-21). The third candidate was chosen: refuse only when
membership is known and says read-only.** It turned out to be the *existing*
predicate rather than a new one — `UntrustedImportRules.receiverMayImport`
already permits on a null role — so the substance of the task was establishing
that abstaining is the design on this path rather than a loophole in it, and
writing that down where the next reader will look. Recorded in
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.19 clause 6, §4.19.1 (whose clause-6 enumeration
now shows no open instance), §4.19.2 clause 0, §4.21, and §5.10 for the
residual.

Three things the code turned up that the plan entry could not have:

- **Position is a live attack, not a style preference.** The check must run
  before any row of the archive is applied, because the archive carries the
  project's own `Project_Memberships` rows. Moving it below `_apply` was tried:
  the file's row naming the importer as `owner` had made them one by the time
  the question was asked, and the check **permitted**. Both self-authorization
  tests go red on that mutation.
- **It must resolve the role in the project the *manifest* names**, not the
  project the app happens to have open — otherwise an owner of project A can
  restore an archive of project B they may only read.
- **This path has no screen gate and cannot have one.** Which project an archive
  is for is unknown until the file is picked and decoded, so there is no button
  to withhold — unlike the share path, where 11.14 added the screen gate and
  11.19 added the write-path check. Task 11.14's sweep did not miss this one; it
  was not constructible. The merger's check is the whole of the device-side
  answer.

**Candidate 2 was rejected for a reason worth keeping:** the only local signal is
the same absent membership row, so "warn that these records may be refused at
sync" fires on *every* fresh-device restore — including the project owner's,
where nothing will be refused. A warning that is usually wrong and always shown
is the dialog §4.19 clause 4 exists to avoid.

**For 11.9:** this is now an owned, closed item with an accepted residual at
§5.10 — a viewer who clears the app and restores onto a device with no
membership rows still passes; the server refuses their rows, so the divergence
is confined to their own device. Confirm the residual rather than rediscover it.

### Task 11.21 — The H-3 gate instrument does not probe the 12th table
**Status:** Done (2026-08-21)
**Model:** **Opus** — it needs the same security judgment 10.45 made, not a list edit.
**Depends on:** 11.7. **Run before 11.9.**

**Found by 11.17.** `scripts/verify_h3_existence_oracle_sweep.py` was written
against eleven synced tables and never updated when task 11.7 added
`Observation_Exclusions`. So the sweep's "complete" claim in
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.13 is **unverified for one table**, and has been
since 11.7 landed.

**Why this is Opus and not a one-line list update.** The sweep asks whether
claiming a primary key another caller holds is distinguishable from claiming a
free one. Adding a table means deciding **what the correct answer for that table
is** — the same judgment task 10.45 made for the other eleven, where the verdict
was accept-with-a-reason for two of them. Guessing here and getting it backwards
would put a wrong verdict into §4.13 with a passing instrument behind it, which
is worse than the current honest gap.

- Until it runs, §4.13's claim should read as covering eleven of twelve tables.
  Say so there rather than leaving the claim broad.
- **The root cause is shared with 11.22 and is the more valuable finding**: a
  new synced table does not automatically appear anywhere it needs to. Whatever
  you conclude about `Observation_Exclusions`, note whether the sweep can be
  made to derive its table list rather than carry one.
- **Acceptance:** the sweep probes all twelve; the twelfth has a written verdict;
  §4.13's coverage claim matches the number of tables actually probed; and
  deleting a table from `syncTables` changes what the sweep does.

**Outcome (2026-08-21). All four acceptance points met, run live against the
e2e stack; 12 of 12 tables probed, exit 0.**

- **The twelfth table's verdict: `Observation_Exclusions` is indistinguishable.**
  A stranger claiming an `exclusion_id` the victim holds and a stranger claiming
  a free one both answer `inserted`. It joins the eight already-covered tables,
  and the accepted-findings list is unchanged at three (`Projects`,
  `User_Emails`, `Tags`) — **no fourth carve-out**. This is the ordinary task
  10.35 outcome for the ordinary reason: the key is `(exclusion_id, project_id)`
  so the claim lands in the prober's own project and never collides.
- **The judgment the task asked for was in the probe's design, not the verdict.**
  The probe pushes a `superseded` mark rather than an `excluded` one, because
  `RowAuthorizer._authorizeExclusionKind` refuses `excluded` from a non-owner
  *before* the row is looked up — an `excluded` probe would have a check standing
  in front of the key comparison that could only make the two arms agree more
  often, i.e. would manufacture the COVERED verdict it was supposed to test for.
- **Yes, the sweep can derive its table list, and now does.** It comes from
  `gate_wire.PRIMARY_KEYS`, already parsed out of `sync_tables.dart` for the
  primary keys. A synced table with no probe **aborts the run** naming itself;
  a probe for a table `syncTables` no longer declares aborts too. Both were
  demonstrated by doing them. What cannot be derived is each table's *row
  shape* — a minimal-but-valid row needs semantics no descriptor carries (which
  enum value `kind` takes, that a latitude is a real number) — so the deriving
  is of the list, which is the part that silently rotted.
- **Two further instrument defects found and fixed while in there**, both the
  same carried-number shape: `gate_wire._parse_primary_keys` guarded its parse
  with `if len(keys) < 11`, a bound written when there were eleven tables that
  went on passing while saying nothing about the twelfth — it now counts the
  `name: Tables.X` declarations in the file and requires the key parse to match
  every one. And the sweep's own closing integrity line claimed to have re-read
  "12 of 12" of the victim's rows when it checks 9 (the three globally-keyed
  rows arrive by reachability, not by the project's pull); it now says 9 of 9
  and names what it does not check.
- **New: a per-probe non-vacuity assertion.** Every probe must claim the exact
  id the victim holds on the held arm and a different one on the free arm, and
  the derived expectation is asserted rather than assumed — a scope-separated
  table's two full keys must genuinely differ, a globally-keyed table's must
  genuinely match. Without it a forgotten seed row would make a probe compare
  two unheld keys and print COVERED for a table nobody tested. Demonstrated
  firing.
- **Also corrected, same 11.7 root cause, one word each:** §4.21.1 and
  `sync_tables.dart`'s `insertIsAGrant` doc comment both said "the remaining
  five are field records." It is six. See the report's note on the four
  remaining "eleven synced tables" phrases, which are **not** fixed here.

### Task 11.22 — A test that every governing column is type-checked
**Status:** Done, 2026-08-22.
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 11.7, 11.21.

**Found by 11.17, independently of 11.21, and the two share a root cause.** The
plan's own write-ups for tasks 10.64 and 10.68 enumerate the tables whose
"which column authorizes this row" value is type-checked by `RowValidator`
before authorization reads it — and both lists are missing
`Observation_Exclusions`, for the same reason the H-3 sweep is.

That matters because of what 10.64 found the hard way: an unchecked governing
column crashed an entire push, and the *tempting* fix — default the bad value to
null — would have turned the crash into an authorization **bypass**, because null
means permitted there.

- **Do not fix the two lists.** Write the test: enumerate every `SyncTable` whose
  `MutationRule` has a non-null governing column, and assert `RowValidator`
  type-checks that column. Then a future table cannot land unshadowed without
  something going red.
- This is 11.17's own rule applied one level in — a hand-maintained list that
  mirrors what the code knows needs a test, not more careful reading. Two of
  those lists have now drifted the same way in the same week.
- **Acceptance:** the test passes today; adding a synced table with a governing
  column and no validator check turns it red, demonstrated by doing it.

**Second part, added 2026-08-21 — the planning decision 11.21 asked for.** Task
11.21 left four prose sentences in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` still saying
"eleven synced tables" when there are twelve (§4.19, §4.19.2 twice, §4.20), and
was right not to fix them one at a time. **The decision: stop writing the number
at all.** Replace each with "every synced table" and, where the reader needs to
know which ones those are, point at the single enumeration rather than restating
a count. A number in prose is a hand-maintained copy of something the code
already knows — the same defect this task's test exists to kill, in a document
instead of a list.

- **Do not find-and-replace.** Other "eleven" mentions, in §7 through §14, are
  dated records of what a particular gate run measured on the day it ran. Those
  are correct as written and rewriting them would turn accurate history into
  false history. Only present-tense claims about the system change.
- The standing rule is now recorded in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` so table
  thirteen does not reopen this.
- **Acceptance for this part:** no present-tense sentence in the security model
  states a count of synced tables; the dated gate-run history is untouched,
  and you say in your report how many you changed and how many you left.

**Outcome (2026-08-22).** Both parts done; both acceptance criteria met.

- **The test is `packages/tritrack_sync/test/row_validator_test.dart`'s
  `'every table whose MutationRule has a governing column has that column
  type-checked by RowValidator'`.** It reads `tableMutationRules` and
  `MutationRule.governingColumn` directly — no hand-copied table list — and
  for each non-null governing column builds a row with a wrong-typed value for
  that one column and asserts `RowValidator.validate` reports an issue on it.
- **It found a real gap, not a hypothetical one.** `User_Emails.user_id` —
  `MutationRule.author`'s governing column for that table — was not
  type-checked by `RowValidator` at all. Unlike `Users`, where `user_id` is the
  primary key and so already caught by the pk-length/shape loop, `User_Emails`
  keys on `user_email_id`; `user_id` is a plain column the switch statement
  never touched. This is exactly task 10.68's own finding, left open at the
  time because `RowAuthorizer`'s explicit type guard (task 10.64's backstop)
  already made it safe *during authorization* — but the backstop only fires on
  the authorization path, not at this earlier, wider gate every write path
  (including the merge path's raw column-maps) runs through. **Fixed**: added
  `identityColumn('user_id')` to `RowValidator`'s `Tables.userEmails` case, the
  same call every other `author`/`authorOrOwner` table's non-pk governing
  column already gets. The test could have been written to skip the table the
  way it skips `anyUser`'s null governing columns — that would have satisfied
  "passes today" without closing anything. Fixing the validator was the
  smaller, more literal reading of the task and the one that leaves nothing
  unshadowed; flagged here rather than assumed, since the task's own acceptance
  line ("the test passes today") is only true because of this fix.
- **The red-test proof:** temporarily added `'Demo_Unshadowed_Table':
  MutationRule.author` to `tableMutationRules`, ran the suite — the new test
  failed, naming the fake table and its ungated `user_id` — then reverted;
  `git diff` on `mutation_rules.dart` was empty afterward and the suite is
  green again (229/229 in `packages/tritrack_sync`, plus the app's and
  server's own `RowValidator`/merge/import suites re-run and unaffected).
- **Doc sweep: four sentences changed, all four the ones named** (§4.19,
  §4.19.2 twice, §4.20) — each "all eleven synced tables" replaced with "every
  synced table (`sync_tables.dart`)", pointing at the code's own list rather

  history:** §4.13's "All twelve was all eleven for four months" narrative
  (an explicit record of the H-3 sweep's own past drift, correctly a comment
  about history, not a current count); §4.20's "arrived as a non-empty String
  and went into a primary key on eleven tables" (a description of what a fixed
  bug used to do, task 10.75/K-4's own past-tense record); §16.4's "every other

### Task 11.9 — Team-surface security review (bounded)
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-22).** Six new trust boundaries added to
`SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §3 (entries 21–26) *before* anything was attacked,
then attacked live: eighteen probes over a real team in
`scripts/verify_11_9_team_surface.py`, plus
`test/security/exclusion_reference_scope_test.dart` for the half the wire cannot
measure. **Verdict reached: no new blocker on either gate.** Gate C still fails
on the NAU review alone; Gate D still passes. **One open finding — N-1, below
the bar, and it needs a decision from this session:** a contributor can put a
teammate's name on an observation or an exclusion mark that teammate never made.
Six findings accepted with reasons, seven claims chased and refuted. Full
verdict in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §18; the reference question the task
names is answered at §4.22; the advisory-vs-enforcement property 11.11 asked
for is stated once at §4.23.
**Model:** **Opus** — high effort, fresh context, run alone.
**Depends on:** 11.1–11.5, 11.7

**This is bounded by `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md`, and that is deliberate.** As
originally written this entry said "review the team surfaces," which is exactly
the unbounded instruction that kept Gate C open across eight rounds. It is not
a ninth gate; it is Gate C and Gate D re-run over the new surface.

1. **Add the new trust boundaries to §3's inventory before attacking anything.**
   At minimum: the invite-token redemption endpoint; membership and role
   mutations; the cross-project isolation surface across every endpoint; and
   teammates' rows arriving through sync now that they are authored by people
   with different rights rather than by the same user on another device.
   **`Observation_Exclusions` is a required inventory entry, named here by
   task 11.21 so it cannot be left to be noticed.** In plain terms: this is the
   table behind "exclude this observation from the analysis," and it is the only
   write in the app where one person acts on somebody else's record. Before
   11.21 the security document did not mention it anywhere; 11.21 added one
   paragraph (§4.13) answering exactly one question — that knowing an exclusion
   row's random identifier tells you nothing — and no others. **The unasked
   question, specifically:** an exclusion row names the observation it applies
   to, and there is deliberately no database constraint on either side of the
   wire tying that name to an observation the writer is allowed to see. Nothing
   currently checks it. That is a question about *references* rather than about
   *keys* (the §4.17 / §5.9(b) shape), so no existing instrument asks it. Ask
   it: can a mark name an observation in another project, or one the writer
   cannot reach, and what happens to the analysis if it can?
2. **Attack each new entry** and try to falsify its stated verdict, as
   adversarially as any Phase 10 round. Eight rounds of that rigour found real,
   serious things.
3. **Judge against §4's four-clause bar. Nothing new.** B1 silent or
   unrecoverable data loss, B2 disclosure of coordinates or observer identity,
   B3 unauthenticated access or authorization bypass, B4 a claimed control that
   does not fire.
4. **Everything below the bar goes to §5's register with a written reason, and
   does not get a task.** "Accepted" is a complete answer and should be the
   common one.
5. **The stopping rule applies.** A newly discovered path is added to the
   inventory and reported; it blocks **only** if it meets the bar. Finding
   something minor must not prevent reaching a verdict.

- **Two unbounded-write items from 11.2, to fix or accept explicitly:** an
  owner can create any number of invitations, and nothing ever deletes expired
  or used ones. Neither discloses anything — creating one requires ownership and
  the stored rows are hashes — so both are storage growth rather than a leak.
  Decide: a cap, a cleanup job, or an accepted risk with the reason written down.
  **Outcome (2026-08-21): accepted, and 11.9 measured it — 60 issued in a row,
  all 60 stored.** Recommendation to Michael is to leave it accepted for the
  beta: it is storage growth in his own project, created by him, with no address
  exposed to anyone but the owner, and a cleanup job is housekeeping work that
  would be the only thing in the phase not driven by a finding.
  **One angle neither 11.2 nor 11.9 raised, and it is the reason this is worth a
  sentence rather than nothing:** an invitation row is bound to the address it was
  sent to, so never deleting used or expired ones means the project retains a
  permanent list of every email address anyone was ever invited with, including
  people who declined or never replied. That is not a leak and it is not a
  security finding — it is a **data-retention** question, and it is exactly the
  kind of question an institutional security office asks. It has therefore been
  added to the NAU letter's list of accepted decisions rather than left as a
  purely internal note, so the reviewer can tell us if indefinite retention is
  the wrong answer.
- Carry forward 11.3's two explicitly deferred items (orphan `Tags`
  writability, the unvalidated id-list columns) — they are on this list by name
  so they cannot be rediscovered as new. **Both were re-derived by 11.3 and both
  stayed accepted, with new reasons**; see `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §5.9.
  What 11.3 left open, specifically: **an orphan tag can be *linked* into a
  project by anyone holding its id**, and thereby adopted. That operation has to
  stay open — it is how a tag becomes a project's at all — and what it exposes
  is a tag no project references, to somebody who already had to know an
  unguessable identifier. Attack it anyway.
- **The diagnostics console is the one place a `project_id` is accepted with no
  per-project authorization**, and 11.3 gave it a verdict rather than a pass
  (§4.21.2). It is correct today because the console has no user session at all
  — a loopback peer plus an operator token, so there is no user identity to
  isolate one project from another *for*. **The verdict is conditional: the day
  it grows a per-user session, this is a live cross-project gap.** Confirm the
  condition still holds and that the two project routes are still reachable only
  with the operator token.
- **`_establishedThisPush`, and the class 11.3's own Gate B run found.** Within-
  push provenance recorded from a branch that does not write is what let a
  losing copy of another project's tag authorize a winning one
  (§4.21.3). Closed, but the class is "a bookkeeping set populated from a
  permissive branch", and there are two more of them —
  `_ownershipsRemovedThisPush` and `_membershipsGrantedThisPush`. 11.3 checked
  both by hand and neither is exploitable: the first is written after the rule
  dispatch has already allowed, and the second is written before it but under
  *the same condition the dispatch then applies*, so a marked row cannot go on
  to be refused. **The second one's safety is not structural**, though — it
  rests on those two conditions staying identical, and if the rule ever tightens
  a marked-then-refused row would block a second membership insert in the same
  push. Note the direction before spending time on it: that failure is an extra
  refusal, never an extra grant. Confirm it still holds; do not assume it.
- **A push may carry two rows with the same primary key**, and `applyPush` does
  not de-duplicate them: both are decided against one pre-push snapshot and
  applied in order. That is what made the finding above reachable. Ask whether
  any other check reads state that an earlier row in the same batch could have
  set.
- **Added 2026-08-22, and it is the same question from the other end: which rows
  must travel together, and what happens when a batch limit splits them?** Task
  11.32 found one such pair — a new tag and its first version — where a split would
  leave the second row refused forever and every bearing on that tag with no
  recorded frequency, **silently**. 11.32 worked around it by making the second row
  contributor-writable, which is defensible on its own merits but is not a fix for
  the splitting. **Enumerate the pairs.** A permission loosened to route around a
  batching hazard is a shape that comes back as a finding, so either the pairs are
  atomic or the hazard is written down per pair with what it costs.
- **State once, in plain language, that the app's permission checks are
  advisory and the server is the enforcement.** A contributor with access to
  their own device's database file can edit anything locally; their change is
  refused on the next sync. That is true of every permission in this app, not
  just tags — 11.11 raised it because it keeps being rediscovered per feature.
  Write it in the security model as a general property so the next reader does
  not treat it as a finding.
- **Confirm §5.10's accepted residual; do not rediscover it.** Task 11.20 closed
  the restore-path authorization gap and accepted one thing knowingly: a viewer
  who clears the app and then restores an archive of a project they may only
  read passes the check, because a reinstalled device has no membership rows and
  clause 6 abstains rather than break the reinstalled-phone restore. Their rows
  are refused at the server, so the divergence is confined to their own device,
  and they could already have exported the same data to CSV. **Attack it anyway
  — it is on this list by name so it cannot come back as a new finding** — and
  if it holds, say so and move on.
- **Every instrument gets a positive control that fires in the same run.** Eight
  consecutive gates found the instruments to be the most dangerous thing in the
  room; the last one caught three of its own probes measuring nothing.
- **Acceptance:** every new inventory entry carries a verdict backed by a failed
  live attack; no open finding meets the bar; the register is complete with
  reasons; a verdict is reached.

**Two things from this run the planning session wants kept where they will be
read again.**

**The instrument discipline paid for itself a ninth time.** Every attack was
paired with the nearest legitimate request that must succeed, and that pairing
caught **four of this run's own probes silently broken** — a bad enum value and
three wrong column names. Each would otherwise have printed "refused" and been
reported as a control holding. Nine consecutive gates have now found the
instruments to be the most dangerous thing in the room; this is the first one
that caught its own.

**The exclusion-reference question was answered, and the answer was not the one
the code claimed.** A mark *can* name an observation in another project, or one
that exists nowhere, and the server accepts it. Nothing happens as a result — but
for a different reason than the code comment asserted: every read filters by
project first, which the comment did not say. Accepted **with a written
condition**, and the condition is the part that matters: the day any feature looks
up a mark's observation *without* filtering by project — a "where else does this
bearing appear" view, an export that follows the replacement link — every value
stored under today's unchecked rule becomes a live cross-project problem at once.
**N-1 is scheduled as task 11.24; N-7 widened task 10.97 rather than becoming a
task of its own.**

### Task 11.23 — Write down who may do what, and check it against the code
**Status:** Done (2026-08-22) — `CLAUDE_DOCS/PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` is filled
from the code. Every cell carries a symbol and a security-model section; the
inventory diff is reported in both directions; N-1's siblings are enumerated as
a class over all twelve synced tables and found a third table plus two
different-shaped arms; §8 holds eleven open cells, each with a disposition, and
they are mirrored in this phase's Discovered Scope. **Two of them change other
tasks: 11.24 must be widened before it starts, and 11.25's enumeration must
include the shared tables.**
**Model:** **Opus** — the work is spotting the cells nobody has answered, which
is judgment, not transcription.
**Depends on:** 11.9. **Run before 11.24.**

**Why this exists.** Phase 11 shipped roles, invitations, shared recordings,
corrections to other people's records, and tag management. Each was decided
correctly and separately, and the result is a set of rules no one person can hold
in their head — including the sessions that wrote them. Finding N-1 is what that
costs: an exemption written when a project reached one person's own two devices
became "every teammate may be named" the moment membership rows joined the
reachability query, **and nothing was written down when that took effect.** A
capability matrix is the artifact that would have made it visible.

**The skeleton already exists** and is not yours to redesign — it defines the
five people-columns (including *Unknown*, a device with no membership record
yet), the six-mark notation, the three enforcement layers, a 44-operation
inventory, and twelve worked scenarios. Fill it.

1. **Fill every cell from the code.** Each filled cell cites the symbol that
   implements it and the security-model section that reasons about it. **No cell
   may be left empty** — `n/a` with a stated reason and "nobody has decided
   this" are both complete answers; blank is not, because blank reads as safe
   and means unasked, which is where the last five findings lived.
2. **Diff the hand-written operation inventory against what the app actually
   exposes, and report both directions.** The inventory was written *without*
   reading the code, deliberately, so it is an independent list. Operations the
   app has that are not on it are the interesting ones. Operations on it that do
   not exist are worth knowing too.
3. **Look for N-1's siblings specifically.** N-1 is "a row may name a person
   other than the caller." Enumerate every place that is possible and give each
   a verdict. Fix the class, not the instance — 10.66's standing rule, and 11.9
   found N-1 by asking this question once.
4. **Every unanswered cell lands in §8 with one of three dispositions**: a
   decision for Michael, a question for the code, or a task number. A question
   recorded without one of those is the failure that has cost this project six
   weeks twice.
5. **Change no behaviour.** This task reads and writes one document. If you find
   something that needs fixing, it goes in §8 and in Discovered Scope.

- **One cell is already known to need checking and is the reason this is Opus:**
  whether a contributor may exclude a *teammate's* bearing from the analysis, or
  only an owner may. The project's own stated dividing line — additive writes
  that unblock field work are contributor-level, subtractive writes that change
  what the whole team sees are owner-level — argues owner-only. Nobody has
  confirmed what task 11.7 built. **Read it; do not reason it.** If the code says
  contributor, that is a decision for Michael and not yours to change.
- **Acceptance:** every cell in every table is filled or explicitly dispositioned;
  the operation-inventory diff is reported in both directions; N-1's siblings are
