### Task 11.24 — N-1: a contributor can sign a record with a colleague's name
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-22).** Option (b) taken after measuring it, and
widened past what the entry asked for on both axes. The affected set is derived
from `MutationRule.namesRowAuthor` rather than listed, with a test that has been
watched to fail. **The fix covers the update path**: an update must name the
caller in the audit column, on every table, which closes task 11.18's
"withdrawn by" sentence at its root. Task 11.9's baseline is empty — both N-1
entries were removed because both are refused. **Task 11.26 was carried as the
second half**: its known instance was reproduced live, judged against §4's bar
and found to **meet it** (B4→B3 — the first finding since the eighth run to do
so), then fixed; the class sweep found two more, one fixed and one shown to be
unfixable at the server and recorded as an accepted risk needing Michael's
sign-off. Full record: `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §19, and §4.17 is amended
rather than annotated.
**Model:** **Opus** — high effort. The task is a design decision; the code change
after it is small.
**Depends on:** 11.9, 11.23.

**What is wrong, in plain terms.** A contributor on a project can record a
bearing — or a mark retiring somebody's bearing from the analysis — and put a
teammate's name on it as the person who did it. The server accepts it and the
teammate's next sync delivers it. So a bearing can appear in a project credited
to an observer who never took it, and a judgement that somebody's data was bad
can appear credited to a colleague who never made it.

**Why it is not an emergency.** The person doing it has to already be a
contributor the owner deliberately invited, and that person could already record
bad bearings under their own name and pull the position estimate just as far off.
Nothing is destroyed, rewriting an *existing* record's author is still refused,
the fabricated record appears in the Team log with the name on it, and it can be
removed. Full reasoning at `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §18.3.

**Why it must not just be accepted.** Phase 11 shipped two features whose entire
purpose is saying who recorded what — the Team log, and observer provenance in
position estimation — and this is the one input that makes both of them state
something false. **For a wildlife biologist that is the part that matters:** a
bearing credited to the wrong observer is a record that cannot be defended in a
permit file, a data-management plan, or a paper. It is not a data-loss problem;
it is a scientific-record problem.

**The two shapes 11.9 wrote down, and the planning session's lean.**

- **(a)** Narrow the "this project already reaches them" rule to a real
  provenance record — a different query, not a tightening of the existing one.
- **(b)** Keep that rule for rows carrying shared project vocabulary, and drop it
  for rows that name an author, so **a record that names an author must name the
  caller.** Its cost is the first publish of a colleague's imported observations,
  which is the trade §4.17 already accepted in Phase 10 and which the held-row
  store already makes payable.

**The lean is (b), and (a) is rejected for a stated reason:** (a) invents a new
provenance mechanism, and nine rounds of evidence on this project say new
mechanisms are where findings come from. (b) reuses a trade already accepted and
a hold path already built.

**But that lean is a plan-document opinion, and the first step is to measure it
rather than adopt it.** Option (b) is only cheap if very little legitimate
traffic names an author who is not the caller. **Count the paths that construct
an author-naming row with a non-caller author** — the share-an-observation
feature, project-file import, backup restore pushed to the server — and say how
many rows each would send to the held store in a realistic season. If that number
is large, (b) is not cheap and the lean is wrong; say so and take (a).

- **Consider stamping the pusher separately from the author, as a companion
  rather than an alternative.** The server knows who called it, so a
  server-written "delivered by" value cannot be forged by a client, and it would
  make whatever legitimately crosses author boundaries honest instead of
  invisible. Two cautions: it must stay optional, because Phase 10's invariant is
  that no server-supplied column is *required* and the app must work with no
  server at all; and **visibility alone is not the fix.** 11.9 flagged its own
  uncertainty precisely here — it confirmed the fabricated row is delivered and
  carries the victim's name, but not that a person would notice it among a
  season's observations. Treat "it shows in the log" as the weakest link in the
  argument, not the strongest.
- **Whichever shape is chosen, write down why**, and write down what took effect
  when membership rows entered the reachability query — because the root cause of
  this finding is that nobody did.

**Widened 2026-08-22 after task 11.23, and the widening changes the answer — read
this before starting.**

- **Do not scope this to a list of tables. Derive the set from the rule.** 11.9
  named two tables (bearings and exclusion marks). 11.23 read the code and found
  a **third** — `Non_Detections`, the record that says "I listened here and heard
  nothing," which can also be filed under a colleague's name. A fix scoped to
  two tables closes two of three, and a fourth table will arrive. Enumerate every
  table whose rule names an author, from the rule definitions, and assert the
  coverage in a test so table thirteen inherits it. This is 10.66's standing rule
  and it is the second finding this week that a hand-kept list would have missed.
- **The preferred shape as written would not close the whole finding, and this is
  the time-sensitive part.** Option (b) requires that a row naming an author names
  the caller **on insert**. Task 11.18 shipped a "withdrawn by" name in the Team
  log, and that name is reachable through the **update** path, which permits a
  name that merely matches what is already stored. Insert-only means 11.18's
  feature keeps displaying something a contributor can forge. **Decide explicitly
  whether the fix covers the update path**, and if it does not, say what carries
  the remainder — do not leave it implied.
- Worth knowing before you start: an earlier round already recorded this shape
  for `Non_Detections` alongside `Observations` (see the fabricated-row item in
  Phase 10's record). It was never given a task number. That is the pattern task
  10.72 exists to stop, and it is why this entry now names the tables' *source*
  rather than the tables.
- **Acceptance:** the cost of (b) is measured before it is chosen; the chosen
  design is implemented with the reasoning recorded; 11.9's baseline for this
  finding flips from "expected to succeed" to "expected to be refused" and the
  harness goes red if it regresses; a legitimate cross-author case still works or
  its refusal is deliberate and documented.

### Task 11.25 — Make the permissions matrix a test, not a document
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-22).** Task 11.27 was merged into this task and is
closed by the same commit — see its own entry below for what changed. New
file: `server/test/authz/permissions_matrix_test.dart`, 33 tests, all run
live against Postgres alongside the full existing `server/test/authz/` suite
(149 tests total) with no regressions. Three groups: **(1)** structural
completeness — the set of tables `tableMutationRules` declares must equal the
set this file has a cross-cutting case for, in both directions, with a
regression-proof test that hands the comparison a deliberately corrupted set
and watches it throw naming the table (also demonstrated live by temporarily
adding a fake table to `tableMutationRules` and watching the real test go red
— reverted before committing); **(2)** §4.0's cross-cutting rule — an update's
`last_modified_by` must name the caller — asserted once per table, across all
thirteen synced tables, each with a positive control (an honest update still
works) alongside the refusal; **(3)** the three shared tables
(`Triangulation_Sessions`, `Estimated_Positions`, `Actual_Tag_Locations`)
tested in the cross-author direction for the first time — a contributor may
alter and soft-delete a colleague's row, deliberate per §4.21 and previously
untested outside `Observations`. The ~40 named operation cells in §4 and §7
are not re-derived from scratch; they continue to be pinned by the per-feature
tests each row already cites, which this task verified are still passing
rather than duplicating.
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 11.23, 11.24.

Every cell in the matrix becomes a case the suite asserts, so the document is a
rendering of a passing test suite rather than a description of intended
behaviour.

- **Why this is not optional polish.** A stale permissions matrix is worse than
  no matrix, because it is the document the next person reasons *from*. One added
  table left a wrong count in six document sections, two task write-ups, a source
  comment and **two gate instruments** inside a single week. The same fate awaits
  a hand-kept table of forty operations by five roles.
- Enumerate from the code — roles from the role type, operations from the
  mutation rules and `tableSpecs` — and fail on any operation the matrix does not
  cover, in both directions.
- **Prove the guard can fail:** add an operation with no matrix row and watch it
  go red. A guard nobody has seen fail is not a guard.
- **Some rules are not cells, and enumerating only cells will miss them. This is
  the correction task 11.24 asked for.** A rule like *"the column recording who last
  touched a row must always name the caller"* applies to **every row of every
  table** — it is not one square in the grid, it is a property of the whole grid.
  Task 11.24 changed three permission rules underneath this task and one of them has
  that shape. **So the fixture needs two kinds of case:** per-cell, and
  cross-cutting rules asserted **once per table** rather than once. Enumerate the
  cross-cutting rules explicitly and by name, and fail if a table is missing a case
  for any of them.
- **The permissions document needs somewhere to put them**, and today it does not
  have one — its structure is cell-shaped. Add a section for rules that apply to
  every row, and treat a cross-cutting rule with no home as a documentation gap in
  its own right. **That gap is why 11.24 had to ask:** a rule that fits nowhere in
  the record is a rule nobody re-checks.
- **The enumeration must include the shared tables, not only the author-governed
  ones.** 11.23 found that triangulation sessions, saved position estimates and
  ground-truth points have no author column at all, so a contributor may alter or
  delete a colleague's row in any of the three. **That is deliberate and is not
  being challenged** — what is missing is a test. The permitted direction is
  covered; the cross-author direction is asserted only for bearings. A cell in
  this document becoming a case is what closes that by construction, which is the
  whole argument for this task.
- **Three cells changed under you on 2026-08-22 and the enumeration must pick
  them up** (task 11.24): `Project_Tags` deactivation and tombstoning are now
  owner-only *at the server* (`_authorizeProjectTagRemoval`); the exclusion rung
  is judged on the **stored** `kind` as well as the pushed one; and
  `last_modified_by` must name the caller on every update. The last of those is
  not a cell — it is a rule that cuts across every row of the document, and it
  belongs in the enumeration as its own case rather than being folded into each.
- **One shape 11.24 found is worth copying rather than re-deriving:** it does
  not enumerate tables, it enumerates *rules*, and asserts that the set of
  probed tables equals the set the rule picks out — then proves the assertion
  fires by deleting a case and watching it go red naming the table. That is the
  same guard this task is asked to build, one layer down.
- **Acceptance:** the suite covers every cell, including the three shared tables
  in the cross-author direction; adding an unlisted operation turns it red,
  demonstrated by doing it; the document is regenerated or checked from the
  fixture rather than edited by hand.

### Task 11.26 — Every owner-only rule the app claims, checked at the server
**Status:** **Done as task 11.24's second half (2026-08-22).** Every acceptance
criterion met: the gap was reproduced live before it was fixed, every owner-only
cell in the matrix has a stated server-side answer, each fix has a test that
fails without it, and the bar judgement is written down — it **meets** the bar.
See `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §19.3 and §19.4.
**MERGED into task 11.24 (2026-08-22). Do not run `/11-26`; run `/11-24`.**
Both ask the same question — what the server actually enforces, as against what the
app claims — in the same file, needing the same live harness and the same judgement
against the bar. Running them apart builds that scaffolding twice. The spec below
still applies in full and 11.24 carries it as its second half.
**Model:** **Opus** — high effort. The known instance is a small fix; finding its
siblings is the task.
**Depends on:** 11.23. **Run before 11.28 and 11.29**, both of which add rules
this sweep should then cover.

**The known instance, in plain terms.** The app says only a project owner may take
a tag out of a project — and the server was never told. Anyone who can edit their
own phone's database file, which the security model states plainly is always
possible, can push that change and the server accepts it. The tag then disappears
for the whole team. This is subtractive and changes what everybody sees, which is
exactly why the rule was made owner-level in the first place.

**Why this is Opus and not a two-line fix.** The class is *"the app asserts a rule
the server does not enforce,"* and 11.23 found this one by reading a single file.
**Derive the whole set:** every operation the permissions matrix marks owner-only,
checked against whether the server actually refuses it. Fix the class, not the
instance — 10.66's standing rule, and the reason to run this before the two tasks
that add new owner-only rules.

1. **Reproduce before fixing.** 11.23 read this from the code and explicitly did
   not attack it live. An unreproduced finding has been wrong on this project
   before, in both directions. Push the row against a running server and watch it
   be accepted; that measurement is what makes the fix's test mean something.
2. **Judge it against the bar in `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §4 and say the
   answer out loud.** The planning session's read is that a contributor
   successfully performing an owner-only, team-visible, subtractive write is
   **B3 — an authorization bypass at the server** — and if that holds, this is
   the first finding since the eighth gate to meet the bar. It does not change
   any decision, because Gate C is already shut on the review, but **a finding
   that meets the bar and is recorded as "the clearest thing to fix" instead of
   as blocking is how the register becomes a lie.** If the judgement is that it
   is below the bar, write the reason.
3. **Then sweep**, then fix, with the template that already exists a few lines
   away in the same file for exclusion marks.

- **Acceptance:** the gap is reproduced live before it is fixed; every owner-only
  cell in the matrix has a stated server-side answer; each fix has a test that
  fails without it; the bar judgement is written down either way.

### Task 11.27 — Three records that are wrong, and one acceptance with no number
**Status:** **MERGED into task 11.25 (2026-08-22). Do not run `/11-27`; run `/11-25`.**
Every correction here needs a test that stops it drifting back, which is exactly
what 11.25 builds. The spec below still applies in full and 11.25 carries it.
**One change to item 4:** the security model's tag section should now describe the
copy-on-add decision (task 11.34), not task 11.29, which is cancelled.
**Model:** Sonnet — no design decisions; all four answers are given below.
**Depends on:** 11.23.

Documentation and comments only, except where a test is named.

1. **A comment claims a control that does not exist.** `auth_routes.dart:509` says
   that removing a member revokes their sign-in sessions server-side. There is no
   such call, and there could not be: removal is an end-date on a synced row, not
   a request to the server. **The decision is to correct the record, not to build
   the control** — and the reason is worth writing into the correction, because
   the planning session got this wrong once already and had to be corrected by
   Claude Code in task 11.2. **Sessions belong to a person, not to a project.**
   Revoking them on removal from one project would sign that person out of every
   other project they belong to. So the accurate statement is: removal takes
   effect because every request re-resolves membership, and task 11.9 measured a
   removed member losing read, write and directory access on their very next
   request. Correct the comment, correct §4.3 where it reads as though removal
   revokes sessions, and **add a test that pins the real mechanism** so the next
   reader finds an assertion rather than a sentence.
2. **Notice the shape, because this is its third appearance in two weeks.** A
   comment asserted one property; a different property was actually holding.
   11.9's exclusion-reference finding was the same, and so was 11.23's discovery
   here. **A control that works for a reason other than the documented one is one
   refactor away from not working at all**, because whoever preserves the
   documented reason will not know to preserve the real one. Say that once, in
   the security model, as a general property.
3. **The merge tiebreak — accept it in writing. Michael decided this on
   2026-08-22: status quo.** When two edits collide with the same clock value, the
   final tiebreak is an identifier the device chooses for itself, so a device can
   be set up to win every tie. It has sat in the record since Phase 10 as
   *"probably acceptable"* with no task number, which is precisely the shape task
   10.72 exists to prevent. Give it a register entry with a reason and a number:
   the attacker must already be a trusted contributor, the loser's row survives
   for provenance, and no coordinate is disclosed.
4. **The security model's tag section is written as though a tag belongs to one
   project.** It does not — tags are global and projects select them. Say so, and
   cross-reference task 11.29.

- **Acceptance:** no comment or security-model sentence asserts session
  revocation on member removal; the real mechanism has a test; the tiebreak has a
  numbered acceptance; the tag section reflects that tags are shared.

### Task 11.28 — Controls that exist on the server and cannot be reached from the app
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-23), with one half of one acceptance criterion
knowingly unmet — see the note at the end of this entry.** Parts 1 and 4 are
complete and tested. Part 2 ("sign out everywhere") is complete. Part 3
("I lost my phone") is answered but by the all-devices control rather than the
per-device one, because the per-device route needs a device id nothing can
supply — see Discovered Scope.
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. Part 1 adds a narrow exception to an
authorization rule, which is where task 11.9 found things.
**Depends on:** 11.23, 11.26.

Three things a person cannot currently do, all of which the design assumes they
can.

1. **Leave a project. Michael decided this on 2026-08-22: yes, a viewer or a
   contributor may leave.** Today there is no control and no route, membership
   rows are owner-only to write, and a device that tries anyway throws an error
   no screen catches while the server refuses the row forever — leaving that
   device permanently out of step. **This is the security-sensitive part**, because
   it needs a narrow exception: a person may end **their own** membership row and
   nothing else. Write the exception as narrowly as it can be written, and attack
   it — the obvious mistake is an exception that also permits ending somebody
   else's. Two rules it must not break: a project cannot be left with no owner
   (11.9 verified that, including two owners ending in one batch), and this must
   not become a way to remove a person other than yourself. Michael did **not**
   ask for owner confirmation, so a person may leave without permission.
2. **"Sign out everywhere."** The route exists, is correctly built — the person
   revoked is always the authenticated caller, taken from the session and never
   from the request — and no screen calls it. The security model names this as the
   answer to "I think somebody has my token," so today that answer is that the
   person can do nothing.
3. **"I lost my phone."** Same story, same section, same absence.
4. **Added 2026-08-22 — the publish screen must say who is about to become the
   owner.** Task 11.24 reproduced this live: if you hold a copy of somebody else's
   project — from a shared project file, or a restored backup — and you publish it
   before its real owner does, **you become its owner on the server and the real
   owner is locked out permanently**, because a project's identifier is baked into
   every row and cannot be renumbered. Michael accepted the risk on 2026-08-22
   rather than making projects re-numberable, and that is the right call for the
   malicious case, which needs the attacker to already hold the project.
   **But the likely path is an accident, not an attack**, and the app actively
   encourages it: the share screen suggests sending a project file by message or
   email, and the colleague who receives it has a publish button. So **the
   acceptance is conditional on this warning existing.** The publish action must
   name the account that will become the owner, and must say plainly when the
   project was imported rather than created on this device. That converts a
   permanent, silent lockout into a moment of doubt, and it is a sentence rather
   than a schema change.

- Parts 2 and 3 are wiring, and low risk. Part 1 is not; if the exception cannot
  be made narrow enough to be obviously correct, **stop and say so** rather than
  shipping a broad one.
- **Acceptance:** a contributor can leave a project and their device stays in
  step; a viewer can too; nobody can end anyone else's membership through the new
  path, demonstrated by a test that tries; the last owner cannot leave; both
  revocation controls are reachable from the app.

**Outcome, 2026-08-23.**

- **The exception was narrow enough, and it is one sentence:** a person may set
  `end_date` on their own currently-open membership row, changing nothing else
  about it. It lives in the shared package (`isSelfDeparture`) so the app and
  the server cannot disagree about what a departure is, and it overrides exactly
  two refusals — the role gradient, so a `viewer` can leave, and the
  `projectOwner` rule, so a non-owner can. The last-owner guard and task 11.24's
  audit-column rule both still bind, because the exception is ORed into the
  ownership branch rather than allowed ahead of it. The columns a departure may
  move are **derived from the table spec**, so a column added later is immutable
  during a departure without anybody remembering to say so. Attacked by 24
  server cases and 24 predicate cases, including every "and also…" shape:
  promote, demote, tombstone, re-date, renumber, move project, reopen, rejoin,
  end somebody else's, end somebody else's while relabelling it as yours.
- **The device-divergence half is closed too, in both the online and the
  offline case.** Online: the app syncs that project *before* writing the
  departure (so it is not built from a stale copy of a row an owner changed
  while the device was offline), writes it, and unlinks the project only once
  the server has confirmed the row. Offline — the normal case in the field —
  the departure is pending for days, so the refusal is handled where it lands:
  a `403` on a project this device's own records say the person already left
  unlinks it. The "already left" half is what keeps that narrow; a bare `403`
  is also what a member removed by an owner sees, and theirs must keep trying.
  Two things worth recording because they were **defects found while reviewing
  my own work, not by the tests**: `syncNow()` syncs the *active* project only,
  so leaving any other project would never have pushed the departure at all
  (fixed with `SyncController.syncProjectNow`); and the receipt check compared
  a re-encoded timestamp against the raw string a receipt stores, which would
  have read a confirmed departure as pending forever if the codec ever stopped
  round-tripping exactly.
- **Acceptance criterion not fully met: "both revocation controls are reachable
  from the app."** "Sign out everywhere" is reachable. Per-device revocation is
  not, and the obstacle is not a button: `/auth/sessions/revoke-device` needs
  the lost device's id, and **there is no route that lists a caller's own
  sessions**, so nothing on the device can offer a picker. Adding one is a new
  authenticated route with its own field-bounds and rate-limit checklist (task
  10.56's class rule), which is more than the "wiring" this part was scoped as,
  so it was not improvised here. The user need behind part 3 *is* met — signing
  out everywhere locks a lost device out from that moment, at the cost of one
  sign-in on each device still held, and the screen says exactly that. See
  Discovered Scope for the task this needs.

### Task 11.32 — What a bearing remembers about its tag
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-22).** Schema v9: `Tag_Versions`, plus
`Observations.tag_version_id`. Column set derived from `tagColumnKinds`; colour
declared `display` and never versioned; the edit asks correction-or-change with
no default, and only when a versioned field moved. All acceptance criteria
tested and green in the app and shared suites. **The server's Postgres-backed
tests could not run** — no Docker and no Postgres on the execution machine — so
the twelve new server cases are written and analyzed but unexecuted; see this
phase's Discovered Scope.
**Model:** **Opus** — high effort. It decides what a historical scientific record
means, and the obvious version of the fix is wrong.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Run before 11.34** — this is what makes tag editing
safe, and 11.34 is not safe without it.

**The problem, in plain terms.** A bearing does not record the frequency it was
taken at. Frequency lives only on the tag record, reached through the tag's
identifier. So the moment anybody edits a tag's frequency — which they must be
able to do, because transmitters drift — **every bearing ever recorded against
that tag retroactively claims to have been taken at the new frequency.** Nobody
did anything wrong and the dataset now says something false.

This was found while answering a different question (whether one project should be
able to re-tune another project's tag). That question turned out to be a special
case of this one, and this one happens **inside a single project**, where nothing
was guarding it at all.

**It is not only frequency, and this is why the task has been reworded.** Michael
raised this on 2026-08-22: the tag **name** has the same problem and is arguably
worse. A renamed tag makes every earlier export, map figure and field note
unmatchable against current data — and the data model already notes that two tags
may legitimately share a name, so there is no fallback identity. Colour is a
smaller version of it: a tag recoloured after a figure was published means the
figure no longer matches the dataset.

**And the obvious fix — copy frequency, pulse rate and name onto the observation —
is the same defect one size up.** "The fields worth copying" is a hand-maintained
list, and it drifts the moment somebody adds a column to the tag table. That exact
pattern has been found four times in two weeks: the stale count of synced tables,
the two governing-column lists, task 10.97's seven named text columns, and N-1's
three tables. **Do not add a fifth.**

**The fix: an observation references the tag as it was, rather than copying selected
fields from it.** Record a version of the tag's full state whenever any of it
changes, with the moment it took effect, and have each observation point at the
version that was current when it was recorded.

**Not every field, though — and this is the correction that makes the design
right.** Michael asked on 2026-08-22 what happens to **colour**. Under a rule that
freezes everything, recolouring a tag would redraw last season's bearings in the old
colour, which is nobody's intent: colour is a display key a person chooses, not a
measurement taken in the field. Freezing it would be as wrong as letting frequency
float.

**So every tag column is one of three kinds, and the kind is declared, not
guessed:**

1. **Display — always current, never versioned.** `color_hex`. There is no such
   thing as "the colour it was then"; a recolour is meant to apply everywhere,
   immediately, including to every record already drawn.
2. **Measurement context — versioned, and an edit must say whether it is a
   correction or a change.** `frequency_mhz`, `pulse_rate`, `pulse_pattern`,
   `tag_name`. See below — this is the interesting one.
3. **Facts about the tag itself — current state only, no per-observation copy.**
   `date_put_on`, `date_removed`, `capture_date`, `status`, `notes`. A bearing has no
   use for its own copy of these; they describe the collar's life, not the moment a
   bearing was taken.

**Correction versus change, and it is a distinction only the person can make.**
Editing a frequency because the transmitter drifted is a *change*: the old bearings
were genuinely taken at the old frequency and must keep it. Editing a frequency
because it was typed in wrong is a *correction*: the old bearings were always at the
new value and the record was simply wrong. Renaming has both cases too — fixing a
mislabelled collar should propagate, re-collaring the same animal should not.

**The app cannot tell these apart, so it must ask.** Two options on a tag edit:
*"fixing a mistake — update every record"* or *"it changed — leave earlier records as
they were."* This is the same question, in the same shape, as the supersede-versus-
overwrite decision already taken for observations, and it should read the same way to
the user.

- **Only prompt when a versioned field actually changed.** A colour-only edit must
  never ask anything. Keeping the common case frictionless is part of the
  requirement, not a nicety.
- **No default on that prompt.** Drift and typo are both common, so either default
  is silently wrong a good fraction of the time, and the whole harm being fixed here
  is silence.

**Every tag column must declare its kind, and a test derived from the schema must
fail if any column has not.** This is the part that keeps the classification from
becoming the hand-kept list this task exists to avoid: adding a column to the tag
table **forces** the decision rather than letting it default. Same pattern as task
11.22's governing columns and task 10.97's text bounds — the judgement cannot be
automated, but omitting it can be made impossible. **An undeclared column must fail,
not fall back**: "current" and "versioned" are each silently wrong half the time.

- **Versioned columns inherit correctness for free once declared** — nobody has to
  remember to copy them anywhere.
- **Two different reads, and they must stay different.** "What was this bearing
  recorded against?" resolves through the version. "What is this tag now?" reads the
  tag row. A future reader must not reconcile them — the difference *is* the drift
  record.
- **Rejected alternative, with its reason:** storing the tag's state as an opaque
  blob on each observation. It would inherit new columns too, but an unstructured
  value on a synced table is exactly the unknown-column surface that took several
  rounds to harden, and the validator cannot check it. Structured versions, not
  blobs.
- **This is a new synced table, and we now know exactly what that costs.** All four
  drift findings above were caused by a table arriving without its instruments. So
  it lands **with** its coverage in the same commit: schema-derived validation
  bounds (task 10.97), the governing-column test, the disclosure sweep, a row in the
  permissions matrix, and a case in task 11.25's fixture. **Shipping it without
  those reproduces the defect this task exists to fix.**
- **How this sits with copy-on-add (task 11.34):** the shape is the same either way.
  If tags become project-local copies, the versions live with the project's copy.
  **Decide the versioning here; 11.34 must not redesign it.**

**A sanity check on the size of this:** tags change rarely — a drift correction, a
rename, a status change. Single-digit versions per tag over its whole life, so the
table stays small and the lookup stays cheap. This is a few rows per collar, not a
history system.

- **Say plainly, in the data model, what each copy means:** the value on the
  observation is what the receiver was tuned to when the bearing was taken and is
  never edited afterwards; the value on the tag is current state and may be edited
  freely. Write that down, because the whole point is that a future reader must
  not "helpfully" reconcile them.
- **This turns drift into data rather than damage.** A tag whose bearings read
  148.520 for six weeks and 148.535 afterwards *is* a drift record, and that is
  more useful to a biologist than a tag row that only remembers today.
- Cover every write path, not just the record screen: shared observations,
  project-file import, spreadsheet import, and rows arriving by sync. A row that
  arrives with no version reference must not have one invented for it — an older
  record genuinely does not know, and **that means "not recorded", never "whatever
  the tag says now."**
- **Say what the export does**, since a spreadsheet is where this is most visible.
  An export should carry the values as recorded, so a spreadsheet made today and one
  made after a rename agree about the same bearing. That is the harm Michael named.
- **Acceptance:**
  - A bearing's frequency and name are unchanged by a tag edit marked *"it
    changed"*, and **do** change under one marked *"fixing a mistake"* — both
    demonstrated by tests.
  - **Recolouring a tag changes the colour of every record already drawn**, and
    asks the user nothing. Tested.
  - **Adding a column to the tag table with no declared kind fails a test**,
    demonstrated by adding one.
  - Rows with no version reference stay unresolved rather than backfilled.
  - Every write path is covered.
  - The new table lands with its validator, sweep, matrix and fixture coverage in
    the same commit.

### Task 11.33 — Record where the animal or collar actually was
**Two things settled by the planning session on 2026-08-31, after the report.**

**1. The segmented control's label scaling is ratified.** With five options the shared
control clipped "Directional" to "Direct…", and the task changed it app-wide to scale a
long label down instead. **Scaling is strictly better than truncating** — a truncated
label can be *wrong* rather than merely small, and nothing changes where a label already
fits. **Flagging it rather than making it silently was the right call.** The open question
underneath — whether five options belong in a segmented control on a phone at all — is a
look-at-it-on-a-real-screen question, not a reasoning one, and it goes on the hardware
list rather than into a task.

**2. The hardware check waits for 11.92.** Michael's decision: he will run the truth-point
entry test — GPS-fix entry and dropped-pin entry, and whether a phone's reported accuracy
is a sensible default for the precision field or so pessimistic it always gets overwritten
— **once the ground-truth work is complete**, so one hardware session covers 11.33 and
11.92 together instead of two.

**Status:** **Done 2026-08-31.** A fifth entry type ("Truth") on the record
screen writes an `Actual_Tag_Locations` row: position through the existing
"use current location / set position on map" control, a radial precision in
metres, the three-way animal-and-collar / animal-only / collar-only choice,
notes and the time. Schema v10 adds two nullable columns to that table —
`found_kind` and `tag_version_id` — with no backfill and no foreign key on the
version, mirrored in the server's Postgres migration. The precision field
prefills from the phone's reported horizontal accuracy for a GPS fix and says
so; **it prefills nothing for a map pin, and a prefilled figure is taken away
again if the position becomes a pin**, while a figure the user typed survives.
The solver invariant is a test that solves with and without a truth point
beside the bearings and carries its own negative control. The two "no"
answers (`Estimated_Positions`, `Triangulation_Sessions`) are written into the
schema and the technical context rather than left blank. **Not done here, by
design:** no accuracy statistic is computed, and nothing exports, edits or
displays a truth point's new fields — see Discovered Scope. **BETA-BLOCKING — Michael decided this on 2026-08-29**, asked
twice and answered plainly: marking where the animal actually was is needed for the
beta. It is the only feature on the beta list; everything else blocking is a defect or
a check. Treat its schedule accordingly — it is not the tail of the queue.
**Model:** **Opus, medium — raised 2026-08-31**, when Michael widened the budget to buy
fewer oversights. The design below really is fully specified, so this is not a rating the
work demands; it is one the *consequence* demands. **This is the only feature in the beta,
and what it writes ends up in somebody's analysis** — a data-model mistake here is
discovered by a biologist months later with field seasons already recorded against it.
**One invariant needs a test, not judgement.** *(Correction: the planning session's run
tables said "Opus, medium" for several turns while this line and the command file both
said Sonnet. The plan was right and the table was drifting. It is Opus now by decision,
not by retrofit.)*
**Depends on:** nothing.

**What this is for.** Triangulation gives you an estimate. This records the truth —
where the animal or the collar actually turned out to be — which is the only way to
find out how accurate the estimates are. The table, its sync rule, its storage code
and a map layer that draws its points **already exist**; nothing in the app ever
calls the save, so today a truth point can arrive from a teammate and be drawn but
can never be entered. That was task 11.23's finding and Michael confirmed on
2026-08-22 that the feature was intended.

**A new entry type on the record screen**, alongside recording a bearing:

1. **Position.** "Use current location" is the default; "select position" opens the
   map picker. These are the two conventions the schema already has — a GPS fix and
   a placed pin — so **reuse them and their existing meanings rather than inventing
   a third.**
2. **Radial precision, in metres, editable in both modes.** The phone reports its
   own horizontal accuracy and the app already stores it for bearings, so
   **prefill that number for a GPS fix and tell the user where it came from.** The
   user may raise or lower it freely, including below the phone's figure.
3. **What was found** — a three-way choice: **animal and collar together**,
   **animal only**, **collar only**.
4. **Notes**, kept as on any other record. "Found in burrow" is exactly the kind of
   thing that matters two seasons later.
5. **Time**, captured as it is for a bearing. A truth point is only comparable to
   estimates near it in time, because animals move.

**Do not prefill 0 for a map-selected point.** A pin is not automatically more
precise than a GPS fix; it is only as good as the person's ability to identify the
exact spot in the imagery, and satellite base-map registration is itself commonly
off by a few metres. Leave it to be entered deliberately, so the number is always a
claim somebody made rather than a default nobody noticed. **This is the one place
where an over-confident default would quietly corrupt the accuracy statistics the
feature exists to produce.**

**Why the three-way choice matters, and it is not cosmetic.** Only *animal and
collar together* validates the triangulation of a live collared animal. A *collar
only* point tells you where the transmitter was, which may be where it was shed
days earlier — comparing it to estimates from when the animal still wore it would
make the app look wrong when it was right. An *animal only* point is not validating
a radio signal at all. **So whichever kind is being recorded must be available to
whatever later computes accuracy**, and the obvious default is that only the first
kind counts unless the user says otherwise. Do not compute accuracy statistics in
this task; do make the distinction storable and say in the report what you think
the default should be.

**Added 2026-08-22 after task 11.32, and it must not be skipped: a truth point
records which tag version it was taken against.** Task 11.32 made a bearing remember
what its tag read at the time. Three other tables name a tag and record nothing about
what it read, and 11.32's report is right that this is the one that matters:

- **Ground-truth points — yes, record the version.** A truth point is a field record
  somebody took while standing in front of a collar, which is the same kind of thing
  as a bearing. Without it, an export of truth points made after a rename cannot be
  matched to the animal it describes — exactly the harm 11.32 exists to prevent. **The
  plumbing is one nullable column and one call**, and this task is building the screen
  that creates these records, so **shipping without it ships the fourth instance of a
  problem that was just fixed.**
- **Saved position estimates — no, and write down why.** An estimate is derived from
  bearings that each already know their own version, so the information is reachable
  without duplicating it.
- **Triangulation sessions — no, and write down why.** A session is a grouping label,
  not a measurement.

Recording the two "no" answers matters as much as the "yes": an unexplained absence
gets rediscovered as a gap by the next sweep.

**The invariant, and it needs a test rather than care:** a truth point must never
enter the position-estimate solver. It lives in its own table and not as a new kind
of observation — deliberately, because a solver query that has to *remember to
exclude* a row type is an exemption, and this project's own recurring finding is
that wherever a control deliberately ignores something, that exemption is where the
next problem is. **Add a test that puts a truth point next to a set of bearings and
asserts the estimate is identical with and without it.**

- **Acceptance:** a truth point can be entered both ways; the precision field
  prefills from the device for a GPS fix and is not prefilled for a pin; the
  three-way kind is stored; the solver test above passes; a truth point still
  renders on the map as it already does.

### Task 11.34 — Decouple project tags from the tag log: measure and design, do not implement
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-09.** Output is `CLAUDE_DOCS/TAG_COPY_ON_ADD_DESIGN.md`; no
production code changed. All three questions answered as measurements. **(1)** `Tags`
and `Tag_Versions` both sync today — two of the four *global* tables on the wire — so
copy-on-add takes the wire from thirteen tables to twelve and from two global reach
sets to one, and retires roughly 200 lines of tag-specific server authorization plus
the offer-order constraint. **(2)** Every reader that computes a *result* — map,
legend, Log, exports, pickers, estimator, archive — is already project-scoped and
simplifies; four readers walk the whole device tag list and all four are *choosing*
screens. **(3)** Migration moves almost nothing: a tag in exactly one project keeps its
identifier and gains a `project_id`, which is schema v6's trick again; only a tag in
two or more projects on one device needs forking.
**Three things the measurement found that the plan did not know.** The server has
refused cross-project tag sharing since task 11.3 — for the same owner too — while the
app still offers it and holds the row forever with *"the server did not say why"*. The
shared-bearing paste screen matches a payload against every tag on the device, so an
imported record can name another project's tag. An archive import can rewrite a row in
your own tag log, because the merger's project check is skipped for tables with no
project column. **And the brief's own load-bearing premise is false: adding a tag to a
project is contributor-level, not owner-only** — see Discovered Scope, which Phase 12
depends on.
**Model:** **Opus** — high effort, fresh window, run alone.
**Depends on:** 11.32. **This task deliberately writes no production code.**

**The decision Michael made on 2026-08-22.** When a tag is added to a project it
should be **copied** into that project, so a project's tag is its own and editing it
neither changes the person's own tag log nor any other project. The user must be
told plainly that the copy is a copy — in both directions, since the confusion that
will actually happen is somebody editing their tag log and expecting the project to
follow.

**Why this is worth doing, stated so it can be argued with.** It does not solve a
problem; **it deletes one.** There is no longer a cross-project tag to coordinate,
so: no cross-project authorization rule, no frozen shared tag, no refusal message
that risks disclosing another project's existence, and the long-accepted orphan-tag
residual — a tag no project references, adoptable by anyone holding its identifier —
stops existing. After nine rounds of findings, removing an authorization question is
worth more than answering one.

**Why it is measure-and-design only, and why that is cheaper than the alternative.**
This is a change to the core data model. Implementing it on assumptions and
discovering a wrong one afterwards costs a rewrite plus a migration; the same
mistake found in a report costs a paragraph. Task 11.20 worked exactly this way and
it was the right shape.

**Establish these before proposing anything, and report each as measured or
unknown:**

1. **Does the tag table sync today?** If it does, this change removes a synced
   table from the wire, which is a real reduction in attack surface and should be
   stated as a benefit. If it does not, the change is larger than it looks. **Do
   not assume either way** — the planning session could not tell from the
   documentation and did not guess.
2. **What reads a tag across project boundaries today?** Analysis, map rendering,
   the legend, exports, the duplicate-frequency warning, and Phase 12's merge. Each
   one either stops needing a cross-project answer or breaks; say which.
3. **What does migration do to data that already exists?** Projects today reference
   shared tags. A migration has to produce copies without losing the link that says
   two projects were once talking about the same collar.

**Task 11.32 lands first, and its versioning design is settled — do not redesign
it.** 11.32 decides what a bearing remembers about its tag: a reference to the tag's
state as it was, not a copy of selected fields. Your question is where those
versions live once a tag is project-local, not whether they exist.

**Two constraints on the design:**

- **Keep a provenance pointer on the copy** — "copied from this tag in your log, on
  this date" — explicitly non-authoritative and never read by anything live. Without
  it you permanently lose the fact that one project's "Coco" and another's are the
  same physical collar, which is exactly what a multi-year or cross-project analysis
  needs. It is cheap now and unreconstructable later.
- **No message about a tag may reveal that another project exists.** That
  constraint is inherited from cancelled task 11.29 and it survives the
  cancellation, because the provenance pointer above is a link to something the
  reader may have no access to.

**One thing to say out loud in the report, because the naive reading is backwards:**
copying looks like it creates more duplicate tags, and it does — but it makes Phase
12 *smaller*, because cross-project duplicates stop mattering by definition and only
within-project ones ever affected an analysis. ~~Also note that within-project duplicates are held down by an existing decision: adding a
tag to a project is owner-only, so one person does the adding. **That decision is now
load-bearing for this one** — say so, so nobody relaxes it later without knowing.~~
**STRUCK 2026-09-10: this was false and it was the planning session's own sentence.** Task
11.34 measured it: **adding a tag to a project has been contributor-level on all three layers
since 2026-08-21**, deliberately. **What is owner-only is *removing*.** Nothing holds
within-project duplicates down except a near-duplicate warning whose buttons are *"Go back"*
and *"Create anyway"*. **The claim that copy-on-add makes Phase 12 smaller survives** — that
rests on cross-project duplicates ceasing to matter, which is untouched. **The claim that the
remaining duplicates will be rare does not, and that was the argument for deferring Phase 12
past the beta.** See the note on task 11.29 below.

- **Acceptance:** the three questions above are answered as measurements, not
  assumptions, with "I could not determine this" stated where true; a migration plan
  exists; the consequences for each cross-project reader are enumerated; **no
  production code is changed.** Implementation is a separate task once Michael has
  read this.

### Task 11.35 — Finish what 11.28 could not: your own sessions, and a two-device test that is possible to run
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-23.** Part 1: `GET /auth/sessions` returns the
caller's own devices — one row per device (matching the revocation's own
granularity), carrying a device id, first sign-in, last-used, expiry and
whether it is this device, and **deliberately no source address and no token**.
There is no device label because the server stores none. Keyed on the validated
session, reading nothing from body or query; bounded and rate-limited per
authenticated user. Permissions matrix row M9, trust-boundary inventory entry
27 (verdict **Open** — built, not yet gate-attacked), Security Model §4.3
rewritten. 16 new tests. **No screen calls it yet** — see Discovered Scope.
Part 2: `docker-compose.dev-lan.yml` turns the file-based magic-link sender on
without touching `ports:` or the publish address, verified by rendering the
merged config; `README.md` §4 now carries the two-device walkthrough, naming the
licensed Ubuntu/Parallels host, why Docker Desktop cannot host it, and the
debug-build `http://` trap. **The walkthrough itself has not been executed** —
it needs the VM and two physical devices. Server suite 682 → 701 green; app
suite 1258, unchanged.
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. Part 1 is a new server surface, however small.
**Depends on:** 11.28.

Two unrelated things, bundled because both are the difference between task 11.28
being written and task 11.28 being *finished*.

**Part 1 — a route that lists your own signed-in devices.** Task 11.28 wired up
"sign out everywhere" but could not offer **"sign out just my lost phone"**, because
nothing tells a person which devices they are signed in on. 11.28 was right not to
add this on its own judgement: it is a new authenticated read, not wiring.

- It returns **only the caller's own sessions**, resolved from the session the
  request arrives on and never from anything in the request body. That is the same
  rule the two existing revocation routes already follow and the reason they were
  found to be correctly built.
- **Say what each row may contain, and default to less.** A device label and a last-
  used time are enough to pick your lost phone out of a list. **A source address is
  not**, and adding one would put location-revealing data on a new read for a
  convenience. If a label is not already stored, say so rather than inventing one.
- Add it to the permissions matrix and to the trust-boundary inventory as a new
  entry, with a verdict, in the same commit. A new server surface arriving without
  its inventory line is what the last four drift findings were made of.
- **Acceptance:** a caller sees their own sessions and nobody else's, demonstrated by
  a test that tries; the route is unreachable unauthenticated; revoking one listed
  session ends that device's access on its next request and leaves the others alone.

**Part 2 — make a two-device test possible at all.** 11.28's acceptance needs one
person leaving a project on a second device, and **that test cannot currently be
run**, for a reason that has nothing to do with 11.28:

- The base compose stack resolves its mail sender to one that **silently discards**
  the magic link, because `TRITRACK_DEV_MAGIC_LINK_DIR` is set only in the
  end-to-end overlay — and that overlay pins the published port back to loopback,
  so it is unusable from a phone. **So on a LAN-reachable stack, nobody can sign in
  at all.** Two devices means two sign-ins, so the whole class of multi-device
  testing is blocked on this.
- **Add a dev-only overlay that turns the file-based sender on without touching the
  publish address**, so the documented LAN setup and a readable magic link can
  coexist. Keep the existing production guard — the file sender must still refuse to
  exist when the environment says production.
- **Then write the walkthrough into `README.md`**, because §4 of that file currently
  *withdraws* the LAN instruction and points at the source-identity refusal, which is
  correct and leaves a reader with no route at all. The walkthrough must name the
  licensed host — the Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 VM under Parallels with native Docker, the
  one configuration measured as preserving caller addresses — and say plainly that
  Docker Desktop on the Mac cannot host this and why.
- **Note the trap for whoever writes it:** the app accepts a plain `http://` address
  **only** in a debug build **and** only for a private or loopback host. So a release
  build on the phone will refuse the VM's address with no obvious explanation. Say
  that in the walkthrough rather than letting the next person discover it.
- **Acceptance:** a person following the README can sign two different accounts in on
  two real devices against one LAN server, with no step that is not written down.

**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. The screen is small; the coverage half needs a

Task 11.35 built the route that lists your own signed-in devices, and nothing in the
app calls it. So per-device sign-out is now possible and still not offered, which is
the same shape 11.28 found and closed for two other controls.

**The design question 11.35 raised, answered here: do not add a device label.**
11.35 is right that a list of five identifiers is not something a person can pick
their lost phone out of. But a label is a schema change *and* a new piece of
free text the phone chooses and the app then displays — which brings length bounds,
control characters and every other question this project has already paid for on
imported text. That is a large new surface for a convenience.

**Use what the server already records, which the phone cannot choose:**

- **Last used**, leading the row. This is what actually distinguishes devices — you
  know roughly when you last used the phone you lost.
- **Signed in on**, secondary. "Signed in 3 August, last used 12 August" identifies a
  device to its owner surprisingly well.
- **"This device"** marked plainly on the session the request is arriving on, so
  nobody signs themselves out while trying to sign out something else.
- Most recently used first.

If that turns out genuinely insufficient in use, a label becomes a considered
follow-up rather than the first thing tried.

- Put it on the Server Connection screen, with a revoke control per row.
- **Revoking must take effect on that device's next request**, which is the property
  the whole session design exists for — not on a timer.
**Second half, added 2026-08-27 from task 11.45: an end-to-end test per auth route.**
Deriving the coverage — rather than reading a list of it — turned up that **three of
the five things the app can ask an auth server for have never been tried against a
real one:** the sign-in poll, sign-out, and "sign out everywhere".

- Two of the three are unsurprising and belong here naturally: task 11.28 found that

  task is where they finally get one. A control with no caller has no end-to-end path

- **The sign-in poll is the uncomfortable one, and it must not ride along.** It is on

  and the most consequential. Say in the report which of the three you wrote and
  which, if any, you did not.
- Task 11.45 left a note in the guard itself that fails if somebody closes one of
  these without removing it. **Do not remove the note until all three tests exist**,
  not merely when this task closes.

**Third half, added 2026-08-28 from task 11.47 — and it forces this task to state an
order.** A sweep found that **no app-side test has ever pushed a shared record
carrying somebody else's edit stamp.** Every fixture stamps them with the pusher. So
if 11.47 had relaxed authorship as well as the audit column — breaking task 11.24 —
**the entire app suite would still have gone green.** The server suite does cover it,
which is why this is a gap and not a hole.

- Its natural home already exists: the two-people end-to-end test, which is the only
  place two different people are signed in.
- **The coverage guard will not flag the absence, and that is the third instance of
  one defect this month:** it counts routes, not authorization causes. Task 11.45

  third. Make it assert the cause, or say why it cannot.

**Priority order for this task, because it has accumulated four parts and they are
not equally urgent. If time runs out, stop at the line you have reached:**

1. **The sign-in poll's end-to-end test.** On the path every user takes, and its one
   known failure was found by hand rather than by any test.
2. **The teammate-stamped shared record test.** It is the guard against silently
   undoing 11.24.
3. **The two revocation route tests.** Real, but those controls had no caller at all

4. **The device-list screen itself.** The nominal subject of this task and the least

  signs you out here and says so rather than appearing to fail; **all three untested
  auth routes have an end-to-end test against a real server; a shared record carrying
  a teammate's edit stamp is pushed by a test and does not hold up the pusher's own
  bearings** — or the report names what was not done, and where it stopped.

**Added 2026-08-29, from task 11.37's handoff, and it changes what two of these tests
must assert.** Task 11.37 altered the behaviour of two of the three routes this task
is about to cover, so tests written against the old behaviour **would pass and prove
nothing:**

- **Asking the server what happened to a sign-in link** used to report "still
  waiting" forever when the address was wrong. It now reports an error.
- **Signing out** used to say "Signed out" even when the server never confirmed it.
  It now reports a failure.

So each of those two tests must **point at a deliberately wrong server address and
require a typed server error** — not a silent wait, and not a false success. A test
that only exercises the happy path against a good address cannot tell the new
behaviour from the old, which is this project's standing rule about checks that
cannot fail for the reason you care about.


### Task 11.37 — What the two-device walkthrough found by being run
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-28).** All five items. The full Flutter suite (1422
tests) and the full server suite against a real Postgres (711 tests) are green.

**Item by item:**

1. **Trailing slash — done, at the class.** `ServerConfig`'s constructor now
   normalises (`normalizeServerBaseUrl`), so **no `ServerConfig` can hold a
   non-canonical address** and all five call sites that append to `baseUrl`
   inherit it. Crucially it runs on **read**, not only on save, so a device that
   already stored the bad value is fixed without anyone re-typing the field —
   which a save-time fix would have missed entirely. Query and fragment are
   dropped too (they produce the same broken URL). A guard in
   `test/core/providers/server_url_normalization_test.dart` scans `lib/` and
   fails if any `baseUrl:` argument anywhere comes from something other than a
   `ServerConfig`, so a sixth call site inherits the fix without knowing it
   exists; a companion test proves that scan can see a violation.
   **A bug was found by writing the test:** `Uri.isAbsolute` is false whenever
   a fragment is present, so the first version skipped normalising exactly one
   of the shapes it existed to flatten.
2. **The two messages — done, and wider than specified.** New
   `AuthServerError` separates "the server answered" from "nothing answered".
   `requestMagicLink` was not the only site: `linkStatus` reported any non-200
   as `pending` (a wrong address polls forever), `redeem` reported any non-200
   as a bad code (which sends somebody to spend a second code against the same
   wrong address), and `signOut` discarded the status entirely and reported
   success. All four fixed through one `_requireStatus`. The screen's blanket
   `catch` is now four branches, and the residual one no longer blames the
   network for faults in this app.
3. **Profile points at Server Connection — done.** A tappable notice; a test
   navigates through it rather than matching the path string, since a wrong
   path is what a string comparison would agree with.
4. **The rate limit is documented — done**, in `README.md` §4 as its own
   subsection: the cap, that the response is identical, one bucket per address,
   the honest per-source `429` as the contrast, the in-process limiter and the
   restart that clears it, and the `rate_limit_tripped` / `email_limited` audit
   rows an operator can read. **No client-visible signal was added.**
5. **Issue time in the dev link file — done**, and the e2e reader now uses it:
   `waitForMagicLinkToken` takes `issuedAfter` and refuses a link written
   before the request, which is exactly the confusion the second-link case in
   `magic_link_sign_in_e2e_test.dart` was exposed to.
6. **The sweep — done.** Eight steps converted, ten left manual with a written
   reason each, recorded in `README.md`'s new "Steps that stay manual, and why".
   **The source-identity probe's verdict was deliberately left alone**, for the
   reason the spec gave: the value is the operator asserting a measurement
   about their own network, and a tool writing it would be the tool making the
   claim. Two new scripts (`scripts/dev_magic_link.sh`,
   `scripts/dev_lan_address.sh`) replace the two highest-risk prose steps.

**What the sweep found that the spec did not anticipate: task 11.38's own
conversion left the repudiated instruction behind in a second file.**
`macos/Runner/Configs/Signing.xcconfig.example` still opened with "Copy this
file to `Signing.xcconfig` and fill in your own Team ID" — the exact
instruction README.md step 3 replaced *because it named the wrong field* — and
README.md still pointed readers at it. Fixed, and
`test/platform/macos_keychain_entitlement_test.dart` now fails if that sentence
comes back. **The class: converting a step does not remove the copies of it
that live elsewhere, and nothing looks for them.**

**Not verified, and it should be said plainly:** the two backup-key extraction
commands added to `server/README.md` and `.env.example` (`age-keygen`'s public
key, `minisign`'s verifying key) were written from the documented output
formats — **neither tool is installed on this machine, so neither command was
run.** Likewise, both new scripts were exercised on macOS only; the Linux
`ip -o -4 addr` branch of `dev_lan_address.sh` has never run on the Ubuntu VM.

**Original spec below.**

**Status when written:** Not started
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. Items 1–4 are small; item 5 is a judgement about
which documented steps should stop being documented steps.
**Depends on:** nothing.

Task 11.35 wrote the walkthrough and demonstrated none of it. Michael ran it on
2026-08-26 and hit both of these. **That is the walkthrough working as intended** —
its acceptance criterion is "no step that is not written down", and the way you find
the missing steps is to walk it.

1. **A trailing slash on the server address produces a 404 that reads like the
   server is down.** Reproduced: a saved URL of `http://192.168.0.136:8080/` becomes
   `http://192.168.0.136:8080//auth/magic-link`, the server answers 404, and the app
   shows **"Could not reach the server. Try again."** Every visible signal points at
   the network, and the network is fine.
   - **Normalise the stored address**: strip trailing slashes when it is saved, so
     one canonical form reaches every caller. Do not fix this at the one call site
     that happened to be hit — the sign-in request is one of several paths that
     append to this value, and fixing the instance leaves the others.
   - **And separate the two failures in the message.** "Could not reach the server"
     for a connection that never completed; something else for a server that
     answered with an error. A message that names the wrong cause cost this
     walkthrough its first hour, and the same conflation will cost a field user a
     day when they have no terminal to check.
2. **Nothing on the Profile screen says that signing in lives somewhere else.**
   Profile asks for a name and an email address and offers Save; Server Connection is
   where the sign-in code is requested and entered. Both screens ask for an email, one
   signs you in, and nothing connects them. Michael reasonably concluded sign-in had
   not been built.
   - The Profile screen's email is local identity and works with no server, which is
     correct and should stay. **It just needs one line pointing at Server Connection**
     for anybody looking for sign-in.
   - **Acceptance:** somebody who opens Profile looking for sign-in is told where it
     is.

3. **The walkthrough sends the reader straight into the per-address rate limit, and
   the limit is invisible by design.** Sign-in requests are capped at **three per
   email address per fifteen minutes**, and when that trips the server returns the
   **identical** accepted response and writes no link file. That silence is correct
   and must not change — a distinguishable response would tell a caller that somebody
   recently requested a link for a third party's address, which is the oracle §4.5
   exists to prevent. **The defect is the walkthrough, not the control.** It tells the
   reader to request a code, and anybody debugging will request several, and then the
   documented `cat` returns nothing with no explanation available anywhere.
   - **Write it into `README.md` §4:** the cap, that the response is identical when
     it trips, that each address has its own bucket, and that the limiter is
     in-process so `docker compose … restart server` clears it. Reproduced on
     2026-08-26 — it cost a working session.
   - **Do not add a client-visible signal.** The right fix is documentation plus the
     audit row an operator can already read, not a hint that undoes the control.

4. **The dev sender's file is named per address and overwritten, so there is no way
   to tell a stale link from a fresh one.** Reading the file after a limited request
   returns the *previous* link, which then fails redemption as already used — which is
   how this session concluded the token had been spent when the real cause was one
   step earlier. **Put the issued time in the file** (it already carries an expiry, so
   this is one line) so a reader can tell whether they are looking at the link they
   just asked for. Development-only affordance, no production surface.

5. **Added 2026-08-27, and it is the class the other four are instances of: a
   documented command whose output a human has to read and retype into a config file
   cannot be checked by anything.** Task 11.38 hit one — a README line named the wrong
   field to copy, and the only symptom was an unrelated-sounding build failure much
   later. Nothing could have caught it, because it is prose.
   - **The fix pattern is the one 11.38 already applied: have the command write the
     file.** A step that produces a value a person then types somewhere is a step that
     will be wrong eventually, and wrong silently.
   - **Sweep the README for the rest of them.** 11.38 named three candidates: the
     source-identity probe, the LAN address lookup, and the magic-link file. Find any
     others rather than working from that list.
   - **This is judgement, not mechanics, which is why the model moved up.** Some of
     these should stay manual — the source-identity probe's verdict is deliberately
     something a person must read and act on, because writing `peer-verified`
     automatically would be the tool asserting a measurement about the operator's
     network. **Decide per step, and say why for each**, including the ones left
     alone. Automating that particular one would undo a control.

- **Acceptance:** a trailing slash on the saved address works; a server that answers
  with an error does not report as unreachable; Profile points at Server Connection;
  the rate limit and the restart-to-clear are in the README; the link file says when
  it was issued; every retype-this-value step is either converted or has a written
  reason for staying; **the walkthrough runs end to end with no step that is not
  written down** — the criterion task 11.35 was given and could not verify.

### Task 11.38 — Sign-in has never worked on macOS
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-27).** **The macOS keychain works, measured on
Michael's Mac.** `./scripts/verify_session_store_keychain.sh` passes in debug
and profile: the real signed app bundle writes a session to the real keychain
and reads it back, `ensureWritable` succeeds, the probe leaves an existing
session intact, and `clear` removes it. Sign-in on macOS is possible for the
first time since desktop support was added.

**Two errors were made and corrected during the hand-off, both worth keeping
because they are the kind that cost hours:**

1. **The Team ID was read from the wrong field of the certificate.** Claude
   Code took the parenthesised value in `security find-identity`'s output
   (`Apple Development: michael.shafer@nau.edu (KYKW9L6G57)`) to be the Team
   ID. It is not — it is Apple's per-developer *user* identifier. The Team ID
   is the certificate's organizational-unit field, `TT5775B757`. The symptom is
   `No Account for Team "KYKW9L6G57"`, which reads like a missing Apple ID
   account and is in fact a wrong ten-character string, so it sends you to
   re-do the Xcode sign-in that was never the problem. README.md and
   `Signing.xcconfig.example` now print the OU field and warn against the
   other one by name.
2. **`Release.entitlements` cannot be exercised by any integration test.**
   `flutter drive` refuses release mode outright, and profile builds use
   `DebugProfile.entitlements` — the same wall task 10.50 hit. The verify
   script asked for a release run and reported a failure that was its own.
   Corrected to debug + profile, with the limitation stated in the script
   rather than left to be rediscovered. What covers the release entitlements
   file instead is the drift test in
   `test/platform/macos_keychain_entitlement_test.dart`, which holds it
   byte-identical to its debug counterpart apart from the keychain block. That
   is weaker than a run and is named as such.

**Two things this task found that the spec did not anticipate, both measured:**

1. **The prescribed fix, applied literally, breaks the macOS build for
   everybody.** Adding `keychain-access-groups` to the base entitlements files
   makes Xcode refuse to *compile* the app without a development certificate
   ("Runner has entitlements that require signing with a development
   certificate"). That would trade "builds and runs but cannot sign in" for
   "does not build", which is worse for anyone who just wants to look at the
   app. Resolved by putting the entitlement in `DebugProfile-Signed`/
   `Release-Signed` variants selected by `TRITRACK_ENTITLEMENTS_SUFFIX`, which
   `Configs/Signing.xcconfig` (untracked) sets. A clone with no signing setup
   still builds ad hoc, exactly as before.
2. **A signing identity in the keychain is not enough** — Xcode must also hold
   the Apple ID *account*. Michael has a valid `Apple Development` certificate
   for team `KYKW9L6G57` and the build still fails, because automatic signing
   cannot mint a profile for an account Xcode does not know about. This is why
   the task cannot be closed by this session.

**The coverage question the spec asked, answered: nothing covered it, and the
reason is structural.** All eight test files that touch sign-in install
`FakeSessionStore`, including `auth_provider_test.dart`, whose own header
claims to run `completeSignIn` "through the real provider stack". They do that
because `flutter test` has no platform channels, so a real `SessionStore.read()`
never completes. The workaround for the untestability was also what guaranteed
the defect stayed invisible. `test/e2e/` re-implements the sign-in sequence
without the store at all. There is no CI, and `flutter build macos` appears in
no tracked file. So the real `write` — the one line that failed — had never been
executed by anything in this repository, on any platform.

**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. The fix is small; what it implies is not.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Run before any further multi-device testing** — it is
currently blocking it.

**Reproduced by hand on 2026-08-26**, on the two-device walkthrough. Signing in on
the macOS build fails with keychain error **`-34018`, "a required entitlement isn't
present"**, thrown by the secure store when it tries to write the session. The
sequence is worse than a plain failure: the server is reached, **the sign-in code is
consumed**, and only then does storing the session fail — so the person is signed out,
their code is spent, and the message they get says "could not reach the server."

**The cause, and it is not subtle.** Neither `macos/Runner/DebugProfile.entitlements`
nor `Release.entitlements` declares `keychain-access-groups`, and the macOS target
signs with `CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY = "-"` — ad hoc, no team. On macOS the keychain refuses
without both. iOS works because it is signed with a real team.

**What this means, and it should be stated plainly rather than buried in a fix:
sign-in and therefore sync have never worked on macOS, in any build.** Phase 5 added
desktop support and this was never exercised. **Establish and report how that
happened** — specifically whether any test or check covers sign-in on the desktop
build, because if none does, the fix without a guard leaves the same hole open for
the next platform.

1. Add `keychain-access-groups` to both entitlement files, and set the macOS target
   to sign with a real team rather than ad hoc. Say in the report what a person
   cloning this repo now has to do, because a signing identity is not something the
   repository can carry for them — **that instruction belongs in `README.md` beside
   the two-device walkthrough**, which currently sends the reader straight into this.
2. **The order of operations in sign-in is a second, separate defect, and it is the
   one that cost a working session.** The code is consumed before the session can be
   stored, so a storage failure leaves the user signed out with a spent code and no
   way to tell why. Either verify the store is usable *before* redeeming, or report
   the failure honestly enough that the person knows their code is gone and storage
   is the reason. **Do not fix only the entitlement** — any future storage failure,
   on any platform, reproduces this.
3. **Add whatever guard would have caught it.** A test that the desktop build can
   write and read back a session is the obvious candidate; if the harness cannot do
   that, say so and say what could.

- **Acceptance:** a session survives sign-in and an app restart on macOS; a
  simulated storage failure does not consume the code, or says clearly that it did;
  something in the suite fails if the entitlement is removed again.

**Acceptance, item by item (2026-08-26):**

- *A session survives sign-in and an app restart on macOS* — **demonstrated
  2026-08-27**, on Michael's Mac (macOS, darwin-arm64, team `TT5775B757`).
  `integration_test/session_store_keychain_test.dart` passes in debug and
  profile via `./scripts/verify_session_store_keychain.sh`: four tests, real
  signed app bundle, real keychain, write and read back. Reading back a session
  the OS stored is the same property as surviving a restart. **Not yet done:
  an actual sign-in against a live server on macOS** — that needs the LAN stack
  and is task 11.35's walkthrough, now unblocked.
- *A simulated storage failure does not consume the code, or says clearly that
  it did* — **both, done.** `SessionStore.ensureWritable()` round-trips a
  throwaway value through the keychain **before** `completeSignIn` redeems, so
  the ordinary case never spends the code; the rare case where the store fails
  after the check throws `SessionStorageFailedAfterRedemption`, and the screen
  says the code is used up and that this device is the reason. Four provider
  tests and three widget tests, each verified to fail when the fix is reverted.
- *Something in the suite fails if the entitlement is removed again* — **done**,
  `test/platform/macos_keychain_entitlement_test.dart`, eight tests in the
  default offline suite. It guards four distinct regressions, not one: deleting
  the entitlement, the two entitlement files drifting apart, hard-coding the
  path back into `project.pbxproj`, and dropping the optional signing include.
  Each was verified to fail by reintroducing it.

**Status:** **Done 2026-08-29.** All three parts, plus task 11.52 and both of

**Part 3's contradiction is settled** in `RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` Part 4: 10.84
