**(Original spec follows.)**
**Status (original):** Not started
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. The value is in the honest division, not the
scripting.
**Depends on:** 11.38.

Two things task 11.38 asked for, together because they are one question asked from
both ends: **what does this project verify without a human, and what can it not?**

**Part 1 — sweep every capability the operating system has to grant.** Location,
background modes, the cloud-folder bookmark, notifications, the keychain, and
whatever else the sweep turns up. For each, decide whether it needs a test on real
hardware, and record the answer either way.

**Why, in one sentence: both hardware tests in this repository exist because somebody
hit a bug by hand first.** Task 11.38's keychain failure is one instance of a class,
and it had gone undetected since Phase 5 added desktop support. **Nobody should have
to reproduce a `-34018` to discover the next one.** Enumerate the capabilities from
the platform manifests and entitlement files rather than from memory, so the list
cannot quietly omit one.

**Part 2 — there is no continuous integration at all.** Nothing runs on a commit.

- The offline suite is around 1,270 tests, fast, and needs no server — so it is
  cheap and should run on every commit.
- The server suite needs Postgres in Docker, which is ordinary for CI.
- **The hardware tests genuinely cannot be automated** without a signed macOS runner,
  and **the task must say so plainly rather than configure something that implies
  they are covered.** A green badge that omits the class of defect 11.38 found would
  be worse than no badge, because it would be read as coverage. This project's own
  recurring finding is that a check which cannot fail for the reason you care about
  is not a check.
- **Output a written division:** what CI covers, what it deliberately does not, and
  what a person must therefore do before a release. That list is a release checklist,
  which this project does not yet have and will need for the beta.

**Carries task 11.52 as of 2026-08-29** — read its entry, which stands unchanged.
One file owns each setup step and every other mention points at it rather than
copying it, enumerated from the files rather than from the four known copies, and
**guarded by a test watched to fail.** It is here because it is the same question this
task asks: what does this project check without a person, and what does it only claim?
A guard with nothing running it is precisely what this task exists to refuse, and this
task is the one standing up the thing that runs guards.

**A third thing, added 2026-08-29 from task 11.36, and it is explicitly the last item
here — drop it and say so if the two above run long.** The end-to-end suite's
magic-link reader **reports a timeout as the rate limit**. Twice on 2026-08-29 a run
failed saying the server had accepted a request and written nothing, *"which is what
the per-address rate limit looks like from the outside"* — but every address involved
was freshly minted and the limit is three per address per fifteen minutes. What fits
is that the server's write took longer than the reader's ten seconds and **the reader
offered the stale file it last saw as evidence of a limiter that was never tripped.**
**It sends whoever is debugging to restart the server for no reason** — task 11.37
item 1's shape, this time inside the instrument. **11.36 could not reproduce it on
demand**: four later full runs were green, two on a cold stack.

It belongs here because **this task is standing up the thing that will run that
harness unattended**, and an instrument that misreports why it failed is a continuous
integration problem the moment continuous integration exists — *"when an instrument
cannot tell you what happened, fix the instrument before the thing it was pointing
at."* At minimum, make the reader distinguish "I waited and nothing appeared" from "a
limiter refused this", and never assert the second.

**A part of this task that task 11.49 identified, and it is not a checklist item — it
is the point of the continuous-integration half.** 11.49 found three defects in the
gate's own instruments, and **all three have one root: these instruments only run when
somebody remembers.** (a) `verify_11_24_attribution.py` had been in neither of
`gate_smoke_test.sh`'s lists since it landed on 2026-08-22, so the closure of the
attribution finding had **no automated re-run at all.** (b) `gate_smoke_test.sh` itself
has been **red since 2026-08-28 and nobody ran it.** (c) The adversarial pass's timing
check measured the laptop rather than the server, and failed a live gate run doing it.

**A guard that only runs when remembered is a hand-maintained list one layer up**, and
this project has now found that shape in its instruments three times. **The sixteen
committed instruments run in 3 minutes 21 seconds against a stack they bring up and tear
down themselves, needing only Docker** — measured by 11.49, which is well inside what
continuous integration can carry. **Whatever this task builds must run them**, or say
plainly why not: a green badge that omits the gate's own instruments is exactly the
false coverage this task exists to refuse.

**Michael decided on 2026-08-30: no self-hosted macOS runner.** He has no Mac he can
leave running, so **the two hardware tests run by hand before a release** and stay on the
human half of the checklist rather than being implied to be covered. That is the honest
division this task was written to produce, and it is the right answer for two tests. **If
they are ever skipped twice in a row, revisit it** — "run when somebody remembers" is how
this project has lost instruments three times.

**Two things task 11.64 asked this task to carry, added 2026-08-30.**

- **Re-run `scripts/verify_round8_broken_control.py` after touching the sync envelope or
  the auth routes.** It takes ten minutes and **it is the only thing proving the 152 new
  gate checks can fail.** It is deliberately *not* inside `gate_smoke_test.sh` — a
  ten-minute build inside a three-minute run would stop the run being used, which is
  exactly the shape that loses instruments, found three times on this project. So it
  needs a **trigger** rather than a schedule, and this task owns choosing one.
- **A workflow fix is incomplete while any document still spells out the broken
  invocation.** Task 11.37 built `scripts/run_e2e_tests.sh` precisely to remove a trap —
  running the end-to-end suite without its two environment variables tests nothing and

  gate reads**, which this round then fell into. That is the same class as task 11.52's
  copies of converted setup steps, which this task already carries, and it is the second

**A second checklist item, added 2026-08-29 from task 11.59:** *measure what automatic
sync costs in battery and cellular data on a real phone, in the field, for a day,
against a real server.* Nobody has ever measured it; the fifteen-minute default ships
on task 10.8's reasoning, and Michael's confirmation after running the build was an
observation — his phrase was "seems to work" — not a measurement. **This is squarely in
this task's remit: a thing only a person with a device in the field can check.** If it

**One item the checklist must carry, decided 2026-08-29:** *check the "Records that
did not arrive" section on every beta device, and ask every beta user to report one if
they see it.* That section is the only signal that a teammate's record was refused and
will never arrive on its own, and it is the written trigger for deferred task 11.50.
A trigger nobody is looking for is not a trigger.

**Part 3, added 2026-08-29 — the checklist has to settle a contradiction nobody has
settled.** `SESSION_HANDOFF.md` §8 calls three unscheduled Phase 10 tasks

field record). Each of those three plan entries says **"Not blocking"**, and
`SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` records **Gate D as passing**, whose stated question is

is somebody reading "Gate D passes" as clear-to-ship. **The release checklist is where
this gets resolved:** for each of the three, state whether it must close before a beta
ships or is accepted for the beta with a reason, and say which of the two documents
was wrong. Do not quietly pick one — name the disagreement, then answer it. If the
answer is genuinely Michael's rather than yours, say so and put the choice in front of
him rather than leaving both sentences standing.

- **Acceptance:** every OS-granted capability has a stated verdict on hardware

### Task 11.41 — Rows stuck forever on the owner's device after a teammate syncs
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-27** (commit `a4176e8`). Two independent defects,
both measured. **Both hypotheses below were disproved** — see "What was found"
at the end of this entry.
**Model:** **Opus** — high effort, fresh window. A live two-device reproduction
exists and will not exist again cheaply.
**Depends on:** 11.24. **This is the highest-value thing in Phase 11 right now.**

**Observed on real hardware, 2026-08-27**, running task 11.35's walkthrough — a Mac
and an iPhone signed in as two different people against one LAN server. The iPhone
recorded bearings and synced successfully. **The Mac then reported two records that
could not be sent, and they never clear.** The waiting-to-sync screen shows them
under **Tags** and **Users**. Nothing appears in the server log and nothing prints in
the client console, so the rows appear to be held on the device **before** they are
ever sent.

**Fix the instrument first, because it is why this had to be diagnosed by guessing.**
The banner says *"two records aren't on the server. Tap to see why"* and the screen it
opens **does not say why.** A control that promises a reason and gives none is the
same defect class as a check that cannot distinguish success from its own failure —
and here it directly cost a diagnosis. **Make that screen state, per row: which
record, which rule held it, and what the person can do about it.** Do this first; it
makes everything below observable instead of inferred.

**A hypothesis, offered so it can be disproved rather than adopted.** `Tags` and
`Users` are exactly the two tables carrying a record that names a person who is not
the caller. Task 11.24 landed the rule that a record naming an author must name the
caller. If a device puts **rows it received from the server** into its own outbound
queue, those rows name their original author, the new rule holds them, and they are
stuck permanently. **That would mean every device accumulates permanently-held rows
for every teammate it ever syncs with**, and no Phase 11 test would have caught it,
because all of them ran on one device.

**Measure before believing that.** Two rival explanations that fit the same symptom:

- The project was created on the Mac **before** signing in, so those rows were
  authored under a locally-minted identity; identity adoption remapped some and not
  others. Michael could not recall which order he did it in, so **establish whether
  the order matters and say so** — if it does, "use the app offline first, sign in
  later" is the app's own advertised path and it would break for every user.
- The rows are genuinely the teammate's and are correctly refused, and the defect is
  only that they sit in a queue that will never drain and tell nobody.

**If the hypothesis holds, fix the class, not the row.** The question is not "should
this row be held" but **"why is a row the device received ever in the outbound queue
at all"** — and whatever answers that covers every table, not the two that happened to
show up.

- **Reproduce it from a clean state**, so the fix has a failing test. If a two-device
  reproduction cannot be automated, say so, and write the manual reproduction into the
  README's walkthrough as a check somebody must perform.
- **Report what a person sees today**, in plain terms: a red bar that never goes away,
  a screen that will not explain it, and no way to tell whether their data is safe.
  Even if the rows are correctly refused, that experience is the finding.
- **Acceptance:** the waiting-to-sync screen names the rule that held each row; the
  cause is established by measurement rather than argument; if rows are wrongly held,
  the fix is derived from what may enter the outbound queue rather than from these two
  tables; a test fails without it.

#### What was found, 2026-08-27

**Everything below was measured against the code, not argued.** The two rows on
the Mac could not be inspected from here, so each candidate explanation was
reproduced or refused on its own.

**The instrument was the first fix, and it is also the diagnosis Michael can
still run.** The screen showed the bare words "Tags" and "Users", one paragraph
of copy covering three unrelated causes, and a retry button. It now names the
record, states why *that record* is waiting, and says what to do — so the two
rows on his Mac, which are still in its database, will identify themselves the
moment he opens that screen on the new build. `HeldRowReason.explanation` was
deleted along the way: it was user-facing copy no production code read any
more, and it had been reworded twice (tasks 10.34 and 11.24) trying to cover
causes an enum value cannot tell apart.

**Cause 1 — a project offered global rows it does not reach.** `Users`,
`User_Emails`, `Tags` and `Tag_Versions` have no project column, and
`SyncEngine._pendingClause` narrowed them by nothing at all, on a premise its
own comment stated and that was false: *"they are reachable from this project's
data by design."* A device holds one `Tags` table for every project it has ever
had. Measured: a second, never-published local project's tag **and its owner's
`Users` row** were offered to this project's server. The server refuses what a
project does not reach, so both were refused and held permanently — exactly two
tables, exactly the two Michael saw. Fixed by narrowing global tables with the
same reachability the server narrows pull by, derived from a new shared
`reachColumnsFor` that the server's `ProjectReachability` now reads too.

**Cause 2 — a hold could only be settled by the one event it prevented.** A
hold was cleared only by a *successful push*, and a held row is deliberately
suppressed from every subsequent push. So once refused, a row could never clear
on its own. In particular, a row the server itself delivered on the next pull
stayed marked "not on the server" forever — which is precisely the resolution
`HeldRowReason.notPermitted`'s copy promised (*"it will arrive from their device
when they sync — you do not need to do anything"*). That promise had never been
kept in any version. `SyncEngine._reconcileHolds` now settles a hold whenever
the row has left this project's outbound set, asked of the push's own predicate
rather than as three special cases.

**Disproved: the leading hypothesis.** A device does *not* put rows it received
from the server into its own outbound queue. `_recordDeliveredReceipts` already
accounts for every delivered row as the page commits. Kept as a test so it stays
disproved, since nothing else in the suite pinned it — every pull test stopped
after one round.

**Disproved: the offline-first order.** Whether the project was created before
or after signing in does not matter. `ServerIdentityAdopter` remaps every user
column onto the server's id, leaves exactly one `Users` row, and the resulting
push is correctly attributed. **"Use the app offline first, sign in later" is
not broken**, and the question can be closed.

**Two existing tests were passing for the wrong reason** and are corrected: one
asserted a colleague's `Users` row was pushed while never giving the project any
row that named them, and one filled an early table with `Users` rows nothing
referenced. Both would have kept passing against a build carrying cause 1.

**Measured on 2026-08-27, after Michael started Docker.** Everything the entry
above said was unverified has now been run: the server's Postgres suite is
**701/701 green**, which is the real check on the `ProjectReachability` edit
rather than the equivalence argument that stood in for it; and the e2e suite is
**36/36 green** against a live server, including the new
`two_people_one_project_e2e_test.dart` — the first test in this project's
history to sign in **two different people** on one project.

**The two tests carrying this task's findings passed on their first real run.**
The third failed, in the test rather than the app, twice for the same reason: a
device was made to hold a record referring to something it had never been told
about, and SQLite refused it both times. And the first attempt to fix that used
`ConflictAlgorithm.ignore`, which skips a row violating *any* constraint — so it
could not tell "already present" from "this insert was broken", and silently did
the second while looking like the first. **That is this task's own defect class,
written into the test for it**, and it is recorded in the file's header rather
than tidied away.

### Task 11.42 — The undo bar after deleting a project never goes away
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-28.**
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** nothing. **Small, and not blocking anything.**

Observed on macOS, 2026-08-27: deleting a project shows the white undo bar and it
never dismisses. It should time out, and it should dismiss on the next navigation.

- **Check the other undo bars in the app rather than this one only.** If the timer is
  shared, they are all wrong; if it is per-screen, that is worth knowing before the
  next one is written.
- Worth a moment's thought about what an undo bar that never expires implies: if the
  undo is still live, the deletion may not be committed — establish which, because
  "the bar is cosmetic" and "the delete is in limbo" are very different findings.

**Root cause, found by reproducing it in isolation before touching the app's own
code at all.** Flutter's `SnackBar.persist` defaults to `true` whenever the
SnackBar carries an `action` — Material 3's own default, stated in its doc comment:
*"if not provided, but the snackbar action is not null, the snackbar will persist as
well."* The dismiss timer still gets created and still fires on schedule, but its
callback is `if (snackBar.persist) return;` — a silent no-op. So every one of this
app's undo bars, all built the same hand-written way, set a `duration` that was dead
the moment it also had an UNDO action: `projects_screen.dart` (delete project),
`project_setup_screen.dart` (remove tag), `log_screen.dart` (delete observation),
`position_estimation_screen.dart` (delete estimate) — plus one that is not an undo
bar but has the identical shape, `projects_screen.dart`'s publish-refused "Details"
snackbar. **The timer is per-screen, not shared — the finding is that all five
independently hand-wrote the same omission, four weeks running the pattern this
project keeps finding.** Fixed by adding `persist: false` to all five, each with a
comment pointing at this task rather than re-deriving the explanation five times.

**Established separately, per the second bullet, because it needed proving rather
than assuming:** every one of the four undo-bar screens `await`s its soft-delete
before ever showing the snackbar. The delete is committed before the bar exists, so
undo is a genuinely separate write (`restoreById`/`restore`), not a pending
transaction the bar is holding open. **The bar was stale. The delete was never in
limbo.** Confirmed for the project-delete case by reading the row back from the
database mid-bar in a test, rather than argued from reading the code.

**"Dismiss on next navigation" was a second, genuine gap, not a restatement of the
first.** `ScaffoldMessenger` sits above the whole `Router` — `MaterialApp` wraps its
routed content in exactly one, app-wide, a fact established by tracing Flutter's own
source rather than assumed — so a route change means nothing to it on its own; an
undo bar shown on one screen floats over whatever screen comes next until its own
timer eventually fires. Closed with `dismissSnackBarsOnNavigate` in
`lib/routing/app_router.dart`: it listens to `GoRouter.routerDelegate`, which
notifies on every navigation the router performs (a push, a pop, a tab switch), and
clears the current snackbar on each one — one place, rather than every destination
screen having to remember to do it on the way in. Needed a
`GlobalKey<ScaffoldMessengerState>` threaded from `app.dart` into the router
provider, since a provider builder has no `BuildContext` of its own to reach
`ScaffoldMessenger.of()` with.

**A `flutter_test` pitfall worth recording here rather than only in code comments,
because it will bite the next screen-with-a-timed-snackbar test too:** a
`dart:async Timer` created from *inside* `tester.runAsync()` — including one created
indirectly, by a `pumpAndSettle()` call placed inside `runAsync` — is bound to real
wall-clock time, not the test's fake clock. Every subsequent `tester.pump(duration)`
after leaving `runAsync` advances only the fake clock, so that Timer can never be
reached and the bar reads as permanently stuck **in the test**, correctly fixed or
not. Cost real time to track down: the identical widget, tapped the identical way,
timed out correctly outside `runAsync` and never did inside it. The fix is ordering —
do the real async work (the DB write) inside `runAsync` with a real delay, but do not
call any `pump`/`pumpAndSettle` there; let the entrance-animation-completing pump
that creates the Timer happen afterward, back in the normal fake-clock zone.

Tests: `test/features/more/projects_screen_test.dart` (two new cases — times out on
its own, with the delete's commit read back from the real in-memory database mid-bar
rather than assumed; and a second delete shortly after the first replaces rather
than queues) and a new `test/routing/app_router_test.dart` (four cases for
`dismissSnackBarsOnNavigate`, including one that documents the pre-fix behaviour by
constructing the router *without* the wiring and asserting the bar survives
navigation). `flutter analyze` clean; full suite green (1372 tests).

**Checked and deliberately left alone:** `map_screen.dart`'s "no elevation data —
Download" snackbar also carries an action and therefore also now persists
indefinitely by Material 3's default — but it sets no explicit `duration`, so
nothing here was ever silently dead, and persisting until the user acts on an
offer to download data is arguably the correct read of Material 3's own default
rather than a defect. Left as `persist`'s default (`true`) rather than touched to
match the pattern; noted here so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

### Task 11.43 — Decide what publishing a project actually sends
**Status after the reopen: Done 2026-09-01.** `Project_Tags` now sits between `Tags` and
`Tag_Versions` in `Tables.all`, so the link that vouches for a tag is committed by an
earlier request than the version row that needs it. **Checked before changing, because the
old position was argued for rather than accidental:** `Tag_Versions` sat immediately after
`Tags` for two stated reasons — the merger's FK-safe insert order, and the server
authorizing one push's rows in that order so a tag created in the same push is already
established. Moving `Project_Tags` up preserves both (`Project_Tags` references only
`Projects` and `Tags`, both still earlier; the same-push escape is unaffected and now fires
one table sooner), so this is a correction and not a trade.

**The gap, which mattered more than the row.** Three suites were green while this shipped.
The fix therefore comes with the replay the reopened acceptance asks for:
`server/test/integration/publish_request_sequence_test.dart` sends **one table per HTTP
request**, taking its order from `Tables.all` — the same declaration `ProjectPublisher`
iterates, so the replay cannot drift from the thing it replays — and its second case
replays the order that *shipped* and asserts the server refuses exactly the `Tag_Versions`
row, so the test is evidence rather than decoration. `test/e2e/publish_and_join_e2e_test.dart`
gains the same case through the real `ProjectPublisher` against a live server, and was
watched to fail against the old order before the order was fixed. The e2e suite had been
green throughout because every project it published had **no tag**.

**The class, not the instance.** `packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/offer_order.dart` states
the rule once — *a table that names a global id is offered only after the table that
establishes the project's claim on that id* — and derives the establishing table
(`reachLinkTableFor`: the project-scoped table keyed by exactly its project scope plus the
reach column) rather than naming `Project_Tags`.
`assertOfferOrderEstablishesReachBeforeItIsNeeded` takes the order as a parameter so it can
be handed the order that shipped and watched to refuse it. Where a reach set has **no** link
table — the user set — the file says why ordering is not the mechanism there (§4.17 clause 1
vouches for a row naming the caller; a field row naming a colleague is the refusal §4.17
accepts and explains) and still refuses one shape: a *global* table naming an id nothing
vouches for, whose refusal would never clear.

Suites: app **1815** green, shared package **313**, server **794** in Docker, e2e **74/74**
against a live server.

**REOPENED 2026-08-31. Its acceptance was not met on real hardware, and the way that was
discovered is the point.**

**Every first publish refuses one `Tag_Versions` row.** The publisher sends **one table per
HTTP request**, and `tagVersions` is ordered **before** `projectTags` — so when the server
reads it, the reachability escape has not been established yet
(`row_authorizer.dart:1899`). It clears itself on a later sync, about four minutes on the
device 11.66 used. **In between, the person gets a red banner and a card telling them this
"is not a case the app expects" and asking them to report it.** On their first publish.

> **Why no test caught it, and this is the finding rather than the row:** the existing client
> test uses a fake transport that **models no reachability rule**, and every server test
> **pushes the tables together in one request.** So both sides test a sequence the app never
> sends. **Neither test is wrong on its own terms; between them they leave the real request
> order untested**, which is how a task reaches "Done" with its acceptance unmet.

**The reopened acceptance adds one requirement: a test that replays the publisher's real
request sequence** — table by table, in the order it actually sends them, against a server
that enforces reachability. **Fixing the ordering without that test would close the instance
and leave the gap.**

**Status before this:** **Done (2026-08-28).** The planning session's reading was checked and
is **correct, with one correction worth carrying**: redemption is enough, but not
because the teammate syncs first. The server writes a `Users` row *itself* at
redemption — carrying the address it authenticated and, deliberately, no invented
name — because `Project_Memberships.user_id` is a foreign key into `Users` and the
membership could not otherwise be written. So the server knows **who** a member is
the instant they redeem, and learns their **name** when their own device pushes it.
Established by running the flow end to end (`two_people_one_project_e2e_test.dart`,
third group) rather than by reading the redemption code.

**The rule, stated:** *a device offers the server every row of the project except
the records the server keeps for itself — who somebody is, and what they may do.*
Derived from each table's declared `MutationRule` and project scope in
`packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/offer_rules.dart`, so a fourteenth table is
classified by definition; the covered set today is `Users`, `User_Emails`,
`Projects`, `Project_Memberships`. §4.17's clause-2 predicate moved to
`MutationRule.vouchesForAForeignName` and `RowAuthorizer._replicableName` is now a
name for it rather than a second copy.

**Withholding is safe because it withholds only unconditional denials** — clause 2
applies exactly where `vouchesForAForeignName` is true and that is false for all
four tables, so nothing withheld could ever have been accepted. Asserted, not
argued.

**One deliberate departure from the acceptance line, flagged rather than buried:**
"no refused record" holds for records about **people**. A replica of a colleague's
*bearing* is still offered, refused and held — the server has no other way to
obtain one, and §4.17's accepted cost is stated in terms of the user being told, so
withholding it would convert a visible, self-clearing wait into a silent omission.
A first publish now holds their bearing and not their name.

**Both paths read the one rule, and had to:** fixing only the publisher would have
left the very next sync putting the same rows back on the wire. Because
`_reconcileHolds` asks the push's own predicate, **every record already stuck on a
device resolves on the next sync** — no migration, no button.

Also closed: publishing a project whose recorded owner is somebody else now fails
by name before anything is sent (`PublishNotYoursToMake`) instead of partway
through with a foreign-key violation.

Three existing tests asserted the old behaviour and now assert the new one, with
the reversal written into each. **Task 11.41's sentence here was the right answer
to the wrong question** — *"the narrowing must not be 'never offer anybody else's
row'"* — because reachability decides what a **pull** delivers, not what a push may
author. One new test passed with the fix removed and was strengthened; every guard
was watched to fail. Suites: app **1316** green, shared package **261**, server
**701** in Docker, e2e **39/39** against a live server (36 before).
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. It is a design decision about a payload, not a
bug in one.
**Depends on:** 11.41.

**Found on real hardware, 2026-08-27.** Publishing a project uploads more
people-records than the server will accept, so **a first publish of any project two
people have touched produces a stuck record, every time.** Task 11.41 made those
records visible and no longer permanent, which is why this is now an annoyance rather
than a trap — but the app is still offering the server something it will always
refuse, and telling the user about it.

**The planning session's reading, offered to be checked rather than adopted:** the
publish payload sends every person-record the project references, including the
teammate's, and task 11.24's rule correctly refuses a record naming somebody who is
not the caller. **If so, the fix is that publishing should not send them at all** —
the server learns about a teammate when that teammate redeems their invitation, which
is their own authenticated action, so the owner never needed to upload them.

**Verify that before building on it**, because if it is wrong the alternative is
worse: a project referencing a person the server does not know about. **Establish
what the server actually knows about a member after redemption**, and say so, rather
than assuming redemption is sufficient.

- **State the rule the payload is built from**, whatever is chosen — "send the rows
  this caller may author" is a rule; "send these tables" is a list, and lists on this
  project drift. Whatever is decided must survive a new table being added.
- **Acceptance:** a first publish of a project two people have touched produces no
  refused record; a member is still fully resolvable on the server afterwards, shown
  by a test rather than argued; the payload's contents follow a stated rule.

### Task 11.44 — A record your device refuses on arrival should leave a trace that survives a restart
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-28.**
**Model:** Sonnet — the outgoing side already shows what this looks like.
**Depends on:** 11.41.

Today, when this device refuses a record that arrived from the server, an amber
warning tells you at the time and **the count resets on restart.** The outgoing side
solved exactly this in task 10.28 and the incoming side never got the same treatment.

**Why it matters to a person rather than to a log:** a refusal that vanishes on
restart means a teammate's record can be dropped by your device and, once you restart
the app, nothing anywhere says it happened. You cannot answer "did I get everything?"
— and in a field season that question has a real answer that matters.

- **Do not build a second mechanism.** Task 10.28 already made outgoing refusals
  durable; use its shape, so the two directions can be read the same way and one fix
  serves both later. **A parallel mechanism for the mirror-image problem is how the
  two halves drift apart.**
- Per the standing rule added 2026-08-27, whatever surfaces this must name **which
  record and which rule**, not a count.
- **Acceptance:** an incoming refusal survives a restart; it names the record and the
  reason; the outgoing and incoming views are recognisably the same thing.

**What was built.** A new client-only table, `Sync_Dropped_Rows`
(`lib/data/sync/sync_dropped_rows.dart`, `SyncDroppedRowStore`), built to
`SyncHeldRowStore`'s exact shape: one row per refused identity (not one per
refusal — the same bound task 10.30 forced server-side), created with
`IF NOT EXISTS` rather than migrated, and holding no copy of the row's data.
It departs from the outbound store in the one place the two situations
genuinely differ: a dropped row was never written to this device, so there is
no local copy to read a name from, and it keeps the validator's own
`field`/`message` explanation instead — the same pair already shown on the
restore-preview screen.

`SyncEngine.run` records every one of a round's drops durably **before**
anything downstream can report a result, mirroring `_push`'s own ordering for
holds. `SyncStatus.droppedOnArrivalCount` is now read from the store via
`SyncEngine.droppedRowCount` — the same way `heldCount` already reads from
`SyncHeldRowStore` — rather than from `report.droppedOnArrival.length`, so
`SyncController.build()` answers it correctly the moment the app opens, and
every intermediate `SyncStatus` this controller constructs (running, an
offline failure, an unexpected error, toggling automatic sync) now carries it
forward instead of silently defaulting to zero. `SyncRunReport` gained a
`droppedCount` total, and `everythingArrived` now reads that total rather than
this round's list — the same fix task 10.28 made to `everythingReachedTheServer`
using `heldCount` instead of a round's `refused` list, and for the same reason:
a later round that drops nothing new must not read as clean while an earlier
drop is still missing.

**Resolution is shaped differently, deliberately, because the two directions
resolve differently.** A held row is this device's own data; the next push
re-offers it automatically, so `_reconcileHolds` can ask "would this still be
offered?" A dropped row is the opposite: the pull that skipped it has already
advanced past it, and the app has no "fetch everything again" action, so the
only way this device ever gets it is the record changing again wherever it was
written — which arrives at a later `server_seq` the way any ordinary update
does. `SyncEngine._reconcileDrops` runs after every pull and asks the simpler
question that shape allows: does a row with this exact identity now exist
locally? Covered by a test where a corrected version of a previously-dropped
observation arrives on a later round and the drop resolves itself.

The status screen gained a "Records that did not arrive" section
(`_DroppedRowsSection` / `_DroppedRowTile`) — same position as "Waiting to
sync," same three labelled parts (which record, why, what to do), no "Try
again" button, because there is no local retry for a record this device never
stored. **Fixed in passing, because it sat right next to the new, honest
version of the same sentence:** the status card's summary paragraph used to
claim "updating the app and syncing again should bring it in," which is false
once a drop has already scrolled past the pull cursor — there is no
"re-fetch everything" action, so an app update alone does not retroactively
recover it. The card now says so plainly and points at the new section.

Tests: `sync_dropped_rows_test.dart` (11 cases, mirroring
`sync_held_rows_test.dart`), four new cases in `pull_drops_test.dart` covering
durability across a clean round, durability from a fresh `SyncEngine` reading
only the database, that the record/field/message survive independent of any
report, and self-resolution; a `sync_provider_test.dart` case constructing the
drop directly in the database and reading it back through a brand-new
`ProviderContainer` (an app restart, in effect); and `sync_status_screen_test.dart`
cases asserting the three named parts and the absence of a retry control.
`flutter analyze` clean; full suite green (1367 tests, unrelated pre-existing
skips only).

### Task 11.45 — Two guards that count artifacts instead of asserting the property
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-28.** Both guards now derive their subject from the
code, and both have been watched to fail. The announcement of arriving data
moved out of the five providers that happened to call an inbound writer and
into the writers themselves (`DataArrival`), so there is nothing left for a
caller to forget; the derived guard immediately found **six** write paths the
hand-written list of five never named, all fixed here. The e2e file count is
replaced by coverage derived from `SyncTransport` and `AuthClient` plus a
two-different-people requirement, in an untagged file that runs on every plain
`flutter test` rather than only when a server is up. What each guard still
cannot see is written into the guard. New standing rule: "A Guard Derives Its
Subject" in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`.
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. Both need a design decision about what to assert.
**Depends on:** 11.41.

Two instances of one defect, together because the fix is the same shape and because
**this is the fourth week running that a hand-maintained list has been the finding.**

1. **The guard on "tell the screens when data arrives" is a hand-written list of five
   files.** A sixth path in an unlisted file is silently exempt, and **the symptom is
   field data on the device that never appears on screen** — which is the worst
   category of bug this app can have, because nothing looks wrong.
2. **The end-to-end coverage check counts files rather than requiring a two-people
   test.** Task 11.41 added the first test that signs two different people in; today
   nothing stops that quietly regressing to a file that no longer does it.

**Make both structural.** Derive the set from the code rather than from a list, in
whatever way the code makes possible, and **prove the guard can fail** — add an
unlisted path, watch it go red, then remove it. A guard nobody has seen fail is not a
guard.

- If a property genuinely cannot be derived, **say so explicitly and say what the
  list costs**, rather than leaving a list that reads as coverage. That answer is
  acceptable; an unstated one is not.
- **Acceptance:** neither guard depends on somebody remembering to add a line;
  each has been watched to fail; if either remains a list, its limits are written
  down where the next reader will look.

### Task 11.46 — Publishing dies with a raw database error on any project built from a colleague's data
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-28.** All three parts. **Part 3's answer is no — the
condition survives copy-on-add, and the remainder is not 11.34's to absorb.**
See the Discovered Scope entry below, which carries the measurement and the
recommended follow-up.
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. The judgement is about how much of this to fix,
not how.
**Depends on:** 11.43. **Read the "how much to fix" note below before starting.**

**Found by task 11.43 while measuring the publish payload, not caused by it.** A first
publish can fail outright with a **raw database error** if the project uses a tag a
colleague last edited: the tag is refused, and the person's own bearings then point at
a tag the server does not have.

**What a person sees:** a publish that dies with an unexplained error, on **any project
built from a colleague's archive or from shared observations** — which is a normal way
to start a project, not an edge case.

**Three parts, and they are deliberately not equal.**

1. **The crash and the message must be fixed now, whatever else is decided.** A raw
   database error reaching a user violates the standing rule added 2026-08-27 in
   `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`: a check must name what is wrong and what to do.
   Publishing must fail — or partially succeed — in a way that names the tag and tells
   the person what to do about it. **This part does not depend on anything below.**
2. **A source comment in the server claims this case works. Establish whether it
   does, first.** That is 11.43's own discipline applied here, and **it is the third
   time in three weeks that a comment has asserted a property that was not the one
   actually holding** — the exclusion-reference comment (11.9) and the
   session-revocation comment (11.23) were the other two. Whatever is found, the
   comment ends up true. Record it against the general property task 11.25 is already
   writing up, rather than as a third isolated instance.
3. **Do not over-invest in the deeper repair, and this is the planning call.** This
   failure requires a project to use a tag **a colleague last edited**. Task 11.34's
   copy-on-add decision means a project's tag becomes its own copy, so that case
   largely stops existing. **So: fix the crash, fix the message, fix the comment — then
   say in the report whether the underlying condition survives copy-on-add.** If it
   does not, the remainder is 11.34's to absorb and should not be built twice. If it
   does, say so and it gets its own follow-up.

- **Acceptance:** publishing such a project no longer produces a raw database error;
  the failure names the tag and the action; the server comment is true; the report
  states plainly whether copy-on-add dissolves the rest.

### Task 11.47 — Who last *edited* a shared record should not block your own field data
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-28.** The claim is decided and written into Security
Model §4.17: **clause 2 is not asked of an audit name.** Derived from
`MutationRule.replicatesAForeignAuditName` + `auditUserColumn`, not from the five
tables — it picked up `Tag_Versions` as a sixth by declaration. Identity columns
untouched on every table, pinned by a test in the same push as the half that
moved. **One consequence worth the planning session's attention: clause 2 is now
unreachable** — see the Discovered Scope entry below.
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. The scope boundary below is the task, and it is
easy to wander over it.
**Depends on:** 11.46. Full measurement in Phase 11's Discovered Scope.

**Read the boundary before anything else, because the obvious version of this task is
the wrong one.** Michael decided on 2026-08-28 that **a record restored from a
colleague's archive keeps their name** — provenance beats publishability. So
restamping an imported record as the importer is **off the table**, and the settled
consequence is that a colleague's bearings can only ever be published from their own
device. **That is an accepted outcome, not a defect. Do not reopen it, do not propose
a workaround for it, and do not treat a refused bearing as a bug.**

**What is left is narrower, weaker, and much safer** — and it is the expensive half.

Five tables — `Tags`, `Triangulation_Sessions`, `Project_Tags`,
`Estimated_Positions`, `Actual_Tag_Locations` — have **no author column at all.**
Their only user column records **who last edited this shared vocabulary**, not who
recorded an observation. Refusing a row on that basis is a far weaker claim than
task 11.24's rule about who authored a measurement, and **it is not what Michael's
decision protects.**

**The asymmetry is the whole case for this task, and it is worth stating in plain
terms.** A refused `Tags` row makes every bearing *of your own* that uses that tag
point at something the server does not hold — **so a note about who last renamed
somebody else's tag blocks your own field data from reaching the server.** A weak
claim with a heavy cost. That is a different argument from the one task 11.24 settled,
and it deserves its own answer.

- **Establish what the right claim is for a column that means "who last edited
  this", as against one that means "who recorded this".** The five tables above are
  the instances; the answer should be a rule about the *kind* of column, so a sixth
  such table inherits it. Deriving from `MutationRule` rather than from that list of
  five is the shape to aim for — 11.24 already does this for author columns.
- **Say what a person can do today**, because right now the only remedy is opening
  and editing each row by hand to restamp it, which works for three rows and not for
  a season, and **nothing tells anybody that is the remedy.** Even if the underlying
  rule is left alone, that is a finding on its own.
- **Held indefinitely is the actual harm, not held.** These rows wait on a person who
  is not on the project and never will be. Nothing errors and nothing is lost — task
  11.46 fixed that — but nothing ever drains either.
- **Acceptance:** the claim made by an edited-by column is decided and written down;
  whatever is chosen derives from the column's kind rather than a list of five tables;
  a person whose rows are held knows what to do; a test covers the case where the
  editor is not and never will be a member.

**What was decided.** Security Model §4.17 gains its second narrowing, on the
other axis from task 11.24's — the column's *kind* rather than the table's rule:

> **Clause 2 is not asked of an audit name.** `last_modified_by` records *who
> last edited this*, not *who this record is about*, and on a table whose rows
> name no author it may be replicated without the project reaching the person it
> names.

The two harms §4.17 names come apart on this column, which is the whole
argument. **Disclosure does not arise:** an identity column is a reachability
edge — naming somebody in one is *why* their `Users` row gets delivered on the
next pull — and `ProjectReachability.resolve` excludes the audit column by
construction, via `SyncTable.identityUserColumns`. It is a foreign key on
neither side of the wire, so nothing is delivered on the strength of it.
**Attribution is bounded one line earlier**, by task 11.24's
`namesRowAuthor` check, and this narrowing sits strictly inside it.

**Derived, and it proved the point immediately.** The predicate is
`MutationRule.replicatesAForeignAuditName` beside the rule table, firing on
`auditUserColumn`. Measured rather than assumed: it relaxes exactly six
tables — the five named above **plus `Tag_Versions`**, which nobody listed and
which inherited it by declaring `anyUser`. Every relaxed table has
`identityUserColumns == []`, so the relaxation cannot reach a column that says
who a record is *about*.

**The guard asserts the premise, not the conclusion**, and was watched to fail.
`mutation_rules_test.dart` asserts that every relaxed table has no identity
column — the fact the safety argument rests on — rather than re-listing the six.
Forcing the predicate true made all four of its cases go red with actionable
messages naming `Users` and `Observations`; restored, green.

**The boundary is pinned in the same request as the change.** A new server test
pushes a session a colleague last edited **and** a bearing that colleague
authored together: the session inserts, the bearing is still `unauthorized`.
Without it the positive test would have passed just as well against a build that
had wrongly relaxed identity columns too.

**Two tests were corrected rather than relaxed**, both because the cause they
used has stopped existing:

- `publish_and_join_test.dart`'s colleague's-tag test is **inverted** — it was
  the reproduction this task exists to fix.
- Its sibling was task 11.46's **only** behavioural proof that a dangling
  reference is refused cleanly rather than dying at `COMMIT`. This change
  removed the mechanism it used to manufacture a refused referent, so left alone
  it would have gone green while reproducing nothing. Re-expressed onto a cause
  11.47 does not touch (a session referencing an unreachable tag), with an
  assertion that says so if that cause ever goes the same way.
- `membership_and_invites_test.dart`'s before/after is now an
  **inserted-then-no-op**, because the tag lands on the *first* push. Verified
  against the real server rather than guessed.

**What a person is told, which was the third bullet.** The remedy was real and
was the tail of a sentence beginning "Nothing." The held-row card for a record
of your own that a colleague last touched now leads with it: *open the record,
change anything and save — that records you as the last person to change it, and
it syncs on the next round.* And the permanent case is now honest rather than
open-ended: where a colleague **authored** the record, the card says that if
they are not on this project and are not going to be, it stays on this device
for good, and to keep the device backed up. It no longer implies a wait that
will end.

Full server suite green against real Postgres (707); client suite green (1367);
shared package green (265); analyzer clean.

### Task 11.48 — One declaration of which column points at which table
**Status:** Not started
**Model:** Sonnet — small.
**Depends on:** 11.46. **Do not run this yet — see the trigger.**

Task 11.46 gave held records a sentence saying which record they are waiting on, and it
finds that link **by convention**: matching a held row's whole primary key against
same-named columns. That is true of every reference in this schema except one, which
the naming rules already cover. The declared foreign-key graph exists only on the
server.

**The trigger, and it is deliberate: run this when a third consumer needs the
graph, and not before.** Two consumers of a convention is not yet a problem; three is
where a convention starts being maintained in three places. Moving the declaration
into the shared package would make the client's explanation derived rather than
conventional — the same one-definition move task 11.43 made for its own rule.

- Until then the convention and its single exception are written down at the method
  that relies on them, which is the right amount of ceremony for two consumers.
- **Recorded rather than done, so it is not rediscovered as new.** This is the
  opposite failure from the one this project keeps hitting: here the risk is doing
  structural work before there is enough evidence to shape it correctly.
- **Acceptance:** when triggered, one declaration serves client and server, and the
  client's held-record explanation is derived from it.

**Status:** **Done (2026-08-29).** Entries 27 and 28 are both **Hardened** —
115 live checks refused, every positive control fired, and 27 of 27 named probes
watched flipping to ADMITTED against three deliberately broken servers. The
§4.13 timing claim task 11.60 left unmeasured is measured with numbers; the
unrecognised-`role` leftover has a verdict (**accepted**, and unreachable
through the front door — measured); the app shows no bare identifier for the
removing account, because it shows no account at all. `/projects/mine` was
**not** attacked, per §6's stopping rule, and is recorded as finding P-1 in
Discovered Scope with what has and has not been asked of it. The re-run is
priced in `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §6.1 and was not run. Full record:
Security Model §20. Three things were found and fixed on the way — a gate
instrument nobody had run since 2026-08-22, a timing check that failed a live
gate run by measuring the laptop, and a test file cited in four places that
never existed.
**Model:** **Opus** — an adversarial pass with a stopping rule, not a fix.
**Depends on:** 11.35, which created the surface. **Not blocked by the NAU letter**,
and that is the point of scheduling it now.

**Updated 2026-08-29 from task 11.36: entry 27 now has a caller.** The verdict is
unchanged and still accurate — nothing has attacked it, and attacking it is this
task's job — but the route was previously reachable only by code nobody had written,
and **the app now calls it on every visit to the Server Connection screen while signed
in, and calls the per-device revocation from it.** Same verdict, different urgency:
this is no longer a dormant surface. **Task 11.60 adds a second entry to attack in the
same pass — run 11.60 first.**

**Task 11.60 ran on 2026-08-29 and entry 28 is now on the inventory, Open.** It is
the **closed-membership disclosure**: `POST /sync/pull` answers a caller whose stint
on the project has ended with that person's own closed membership rows and nothing
else, so their device learns it was removed. Security Model §4.27 states it. **What
this task must attack, beyond the entry's own claims:**

- **It is an exemption on a refusal path**, which is where this project's findings
  come from. The question is not "does it return little" but *"can anybody who is
  not its subject observe that the branch exists"*.
- **Two instruments already probe it and both passed on 2026-08-29** —
  `verify_c2_existence_oracle.py` gained a section that probes with a caller who
  *can* reach the disclosure on one project and must still learn nothing about ids
  they hold no row for, and `verify_11_9_team_surface.py`'s probes 7 and 10 now
  assert what comes back rather than a status code. **A gate that only re-runs
  those is re-running somebody else's checks**; the value here is the attacks
  nobody thought of.
- **The disclosed row carries `end_date` and `last_modified_by`** — when the stint
  ended and which account ended it. §4.27 argues both are columns of the caller's
  own row and that blanking one would make the device disagree with the server
  forever. **That argument is the thing to attack**, not the code.
- **The fail-closed leftover, recorded rather than fixed:** an open membership row
  whose `role` string this build cannot interpret leaves somebody with no access
  and no disclosure. They still see "the server is refusing access". Whether that
  matters is a verdict this task can reach; task 11.60 deliberately did not.
- **Confirmed by the planning session on 2026-08-29 — this section says what it should
  say, with two additions.**
  - **A §4.13 claim was closed on the way and never measured.** Task 11.60 found that
    asking about a project id naming nothing cost one database query while asking
    about a real project belonging to somebody else cost two — the two answers §4.13
    requires to be indistinguishable from outside, differing in work done, which is
    also observable from outside. It equalised them rather than build a third query on
    top, and **said plainly that it did not measure whether the difference was
    detectable over a network.** Two gates walked past this. **This task should decide
    whether an unmeasured timing claim is an acceptable verdict on that path, or
    whether it needs a measurement** — and if the answer is "below the noise", say so
    with a number rather than a belief.
  - **Check what the app renders when it cannot resolve the account that removed
    somebody.** The disclosed row names that account, and a removed member whose last
    successful sync predates that owner joining will not have their name. **A bare
    identifier on a screen is not an acceptable answer** — it is a raw internal value
    shown to a person, and it confirms that an account exists without naming it. Say
    what it shows today.

**Why this exists.** `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §2 says Gate C's current blockers
are "the NAU review — and nothing else." §6 of the same document says entry 27 —
`GET /auth/sessions`, the route that lists your own signed-in devices — **is Open,
because task 11.35 added it to the inventory before anything was attacked, which was
the correct discipline** — and Gate C's own criterion 1 requires every server entry
to carry a verdict. Both sentences are in one document and they disagree. **So Gate C
cannot pass today even if the NAU letter came back tomorrow**, and until this runs,
"NAU is the only thing standing between us and a deployment" is not true. That is an
open verdict with no task number, which is the failure that cost this project two
blocking items six weeks. §2's blockers row is corrected to name both.

**This is a read, and every attack the inventory records was aimed at a mutation.**
A read fails differently: it corrupts nothing, it *tells somebody something*. So the
attacks are disclosure-shaped, not escalation-shaped:

- **Can the route be made to answer for somebody else?** The `user_id` is supposed to
  come from the validated session and from nowhere else — try to supply one in the
  body, the query string, a header, a path segment, a second session id, a forged
  `device_id`, a revoked session and an expired one, and confirm each is ignored or
  refused rather than honoured.
- **Does the response carry anything the design says it does not?** No token, no token
  hash, no source address. `ListedSession` records the no-source-address decision;
  attack the claim rather than reading it.
- **Do the bound and the per-user rate limit actually fire, and can they be watched
  failing?** A limit nobody has seen refuse is not known to be a limit.
- **Does a revoked device leave the list at the moment the revocation takes effect**,
  rather than on a timer.
- **Every one of these must be watched to fail** against a deliberately broken
  control, per task 10.66's standing criterion. A check that cannot distinguish
  success from its own failure is not a check.

**Do not widen, and this is the whole reason §6 has a stopping rule.** Entry 27 is
the subject. `/projects/mine` is the inventory's only other server read and it was
folded into item 15 and attacked as a route rather than as a read — **if that turns
out never to have been asked the questions above, record it as a finding with a task
number and stop**, rather than attacking it in this run. Eight gates went the other
way and none of them reached a verdict.

**Second half, and it is the part Michael actually needs: price the re-run without
running it.** Criterion 1 does not only require entry 27 to have a verdict — it
requires every entry marked Hardened to carry a failed live attack **from the current
round**. Nobody has said what that costs now. **Report it:** which entries' last live
attack is from round 8 or from task 11.9, what hardware and which stack each needs,
what is scriptable and what is not, and roughly how long. Do not run it here.

- **Acceptance:** entry 27's verdict in `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §3 becomes
  **Hardened** with the refused attacks named and dated, or **Accepted** with a
  written reason, or stays **Open** with a finding that has a task number — never
  Open with nothing; every attack was watched to fail against a broken control; §2's

  afterwards; and the report states what a full Gate C re-run of criteria 1–4 would

### Task 11.50 — Ask again for a record this device refused
**THE TRIGGER FIRED, AND THE PLANNING SESSION'S DECISION 2026-08-31 IS: STAY DEFERRED, WITH
THE TRIGGER RE-ARMED.**

Task 11.66 saw a refused record on the first publish from a clean device, which is exactly
what release-checklist F2 and this entry named as the trigger. **But the cause is understood,
local, and about to be removed:** it is task 11.43's request ordering, reopened the same day.
**A trigger that fires for a reason another task is already fixing is not evidence that this
task is needed** — it is evidence that 11.43 was not finished.

> **Re-armed, and narrower than before: if a refused record is seen again *after* 11.43's
> ordering fix lands, that is a real trigger and this task runs.** The distinction matters
> because the original trigger was written to catch "the app refuses records for reasons we do
> not understand", and this one was understood within an hour.

**11.66 was right to raise it rather than decide it** — the trigger fired, and a trigger
nobody adjudicates is a trigger that stops meaning anything.

**Status:** **Deferred by decision (2026-08-29), re-armed 2026-08-31. Do not run `/11-50`
until the re-armed trigger fires.**
**Model:** **Opus** when it runs — it adds a mechanism to the sync path, which is
where this project's findings come from.
**Depends on:** 11.44, which made the refusal durable and named.

**What the gap is, in plain terms.** The server keeps records in one numbered line
and each device keeps a bookmark saying how far it has read. When a record arrives
that this device cannot store — most often because two devices are running different
builds of the app, which is the normal state during development — the device skips it
**and still moves its bookmark past it.** The record is now behind the bookmark, so
nothing ever asks for it again. The only thing that brings it back is somebody editing
that record on the device where it was written, which puts it in the line again at a
higher number. So a teammate's bearing can be on their device and on the server and
permanently not on yours.

**Why it is deferred rather than open.** Task 11.44 made the refusal **durable and
legible**: the sync screen names the record and the reason, the notice survives a
restart, and 11.44 correctly deleted the status card's old claim that syncing again
would bring it in, which was false. So this is a *visible* gap rather than a silent
one, which is what keeps it below `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §4's bar — B1 is
silent or unrecoverable loss **and the user is not told**, and the user is now told.
Against that, the fix is a new mechanism on the client path whose failure mode is
losing a field season, and nobody has measured how often a refusal actually happens
in ordinary use. **The same trade, in the same shape, was accepted for the
viewer-restore dialog at task 11.20's Discovered Scope entry.**

**The trigger — any one of these, and this task becomes scheduled:**

1. **A beta user reports a record that never arrived**, or the "Records that did not
   arrive" section is found non-empty on any device that is not running a development
   build. One instance is enough; this is not a rate.
2. **The beta team is knowingly running mixed app versions** for more than a few days,
   because version skew is this defect's main trigger and a mixed fleet turns a rare
   event into a standing one.
3. **The refusal ever becomes silent again** — if any future change removes the named,
   durable notice, this stops being below the bar and becomes B1 immediately.

**What the task would be when it runs, so the shape is not re-derived under pressure:**

- **Store the record's position in the line at the moment it is refused**, alongside
  the entry 11.44 already writes. That is the one piece of information the retry needs
  and the only part that must be captured *now* rather than reconstructed later.
- **Replay from that position, not from zero.** A button that re-downloads the whole
  project is slower than the problem it solves and is unusable on a phone in the
  field. Bound what one retry may fetch.
- **A retry that fails must say the same thing twice.** If the record is still refused
  for the same reason — the other device is still on a newer build — the second answer
  must be recognisably the first answer, not a new-looking failure. Per the standing
  rule of 2026-08-27, it names which record and which rule.
- **Do not build a second mechanism.** Outgoing refusals resolve through
  `SyncHeldRowStore` and `_reconcileHolds`; incoming ones through
  `SyncDroppedRowStore` and `_reconcileDrops`. This is a third path on the incoming
  side and it must read the same store, for the reason 11.44 gave: a parallel
  mechanism for the mirror-image problem is how the two halves drift apart.

- **Acceptance, when it runs:** a record refused on arrival can be asked for again
  from the device that refused it; the retry fetches a bounded range rather than the
  project; a retry that fails again explains itself in the same words as the first
  refusal; and the trigger that scheduled it is recorded with its date, so the
  deferral reads as a decision rather than a delay.

### Task 11.51 — Pointing the app at a different server silently delivers nothing
**Status:** **Partly done inside 11.54 (2026-08-29), and the engine half is
still open.** 11.54 built the classification this asked to join
(`SyncFailureCause`), and **deliberately did not add a value for "my bookmark
belongs to a different server", because no code path could produce one** —
nothing in the protocol can tell one server's database from another's, and an
unreachable state in a classification reads as covered. The mechanism is now
reproduced at the engine in
`test/data/sync/stale_cursor_new_server_test.dart` (three cases, all passing),
which also found a **second, worse carrier than the cursor**: row receipts are
deliberately kept across an unlink, so a receipt minted against the old database
keeps a local row off the new server too, and that one does not self-heal.
**Closing this needs a server-minted database identifier on the wire and is its
own task** — see Phase 11's Discovered Scope. **Do not run `/11-51`; the
remaining work needs a fresh entry.**

**(Original status)** **MERGED into task 11.54 (2026-08-29). Do not run
`/11-51`; run `/11-54`.** The spec below still applies in full and 11.54 carries it. Merged because
both are one question — **does the sync surface tell the truth about its own state?**
11.54 must teach it to distinguish "no network" from "the server refused you" from
"you are no longer a member"; this adds "my bookmark belongs to a different server" to
that same set. One classification, not two.
**Model:** **Opus** — it is a question about what a sync cursor belongs to, which is
the sync engine's core bookkeeping, not a screen fix.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by Michael on 2026-08-29**, from the two-device
walkthrough being run repeatedly rather than once.

**The symptom this was written from was misdiagnosed, and the correction is recorded
here rather than quietly edited out.** Michael reported that typing a new address in
and saving it did not work and that he had to sign out on both devices. On 2026-08-29
he established the actual cause: **the server was not running.** With the stack up,
changing the address and syncing works with no sign-out. **The planning session
offered a code reading as the explanation of a symptom it had not reproduced, which is
the mistake this project has already recorded once** — do not offer a prediction as a
finding. There was no cursor staleness in his case because the database persisted
across his restarts, so the bookmark was still valid for that same server.

**The structural finding survives the misdiagnosis, and it is the whole task now.**
The sync bookmark still records nothing about which server it came from, and that is
measured rather than inferred — see below. What is *no longer* claimed is that this
explains anything Michael saw. The task's subject is the field case, not his.

**What the planning session measured in the code, and it should be reproduced rather
than believed.** The device's sync bookmark — the number saying "I have read the
server's records up to here" — is stored under a key built from the **project id
only**: `sync_cursor_v1_<projectId>`, in `lib/data/sync/sync_state_store.dart`.
**Nothing in that key, or beside it, records which server the number came from.**
`SyncStateStore.clear` does erase it, and its own comment says it is called on
sign-out *"so a later sign-in as a different identity does not inherit a stranger's
cursor."* **Changing the server address is not sign-out, so nothing clears it.** That
is a complete explanation of Michael's symptom and it is a reading of the code, not a
reproduction — **step 1 is to reproduce it.**

**Why this is a finding and not a nuisance.** A bookmark from one server's database
applied to another's means the device asks for "everything after 4,812" of a line
that starts at 1. The server correctly returns nothing. The app correctly reports a
successful sync. **The person is told everything is up to date, and nothing arrived.**
That is silent, and the user is not told — the shape `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §4
calls B1. In development it costs a sign-out. In the field it fires whenever a server
is **restored from backup, rebuilt, or replaced** — and this project has a restore
drill precisely because that is expected to happen.

**Establish these, in this order, and report each as measured or unknown:**

1. **Reproduce it against a genuinely different database**, which is the case that was
   never tested: bring the stack down **with its volumes removed** so the server comes
   back with an empty database, then sync a device that already holds a bookmark from
   the previous one. Watch whether the sync reports success and delivers nothing. **A
   failure to reproduce is a useful result — say so and stop.** Note that simply
   restarting the stack does *not* exercise this, because the database survives; that
   is why Michael's rounds never hit it.
2. **What else carries across a server change?** The cursor is the one this session
   found. Row receipts are deliberately *not* cleared on sign-out (the store says
   why); ask whether that reasoning survives the server changing underneath them,
   because "a statement about what the server holds" is a statement about **which**
   server. The linked-project flag is in the same file. **Derive the set from the
   store rather than from this list.**
3. **What should identify a server?** The planning session's lean, stated so it can be
   argued with rather than inherited: **the server should tell the client which
   database it is** — an identifier minted once when the schema is created and
   returned on sync — and the client stores it beside the cursor and resets the cursor
   when it does not match, saying so on screen. That makes the check derived and
   self-announcing rather than depending on somebody remembering to clear state at
   each of the places an address can change. The cheaper alternatives are to clear
   sync state whenever the address changes, or to namespace the cursor key by address
   — **both are worse for a reason worth stating: an address is not an identity.** The
   same server reachable at two addresses would reset needlessly, and two different
   servers at the same address over time would not reset at all, which is exactly
   Michael's case. **Measure the cost of the lean before adopting it** — it is a
   protocol change and task 10.18's compatibility guarantee applies.
4. **What the person should see.** Not silence. If a device's bookmark is discarded
   because the server is a different one, that is worth a sentence on the sync status
   screen naming what happened, in the same voice as the "Records that did not
   arrive" section task 11.44 built.

**And fix the walkthrough's own cause, which is separate and cheap.** The address
changes because the virtual machine takes a new one from the router each time.
**Document a stable address** in `README.md` §4 — an mDNS `.local` hostname published
from the virtual machine, or a fixed lease on the router — so the walkthrough stops
requiring a value to be re-typed on two devices per run. That is task 11.37 item 5's
class exactly: a step whose value a human reads and retypes is a step that will be
wrong eventually. **Check whether a `.local` hostname is reachable from the app on
iOS**, which needs the local-network permission and may interact with the cleartext
exemption in the platform configuration — the planning session does not know and did
not guess; task 11.40's capability sweep is the natural place for the general
question, but this task needs the specific answer to write the step.

- **Acceptance:** the reading above is reproduced or disproved, and the report says
  which; a device pointed at a different or rebuilt server either receives its data or
  says plainly why it cannot, and never reports a clean sync having delivered nothing;
  whatever identifies a server is derived rather than kept in step by hand; and the
  walkthrough documents an address that does not change between runs.

  class then a guard replaces the list and has been watched to fail; the header's
  cause is identified as this app's or the platform's, with the scope of the change
  stated; and any decision left for Michael is named rather than made.

### Task 11.54 — Leaving a project tells you the wrong thing and leaves you nowhere
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-29).** Items 1–4 of the merged running order are
built and tested. **Michael then ran the new `README.md` §4 walkthrough and
confirmed one of the two risks it had recorded as unverified:** leaving,
deleting and being invited back brought the project back **invisible**. That is
now reproduced, fixed in `ProjectJoiner.join`, and covered by
`test/data/sync/rejoin_after_delete_test.dart` — and the delete warning's copy
was corrected with it, because it had promised "you get back what the server
holds, not what this device held", which was the plan's sentence for a
destructive delete and this is not one. Re-joining otherwise works, tested on
hardware. Also: item 5 (the bookmark's server identity) is **measured and
reproduced but not fixed** — see 11.51's status below and the Discovered Scope
entry — and item 6 (the "More" header) is **measured and needs a decision from
Michael**, not a code change. `README.md` §4 now carries the whole round trip as
"Check 2 — leaving a project, and coming back".
**Model:** **Opus** — the message half is the third instance of a class, and the
dead-end half is a decision about what a project you have left *is* on your device.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by Michael on 2026-08-29** by running the
leave-a-project checks on real hardware, which had never been run.

**Carries tasks 11.51, 11.53 and 11.55 as of 2026-08-29** — read all three entries,
which stand unchanged in this document. They are here because they are one subject
wearing four titles: **the sync surface does not tell the truth about its own state,
and the leave-and-return cycle has never been walked end to end.**

**The order, and stop where you run out rather than going wide:**

1. **The sync surface learns to name what is actually wrong.** One classification
   covering: no network; the server answered with an error; **you are no longer a
   member of this project**; and — from 11.51 — **this device's bookmark belongs to a
   different server.** Doing these as one set is the whole reason these tasks merged;
   doing them one at a time is how a fifth cause arrives with no home.
2. **Leaving no longer reports itself as a failure**, and a project you have left can
   be deleted (items 1 and 3 below).
3. **The bar that never goes away** (11.53 item 1). If it is a snackbar, the finding
   is that 11.42's sweep was a list of five call sites rather than a derivation — fix
   the class with a guard watched to fail, not a sixth `persist: false`.
4. **Re-invite a past member** (11.55), which is what makes the walkthrough a round
   trip rather than a one-way street.
5. **The bookmark's server identity** (11.51's engine half). Lowest because it is a
   field case — a server restored or rebuilt — not something Michael can hit today.
6. **The oversized "More" header** (11.53 item 2). Cosmetic, and already narrowed to
   the platform rather than this app.

**Write the whole round trip into `README.md` §4** — leave, observe, re-invite,
rejoin — because §4 contains no leave step at all today and a cycle tested in one
direction is half tested.

**Three of the six checks passed and are recorded so they are not re-tested:** the
departed member's bearing is still on the owner's Mac under their name; the owner's
members list still shows them as a past member; and the data is still on the phone,
which is the known limitation, working as accepted. **The design decisions hold. What
fails is everything the app says and offers afterwards.**

**1. Leaving succeeds, then the app immediately reports that sync is broken.** A white
confirmation bar says leaving worked, and a red bar arrives at once saying *"sync
isn't working, tap to check."* The app tried to sync a project the person had just
left. **That is not a failure; it is the expected consequence of the action they just
took, reported as breakage.** Either do not sync a project on the way out of it, or
say what actually happened. Decide which, and say why.

**2. The message names the wrong cause, and this is the third instance of that class.**
Tapping through gives *"Sync has failed repeatedly. If this continues, contact whoever
manages your project server"* (`sync_status_screen.dart:210`). **The truth is "you
left this project," and the app tells them to contact the project's manager** — advice
that is not merely unhelpful but points away from the answer. Task 11.37 closed this
shape once for "could not reach the server" versus "the server answered with an
error," and task 11.42's stale bar was a third relative. **Fix the class:** a status
surface that cannot distinguish "the network is down," "the server refused you," and
"you are no longer a member" is not a status surface.

**The measured lead, and it makes this sharper rather than simpler.** The app already
has a control for exactly this case: `SyncController._unlinkIfWeAlreadyLeft`
(`sync_provider.dart:525`) fires on a `403`, checks the project is linked, and unlinks
it when `findForUser` returns no open membership — which is precisely Michael's state,
since his phone shows him as a *past* member and `findForUser` filters to open stints.
**So either the control did not fire, or it fired and nothing told the user.** Those
are different defects and the report must say which. Note the message he saw is the
*repeated-failure* branch, which suggests the second: the state was tidied and the
screen kept showing a schedule-level message that outranked the real reason. **A
control that works and says nothing is half a control** — the standing rule of
2026-08-27.

**3. A project you have left is a dead end on your device.** It still appears in the
list; the leave control is gone, correctly; and **the delete control is greyed out**,
so the person can neither participate in it nor get rid of it. Nothing in the accepted
design requires that: the known limitation says a departed member's copy *cannot be
taken away from them* — it does not say they may not delete it themselves.

**Michael decided this on 2026-08-29: yes, they may delete it. Do not re-open the
question; build it.**

- **Re-enable the existing delete control for a project the person has left.** Use the
  delete path the projects list already has, including its undo bar — task 11.42 has
  just been through that code and established that the delete is committed before the
  bar appears and undo is a separate write. **Do not build a second deletion
  mechanism** for this case; a parallel path for the mirror-image situation is how two
  halves drift apart.
- **The warning has to say the thing that is actually at risk, and it is sharper than
  "this is your only copy."** Once someone has left, **anything on that device that
  never reached the server never will** — their own bearings sitting in "waiting to
  sync" are refused from now on. So deleting the project destroys those permanently,
  while everything that did sync survives on the server and on teammates' devices.
