  **Say both halves**, because "you will lose everything" and "you will lose only what
  never synced" lead a person to different decisions, and only one of them is true.
  Check whether anything is actually waiting before warning as though something is.
- **Rejoining later brings back what the server holds, not what this device held.**
  Say so in the same warning rather than leaving it to be discovered.
- Task 10.19's invariant that no *failure path* deletes data is untouched by this —
  it is about failures, not about a deliberate choice a person makes and confirms.

- **Acceptance:** leaving a project does not report a sync failure caused by leaving;
  the sync surface distinguishes "no network," "the server refused you," and "you are
  no longer a member of this project," and the last of those says so in words a person
  can act on; whether `_unlinkIfWeAlreadyLeft` fired is measured and stated; **a
  project the person has left can be deleted from their device**, through the existing
  delete path rather than a new one, with a warning that distinguishes what was
  already synced from what never will be; and
  the six leave-a-project steps are written into `README.md` §4, because **§4 contains
  no leave step today** and the walkthrough's own criterion is "no step that is not
  written down."

### Task 11.55 — Invite a past member back without retyping their address
**Status:** **Done inside 11.54 (2026-08-29).** A re-invite control on each past
member's row opens the ordinary invite sheet pre-filled with the address on the
record and the role they last held, both editable, with the removal disclosure
still gating the send. The membership rule needed no work: the server already
creates a new row and never nulls the old `end_date`
(`InviteService.redeem`), and `server/test/projects/invite_service_test.dart`
already asserts it. Disabled with a reason where this device holds no address
for the person.

**(Original status)** **MERGED into task 11.54 (2026-08-29). Do not run
`/11-55`; run `/11-54`.** The spec below still applies in full and 11.54 carries it. Merged because
**a leave-a-project walkthrough that cannot end in rejoining tests half a cycle**, and
11.54 is the task writing those steps into `README.md`. Leaving and coming back is one
round trip and a field season contains both.
**Model:** Sonnet — the membership rules it needs are already decided.
**Depends on:** 11.2. **Asked for by Michael on 2026-08-29** while looking at the
owner's members list with a departed member on it.

The owner's members screen already shows past members with their stint. **A returning
field technician is the normal case, not an edge case** — the same person on next
season's crew, or somebody who left mid-season and came back. Today the owner has to
issue a fresh invitation and retype the address, which they can already see on screen.

- **A re-invite control on each past member's row**, issuing the same invitation a new
  invite would, addressed to the address already on the record.
- **The membership rule is already settled and must not be re-decided here:** rejoining
  **creates a new membership row; it does not null the old `end_date`.** The old stint
  is the record of when they were there, which is the whole reason it is kept. The
  invariant to hold is at most one open membership per (project, person) pair.
- **Re-invite is an invitation, not a reinstatement.** It produces a code the person
  redeems, exactly as a first invitation does. An owner must not be able to put
  somebody back into a project without that person acting — that would be the owner
  asserting a membership on somebody else's behalf, which is the shape task 11.24's
  rule exists to refuse.
- **Ask what role a re-invite offers.** The obvious default is the role they last
  held, shown and editable before sending, because a returning member is often
  returning to a different job. Do not silently reuse the old role.
- **Acceptance:** an owner can re-invite a past member from their row without typing an
  address; redeeming it creates a new open membership and leaves the closed one intact;
  the pair invariant still holds, shown by a test; the offered role is visible and
  changeable before the invitation is issued.

### Task 11.56 — Start next season from last season's project
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-16.** Held back until task 11.34's design landed as task
11.219 on 2026-09-10 (a project's tags are its own copies, so there was never a
cross-project branch to design) and until 11.246 had put `Individuals` and `Deployments`
into the permissions matrix. Built as `SeasonClone` (`lib/data/repositories/season_clone.dart`),
the **New season** screen (`new_season_screen.dart`, reached from *Start next season* on a
project's ⋮ menu), and schema **v18** — a minor — adding `Projects.lineage_id` and
`Projects.copied_at`, sealed by `provenanceColumns` like the tag's and the animal's.
**The questions this entry recorded are answered in the code, with a guard each:**
- *What copies* is `seasonCloneDispositions` — one entry per table in `Tables.all`,
  and `season_clone_test.dart` fails if a table has none, then checks each verdict
  against what a clone actually wrote into a source seeded with a row in every table.
  Individuals and tags copy (fresh id, same lineage, `copied_at` stamped); deployments copy
  where both ends did, both re-pointed; the project row copies its study area and settings;
  memberships do not copy — the creator is the only member; every observation table stays,
  except the last-known-position rows the next-but-one bullet describes, and only when asked.
- *Both ends* — asserted, and also structural: the composite foreign keys refuse a
  deployment with one end in another project on the device, which a sabotage run showed
  (fifteen red tests, `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`).
- *Tag versions:* **a copied tag starts a fresh history**, and the reason is on
  `SeasonCloneDisposition.freshHistory` — a version row is what one project's bearings
  point at, the old chain stays beside the old bearings, and a re-tuned collar next
  season is an ordinary drift recorded against the copied reading. Cross-season
  comparison is by `lineage_id` in an export.
- *A dead bird stays dead* (status copies), and **whether it copies at all is a switch on
  the screen, shown only when the source has one, default on** — Michael's call on the
  default is in the comms entry.
- **Where each animal was last — added the same day at Michael's request:** a second
  switch, default on, brings over each copied animal's *most recent* position estimate and
  *most recent* truth point, attributed the way a bearing is (by which animal wore the
  collar at that moment), so a crew going back out can re-establish where the animals are.
  Nothing else from either table crosses. A copied truth point keeps its finder only when
  that is the person cloning — the server refuses a new row naming anybody else — and drops
  its tag-version pointer rather than name a version in last season's chain; an estimate's
  list of bearings used is carried as the record of what it came from. Reasoning on
  `SeasonCloneDisposition.lastKnownPerAnimal`.
- *Members carry over as invitations* was decided against a mechanism task 11.81 has since
  removed; the consequence is unchanged and built: nobody is on the new season until they
  join by the join code, and the screen says *"Only you, as owner"* in those words.
- *Provenance* is the project's `lineage_id` (the first project of the line, carried
  through every later season) and `copied_at`, on 11.34's terms: read by nothing live,
  never resolved into words about another project.
**What it costs Michael:** one beta-server redeploy, because a v17 server stores only the
columns it declares and would drop a season's lineage on the way through.
**Model:** **Opus** when it runs — it is a data-model question wearing a feature's
clothes.
**Depends on:** 11.34. **Michael's idea, 2026-08-29**, and it is a real field workflow
rather than a convenience.

**The case, in his words and worth keeping:** going back out for another field season
with a similar team — a few new people, a couple who dropped off — reusing the same
tags, or tracking the same animals with new collars whose frequencies need updating.
**The team and the tags should carry over. Last season's observations must not.** The
study area carries over as a starting point and is editable.

**Why it is deferred rather than scheduled, and the reason is sequencing, not
priority.** Task 11.34 is deciding whether a project's tags are **copied into the
project** rather than shared with the person's tag log. Cloning a project is exactly
the operation whose meaning changes depending on that answer: if tags are project-local
copies, cloning copies them and there is no cross-project question at all; if they are
shared, cloning has to decide what a second project referencing one tag means — which
is the question 11.34 exists to delete. **Designing this first would design it against
a data model that is about to change**, and this project has paid for that shape
before.

**Questions it will have to answer, recorded now so they are not rediscovered:**

- **What exactly copies.** The membership list, the tags, the study area. Not
  observations, not position estimates, not triangulation sessions, not ground-truth
  points. Say so explicitly for every table rather than for the ones that came to mind
  — derive the list from the schema, which is this project's standing rule.
- **The individuals copy too — added 2026-09-13, and this is now the point of the
  feature.** Task 11.240 makes the animal a row of its own. **Michael's case is
  Ponui 2025 → Ponui 2026: "mostly the same animals but a few new chicks and a few
  mortalities."** Re-entering a season's worth of birds by hand is the work this task
  exists to remove — **more so than the tags, because a collar changes between seasons
  and the animal does not.**
  - **Copied individuals carry the same `lineage_id`**, exactly as the tags do, so an
    export covering both seasons can show Marie-2025 and Marie-2026 are one bird. **It
    stays invisible in the app** (the standing rule from cancelled task 11.29).
  - **A copied collar keeps its link to the copied animal.** ~~The clone must re-point
    `Tags.individual_id`.~~ **Corrected 2026-09-14: there is no `Tags.individual_id`.**
    The clone copies the project's **`Deployments`** rows and must re-point **both ends**
    — tag and individual — at the new project's rows, carrying the attached and removed
    dates unchanged. **Two ends, not one, is the trap**: re-pointing the tag and leaving
    the animal (or the reverse) makes a deployment that spans two projects, which is
    the same class of mistake 11.239 spent a task on, one table over.
  - **An individual's status copies; a dead bird does not come back to life in the new
    season.** Whether a mortality should be copied at all is Michael's call and belongs
    in this task's questions.
- **Members carry over as invitations, not as members. Michael decided this on
  2026-08-29 and it is settled — do not re-open it.** Copying an open membership row
  would put people into a project without their acting, which is the same thing task
  11.55 refuses and the same shape task 11.24's rule exists to prevent. A clone
  produces a pending invitation per carried-over member, which each person redeems as
  they would any other. **Consequence to design for rather than discover:** a cloned
  project has no members until people accept, so the clone's creator is its only owner
  at the moment it is made, and the screen should say that plainly rather than showing
  a team that is not yet there.
- **What a copied tag means for its version history.** Task 11.32 made a bearing
  remember what its tag read at the time. A new season's tag with an updated frequency
  is a *drift*, not a correction — the decision of 2026-08-22 — so the question is
  whether a clone starts a fresh version history or carries the old one forward. There
  is a right answer here and it matters to anybody comparing two seasons.
- **Provenance.** The clone should record which project it came from, on the same
  terms as 11.34's provenance pointer: explicitly non-authoritative, never read by
  anything live, and never disclosing a project the reader cannot access.
- **Acceptance, when it runs:** a project can be started from a previous one; what
  copies is derived from the schema and stated table by table; no observation data
  crosses; people join by their own action; and the tag-version question is answered
  with a reason, not a default.

### Task 11.57 — The membership cycle, in every order, on two devices
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-29.** All five items ran; nothing was left for a later
pass. The matrix is `test/e2e/membership_cycle_matrix_e2e_test.dart` — nine walks
against the real server on two different accounts, eight of them the enumerated
cross product of *how the stint ends* × *when the local copy is deleted*, plus the
field ordering (a departure that never got sent, then the delete). The sync-bar
enumeration is `test/core/providers/sync_bar_through_the_cycle_test.dart`.

**What running it changed, beyond the five items:**

- **Item 3's leading hypothesis is refuted by measurement.** A departure from a
  device that can reach the server is accepted on the first attempt — the server's
  own table shows the stint closed. The byte-identity rule was never the problem.
  What *is* true is that the round always throws afterwards, because the pull that
  follows the accepted departure is refused: the person is no longer a member. The
  leave path already tolerates that; the finding is that "leaving reported a sync
  failure" was that, and it is expected rather than a fault.
- **The direction that had never been walked was broken, and silently.** An owner
  removing a member — or changing their role — wrote a row naming the *member*,
  which `offer_rules.dart` withheld from every push. The removal never left the
  owner's device; the person stayed a member on the server; and because the
  "records waiting" count is computed from the same rule, nothing anywhere said
  so. Closed by an ownership waiver bounded to writes the server accepts (see
  `namingRequirementsForOffering`). The safety property that file stated —
  *"nothing withheld could ever have been accepted"* — was true of inserts and
  had been applied to updates; it is now written correctly.

**Model:** **Opus** — items 1 and 2 are small and mechanical; item 3 is a live sync
defect with four candidate causes and needs judgement about which to test first.
**Depends on:** 11.54. **Requested by task 11.54's field report after Michael ran two
more rounds on hardware, 2026-08-29.**

**Why a matrix and not four bug fixes.** Four symptoms came out of running **two
orderings, once each**. Each step of the cycle is fine in isolation; the *transitions*
are not. So the acceptance is the matrix — **add → invite → join → leave → remove →
delete → re-invite → rejoin**, in every ordering that can occur, on two devices —
rather than the four symptoms below, which are examples of it. **Both directions of
removal belong in it:** the person leaving, and an owner removing them. **Only the
first has ever been walked.**

**Run in this order and stop where you run out, saying where:**

**1. A device can be permanently locked out of a project it is a member of, and this
is measured rather than hypothesised.** Michael left and deleted a project on his
iPhone; the Mac issued a fresh invite code; the code was refused with *"You're already
on that project. If it isn't on this device yet, use 'Join a project' instead."* And
**the project is not in that list either.** `ProjectDirectoryClient.listAvailableToJoin`
queries `Projects` with **no `deleted_at` filter**, so a tombstoned local row counts as
"already have it" and the project is excluded. The server is right to refuse the code —
he really is a member — so **there is no route back to that project on that device.**

**This was written down on 2026-08-29 as "currently unreachable — nobody can reach it
today," and Michael reached it the same day.** Task 11.54's report says so itself and
names it as its own error. **That is a prediction offered as a finding, which this
project has now recorded three times.** Fix the exclusion.

**2. The refusal recommends a remedy the app cannot deliver.** *"Use 'Join a project'
instead"* is good advice only when the project is listed there, and item 1 is exactly
when it is not. **This is task 11.54's own subject — a surface naming a remedy that
does not exist — so treat the message and the listing as one fix**, not two. Items 1
and 2 need no server and no second device; **they are what unsticks Michael's phone,
which is why they are first.**

**3. A departure never reached the owner's device, and on 2026-08-29 an identical
departure did.** Clean run: create on the Mac, join on the iPhone, leave on the
iPhone, delete on the iPhone. **The Mac still shows him as a current member.** A
second invite code was then refused as "already a member" while the project stayed
invisible. Something differs between the two runs. Task 11.54's report carries the
measurement, and it is worth repeating rather than re-deriving:

- **Ruled out by measurement:** "the device never sends it." A departure row names
  only the caller, so `offer_rules.dart` does not withhold it.
- **The hypothesis to test first:** the server accepts a non-owner's membership write
  only as a *departure*, which requires every column but `end_date`, `updated_at`,
  `revision`, `last_modified_by` and `origin_device_id` to be **byte-identical to the
  stored row.** In this run that row was **written by the server at redemption**; in
  the run that worked it may not have been. If the iPhone's copy differs in any
  immutable column the departure is refused and held — **invisibly**, because he then
  deleted the project and the held-row warning lives on that project's sync screen.
- **Not ruled out:** the departure reached the server and the Mac never showed it.
  That is task 11.41's shape. **Read the server's own table before blaming either
  client.**

**4. A departure that fails on the way out has no route out afterwards, ever — and
this is true regardless of what caused item 3.** If the server does not confirm it,
`MembershipController.leaveProject` leaves the project **linked** with the row
pending; `SyncController.syncNow` and `syncIfDue` both operate on the **active**
project only; **a deleted project is never the active one.** So the pending departure
can never be retried. **This needs its own acceptance line** — it is a trap that
exists today independent of anything above.

**5. The sync bar's visibility is a function of this cycle, and it has changed
underneath us.** On 2026-08-29, after leaving and deleting projects on the iPhone,
Michael reports **there is no sync bar at the top at all** — and that the "More" header
now looks fine. Task 10.12 specified that bar as never hiding itself while sync is
available, and Michael accepted that behaviour deliberately on the same day.

- **Answered by Michael on 2026-08-29, and it is not a regression: that device has no
  project showing at all.** The lockout in item 1 hides the only project it had, so
  there is nothing linked and nothing active, and the bar correctly hides. **Confirm
  that reading rather than adopting it**, and still say what the bar shows at each step
  of the cycle — that enumeration is the deliverable, not this one state.
- **But the consequence is the sharpest thing in this task, and it was not visible
  until his answer.** That phone is a member of a project on the server, holds a hidden
  local copy of it, and **shows the person nothing whatsoever** — no project, no bar,
  no warning. The lockout is not merely "cannot rejoin"; it is **cannot rejoin, and
  nothing says so.** Silence is the property this phase has spent three tasks removing
  from the sync surface, and item 1 puts it back by a side door.
- **So establish, before fixing anything, whether records are stranded on that
  device.** If any row for that project never reached the server, it is now sitting in
  a hidden project with no screen that can reach it. **The fix in item 1 must restore
  access without discarding what is on the device** — relinking the existing local copy
  rather than fetching a fresh one over the top of it. Say what you found either way;
  "nothing was waiting" is a result worth writing down.
- **This probably also settles task 11.53's "More header is too large", and cheaply.**
  The code says all 22 app bars share one 18px style with no per-screen override, so
  "More" cannot be larger than any other screen's. **The likely answer is that the
  header never changed — the sync bar sat directly above the title and the two read as
  one tall block.** That is a hypothesis, not a finding: confirm or refute it in one
  sentence and close the item either way rather than leaving Michael owing a
  photograph.

- **Acceptance:** the cycle is walked in every ordering that can occur, on two
  devices, with an owner-initiated removal as well as a member-initiated one, and the
  orderings are enumerated rather than chosen; **the sync bar's visibility is stated
  for every step of the cycle, and the oversized-header question is closed with a
  reason;** a device is never left holding a
  project it is a member of and cannot reach; no message recommends a remedy the app
  cannot deliver; a departure either reaches the owner's device or is visibly pending
  somewhere the person can still find it; a pending departure on a deleted project has
  a route out; and where the run stopped is stated.

### Task 11.58 — A sync bookmark that knows which server it came from
**Status:** **Done (2026-09-29), commit `efc2878`.** The server mints a database identifier
once (`server_database_identity`, ensured on every start) and returns it as `database_id` on
every push and pull; the app keeps it beside the cursor and, when a response names a different
one, resets the cursor, forgets the project's receipts, **releases its holds** (the third
statement about one database, which the brief did not name), and runs the round again from the
top. The status screen says so in one dated sentence. A second change inside the restarted round
is `SyncFailureCause.serverDatabaseChanged`, and the enum's "deliberately not here" note is
rewritten. **Task 10.18's guarantee holds — the change is additive and no version moved.**
**The brief missed one thing that decided the design:** "minted once at schema creation" alone
would have been copied by every restore, because a backup dumps every table — so `backup.sh`
now dumps the table without its row and `restore.sh` empties it, and the restore drill checks
that a restored database holds no identifier. Two blind spots are stated rather than closed, and
are in Discovered Scope: a device's first round after updating adopts whatever answers, and a
whole-disk restore (a VM snapshot) brings the old identifier back. **Not run: a real app against
a real server that was actually restored** — the halves are each tested against real components
(the wire over HTTP against Postgres, the restore in the drill, the device against the fake
server), and nothing yet joins them over the network.
**Model:** **Opus** — it is a protocol change, and task 10.18's compatibility
guarantee applies.
**Depends on:** 11.54, which reproduced it. **This is task 11.51's remaining half**,
given its own number because 11.54 closed the rest and deliberately did not fake this
part.

**Why it is a separate task rather than a loose end.** Task 11.54 built the
classification that tells a person what is actually wrong with a sync. It
**deliberately did not add a cause for "this device's bookmark belongs to a different
server," because nothing in the protocol can produce one** — and an unreachable state
sitting in a classification reads as covered when it is not. The mechanism is
reproduced in `test/data/sync/stale_cursor_new_server_test.dart`.

**What the reproduction found that the original reading missed, and it is worse than
the bookmark.** Row receipts are deliberately kept when a project unlinks, on the
stated grounds that *"a receipt is a statement about what the server holds, which does
not stop being true."* **That reasoning does not survive the server changing
underneath it** — it is a statement about *which* server holds it. A receipt from the
old database keeps a local row out of the new server's push set, and **unlike the
bookmark it never self-heals.** This is the recurring finding that a control which
works for a reason other than the documented one is one refactor from not working:
the documented reason is "this is still true", and the real one was "the server has
not changed."

**What it needs:** the server minting a database identifier once at schema creation
and returning it on sync; the client storing it beside the cursor; **resetting both
the cursor and the row receipts** on a mismatch; a sentence on the sync status screen
saying what happened; and the missing failure cause so the classification is complete.

**When this stops being a field case and starts blocking:** the moment a server that
real devices have synced against is **rebuilt or restored**. Today that is a
development inconvenience. **If the beta server is ever restored from backup, every
beta device silently pulls nothing and reports success** — so this is on the release
checklist task 11.40 produces, as a thing that must land before a server carrying
other people's data is rebuilt.

- **Acceptance:** a device pointed at a different database is told so and recovers
  without a sign-out; both the cursor and the receipts reset; the classification has
  no unreachable states left in it; and the compatibility guarantee is honoured or the
  break is stated.

### Task 11.59 — The app syncs by itself, and the user can say how often
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-29).** The foreground hook in `app.dart` calls
`syncIfDue`; the sync screen offers four named choices under "Sync while
TriTrack is open"; the bar names "Only when I ask" in those words when it is
chosen; the setting and the last-attempt time are now persisted, which the
previous on/off switch was not. **The battery and data cost was not measured on
hardware — the reasoning is what shipped**, and it is stated with the two
findings below. Three things worth reading before the next task touches this:
the frequency is now a *ceiling* on how often the app reaches out (the failure
backoff can no longer retry faster than the setting), `SyncSchedule.resumed` is
the second method in that file with no caller, and both are written up in
Discovered Scope.

**Michael, 2026-08-29, after running the build: "Auto Sync seems to work", and
the fifteen-minute default stands.** His reason is the one that settles it and
is worth keeping in his words — *"other team data needs to be timely"* — with
"Sync now" there for anybody who wants their records off the device sooner.
That is the shipped behaviour exactly, so **nothing changed in response**; it is
recorded so the question is not re-asked. **It closes the choice, not the
cost:** the battery and data measurement is still not done, and what he reported
is an observation on a running build rather than a measurement — "seems to work"
is his phrasing, not a stronger claim.
**Model:** **Opus** — the machinery exists and the wiring is small; **what the control
promises is the part that can be wrong**, and this is the fourth task in a row whose
subject is a surface describing a mechanism the code does not have.
**Depends on:** 11.57, which found it.

**Michael decided this on 2026-08-29: yes, the app should sync automatically, and the
sync screen should let the user change how often.**

**What task 11.57 found, and it is the largest thing that run turned up. Nothing in
the app ever starts a sync on its own.** `SyncController.syncIfDue` exists, documents
itself as the opportunistic foreground attempt, respects the schedule, and **has no
caller anywhere in `lib/`**. Syncing happens only when somebody opens the Sync Status
screen, retries a refused record, or changes a membership. **A person recording
bearings all day and never opening that screen has nothing on the server** — while the
bar says *"N records waiting to sync"*, which reads as *about to* and means *not until
you ask*.

**Why this is beta-blocking:** the whole premise of a team beta is that a colleague's
records reach the team. A field tech who never opens one particular settings screen
contributes nothing, and is told the opposite.

**The wiring is small.** `SyncSchedule` (task 10.8) already has the on/off setting
defaulting to **on**, a fifteen-minute minimum interval, exponential backoff from one
minute to a two-hour ceiling, and a terminal stop for a revoked session or a version
mismatch. What is missing is the call site — `syncIfDue()` from the foreground hook in
`app.dart`, beside the stuck-departure recovery 11.57 put there — and the setting.

**The control must be labelled for what the app actually does, and this is the part to
get right rather than the interval values.** Task 10.8 decided deliberately, with
reasons, that **there is no background sync**: iOS runs background work when it feels
like it, which on a phone that spends the day in a pack is close to never, and
registering for it costs battery on every wake. So "frequency" does not mean *how
often the app syncs* — it means *how long after the last attempt a foreground counts
as due*. **If the app is closed all day, nothing syncs at any setting.** A control
reading "Sync every 15 minutes" would describe a mechanism the code does not have,
which is the class tasks 11.54 and 11.57 both existed to close, arriving by a new
door. **11.57's proposed shape is accepted as the starting point** — change it if
building it shows something better, and say why:

> **Sync while TriTrack is open**
> Every time I open it · **Every 15 minutes (recommended)** · Hourly · Only when I ask
>
> *TriTrack syncs while the app is open. It does not sync in the background.*

Named choices rather than a free minutes field: a free number invites "1", which
spends battery and data for nothing, and "1440", which is indistinguishable from off
and does not say so.

- **"Only when I ask" must be visible on the sync bar, and it is an acceptance line
  rather than a nicety.** Turning automatic sync off is legitimate — satellite billing
  is the case task 10.8 named — but a device quietly not syncing while showing "3
  records waiting to sync" is telling somebody it is about to do something it never
  will. **Three tasks in a row have removed exactly that silence from this surface. A
  new setting must not put it back.** The bar says sync is off, in those words.
- **Two properties that already hold become acceptance lines so they cannot regress:**
  manual "Sync now" ignores the setting entirely (`syncNow` bypasses the schedule —
  the trailhead case task 10.8 was designed around), and the fifteen-minute floor
  exists so that constant foregrounding, which field use does between the map and the
  record screen, is not a round trip each time. **An "every time I open it" option
  removes that floor and should be offered knowing so.**
- **Say the data cost on the same screen.** Automatic sync is **not Wi-Fi-only** and
  can spend cellular data; `SyncSchedule`'s own header says so and says the remedy is
  to turn it off. A real "unmetered connections only" setting needs interface
  detection and is filed as follow-up scope. If a person is being handed a frequency
  control, that sentence belongs beside it.
- **The battery and data cost of a fifteen-minute foreground cadence has never been
  measured on hardware** — task 10.8's numbers are reasoning. **Decide whether this
  task wants a measurement or is content to ship the reasoning, and say which.**

- **Acceptance:** the app syncs on foreground without anybody opening a screen; the
  setting exists with named choices; **no label promises background syncing**; "only
  when I ask" is stated on the bar in those words; manual sync still ignores the
  setting; and the cellular-data caveat is on the screen.

### Task 11.60 — A removed member is told nothing and cannot get rid of their copy
**Confirmed on hardware by Michael, 2026-08-29, in full.** Removing a member from the
Mac reached the iPhone and the membership was revoked on its next sync; **the phone
reads "You're not on this project" and offers a Delete that works with no "Leave"
step.** Both halves are done on real devices, not only against a server.

**One deviation from this brief was shipped and flagged rather than buried, which is
`CLAUDE.md`'s rule of 2026-08-29 working on its first outing.** The brief said the
disclosed row must not say who removed somebody or when. As shipped it says both,
because they are columns of the caller's own row: **when** is the entire message —
without it the row says nothing — and **who** is the audit column, which could have
been blanked and was not, because blanking it would leave that device holding a row
that permanently disagrees with the server's copy, which is the class of defect the
shared sync package exists to prevent. The disclosure cost is narrow: a removed member
already held that project's member list, so the only account new to them is an owner
added after their last successful sync — and their device was never sent that person's
name. Reasoning at `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.27. **Michael confirmed the deviation on 2026-08-29 and it stands as shipped.**
**Task 11.49 is still asked to attack that argument rather than the code, and to check
what the screen renders when the account cannot be resolved** — a confirmed decision is
not an unattackable one.

**Status:** **Done, 2026-08-29.** The server hands a removed member their own
closed membership row through the existing pull, as a stated exemption; the
device learns it was removed, and deleting its copy then works through the
departed-member path that already existed — no second mechanism. Inventory entry
28 was written and committed **before** any code (commit `7d00bb7`), Security
Model §4.27 states the exemption, and three deliberate mutations were each
watched to turn the right test red. Two client changes were needed for the news
to be reachable at all and both are in this task's report: a refused push no
longer buries the pull that answers it, and a page that does not move the cursor
is not acknowledged. **What is Open, deliberately:** entry 28 carries no live
attack and therefore no verdict, which is task 11.49's, and Gate C's exit
criterion 1 now names two Open entries rather than one.
**Model:** **Opus** — Michael's decision of 2026-08-29 (below) turned this from a
local screen fix into **a new thing the server tells somebody**, which is a security
surface and not a small edit. It was Sonnet for one day.
**Depends on:** 11.57, which measured it.

**Both are the same shape and that is why they are one task: a membership operation
that does not work and does not say it did not work.**

**1. Somebody an owner removed cannot delete their local copy without first pressing
"Leave".** Measured, and asserted in both halves by
`test/e2e/membership_cycle_matrix_e2e_test.dart`. The departed-member exemption checks
the *local* membership rows, and **a removed person's device never learns it was
removed** — the pull that would tell them is the request being refused. A route out
exists (press Leave, then Delete) and nothing anywhere tells anybody to use it. Their
device shows an amber "the server is refusing access" and a delete control that does
nothing.

**Michael decided (b) on 2026-08-29, reversing his own choice of (a) taken the same
day, and against the planning session's stated lean. The reversal is right and the
reasoning is recorded because it is better than the reasoning it replaced.**

**The decision: the server hands a removed member their own closed membership row, so
the device learns it was removed.**

**Why (a) was worse than it looked, which only became clear after it was chosen.**
Under (a) the device never learns anything, so the screen could only report what it
observes — *the server is refusing this device access* — and must never say *you have
been removed*, because that would be false if the cause were a revoked session, a
rebuilt server, or an outage. That is a real constraint and it is a **workaround for
not knowing**, on the very surface this phase has spent four tasks making say what is
actually true. (b) removes the reason for the workaround instead of wording around it.

**And (b) deletes the special case rather than adding one.** Once the device holds its
own closed membership row, the departed-member exemption that already exists — the one
that reads local membership rows — is satisfied, so **deleting the copy works through
the path that is already there.** (a) would have added a second way to delete a
project, and "do not build a parallel mechanism for the mirror-image problem" is this
project's own standing rule. The planning session's lean missed that, and it is the
strongest argument on this question.

**What (b) costs, stated plainly because it is more than (a) cost.**

- **It is a new server surface**, and this project's discipline is that a new surface
  is **added to `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §3's inventory before it is built**, not
  after — that is what entries 21–27 did and it is the answer to four drift findings.
  **Add the inventory line first.** Gate C's next run then has one more entry to
  attack, which is a real cost and belongs on task 11.49's ledger.
- **It is a read that answers a caller the server is otherwise refusing**, which is the
  shape existence oracles are made of. **The response must be indistinguishable
  between: a project that does not exist; a project the caller was never a member of;
  and a project whose membership is closed but whose rows are refused.** If those three
  differ in any observable way — status, body, timing, order — the route becomes a
  probe for whether a given project id exists, which is exactly what §4.5's
  byte-identical response exists to prevent. **Demonstrate it with a test rather than
  asserting it.**
- **Prefer no new route at all.** The narrowest shape is to deliver the closed row
  through the **existing pull**, as a stated exemption: for a project where the caller
  has a closed membership, the pull returns exactly their own closed membership row and
  refuses everything else. That adds no endpoint and reuses reachability. **But an
  exemption is precisely where this project's findings come from** — "wherever a
  control deliberately ignores something, that exemption is where the next problem is"
  — so the exemption must be written down, attacked, and watched to fail, not merely
  implemented.
- **Nothing beyond their own row.** Not the project's name, not its members, not who
  removed them, not when relative to anything else. One row, about themselves.

**Item 2, the silently-failing ownership transfer, MOVED OUT to task 11.62 on
2026-08-29.** Task 11.59 found a third method with no caller, which makes the finding
the class rather than the instances — see 11.62. This task keeps only the removed
member, which is the half carrying a security surface.

- **Acceptance:** a removed member's device learns it was removed, through its own
  closed membership row and nothing else; the delete then works through the existing
  departed-member path with **no second deletion mechanism added**; the new surface has
  an inventory entry in `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §3 **written before it was built**;
  a test demonstrates that a caller cannot distinguish a project that does not exist
  from one they were never in from one they were removed from; the exemption is written
  down and has been watched to fail; and nothing changes about who may be an owner.

### Task 11.61 — An app that had to be force-killed, and no request that can ever give up

> **NEW EVIDENCE 2026-09-03, from task 11.142 — recorded against Michael's decision rather than
> overturning it.** He decided on 2026-08-29 that this is not beta-blocking. **What is now known
> that was not then:** nothing this app sends can give up, and on the *server did not answer* path
> the Members screen's two sections **genuinely spin forever** — 11.142 gave that case an honest
> sentence, **but the sentence is only reached once the request fails, and a request that cannot
> fail never reaches it.** So the honest empty state is unreachable exactly when a person most
> needs it. **This is a reopen trigger for his decision, not a reversal of it**; the question to
> put to him is whether a beta tester on a flaky connection meets this, not whether the code is
> untidy.
>
> **And the written trigger does not fire, because it was written around the other half.** It
> says: *if this state turns out to be reachable by an ordinary session expiry rather than only by
> a remote sign-out.* **The new evidence is not about sign-out at all** — it is about a server that
> does not answer, which is a different path, has nothing to do with session expiry, and is the
> commonest thing that happens to a phone on a ridge. **The 2026-08-29 decision rested on remote
> sign-out being rare. That estimate is still right and it does not cover this.**
>
> **Michael asked on 2026-09-03 what to do. The planning session's recommendation, in full, so it
> is not re-derived:**
>
> **1. Put a deadline on the request. Do not put a timer on the screen.** A screen that says
> *"the server is not responding"* after N seconds is **a second mechanism that can disagree with
> the first** — the request is still running, may succeed a minute later, and will then overwrite
> the message with a result. It also leaves the request holding a socket and a wakelock on a
> phone. **The app already has honest sentences for a failed request** — task 11.122's default,
> 11.135's tile band, 11.142's four Members sentences, the sync bar's own states. **They are
> unreachable only because the request never fails.** Give it a deadline and every one of them
> starts working. **This shape needs no new user-visible copy at all**, which is the strongest
> argument for it.
>
> **2. Connect deadline plus inactivity deadline — not a cap on total duration.** A first sync of
> a season's data at a trailhead is **slow and progressing**, and a wall-clock cap kills exactly
> the case the app exists for. What must fail is *no bytes at all*: `HttpClient.connectionTimeout`
> for the handshake, and an idle watchdog for a connection that stops delivering. **Measure
> progress, not elapsed time.**
>
> **3. Budgets per operation, derived from what the operation does.** A join-request poll is
> seconds; a sync page is not. **`SyncEngine` already chunks at 500 rows**, so each request is
> bounded even though a whole sync is not — the budget belongs on the request, and the chunking is
> what makes that sufficient.
>
> **4. Compute the combined bound and state it, because this fix can undo task 11.107.** Once
> requests can fail, **the retry policy applies to them** — so a dead server becomes timeout ×
> attempts. That is how a 1.6-second failure becomes a 38-second one again. **The total a person
> waits must be a number this task writes down, not one somebody discovers.**
>
> **5. Cancel; do not abandon.** A request that is given up on but left running can complete later
> and write state behind a screen that has moved on.
>
> **6. Replace the four ad-hoc `.timeout()` call sites, do not add a policy beside them.**
> `join_request_watcher.dart`, `project_setup_screen.dart`, `map_screen.dart` and the one
> `server_config_screen.dart` documents already time out by hand — **a policy plus four survivors
> is the hand-maintained list this project names oftenest.**
>
> **Recommended rating: above the line.** Not because the code is untidy — because **the honest
> messages three separate tasks have just built are unreachable on the one path a field user is
> most likely to meet.** Michael's call.
**Status:** **Done (part 1) and reported unreproduced (part 2) — 2026-09-03.**

**Part 1 shipped.** Every request the app sends is bounded at the one seam that builds a
client (`lib/core/net/request_deadline.dart`): a **connect-plus-first-response deadline** —
30 seconds for a small request (Michael's figure), 5 minutes for a sync page — and a **60-second
inactivity deadline** on the body, so a slow but progressing transfer is never interrupted. A
reached deadline **cancels**, names the request and which half of the exchange stopped, and
becomes its own cause (`SyncFailureCause.timedOut`) rather than any 11.54 already had. **No new
user-visible copy.** `appRetryPolicy` no longer retries a spent deadline, which is what stops
this undoing task 11.107 — the total a person waits is **30 s** for a small request, **5 min**
for a sync page and then the schedule's fifteen-minute floor. **A fifth unbounded path nobody
had listed was found and fixed**: `cached_tile_provider.dart`'s `http.get`, which is every
basemap tile.

**Part 2 is not reproduced, and is deliberately left open.** The candidate mechanism is real —
`test/features/more/device_list_reload_loop_test.dart` breaks the identity comparison and
watches the loop appear, 13 fetches across 25 frames — but the app does not reach it: in the
state Michael described, the screen asks **once** and stops. `CurrentSession` is `keepAlive`,
nothing in `lib/` invalidates it, and every other way its value changes is a genuinely different
value. **The file is left behind as the instrument** for the next occurrence.

**Superseded status, kept as the record: Not started. ABOVE THE LINE — Michael's decision,
2026-09-03**, on the recommendation in the block above: the honest messages three separate tasks
have just built are unreachable on the one path a field user is most likely to meet. **This
supersedes the rating below rather than contradicting it** — his 2026-08-29 reasoning was about how rare a remote
sign-out is, which is still true and is about part 2. **Part 1 is not about sign-out at all.**

**Part 1 ships even if part 2 stops**, and part 2's own entry already says to stop rather than fix
a candidate. **The three facts part 2 needed were answered on 2026-08-29 and are recorded below,
so nothing here waits on Michael.**

**Superseded rating, kept as the record: NOT beta-blocking — Michael's decision, 2026-08-29,
overruling the planning session's call.** His reason: being signed out remotely is very
rare, and if the app does freeze the person restarts it. **The revisit trigger is
written into "the line" below and it is narrow: if this state turns out to be reachable
by an ordinary session expiry rather than only by a remote sign-out, the frequency
estimate the decision rests on is wrong and the rating must be re-made.**
**Model:** **Opus** — part 1 is a timeout policy on the path everybody uses, and part
2 is an unreproduced freeze with more than one suspect.
**Depends on:** 11.36, which found both. **Part 2 needs three facts from Michael that
only he has, and they decay — get them first.**

**Michael signed his iPhone out from his Mac on 2026-08-29. The revocation worked —
after a force-restart the iPhone was properly signed out — but the app had to be
killed. That is the most severe thing anybody has reported on this project.**

**Part 1 — no request this app makes to a server has a timeout. This is certain, and
it does not depend on diagnosing the freeze.** Measured by 11.36: not one call in the
sign-in client or the sync transport is bounded, and neither HTTP client sets a limit.
**A stalled request leaves the control that started it disabled for 60 seconds on an
iPhone and forever on Android or Linux** — the platform default is the only thing
ending it, and on two platforms there is no default. **That looks exactly like a
frozen app**, which is why it is part 1 whether or not it explains part 2.

**The length is a decision, not a default, and it is Michael's.** Too short and a
large sync over a slow field link dies partway, which on this project's own terms is
worse than a stall — a field season's records not arriving because a timeout was tuned
for an office. **Do not pick one number for everything.** The planning session's
starting proposal, offered to be measured against rather than adopted:

- **Small requests — sign-in, the session list, revocation, ack: 30 seconds. Michael
  approved this figure on 2026-08-29.** Nothing legitimate takes longer, and a person
  is watching.
- **A sync page — push or pull: generous, and never unbounded.** Establish what a
  realistic page actually takes over a deliberately slow link before choosing; a
  number picked from an office network is a number that fails in the field.
- **Prefer an idle timeout to a total one where the client supports it** — "no bytes
  for N seconds" survives a slow-but-progressing transfer, which a total deadline
  kills. Say whether the clients in use can express that; if not, say so and pick
  totals.
- **Whatever is chosen, a request that gives up must say which request and why**, per
  the standing rule of 2026-08-27, and must not be reported as any of the causes task
  11.54's classification already names.
- **Know what a timeout now costs before choosing one — task 11.59 changed the retry
  curve on 2026-08-29 and this task is the first to interact with it.** The chosen sync
  frequency is now a **ceiling** on how often the app reaches out: the wait after a
  failure is the longer of the backoff curve and the chosen interval, because under the
  new "Hourly" choice a one-minute backoff would have meant an attempt every minute for
  as long as a server stayed unreachable. **The visible consequence at the default: a
  transient failure is retried after fifteen minutes rather than after one.** So **a
  timeout that fires becomes a fifteen-minute wait**, not a quick retry — which argues
  for a generous sync-page timeout rather than a tight one, and is exactly the trade to
  state rather than discover.

**Part 2 — the freeze itself, which is unexplained and must not be guessed at.**

- **A revoked device should get a prompt refusal, not a stall**, so the missing timeout
  **does not on its own explain this.** 11.36 says so plainly and it is right to.
- **The new device-list screen is a suspect and was not cleared.** Reading it found no
  loop, **which is not the same as there being none** — this project's own rule about
  what a reading is worth.
**Michael answered the three questions on 2026-08-29, and the answers narrow it
sharply:** the iPhone was **on the Server Connection screen** — the one task 11.36 had
just built; **he touched nothing**, the app was already unresponsive when he came back
to it after signing that device out from the Mac; and **nothing was spinning**, meaning
no loading indicator was visible.

**A candidate that fits every one of those, found by reading
`server_config_screen.dart` and offered as a reading rather than a finding — this
session has had four readings overturned by measurement in a week, so test it, do not
adopt it.** The device-list section's `build` watches the stored session and compares
it to the last one with **`identical`**, which is reference equality; when they differ
it schedules `_reload()` in a post-frame callback; `_reload()` fetches and calls
`setState`; `setState` runs `build` again. **If that provider ever emits a new object
that is equal but not identical — which a re-read of the stored credential, or an error
state settling, can do — the comparison is false every pass and the screen reloads
forever.** A revocation is exactly the moment the session changes and the fetch starts
failing.

**Why that matches the symptoms better than a hung request:** a stalled network call
would leave a spinner and would not block taps; **an unbounded rebuild-and-refetch loop
saturates the interface thread, which is unresponsive with nothing spinning.** It also
explains why it happened with nothing touched.

- **Test that mechanism first**, and **watch it fail** — break the identity comparison
  deliberately and confirm the loop appears, so the fix is known to address the cause
  rather than to coincide with its disappearance.
- **If it cannot be reproduced, say so and stop rather than fixing a candidate.** Part
  1 is a real fix and stands alone. **A speculative fix to an unreproduced freeze
  leaves everybody believing it is closed**, which is worse than an open entry — and
  this project has now had four readings overturned by measurement in one week.

**The line — drawn by the planning session, overruled by Michael on 2026-08-29, and
both are recorded because the disagreement is the useful part.** The planning session
called it beta-blocking: an app a person must force-quit looks in the field like a
phone that has died, and a field tech with a dead phone stops recording. **Michael
overruled it: being signed out remotely is very rare, and the remedy is restarting the
app.** That is a reasonable trade and it is his to make.

**But the decision rests on a frequency estimate, and the estimate has not been
checked.** "Remote sign-out is rare" is true. What is not established is whether a
remote sign-out is the only way to reach this state. **The screen re-reads whenever the
stored session changes, and a session also changes when it expires** — which happens to
everybody eventually — **and when somebody uses "sign out everywhere", and when the
server is rebuilt.** If any of those reaches the same state, this is not rare at all
and it will meet beta testers whose sessions simply timed out.

**So the first question is not the freeze, it is the frequency, and it is cheap:** does
an expired or otherwise invalidated session reach the same state as a remote
revocation? **That can be answered without reproducing the freeze**, in minutes.
**If the answer is yes, this rating is void and must be re-made** — that is the revisit
trigger, and it is the reason to answer it early rather than after a beta.

- **Acceptance:** every request the app makes to a server is bounded, with the bounds
  chosen against a measurement rather than a guess and stated per request class; a
  request that gives up names itself and its reason and is not confused with any
  existing failure cause; and the freeze is either reproduced and explained, or
  reported as not reproduced with what was ruled out — **never closed by a plausible
  fix**.

### Task 11.62 — Three methods nobody calls, and nothing that would have noticed
**Status:** Done, 2026-09-09. All three disposed of; a derived guard now watches the
class, and it found three more on its first real run. **Below the line** — none of the
three costs anybody data, and two cost nothing at all today.

**What happened to each of the three, and what the guard found beyond them:**

1. **`SyncController.syncIfDue`** — already fixed by task 11.59 (`lib/app.dart` calls it
   on every foreground). Nothing to do here; confirmed wired.
2. **`SyncSchedule.resumed()`** — deleted. Its actual job was clearing the persisted
   `sync_last_attempt_v1` key on `SharedPreferences`, which `SyncSchedule` (an in-memory,
   rebuilt-fresh-every-launch value object) cannot reach on its own — the two live in
   different places. Added `SyncStateStore.clearLastAttemptAt()` and call it from
   `CurrentSession.completeSignIn` once a session is established, so signing in again
   makes the next `syncIfDue` check find a round due immediately, which was the whole
   point of `resumed()`. `consecutiveFailures`/`stoppedReason` needed no equivalent fix —
   they are never persisted and already reset to their defaults on the rebuild that
   follows a session change.
3. **`ProjectMembershipRepository.grantOwner`** — deleted. Its insert branch (a fresh
   membership row naming somebody not yet a member, at `owner`) named a stranger on a
   client-pushed insert, which the server's `RowAuthorizer._authorizeNaming` refuses
   unconditionally — confirmed by reading it, not assumed. Its promote-an-existing-member
   branch duplicated `MembershipProvider.changeRole` (an ordinary update). Both halves
   were redundant with something that already works; deleted rather than fixed, per the
   task's own "delete it may be the whole answer." Three tests that used it as scaffolding
   (`project_ownership_test.dart`, `leave_project_test.dart`) were rewritten against the
   real equivalents (`MembershipInsertAuthority.replication` for "a co-owner arrived by
   invitation", direct `update(...role: owner)` for "promote an existing member").
4. **`permission_handler` dependency** — removed from `pubspec.yaml`. `flutter build ios
   --no-codesign --debug` and `flutter build apk --debug` both succeeded afterward
   (confirming the acceptance criterion the plan asked for: "remove it and build both").

**The guard: `test/architecture/sync_auth_uncalled_methods_test.dart`.** Textual, in this
project's established style (`test/support/dart_source.dart`), not analyzer-based — it
parses `returnType name(` at class-member indentation across `lib/data/sync/`,
`lib/data/auth/`, the two provider files, and `project_membership_repository.dart`, skips
`@override`s and `Object` methods (the trap: an interface or framework callback must not
be flagged), and fails any survivor whose name has no call or tear-off anywhere else in
`lib/`. **Watched to fail**: temporarily commented out `lib/app.dart`'s only call to
`syncIfDue` and confirmed the guard went red naming it, then restored the call.

**On its first real run it found three more instances nobody had reported**, all in
`project_membership_repository.dart`: `findByUser` (zero callers anywhere, including
tests — deleted), `roleForUser` (superseded by `BaseRepository.projectRoleFor` per task
11.12's own doc comment, which says the two used to disagree — deleted, two test call
sites rewritten to use `findForUser(...)?.role`), and `SyncRowReceiptStore.forgetProject`
(an intentional, tested recovery primitive — "forgets every receipt so the next push
re-offers the project" — with no UI affordance anywhere that triggers it). The first two
are fixed; `forgetProject` is registered in the guard's `_deliberatelyUnused` map pending
a decision below.

**For the planning session:** `SyncRowReceiptStore.forgetProject` is a working, tested
"force a full resync" primitive with nothing in the app that can reach it — there is no
button anywhere for "this project's sync looks wrong, start over." Worth a small task to
add one (probably on the project's More/sync-detail screen, owner-gated or not depending
on whether a contributor should be able to trigger it), or a deliberate decision to leave
it as a debug-only tool and say so. Either is fine; what shouldn't happen is leaving it
silently in the exemption list indefinitely.

**Discovered Scope:** the guard's scope is deliberately narrower than "every public
method in `lib/`" — see its own file-level doc for why (`ObservationRepository
.findBySession` is a known, deliberately-kept exception one level up, outside this
guard's scope entirely). Widening it to the rest of `lib/data/repositories/` is real
future work, not done here.

> **One method that is not yours, added 2026-09-07 by task 11.197.**
> `ObservationRepository.findBySession` **has no callers and now has no data source either** —
> nothing writes a triangulation session any more. **It stays on purpose**, and the doc comment says
> so: it is the only way to read back rows that already exist on people's devices. **Do not report it
> as dead code; it is retired code with a reason.**
**Model:** Sonnet — three dispositions and one guard.
**Depends on:** 11.57 and 11.59, which found the second and third by accident.

**This is the class, not the three instances, and that is why it is one task.** Three
tasks in three days each found a public method in the sync or auth seams that is
documented as doing something useful and **has no caller anywhere in the app.** Each
was found by somebody happening to look. **Nothing in this project would have noticed
any of them** — the same shape as every hand-maintained list this phase has replaced
with a derivation.

1. **`SyncController.syncIfDue`** — found by task 11.57, fixed by 11.59, and **the
   expensive one.** It was the whole reason the app never synced by itself: somebody
   recording bearings all day had nothing on the server. **Listed here as the proof
   this class is not cosmetic** — one uncalled method was, for months, the difference
   between a team app and a solo one.
2. **`SyncSchedule.resumed()`** — found by task 11.59, and the reason this task exists.
   It exists so somebody who has just signed in again syncs immediately instead of
   waiting out the interval. Nothing calls it. **11.59 made it slightly more visible:**
   the time of the last attempt is now saved to disk, so a person who signs out and
   back in within their chosen interval waits out the remainder, where before any
   rebuild forgot the time. **Nothing is lost, the bar does not lie about it, and "Sync
   now" is on the same screen** — which is why 11.59 left it rather than widening
   itself, correctly. **Fix: clear the saved attempt time when a session is
   established, or delete the method.**
3. **`grantOwner`** — found by task 11.57, moved here from task 11.60 on 2026-08-29. It
   inserts a membership row naming somebody else; the server refuses it unconditionally
   and the client correctly withholds it, **so it fails at both ends and reports
   nothing.** No interface calls it, which is the only reason nobody has hit it. **An
   invitation issued at the `owner` role does work end to end** — 11.57's matrix walks
   it — **so "delete it" may be the whole answer.** Otherwise make it refuse out loud
   with a pointer at the invitation route. **A path that fails silently at both ends is
   worse than one that does not exist**, because the next person to wire a button to it
   will believe it. Task 11.1's ownership rule is untouched either way.

4. **The `permission_handler` dependency** — found by task 11.40 on 2026-08-30, and it
   is the same class one layer out: **zero references anywhere in the source.** Today it
   contributes no capability, but it is a large latent permission surface sitting behind
   a dependency nobody uses. 11.40 did not remove it because confirming the removal
   needs an iOS and an Android build, which it could not run. **Remove it and build both,
   or record why it stays.**

**The guard is the point of the task.** Three in three days, each by accident, means
the next one is already waiting. **Derive it** — public methods in the sync and auth
seams with no caller in `lib/`, failing on any that is not explicitly registered as
deliberately unused with a reason. **Watch it fail** before believing it: delete a real
call site and confirm it goes red.

- **A trap worth a moment's thought rather than a grep.** A method reached through an
  interface, a callback, a generated provider file, or a test is not uncalled — a naive
  search reports a wall of false positives and the guard gets turned off within a week.
  **If the honest version cannot be made quiet enough to keep, say so and fix the three
  instead.** That is a legitimate outcome and better than a guard nobody trusts.

- **Acceptance:** each of the three has a disposition — wired, deleted, or registered
  as deliberately unused with a reason; a guard finds the class, or a written statement
  says why it cannot be made quiet enough to keep; and if the guard exists it has been
  watched to fail.

**Added 2026-09-04 by task 11.154 — this task's shape would close a limit somebody else wrote
down, and that is a reason to keep it rather than a reason to raise it.** 11.154 made the app's
two refresh lists check themselves and then stated plainly what neither instrument can see:
**a provider that ought to be refreshed and is read by nothing already on a list.** The
derivation starts from the lists, so a screen nobody ever added is invisible to it. **The
closing move is this task's move** — enumerate the app's providers and ask which read the
membership or tag tables, rather than starting from who remembered to say so. 11.154 did not
do it because it is much larger work than that task. **If this task is ever run, it should
close that limit too**, and `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`'s *Where the Invalidation Audit
Stops* is the paragraph it answers.


### Task 11.63 — The strip of dead grey under the sync bar
**Status:** Done, commit e92ee21. **Candidate 2 confirmed,
candidate 1 already dead code.** `BackupHealthBanner` already returned
`SizedBox.shrink()` when it had nothing to report — that part of the earlier "optical
illusion" close was never the mechanism. Candidate 2 was right: `_TabShell`'s
`Scaffold.body` had no top `SafeArea`, so the ambient top inset (notch/Dynamic Island
height) reached every descendant unconsumed, and `SyncStatusBanner`,
`BackupHealthBanner`, and each tab's own `Scaffold`+`SafeArea` (map/compass/record/
position) or `AppBar` (More) each independently reserved it again — a widget test
reproducing `_TabShell` (renamed `TabShell`, made public for exactly this) through a
throwaway two-branch router measured a 73px gap between the sync banner and More's
header where the fix requires under 59px, and a stray 59px gap above the map-shaped
tab, confirming both of Michael's symptoms come from the same cause. Fixed by moving
the top `SafeArea` to wrap `_TabShell`'s whole `Column` once, and removing the
now-redundant per-banner `SafeArea` from `SyncStatusBanner` and `BackupHealthBanner`.
Verified across both banner-shown and banner-hidden states; the fix does not touch any
individual tab screen. **Below the line, and the highest-value thing below it** — it
is not a defect that loses data, but it is on the map, which is the screen a field user
looks at all day, and vertical space on a map is the product.
**Model:** Sonnet — two concrete candidates, both cheap to test.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Reported by Michael on 2026-08-29** after three separate
sightings.

**What he sees:** on the map, **the sync bar, then a grey bar below it roughly twice
the sync bar's height, then the map.** He first reported it as "the More header is very
large", then noticed the header looked fine once the sync bar was gone, and now sees
it on the map as well.

**A correction the planning session owes, and it matters more than the bug.** On
2026-08-29 this was closed as *"two reports, one observation — the sync bar sat above
the title and the two read as one tall block; the header never changed."* **That was
wrong.** The reports were indeed one cause, but the cause is a layout defect and not an
optical illusion, and closing it meant Michael reported the same thing a third time
before it was believed. **This is the fifth reading this session that measurement
overturned**, and the pattern is specific enough to name: *the planning session keeps
offering a mechanism derived from reading code as though it were a finding.* A reading
narrows where to look. It does not close anything.

**Two candidates, from reading `lib/routing/app_router.dart` and `map_screen.dart`.
They are readings — test them, do not adopt them, and check for a third.**

1. **There is a second banner directly beneath the first.** `_TabShell` builds
   `Column(children: [SyncStatusBanner(), BackupHealthBanner(), Expanded(...)])`.
   **`BackupHealthBanner` is literally the grey bar's position**, and if it renders a
   sized container when it has nothing to report rather than a zero-height box, that is
   the whole bug. **Check what it returns when there is nothing to say.**
2. **A duplicated top inset from nested scaffolds.** `_TabShell`'s `Scaffold.body` is a
   bare `Column` with **no `SafeArea`**, so it starts under the status bar; the map then
   builds its own `Scaffold(body: SafeArea(...))`. **Nothing has consumed the top
   padding, so the inner `SafeArea` inserts the full status-bar height a second time,
   below the banner.** On an iPhone with a Dynamic Island that inset is around 59
   logical pixels, which would read as "about double" a compact banner. The fix for
   that shape is `MediaQuery.removePadding` around the shell's body once the banner has
   consumed it — **not a hand-tuned negative margin**, which is the fix that looks right
   on one device and is wrong on every other.

**Whatever it turns out to be, check every tab and not only the map**, and check it
with the banner shown and hidden. **The two states differing is the whole report.**

- **Acceptance:** the cause is measured rather than reasoned about; no screen gains
  vertical space it does not use when the sync bar is shown; the fix is expressed in
  terms of insets or widget structure rather than a tuned constant; and the behaviour
  is checked on every tab in both banner states.

### Task 11.64 — Gate C, run from instruments that survive the run
**Status:** **Done, 2026-08-30 — Gate C now fails on criterion 5 alone, and criterion
1 is met for the first time.** Round 8's checks and its twelve-shape refusal matrix
are committed instruments (`scripts/verify_round8_server_surface.py`, 152 checks;
`scripts/verify_deployment_refusal_matrix.sh`, 12 shapes), both watched to fail.
Finding P-1 is closed. The full round ran from instruments: **18/18 in 3 min 45 s**,
724 server tests, 1520 app tests, 60 end-to-end, and the adversarial pass matching its
baseline exactly. Two new findings, neither at the bar (Q-1, Q-2). See Security Model
§21. **The only thing now standing between this project and a deployed server is the
NAU letter.**
**Model:** **Opus** — an adversarial round, plus the judgement about which hand-written
checks are worth committing.
**Depends on:** 11.49, which priced it. **Do not start it as a re-run. Start it as
instrument work that happens to produce a round.**

**The finding task 11.49 handed over, and it is the reason eight gates cost what they
did.** Round 8 attacked entries 14–20 with **about ninety checks written by hand during
that run and never committed**, plus a twelve-shape deployment refusal matrix, also
never committed. So "re-run Gate C" has always meant "write those again" — about half a
day of Opus time — **and every round has paid it afresh.** Meanwhile the committed half
of the gate is **3 minutes 21 seconds** for sixteen instruments, measured. *That* is the
difference between a gate that gets run and one that gets deferred.

**So the order is the whole task, and inverting it wastes the round:**

**One entry is already current, and do not waste the round re-running it.** Michael
re-ran `verify_source_identity.sh --assisted` on the Ubuntu VM on **2026-08-30** with
two real phones as the off-host callers: both shapes `PRESERVED`, 13 checks, source
addresses stayed distinct. **Entry 19 therefore carries current-round evidence already**
— count it, and record the host, OS, virtualisation and Docker flavour beside the
declaration as §4.4.3 requires, since that run licenses *that machine* and not the
platform.

1. **Commit round 8's checks and the refusal matrix as instruments first**, in the shape
   the existing sixteen use, so entries 14, 15, 17 and 20 move into the
   three-and-a-half-minute column.
2. **Add finding P-1's probe group and fix what it found** (below). Task 11.49 says the
   probes already exist in its new instrument and this is one more group.
3. **Then run the round** — its evidence is then reproducible by construction rather
   than by somebody's memory. **A round whose checks vanish when it ends has not really
   been run**; it has been performed.
4. **Reach a Gate C verdict** against §6's criteria, and update §2, §3 and §6 to say
   what it is.

**Finding P-1 — `/projects/mine`, the inventory's other server read, folded in here.**
It has only ever been attacked as a *route*, never as a read. Task 11.49 recorded it and
**deliberately did not attack it**, because §6's stopping rule says record and stop —
the discipline that finally got a gate to a verdict. It is **below the bar**. What it
lacks, measured:

- **Nothing measures that a caller-supplied `user_id` is ignored.** The sessions route
  has a test that tries body and query; this has none.
- **No document says which fields a row may carry.** It returns `owner_user_id`, which
  is another person's identifier.
- **No `LIMIT` on the query, and no per-user rate limit** — `/auth/sessions` got both
  under task 10.56's standard treatment and this did not.
- **No `cache-control: no-store`**, which the sessions listing does send.

**Give it 10.56's standard treatment rather than inventing one**, and **write down which
fields the row may carry** — the absence of that sentence is what makes "does it leak?"
unanswerable rather than merely unanswered.

**One thing this task must not do.** Do not widen from P-1 into a free-range review.
§6's stopping rule is what ended eight rounds of treadmill, and the instrument work
above is the reason this round should be cheaper than the last, not more thorough.

- **Acceptance:** round 8's hand-written checks and the refusal matrix exist as
  committed instruments and have been watched to fail; `/projects/mine` carries 10.56's
  treatment and a written statement of the fields it may return; a full Gate C round has
  been run from instruments rather than from memory; §2, §3 and §6 record the verdict
  and the date; and **the cost of the next round is stated and is lower than this
  one's.**

**Status:** **Done (2026-09-10).** The full explanation now lives in

(A) `forgetProject`'s exemption now carries the 2026-09-10 date and its reopen trigger

`TagVersionRepository.historyFor`, `UserEmailRepository.findByUserId`, plus the

**Model:** Sonnet — the shape is decided below; the work is mechanical plus one guard.

**What was found.** The meaning of `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=peer-verified` and
`TRITRACK_PROXY_SOURCE_IDENTITY=probe-verified` is explained in several operator-facing
files at once. **This entry used to say "seven places" and name six of them; task 11.212

it named neither `docker-compose.yml` nor `proxy/Caddyfile`, and "seven" matched neither
the file count nor the mention count — and nobody was maintaining it.

**The surface is derived, and the derivation prints itself.**
`server/test/security/source_identity_warning_test.dart` walks the repository for files
playing an operator-facing role, keeps the ones that actually *assign* either variable,
and **names each one in its own test and prints the list and the count on every run.**
Read that output rather than a number written here. As derived on 2026-09-09 it was five

`SERVER_DEPLOYMENT_PRIMER.md` and `proxy/Caddyfile` mentioning the variables in prose
without asking anybody to type a value. **That figure is a snapshot, not a claim about
today; run the guard.**

**Task 11.40 swept the setup-step copies and deliberately left this one, and its reason
is right:** every copy sits next to the variable it governs, and **a person editing
`.env` who is sent somewhere else to learn that the value is a claim about their own
network is a person who will set it without reading.** That is not a documentation
preference; it is the control. This value is the one place in the repository where a
human asserts a measurement, and the warning has to be where the hand is.

**The shape, decided by the planning session on 2026-08-30 so it is not re-derived
under pressure — and it satisfies both halves rather than choosing one:**

  only thing that can license it."* **A bare cross-reference is what 11.40 rightly
  refused.** The pointer carries the reasoning; the warning stays put.
- **A guard asserts the one-line claim is present at every site**, derived from the set
  of files that mention either variable rather than from a list written here — a list of
  seven files is the defect this task exists to stop, one level up. **Watch it fail.**

- **Acceptance:** the full explanation exists once; every site that mentions either

  network; a guard fails when a mention appears without that warning and has been seen
