### Task 11.66 — Nothing on Android has ever been exercised by a person
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-31), with one stated limit: the walk was run on an
`android-36` emulator, because no Android phone was attached to the machine.** The
whole path was walked and written down in `README.md` ("Walking the whole app on
Android"); the capability enumeration was derived from the *built* merged manifest
and is in `CLAUDE_DOCS/CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md`; eight findings are in Phase 11's
Discovered Scope, each with a named action. **Release-checklist item H2 is met**
(the Android location dialog appears and a bearing records at a real fix) and item
H4 is obsolete (cloud backup was retired; the app has no platform channels).
**What an emulator cannot answer stays open** — a real magnetometer, real GPS
acquisition and drift, battery cost, a device with no Google Play services, any
manufacturer's own permission layer, and anything needing a second device. Those
are listed in the README section's "What was not run".
**BETA-BLOCKING — Michael confirmed on 2026-08-30 that Android is in the beta.**
**Model:** **Opus, HIGH effort, fresh window, run alone — raised 2026-08-31.** This is the
task most likely to be quietly under-served by a cheaper rating, because **its output when
it goes badly is a clean report.** A walkthrough that notices nothing looks exactly like a
platform that works.

**One rule added 2026-08-31, and it is what keeps the scope bounded: fix only what blocks
the walk; report everything else.** A missing permission that stops you testing location
gets fixed, because otherwise the walk stops. A layout that is wrong on Android gets
*written down*, not fixed. **A task that both explores an unknown platform and repairs
everything it finds has no scope at all**, and this project's own record says exploratory
tasks generate follow-ups regardless — 11.74 designed and 11.81 built, and that split
worked. Expect this to produce several tasks; that is success, not overrun.

It is a walkthrough that has to decide what it is looking for, not
a fix.
**Depends on:** 11.40, which found the first instance.

**The finding, and it is bigger than what was fixed.** Task 11.40 found that the Android
build **declared no location permission at all** — so the app's core action, recording a
bearing at your position, could not work, and the app told the user *they* had refused.
It was added and Michael confirmed on 2026-08-30 that recording and syncing a bearing on
a real Android phone now works.

**What that fix does not close: the reason it was there.** A missing declaration for the
app's single most important capability survived because **no part of the Android build
had ever been exercised by a person.** One permission is fixed; the question is not.
This project's own most expensive lesson is the same shape — sign-in had never worked on
macOS since Phase 5 added desktop support, and the two-device walkthrough found seven
real defects on its first honest run, none of which any test caught, because every test
ran on one device.

**So this is a walkthrough, and the two that came before it are the model.**

- **Enumerate what Android has to grant from the platform manifests and entitlement
  files, not from memory** — the same derivation task 11.40 used, applied to the one
  platform it could not run. Location was found that way; assume it was not alone.
- **Walk the app's whole path on a real Android device**: first run, permissions,
  recording a bearing, the map and its tiles, the compass, sign-in, joining a project,
  syncing both directions, export, and the file picker. **Write the walkthrough down as
  you go, the way `README.md` §4 was written** — a step that is not written down is a
  step nobody can repeat.
- **Say what you could not run and why.** Michael has one Android phone; anything
  needing two is his to schedule.
- **Do not fix defects silently.** Each one gets named, and anything larger than a small
  fix gets a task rather than being absorbed here — that is how a walkthrough stays a
  measurement instead of becoming a rewrite.

- **Acceptance:** every capability Android grants is enumerated from the platform files
  and has a stated verdict; the app's main path has been walked on a real device with the
  steps written down; every defect found is named, and each is either fixed or has a task
  number; and the report says plainly what was not run.

everywhere, to make room) on a bearing record, and a left-justified row of its own on the
record types with no signal line. The label carries the number when set; every tap opens the
sheet; the separate line at the top of the form is gone, the lapse notice stays. The design
paragraphs below describe the icon and are superseded by this note.
**Was: below the line — Michael decided on 2026-08-30 that aerial
tracking is not in the beta**, and gave a scope principle worth keeping verbatim:
*"aerial tracking is so rare that we shouldn't let it drive too much of the design of our
software."* **That is a constraint on this task, not just a schedule for it.** Whatever
it eventually proposes must not complicate the ground case, which is what essentially
every user is doing. If the design starts adding choices to the record screen that a
person on foot has to read past, it has gone wrong.

**One part of what this investigation found is NOT aerial and has been moved out** — see
task 11.30, **which has now landed and done half of it.** `altitude_agl` was **removed
from both CSV exports** rather than continuing to export a zero nobody measured. **The
column still exists and still cannot be set by anyone** — that half is this task's, and
**when it becomes settable the exports need it added back.** Do not leave that as an
implied consequence: it is an acceptance line here.
**Model:** **Opus** — the schema turns out to be ready, so what is left is a
field-methods design question, which is the kind this session gets wrong alone.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Raised by Michael on 2026-08-30**, from the observation that
a receiver in a small aircraft is not on the ground.

**The good news first, and it inverts the question he asked.** He asked whether this
needs a schema change. **It does not.** `Observations` and `Non_Detections` already
carry both:

- **`elevation`** — the ground elevation at the recorded position, from the terrain
  tile.
- **`altitude_agl`** — the receiver's height **above ground level**. `viewshed.dart`
  already reads it and notes that *"1.5 m is a reasonable held-antenna default"*.

**So the app already models "how high is the antenna above the ground". Nobody can set
it.** The model defaults it to `0`, the viewshed substitutes a standing person, and no
screen offers the field. **For an aircraft at 300 m that default is not slightly wrong;
it is the wrong quantity**, and it silently feeds the viewshed.

**Establish these before designing anything, and report each as measured or unknown:**

1. **What actually reads `altitude_agl` today?** The viewshed is one reader. **Does
   anything in position estimation use it, or is the solver purely two-dimensional?**
   That single answer decides whether this is a provenance improvement or a correctness
   defect — do not assume, and the planning session deliberately did not.
2. **What does `elevation` being `nullable: false` cost an aerial observation?** The
   terrain tile is required. Over ground with no tile cached, or over water, what is
   stored?
3. **Which altitude source is worth having, and this is the part Michael asked about.**
   The phone's GPS altitude is already available. A barometric reading is a *different*
   measurement with real caveats worth stating rather than discovering: phones expose
   pressure-derived altitude that is **relative** unless calibrated against a reference
   pressure, that reference **drifts with the weather**, and **in a pressurised cabin it
   measures the cabin.** In an unpressurised small aircraft it is usable and needs
   calibration. **Measure whether it beats GPS altitude for this purpose rather than
   assuming it does** — and note that `altitude_agl` can also be derived as *absolute
   altitude minus ground elevation*, which may need no new sensor at all.
4. ~~**Does an observation need to record that it was taken from the air?**~~ **ANSWERED by
   Michael, 2026-09-12: no.** *"I don't think we need a separate mark that it was taken
   from the air. Altitude should say it all."* **Do not add an aerial flag, a mode, or a
   record type.** A non-zero `altitude_agl` is the fact; anything else is a second way to
   say the same thing that can disagree with the first.

#### The design, decided with Michael on 2026-09-12

**He designed this and it is not a starting point to improve on.** What follows is settled;
the open work is the four measurements above and the details called out as unresolved.

**The entry surface: one small icon on the record screen that expands.** Not the advanced
section, and not a field in the main flow. Collapsed, the ground user sees an icon and
nothing else — **that is what satisfies the 30 August constraint.** Expanded, it offers:

- an altitude value,
- a switch for **AGL / MSL**,
- a switch for **metres / feet**.

~~**The icon is NOT an aeroplane.**~~ **SUPERSEDED 2026-09-12 — there is no icon.** The
gauge mark was built, Michael looked at it on the device, and it was *"too small and hard to
tell what it means"*; the entry surface is an **"At altitude" checkbox** instead. **The
reasoning below still stands and still binds anything that replaces it:** an aeroplane glyph
means *aeroplane mode — radios off* on every phone, and this app exists to listen to a radio,
so an icon a user reads as *"receiver disabled"* is a bad ten seconds to hand somebody in an
aircraft. A test still refuses `flight`, `airplanemode_active` and their neighbours. **The
wider lesson is the one worth keeping: a small glyph asked to carry a word it has no
convention for is a guess, and the device look is what settles it** — words are cheaper to
read than symbols are to learn.

**Sticky-if-non-zero, with a rolling four-hour window.** Once a person sets a non-zero
altitude, the next observation defaults to it; a small indicator **above the fold** says
the altitude is non-default, so the value in use is visible without opening anything. The
window is **four hours since the last record**, not four hours since the value was set —
**those are different clocks and the rolling one is meant**, so a working flight keeps the
value and the next morning starts clean.

##### The one part of this that is a defect if built naively, and it must not be

**A timer that silently returns the number to zero is the defect this whole task exists to
fix, rebuilt one level up.** At four hours and one minute — a fuel stop, a lunch break, a
weather hold — the app would quietly resume recording ground observations from an aircraft.
The mirror failure is no expiry at all, and tomorrow's walk-in recorded at 300 m.

> **The answer is not a better timer. It is that the number never changes silently.**
> Keep the four hours, and make the **first record screen after the window lapses say so** —
> *"altitude cleared — was 300 m"* — visible until one record is saved. Then both
> directions are honest and it costs no taps in the air. **A default that changes without
> saying so is this project's most repeated defect and it is being deliberately declined
> here.**

##### MSL is where a wrong number can be produced quietly

The app stores **AGL**. An MSL entry becomes AGL by subtracting ground elevation, which
comes from the terrain tile — **and item 2 above is exactly about the tile not always being
there.** Over water, or over ground with nothing cached, **an MSL entry has nothing to
subtract.**

- **No ground elevation means no MSL conversion**, said on screen, rather than a plausible
  AGL derived from a missing quantity. **A refusal is the correct output here.**
- Item 2 stops being background and becomes load-bearing: **measure what `elevation` holds
  in those cases before designing the refusal**, because the refusal has to key off
  something real.

##### Units

**Store metres.** US altimeters read feet, so a pilot reading a number aloud is reading
feet — **default the display to whatever was chosen last, and hard-code neither.**

##### Still open, and for the task to settle

- **Where the sticky value lives** — it survives app restart or it does not, and which is
  right depends on whether four hours can span a restart in practice. Decide and say why.
- **What the above-the-fold indicator shows** — the number, or only that it is non-default.
  **Show enough that nobody has to open the panel to know what is being recorded.**
- **Non-detections too.** `Non_Detections` carries `altitude_agl` as well. **The same
  sticky value must reach it**, or a flight's no-signal records claim ground level while
  its detections do not.

- **Acceptance:** what reads `altitude_agl` is enumerated from the code rather than
  assumed; a person can set it, see what it is set to without opening anything, and **is
  told when the sticky value lapses rather than discovering it in the data**; the MSL path
  refuses rather than guesses when ground elevation is unavailable, and that refusal is
  watched happening; the icon is not the aeroplane-mode glyph; the sticky value reaches
  `Non_Detections`; **`altitude_agl` is added back to both CSV exports** (task 11.30
  removed it because nothing could set it — that precondition ends here); the ground
  record screen is unchanged but for one collapsed icon; and any altitude source added is
  justified by a measurement rather than by which sensor sounds better.

### Task 11.68 — The committed-secrets check is red, so it cannot report a real secret
**Status:** Done. **Above the line — it is twenty minutes and it is a broken
control, not a defect in the thing it guards.**
**Model:** Sonnet.
**Depends on:** 11.40, which introduced the literal. **Found by task 11.30 on a clean
tree**, verified by stashing all its own work and re-running, so it is not that task's
doing.

`test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart` **fails both its working-tree check and
its history check** on `POSTGRES_PASSWORD=ci-not-a-real-password` in
`.github/workflows/offline-suite.yml` (commit `5245e9a`). The value is a continuous
integration placeholder and not a real secret — **and that is not the point.** The check
is red on `main` right now, **so it cannot report a real secret if one lands.** This is
the standing class: *a check that cannot distinguish success from its own failure is not
a check.*

**Prefer moving the value out of the file to allowlisting it.** An allowlist entry makes
the guard permanently blinder by exactly one string, and the next placeholder will want
one too; reading it from a continuous-integration variable leaves the guard at full
strength and costs a line of workflow configuration. **If the allowlist is chosen
anyway, say why**, and make the entry name the specific literal rather than a pattern.

**Watch it fail before believing it fixed.** Put a plausible-looking secret in a file,
confirm the check goes red, remove it. **A guard that has been red for days is not
evidence that it works when green** — it is evidence nobody was looking.

- **Acceptance:** the check passes on a clean tree, both its working-tree and history
  halves; it has been watched to fail on a planted secret; and the fix is a value moved
  rather than an exemption, or the exemption is justified in writing.

### Task 11.69 — The workflows have now run, and three of four fail
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-30, under a re-scoped acceptance.** The original read *"all
four workflows pass on a clean runner."* **Two do. The other two are red for true
findings this task does not own** — the gate instruments workflow for the timing oracle
now scheduled as task 11.72, and the broken-control workflow for task 11.71's blind
check. **The acceptance is re-scoped to "no workflow is red for a difference between a
developer's machine and a runner," which is met** — the task proposed that itself and it
is the right line, because the remaining reds are the workflows working.

**Closed on GitHub, not locally: three commits and five runs**, after being reopened for
verifying a fix on the machine the bug could not exist on. That is the rule this task
ended up establishing and it should outlive the task.
**Model:** **Opus** — three failures, two root causes, and one of the fixes is a
security-shaped decision rather than a configuration change.
**Depends on:** 11.40, which wrote the workflows and said plainly they had never
executed anywhere. **They have now.** Michael pushed on 2026-08-30 and the Server suite
passed; the other three failed.

**Nothing here is a defect in the app.** Every suite passes on Michael's machine and the
Server suite passes on GitHub. **These are differences between his machine and a clean
Linux runner** — which is the entire reason the workflows were worth having.

**Failure 1 — Offline suite: `flutter analyze` reports every symbol in the server's
tests as undefined.** Measured, not inferred, from three facts: `server/` is **its own
package with its own `pubspec.yaml`**; the workflow runs **only the root
`flutter pub get`**; and the root `analysis_options.yaml` has **no `exclude`**. So the
analyzer walks into `server/test/` where that package's dependencies were never
resolved, and every name in it is unknown. **It passes on Michael's machine because he
has run `dart pub get` in `server/` at some point and the resulting
`.dart_tool/package_config.json` is not in git.** A file that is not committed is not
part of the build, and this is the plainest instance of that this project has produced.

- **Two fixes exist and they are not equivalent — choose deliberately and say why.**
  Resolving `server/`'s (and `packages/`'s) dependencies before analyzing keeps analysis
  covering the whole repository. **Excluding `server/` from the root analyze is a
  reduction in coverage wearing the costume of a fix**, and this project's standing rule
  is not to close a gap by exempting the thing that revealed it. **The exclude is only
  defensible if the Server suite's own analyze genuinely covers what the root one would
  have** — establish that rather than assuming it.

**Failure 2 — Broken-control check: the runner cannot read the magic-link file.**
Measured, and the error names it: `PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied:
'.e2e_magic_links/gate-preflight-…link'`. The development magic-link sender writes that
file **from inside the container, as root, mode 600** — deliberately, because it is a
live credential — into a bind-mounted directory. **On Docker Desktop that ownership is
remapped to the developer's own user; on a Linux runner it is genuinely `root:root` and
unreadable.**

- **This is a security-shaped decision, not a `chmod` in a workflow.** Whatever changes
  must apply **only to the development and end-to-end compose overlays and must not
  touch what a production deployment does** — the file is 600 and root-owned on purpose.
  Say explicitly which shape you changed and prove production is untouched.

**Failure 3 — Gate instruments: thirteen of eighteen fail, and the five that pass are
the five that need no live server.** `verify_c3_cleartext_defaults`,
`verify_i1_source_identity`, `verify_source_identity`,
`verify_deployment_refusal_matrix` and `verify_instrument_unchecked_returns` pass;
everything that talks to a running server fails. **The planning session's reading — and
it is a reading, so test it first — is that this is failure 2 wearing a different hat:**
the instruments that need to sign in need to read a magic link, and cannot. **Confirm
against the per-instrument logs the run kept** (`/tmp/tritrack-gate-smoke.*`) before
fixing anything; if some of the thirteen fail for a second reason, that reason is the
interesting one and must not be hidden by fixing the first.

**One thing that must not happen.** **Do not make a workflow pass by narrowing what it
checks.** Every one of these is a real difference between a developer's machine and a
clean checkout, and each is exactly the class of defect this project has paid for twice
on real hardware — sign-in that had never worked on macOS, and an Android build that
declared no location permission. **A red workflow that is telling the truth is worth
more than a green one that has been persuaded to stop.**

- **Acceptance:** all four workflows pass on a clean runner; each fix is a resolved
  dependency, a corrected environment or a deliberate scoping decision **rather than an
  exemption**, and where an exemption was chosen the report says what coverage was given
  up; the magic-link change is proven to affect only the development and end-to-end
  shapes; and any of the thirteen instruments failing for a reason other than the
  magic-link file is named separately.

### Task 11.70 — Encrypted backups do not work on a Linux server, and the error blames the wrong thing
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-30 — commit `461493c`.** Shape (a) as Michael decided:
`docker-compose.yml`'s `backup` service declares the `user:`, a helper sets it to the
invoking user, and **the signing key stays the operator's rather than a shared
account's.** An operator following the instructions on Linux now gets an encrypted
archive, and when they do not, **the error names which user could not write which
directory instead of blaming the database.**

**The second cost this task was given is also closed, and that is the part worth
noting.** Task 11.69 had made the drills pass on Linux by overriding the container user,
which left the instrument green while the shipped procedure stayed broken. **Both
overrides are removed**; the drills take the user from the same compose declaration an
operator gets, and a new step 0 fails if it is not the invoking user, **watched failing.**
`SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` entry 16 records that its evidence measures the documented
procedure again.

**One limit, stated by the task rather than discovered later.** Every Linux behaviour was
reproduced on a Mac using Docker **named volumes**, which pass ownership through the way a
Linux bind mount does — the refusals and the fix were **watched, not reasoned about**.
**What has still never run is the documented procedure on a real Linux server with a real
`backups/` directory.** The gate-instruments workflow exercises it on its next run, since
the drills no longer override the user.

**Verified 2026-08-31, by task 11.88, from the runner itself.** The drill's own log from a
real GitHub Actions run reads *"the backup container runs as '1001:1001', but this drill
runs as 1001:1001"* — an exact match. **This half of the verdict, withdrawn on 2026-08-31
when the drill was found never to have passed on a real Linux runner, is restored: this
project's operating-user fix does hold on a real Linux host, confirmed rather than
assumed.** The drill had never actually exercised this on a real runner because of a
separate instrumentation bug (task 11.88 fixed it) that made the check fail regardless of
the true values; it now passes.
**Model:** **Opus** — it is a §4.9 key-custody decision, not a permissions fix.
**Depends on:** 11.69, which found it while fixing something else.

**What a person following the documented procedure gets today.** `server/README.md`
tells an operator to create a `backups/` directory and generate a mode-600 signing key.
On a Linux server **the backup container runs as its own `postgres` user (uid 70)**, so
it can neither create a file in that directory nor read that key. `backup.sh` then
reports **`pg_dump | age pipeline failed; no archive written`** — which names the wrong
cause, sending the operator to look at their database.

**The harm, stated plainly: they follow the instructions, see something that reads like
a transient error, and believe they have encrypted backups when no archive was ever
written.** That is the shape this project treats most seriously — not a loss today, but
a person holding a false belief about where their data is. It works on Michael's Mac
because Docker Desktop remaps ownership, the same difference behind every finding in
task 11.69.

**A second cost, and a security gate must know about it: the backup drill passing is no
longer evidence that a real deployment can write an archive.** Task 11.69 fixed the two
drill scripts so the instruments run on Linux. **That makes the instrument green while
the shipped procedure stays broken** — a control that no longer measures the thing it is
cited for. **Whatever this task does must re-establish that link**, or say plainly that
the drill covers only the drill.

**The decision, and it is Michael's because the three shapes differ in who can read the
signing key on a shared machine — which is what decides whose backups a restore will
trust.**

- **(a) The compose file declares a `user:` for the `backup` service.** Explicit,
  committed, versioned, travels with the repository.
- **(b) The documented procedure gains a `chown` step**, performed by the operator.
- **(c) The image stops running as `postgres`.** Changes the container itself.

**Michael decided (a) on 2026-08-30: the compose file declares a `user:` for the
`backup` service. Build it; do not re-open the question.** The signing key stays owned by
the operator rather than by a shared internal account, and the fix travels with the
repository instead of depending on a step somebody performs correctly.

**The reasoning that produced that lean, kept because it generalises.**
Option (b) is **a documented step a human must perform correctly and which nothing can
check** — precisely what task 11.37 item 5 was written to eliminate, and 11.38 paid its
cost: a README naming the wrong field to copy, whose only symptom was an
unrelated-sounding failure much later. **A backup that silently does not happen is a
worse instance of that class than the one that motivated the rule.** (a) is verifiable by
rendering the merged configuration — the technique 11.69 already used to prove production
was untouched. **Michael decides; this is a lean, not an answer.**

- **Acceptance:** an operator following `server/README.md` on a clean Linux server gets a
  written, encrypted archive; a failure to write one **names its own cause** rather than
  blaming the database; the chosen shape is recorded with who can read the signing key
  under it; and the backup drill either measures the shipped procedure again or states
  that it does not.

### Task 11.71 — One check in the round-8 instrument cannot fail
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-30 — commit `eeb5950`.** **The answer was the second
explanation, the one the brief called the more interesting: the control was holding for a
reason other than the documented one.** The check was correctly written and looking in
the right place; **round 8's five traversal addresses simply could not put a file anywhere
it looks.** On Linux two of them are ordinary filename characters and never leave the
directory, two more name subdirectories the sender does not create, and the only one aimed
outside is refused by **the filesystem**, because the container runs as an unprivileged
user.

**The real defence is now named, written down, and measured to be narrower than it
looks.** The unprivileged user keeps an escape out of `/etc` and **does nothing about
`/tmp` or `/var/tmp`** — the same user writes to both freely — and the end-to-end compose
overlay's `user:` falls back to `0:0`, so a stack brought up without its helper script
gets `/etc` back. **And the sanitiser is load-bearing, now measured rather than assumed:
delete it and an unauthenticated address makes the server create a caller-named file in
`/tmp`.** Recorded so a later refactor cannot read the unprivileged user as cover for
removing the sanitiser.

**A false sentence was corrected, and it was false rather than merely over-stated.**
`SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` entry 20 ended *"watched to fail: with the sanitiser deleted,
the escape appears and the probe goes red."* **That was written before the harness had
ever run on a machine that could run it**, and its first real run flipped seven of eight.
Entry 20, its cost-table row and §21.1–21.2 now say what happened. **Entries 14 and 15 are
unaffected** — different probes, every one watched flipping — and entry 20 is `Accepted`,
so **no `Hardened` verdict falls and nothing needs re-running.**
answer is the second one's shape: the check was fine and the corpus it was given could
never reach it.**

**What was wrong, in one sentence.** The comprehensive search — "is there a `.link` file
anywhere on this container's filesystem outside the directory it was told to use" — was
correctly written and looking in the right place; **none of round 8's five traversal
addresses could put a file anywhere it looks**, so for two rounds it was searching for
something nothing in the run could create.

**Measured in the running container rather than reasoned about**, address by address:

- `..%2f..%2f…` and `..\..\…` **never leave the directory at all.** Nothing URL-decodes
  the JSON body and a backslash is an ordinary filename character on Linux, so both land
  inside the link directory whatever the sanitiser does.
- `a/b/c-…` and `....//....//…` name subdirectories that do not exist. `FileEmailSender`
  creates the link directory (`createSync`) and not the file's parents, so both fail
  `ENOENT`.
- `../../../../etc/…` is the only one naming an existing directory outside — and the
  write is refused by the **filesystem**, because the container runs as an unprivileged
  user (`docker-compose.e2e.yml`'s `user:` line, task 11.69). Verified by trying it as
  that user: `Permission denied`.

**So the control was holding for a reason other than the documented one, and the real
defence is narrower than it looks.** The unprivileged user keeps an escape out of `/etc`.
It does nothing about `/tmp` or `/var/tmp`, both of which the same user writes to freely
— verified — and `user:` falls back to `0:0`, so a stack brought up without
`scripts/lib/host_user.sh` gets `/etc` back. **The sanitiser is load-bearing and that is
now measured**: with it deleted, `../../../../tmp/…` makes the server create a
caller-named file in `/tmp`, watched happening. Written into §15.3 M-9 so a later
refactor cannot read the unprivileged user as cover for removing the sanitiser.

**The fix strengthens the check rather than weakening it.** The instrument now asks the
container which directories outside the link directory it can actually write to — by
trying the write, because that is the property, and a permission bit is only a
description of it, and requiring the same filesystem as `/` because the search is
`find / -xdev` and a target on another mount would be an escape the search steps over.
It aims one address at the first such directory; its label deliberately does not name the
directory, because the broken-control harness matches attacks by name and a name that
moved with the host would be a required flip that quietly stopped being required. **A new
positive control plants a `.link` where an escape would land and requires that same
search to report it**, and the run fails outright if the container has no writable
directory outside the link directory — a run that cannot test the escape now says so
instead of passing.

**Watched to fail, for real.** `verify_round8_broken_control.py`: **155 checks clean
against the intact server (127 attacks, 28 controls, none admitted, none blind), 17 of 16
required flips on the envelope variant and 9 of 9 on the sanitiser variant** — including
both the new address and the filesystem-wide search, which is the line that could not go
red before. Exit 0.

**The gate's record is corrected in three places, and the correction is a false sentence
rather than a downgrade.** Entry 20 is `Accepted`, so no `Hardened` verdict is overturned,
and **entries 14 and 15 are untouched** — their evidence is different probes, all of
which were watched flipping. What was wrong is that entry 20 and §21.1 both claimed the
escape probe had been *watched to fail*, written before the harness had ever been run on
a machine that could run it. Its first real run flipped seven of eight, not eight of
eight. `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` entry 20, its cost table, and the security model's
§21.1 and §21.2 now say what happened and what closed it.

**Superseded below.** The brief as written before the work, kept because it named both
explanations and the answer was between them.
**Model:** **Opus** — the interesting outcome is the one where the check is fine and the
reason it passes is not the documented one.
**Depends on:** 11.64, which committed the instrument. **Found by the broken-control
workflow on its first real run, 2026-08-30 — which is the harness working exactly as
designed.**

**What the run established, and most of it is good news.** The healthy server was clean:
**152 checks, 126 attacks, 26 positive controls, none admitted and none blind.** Against
a server with the envelope's type-checking removed, the instrument caught it — 17 attacks
admitted where 16 were required. Against a server with the address sanitiser removed it
caught that too, 10 admitted where 8 were required.

**But one check stayed `refused` against a server whose control had been deliberately
removed**, and the harness refused to call the instrument trustworthy because of it:

> `sanitiser: 1 attack stayed 'refused' … ['any .link file anywhere outside the link
> directory']`

**That is the standing class, caught by the one mechanism built to catch it: a check that
cannot fail is not a check.** Every other check in this instrument has now been watched
to fail. This one has not, so **whatever it has been reporting for two rounds is not
evidence.**

**Two explanations, and they are not equally interesting. Distinguish them before fixing
anything.**

1. **The check is broken** — it looks in the wrong place, or its search cannot see a file
   the attack would create. Then it is a defect in the instrument and the fix is
   mechanical.
2. **The check is fine and nothing escaped, because something other than the sanitiser
   prevents it.** Then **the control is holding for a reason other than the documented
   one**, which is this project's most-repeated finding and is worth more than the check:
   whoever preserves the sanitiser in a future refactor will not know to preserve the
   real defence. **If this is the answer, name the real defence and write it down**, and
   say whether the sanitiser is then load-bearing at all.

**Do not make this green by weakening the check or by deleting it.** A blind check
removed is one fewer lie; a blind check *replaced by one that has been watched to fail*
is the point. **And do not let the healthy run's cleanliness stand in for it** — 152
clean checks say nothing about the one that cannot go red.

**Note for the gate's record either way.** The inventory's entry 20 is **Accepted**
rather than Hardened, so this does not overturn a Hardened verdict. But the round-8
surface evidence for entries 14, 15 and 20 was cited on 2026-08-30 as current-round, and
**one of its checks is now known not to be evidence.** Say in the report whether that
changes anything in `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md`, and correct it if so.

- **Acceptance:** the blind check either fails against a server with the sanitiser
  removed, or is replaced by one that does; if nothing escapes without the sanitiser, the
  actual defence is identified and written down and the sanitiser's role is stated; the
  instrument reports itself known-to-work; and the gate's record is corrected or
  explicitly confirmed unchanged.

### Task 11.72 — The refusals say the same words and take different times
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-30 — closed by fixing it, not by accepting it. One residual
is accepted in writing and is subject to Michael's review.** Both differences are down by
a factor of forty to a hundred and **neither is zero**: on the runner, **+6.0
microseconds** between a real project and a fictional id and **+4.0** between a
fifty-member project and a one-member one, against a **measured per-id noise floor of 4
microseconds on the same run** — so the residuals sit *on* the floor rather than above
it. They cannot reach zero because an index probe that finds a row fetches it and one
that finds nothing does not; **only padding removes that, and padding is rejected in
writing** (§4.13) — the pad must exceed the slowest real project, it grows as teams grow,
and `/sync/pull` has no per-user rate limit, so a padded refusal is a resource an
attacker can hold open. **The reopen condition is a check rather than a promise:** each
pair bounded at 25 microseconds, or four times the run's own floor if that is larger. **Michael reviewed and accepted it on 2026-08-30**, so the
acceptance is his rather than made on his behalf, and the alternative he declined —
padding every refusal to a fixed delay — is recorded with its reasons at §4.13. The
planning session's lean below was "below the bar, accept in writing"; the task's own
instruction to *establish what costs the extra time before choosing* is what changed the
answer, and the entry below is left intact so the reasoning can be checked.

**What the attribution found, and why it made the fix the right option.**
`ProjectAuthorizer.resolve` ran the same two statements on both branches — task 11.60's
fix — but the second read **every membership row of the project**. A fictional id returns
none; a real project returns one per member, and fetching and decoding those rows is
work. Measured directly against Postgres rather than through HTTP: **+7 µs at one member,
+17 at three, +71 at twenty, +213 at fifty**, sign unanimous from three members up. **So
the leak was never one bit.** It was a monotone reading of *how many people are on a
project the caller has no access to* — and equalising only the absent-versus-forbidden
pair the probe measures would have turned the workflow green and left that standing,
which is the instance rather than the class (task 10.66).

**The fix is a narrowing, not a padding.** Both statements now return a result whose size
does not depend on the project: one row of scalar facts (`EXISTS` for the project row and
for "anybody holds an open owner membership", plus the creator column), and **only the
caller's own** membership rows — empty for any non-member, real project or fabricated id
alike. `resolveProjectRole` gets exactly what it needed. Constant-time padding was
considered and rejected in writing (§4.13): the floor has to exceed the slowest real
project and grows with the team, `/sync/pull` has no per-user rate limit so a padded
refusal is a resource an attacker can hold, and work added after the deadline reopens it
silently.

**Measured after, on the GitHub runner and not only on this Mac — and the runner is what
corrected the first version of this answer.** Existence pair **+6.0 µs**, team-size pair
**+4.0 µs**, against a measured per-id noise floor of **4 µs** on the same run; the old
formulation in the same interleaved pass still shows **+256 µs at 9/9**, so the run proves
it could still see the effect. **The residuals sit on top of that floor rather than
comfortably above it** — the team-size pair's sign is 9 of 9 at four microseconds, which
is a stable sign on a difference the run cannot separate from its own noise, and that is
the honest way to read it. **Both differences are down by a factor of forty to a
hundred and neither is zero**, and the first version of the instrument — which asserted
"no stable sign" — was refused by the runner reporting the *null pair* of two fictional
ids unanimous at 4.1 µs. That is real: two fabricated ids land on different pages of the
same index. Writing "no stable sign" would have repeated this task's own lesson.

**So a few microseconds are accepted in writing**, with the reason (an index probe that
finds a row does a heap fetch; one that finds nothing does not, and only padding removes
that) and a reopen condition that is a check rather than a promise: the instrument bounds
each pair at 25 µs, or four times the run's own measured floor, and goes red above it.
**Accepted by Claude Code, 2026-08-30, subject to Michael's review** — it is a hundredth
of the question he was going to be asked, but it is still his call.

**What is not claimed:** this is not a constant-time guarantee and §4.13 says so.

**The instrument moved, and that is the part worth keeping.**
`server/test/security/authorization_timing_test.dart` times the function directly against
Postgres, resolves single-digit microseconds where the HTTP probe needs 900 requests to
see a fiftieth of a millisecond, runs in the ordinary server suite on every commit, and
**fails rather than passes on a host that cannot resolve the effect** — its positive
control is the old formulation measured in the same pass. **It has been watched to fail**
(+211.7 µs at 9/9 on the existence pair, +196.6 at 9/9 on the gradient). The two HTTP
probes are kept as the end-to-end view and now say in their own comments that they are
not the measurement.

**§4.13 is corrected either way, as the brief required.** Its opening claim now says that
"indistinguishable from outside" covers the *work done* and not only the answer; the
clause in the task-10.29 paragraph asserting the routes were identical "including by
timing" is marked false where it stands; §20.3's verdict is overturned in place with the
runner's numbers; and inventory entry 28 is amended. **One correction to the brief
itself:** the two probes that found this are independently written but run against the
**same route**, so their agreement rules out one instrument being wrong and never ruled
out one handler being wrong. The narrowing covers all four routes that call the function.

**Superseded below.** Everything from here to the acceptance line is the plan as written
before the work, kept because the decision it was steering toward was the other one.

**Above the line.** It is an unresolved security question on a
server that is about to be reachable, **and it makes the gate instruments workflow red in
about four runs of five** — which corrodes the habit of reading red at all.
**Model:** **Opus** — a bar judgement and a §4.13 correction, not a performance fix.
**Depends on:** 11.69, which found it.

**Two further corrections to this brief, recorded because the brief was wrong and the
task said so.** *"It shows on two different routes, so it is unlikely to be one handler's
accident"* — **that was not what was measured.** The two probes are independently
written, which rules out one *instrument* being wrong; both call the same route, so
nothing ruled out one *handler* being wrong. The conclusion was right by luck: the
function is called by the project-detail route and all three sync routes, so the fix
covers four. **And the residual acceptance below was made on Michael's behalf and awaits
his review.**

**What was measured, and the measurement is well made.** Somebody signed in but not on a
project asks the server for it. **The refusal is byte-identical whether or not the
project exists — and the one for a project that really exists is consistently about 54
microseconds slower.** Three separate runs: +0.052, +0.061 and +0.049 ms, **sign positive
in 9 of 9 trials each time**, while the check's own control pair — two invented ids whose
true difference is zero — **flipped sign every run.** That control is what makes this a
measurement rather than noise. It shows on two different routes, so it is unlikely to be
one handler's accident.

**Why four security gates missed it, and it is the week's recurring lesson one more
time.** *A developer's Mac cannot resolve 54 microseconds and a clean Linux runner can.*
**Task 11.60 equalised the query count on this path without measuring**, and task 11.49
was then asked to put numbers on it and reported hundredths of a millisecond against an
8–24 ms spread **with no stable sign** — a correct answer, produced on the wrong machine.
**The beta server is a Linux machine.**

**The planning session's reading against `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` §4, offered so it
can be argued with rather than inherited — and Michael decides:**

- **B1** — no field data is lost or corrupted.
**CORRECTED 2026-08-30 by the task, and the correction is why fixing beat accepting.**
**The leak was bigger than this analysis describes.** `ProjectAuthorizer.resolve` read
**every membership row of the project**, so the refusal's time grew with the size of the
team: about **7 microseconds** slower than a fictional id at one member, **17** at three,
**71** at twenty, **213** at fifty, sign unanimous from three members up. **So somebody
with no access could read off roughly how many people are on a project — not merely that
its id is real.** Team size was not on the table when the reading below was written, and
the reading is left standing only as a record of what was argued. **It still lands below
the bar** — team size is neither a coordinate nor an observer's identity — **but "it only
confirms an id you already hold" was not a true description of the finding**, and a bar
judgement is only as good as its description of what leaks.

- **B2** — **no animal coordinates and no observer identity are disclosed.** What leaks
  is that **a project id the caller already holds names a real project on this server.**
- **B3** — nothing is bypassed; the caller is authenticated and still refused.
- **B4, and this is the one that needs stating rather than waving past.** §4.13 asserts
  the two answers are **indistinguishable from outside**, and that claim is now **false
  as written** — a timing difference is observable from outside. §15.0 settles that B4 is
  a route to B1–B3 rather than an independent bar, so the question is what the weakened
  control leaves undefended: **the existence of an id the caller already possesses.**
  That is not B1, B2 or B3.
- **The bound that made every earlier existence-oracle finding acceptable still holds:**
  ids are client-minted 122-bit UUIDv4s. **Timing does not help anybody guess one** — it
  only confirms a candidate already held, and the population of candidates a stranger
  holds is empty.

**So the lean is: below the bar, accepted in writing with a reason and a reopen
condition — and §4.13's wording corrected regardless.** An accepted finding does not
excuse a document that says something untrue.

**Whatever is decided, the workflow cannot stay red four runs in five.** That is the
outcome task 11.40 exists to prevent, and this project has lost instruments to it three
times. **Task 11.69 was right not to widen the threshold silently** — the check is
telling the truth. **So the check must be reconciled with the decision, not with the
inconvenience:** if the finding is accepted, the check's baseline records the accepted
difference and goes red on any *change* to it; if it is fixed, the check stays as it is.
**A threshold widened to make a run quiet, with no decision behind it, is the one
outcome that is not allowed.**

**And nobody has looked at what costs the extra time.** 11.69 says so plainly and did not
guess; it may be as ordinary as one index lookup. **Establish it before choosing** —
whether it is cheap to remove changes which option is right.

- **Acceptance:** the finding is either closed or registered with a written reason, a
  named person and a date; §4.13's claim is corrected to say what is actually true;
  the gate instruments workflow is green for honest reasons and goes red if the timing
  difference *changes*; and the report says what actually costs the 54 microseconds, or
  states plainly that it could not be established.

### Task 11.73 — A widget test can reach for a real device folder, so every screen test is a coin flip
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-30 — commit `c0a24a9`.** Fixed as the class rather than as
two tests: a fake `path_provider` is installed for **every** widget test by default via
`test/flutter_test_config.dart`, so a screen cannot acquire this exposure by being
written.

**One thing recorded for whoever writes the next screen test.**
`project_extent_picker_screen.dart` has the same exposure — it renders a live map through
the same tile provider — but **has no widget test yet**, so it was not in the five-screen
count this task closed. **Nothing to do now.** When that screen gains a test file, the
global fake already covers it and **no opt-in is needed** — which is the point of having
fixed it globally.
every live-map screen uses), which reaches `path_provider` the instant a tile is asked
for. Fixed at the class via `test/flutter_test_config.dart`, which now installs the fake
`path_provider` before every widget test in the suite by default, rather than each
screen's test file having to remember to opt in. **Five screens carry this exposure**
(`MapScreen`, `PositionEstimationScreen`, `RecordPositionPreviewScreen`,
`OfflineDataMapScreen`, `ProjectExtentPickerScreen`); of the four with a test file, two
(`position_estimation_screen_test.dart`, `record_position_preview_screen_test.dart`) had
never been given the fake and are the ones this task closes.
`test/support/plugin_channel_guard_test.dart` is the derived guard: it puts the real,
unstubbed channel back for its own run and awaits it directly (not via a detached
background Future), proving the failure is deterministic rather than a race — confirmed
by disabling the global fake and re-running the two previously-unprotected screen tests,
which reproduced the exact background `MissingPluginException` the diagnosis described
(the fake is what stops it, not luck).
**Model:** Sonnet — the diagnosis is done and it points at one mechanism.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by task 11.72 while its own workflow runs kept going
red for something that was not its.**

**What was measured, and it is better than "a flaky test".** The offline suite failed on
GitHub **three times in eleven runs**, on two different screen tests
(`position_estimation_screen_test.dart` twice, `map_screen_test.dart` once), and **at
least once on a commit that changed four documentation files and no client code at
all** — so nothing introduced it. The log names the cause **59 times**:
`MissingPluginException` on `path_provider`'s `getApplicationSupportDirectory`. Something
running in the background during a widget test asks for a real device folder, and there
is no device.

**The part that makes this cheap rather than nasty: it is not a race and not a runner
problem.** 11.72 ran that file on the Mac and **the same exceptions appear there while
the test still passes.** So the exceptions are **unconditional**; what varies is only
whether they land **inside a test body**, where the framework counts them as a failure,
or **after it**, where nobody looks. **That is a timing lottery, not a rare condition.**

**Fix it as the class, because it is already the second instance.** Task 11.69 fixed one
race in the map screen and **said plainly it could not prove there was only one.** This
is the second. **If a plugin channel can be reached at all from a widget test, then every
screen test in this suite is a coin flip** — the two that have failed are the two that
happened to lose. So:

- **Find what reaches the channel and stop it reaching**, rather than making two tests
  tolerate it. A test that swallows the exception still has the background work running.
- **Then derive the guard:** a widget test that provokes a `MissingPluginException`
  should fail loudly and by name, so the next screen to acquire one is found by the suite
  rather than by a run that happened to lose. **Watch it fail.**
- **Say how many screen tests were exposed**, not just how many were failing. That number
  is the finding.

- **Acceptance:** no widget test reaches a platform channel; the offline suite runs green
  on the runner several consecutive times, not once; a guard fails when a widget test
  provokes a plugin exception and has been watched to fail; and the report states how
  many screen tests were exposed to this before the fix.

### Task 11.74 — One join code and an owner's approval: measure and design, do not implement
**Status:** **Done, 2026-08-30.** The measurement, the design and the migration plan are
in `CLAUDE_DOCS/JOIN_CODE_AND_APPROVAL_DESIGN.md`; the drafted inventory entries for 23,
24 and a new 29 are in its §1.4. **No production code was changed.** Five decisions are
waiting on Michael in that document's §5 — the largest is whether an owner may re-read
their project's join code, which needs an exception written into the security model's
token rule if the answer is yes. **BETA-BLOCKING — Michael's judgement on 2026-08-30 that the
current join flow does not scale to a real team, and the beta is a real team.**
**Model:** **Opus** — high effort, fresh window, run alone. **This task deliberately
writes no production code.**
**Depends on:** 11.2, 11.3, 11.54.

**Michael's design, decided 2026-08-30 and settled — do not re-open any of it:**

1. **One shared join code per project, replacing per-address invitations entirely.** It
   is meant to be emailed, sent over WhatsApp, or written on a whiteboard at a field site.
2. **Joining with the code creates a request, not a membership.** The person appears in
   the owner's member list under **pending approval**, with their name and email.
3. **The owner approves, and chooses the role at approval.** *Planning session's default:
   contributor unless changed.* The role is never carried in the code — a leaked
   owner-level code would be a far worse leak, and per-role codes are the thing this
   change exists to escape.
4. **The owner can rotate the code or switch joining off.** Pending requests **survive** a
   rotation by default.
5. **Rotating offers "also clear pending requests", defaulted off.** It is reachable only
   by deliberately rotating — never by mis-tapping a list.
6. **One team-size limit on the project, owner-changeable, default 50. Pending requests
   count toward it**, and the screen says so plainly when it refuses somebody.
7. **No bulk reject. Michael's reasoning, and it is better than the planning session's:**
   an accidental "reject all" would force every legitimate requester to ask again and be
   contacted individually, and **that accident is far likelier than the flood it would
   defend against.** The more probable failure wins.

**Why this is safer than what it replaces, stated so nobody argues the wrong way round.**
Today, possessing an invite code **is** membership. Under this design, possessing the
code buys only the right to **ask**, and the owner is the gate. **A leaked code stops
being a credential and becomes an address.**

**Establish these before proposing anything, and report each as measured or unknown:**

1. **Does the requester have to type anything at all?** Requesting requires being signed
   in — that is already true of redemption today — so **the server already knows their
   authenticated email, and their display name already exists on their profile and
   already syncs.** If the request takes both from the session, **there is no new
   untrusted-text path** and the length, control-character and bidirectional-override
   questions never arise. **This is the planning session's assumption and it is
   unverified — check it first, because everything downstream depends on it.**
2. **What enforces that a pending row is not a grant?** This is the deep one. **The
   permission model currently treats the existence of a membership row as the grant** —
   `insertIsAGrant`, `RowAuthorizer` and `offer_rules` all rest on it. A pending member is
   a membership-shaped row that must **not** grant anything, **enforced at the server and
   not by a screen showing a different list** (task 11.26's rule). Say exactly what
   changes and what else depends on the current reading.
3. **What is the schema change and what does migration do to what exists?** Existing
   members, existing outstanding invitations, and a project with no code yet.
4. **Which server routes go, which arrive, and what happens to the security inventory?**
   Entry 23 (invitation issuance, listing, revocation) largely disappears; entry 24 (the
   one route where a signed-in stranger asks to join) **changes shape rather than going
   away**. **Write the inventory entries before anything is built** — the discipline that
   has now worked twice, and the answer to four drift findings.
5. **What happens to "re-invite a past member"?** Task 11.54 built that button on the
   address-bound path this change removes. It needs a new meaning, not deletion.

- **Acceptance:** the five questions are answered as measurements with "I could not
  determine this" stated where true; a migration plan exists; the inventory entries are
  drafted; **no production code is changed**; and the report is written for Michael to
  read and approve before anything is built.

project-file reference passes every test and fails a device build. Michael built iOS and

**The constraint that decides the design, measured on 2026-08-30.** The repository is
**private on a free organisation plan**: roughly 2,000 Actions minutes a month, Linux at
1× and **macOS at 10×**. Current usage is **195 minutes**. A Flutter iOS build takes
10–15 minutes of Mac time, so **one run of iOS plus macOS costs around 200 billed minutes

- **Android builds on every push.** Linux, same as the existing workflows, effectively

### Task 11.77 — Which instruments have ever been watched to detect, rather than to abort
**Status:** **Done as population 1 of task 11.119, 2026-09-01 — see
`CLAUDE_DOCS/UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md`, "Population 1 — Instruments".** All 26 instruments are
listed with a verdict; the comprehensive-search shape was checked for by name and **both known
instances had already been closed by tasks 10.95 and (in `verify_c5_denial_audit.py`) its own
author** — a negative result. An order is proposed and nothing was rewritten.
**MERGED into task 11.119 on 2026-09-01. Do not run `/11-77` separately** — it
is the instrument population of that task's survey. **Everything below is unchanged and is
still the spec.** **Below the line, and it is the item there that most changes what a gate
verdict is worth.**
**Model:** **Opus** — the judgement is which instruments even have a "control to delete",
and that is not obvious from reading them.
**Depends on:** 11.71, which found the class. **Task 11.71 deliberately did not file this
as its own follow-up**, on the grounds that it is new work rather than a loose end — that
was the right call and this is the task.

**The class, and it is not the same as a check that cannot fail.** Task 11.71's blind
check was **correctly written, looking in the right place, and every control inside the
instrument was firing.** What was wrong sat **upstream of all of them: the attack corpus
could not reach the check.** Four of round 8's five traversal addresses were, on Linux,
decoration. **Only an outside harness that deletes the control could see that** — no
amount of reading the instrument would have.

**Why it matters beyond one check.** The ninth Gate C round's criterion 1 was met on these
instruments' evidence. One of them had been reporting a clean result for two rounds
**without being able to report anything else.** That instance is closed. **The question
this task asks is how many others have the same shape**, and nobody knows.

**The precise gap, and stating it precisely is most of the work:**

- **The broken-control harness proves *detection*** — it deletes a real control and
  requires the instrument to notice. **It covers round 8's instruments only.**
- **`gate_smoke_test.sh`'s self-test proves *abortion*** — it forces a stale schema major
  and requires every wire-speaking instrument to fail loudly rather than pass vacuously.
  **That is a different property.** An instrument that aborts correctly when the world is
  wrong may still be unable to detect the thing it exists for.
- **So for most instruments, "watched to fail" means "watched to abort", and that has
  been read as though it meant "watched to detect."**

**What to produce:**

1. **A list, derived from `scripts/` rather than from memory, of every instrument, and for
   each one: has it ever been watched detecting its own subject being removed?** Expect
   the honest answer for most to be no.
2. **For each, whether a control even exists to delete.** Some instruments assert a
   property of configuration or of the code rather than of a running server; deleting a
   control is not always meaningful, and **saying so is a result, not a gap.**
3. **The specific shape 11.71 names, checked for directly: an instrument whose final
   assertion is a comprehensive search** — a `find` across a filesystem, a grep of a whole
   log, a scan of a whole table. **Those look thorough and are exactly where a corpus that
   cannot reach the check hides**, because the search finding nothing is indistinguishable
   from there being nothing to find.
4. **Do not fix them all.** Rank by what a gate verdict actually cites, propose an order,
   and let Michael choose how far to go. **A sweep that turns into a rewrite is how eight
   gates cost what they did.**

- **Acceptance:** every instrument in `scripts/` is listed with a verdict of watched-to-
  detect, watched-to-abort-only, or no-control-to-delete-with-a-reason; the comprehensive-
  search shape is checked for by name; the list is derived rather than hand-written; and
  the report proposes an order rather than doing the work.

ever taken was on 2026-08-31. **Where the 16 August date came from is unknown** and was not
established. Recorded because the planning session repeated the claim to Michael as fact,
and because **a report asserting a date it had not checked is the same class as a reading
offered as a finding** — the one this session has now had overturned six times.

**Two decisions the task made and recorded, both endorsed by the planning session on
2026-08-30.**

- **Who is meant to notice: the operator, and nobody else.** A project owner in the app is
  not told and cannot find out — the diagnostics console is off by default and
  loopback-only, and the sync screen belongs to a project rather than to a server.
  **Accepted for the beta because Michael is both**, and written into `server/README.md` in
  those words. **Reopen condition: the first time somebody runs the server who is not also
  a project owner** — at which point the owner has no signal at all, and giving them one
  needs a new authenticated route and a disclosure decision about what one project's owner
  may learn about a server.
- **Staleness threshold: 48 hours.** One missed daily run is a reboot; two consecutive
  misses is a schedule that has stopped, and it bounds what is at risk to two days of
  observations. One line in `.env`. **Michael has the final say and changing it costs
  nothing.**

**What the task left open and could not close itself: the signal is a red container and a
log line, and nothing pages anybody.** The belief is now **falsifiable**, which it was
not before — but it is **not falsified automatically**, so a stopped backup stays
invisible for as long as nobody runs `docker compose ps`. **Going further needs a decision
from Michael about where a push would go** before it can be a task.

**Status:** **Done 2026-08-30.** A `backup-scheduler` service in
`docker-compose.yml` takes a backup every `TRITRACK_BACKUP_INTERVAL_HOURS`
(default 24) and comes back after a reboot, so the schedule is a declaration in
the repository rather than a cron line somebody was trusted to write. Its Docker
healthcheck runs `tritrack-backup-freshness`, which reads **the age of the newest
archive** and knows nothing about whether the loop is running — so a wedged
scheduler, an empty recipients list, a full disk and a `.env` edited last month
all go red, because to a person they are one fact. `docker compose ps` shows it;
`scripts/backup_status.sh` prints the same sentence. Absent and stale are
deliberately different sentences. Watched going green, then red, on a real stack
on 2026-08-30: an archive was taken with nobody running anything, and deleting it
turned the service `(unhealthy)` with "NO BACKUP HAS EVER BEEN TAKEN" as the last
line of Docker's own health log.

**Three answers to the questions the brief said to establish first.**

1. **Who is meant to notice: the operator, and nobody else.** The diagnostics
   console is off by default and loopback-only, and the app's sync screen belongs
   to a project rather than to a server, so neither could carry this. **A project
   owner in the app is not told and today has no way to find out** — an operator
   and a project owner may not be the same human being, and only the one holding
   the machine can fix a stopped backup. If they are different people, somebody
   has to look at `docker compose ps`; nothing in this repository can make them.
   Written down in `server/README.md` in those words rather than left implied.
2. **The staleness threshold is 48 hours and it was chosen, not inherited.** One
   missed daily run is a reboot or a slow dump, and paging somebody for that
   teaches them to ignore the one signal that would tell them backups had
   stopped — the only failure mode that puts us back where this started. Two
   consecutive misses is a schedule that has stopped. 48h bounds what is at risk
   to two days of observations: a bad week rather than a lost season. One line in
   `.env` (`TRITRACK_BACKUP_MAX_AGE_HOURS`); **Michael has the final say and the
   reasoning is in `server/README.md` so the next person can argue with the
   argument rather than the default.**
3. **The audit purge has exactly the same gap and it is NOT closed here** — see
   Discovered Scope below. It is a smaller harm and a different one: an unrun
   backup loses data, an unrun purge keeps rows past the window that justified
   holding them. **A second defect was found in it:** the command
   `server/README.md` gave cannot run in the shipped server container at all.

**One thing worth knowing about the freshness check.** The age comes from the
archive's *filename*, and a filename is believed only when its signature verifies
under that exact name — retention's own predicate (tasks 10.44/10.53), against
the same attacker. Otherwise anyone who can write into `backups/` plants
`tritrack-29991231T235959Z.age` and the staleness alarm is green forever, which
is a thing an attacker wants more than they want to delete an archive. Without
`TRITRACK_BACKUP_VERIFY_KEY` the age is still reported and labelled `UNVERIFIED`.
Not mtime, which whoever can write the directory can `touch`.

**Original spec below.**

**Status when written:** Not started. **BETA-BLOCKING, on exactly the reasoning that made task 11.70
blocking.** The end state for a person is identical: **they believe they have encrypted
backups, and the newest archive is from the week they set the server up.**
**Model:** **Opus** — the visible half is a design question about what a person sees and
when, not a cron line.
**Depends on:** 11.70, which fixed the other half of the same harm and named this one.

**What 11.70 fixed and what it did not.** A backup now *works* when it runs. **Nothing
runs it.** `server/README.md` says to *"schedule it the same way as the audit purge — a
daily cron"*, which is **a documented step a human performs and nothing checks** — the
exact class 11.70's own decision rejected when it chose the compose declaration over a
`chown` in the instructions. **The fix and the remaining gap are the same shape**, and the
gap is now the larger one: **11.70 turned a backup that fails loudly into a backup that is
never taken**, and nothing anywhere would say so.

**The smallest honest version, named by 11.70 and adopted here as the floor rather than
the ceiling: something visible names the age of the newest archive.** A person who can see
*"newest backup: 34 days old"* cannot hold the false belief. **That sentence is the
deliverable**; scheduling is how it becomes true rather than the point.

**Establish before designing:**

1. **Where does a person actually look?** The server has a diagnostics console that is off
   by default and loopback-only, and the app has a sync status screen that belongs to a
   project rather than to a server. **An operator and a project owner are not the same
   person and may not be the same human being.** Say who is meant to notice, and be honest
   if the answer is that today nobody would.
2. **What schedules it, and does the schedule check itself?** A cron entry that stops
   firing is silent in exactly the way this task exists to end. **Whatever schedules the
   backup, the age of the newest archive is the thing measured** — not whether a timer
   exists. That distinction is the whole task.
3. **Does the audit purge have the same shape?** The README points at it as the model to
   copy. **If it is also an unscheduled documented step, say so** — the class matters more
   than this instance, and copying a broken pattern is how this arrived.
4. **What is a sensible age to complain at**, and who decided? A field season's data is
   worth more than a tidy screen. Propose a number with a reason rather than inheriting a
   default.

- **Acceptance:** a backup runs without a person remembering to run it; **the age of the
  newest archive is visible to whoever is meant to care, and stale is distinguishable from
  absent**; the guard measures the archive rather than the timer, and has been watched
  going red; and the audit purge is either confirmed to be scheduled or named as having
  the same gap.

**Two facts, and the second is not the one that was expected.**

1. **Nothing runs `AuditRetentionService.purge()`.** So the retention windows the
   documentation promises — a year for sign-in events, 180 days for sync traffic —
   **describe an intention rather than what is on disk.**
2. **The command the documentation gave cannot run at all in the shipped container.**
   `dart run bin/purge_audit_logs.dart`, offered as *"e.g. a daily cron inside the
   container"*, needs a Dart SDK and source; **the server image contains a compiled binary
   and neither.** It works only on a developer's laptop. **So the documented remedy was
   never available to the person it was written for** — task 11.70's class exactly, found
   because the same question got asked twice.

**Why it is not beta-blocking, and the distinction is worth keeping.** An unrun backup
**loses data**. An unrun purge **keeps rows past their window** — a liability that grows
rather than a loss. **But it grows with other people's data in it**, which is why the
trigger is the beta rather than a date.

**SCOPE WIDENED 2026-08-31 by task 11.85's finding R-2, and the table is named because
this entry did not name it: `project_join_requests`.** Measured rather than argued — six
rejections on a fresh project left six rows, and the only bound anywhere is a 200-row cap
on what the list routes *return*, which bounds the response and not the table.

**Michael decided the design half on 2026-08-31, and he chose both options rather than
one, which is right — they solve different problems.**

> **1. Freeze the project's name onto the request at the moment it is made.** Today a
> refused requester's phone goes on showing whatever that project is currently called, so
> renaming "Field season" to something specific hands the rename to somebody you turned
> down. **This is the pattern the design already uses one column over:** the requester's
> email is copied onto the request row at request time rather than joined from elsewhere.
> The project name is the same shape of thing and gets the same treatment.
>
> **2. Expire decided requests, so a rejection does not sit on their screen for ever.**
> Michael's words: *"we wouldn't want that on their screen forever."* Correct, and it is
> also the durability bound this task already owed.
>
> **Both, because each covers what the other does not.** Expiry alone still leaks renames
> for the whole retention window. Freezing alone leaves a rejection on somebody's phone
> permanently. Neither is redundant.

**The window: 30 days, unless Michael says otherwise** — long enough that somebody who
asked and then spent three weeks out of signal still gets their answer, short enough that
it is not clutter. **Make it the same shape of knob as the other two windows here**, not a
special case.

**One detail that decides whether this reads as tidy or as broken:** when the row expires,
the card must simply be absent, not an error and not an empty state that looks like a
failure. **The person has already had the news; this is the notice being taken down, not
lost.** And expiring a rejection changes nothing about asking again — the partial unique
index only covers undecided requests, so a refused person could always ask again.

**A third retention class arrived on 2026-08-31 and belongs here rather than on its own
(task 11.81's request).** Decided join requests — approved, rejected and cleared — are
kept **deliberately**: deleting a rejected request is what would leave somebody staring at
"pending" forever, which is the defect `GET /projects/join-requests/mine` exists to
prevent. So the answer is a **retention rule, not a delete**, and it is the same
mechanism, the same scheduler and the same measurement as the two windows above. Inventory
entry 23 says this needs a bound before it can be accepted. **Pick the window and write
down why**; a rejected person has no reason to be a row on this server a year later.

**The shape is task 11.78's and should not be re-derived:** compile the purge entrypoint
into the server image, schedule it the way the backup scheduler is scheduled, and
**measure the age of the oldest surviving row rather than whether a timer exists.** That
last clause is the point — a timer that exists and does not fire is what both of these
tasks are about.

- **Acceptance:** the purge runs without a person remembering; the documented command is
  one that works in the shipped image; **the age of the oldest surviving row is visible and
  goes red when it exceeds its window**, watched going red; and the retention windows in
  the documentation describe what is on disk.

**Model:** **Opus** — the destination is a custody decision, not a copy command.
**Depends on:** 11.78. **Found by Michael on 2026-08-30**, asking what the server's own
backup was even for.

**What the archive protects against today, and what it does not.** `backup_db.sh` dumps
the server's database, encrypts it, signs it, and writes it into a folder **on the same
machine.** That covers a corrupted database, a bad migration, a botched restore. **It does
not cover losing the machine** — and the machine is a virtual machine on one laptop.

**What is actually at risk, measured rather than assumed.** The server holds fourteen
tables that also live on every device **and ten that live nowhere else**: `auth_accounts`,
`auth_sessions`, `auth_magic_links`, `auth_link_requests`, `auth_audit_log`,
`project_invites`, `sync_cursors`, `sync_seq_counter`, `sync_traffic_log` and
`tombstone_purge_floor`. **So losing the machine does not lose field data** — every device
keeps its own copy — **it loses every account, every session, the sign-in audit trail,
outstanding invitations, and the numbered line every device's sync bookmark points into.**
That last one is task 11.58's failure arriving by a different road: every device left
holding a bookmark into a line that no longer exists.

**Why this is a gap rather than a choice, and it is the strongest argument here.** The
archive is **encrypted to a key that deliberately does not live on the server**, and
signed so a restore can tell a genuine archive from a planted one. **That design only makes
sense if the file goes somewhere the server cannot read.** Something was meant to carry it.
**Nothing does** — no script, no step, no instruction anywhere in the repository.

**The decision, and it is Michael's: where does it go?** A second machine, an external
drive, object storage. **Say plainly that this does not reverse his decision of 2026-08-30
to remove the app's cloud backup** — that removed **unencrypted project data, on by
default, to a third party.** This is an archive **encrypted to a key the destination does
not hold and signed against forgery**, moved deliberately. **Those are different
propositions and the entry says so, so nobody reads one as undoing the other.**

**A third item, found on Michael's own server on 2026-08-31 and small: the failure
message names the right cause and prescribes a remedy that does not fix the commonest
case.** His first backup failed with `cannot create a file in /backups` — and the message
correctly explained the uid/gid mismatch, correctly explained why it works on a laptop and
fails on a server, and then offered **one remedy: use `scripts/server_up.sh` instead of a
raw compose line. He had used `scripts/server_up.sh`.** The directory was owned by root
from an earlier bare `docker compose up` **taken before task 11.70 landed**, and 11.70's
chosen shape — declaring the user in the compose file — **fixes new installations and
leaves existing ones stranded with no instruction.**

**This is the project's most-repeated shape one level in.** Not a message naming the wrong
cause, which 11.70 fixed, but **a message naming the right cause with an incomplete
remedy** — which is worse in one specific way: the reader follows it exactly, fails again,
and now doubts the diagnosis as well. **Add the missing branch** — if the directory exists
and is owned by somebody else, say so and give the one-line `chown` — **and a line in
`server/README.md` for installations that predate 11.70.** It is a few lines and it belongs
here because this task is already in that code.

**Two constraints that are not negotiable, both from tasks that just ran:**

- **Measure the copy, not the command.** Task 11.78's whole lesson: a timer that exists and
  does not fire is invisible. **The thing to check is that a recent archive exists at the
  destination**, in the same four-sentence shape 11.78 used — present and fresh, present
  and stale, absent, or unreachable.
- **The restore drill either exercises restoring from the off-machine copy, or says it does
  not.** Task 11.70 made the drill measure the shipped procedure again after 11.69 had
  quietly made it measure a variant. **Do not let a copy exist that no drill has ever read
  back.** A copy nobody has restored from is a belief, not a backup.

- **Acceptance:** an archive reaches a second location without a person remembering; its
  presence and age at that location are visible, with stale distinguishable from absent and
  from unreachable; a restore has been performed **from the off-machine copy** or the
  report says plainly that it has not; and the destination decision is recorded with who
  can read what is stored there.
