  them here; they are listed in Phase 11's Discovered Scope.
- **Put the three drafted inventory entries into `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` when this
  task starts, not when it finishes** — a replacement for entry 23, a replacement for
  entry 24, and a new entry 29 for the requester's read of their own pending requests.
  **All three keep the verdict `Unexamined` until somebody actually attacks them.** A new
  entry arriving already marked Hardened is the drift those entries exist to prevent.
- **Nothing about the app's database, the sync protocol, or any device in the field
  moves** — the design says so and it is what keeps this buildable in one pass.

- **Acceptance:** the design document is implemented as written, with the five decisions
  above; the name is bounded exactly as an existing name column is and the screen
  distinguishes authenticated from claimed; §4.2 carries its written exception; approvals,
  rejections and rotations appear in the audit log; the three inventory entries exist and
  say `Unexamined`; every now-false sentence is corrected; and the report says what the
  test rewrite actually cost against the estimate.

**Status:** **DONE 2026-09-02, inside task 11.124** — do not run `/11-82`. The v8 test stops at

**Model:** Sonnet.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by 11.74 while reading the migration tests; not caused by
it.**

Two things, both about the app rather than the server. **There is no populated-database
upgrade test for schema v9 at all.** And **the v8 test upgrades all the way to the latest
version rather than stopping at v8**, so it is not testing what its name says — it passes
for a reason other than the one it claims, which is this project's most-repeated shape.

**A migration test that does not stop where it says it stops cannot catch a defect

### Task 11.83 — Approved, and the project never arrives
**Status:** **DONE 2026-08-31** (`9a4d974`), **and confirmed on hardware the same day.**
Michael re-ran the walkthrough that found the defect: new project on the Mac, iPhone
requested, Mac approved, and **the iPhone showed the project joined and downloaded with
nobody touching it.** The flow 11.81 shipped is finished.

**One decision Michael made on the report, 2026-08-31, and it is settled: no limit on the
first-download volume, cellular included.** A fresh install signing in as somebody with
several historical approvals downloads all of those projects, bounded only by the server's
200-request window. **He accepts that.** Every project involved is one that person is a
member of, and every bound anybody could design needed a comparison between the device's
clock and the server's — a guess this project does not make. **Registered as an accepted
cost, not a defect, and it does not get a task.** The trigger that would reopen it is
somebody reporting a surprising cellular bill, not a code review.

**What it built.** `JoinRequestWatcher` (`lib/core/providers/join_request_watcher.dart`)
links and syncs an approved project by itself, reusing `joinApprovedProject` and
`SyncEngine` rather than copying the paging loop. `JoinRequestsCard`
(`lib/features/more/widgets/join_requests_card.dart`) replaces `PendingRequestsCard` and
narrates every outcome — pending, approved-and-downloading, approved-and-here,
approved-and-interrupted, rejected, cleared — on **both** the join screen and the
projects screen. The projects screen has pull-to-refresh. §2.3 of
`JOIN_CODE_AND_APPROVAL_DESIGN.md` is corrected in place, with the false sentence struck
through rather than deleted.

**One server change, which the task's own text did not anticipate and which the build
had to make: `GET /projects/join-requests/mine` now returns `project_id` on an approved
request, and on nothing else.** `MyJoinRequest` carried the decision and the project's
*name*; a device cannot pull a project it cannot name, and matching by name would have
been a guess. Approved-only is the disclosure argument in full: an approved requester is
already a member and `GET /projects/mine` hands them the same id, so nobody the owner has
not admitted learns a project identifier. Two integration tests pin both halves.
**The rate limit was not touched**, as instructed.

**Two things the build decided that the spec left open, both flagged for review:**

1. **The foreground check is gated on a durable "this device has join business" flag**
   (`SyncStateStore.joinWorkPending`). Without it, every device asked the server on every
   foreground — including one whose owner had chosen "Only when I ask", which task
   11.59's own suite caught. A device that has never asked to join anything now reaches
   no server at all.
2. **The sync-frequency setting does *not* suppress the poll.** Somebody who has just
   tapped "Ask to join" is asking, and the join card tells them what will happen. If the
   planning session disagrees, the gate is one condition in `_check`.

**Known consequence, stated rather than discovered:** a fresh install signing in as
somebody with several historical approvals will auto-download all of those projects, up
to the server's 200-request window. Every one is a project that person is a member of,
and the alternative bounds all needed a cross-machine clock comparison, which this task
was told not to guess at. If that is not wanted, it needs a decision and a task.
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. Small code, but the decision inside it is a design
correction and the failure it fixes is invisible.
**Depends on:** 11.81. **Found by Michael on real hardware, 2026-08-31**, on the first
two-device walkthrough of the flow 11.81 shipped.

**What he did and what happened.** New project created on the Mac. iPhone requested to
join with the code. The Mac showed the request and approved it. **The project never
appeared on the iPhone.** Nothing errored.

**This is not a defect in 11.81's build — it built what the design specified.** §2.3 of
`JOIN_CODE_AND_APPROVAL_DESIGN.md` says *"How the requester finds out they are in.
Nothing new is needed."* **That sentence is the defect**, and it was the planning
session's. It is true that the project appears in `GET /projects/mine` and that the "Join
a project" screen renders it with a Join button. It is false that nothing is needed,
because **the person has no reason to go back to that screen and nothing tells them to.**

**Confirmed on hardware, 2026-08-31**, which is what separates *the grant never happened*
from *the last mile is a manual step nobody is told about*: after the approval Michael
opened More → Join a project on the iPhone and **the project was there with a Join
button.** The server, the grant and `GET /projects/mine` are all fine. **Everything that
is wrong is on the device, after the approval** — so this task needs no measurement pass.

**The mechanism.** A project only exists on a device once
something calls `ProjectJoiner.join` — which marks it linked and runs a sync from cursor
zero. `markProjectLinked` is called from exactly two places in the app: that join, and
publishing your own project. Automatic sync (11.59) runs against the **active** project
and only when linked, so an unlinked project is not merely empty, it is not a thing the
device does anything about. `MembershipController.joinApprovedProject` exists and does
all of this correctly — **and nothing calls it without a person tapping Join.**

**The sharp version, and it is the one that should drive the fix.** The "Your requests"
card filters approved requests out of its own list
(`join_project_screen.dart`: `if (r.isPending || r.decision != 'approved')`). So at the
exact moment the news arrives, **the one element on the device that was tracking the
request goes blank** — and the thing it was replaced by is one screen away, in a list the
person has no reason to open. **The person is told nothing at the only moment they needed
telling.** That is task 11.60's class — *a person is not told the thing that happened to
them* — reappearing on the other side of the same door. 11.81 met it for rejection, which
its own report says, and missed it for approval.

**The fix is that approval completes on its own**, not that a sentence is added telling
somebody to go and tap Join. The device already polls its own requests; when one comes
back approved it should link and sync that project without being asked, and **the card
should say so while it happens rather than vanishing.** A person who was told "waiting for
approval" should next be told "you're in", and by then it should be true.

**How the device learns it was approved — decided by the planning session on 2026-08-31,
from measurement, and not left to the build.** Michael asked the right question and the
answer is not "on the next sync":

> **The 15-minute sync tick would never deliver this, not in 15 minutes and not in a
> day.** Automatic sync runs against the **active, linked** project
> (`sync_provider.dart`), and somebody joining their **first** project has no linked
> project at all — so there is no loop running to piggyback on. It also never asks
> `/projects/join-requests/mine` or `/projects/mine`. **This is not a slow path; it is
> not a path.** Any plan that says "it will arrive on the next sync" is wrong on the
> most important case.

**Today the only thing in the app that ever asks whether you were approved is the "Join a
project" screen, and only while you are looking at it** — `myJoinRequestsProvider` is
watched in exactly one place. Four changes, in this order:

1. **Poll `GET /projects/join-requests/mine` every 60 seconds while the app is in the
   foreground and this device holds an outstanding request.** **It fits the existing rate
   limit with four times the headroom and needs no server change:**
   `joinRequestListPerUser` is 60 per 15 minutes — one every 15 seconds — and that bucket
   exists, in its own author's words, so that *"a device polling for 'has the owner
   approved me yet' must not be able to deny itself the answer."* The poll was anticipated;
   it just was not built. **It is self-limiting: a device with nothing pending polls
   nothing**, and the population that ever polls is people who have asked to join in the
   last few minutes.
2. **Check once on app resume**, so somebody who closed the app and came back is told
   immediately rather than up to a minute later. This is the common real case — the
   approval usually arrives while the phone is in a pocket.
3. **Pull-to-refresh on the projects screen** (Michael asked for it, 2026-08-31). It is
   the manual override and it is what a person actually reaches for. **The only
   `RefreshIndicator` in the app today is on the Sync Status screen**, which is not where
   anybody waiting to be let into a project is looking.
4. **The news lands on the projects screen, not only the Join screen.** That is where the
   person is, and the whole defect is that the truth was one screen away from where they
   were looking.

**What this promises, stated as numbers so it can be checked rather than believed:** app
open, **at most 60 seconds** from approval to the project appearing, plus the download.
App backgrounded, **the moment they open it**. **App closed, nothing happens until they
open it, and that is not fixable here** — delivering it to a closed app means push
notifications, which need an Apple developer account this project does not yet have.
**Say that rather than implying background delivery.**

- **Do not make the download the person's decision.** It was one under the old flow
  because redemption happened on their own device in the foreground. Here the grant
  happens elsewhere, possibly hours later, and a device that knows it has been let in and
  waits to be told again is the same silence in a new place.
- **A first sync of a season's data on a phone at the end of a track is the case to get
  right.** `SyncEngine` is resumable and this must use it rather than a second copy —
  which is what `joinApprovedProject` already does. **The work is the trigger and the
  telling, not the download.**
- **Say what happens if it fails.** An interrupted first pull must leave the project
  present and behind rather than absent, and the sync surface must be able to say which.
- **Rejection and approval must be told the same way.** The card handles rejection today;
  approval should not be a second mechanism.

- **Acceptance:** on two real devices, an approved requester's project appears without
  them touching anything, and the "Your requests" card narrates it rather than going
  blank; a widget test covers approved-then-arrives; and **the false sentence in
  `JOIN_CODE_AND_APPROVAL_DESIGN.md` §2.3 is corrected in place** rather than left to be
  read again by whoever next builds from that document.

### Task 11.86 — Two red workflows from one push, and they are not the same kind of thing
**Status:** DONE 2026-08-31. All three `ref` reads in the foreground chain now come from
notifiers captured once, before the chain's first `await`; a deterministic widget test
(fakes + `Completer`s, no real timers) disposes the app mid-`syncIfDue` and proves the
join check still runs safely afterward — verified to fail on the pre-fix code with the
exact original stack trace, and to pass on the fix. Offline suite: 1571 passed, 0 failed.
`backup_restore_drill` is a separate, pre-existing red — see Discovered Scope, new task
needed.
**Model:** Sonnet. Small, but **item 3 is a triage and must not be answered by guessing.**
**Depends on:** 11.83.

**1. `ref` used after the widget is gone, in 11.83's own new code.** The offline suite is
1569 passed and one failed, and the failure is thrown *after the test completed*:

```
Bad state: Using "ref" when a widget is about to or has been unmounted is unsafe.
  _TriTrackAppState._checkJoinRequests (app.dart:104)
  _TriTrackAppState._syncOnForeground  (app.dart:83)
```

**This is a real defect, not a test artefact.** `didChangeAppLifecycleState` fires
`unawaited(_syncOnForeground())`, which awaits twice and then calls
`ref.read(joinRequestWatcherProvider.notifier)`. If the app is backgrounded or torn down
while that chain is in flight, the read lands on a disposed element. **In production that
is a person closing the app a second or two after opening it** — not exotic.

**Fix the class, not the line.** There are **three** `ref` reads in that chain — the stuck
departure, `syncControllerProvider`, and the join check. The third failed only because it
is last and has the most awaits in front of it; **all three are the same unsafe pattern
and the earlier two are latent.** One mechanism covering all three, not three guards.

**And note what caught it: nothing that was watching for it.** The test that failed is
`automatic_sync_test.dart`, which is about task 11.59, and it caught this in teardown by
luck of the framework's post-test checks. **There is no test that disposes the app while a
join check is in flight.** Add one; that is the check that should have found this.

**2. Two of 11.83's decisions are ratified by the planning session and this task does not
revisit them:** the durable `joinWorkPending` flag stays, and the sync-frequency setting
continues **not** to suppress the join poll — "Only when I ask" is scoped to records, and
somebody who has just tapped "Ask to join" is asking.

**3. `backup_restore_drill` is also red, and it has nothing to do with any of the above.**
It appeared in the same run as the four invite-404 instruments and it is **not** one of
them — no invitation is anywhere near it.

> **Do not let one explanation cover both.** The four invite failures have a known,
> single, boring cause and this does not. **Establish first whether the drill was already
> red before this push** — workflow history, not code — and then whether it is a broken
> instrument or a genuine backup failure. **Task 11.70's entire finding was a message
> naming the wrong cause**; an answer of "probably the same thing" here would be that
> defect committed on purpose.
>
> If it is a genuine backup failure, **stop and report it rather than fixing it here** —
> Michael's server backups are the one place on this project where a wrong guess costs
> data.

- **Acceptance:** the offline suite is green, with disposal covered by a test that disposes
  the app mid-check; all three `ref` reads in that chain are made safe by one mechanism;
  and **the drill's red is explained with evidence and named as either a broken instrument
  or a finding with a task number.** "Fixed by re-running" is not an explanation.

### Task 11.87 — The viewshed boundary is a staircase, and the code meant to fix it cannot

> **CLOSED 2026-09-02 by the planning session, after four addenda and three designs.** Read this
> block before the entry below it, because the entry describes a design that no longer exists.
>
> **Where it ended: a flat raster fill and no boundary line at all** — the same shape it started
> from — by Michael's decision on a device, after a vector fill was reported *"extremely laggy."*
> `viewshed_contour.dart` and its tests are **deleted, not commented out**, which is this
> project's rule and the right call.
>
> **1. The original complaint is moot rather than fixed, and that is the honest word.** Michael
> reported the boundary line and the fill visibly disagreeing. **It was never reproduced in the
> execution environment**, and the design that carried it has since been replaced twice and then
> removed. **There is no boundary line now, so the two objects that could disagree do not both
> exist.** The complaint cannot recur in that form. **Do not record it as fixed** — nobody ever
> saw it fixed.
>
> **2. The 35 km / 40 km split stands, and the reasoning is ratified rather than tolerated.**
> `ViewshedConfig.maxRangeMeters` is **35 km** — Michael's field figure — and the drag ceiling is
> **40 km**. They differ on purpose: **the drag ceiling is a padded bound on what a person may
> draw, and the viewshed is a prediction the app renders as fact over real terrain.** Rounding
> the *prediction* up would have the app assert visibility across ground where a tag would not be
> heard anyway. **Two constants that deliberately disagree, each with its reason written where it
> lives, are not the defect this project warns about** — that one is two constants agreeing by
> coincidence. **Reopen trigger:** a field report that 35 km is short, not a code review. Compute
> is O(range²) — 41 ms at 10 km, 454 ms at 40 km on a desktop — so raising it is not free.
>
> **3. A seam this task's own acceptance criteria promised no longer exists.** The original design
> kept contour and painter separable **so a feathered band could be swapped in later without a
> rewrite.** That separation was retired in the second addendum and the whole vector path is now
> gone. **If anyone ever wants the feathered band Michael and the planning session discussed on
> 2026-08-31, it is a build, not a swap.** Recorded here so nobody goes looking for a seam that
> was promised in writing and then removed.

**Status:** Done, 2026-09-02. Landed on a flat raster fill with no boundary line — the same
shape this task started from — after two vector approaches in between, both retired for real,
confirmed reasons rather than abandoned mid-stream. See all four 2026-09-02 addenda below for

vector boundary and raster fill unified into one filled vector polygon, at Michael's request;

**Model:** Sonnet — every judgement call is made below.

**Resolution, 2026-09-02.**

**The two range constants (added 2026-09-02 items) are done.**
1. `_maxBearingRangeMeters` (`lib/features/map/screens/map_screen.dart`) raised 20 km → 40 km,

2. `ViewshedConfig.maxRangeMeters` (`lib/viewshed/viewshed.dart`) raised 10 km → **35 km** —
   deliberately *not* 40 km. The drag ceiling is a display bound with its own built-in margin
   above the real figure; this bounds an actual physical prediction ("could I have heard the
   collar from here"), so the honest number is Michael's reported range itself, not the padded
   one. Documented as a judgement call in the doc comment. Cost measured (not guessed) on a
   desktop (M-series Mac, not a phone) with a synthetic 90 m-cell DEM at the app's actual fixed
   cell size (`kDemCellSizeMeters`): 10 km ≈ 41 ms, 20 km ≈ 116 ms, 35 km ≈ 344 ms, 40 km ≈
   454 ms — confirms the O(range²) scaling. A phone will be slower, but the computation already
   runs off the UI thread with a progress bar and a 20-second timeout with a clear failure
   message, so this is a longer wait, not a stall.

**The boundary fix is done as specified: vector, not pixels.** `lib/viewshed/viewshed_contour.dart`
(new) runs marching squares on the *continuous* bilinear-upsampled-and-blurred field
`viewshed_overlay.dart` already built (extracted into a shared, now-public
`buildViewshedBlurredField`, used by both the fill PNG and the contour tracer so they can never
disagree about where the edge is) at the 0.5 iso-level, giving sub-cell-accurate crossing
points, then rounds them with Chaikin corner-cutting (3 iterations by default). Drawn as a
`flutter_map` `PolylineLayer` over the existing flat translucent PNG fill (the fill's own
per-pixel outline coloring was removed — the vector line is now the only boundary, and
`renderViewshedPng` no longer takes an `outlineArgbColor`). Handles multiple disjoint visible
regions and holes (donut shapes) as separate closed loops — tested directly. A region touching
the edge of the computed extent still closes into a loop (one all-zero padding ring added
before tracing) rather than leaving an open curve.

**Both measured numbers, reported as the task asked.**
- **Upsample factor collapses well before 35 km.** At the app's fixed 90 m DEM cell size:
  10 km → factor 9, 20 km → 4, 35 km → 2, 40 km → 2 (target was 11, for ~8 m rendered cells).
  So at the now-default 35 km range, the *old* pixel-based smoothing would have been running at
  essentially no upsampling at all — this is the second, independent defect the task predicted,
  confirmed. It no longer matters for the boundary's smoothness: Chaikin's corner-cutting adds
  curvature regardless of the base contour's density, so the fix does not depend on a high
  upsample factor. `_maxFineDimension` (2048) was **not** raised, per the task's explicit
  instruction — the vector fix is what removes the need to.
- **DEM cell size is a hard-coded constant, not something that needed a device measurement**:
  `kDemCellSizeMeters = 90.0` (`lib/viewshed/dem_tile_store.dart`) — every DEM tile this app
  generates or fetches is resampled to exactly this, by design (`DemTileStore`'s doc comment:
  "no longer a resolution slider").

**The comment claiming smoothness is gone, replaced with the actual finding.**
`renderViewshedPng`'s doc comment now says plainly that the old per-pixel-outline approach's
claim was false (a field screenshot proved it), names why in one sentence (thresholding a
blurred binary field can only bevel corners, not draw a curve), and says what replaced it.
The "no real line-of-sight accuracy" sentence is kept, in both files that now touch this
boundary.

**The DEM is not resampled.** The fix only changes how the existing raster's boundary is
drawn; `ViewshedComputer.compute`'s output is untouched.

**The two 11.105-sweep items are also closed, not left for later:**
- **A failed computation now displays its message.** `ComputationFailed` was reachable only via

- **The "smaller radius" phrase does not exist in shipped code.** Checked directly (grep +

**Tests.** `test/viewshed/viewshed_contour_test.dart` (new): `marchingSquaresLoops` on
synthetic fields (empty, single block, two disjoint blocks, a donut with an inner+outer loop)

Full suite: 2005 passed, 0 failed (15 pre-existing skips, unrelated). `flutter analyze`: clean.

**Addendum, 2026-09-02, same day: Michael sent a screenshot showing the line and the fill
visibly disagreeing** — the vector boundary looped through empty map in some places and left
purple fill outside the line in others, not the small cosmetic mismatch a smoothed line over a
raster fill should ever show. Two real defects were found and fixed while chasing it, but
**the exact defect the screenshot shows was not reproduced or confirmed in this environment**,
because this environment cannot run the app on a device — that gap is why this is an addendum,
not a re-closed task.

**What was found, verified two independent ways (a synthetic-field unit check and a pixel-level
cross-check against the actual rendered PNG's alpha channel), and fixed:**
1. **The raw marching-squares boundary was being handed to Chaikin directly — tens of
   thousands of points for one loop (22,704 on one measured case), the overwhelming majority of
   them collinear "staircase" points a straight run of open sky produces one-per-grid-cell.**
   That is real: wasteful for `flutter_map` to draw regardless of anything else, and (see next
   item) the thing that made the second defect possible. Fixed by a new
   `simplifyClosed` (Douglas-Peucker, written iteratively rather than recursively so a
   pathological run of near-but-not-quite-collinear points can't blow the call stack) run
   *before* Chaikin. Measured: the same 2838-point raw loop that produced 22,704 Chaikin points
   fell to 1504 after simplifying, then 6016 after 2 Chaikin iterations (down from 3, see
   below) — an ~4x reduction overall.
2. **Once edges can be genuinely long — which they can *only* become after simplifying — plain
   1/4-fraction Chaikin cutting is a real, severe bug, not a hypothetical one.** Measured
   directly: on one real (simplified) loop, cutting a flat 1/4 of every edge moved a point by
   up to **61.9 fine pixels** (at the case's factor, on the order of 500 m) — a corner-rounding
   step should never move a point by half a kilometer. `chaikinSmoothClosed` now caps the cut
   distance at a small constant (`maxCutFinePixels`, default 2.0) instead of a bare fraction: on
   the short edges a raw (unsimplified) boundary produces the cap never binds and nothing
   changes, but a long straight run stops being dragged in from the middle. Also reduced the
   default `chaikinIterations` from 3 to 2, since simplifying first means fewer, more
   meaningful corners are left for Chaikin to round — the earlier 3 was tuned against the
   unsimplified boundary's density.
3. **Re-verified end to end after both fixes**: a pixel-level cross-check that reads the actual
   rendered PNG's alpha channel and checks every contour point lands within a few pixels of a
   transparent/opaque transition found ≤0.5% of points off by more than 3 fine pixels, with the
   rest at or under sub-pixel accuracy — consistent with ordinary cosmetic smoothing, not a
   structural mismatch.

**What was checked and is very unlikely to be it:** the coordinate mapping from a contour
point back to lat/lon (`_finePointToLatLng`) was cross-checked point-by-point against the
independently-derived inverse of the exact mapping `OverlayImageLayer`/`OverlayImage` use
(bounds stretched linearly, pixel (0,0) = north-west) — no offset or axis-swap found. The
marching-squares stitching (which point connects to which) was checked for "jump" distance
between consecutive points in a traced loop — always ≤√2 fine pixels, meaning no loop was ever
built by wrongly linking unrelated parts of the raster together.

**What this addendum could not do, and is why it is not marked resolved:** confirm that
defects 1–2 above are *the* defect in Michael's screenshot, rather than *a* defect that happened
to be real and worth fixing regardless. The screenshot was taken against the version shipped
before this addendum — flat-fraction Chaikin directly on the raw (always-short-edged) boundary,
no simplification step existed yet — and by the measurements above, flat-fraction cutting on an
always-≤1.4-fine-pixel raw edge should not itself have produced the large deviation the
screenshot shows. So the current best guess is either (a) a stale build/hot-reload on the device
that hadn't picked up the fix, or (b) something in `flutter_map`'s own rendering of a
several-thousand-point polyline that this headless environment cannot see. (b) is meaningfully
less likely now regardless, since the polyline handed to it is ~4x shorter.

**What Michael needs to do:**
1. Nothing blocking. Committed, working tree clean.
2. **Do a full rebuild (not a hot reload) and look again.** If the line still visibly disagrees
   with the fill after that, it's evidence for (b) above — flag it back with a fresh screenshot,
   ideally at the same map location/zoom so before/after can be compared directly, since that
   would mean the geometry checks in this addendum, thorough as they were, missed something a
   real device run would catch.
3. **Look at a real device regardless of (2)'s outcome.** Still true from the first resolution:
   nobody has looked at the actual drawn line on a phone in this task, only at test output.
4. The 35 km vs. 40 km split (`maxRangeMeters` vs. the drag ceiling) is still an open judgement
   call from the first resolution above, unrelated to this addendum.

#### Michael's range figure, 2026-09-02, and the two constants it corrects

**Trackers he knows report picking up tags at around 35 km** in good conditions from
elevation — a mountain top to a valley. **He has set the drag cap at 40 km.** That is field
report rather than a datasheet, and it beats both numbers currently in this repository.

1. **Change task 11.131's maximum drag length from 20 km to 40 km.** 11.131 chose 20 km as
   *"roughly twice the best realistic ground-to-ground detection distance for a handheld Yagi at
   150–152 MHz"* and **flagged it as the number it could defend rather than one it had
   measured** — which is exactly why it was put to Michael. It clamps rather than refuses, so
   the change is one constant and whatever test asserts the clamp. **Restate the reason in the
   code as a field report, not a calculation**, so the next person does not re-derive it from
   equipment specifications and get 20 again.
2. **Then look at `ViewshedConfig.maxRangeMeters`, hard-coded at 10 km**, which is the other
   half of this task's own third item — the failure message that says *"try a smaller radius"*
   about a control nobody has. **A viewshed computed to 10 km cannot show terrain that a signal
   reaching 35 km crossed**, and the person most likely to run a viewshed is standing on the
   high ground where that happens. **Say whether 10 km is still the right number given the
   figure above.** If raising it is expensive — it is a DEM-sampling cost, and this task is
   already measuring the upsample factor and cell size — **say what it would cost rather than
   raising or keeping it silently.**

> **These two constants are the same question asked twice — how far does this signal go — and
> until today both answers came from reasoning rather than from anybody who had tracked a
> collar.** Keep them consistent, or say why they differ.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Raised by Michael from a field screenshot, 2026-08-31**, with
the observation that the boundary's resolution *"reminds me of the graphics quality from
Wolfenstein 3D."*

**READ THIS FIRST, added 2026-08-31.** Until task 11.95 landed, **the automatic viewshed
never completed at all** — an error thrown past a `try` jumped the `finally` that ends the
computation. So every judgement anybody has made about how this overlay behaves on launch
was made about a feature that was not running. **It runs now**, and the first pictures of it
show a large purple polygon over the terrain at a 200-metre zoom with several of the
project's own bearings off screen. **Michael's hardware look decides whether that needs a
change**; do not assume the launch behaviour is settled just because it is old.

**The smoothing already exists and does not work, which is the actual finding.**
`viewshed_overlay.dart` upsamples the binary visibility raster to ~8 m pixels by bilinear
interpolation, runs a 3×3 box blur, and its own comment claims this makes the boundary
*"read as a smooth curve rather than a (finer, but still faceted) diamond lattice."*
**The screenshot is evidence that claim is false** — so this is not "add smoothing", it is
a control that does not do the job it documents.

**Why it cannot work, in principle rather than in tuning.** The last step **thresholds the
blurred field back to binary at 0.5** and traces the outline on that. Thresholding a
blurred binary field returns approximately the boundary you started with, with the corners
beveled. **It can cut corners; it cannot make a curve.** The 45° facets in the screenshot
are that bevel — the code doing exactly what it was written to do.

**Two things to measure on the way through, and report as numbers.**

- **The actual upsample factor on a real device.** `viewshedUpsampleFactor` takes
  `min(target, 2048 ÷ grid width)`, so over a large extent the factor falls silently
  toward 1 and **the smoothing stops happening entirely with nothing reporting it.** If
  that is what is happening it is a second, independent defect, and the more interesting
  one.
- **The DEM cell size actually in use.** 30 m against 90 m changes what "smooth" can mean
  at all.

**The fix: stop drawing the boundary as pixels.** Run marching squares on the
**continuous** blurred field at the 0.5 iso-level — that gives a sub-cell-accurate
polyline — smooth it (Chaikin or Catmull-Rom), and draw it with `flutter_map`'s polyline
over the existing translucent fill. Antialiased, resolution-independent, and **crisp at
every zoom**, which fixes something nobody has reported yet: the overlay is a PNG rendered
once at fixed pixel size, so zooming in currently makes it worse.

**TWO MORE ITEMS, added 2026-08-31 from task 11.105's sweep — this is now the viewshed task
rather than the viewshed-boundary task.**

- **A viewshed that fails tells nobody anything.** `ComputationFailed` is referenced only in
  the file that declares it, and the map's progress bar **renders only the *running* case** —
  so on failure the bar simply vanishes and the person is told nothing. Task 11.105's sweep
  wrote a real sentence into that state, **because that is what a renderer would use, and
  nothing draws it.** **A message nobody can reach is not a message.**
- **The failure message points at a control that does not exist.** The 10 km range is
  hard-coded, so *"try a smaller radius"* describes something a person cannot do. **The
  shipped wording works around it; decide whether a range control is worth having** — and if
  the answer is no, the message must stop implying one.

**Michael's decision, 2026-08-31: a sharp line, not a feathered band**, and the reasoning
is kept because it is better than the conclusion. The honest object is a band about one
DEM cell wide — 30 to 90 m — because that is the resolution at which visibility is known.
**But at the 200 m scale bar of a working field view, an honestly-drawn band is a third to
a half the width of the features underneath it**: not a subtle halo, a smear that swallows
the map. It would be both honest and legible only at zooms nobody uses. **So: a sharp
line, and the uncertainty told in words somewhere a person will read it, rather than drawn
at a width that makes the display unusable.**

**The feathered band is the recorded backup, not a dead idea.** Keep the seam: **contour
extraction and painting must be separate**, so switching is a painter swap rather than a
rewrite. **Do not build the second painter** — that is speculative work after the decision
is made. Build the seam.

**One line this task may not cross, and it is research integrity rather than style.**
There is a difference between making the boundary *look* smoother and making it *more
accurate*, and **only the first is available here.** Do not resample the DEM to a finer
grid before running the viewshed: that produces a genuinely smoother boundary by
**inventing terrain nobody measured**, and this app's viewsheds answer *"could I have
heard that collar from here"*, which ends up in a methods section. **Keep the existing
honest sentence that this adds no line-of-sight accuracy**, and make sure whatever
replaces it still says so.

- **Acceptance:** the boundary is a smoothed vector polyline that stays crisp when zoomed;
  the upsample factor and DEM cell size are reported as measured numbers; contour and
  painter are separable; the DEM is not resampled; and the comment claiming smoothness is
  either true or gone.

**Second addendum, 2026-09-02, same day: the mismatch is fixed — a follow-up screenshot shows
the line and the fill tracking each other closely — and Michael asked the design question the
whole two-object approach was always going to invite: "if the boundary line accurately
represents the viewshed then can't you fill in the line? It looks currently like the boundary
line and the purple infill are separately drawn objects."** They were, by this task's own
original design (a raster PNG fill under a vector polyline, per the acceptance criteria's
"contour and painter are separable"). **That design is now retired — with Michael's live
go-ahead, since he asked the question rather than the plan asking it.**

The visible region is drawn as one `flutter_map` `PolygonLayer`, filling the exact same
Chaikin-smoothed vector loops the boundary was already traced from — not a second painter,
the *same* loops, fill and border in one draw call. New `groupViewshedLoopsIntoPolygons`
(viewshed_contour.dart) turns `traceViewshedContour`'s flat loop list into fillable
outer-boundary-plus-holes polygons (a viewshed can have several disjoint visible regions, and
a region can have its own holes from local occlusion; a hole two levels deep is attached to
its *immediate* parent, not the outermost ancestor — tested directly for all four shapes:
single loop, two disjoint loops, a simple donut, and a nested outer/hole/island). This removes
`renderViewshedPng` and the PNG-fill machinery entirely (deleted, not left dead — nothing
called it anymore) along with the `OverlayImageLayer` it fed; `ViewshedBlurredField`/
`buildViewshedBlurredField` stay, since the vector boundary is still traced from that
continuous field.

**One structural finding worth recording, from chasing the original mismatch before this
retirement:** it exposed a real, severe bug the acceptance criteria's "contour and painter are
separable" design would have hit eventually regardless of the specific mismatch reported.
Marching squares alone emits one point per crossed grid cell — thousands, for a real
viewshed's whole boundary — and handing that directly to Chaikin smoothing is both wasteful
and, once a simplification pass is added to fix the waste (new `simplifyClosed`,
Douglas-Peucker, written iteratively rather than recursively so a pathological run of points
can't blow the call stack), genuinely dangerous: plain 1/4-fraction Chaikin cutting on a long
simplified edge moved a point by up to **61.9 fine pixels (~500 m on one measured case)** —
nowhere near the corner it was supposed to round. Fixed by capping the cut distance at a small
constant (`maxCutFinePixels`, default 2.0) instead of a bare fraction. Point count on one real
case: 2838 raw → 1504 after simplifying → ~6000 after 2 Chaikin iterations (default dropped
from 3 to 2, since simplifying first leaves fewer, more meaningful corners to round) — down
from 22,704 with the original unsimplified, 3-iteration approach.

**Still true, and now even more directly testable:** what was checked and found *not* to be
the original mismatch's cause — the fine-pixel-to-lat/lon coordinate mapping (cross-checked
against the independently-derived inverse of the exact mapping `OverlayImageLayer` used) and
the marching-squares stitching (checked for wrong-jump distance between consecutive loop
points, always ≤√2 fine pixels) — both still hold, and now feed the single rendered polygon
directly rather than two objects that could drift apart.

**What Michael needs to do:**
1. Nothing blocking. Committed, working tree clean.
2. **Still true: look at a real device.** This removes the two-object design his own question
   identified as the likely deeper issue, but nobody has looked at the single filled polygon on
   a phone yet either.
3. The 35 km vs. 40 km split and the un-reproduced-in-this-environment original mismatch are

**Third addendum, 2026-09-02, same day: Michael reported the vector-filled `PolygonLayer` from
the second addendum as "extremely laggy" on a real device, and asked to go back to just the
raster fill with no boundary at all.** Done, literally: `renderViewshedPng` — deleted in the
second addendum — is restored verbatim (flat translucent fill, no per-pixel outline; that part
was already retired correctly in the *first* addendum and stays retired), `map_screen.dart`
draws it via `OverlayImageLayer` again, and nothing calls `PolygonLayer`/`groupViewshedLoopsIntoPolygons`/
`traceViewshedContour` for the viewshed anymore.

**Why this is plausible as the actual cause, not just a guess to appease a complaint:**
`flutter_map`'s own `Polygon` documentation warns that a *translucent* fill (`color`'s alpha
not 0 or 1 — which the viewshed fill always is, since overall opacity is user-adjustable) costs
real performance because its internal canvas has to be drawn to and saved far more often. On
top of that, `PolygonLayer` re-projects and repaints every point of every polygon on every
frame during pan/zoom — several thousand points per loop even after this task's own
simplification work — where the raster approach draws a bitmap once and then GPU-samples it
like any other map tile, independent of how complex the underlying shape was. A static bitmap
being cheap to pan/zoom and a many-thousand-point translucent vector shape being expensive to
redraw every frame is exactly the asymmetry "extremely laggy" describes.

**`viewshed_contour.dart` (marching squares, `simplifyClosed`, `chaikinSmoothClosed`,
`groupViewshedLoopsIntoPolygons`) is left in the tree, not deleted.** It is unused by
production code as of this addendum, correct, and fully tested (test/viewshed/viewshed_contour_test.dart,
15 tests, all passing) — kept rather than deleted because "go back to the raster fill for now"
reads as a live performance tradeoff, not "the vector approach was wrong and should never come
back." **This is a judgement call, not something Michael asked for either way — flagged for
the planning session in case the project's usual "delete code once you're certain it's unused"
rule should apply here anyway.** If a future task wants the boundary smoothed again, the path
back is a cheaper rendering strategy on the same already-tested geometry (e.g. baking the
polygon into a bitmap once instead of redrawing it as vectors every frame) rather than
rebuilding the marching-squares/simplify/Chaikin pipeline from scratch.

### Task 11.88 — Checks that have never passed where it matters, and could not say why
**Status:** **DONE 2026-08-31 for the reporting fix, the backup drill, and the
never-passed list — commits `e22e986`, `b884a7f`, `9f25462`. The Broken-control workflow's
own red is now two DIFFERENT, newly-discovered problems, neither owned by this task.**
**Model:** Sonnet for the first two items; the third is whatever they reveal.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by 11.86, which was told not to guess at it and did not,
and widened by 11.85's push.**

**Resolution, 2026-08-31.**

**Reporting (item 2): fixed and proven, twice, by real failures rather than a synthetic
one.** `gate_smoke_test.sh`'s `run_instrument` now greps a failing log for
FAIL/ERROR/ADMITTED/traceback lines with 8 lines of trailing context (a finding's
explanation often continues on lines that do not repeat the marker word — the drill's own
uid:gid values sit on the line *after* the one that says FAIL, and a bare per-line grep
would have dropped them exactly as `tail -n 5` did), and the full per-instrument logs are
now uploaded as a CI artifact (`gate-instrument-logs`) whenever any instrument fails. Both
halves were watched working on real, organic failures, not a deliberately-broken one: the
drill's own log (below) and one occurrence of an unbaselined `gate_c_adversarial_pass`
finding (see Discovered Scope) both became legible in the console, and the artifact
downloaded cleanly (21 files, 37 KB) from
`https://github.com/dynamic-and-active-systems-lab/tritrack/actions/runs/33398725098`.

**The backup drill (item 1): task 11.70 holds. Confirmed from the runner, not guessed.**
The uploaded log from a real failing run reads, once the build-log noise around it is set
aside: *"the backup container runs as '1001:1001', but this drill runs as 1001:1001"* — an
exact match. **11.86's guess that the fix did not hold on Linux was wrong, and it was
right not to act on it rather than guess further.** The check still failed because of a
second, separate, previously-invisible bug: step 0 asks the container who it is *before*
the backup image is ever built, so a fresh checkout's implicit `docker compose run` build
prints its own progress text onto the same stdout the check reads, ahead of the real
value, corrupting the comparison. Fixed by building the image on its own line first.
`backup_restore_drill` now **passes on the real GitHub Actions Linux runner for the first
time since task 11.70 landed** — 0 for 7 before this fix, confirmed at

**1. `backup_restore_drill` has never once passed on the real GitHub Actions runner.** It
has failed at the same step — *"the shipped compose file decides who the backup container
is"*, added by task 11.70 — on **every** CI run since 11.70 landed on 2026-08-30. It
passes 39/39 locally on Michael's Mac under Docker Desktop, **and that is not evidence it
is fine: the drill's own comments say Docker Desktop hides exactly this class of bug.**
The platform the check and the fix were both written for is a real Linux host, and that is
the only platform where it has never worked.

> **This costs 11.70 part of its verdict, and the plan says so rather than leaving the
> claim standing.** 11.70 is recorded as *"an operator on Linux now gets an encrypted
> archive, and the drill measures the shipped procedure again rather than a variant of
> it."* **The first half still stands** — Michael's own server takes backups and
> `backup_status.sh` reports their age. **The second half does not**: the drill has never
> measured the shipped procedure on a real Linux host. That is not a data-loss finding, it
> is an unverified guarantee, and the difference matters.

**2. The harness guarantees that a well-behaved instrument's finding is thrown away.**
11.86 could not read the actual uid/gid values the runner produces, and the reason is
structural rather than incidental. `gate_smoke_test.sh:226` prints `tail -n 5` of a failing
instrument's log, and the per-instrument log file is never uploaded anywhere. **`tail -n 5`
assumes the failure is the last thing an instrument says.** Any instrument that tears down,
cleans up, or prints a banner after failing has its finding pushed out of the window — and
tearing down after a failure is *correct* behaviour. **So the better an instrument
behaves, the more likely the harness is to discard what it found.**

**This is the project's own rule — an instrument's last words must be a finding, not a
name — inverted by the thing that prints them.** The four invite-404 instruments were
readable only by luck: their assertion happened to fall inside the last five lines.

**CONFIRMED LIVE, 2026-08-31.** Michael's latest run shows the reporting defect exactly as
described. The console now reads:

```
DRILL FAILED during: 0. The shipped compose file decides who the backup container is
Tearing down
  removed throwaway key and drill volumes
```

**It names the step and not the values.** *An instrument's last words must be a finding,
not a name* — and here they are literally a name followed by a teardown banner. **This is
the second run in a row where the thing that would explain the failure was thrown away by
the harness rather than by the instrument.**

**Do the reporting finding first.** Until a failing instrument can say what it found,
nothing else on that workflow can be diagnosed either — this is not specific to the drill. **Fix
it as a class**: print the failure lines themselves rather than a fixed tail (grep the log
for the instrument's own failure marker), **and** upload the full per-instrument log as a
CI artifact on failure, so the next person has the whole thing rather than an excerpt
somebody chose in advance.

**Then resolve step 0 against the real value.** With the actual numbers in hand, decide
whether task 11.70's fix for the backup container's operating user holds on a real Linux
host. **11.86's guess is that it does not, and 11.86 was right not to act on it** — that
guess is written here so it can be checked, not inherited.

**If the answer is that backups on a real Linux host run as the wrong user, stop and
report it before fixing.** Michael's backups are the one place on this project where a
wrong guess costs data, and 11.78 already had one report about them turn out to be false.

- **Acceptance, resolved 2026-08-31:** a failing instrument's finding is legible from the
  GitHub Actions console **and** its full log is downloadable — met, demonstrated by real
  failures rather than a deliberately-broken one. **The Broken-control workflow's healthy
  run is clean, with the compose-project mismatch named rather than worked around** — met;
  the mismatch is fixed and confirmed, and the healthy run reached and passed against the
  real server on a re-run. The drill's real uid/gid mismatch is quoted from the runner —
  met (1001:1001 = 1001:1001, an exact match). The drill now **passes** on the runner —
  met, for the first time since 11.70 landed. **The list of instruments that have never
  passed in CI exists and is written into the plan** — met, table above. **11.70's entry is
  corrected to say what was and was not verified** — met, below. **Not met by this task,
