### Task 11.89 — R-1: a stranger chooses what the second line of your approval tile says
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-01.** The rule is an allowlist; R-1 is closed in §22.4, verified
live (probe 9's name attacks now 24 of 24 refused, its two baseline entries deleted, eleven
positive controls accepted and stored byte-exact) and on screen (the rendering test asserts
the property rather than the two characters). **What widening it costs an existing row is
measured in both directions**, not stated — `test/data/sync/name_rule_widened_existing_rows_test.dart`.
**Below the line** — below §4's bar, and round 9 measured why.

> **Michael's decision, 2026-09-02, on the one item the build flagged as a product choice
> rather than a security one: brackets stay refused.** The allowlist necessarily refuses more
> than the two characters R-1 named — brackets, at-signs, slashes, symbols and emoji are all
> outside "letters, marks, digits, dashes, spaces, apostrophes, full stops and commas", so
> **`Dana Reyes (PhD)` is refused.** The build offered to put brackets back (one character
> class, one place, tests naming where) and **Michael declined.** The reasoning it gave is
> the reason to accept it: **R-1's payload was an address on a second line, and the same
> address on one line is the same forgery with the break taken out** — so a rule that stops
> the break and allows the payload has stopped the wrong half.
>
> **The reopen trigger, so this is a decision and not an assumption:** somebody joins whose
> real name contains a refused character and is told to drop part of their own name. That is
> a cost paid by a person rather than by the project, and it is the only thing that should
> reopen this. Nobody on the project has such a name today, and the refusal names the exact
> character, so the failure is legible rather than mysterious.

**Model:** **Opus, medium — raised 2026-08-31.** **The regex is the easy part; the
decision underneath it is not** — this changes validation on a **synced** column, so the
blast radius is rows already written on devices in the field.
**Depends on:** **task 11.84's item 3, and this matters.** 11.84 measures what a device
does when a push is refused by the name validator. **Do not widen a validator before you
know what a refusal costs** — widening it is what turns that latent question into rows
that actually get refused. **Also on task 11.122, added 2026-09-01 — and it is met:
11.122's items 1 and 2 shipped on 2026-09-01 (`aa2ded4`), which is all this task
depended on. Item 3 became task 11.124 and this task does not wait for it.** The held-row
screen no longer tells anybody there is nothing they can do, so widening the rule no
longer multiplies a false sentence.

> **11.84 answered the question and the answer was the good one — and it found a worse
> one next to it.** A `Users` row refused for a malformed name is **a reported rejection,
> not a loop**: held once, shown on the sync status screen, never re-offered while
> unchanged, re-offered automatically once corrected. Measured against the real
> `RowValidator`, and the measurement was watched to fail with the suppression removed.
> **So the loop this task feared does not exist.**
>
> **What does exist is the sentence the person reads when it happens.** The held-row
> screen tells them it is *"a fault in the app... not something wrong with what you
> recorded"* and that *"nothing you can do in the app will change the answer."* Both are
> false for a name refusal — editing the name fixes it, measured. **This task widens the
> rule, which is precisely what turns rows already sitting on field devices into rows that
> meet that sentence.** Task 11.122 makes the fallback stop asserting a cause it cannot
> know. **Do not ship a wider rule onto devices before it has.**

**The finding** (`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §22.4). The name a stranger types when
asking to join refuses control characters and bidirectional overrides but **not the two
Unicode line-separator characters, which Flutter treats as hard line breaks.** So a
requester can put a second line — an email address, say — into the owner's approval tile.

**Why it is below the bar, measured rather than assumed:** 11.85 looked at the actual
tile. **The title is the address the server authenticated and is untouched**, and the
claimed name always sits underneath it after the words "Says they are". The impersonation
does not reach the line a person is meant to trust. **That holds because of a layout, and
a layout is not a control** — which is the reason this gets a number instead of a shrug.

**The thing that makes this more than a regex.** That regex is the **shared** declaration
`Users.first_name` and `Users.last_name` use. **Widening it means a `Users` row that
already contains one of these characters starts failing validation on the sync path**, on
devices in the field, for a row that was legal when it was written. That is the same
consequence 11.81's own Discovered Scope entry records, and **it is a decision, not a
typo.**

- **Say what happens to an existing row that the widened rule refuses** — and say it
  before changing the rule. If 11.84 found that a refused push loops rather than reports,
  **this task does not ship until that is fixed**, because widening the rule multiplies
  the rows that hit it.
- **A line separator is not the last character Flutter will surprise somebody with.**
  Prefer a rule stated as what a name may *contain* over a list of what it may not —
  **a hand-maintained list of forbidden characters is already wrong**, and this finding is
  the proof: the previous list was written deliberately, three days ago, by somebody
  thinking about exactly this attack.
- **Do not fix this by changing the tile's layout instead.** The layout is why the finding
  is below the bar; making the layout the fix means the next layout change silently
  reopens it.

- **Acceptance:** a name cannot introduce a line break on the approval tile; the rule is
  expressed as an allowlist rather than a growing denylist; **what happens to an existing
  non-conforming `Users` row is stated and tested**, not discovered; and the §22.4
  register entry is closed with what was done.

### Task 11.90 — R-3: the guard that decides "too busy to measure" cannot tell busy from biased
**Status:** **DONE 2026-09-06.** The rule is out of the instrument and into
`scripts/gate_timing_guard.py`, where it compares the effect against the resolution the
run itself demonstrated rather than against the sign of its own control; its `--selftest`
breaks it on purpose in a second, including on R-3's own numbers, and `gate_smoke_test.sh`
runs that on every gate. **Watched declaring INCONCLUSIVE on a live loaded stack through
all three of its doors**, including the one the repair adds, each run exiting 0 with its
baseline intact. §22.4.1 is closed and Gate C's
criterion 4 no longer carries an unwritten "on a quiet machine". **`Cg` gets no baseline
entry, deliberately** — full resolution in the security model. **Resolution below.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium — raised 2026-08-31.** The repair is named in the write-up, but
what is actually being designed is **a statistical guard that must tell a busy machine
from a biased measurement** — and the previous version of that guard was written by
somebody who thought they had done exactly this. **A second wrong guard would be harder to
find than the first**, because it would be sitting behind a task that says the guard was
fixed.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by 11.85 by refusing to re-run until green.**

**What happened.** During round 9's full run the adversarial pass **reported a Gate C
blocker that three re-runs could not reproduce.** Its timing check carries a guard meant
to answer "inconclusive" on a machine too busy to measure — but **the guard tests the
*sign* of its own control and not the *size***, so a load-driven bias passed the guard and
was scored as a real finding.

**It fails safe** — a false blocker rather than a missed one — **and it still has to be
fixed**, because §6's criterion 4 says the adversarial pass must match its baseline
*exactly*, and an unsound guard quietly turns that into "exactly, on a quiet machine."
**A criterion with an unwritten precondition is a criterion that will be met on paper on
the day it matters.**

**This is the recurring class in its purest form: a check that cannot distinguish success
from its own failure.** Here it is one level up — a *guard* that cannot distinguish a
quiet machine from a biased measurement, which is the one job a guard has.

**And note what nearly buried it.** 11.85 could have re-run until green and reported a
clean round; three re-runs did pass. **It wrote the flake up as a defect in the check
instead**, which is the behaviour that keeps a gate worth believing — a blocker nobody can
reproduce is how a gate stops being believed, in either direction.

**One thing to decide when this lands, deliberately left open by task 11.88.**
`gate_c_adversarial_pass`'s `Cg` check measures the same phenomenon Michael accepted at
§4.13, and 11.88 **deliberately did not give it a baseline entry** — its one observed
failure matched *this* task's defect (a guard testing sign rather than magnitude under
load), not the genuine small residual, and accepting it blanket-style would have hidden
either a future load-driven false positive or a real regression. **That reasoning is
ratified.** Once the guard is sound, **decide whether `Cg` needs its own baseline entry
citing §4.13, and record the answer either way** — an open question that nobody closes is
how a residual becomes permanent by accident.

**And do not reach for a baseline for a signal that is only sometimes stable.** 11.88 made
that mistake, caught it the same day, and it is now a standing rule in `CLAUDE.md`: a
baseline has two modes and a probabilistic fact lives in neither.

- **Acceptance:** the guard tests the magnitude of its control and not merely its
  direction; it is **watched declaring "inconclusive" on a deliberately loaded machine**,
  because a guard nobody has seen fire is not a guard; §6's criterion 4 no longer carries
  an unwritten "on a quiet machine"; and the §22.4.1 entry is closed.

**Resolution, 2026-09-06.**

**The rule.** `Cg` measures two differences per trial: `real - fictional`, the effect, and
`fictional - fictional`, a null whose true value is exactly zero. The old rule failed on a
unanimous effect sign and said INCONCLUSIVE only when the null's sign was unanimous too —
**the null's size was never read.** It now is: the run's **resolution** is `max(|null|)`,
the largest gap that run opened between two ids that are the same in truth, and `Cg` fails
only when the effect's sign is unanimous **and** the effect is larger than that. The old
null-sign case is kept, not replaced; it is an independent symptom.

**Why `max(|null|)` and not a dispersion estimate with a multiplier.** Seven trials make a
standard deviation nearly as noisy as the thing it describes, and any constant on top of it
would be a number somebody picked — which is the defect this task is about, one level along.
`max(|null|)` is a fact the run produced and fits in the sentence the check prints.

**It is not a widened tolerance, and that is measured rather than asserted.** Self-test case
2 holds a 40 ms one-sided effect FAILED against a null five hundred times larger than the
quiet one: load inflates the bar, and it inflates the effect with it.

**Where it lives.** `scripts/gate_timing_guard.py` — a function over two lists of numbers,
so it can be broken on purpose without a stack, three project ids and a minute of requests.
`--selftest` covers six cases and asserts that the **replaced** rule called R-3's shape a
finding; if that line ever stops holding, the self-test has stopped demonstrating the defect
it exists for. Registered in `gate_smoke_test.sh` (23 of 23 derived lines, was 22).

**Watched firing, and how.** Under deliberate load — 24 to 48 CPU spinners on a 14-core
laptop, load average above 200, and up to eight copies of the adversarial pass sharing one
stack, which is R-3's own condition — the check declared INCONCLUSIVE through **all three of
its doors** on live measurements. The one the repair adds: **effect 2.439 ms with the sign
the same in every trial, resolution 4.548 ms**, which the *old* rule would have reported as a
Gate C blocker, its null's sign being 1 of 3 and therefore quiet. The old guard's own door:
null 0 of 7, resolution 8.501 ms. The third: effect 0.062 ms against a 0.060 ms resolution
with the signs disagreeing. Every inconclusive run exited 0 with the baseline intact — a
skipped `Cg` still counts in the check total, so an INCONCLUSIVE run is not a silently lost
check.

**The qualification, stated rather than smoothed over.** The magnitude door needs a unanimous
sign, which at the shipped seven trials is 1 in 64, and **it did not occur once in 46 loaded
runs.** It was reached by running the same instrument against the same live stack from a
throwaway copy with the trial count cut to three; the measurements and the load are real and
only the trial count differs. Across those 46 runs the sign ran 1/7 to 6/7 centred near 4 and
was never unanimous — *less* unanimous than independent coin flips would give, which is why
three quiet re-runs could not reproduce R-3 and why its 7-of-7 was such an outlier.

**11.88's open question, answered: `Cg` gets no baseline entry.** A baseline can hold a fact
that is stably true or stably false and nothing in between; `Cg`'s signal is neither, which
is 11.88's own standing rule. With the guard sound, the case that argued for one is now
INCONCLUSIVE rather than a failure, and a `Cg` failure from here means a one-sided effect
larger than the run's own millisecond-scale resolution — three orders of magnitude above
§4.13's accepted 5 µs residual, and a finding to read rather than to pre-accept. The
residual's own bound stays in `server/test/security/authorization_timing_test.dart`, which
times the function directly, holds it under 25 µs, and runs on every commit.

### Task 11.91 — Two attacks with the same name, and the second one erases the first
**Status:** **DONE 2026-08-31** (`0c77ce4`). Registration is now a hard error on a
repeated name; all five real collisions found (four named below plus one more found by
a mechanical scan) are resolved by route; the healthy sweep and both broken-control
scripts that exercise the fixed routes were re-run live and came back clean, with the
two previously-blind attacks now correctly flipping. **Full resolution below.**
**Model:** Sonnet. The fix is small; the sweep of what it invalidates is the work.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by 11.88 while chasing something else, and confirmed
live rather than by reading.**

**Resolution, 2026-08-31.**

**The keying fix.** `attack()`, `control()` and `discriminator()` now each call a new
`_register(key)` before writing `RESULTS`, which raises `SystemExit` immediately on a
repeated key — naming both call sites (`file:line`) via `inspect.stack()`. A duplicate
name now aborts the run instead of silently discarding a verdict.

**The four named repeats, resolved:**
- *"raising the bound with a limit in the query string"* — a **three-way** collision
  (sessions, `/projects/mine`, `join-requests/mine`), confirmed. Each is now namespaced
  by route, e.g. `"raising the bound on /auth/sessions with a limit in the query
  string"`.
- *"the response carrying anything shaped like a source address"* — confirmed, two-way
  (sessions, `/projects/mine`). Its sibling `discriminator("that address pattern can
  still see one", ...)` **also collided at the same two call sites and was not named in
  the original finding** — caught by the mechanical scan below. Both namespaced by route.
- *"listing with {label}"* — **established: does not collide.** Both call sites are in
  the same route (entry 27, sessions) and their label dictionaries (bad tokens vs.
  malformed auth headers) share no key. Left as written; the new hard error now protects
  it against a future overlap.
- *"the response carrying {label}"* — **established: does collide.** Two of the labels
  (`"the SHA-256 the server stores instead"` and `"the caller's email"`) are used
  verbatim by both the sessions loop and the `/projects/mine` loop. Namespaced by route.

**A fifth collision the plan did not name, found by a static AST scan of every
`attack()`/`control()`/`discriminator()` call in the file** (written to catch what eyeballing
the four leads might miss): `control("a second signed-in caller is not locked out by the
first's flood", ...)` was called with the **identical literal string** at three sites —
the sessions, `/projects/mine`, and `join-requests/mine` per-user rate-limit probes.
Namespaced by route, same as the others. The scan found no other duplicates; a second
pass after all fixes landed confirms zero.

**What it invalidated, and the disposition of each.** Re-run rather than reasoned about,
per this task's own instruction, since task 11.64 made re-running cheap:

1. **The healthy sweep itself (`verify_11_49_server_reads.py` against an unbroken
   server) — re-run live, exit 0, clean.** All attacks refused, all controls fired, all
   discriminators sensitive, no duplicate-name error. This is the same sweep task 11.49's
   and round 9's entry verdicts (27, 28, 15, 29) cite; a collision cannot corrupt a
   healthy run's verdict (refused silently overwriting refused changes nothing), but it
   is re-confirmed clean anyway rather than assumed.
2. **Task 11.49's Hardened verdicts for entries 27 and 28, evidenced by
   `verify_11_49_broken_control.py`'s three variants — re-run live, exit 0, and this is
   the one that actually mattered.** The "shape" variant's `must_flip` list is exactly
   where the collision bit: with the fix in place, **all 9 of 9 required attacks now flip
   to ADMITTED**, including the two the Discovered Scope entry named as staying BLIND —
   `"raising the bound on /auth/sessions with a limit in the query string"` and `"the
   response carrying anything shaped like a source address, on /auth/sessions"`. The
   "scope" and "disclosure" variants (12/12 and 6/6 required flips) were never at risk —
   neither references a collided name — but were re-run anyway. **Task 11.49's verdicts
   stand, now on fresh, valid evidence rather than evidence known to have been capable of
   lying.**
3. **Round 9's (task 11.85) Hardened verdicts for entries 23, 24 and 29, evidenced by
   `verify_11_85_broken_control.py` — re-run live, exit 0.** Its `must_flip` lists (the
   "owner", "grant" and "mine" variants) were checked against every renamed string and
   reference none of them, so this evidence was never actually at risk from the
   collision — but was re-run anyway rather than argued about. The "mine" variant, which
   scores entry 29 through this same `verify_11_49_server_reads.py` instrument, flips all
   6 of 6 required attacks. **Round 9's verdicts stand, re-confirmed live.**

**Acceptance, checked against what was asked:** duplicate descriptions are refused at
registration with a message naming both call sites — yes. The four known repeats are
resolved (one, `"listing with {label}"`, established as not colliding and left alone;
the fixed guard now protects it) and the two unconfirmed ones established either way —
yes, and a fifth, previously-unknown collision was found and fixed along the way. The
sweep re-runs clean — yes, watched live. The list of previously-recorded results taken
while a collision was live is written down with a disposition each — yes, all three
stand, above.

**The defect.** `scripts/verify_11_49_server_reads.py` calls `attack()` with the **same
description string** for unrelated checks on different routes, and the result structure is
keyed on that string — so **a later check silently discards an earlier one's result.**
Two collisions are confirmed: *"raising the bound with a limit in the query string"*
across the sessions, `/projects/mine` and `join-requests/mine` routes, and *"the response
carrying anything shaped like a source address"* across the sessions route and a separate
disclosure route. Two more repeated names (`"listing with {label}"`, `"the response
carrying {label}"`) were found by a mechanical scan and are **not yet confirmed to collide
in practice** — check them.

**Why this is worse than a bookkeeping bug, and it was confirmed rather than reasoned
about.** This is why the "shape" broken-control variant reported **two required attacks
staying blind when the server's behaviour had genuinely changed.** So the failure mode is
not "a check is missing" — it is **an instrument reporting that an attack did not detect a
deliberately broken server when in fact it did.** That is the class this whole apparatus
exists to prevent, occurring inside the apparatus: **a check that cannot distinguish
success from its own failure.**

**Fix the class, and the class is the keying, not the four strings.** Renaming the
duplicates leaves the next duplicate free to do this again, silently, and the next one
will be written by somebody being careful — these were. **A duplicate description must be
a hard error at registration time**, so the instrument refuses to run rather than
reporting a smaller truth. **A structure keyed on a string a person types is a
hand-maintained list wearing a different hat.**

**Then say what it invalidates, which is the part that must not be skipped.** Any
broken-control result recorded while a collision was live is suspect. **Name the runs and
the verdicts that rest on them** — including task 11.49's and round 9's, if they are
affected — and say for each whether it stands, must be re-run, or cannot now be
established. **"Probably fine" is not one of the three.**

- **Acceptance:** duplicate descriptions are refused at registration with a message naming
  both call sites; the four known repeats are resolved and the two unconfirmed ones are
  established either way; the sweep re-runs clean; and **the list of previously-recorded
  results that were taken while a collision was live is written down, with a disposition
  each.**

### Task 11.92 — A truth point you cannot read, correct, or get out
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-31 — see `TASK_COMMS.md` for the commit.** All four halves
landed: truth points export as their own CSV (`observations_<date>_truthpoints.csv`) with
both tag names, tested end-to-end through a real rename; the map's info panel shows the
precision and what was found and offers Edit and Delete; the Log lists them in both tabs;
and edit and delete go through the repository, with the delete soft and undoable.
**One thing Michael has not yet confirmed: nothing here has been run on a phone.**
**BETA-BLOCKING** — not because it breaks anything, but because
**11.33 shipped a feature whose output cannot leave the device or be corrected**, and a
beta records real points against real animals.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The work is ordinary; the reason for the rating is that this
is where 11.33's data model meets three surfaces at once and a wrong choice about what a
point *means* propagates into an export somebody analyses.
**Depends on:** 11.33. **Both halves raised by it, merged here on Michael's instruction**
— they are one feature area, one commit, and one hardware check rather than two.

**The shape, in one line: a truth point can be created and nothing else.**

**Half one — it cannot get out.** Nothing exports `Actual_Tag_Locations`; the export screen
never reads the table. As shipped, **a season of truth points can only leave the device
inside a full backup.** The export must carry position, precision, what was found, the
time, **the recorded tag version and the tag's current name** — both, because the recorded
version is what makes an export matchable after a rename and the current name is what a
person recognises. That column exists precisely for this and nothing uses it yet.

**Half two — it cannot be read properly or fixed.** The map draws the point, but the info
panel shows only tag, position and time. **It does not show the precision, and it does not
show whether the animal, the collar, or both were found — which are the two things that
decide what the point means.** The Log tab does not list truth points at all, and there is
no edit and no delete anywhere, **although the repository already supports both.**

> **This is the defect 11.33 existed to fix, one step further on.** 11.33 was "you cannot
> record where the animal actually was." This is "you can record it, and then you cannot
> see what you recorded, correct a typo, or use it." **A feature that only writes is not a
> feature.**

**Michael's decision, 2026-08-31, recorded before anything computes a number.** When
something eventually reports *"the estimates were accurate to within X metres"*, that
figure counts **animal-and-collar points only by default**, with the other kinds
includable deliberately, **and the screen must say which kinds a figure counted.** The
reasoning is 11.33's and it is the right one: **a collar-only point may be where the collar
was shed days earlier**, so scoring an estimate against it reports the app as wrong when it
was right. **This entry is where that decision lives until a task computes such a number**
— no task does today, and none may without carrying this line.

- **Acceptance:** truth points export with all seven fields including both tag names; the
  info panel shows precision and what was found; the Log lists them; edit and delete exist
  and use the repository support that is already there; and the export is checked against
  a renamed tag, because that is the case the version column exists for.

### Task 11.93 — Who found the truth point, how the position was got, and letting it be nudged
**Status:** **Done, 2026-08-31.** Schema v11 ships `Actual_Tag_Locations.user_id` and
`.position_source`; the position is editable through the record screen's own map picker;
the edit gate is unchanged and three tests assert it (client repository, on-screen verdict,
and the server boundary). **Two columns, not three** — the acceptance criterion said three,
and item 2 (the editable position) needs no column of its own: what records it is item 3's
new `PositionSource.gps_fix_adjusted` value. Nothing was dropped. **One defect was found and
fixed while testing this**: on an *update*, the server let a caller write their own name
over an identity column somebody else's row carried, so a colleague could have taken credit
for finding another person's truth point. See Discovered Scope.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Three additive columns and one migration is ordinary work; the
rating is for the backfill question and for one gate this task must be careful **not** to
tighten.
**Depends on:** 11.92. **All three items merge because they are one schema v11 migration** —
splitting them would mean two migrations for one feature, which is the expensive mistake.

**1. A truth point records who found it.** Michael, 2026-08-31: *"the truth point should be
recorded with the user that logged it."* Today the only person-shaped column is
`sync.last_modified_by`, which names whoever last touched the row — **not who walked in and
found the collar.** Consequences already shipping: the Log's observer filter hides every
truth point, and the Team tab's member sort puts them last.

> **Michael also settled what this must NOT do, and the task may not quietly do it anyway:
> recording the author does not make editing author-only.** Any contributor on the project
> may still edit or delete a truth point, exactly as 11.92 shipped it. `user_id` records
> **who found it — a fact about the record, not a permission.** His reason is the lion
> case: **the person who saw the pride and the person driving the truck may not be the same
> person.** Leave `truthPointEditVerdict` alone.

**2. The position becomes editable, and 11.92's reasoning for locking it was wrong.**
11.92 argued that somebody who stood in the wrong place should delete and re-record.
**Michael's counter-example is the case the feature exists for: a collared lion tracked
from a truck.** Nobody walks into a pride to stand on the animal, so the recorded position
is a place *near* it — and re-recording does not help, because the person is still in the
truck. **The capability already exists at creation time**: the record screen offers a
manual map pin, with the precision prefill deliberately suppressed because a pin's
precision is not the phone's GPS accuracy. **The missing piece is the same picker on the
edit path, not a new one.**

**3. `position_source`, which nobody asked for and which item 2 makes necessary.** Found by
11.92 while checking the above: `Observations` records whether a coordinate came from a GPS
fix or a hand-placed pin. **`Actual_Tag_Locations` does not.** So a truth point cannot say
whether its coordinate was measured standing at the collar or eyeballed across 200 m of
savannah, and the precision radius carries that distinction only by convention.

> **Today that is tolerable. The moment a position becomes editable it stops being
> tolerable** — a point that began as a GPS fix and was later nudged by hand is a third
> thing again, and nothing would record it. **This is why the three items are one task:
> item 2 without item 3 ships a column whose meaning silently changed.**

**The backfill is a question, not a default.** Existing truth points have no author and no
position source. **Do not invent either.** An author backfilled from `last_modified_by`
would be a guess wearing a fact's clothing, and this app's whole value is that its records
mean what they say. Leave them null, make the screens say "not recorded" rather than blank,
and say in the report how many rows are affected — on Michael's own device it is probably a
handful.

**CORRECTION 2026-08-31, after the task ran: the acceptance below says "all three columns"
and there are two.** `user_id` and `position_source`. **Item 2, the editable position, needs
no column of its own** — what records it is `position_source`'s new value
`gps_fix_adjusted`, *"a GPS fix somebody later moved by hand."* **Nothing was dropped and all
three items shipped**; the wording was the planning session's and it would have sent a later
reader looking for a column that was never needed.

**Michael's backfill decision, 2026-08-31: leave the old rows null.** They read "not
recorded" rather than going blank, there are at most a few days of them — truth points only
became recordable on 2026-08-31 — and **an author inferred from `last_modified_by` would name
whoever last edited the row, not who found the collar.** A guess wearing a fact's clothing is
the one thing this app cannot afford. No task, and no backfill.

**A security defect was found by this task's own new tests and fixed in the same commit —
recorded here as finding S-1 rather than left as a line in a diff.**

> **S-1.** The server's row-naming check asked *"does this row name the caller?"* **before**
> it asked the update rules, so a caller could write **their own** name over an identity
> column on **somebody else's** row. **In plain terms: a colleague could have taken credit
> for finding another person's lion.**
>
> **It was unreachable until 11.93 existed**, because every table that named a person also
> refused the write itself. `Actual_Tag_Locations` is the first table that is **writable by
> anyone on the project *and* says who a record is about** — so the defect was created by the
> combination, not by either half.
>
> **Fixed for every table, with a server test confirmed to fail before the fix.** Same family
> as N-1 (task 11.24). **Because one change now governs every table, the next gate round must
> attack the generalised fix rather than the one table it was found on** — a fix applied
> everywhere by a single edit is exactly the kind that needs one probe, and 11.93's test
> covers the case it knew about.

- **Acceptance:** one schema v11 migration carrying all three columns; the author is
  recorded and shown, and **the edit gate is unchanged and a test asserts that**; the map
  picker works on the edit path; `position_source` distinguishes fix, pin, and a fix later
  nudged by hand; historical rows stay null and read as "not recorded"; and the export from
  11.92 carries the new columns.

**Status:** **Done 2026-09-02 — commit `f296ae2` (plus `3f409ac` for sweep 4). Full

`server/`, and READMEs — 1 already fixed by 11.125, 1 corrected (`audit_
retention_status.sh`'s claim held but was unverified in writing), 7 verified to

plainly that it had not looked for the rest.**

**MERGED 2026-09-01 — this task now also carries tasks 11.101 and 11.75, whose entries
stand below unchanged and must be read in full before starting.** All three are the same
motion: **enumerate the whole set rather than fixing the instance that was noticed, and
report a denominator.** This one is the prefilled-value-that-means-untouched class.
**11.101 is controls whose only label is a `tooltip:`, which a touchscreen never shows** —
so on the device this app is used on, the control has no label at all. **11.75 is app
icons, and its whole instruction is not to fix the macOS one Michael noticed but to
enumerate every platform target from the platform files** — about fifteen minutes, and the
reason it is here is that fifteen minutes does not deserve its own round trip.

**A FOURTH SWEEP, added 2026-09-02 from task 11.125, and it is not in `lib/`.**
`backup_status.sh`'s header claimed that it and `docker compose ps` *"can never disagree"*,
because they run the same program — **and on 2026-09-02 they disagreed**, one reporting *50
hours old, backups have stopped* and the other *freshness unknown*. Same program, **different
identity**: the script runs as the person typing it, the scheduler ran as uid 70 and could not
read the directory. **11.125 corrected that header and checked exactly one other claim**
(`audit_retention_status.sh`, whose version is true because both sides run as the same user),
and said so rather than implying a sweep. **So: find every "these two cannot disagree" or "this
asserts the same thing as" claim in `scripts/`, `server/` and the READMEs, and give each a
verdict.** The question to ask each one is the one that broke this one: **the two paths may run
the same code and still differ in who they run as, where they run, or what they can see.**

> **Four sweeps, four counts, four denominators, and name what you rejected in each.**
> A merged report that gives one number has lost all four, and **a sweep without a
> denominator does not close a class** — that sentence is already in 11.101's entry and it
> now governs the whole task.

**The class.** A field prefilled by the app, whose test for *"has the person touched this"*
**is the value itself.** Then an empty field and a never-touched field are the same state,
and clearing a prefilled value reads as an empty slot to be filled again.

**Two instances in two days.** 11.92's precision field: prefilled at 4 m from the phone's
GPS accuracy, deleting the `4` to type `10` put the `4` straight back on the next frame, so
the only way to enter 10 was to type `410` and delete the leading digit. **Michael hit this
on hardware within minutes of the feature existing.** The fix was to record the fact —
`truthPrecisionTouched` — rather than infer it from a value with two meanings, and to
replace one boolean setter with three methods that each **name who acted**:
`prefillTruthPrecision` (the app), `enterTruthPrecision` (the person),
`withdrawTruthPrecisionPrefill` (the app taking its own guess back).

**That naming is the pattern to look for and to copy.** A setter that does not say who is
setting is where this class hides.

**A THIRD SWEEP, added 2026-08-31 from task 11.107 — and it belongs here rather than in a task
of its own, for a reason worth stating.** This task's class is **the app asserting something
about state it did not actually check**: a field whose "has the person touched this" test is the
value itself, and a sentence describing a prefill that did not happen. **11.107's open question
is the same assertion one level up.**

Its retry policy makes every awaited provider on every screen fail in **1.6 seconds instead of
38** — **and nothing has checked that each of those roughly thirty call sites renders anything
when it does.** 11.107 read the list and found almost all of them inside a `try`, and said the
right thing: **"inside a try" is not "shows the person something"** — which is exactly the
distinction task 11.105's follow-up found sixty instances of. **It flagged this as uncertainty
rather than as a defect, having found no specific screen that goes blank.**

**So: walk the awaited-provider call sites and confirm each has a visible failure state.** Same
discipline as the other two sweeps — classify all of them, **report the count including zero**,
and name what you rejected. **If the bounded wait turns out to be enough on its own, say so in
writing**; that closes the question rather than leaving it open under a task that ran.

**What this task does: find the rest, and do not assume there are none.** Every place the
app prefills a form field, decide whether "untouched" is stored as a fact or inferred from
the value. **Report the count even if it is zero** — a sweep that finds nothing is a
result, and it is the only way "we fixed both instances" becomes "we know the class is
closed."

**One extra sweep added 2026-08-31, from 11.93, and it is the same defect in prose.** The
truth-point precision helper text claimed *"This was prefilled from the device's reported GPS
accuracy."* **True of a point recorded on a GPS fix. False of one recorded on a map pin**,
where the prefill is deliberately suppressed — and false of any figure the person typed.
11.93 rewrote the sentence in the edit dialog **that it owned**, and said plainly that the
same claim may sit elsewhere in the record screen and that nobody had swept for it.

> **Sweep the copy alongside the code, because it is one class wearing two costumes.** A
> field whose "has the person touched this" test is the value itself, and a sentence that
> describes a prefill that did not happen, are both **the app asserting something about state
> it did not actually check.** You are already reading every prefilled field; read the
> sentence next to each one while you are there.

- **Fix only what is genuinely the same class.** A prefill that can never be legitimately
  cleared to empty is not this defect, and forcing the pattern onto it adds state for
  nothing. Say which candidates you rejected and why.
- **Each fix carries a test confirmed to fail against the old logic**, the way 11.92's
  regression test reproduced Michael's `4` before it was kept.

- **Acceptance:** every prefilled field in the app is classified; those in the class are
  fixed with tests confirmed red beforehand; rejected candidates are named with reasons;
  and the total count is reported **whatever it is.**

### Task 11.95 — Two things wrong with the map screen, found by photographing it
**CONFIRMATION RECEIVED 2026-08-31, and it is positive.** This task's own evidence was a
widget test rather than a simulator run, because the screenshot harness deliberately withheld
the GPS fix that triggered the defect — and it said plainly that when somebody turned the fix
on, that run would be the real confirmation, and that if it still threw it had the wrong
answer and wanted to know. **`/w-06` turned it on. Four runs across two device profiles, every
one reporting no screen throwing while being photographed. Before the fix, giving the app a
position ended the run with no images at all.** The answer was right.

> **And the fix turned on a feature that had never worked.** 11.95 found that throwing past
> the `try` also jumped the `finally`, so **the automatic viewshed never completed** — the
> bar sat at *"Computing viewshed…"* for the session. It completes now, and `/w-06`'s
> pictures are **the first time anybody has seen that overlay finish.** What it does is
> paint a large purple polygon over the terrain and zoom to a 200-metre scale, putting
> several of the project's own bearings off the edge. **That may be right and nobody
> knows** — it is on Michael's hardware list, and whoever next touches task 11.87 should
> read this first.

**Status:** **Done 2026-08-31.** Item 2 committed first as `21d4c61`, item 1 as `2a58ac5`.
**The unknown is answered: there is no second fault.** The unhandled asynchronous error is
the provider write itself — `_computeViewshedAt` is `async` and touched the status provider
before its own `try`, so Riverpod's refusal completed an un-awaited future instead of being
caught, and surfaced twice. Measured both ways: exactly one non-tile-fetch error before the
change, none after. **The field cost the release build kept**: the throw jumped the
`finally`, so the automatic viewshed never ran and the bottom progress bar sat at "Computing
viewshed…" for the rest of the session.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Item 2 is twenty minutes. Item 1 contains something nobody has
explained yet.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by `/w-02` while building the screenshot harness** — not by
writing prose, and not by anybody testing the map.

> **Two commits, in this order.** Item 2 is bounded and unblocks the website; item 1 is an
> investigation that could grow. **Commit item 2 first so it cannot be held hostage** by
> whatever item 1 turns out to be.

**1. The map screen changes provider state while it is building, and something in the same
chain throws asynchronously.** `_MapScreenState._buildBody` calls
`_maybeAutoComputeViewshed` → `_computeViewshedAt`, which sets
`ComputationStatusNotifier`'s state during `build`
(`map_screen.dart:256`, `:990`, `:1501`; `computation_status_provider.dart:44`). Riverpod
refuses it — *"Tried to modify a provider while the widget tree was building"* — and a few
seconds later an unhandled asynchronous error escapes from the same chain.

**Why this is beta-blocking despite being invisible in release.** The assertion is compiled
out of a release build, so **the field never sees the message** — but the rule exists
because modifying a provider mid-build can produce an inconsistent screen, and **the
unhandled async error is a separate problem that release mode does not fix.** `/w-02` could
not determine what throws; it only saw the error escape.

> **An unexplained asynchronous error on the app's primary screen, in the ordinary case —
> GPS fix, project open — is not something to ship without knowing what it is.** The
> `setState`-during-build is the easy half. **Do not fix that and declare the item closed:
> find what throws, and say so.** If it turns out to be harmless, that is a fine answer and
> it must be an answered one.

**2. The map attribution is cut off on every phone.** The `flutter_map` attribution row
overflows by 61 pixels on a 6.9-inch iPhone with the default Terrain basemap, whose
attribution string is the long one. Debug paints the overflow stripes; **release simply
clips the text.** The iPad is wide enough.

**This is not only cosmetic.** Displaying attribution is a condition of the OpenStreetMap
and OpenTopoMap tile licences, and **an attribution running off the edge of the screen is
arguably not displayed.** `/w-02` was right to say the licence judgement is not its call —
it is not this task's either. **Fix the layout so the whole string is readable on a phone;
the licence question then does not need answering.** Wrapping, scrolling, or a tap-through
attribution sheet are all acceptable; a smaller font that still clips is not.

- **Acceptance:** the attribution is fully readable on a 6.9-inch phone, committed
  separately and first; the provider-during-build violation is gone; **what throws
  asynchronously is identified and stated**, whether or not it needed fixing; and the two
  phone screenshots `/w-02` flagged can be regenerated clean, which is the check that this
  actually worked.

### Task 11.96 — The mutation rules have two shadow copies, and one of them is a test
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-02 — commit (see `TASK_COMMS.md`).** Both halves closed. **(1)**
`test/data/repositories/mutation_rule_matches_shared_table_test.dart` asserts every one of
the thirteen `BaseRepository` subclasses' `rule` against `tableMutationRules[repository.table]`
— confirmed red first against a deliberately mismatched `Actual_Tag_Locations` rule, then
reverted. **All thirteen currently agree; zero were disagreeing.** **(2)** The two
authorization groups in `server/test/authz/authorization_test.dart` are unified: task 11.24's
and task 11.93's separately-derived "declared set" tests are now one test deriving over
`SyncTable.identityUserColumns` minus `MutationRule.isAuthorizationState` — proved to equal
the exact union of the two former sets (confirmed red by temporarily making `Non_Detections`
`owner`-ruled, which the derivation correctly excluded, then reverted). The per-table forged-
name refusal loop and its positive control are likewise merged into one group; the two tests
unique to `Actual_Tag_Locations`'s `anyUser` write gate (a colleague may correct the point, may
not rewrite who found it) have no analogue among the author-ruled tables and stay in their own
group, with a comment saying why. **11.117's half (`SyncStatus`) is also done** — see its own
entry below, merged into this one. The full server suite (834 tests) and full client suite
(1994 tests) are green.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium. **Both halves are one idea and one commit** — a rule that is
derived in one place and duplicated in another.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Both found by 11.93 while writing its own tests**, which is the
only reason either is known.

**MERGED 2026-09-01 — this task now also carries task 11.117, whose entry stands below
unchanged and must be read in full before starting.** One principle, applied twice.
**Here it is thirteen repositories each carrying a hand-written copy of
`tableMutationRules`** — proved by flipping the shared table and watching nothing go red.
**In 11.117 it is `SyncStatus`, rebuilt by a fifteen-field constructor call in seven
places, where a dropped field silently means *healthy*** — the hardest signal in the app to
notice being wrong, and it has already bitten twice. **Neither task is the sweep. Both are
removing the invitation** — making the omission unrepresentable rather than finding today's
instances. Do them in one window because it is one judgment made twice, not because they
touch the same files; they do not.

**1. Every repository's mutation rule is a hand-maintained second copy of
`tableMutationRules`.** Measured, not suspected: 11.93 flipped `Actual_Tag_Locations` to
`author` in the shared rule table and **no client behaviour changed and no test went red**,
because each `BaseRepository` subclass passes its rule as a literal. **The shared table is
not the authority it looks like** — it is a document that happens to agree with the code.

**This is the hand-maintained-mirror class that task 10.66 made a standing criterion.** The
fix is one test: `repository.rule == tableMutationRules[repository.table]`, for **every**
repository. 11.93 asserted it for the one table it was about; **the other twelve are
unguarded**, and a mirror that is checked in one of thirteen places is not checked.

**2. `authorization_test.dart`'s task-11.24 group no longer enumerates what it thinks it
does.** It derives the tables it probes from `MutationRule.namesRowAuthor`, which **was** the
same set as "tables that name a person" until 11.93 — and is not any more. **A derived check
whose derivation has silently stopped matching its intent is worse than a hand-written list,
because it still looks derived.**

11.93 added its own derived group for the new shape rather than widening theirs, and **was
right not to widen**: widening pulls in `Projects` and `Project_Memberships`, which are
refused for different reasons and need their own cases. **The question this task answers is
whether the two groups become one derivation over `identityUserColumns`** — and if the
answer is no, that answer must be written down beside both groups, because the next person
will ask again.

- **Acceptance:** one test asserts every repository's rule matches the shared table, and it
  is **confirmed red against a deliberately mismatched rule** before being kept; the two
  authorization groups are either unified over `identityUserColumns` or **the reason they
  stay separate is written next to both**; and the report says how many of the thirteen
  repositories were actually disagreeing with the table, **which nobody currently knows.**

### Task 11.97 — The sync bar's error states cannot be exercised end to end by anything
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-01 — commit `d993e51`.** The app now builds a server
connection in exactly one place, `lib/core/providers/server_transport_provider.dart`; the
sync engine, the membership surface and the join/publish controller all draw from it, where
before each assembled its own. `test/core/providers/sync_bar_states_end_to_end_test.dart`
drives eleven of the sync bar's fourteen presentations from a substituted server — including
all four `/w-05` named — and the file's header table names the other three and why a
substituted server cannot reach them (a refused address is decided before any connection
exists; staleness is a fact about a clock). **Every test was watched against the pre-change
engine, and nine of the eleven failed — all nine reporting `offline`,** which is the finding
in one line: with the engine building its own connection, a substituted server was not a
failing server but no server, so the only two states reachable were the two that describe a
request that never arrived. **No state, once reachable, turned out to be drawing or saying
the wrong thing** — the bar was right about all eleven on the first honest run.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** It is a small architectural change with a large blast radius —
the sync engine is the thing everything else trusts.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by `/w-05`**, which could photograph exactly one of the sync
bar's eight states and said so rather than shipping a guide that implies there is one.

**The finding.** The sync engine **builds its own connection**, so nothing can substitute a
failing server for it. The membership transport is already replaceable — `/w-05` swapped four
seams to drive a whole join with no server — **but the sync engine is not among them, and
deliberately was not swapped**, because a "tap Sync now" picture would have been a real
request to an invented hostname.

**The consequence is much bigger than screenshots, and that is why this is a code task.**
Offline, *records refused*, *records missing*, and *you are no longer on this project* are
four states the app draws, the app explains, and **no test can drive.** Tasks 11.54 and 11.60
exist because two of those states were wrong in ways only a person on real hardware found.
**A state that only a human can reach is a state that regresses silently.**

- **Make the engine's connection replaceable the way the membership transport already is**,
  and copy that shape rather than inventing a second one — `/w-05`'s `joined.dart` documents
  why each seam is where it is.
- **Then exercise the states**, end to end, against a substituted failing server. **The point
  is the tests, not the seam** — a seam with no test through it is refactoring, not coverage.
- **Say which of the eight states are now reachable and which are not**, and why. **Do not
  report "the connection is now replaceable" as the result.**
- **`/w-05` was right that this is an app change rather than a harness change**, and it stays
  that way: this task does not touch `integration_test/screenshots/`. The screenshots follow
  later, from the content lane, once the seam exists.

- **Acceptance:** the sync engine's connection is substitutable; each of the sync bar's
  states is either driven by a test or named as still unreachable with a reason; **at least
  one test is confirmed red against the pre-change behaviour**; and the report says whether
  any state, once reachable, turned out to be wrong.

value reaches a screen again. **(3)** The disclosure decision is written up as
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.29 with its reasoning — **roles yes and member list yes**,
because sync already sends every member's row to every member's device, the log screen
already shows observer names, and the export screen is not role-gated and writes every
member's email into an archive a viewer can take. **(4)** The app bar's unlabelled cloud
icon is gone; joining is a labelled row in the list, present in the empty state too. Each
project row's four-or-five bare icons are now one overflow menu of written labels, with
delete last below a divider of its own and drawn in the error colour, and a refused action's
reason on the item rather than in a tooltip. **Every new property was watched to fail
against the pre-change behaviour.** 1645 app tests and 302 shared-package tests pass; the
website drift check is green, **which is itself a finding — see the comms entry: eight
sentences and two screenshots in the user guide are now false and the check cannot see it.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Two findings, one screen family, one commit. The judgement is
about what a non-owner may see, which is a permission decision as much as a layout one.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Both found by `/w-03`**, which had to write the sentences and
could not.

**1. A contributor or a viewer has no way to find out what role they hold, or who else is on
the project.** The route to the members screen is rendered only for owners —
`projects_screen.dart`, the members icon inside `if (isOwner)`. **The only place the app ever
names somebody's own role to them is inside a failure message, after they have tried
something they were not allowed to do.**

> **What breaks for a person:** a field tech who cannot save a position estimate has no way
> to find out whether that is their role or a bug, and no way to see who to ask. **Writing

**The decision this task must make explicitly, not by default:** a non-owner seeing the
member list is a disclosure — colleagues' names and addresses. **The role gradient already

somebody already on it. **State the reasoning either way**, and if the answer is "roles yes,

**2. The only way into joining a project is an unlabelled icon, and leave sits beside

> **The leave-beside-delete adjacency is the part to take seriously.** Two unlabelled

**A third item, added 2026-08-31 from `/w-06`, because it is on the screen you are already

Same three roles, two spellings, **and the lower-case one is the raw database value rather

- **Acceptance:** a non-owner can discover their own role without failing at something

  into joining a project is labelled in a way that survives having no tooltip; and **leave

### Task 11.100 — A truth point is drawn a hundred metres from where it is
**Status:** **Done, 2026-08-31.** All four items. The truth-point marker now sits on its
coordinate and the screenshot harness printed *opened its info panel* — the first time it
has said that. The shared-observation marker had the identical defect and is fixed, but see
the comms entry: it is verified by arithmetic and by reading, not by a run. Item 4 done —
the bearing rows' four bare icons are now one ⋯ menu.
**Was: Not started. BETA-BLOCKING** — item 1 is a correctness defect on the one
screen where somebody judges whether an estimate was any good.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The fix is small; **the rating is because item 1 is about
whether a record means what it shows**, and because two other markers may share it.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by `/w-07`, which could not write the sentence "tap the
truth point on the map" because that is not what you do.**

> **Four items, in this order. Item 1 is the task; items 2–4 are one line each and ride
> along. If item 1 grows, stop and commit it alone.**

**1. The marker is painted about 28 screen pixels above the position it stands for, and
tapping it does nothing.** At the zoom the screenshots use, that is **roughly a hundred
metres of apparent ground offset** — on a record whose entire purpose is being accurate to
about ±12 m. A tap on the square selects nothing, because the map decides what you tapped by
measuring from the **real** position and accepting 24 pixels. You have to tap the label
underneath, or the blank map below the square.

**What breaks for a person:** somebody comparing an estimate against a truth point on screen
**misjudges the gap by about a hundred metres, in a fixed direction** — and somebody who taps
the dot to read its details concludes the app is broken.

**The cause is identified and the fix is next door.** `map_screen.dart` gives that marker
`alignment: Alignment.topCenter`, which in flutter_map puts the **bottom** of the marker's
36-pixel box on the coordinate. **The estimate marker eight lines above passes
`Alignment(0, 0.5)` and carries a comment saying plain `topCenter` would do exactly this.**

- **Check the shared-observation marker too.** `/w-07` says it has the same alignment and
  **did not test it** — so treat that as unverified rather than as a second defect or a
  non-defect.
- **`/w-07` left you a measuring instrument, not an assertion.** The capture now taps the
  drawn square and prints whether the panel opened; it has said *did NOT open* four times
  across both device profiles with the same 28-pixel gap. **When the anchor is right the
  harness will say so** — that is the confirmation, not a green test.

**2. The Log's menu entry describes less than the code does.** It reads *"Edit precision /
what was found…"* and the dialog it opens **also moves the point on the map** — which is the
headline of task 11.93. Somebody who wants to nudge a position reads that label and concludes
they cannot. **This is copy describing a mechanism the code does not have, inverted.**

**3. "1 truth points".** The CSV export receipt names each kind and its count, and the plural
is unconditional for all three kinds.

**4. Least urgent, and droppable if anything above grows.** On the Log, a truth-point row's
controls are a single ⋯ button while a bearing row two rows up has four icons on the row —
so the guide had to warn a reader away from a pencil that is not there. **Task 11.99 has just
made the opposite move on the projects screen** — four bare icons became one labelled
overflow menu — **so the bearing rows are the ones out of step, not the truth-point row.**
Bring them into line, or write down why not.

- **Acceptance:** the truth-point marker sits on its coordinate and a tap on it opens the
  panel, **confirmed by the harness reporting the tap opened**; the shared-observation marker
  is checked and its state reported; the Log's menu entry names moving the point; the export
  receipt agrees with its own numbers; and item 4 is done or its reason recorded.

### Task 11.102 — The navigation flag points 13 pixels to the left of where it points

> **CORRECTION 2026-09-03, from `/w-09`, and it is the fourth cause proposed for one event.**
> This entry's conclusion — that the Navigate row overflows at a device width of about
> **460–470 logical pixels**, so "every real phone would hit this" — **does not follow from the
> measurement it rests on.** `/w-09` pulled the pre-fix screenshot out of git and looked at it:
> **the harness photographed that panel before the fix and the row fit, with visible space to
> spare.** There was nothing for the harness to report.
>
> **The threshold is real and was measured in the wrong font.** It comes from a widget test, and
> `flutter_test`'s fallback font is roughly **twice Roboto's width** — the caveat `CLAUDE.md`
> already carries from task 11.133. On a simulator running the real app in the real font the same
> three buttons need far less room. **So the number cannot be compared against a device width the
> way the comment in `test/features/map/truth_point_row_overflow_width_test.dart` compares it.
> Correct that comment.**
>
> **The fix is right and stays.** `Wrap` instead of `Row` is correct regardless of what triggered
> the overflow.
>
> **What is still not established is what made Michael's device the one that overflowed.**
> `/w-09`'s best guess, flagged as a guess: **a system text size above the default.** The harness
> renders at text scale 1.0 and has no way to notice.
>
> **The pattern is now four-for-four, and that is the finding worth keeping.** Tag-name length
> (my brief), device width (11.102's own correction), bearing count, and the fixture itself have
> each been named as the cause of this overflow and each been wrong. **Every one of them was
> inferred from an event nobody could reproduce.** See `CLAUDE.md`.
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-01, batched with task 11.106.** The flag glyph was swapped for
`MapPinMarker`, a hand-drawn teardrop whose tip is guaranteed by construction (not a font
glyph's visual bounds) to sit at `Alignment.bottomCenter` — no per-marker fraction needed,
and `map_pin_marker_test.dart` renders the actual pixels to check that promise rather than
trusting the doc comment. The Navigate row's fixed-width `Row` became a `Wrap`, so a device
too narrow to fit all three buttons drops the last one to a second line instead of clipping.
**Corrected from the brief's own guess:** the overflow is not driven by the tag's name —
Edit/Delete/Navigate are fixed labels — it's driven by device width, and the measured
threshold (~460–470px of row width, `truth_point_row_overflow_width_test.dart`) is narrow
enough that **every real iPhone Michael has, not just the Android device, would have hit
this overflow** once a real (non-1200px-wide) screen was involved. Full detail in this
task's `TASK_COMMS.md` entry.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium. **Batch it with another below-the-line task in the same window**
— it is too small to be worth a fresh context on its own.
**Depends on:** 11.100, which found it and deliberately did not fix it.

**The defect.** The navigation-target flag is drawn about **13 pixels to the left** of the
place it points at: it is a **flag glyph — pole down the left edge — anchored as if it were a
pin**, whose tip is at the bottom centre. Same cause as 11.100's truth-point marker, different
axis.

**11.100 checked the record screen's position pin and it is correct**, so this is one site
rather than a class. **But three markers have now been examined and two were wrong**, and both
were wrong for the same reason: **an anchor chosen for a glyph shape the marker does not
have.**

**So the fix is two things, and the second is the point.**

1. **Fix the flag.** It is a judgement call between nudging the anchor and swapping the glyph
   for a pin. **Prefer swapping the glyph** unless there is a reason not to: an anchor
   compensating for an asymmetric picture is a number somebody will "tidy" later, and a pin
   whose tip is its anchor needs no compensation. **Whichever you choose, say why.**
2. **Leave something that makes the next mismatch visible.** Every marker on that map declares
   an alignment, and the correct alignment is a function of what the glyph looks like — which
   is exactly the kind of pairing this project has repeatedly found drifting. **A test, a
   shared helper that takes the glyph and returns the anchor, or a comment convention are all
   acceptable; silently fixing 13 pixels is not.** Say what your answer would and would not
   have caught, including whether it would have caught this one.

**A third item, added 2026-08-31 from Michael's device, and it is the same screen.** Tapping
a truth point overflows the info panel's Navigate row: *"A RenderFlex overflowed by 0.0896
pixels on the right."*

> **The number is the finding.** A row that overflows by a tenth of a pixel is a row that
> fits by **nothing**. A longer tag name, a larger system font, a different locale, or a
> narrower phone turns 0.09 into 20, and then it is stripes across the control somebody taps
> to walk to the animal. **Give the row real slack — let something wrap, shrink or ellipsise —
> rather than buying back a pixel.**

**And it explains why nothing caught it, which matters more than the fix.** The screenshot
harness *does* watch for this: it drains `tester.takeException()` every frame and records what
it finds, and `/w-06` reported *no screen threw while being photographed.* It photographs this
exact panel — task 11.100 made it tap the marker and open it. **So the harness opened the
panel, watched for errors, and saw none, while Michael's device overflows.** The difference is
the content: **the invented fixture's tag name is shorter than a real one.** That is `/w-09`'s
problem, not this task's, but say in the report what length actually overflows — the content
lane needs a number.

- **Acceptance:** the flag points where it points; the choice between anchor and glyph is
  explained; something exists that would surface the next glyph-anchor mismatch, with its
  limits stated; **the Navigate row has real slack and the length at which it used to overflow
  is reported**; and **the shared-observation preview marker's fix — which 11.100 could not
  exercise, because nothing tests it and the harness never photographs it — is either covered
  or named as still unverified.**

### Task 11.103 — A map that does not know where you are shows you the Atlantic
**Status:** **Done (2026-09-01).** The premise question is settled and the answer is **neither
of the two the brief offered** — see "What the premise turned out to be" below. **BETA-BLOCKING.** It is the first thing a beta tester sees on a
desktop, and on a phone whose location permission was refused.
**Model:** **Opus, medium** — the fallback chain is small, but two of its steps are decisions
nobody has made.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by Michael on the macOS app, 2026-08-31.**

**RE-SCOPED 2026-08-31, BEFORE IT RUNS, BECAUSE THE PREMISE IS NOW IN DOUBT.** Michael denied
location on the Android phone and **the map showed the area near his test data, not the
Atlantic.** So the fallback either already works on Android, or that device had something macOS
lacked — a remembered position, or project data to fall back to.

> **Establish why the two platforms differ before changing any code.** The task was written as
> *"the map must never centre on a position nobody supplied"*, and that framing still holds —
> but **"macOS is broken" and "macOS is the case with nothing to fall back to" are different
> findings with different fixes**, and only one of them is about the map. **Reproduce both
> behaviours and say which it is.** If the honest answer is that Android was never affected,
> that is a smaller task and a better record than a fix applied to both.

**The defect as reported.** With no position estimate the map defaults to what looks like
**0°, 0° — the middle of the Atlantic.**

> **This is the null-that-means-two-things class in map form, and that is why it is worth
> more than a default coordinate.** `0,0` is a **valid** coordinate, so nothing errors and
> nothing warns: *"I do not know where you are"* is rendered as *"you are here."* **Fix it as
> "the map must never centre on a position nobody supplied", not as "special-case 0,0."**

**It is not a macOS defect.** macOS just has it permanently. **Any device without a fix takes
the same path** — a phone indoors, a phone before its first fix, and **a phone whose location
permission was refused, which is precisely the state the Android build shipped in.** No
platform check.

**Michael's fallback order, 2026-08-31:** the device's position if there is one; otherwise
**the extent of the most recently recorded data in the active project**; otherwise **the
project's map extent**.

**Two steps of that chain are decisions this task must make rather than assume:**

- **Where a remembered last-viewed map position sits.** For somebody returning to work they
  were doing yesterday, the view they left is arguably better than the project extent. **If
  the app already persists a map position, decide whether it goes ahead of the project extent
  — and if it does not persist one, do not add persistence here**; say so and stop.
- **A project with no data and no extent.** This is the one case with **no honest answer
  available**, and it is a new project's first minute. **Do not invent a location.** A zoomed
  out view, or the map with a line saying there is nothing to show yet, are both honest; a
  coordinate is not.

- **Acceptance:** no code path centres the map on a coordinate nobody supplied; the chain is
  implemented in Michael's order with the two open steps decided and written down; **it is
  exercised with location permission refused**, not only with location absent; and the
  no-data-no-extent case shows something a person can read rather than a place.

#### What the premise turned out to be (written by task 11.103 on completion, 2026-09-01)

**Everything above this heading is the brief as written.** It offered two possible answers —
"macOS is broken" or "macOS is simply the case with nothing to fall back to" — and the real
answer is a third one, which is why re-scoping the task before it ran was right.

1. **There is no platform difference and there never was.** The whole chain is one method with
   no platform branch in it. Both behaviours were reproduced in one process on one machine with
   location permission *refused*: with a project extent the map opened on the extent (the
   Android behaviour); with no extent and no bearings it opened on `0, 0` (the macOS
   behaviour). Same code, same refusal, different project contents.
2. **But the Mac was not "the case with nothing to fall back to" either.** Re-run against that
   same Mac after the fix, the map opens on **a labelled ground-truth point that had been drawn
   on that map the whole time.** The old chain's data step read `data.observations` — bearings —
   **and nothing else**. A project whose recordings are truth points, estimates or
   non-detections fell straight past the step to the Gulf of Guinea *while showing the person
   their own data on screen*. That is the finding, and it is worse than the one the brief
   described, because it was reachable without an empty project.
3. **The order was also inverted.** The project extent outranked the recordings. An extent is
   drawn once at setup; the recordings are where somebody actually is.

**The two open steps, decided:**

- **A remembered last-viewed map position is not in the chain, and this task did not add one.**
  Nothing in the app persists a map camera — `map_settings_provider` stores the chosen basemap,
  `active_selection_provider` stores project and user ids, and that is all of it. The brief said
  not to add persistence here and that is what was done. **Where it would go if it is ever
  added is written into the code**: between the recordings and the project extent — better
  evidence than a box drawn at setup, worse than data recorded in the last day.
- **A project with no data and no extent shows the whole planet and a sentence saying so.**
  `MapCameraTarget.center` is `null` in exactly that case, so a caller cannot accidentally be
  handed a place; the only sanctioned substitute is a named whole-planet framing at zoom 2. The
  sentence names the state and ends with something to try.

**"The most recently recorded data" is defined as** everything recorded within 24 hours of the
newest recording — a window back from the newest point, not a calendar day, because a
dusk-into-the-small-hours session straddles a midnight and a UTC midnight lands mid-evening
across the Americas.

**Exercised on:** macOS (the real app, before and after, with location permission never granted
— the "before" run showed open water at a 500 m scale bar and the "after" run showed the study
area near Kachina Village), and the widget/unit suites on the development machine. **Not run on
Android or iOS by this task** — the code has no platform branch and the tests cover the refused
path, but nobody has watched it happen on a phone.

**New:** `lib/features/map/map_camera_target.dart` (the chain),
`test/features/map/map_camera_target_test.dart`,
`test/features/map/map_with_no_position_test.dart` (permission *refused*, four cases),
`test/documentation/map_never_invents_a_location_test.dart` (the standing guard — it found a
