### Task 11.104 — A release build refuses the address, then blames the network
**Status:** Done (2026-08-31). The refusal now travels as a **value**, not as a thrown
exception: `serverUrlRefusalProvider` answers "will this build use the saved address, and if
not, what does a person do about it", and the sync bar, the sync-status screen and the Server
Connection screen all read that one answer. New `SyncUnavailable.serverAddressRefused` /
`SyncHealth.serverAddressRefused` states reach the bar without any request being attempted.
The URL field's one message for three faults is now five faults with five sentences.
**Task 11.105's brief needs correcting** — see this task's Discovered Scope entry: the
mechanism here is *not* `ProviderException`.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The fix is small; the rating is because the app currently gives
a person a **false cause** and there is no way to find the real one from inside it.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by task 11.66 on a real Android run.**

**The defect.** A release build correctly refuses a plain `http://` LAN server — and then
tells the person their network is broken. The sync bar says **"Offline"**, the server screen
says **"nothing answered at that address"**, and the header still says **"Server
configured"**. `requireValidServerUrl` has the right sentence and **nothing in the app catches
`InvalidServerUrl`.**

> **This is the wrong-cause class, at its most expensive.** *Offline* is not a vaguer version
> of *this address is refused for being insecure*; it is a **different problem**, and it sends
> somebody to check a network that is working. **The beta build is a release build and
> `README.md` §4 ends in an `http://` address**, so this is not an edge case — it is the
> documented path.

**A second, smaller item from the same walk, and it belongs here because it is the same
screen and the same failure:** the server-URL field shows **one error message for three
different faults**. Give each fault its own sentence, and make sure the insecure-address case
is one of them.

- **Say what the person should do.** *"This server is plain http, which release builds
  refuse"* is a diagnosis. **The sentence has to end with what to try** — a `https://`
  address, or how a LAN server gets one.
- **The header must stop saying "Server configured" when the configuration was rejected.**
  Three surfaces currently disagree about the same fact, and the header is the one that reads
  as reassurance.
- **A test that only asserts the exception is thrown has not covered this.** The defect is
  that nothing catches it. **Cover the path from a refused address to what a person sees.**

- **Acceptance:** an `http://` address in a release build produces a message naming the real
  cause and a next step; the three server-screen surfaces agree; the URL field distinguishes
  its three faults; and there is a test that fails if the refusal is ever silently turned back
  into "Offline".

### Task 11.105 — Every typed error test at an awaited provider is dead code
**Status:** **Done (2026-08-31).** **The brief's stated mechanism was wrong and the
correction is the main result** — see this entry's "What was actually measured" below.
Riverpod 3.3.2 does **not** wrap a provider's error in `ProviderException` at
`await ref.read(p.future)`; it delivers the raw exception. What kills a typed catch is
**autoDispose teardown**, which *destroys* the original rather than wrapping it — so no
shared unwrap could have fixed either instance, and the fix is 11.104's: carry the reason
as a value. **The count: one dead typed catch in `lib/`, and it is one of the two 11.66
reproduced** (the other was an exception nothing caught, for the same reason). The other
43 type tests were traced individually and are live. New: `lib/core/providers/provider_error.dart`
(the one unwrap, plus teardown detection), `locationProblemProvider`,
`test/core/providers/provider_boundary_behaviour_test.dart` (pins all three mechanisms
against the real package), `test/documentation/provider_boundary_catch_test.dart` (the
standing guard).

**Model:** **Opus, medium.** One shared unwrap, then a sweep that has to prove each type test
can still fire.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by task 11.66, which reproduced two live instances on the
device from unrelated screens** — location denied, and https required.

**The class.** **Riverpod 3 wraps any error thrown inside a provider in a `ProviderException`
when you await `.future`.** So every `catch (e) { if (e is SomeTypedException) … }` at such a
site **can never match.** The typed branch is unreachable; the generic branch runs; the person
gets the wrong message or none.

> **This is a Riverpod 2→3 migration casualty, not a coding mistake**, which is exactly what
> makes it dangerous: **nothing about the code looks wrong**, it compiles, the tests pass, and
> the branch is simply never taken. Task 11.104 is one visible consequence. **Nobody knows how
> many others there are.**

**Fix it once, in a shared unwrap, then sweep.** Per the standing criterion: fix the class,
not the instance.

- **Every type test found must be proved able to fire.** A sweep that rewrites call sites and
  never demonstrates one matching has replaced dead code with code of unknown liveness. **At
  least one test per distinct exception type, confirmed red against the unwrapped version.**
- **Report the count.** How many sites, how many were dead, how many are now live. **A count
  of two would be a genuine result and would mean 11.66 found all of them** — say so if that
  is the answer.
- **Look for the same shape elsewhere.** Anywhere a framework re-wraps an error — not only
  Riverpod — a typed catch is a guess about a wrapper. Say whether you found another.

- **Acceptance:** the unwrap exists in one place; every awaited-provider type test is either
  live and proved so, or removed; the count is reported; and the two instances 11.66
  reproduced are covered by tests.

#### What was actually measured (written by task 11.105 on completion, 2026-08-31)

**Everything above this heading is the brief as written. The mechanism it names is not the
one that was there** — recorded here rather than edited out, because the brief being wrong in
a specific, checkable way is the most useful thing this task found. All of it is pinned in
`test/core/providers/provider_boundary_behaviour_test.dart`, which fails if a Riverpod
upgrade changes any of it.

1. **`await ref.read(p.future)` delivers the raw exception, not a `ProviderException`.**
   Measured for `FutureProvider`, `StreamProvider`, `AsyncNotifier`, and through a chain of
   providers. So a typed catch at an awaited provider is *not* dead from wrapping, and the
   shared unwrap the brief asked for would have fixed neither instance.
2. **What kills it is autoDispose teardown.** `@riverpod` generates an autoDispose provider;
   `ref.read(...future)` holds no listener across the await; the element is disposed while
   still loading; the caller gets `StateError: "…was disposed during loading state…"`. **The
   original is destroyed, not wrapped**, so nothing at the `catch` can recover it. This is
   what 11.104 measured and what killed both of 11.66's instances.
3. **`ProviderException` is real, at other reads** — `ref.read(syncProvider)` on a
   synchronous provider that threw, and `AsyncValue.requireValue`. Both occur in this app, so
   `unwrapProviderError` exists and is proved to work on a *provoked* nested exception rather
   than a constructed one.
4. **`ref.watch(p)`'s `AsyncValue.error` carries the raw exception**, unwrapped and
   undestroyed. That is why the screens reading errors that way — the audit found several —
   were never affected.

**The count.** 33 `try` blocks in `lib/` type-test an exception, 44 (site, type) pairs in all.
Five sit around an awaited provider `.future`. **One was dead** — `LocationPermissionDeniedException`
in `project_setup_screen.dart`, the instance 11.66 reproduced with location denied. The other
43 were traced individually to a reachable throw site and are live; **none was dead for the
second reason the brief asked about** (a type that can no longer be thrown at all), so nothing
had to be removed. 11.66's second instance — the refused `http://` address — was the same
mechanism but not a dead *catch*: nothing caught `InvalidServerUrl` and, as 11.104 found,
nothing could. **So the answer is the one the brief said would be a real result: 11.66 found
all of them.**

**On resurrecting the message.** The dead branch's sentence — *"Location permission denied —
enable it in Settings to use current location"* — was read, not assumed, and **not restored as
written**. It is wrong for a device whose location services are off (the app's own settings
page does not fix that) and needlessly heavy for an ordinary first denial (the OS will ask
again; no settings trip is needed). It is now four faults with four sentences, each ending in
something to try, checked by test.

**The shape elsewhere.** Ten non-Riverpod boundaries were swept — isolates, platform channels,
sqflite, `package:http`/`dart:io`, zones, `Future.wait`, JSON codegen, zip decoding, Dart
re-throw idioms, and the server's shelf middleware. **One found and fixed:** `BackupArchive.decode`
promised that any malformed archive throws `BackupFormatException`, but `package:archive`
inflates lazily on `ArchiveFile.content`, and both content reads were *arguments* to the
function holding the `try` — so a `.zip` that arrived short over WhatsApp (the transport the
class's own doc names) escaped as a raw `FormatException: Filter error, bad data` and missed
the import screen's typed branch. Everything else in the ten areas either does not exist here
or already converts at the seam.

### Task 11.106 — Three small Android things the walk found
**DONE 2026-09-01, with ONE ITEM UNCONFIRMED AND IT IS THE ITEM THE TASK LED WITH.** The
compass smoothing — bounded, display-only, about 100 ms — **could not be measured on real
Android hardware**: no device and no emulator with a working sensor feed. It is **a reasoned
guess from source inspection** (both platforms' plugins request roughly 30 Hz), not a
measurement, and the task said so.

> **This is the item the whole Android task existed to find, and it is the one thing in the
> batch nobody has verified.** **Michael's next Samsung session is the measurement.** If the
> choppiness is unchanged, the next step is **logging the two platforms' raw sensor delivery
> timestamps on-device** — which is the measurement this task could not take — rather than a
> second guess at the smoothing constant.

**Everything else in the batch is confirmed by automated test:** the back gesture, the basemap
switcher's legibility, two Navigate/position-row visual fixes, and task 11.102's navigation
flag.


**Status:** **Done 2026-09-01, batched with task 11.102.** All four items (the compass, the
back gesture, the basemap switcher, and the two grouped visual defects). The compass fix
could not be measured on real Android hardware — no device or working emulator sensor feed
was available — so item 0 is a source-level finding plus a bounded fix, not a confirmed
measurement; see the item below and this task's `TASK_COMMS.md` entry for what that means
for Michael. Everything else is confirmed by test.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium. **Batch with another Sonnet task.**
**Depends on:** 11.66.

**0. The compass animation is choppy on Android and smooth on iOS — and this is the item to
lead with.** Michael, on a Samsung device, 2026-08-31: *"the animation of it moving is kind of
choppy like the refresh rate is too slow. Looks smoother on iOS."*

> **This is what the whole Android task existed to find and could not.** The emulator has no
> magnetometer, so `/w-02` fed the compass a constant and every screenshot of it is a still
> picture of an invented heading. **A sensor's update rate is invisible to every instrument
> this project owns** — no test, no gate round, no screenshot could ever have produced it.
> **Taking a bearing is the core action of this app**, and a needle that stutters while you
> turn is the difference between an instrument somebody trusts and one they work around.

**Establish the rate before changing anything.** The likely causes are a slower default sensor
sampling rate on Android than iOS, or the widget redrawing only on each raw sample rather than
interpolating between them — **and those have different fixes.** Measure the actual delivery
rate on the device, say what it is on each platform, and only then decide.

**If the answer is interpolation, be careful what you are smoothing.** A compass needle that
lags reality to look pretty is a worse instrument than one that stutters. **Say what the
smoothing costs in responsiveness**, and keep the raw heading as the value any record is
written from.

1. **The Android back gesture never leaves the app.** Whatever it currently does, it does not
   do what an Android user expects, and this is the first platform convention this app has
   ever had to obey.
2. **The basemap switcher draws its unselected options as bare text over the map** — plus two
   other small visual defects `/11-66`'s Discovered Scope entry groups with it, for the same
   reason: they are one screen's chrome.

**One thing to be careful of on item 1.** Back-navigation is where "leaves the app" and
"loses unsaved work" meet. **Say what happens to a half-written observation** when the gesture
is used on the record screen, and make it what a person would expect rather than what falls
out of the router.

- **Acceptance:** the back gesture behaves the way Android users expect and its effect on an
  in-progress record is stated; the basemap switcher's options are legible against a map; the
  two grouped visual defects are fixed or named; **and the report says whether any of it looks
  different on iOS**, since these are shared widgets.

### Task 11.107 — Any failure anywhere looks like a freeze for most of a minute, and one looks like a freeze forever
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-31.** **The 38.2 seconds became 1.6.** The decision: keep automatic
retry, bound it, and hand the person the retry. `lib/core/providers/retry_policy.dart` holds
`appRetryPolicy` — three attempts, 400 ms then 1200 ms of backoff — and the whole reasoning,
including what gets worse: an outage lasting between two and thirty-eight seconds used to be
ridden out invisibly and now surfaces as a failure somebody has to tap past. It is installed on
`main.dart`'s `ProviderScope` (every provider in the running app) and on the container the
full-app widget tests boot, and `test/documentation/retry_policy_applied_test.dart` fails if a
`ProviderScope` is ever added without it. The splash screen now has the `try` it never had:
a failed identity read reaches a panel naming what happened and a "Try again" that really
re-reads, and while a retry is running the tagline slot is replaced by a spinner and "Still
trying…" so *working* is distinguishable from *stopped*. Four splash tests
(`test/features/splash/splash_failure_test.dart`), confirmed red against the old screen for
the behavioural reason, not a compile error. 1723 app tests pass; `flutter analyze` clean.
**Not claimed:** every awaited provider on every screen now fails within 1.6 s, but this task
did not verify that each of those ~30 call sites renders something when it does.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The splash screen is a `try`. **The retry policy is a decision
that applies to every screen in the app**, and getting it wrong is worse than leaving it.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Both found by task 11.105; they are one task because the first
makes the second look different.**

**1. A failed provider makes the app wait 38 seconds before it can say anything.** Riverpod 3
retries automatically — **ten attempts, backoff to a 6.4-second ceiling, measured at 38.2
seconds** — and `p.future` stays pending throughout. **Nothing sets `retry:` on the app's
`ProviderScope`, so this is every awaited provider on every screen.**

> **Nothing is broken by it, and that is what makes it easy to leave.** But a field tech
> whose sync fails watches a still screen for most of a minute before the app admits
> anything, and the reasonable conclusion is that the app has hung. **This project has
> already spent two tasks on people not being told what happened to them; this is the same
> harm arriving by a slower route.**

**It is a decision, not a defect fix.** Either the app sets its own retry policy, or every
awaiting call site gets a timeout. **Task 11.105 bounded only the site it touched, using a
timeout that was already there** — which was right for that task and is not a policy.

- **Whichever you choose, say what a person sees during the wait.** A retry that is invisible
  is the defect; a retry that says *"still trying"* may be fine at 38 seconds.
- **Do not simply switch retries off without saying what breaks.** They exist because a
  flaky field connection benefits from them. **Name what gets worse.**

**2. A failed identity read leaves the app on the splash screen forever, with no message.**
`splash_screen.dart:59-63` has **no `try`** — the error goes unhandled and `context.go` never
runs. **Combined with item 1, the app looks frozen for 38 seconds and then stays frozen.**
That is the first screen a person ever sees.

- **Acceptance:** the retry policy is decided and applied app-wide with the reasoning written
  down; something on screen distinguishes *working* from *stopped* during a retry; a failed
  identity read reaches a screen that says what happened and offers a way on; and **the splash
  path is tested for failure**, which it currently is not.

### Task 11.108 — An untrusted certificate says "this device could not tell why"
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-01.** `HandshakeException` and `AuthProtocolException` (a malformed
response body — found reaching the same catch-all while enumerating it) each get their own
message on `server_config_screen.dart`'s sign-in path and its two revocation controls.
`HandshakeException`'s message best-effort-matches self-signed, expired, or wrong-hostname from
the free-text OpenSSL/BoringSSL string and says plainly when it cannot tell. The remaining
catch-all is documented in place: with those two peeled off, nothing domain-typed reaches it —
what's left is a bug in this app's own code, which genuinely has no actionable cause to name.
Four new widget tests cover the handshake and malformed-body paths.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium. Small, on a screen task 11.104 has just rewritten.
**Depends on:** 11.104. **Found by task 11.105.**

**The defect.** `HandshakeException` is neither `SocketException` nor `http.ClientException`,
so it falls to the catch-all in `server_config_screen.dart` and the app reports **"this device
could not tell why"**.

**Why it is the beta path.** Task 10.49 committed a terminating proxy and §4.1 requires
`https`, so **an untrusted or not-yet-issued certificate is the first thing a tester meets**
when a server is stood up. **Same wrong-cause class as 11.104**, on the same screen, found
one task later — which is the argument for looking at what *else* that catch-all is
swallowing rather than adding one more branch.

- **Do not just add a `HandshakeException` case.** 11.104 fixed one exception on this screen
  and this is the second in two days. **Enumerate what can actually arrive at that catch-all
  and say which of them a person could act on** — then handle those and let the rest be
  honestly unknown.
- **The message must name a next step.** A certificate a device does not trust is usually
  self-signed, expired, or issued for a different hostname, **and those are different
  actions.** Say which, if the exception carries enough to tell them apart; say so plainly if
  it does not.

- **Acceptance:** an untrusted certificate produces a message naming the real cause and what
  to try; the screen's remaining catch-all is enumerated and documented; and a test covers the
  handshake path so it cannot silently rejoin the catch-all.

### Task 11.109 — The Position screen has been furnished until you cannot see the bearings
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-31 — commit `0b81d9b`.** Measured, then fixed, then given the
acceptance criterion it never had.

> **AMENDED 2026-09-04 by task 11.147 — this task's central rule is overridden above the
> ordinary text-size slider, and a reader who stops at the paragraphs below will not know it.**
>
> **The rule.** *The bearings list's height is a floor, not a remainder* — the panel sizes
> itself to show whole bearing rows first and the furniture takes what is left, and the panel's
> minimum is "its furniture plus one whole bearing row" so that the subject cannot be dragged
> away.
>
> **Where it stops holding, and why.** At the five Larger Accessibility Sizes that rule and task
> 11.110's map clear band are **jointly unsatisfiable** on a 6.1-inch phone. This panel's
> furniture plus one *scaled* bearing row is about 470 logical pixels at AX3, and the body has
> nothing like that to give above the map's floor. Both rules were written with reasons and
> neither is wrong; they simply cannot both be obeyed there. **Michael decided on 2026-09-04
> that the map's floor holds and this rule yields.**
>
> **How narrowly it yields.** Only above the ordinary text-size slider, and only for the panel's
> *scroll behaviour*: at those sizes the panel stops being a fixed frame with a scrolling list
> inside it and becomes one scrolling column — header, controls, every bearing and the save row
> together. **It does not yield the priority of the subject** (every bearing is still there, and
> somebody scrolls to one instead of not having it), and **it does not yield the map's floor.**
> At Large and every size below it, this panel is exactly the one this task built, to the pixel.
>
> **What that cost the instrument, stated because it is the part that can rot.** A scrolling
> panel cannot paint the overflow stripe, so a check asserting "nothing overflowed" would have
> gone green because the failure mode was removed. The ladder tests now assert that the last
> bearing row and SAVE POSITION can each be brought fully inside the panel. See task 11.147.

**The number the task asked for: 2.** Measured on a 393x852 phone (iPhone 14 Pro) inside the
real app shell. The bearings list's viewport was **83.5 logical pixels** with no caution showing
and **42.5 pixels** with one; a two-line dense bearing row is about 64 pixels on a device. So
**one whole row was visible at best, and none at all whenever the solver raised any caution** —
including the time-span caution, which fires on exactly the geometry that makes a person want to
scrutinise their bearings. Two is the first count at which the screen has a job to do (an
estimate needs two bearings), and at two you could already only see one of them.

**But the count was never the variable, and that is the more useful finding for `/w-09`.** The
panel was a fixed 5/11 of the screen, so it showed the same one row at 2 bearings and at 200.
**A fixture cannot be built past a threshold that does not exist.** What made the difference was
not how many bearings there were but **whether a caution was showing**, because the cautions
banner sat above the list and pushed it. For a representative picture, seed **at least 8
bearings spanning more than the project's 15-minute triangulation window**, so the caution is
live.

**The drag gesture: it did not break — it was never built.** `git log -S "flex: 5"` puts the
fixed 6:5 split in this screen's very first commit (`55947e0`, Phase 4), and no commit has ever
added a `DraggableScrollableSheet` or a vertical-drag handler anywhere under
`lib/features/position_estimation/`. The Main Map *does* have a draggable sheet, and this panel
is drawn with a 1.5px rule along its top edge that reads exactly like one, so expecting the
gesture was reasonable. It is built now. **Item 1 did not cause it — but the diagnosis behind
the question was right anyway:** the first floor written for the new drag was fractional (a
quarter of the screen), and a quarter of a 6.1-inch phone is *less than this panel's furniture*,
so the drag could have reproduced the defect by hand. The floor is now a pixel floor of
"furniture plus one whole row".

**What changed.** The summary line, the cautions banner and the sort bar were three permanent
bands above the list. They are now one header row (drag handle, estimate readout, a cautions
button that opens a sheet, past estimates) and one controls row (selection count, a sort menu
button, All/None). Panel furniture went from 188-243 pixels to a flat 151.5, **cautions cost the
list nothing at all**, and the split is computed from the furniture rather than the furniture
being subtracted from a constant split: the panel asks for "chrome plus four whole rows",
capped at 60% so the map stays usable. Result on the same phone: **224.7 pixels of list, about
3.5 device rows, at any bearing count and with every caution showing** — and draggable to more.

**The rule is written at the top of `position_estimation_screen.dart`** (five numbered rules
about what earns permanent space) **and enforced by
`test/features/position_estimation/screens/position_screen_space_budget_test.dart`**, which
renders the screen inside the real app shell at real phone geometry and fails if the furniture
grows, if cautions cost the list a pixel, if whole rows stop being visible, or if the drag stops
working. That is the acceptance no task on this screen has ever had.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Small code; **the judgement is what may occupy permanent space on
a screen, and that decision outlives this fix.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by Michael on hardware, 2026-08-31**, and it is the first
defect on this project that nothing built it — **it accreted.**

**What he found.** On the Position screen, the sort options, the Save position button, the
orange warning bar about time, and the ellipse statistics between them take so much room that
**the list of bearings is not visible at all** — and **dragging the lower panel up under the
map no longer works**, so there is no way to reach it.

> **This is the failure mode where every step was right and the sum was never looked at.** Each
> of those four was added by a task that justified it, and **no task's acceptance has ever been
> "and the screen still works with all of this on it."** That is why no test caught it: there
> is nothing wrong with any individual widget. **The defect is the total.**

**And it breaks the screen's actual purpose.** Bearings are what a position estimate is
computed *from*. A screen that shows the statistics of an estimate while hiding the
observations behind it has the priority exactly inverted — **the derived figure is visible and
the evidence is not.**

**Two separate things to fix, and they may have one cause.**

1. **The bearings list must be visible and usable** on a phone, with a realistic number of
   bearings, without scrolling past three panels to reach it.
2. **The drag-up gesture is broken.** Find out whether it broke *because* the panel is
   over-subscribed — a sheet whose minimum content exceeds its collapsed extent often stops
   responding — or for an unrelated reason. **Say which.** If it is the first, fixing item 1
   fixes it, and that is worth knowing before anybody touches the gesture code.

**Decide what earns permanent space, and write the rule down.** This screen will be furnished
again — that is what a screen for a growing feature does.

- **The bearings list is the subject and everything else is furniture.** Start from that.
- **The orange time warning is a condition, not a fixture** — it should occupy space when it
  applies and none when it does not, if that is not already how it works.
- **The ellipse statistics are output, not input.** They may not deserve to be visible at the
  same moment as the thing they are computed from.
- **Do not solve it by making everything smaller.** A screen readable only by somebody with
  good eyes and no gloves is not a fix for a field app.

**One thing to check while you are there, because it explains why no instrument saw this.** The
screenshot harness photographs this screen, and the committed picture looks fine — **because
the seeded fixture has few enough bearings that the list does not compete.** That is `/w-09`'s
problem and it is already noted there; **your part is to say how many bearings it takes before
the screen breaks**, so the fixture can be built past that number.

- **Acceptance:** the bearings list is visible and usable on a phone with a realistic number of
  bearings; the drag gesture works and the report says whether it was a consequence of item 1;
  the rule for what occupies permanent space is written where the next person adding something
  will read it; and **the bearing count at which the screen becomes unusable is reported as a
  number.**

in its worst measured state, and 113 for a contributor.** That is real margin — **and it is the

### Task 11.112 — The certificate message was fixed on the platforms Michael does not test on
**Status:** **Done on macOS 2026-09-01, confirmed by real `NSError` objects, not a live TLS
handshake. iOS not verified — needs Michael and a phone.** `server_config_screen.dart` now
catches `NSErrorClientException` ahead of the generic `http.ClientException` clause (both in the
sign-in path and in `_becauseOf`, the second place 11.108 found `HandshakeException` falling
through) and classifies it by `NSError.domain`/`.code` against six pinned `NSURLErrorDomain`
constants. Dates (`-1201`/`-1204`) get an unambiguous "dates are wrong" message; trust-chain
failures (`-1202`/`-1203`, and the more general `-1200`) get one message covering self-signed,
untrusted-issuer, *and* wrong-hostname together — see the finding below on why those three are
not separable here. Anything else (DNS failure, connection refused, timeout) falls back to the
ordinary "could not reach the server" message, same as a plain `ClientException`. 11.108's
free-text substring lists were pulled into named, `@visibleForTesting` constants and pinned by a
new test group so an edit to any of them is a deliberate, reviewed change rather than a silent
one.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium. The mechanism is identified and the codes are documented; **the care
is in not repeating the fragile half of 11.108's fix.**
**Depends on:** 11.108, which fixed it elsewhere and **said so plainly.**

**The finding.** This app uses a different HTTP client on iOS and macOS — `CupertinoClient` —
and **its TLS failures arrive as a plain `http.ClientException`, not `HandshakeException`.** So
they are still caught by the *"could not reach the server"* branch, and an untrusted or expired
certificate still reports the wrong cause on both.

> **Stated plainly because it changes what "11.108 is done" means: the defect is fixed on the
> platforms nobody is testing on, and live on the two Michael uses.** From his chair nothing
> changed. That is not a criticism of 11.108 — it fixed what its brief named and **disclosed
> the gap rather than letting the green suite speak for it** — but the user-visible outcome
> today is that the defect is still there.

**11.108 found this by reading `cupertino_http`'s source, not by testing on a device**, and said
so. Treat it as a well-supported hypothesis rather than a measurement: **confirm it before
fixing it.** macOS you can test yourself — stand up a server with a self-signed certificate on
the machine you are running on. **iOS needs Michael and a phone**, so say clearly in the report
what was verified where.

**Use the structured codes, and this is the part that makes the fix better than the one it
follows.** `NSURLErrorDomain` carries distinct codes for a self-signed certificate, an expired
one, and a hostname mismatch — **three different problems with three different actions.**
11.108 had to fall back to matching free text on the other platforms because nothing better was
available there.

> **Free-text matching is a control that works for a reason nobody controls.** A Dart or OS
> update changes the message, the branch silently stops matching, and the app quietly returns
> to reporting the wrong cause — **with every test still green.** So: use the codes here, and
> **leave behind a test that fails if the string 11.108 matches on ever changes**, so the older
> half of this fix cannot rot in silence.

**What this task found once it checked the codes, rather than trusting them from either
source.** The six `NSURLErrorDomain` values this task's own note above gives are wrong in three
places — it says `-1201`/`-1203` are both "bad date" codes and `-1204` is "unknown root". The
correct assignment, checked against Apple's published `NSURLError` constants: `-1200` secure
connection failed (generic), `-1201` bad date, `-1202` untrusted, `-1203` unknown root, `-1204`
not yet valid. Both this task's note and 11.108's before it turn out to be exactly the kind of
source that can't be trusted verbatim — which is the whole argument this task makes for pinning
numbers in code and a test rather than writing them once in a comment and hoping.

**Self-signed and wrong-hostname turned out not to be separable by code, and the fix says so
rather than guessing a third way.** Apple's certificate-chain trust evaluation reports one
pass/fail for the whole chain, not per-check reasons — an untrusted root, an unknown root, and a
hostname that does not match the certificate all arrive as the same `-1202`/`-1203` (or, on some
OS versions, the more general `-1200`). The specific sub-reason exists only inside a private,
undocumented `NSUnderlyingErrorKey` chain that this task chose not to parse, for the same reason
11.108 chose not to parse OpenSSL/BoringSSL internals: a layer neither Apple nor this project
documents is not a foundation for a message somebody will act on. So only the date family
(`-1201`/`-1204`) gets a fully specific message; the trust family gets one message naming all
three remaining possibilities plainly, which is still strictly better than 11.108's platforms,
where even the date case was a free-text guess.

**Confirmed on macOS, and how.** Rather than standing up a real server with a self-signed
certificate, this task constructed genuine `NSError` objects directly through
`package:objective_c`'s Foundation bindings (`NSError.errorWithDomain`) and threw them as
`NSErrorClientException` from a mocked HTTP client — real Apple-framework objects with real
`domain`/`code` getters, run through the actual catch clause in `server_config_screen.dart`, not
a simulation of it. Three widget tests pass on this Mac
(`test/features/more/server_config_screen_macos_test.dart`, run manually — this repository's CI
never runs `flutter test` on `macos`, so nothing automated exercises this file yet): an untrusted
cert (`-1202`) names self-signed, a bad-date cert (`-1201`) names the dates, and a plain
connection failure (`-1004`, never reaching TLS) still says "could not reach the server" rather
than a false certificate report. **This was not an end-to-end TLS handshake against a live
self-signed server** — it isolates the one thing 11.108 could not confirm (that `cupertino_http`
throws this exception type carrying these getters) rather than reproducing a full network
failure, which is a narrower but more precise confirmation of the specific hypothesis in
question. **iOS was not tested at all** — no device or simulator was available in this session.

- **Acceptance:** an untrusted certificate on iOS and macOS names the real cause and a next
  step, distinguishing self-signed, expired and hostname-mismatch where the code allows; what
  was verified on a real machine and what was not is stated; and **the free-text branch from
  11.108 is covered by a test that fails if its string changes.**

### Task 11.113 — The app has two classifiers for one question, and only one of them knows about certificates
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-01 — commit `191bc6e`.** The two classifiers are one:
`lib/core/errors/transport_failure.dart` holds the only `classifyTransportFailure`, the
server screen and the sync engine both call it, and
`test/documentation/one_transport_classifier_test.dart` fails if any second file under
`lib/` names a transport exception type (it was smoke-tested against a deliberate
second classifier and named the file and line). A rejected certificate now has its own
`SyncFailureCause`/`SyncHealth` state, ranked with the `http://` refusal rather than with
offline, and reaches the sync bar on the first failed round. 1777 app tests and 302
shared-package tests pass; the three macOS-only certificate tests were run by hand on
this Mac. **Two things the report flags rather than fixes:** staleness alone never
changes the bar's colour (a sync that stopped on Monday shows a calm "Synced 3 days ago"
all week), and "my network is down" and "the server is not running" are still one state,
because nothing on the wire distinguishes them. **Confirmed on hardware by Michael, 2026-09-01:** on the iPhone,
against the same self-signed server, the sync status now reads *"the server was reached
but this device does not trust its security certificate, it is self-signed…"* — the cause
named, on the surface that reported "Offline". The iOS half of the 11.108/11.112/11.113
line is closed.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The branch is trivial. **Making a fifth instance impossible is the
task.**
**Depends on:** 11.104, 11.108, 11.112 — **which is the point.**
**Found by Michael on an iPhone, 2026-09-01, and confirmed against a browser.**

**What he did and what happened.** Pointed the app at a server presenting a self-signed
certificate. Safari on the same phone said *"this connection is not private — this website may
be impersonating…"*, so **the server was reachable and the certificate was genuinely
rejected.** Tapping Sync now in the app produced **"Offline"**.

**The measurement.** `lib/data/sync/sync_failure.dart`'s `classifySyncFailure` contains **no
reference to certificates, `HandshakeException`, or `ClientException`** — a TLS rejection falls
through to offline. Meanwhile `server_config_screen.dart` carries its own, certificate-aware
classification, built by three consecutive tasks.

> **So this app has two classifiers for one question — "why did that request fail?" — and only
> one of them has ever been taught anything.** `sync_failure.dart`'s own header says *"every
> surface switches over the health state"*, which is true and is exactly why this matters: the
> sync bar, the map, the Log and anything added next all inherit its answer.

**This is the fourth instance of one class in a week, and that is the argument.** 11.104 fixed
a refusal reported as a network fault on the server screen; 11.108 found a second exception
reaching the same catch-all; 11.112 found a third route on a different HTTP client. **Each fix
was correct. None of them fixed the class**, because the class is that a cause is decided in
more than one place.

**And the precedent for the shape of the fix is already in the file.** The `http://` refusal
was given its **own health state, deliberately kept "a long way from offline"**, because a
configuration fault is not a transient one. **A rejected certificate is the same shape and was
never given one:** it will not fix itself by walking uphill, and telling somebody they are
offline guarantees they look in the wrong place.

**So do not add a fourth branch and stop.**

- **One place turns a transport failure into a cause, and every surface consumes it.** The
  server screen's classification and `classifySyncFailure` become one thing, or one calls the
  other. **Two surfaces must not be able to disagree about why the same request failed.**
- **Make a third classifier hard to write.** A test that fails if a surface maps an exception to
  a cause on its own, a single exported function, a lint — your choice, but **say what it would
  and would not have caught**, including whether it would have caught this one.
- **Keep the distinction the file already draws.** Offline is transient and expected; a
  certificate fault is neither. Rank it where the `http://` refusal sits, not where offline
  does.

- **Acceptance:** a rejected certificate is named as such on the sync surface as well as the
  server screen; there is one classification of transport failures and the surfaces consume it;
  something makes a third classifier hard to add, with its limits stated; and **the report says
  what the sync bar now shows in each of the four cases** — offline, http refused, certificate
  rejected, server unreachable.

### Task 11.114 — A sync that stopped on Monday looks fine all week
**Status:** Done, commit `9ebfea8`. **BETA-BLOCKING.** The premise of a team beta is that colleagues'
records reach the team, and nothing tells anybody when they stop.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium. **The branch work is routine; the invariant in the second bullet is
what needs care**, and Claude Code was right to say so.
**Depends on:** 11.113, which found it while fixing something else.
**The design is settled and written to be transcribed, in Phase 11's Discovered Scope (commit
`8a5d0ec`). Do not re-derive it.**

**The finding.** Michael's bar read *"Synced 21 hours ago"* in a calm colour, against a server
the app had never successfully contacted. **It only went to a warning when he tapped Sync
now.** So staleness alone never changes the bar, and **today's certificate work only helps once
an attempt has been made and failed.**

> **A field tech whose sync quietly stopped on Monday sees a calm bar all week.** Their records
> exist on one device and nowhere else, and the app knows exactly how long that has been true.

**Michael's two decisions, made 2026-09-01, and the reasoning is his — do not re-open them.**

- **The warning re-arms at 04:00 local**, not 08:00 as first proposed. His reason: *"likely
  before fieldwork begins in most situations"* — **it puts the reminder ahead of the workday
  rather than into the middle of it.**
- **Red with a record count when records are waiting; amber when nothing is pending.**
  **Records waiting means they exist on one device and nowhere else**, which is a different
  severity from merely reading slightly old data.

**The one criterion to write in so many words: the dismiss applies to staleness and to nothing
else.** It must never be able to silence a held record, a rejected certificate, a refused
address, or an ended membership.

> **A dismissable condition is a condition nobody ever fixes.** The dismiss exists because an
> indicator people learn to ignore is worse than none — task 10.12's own reasoning — and that
> argument only holds while the dismiss is narrow. **Make the scope an explicit, tested
> acceptance criterion**, because this is exactly the kind of rule that gets quietly widened by
> whoever implements the control next.

**And say what the bar looks like afterwards.** It gains a dismiss control, and **a real touch
target fights a 12pt strip on a bar that renders above every tab.** Task 11.109 found a screen
crowded into uselessness by four additions each of which was individually justified; **this is
one more addition to a permanent piece of furniture**, so measure it rather than eyeball it.

- **Acceptance:** staleness alone changes the bar, at Michael's thresholds and colours; the
  re-arm is 04:00 local; **a test asserts the dismiss cannot silence any non-staleness
  condition**; and the bar's new layout is measured, not eyeballed.

### Task 11.115 — "No signal" and "the server is switched off" are still one word

> **Item B's closure is ratified 2026-09-02 by the planning session, and the reopen trigger is
> written down so the closure does not read as "impossible" later.** It is not impossible; it is
> **possible on one platform only.** Android's `NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED` genuinely probes for a
> working route; iOS's and macOS's `NWPathMonitor` reports "satisfied" as soon as an interface is
> up. **So the choice was between one honest word everywhere and a better answer on Android with
> a worse-looking non-answer beside it on iOS**, for the same situation, in an app whose two beta
> devices are one of each. **One word everywhere is the right call**, and it is a design decision
> rather than a limit.
>
> **Reopen triggers, either one:** iOS gains an API that probes a route rather than an interface,
> or this app becomes Android-first in a way that makes a platform-divergent message acceptable.
> **Not a code review, and not somebody rediscovering that Android could do it — that is already
> known and written down here.**
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-02.** Item A shipped as copy on `server_config_screen.dart`. Item
B is **closed as not reliably possible**, with the reasoning written into
`lib/data/sync/sync_failure.dart` next to `SyncFailureCause`. See both write-ups below the
original spec.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium.
**Depends on:** 11.113, which named it while fixing its sibling.

**Item A, done.** The waiting sentence on the sign-in screen (`server_config_screen.dart`,
just below the sign-in-code fields) now says, in addition to naming who to ask: *"...this app
cannot tell which way it uses — so it cannot say how long a normal wait is either. If it has
been longer than you would expect and nothing has arrived, ask whoever runs the server for
it."* No duration, no retry count, no mechanism — true on an outage and on an ordinary day
alike, for the same reason task 11.119's fix was. `test/documentation/sign_in_delivery_vocabulary_test.dart`'s
doc comment was updated to quote the new sentence so it does not go stale (task 11.89's rule);
the test itself is a phrase-vocabulary scan and needed no code change, and it still passes.

**Item B, closed rather than implemented.** Investigated what iOS, Android and macOS actually
offer before designing anything, per the task's own instruction. **This project had already
answered the question once**: `sync_schedule.dart`'s scheduling policy (task 10.8) declined to
use any connectivity plugin, for the reason this task exists to re-examine — those APIs report
whether a network *interface* is up, not whether it can reach anything, and say "connected"
behind a captive portal. That finding still holds, and it is worse than the task anticipated:
the platforms are not even consistent with each other. Android's
`NetworkCapabilities.NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED` genuinely probes for a working route: Android
could, in principle, tell "no signal" from "reachable interface, dead server" apart. iOS's and
macOS's `NWPathMonitor` reports "satisfied" the moment an interface is up, with no such probe —
it cannot make that distinction at all. A classifier built on this would give the *same*
captive-portal Wi-Fi a different verdict depending on which phone was holding it — which is a
new instance of the very class task 11.113 exists to close (two surfaces disagreeing about why
the same request failed), just moved from two screens to two platforms. **A check that answers
confidently and wrongly is worse than the single word it replaces** — the task's own acceptance
criterion — so shipping a real check on Android and an honest non-answer on iOS/macOS would
have been a worse product than today's single "Offline" everywhere. Stated confidence: **zero**,
app-wide, on the current tooling. Nothing changed in `classifySyncFailure`; both causes remain
`SyncFailureCause.unreachable`, and the reasoning above is written into that file so the next
person who reaches for a connectivity plugin finds the prior art before writing one.

**Original spec below.**
**Status (original):** Not started. **Below the line, and Claude Code explicitly did not argue
it is urgent.**

**MERGED 2026-09-02 — this task now also carries the sign-in-screen half of task 11.129's
finding, and that half goes FIRST.** They are one question asked twice: **the app cannot know,
so what does it say?**

#### Item A — the sign-in screen, and it ships whatever happens to item B

Task 11.129 gave an **operator** a way to establish afterwards that sign-in was broken. **It did
nothing for the person standing at a trailhead**, who is told *"sent"*, receives no link, and has
no way to tell an outage from a typo in their own address.

> **The fix is not on the wire, and this must not be re-litigated.** Task 11.119 settled it: the
> server answers an identical `202` whether it sent, filed or dropped the link, **because §4.5
> requires it to** — a response that varied would be a way to test whether an address is
> registered. **The app cannot be told why, and it never will be.**

**So this is a copy task.** What does the screen say about *waiting* — how long is normal, what to
do when nothing comes, who to ask? Task 11.119's own fix already stopped it promising an email;
this is the next sentence.

- **Do not add a mechanism.** No retry counter that implies the app knows, no timeout that turns
  into a claim.
- **It must be true during an outage and true on an ordinary day**, because the screen cannot
  tell them apart. **That constraint is the task.**
- **Ship item A even if item B closes as "cannot be distinguished."** A shippable copy fix must
  not wait behind an investigation — that ordering mistake has been made on this project before.

#### Item B — "no signal" and "the server is switched off" (the original entry)

**The finding.** A phone with no signal and a server that is switched off both report
**"Offline"**. **Same class as 11.113** — a cause named wrongly sends somebody to the wrong
place — but **a harder fix, and that is why it is below the line rather than beside it**:
nothing on the wire distinguishes the two. A request that never leaves the device and a request
that leaves and finds nothing look identical from where the app is standing.

**So it needs something the app does not have: a check of the device's own connectivity**,
consulted when a request fails, so *"your phone has no network"* and *"your phone is fine and
the server did not answer"* can be told apart.

- **Establish what the platforms actually offer before designing anything.** Connectivity APIs
  are notoriously willing to say "connected" for a Wi-Fi network with no route to anywhere.
  **A check that answers confidently and wrongly is worse than the single word it replaces**,
  because it would move somebody from a vague right answer to a specific wrong one.
- **If the honest answer is that it cannot be told apart reliably, that is a result.** Say so,
  and the finding closes as accepted rather than staying open forever.

- **Acceptance:** either the two causes are distinguished with a stated confidence and what
  happens when the check is unsure, or **the entry is closed with a written reason** that they
  cannot be.

### Task 11.116 — The sync bar forgets it was failing every time the app restarts
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-01.** The failure cause, the consecutive-failure count and any
terminal stop are now written to `SharedPreferences` per project
(`RememberedSyncFailure`, `SyncStateStore.rememberedFailure`) and restored by
`SyncController.build`, so they survive a restart and a provider rebuild.

**The decision, recorded here as the task asked.** A remembered failure is **shown, and shown
as remembered** — the third of the three options the task named. The bar keeps the same state,
colour and icon a live failure would have, and gains one clause: *"Last tried 3 days ago — not
retried since."* The status screen says it in full. The reasoning is in
`RememberedSyncFailure`'s class note: "the server is refusing us" and "the server was refusing
us when we last tried" are different facts to somebody deciding whether to walk half a mile for
signal, and neither of the other two options can express the difference. The severity is
deliberately **not** softened — downgrading a remembered failure would be discarding it slowly.

**The state is short-lived by construction.** A terminal stop is not restored into
`SyncSchedule`, so a restart still gets its one cheap attempt and the earlier decision behind
`SyncStateStore.lastAttemptAt` (fresh backoff on relaunch) is untouched. The two counts answer
different questions and are kept apart on purpose: the schedule's is *how long to wait*, the
record's is *how much evidence there is*.

**The staleness clock was checked and is correct.** `SyncStatus.health` measures staleness from
`lastSuccessAt`, which is written only by `SyncEngine.run` and `ProjectPublisher.publish` after a
round that connected — never from `lastAttemptAt`. A device that keeps trying and keeps failing
does **not** look fresh. No change was needed.

**A third route to the calm bar was found and closed while in there:** `setFrequency` dropped
`lastFailure` and `lastErrorMessage` when rebuilding the status, so tapping the frequency
control reset the bar to healthy with no restart involved at all.

**Original entry below.** **BETA-BLOCKING**, and it is broader than the case task 11.114 just
closed.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Persisting three fields is small. **Deciding what a persisted
failure means when the app comes back is not**, and it is the part that will be got wrong.
**Depends on:** 11.114, which found it and explained why it did not fold it in.

**The finding.** `SyncController.build` persists only `frequency` and `lastAttemptAt`.
**`SyncFailureCause`, and `SyncSchedule`'s `consecutiveFailures` and `stoppedReason`, are held
in memory only** — so a genuine, ongoing failure **resets to a calm "healthy" bar on every app
restart, and on every provider rebuild.**

> **The bar's memory is shorter than the failure it reports.** And a restart is not a rare
> event: a phone reclaiming a backgrounded app is a restart, and a provider rebuild does not
> even need the app to close. **A device whose sync has been refused for a week can show a calm
> bar several times a day.**

**Task 11.114 limits the damage without fixing it.** Staleness now warns after a day — so the
worst case is bounded rather than unbounded. **But between the restart and that threshold the
app is quietly asserting that everything is fine, having just been told otherwise**, and 11.114
was right not to fold this in: it needs durable per-project state that does not exist yet.

**The decision this task must make explicitly, because it is the part that is not mechanical.**
When the app comes back holding a remembered failure, **is that failure still true?**

- **Showing a remembered failure as current is a claim the app has not re-tested.** The server
  may have come back an hour ago.
- **Discarding it and showing healthy is exactly the defect being fixed.**
- **The honest middle is to distinguish "this is failing" from "this was failing when we last
  tried, and we have not tried since"** — which is a real difference to a person deciding
  whether to walk somewhere with signal. **Say which you chose and why.**

**One thing to check while you are there.** 11.114's staleness warning reads from
`lastAttemptAt`, which **is** persisted. **Establish whether staleness survives a restart
correctly today** — if it is computed from last *attempt* rather than last *success*, a device
that keeps trying and keeps failing may look fresh forever, which would be the same defect
wearing 11.114's clothes.

- **Acceptance:** failure cause, consecutive failures and stopped reason survive a restart and a
  provider rebuild; the app distinguishes a current failure from a remembered one, with the
  choice reasoned in writing; **the staleness clock is confirmed to run from success rather than
  attempt**, or corrected; and a test restarts the app mid-failure and asserts the bar does not
  go calm.

### Task 11.117 — Fifteen fields listed by hand in seven places, and the compiler cannot help
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-02, as part of task 11.96 — commit (see `TASK_COMMS.md`).**
`SyncStatus.copyWith` (`lib/core/providers/sync_provider.dart`) replaces all seven hand-rebuilt
constructor calls; each now names only the fields it changes, and everything else — including a
field added after this method was written — carries over by construction. **A test covers the
frequency-change path this task's brief named**: `test/core/providers/sync_failure_survives_restart_test.dart`'s
new case fails three sync rounds, calls `setFrequency`, and asserts the bar is still `broken` —
confirmed red against the pre-fix hand-listed rebuild, then green after. **The sweep found one
more instance, not fixed**: `SyncSchedule` (`lib/data/sync/sync_schedule.dart`, 5 fields) has the
same shape one size down — see Discovered Scope. **One deliberate behaviour change, noted rather
than silently shipped**: `setFrequency`'s old hand-written rebuild silently reset `running` and
`progress` to false/null on every call (even mid-round), which `dismissStaleness`'s neighbouring
rebuild never did; `copyWith` makes the two consistent by carrying both through, which is more
correct but is a behaviour change from what was there before.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium. **The sweep is easy; the instruction that matters is to make the
mistake unrepresentable rather than to find today's instances.**
**Depends on:** 11.116, which found the second instance while fixing the first.

**The mechanism.** `SyncStatus` is rebuilt by a **constructor call listing fifteen fields by
hand, in seven places** — and **nothing fails if one is left out.** A dropped field silently
becomes its default, which for the sync bar means *healthy*.

**Two instances, both user-visible, both on the app's most important indicator.** Task 11.116
fixed a restart dropping the failure fields. **While in there it found a second: changing the
sync frequency rebuilt the status and dropped them too**, so tapping that control reset the bar
to healthy **with no restart involved at all.**

> **This is the hand-maintained-list class wearing a constructor.** The seven call sites are a
> list somebody maintains by remembering; **the compiler cannot help because every argument is
> supplied and every one is valid.** The only feedback is a bar that looks calm, which is the
> hardest signal in the app to notice being wrong.

**So the task is not the sweep. The task is removing the invitation.**

- **Prefer `copyWith` — or whatever makes "everything as before, except this" the only easy
  way to write it.** If a rebuild cannot omit a field, no sweep is needed for the next one.
- **Then sweep, because the change does not retrofit itself:** other providers that rebuild a
  status object field-by-field have the same shape. **Report the count including zero**, and
  name what you rejected.
- **A field that legitimately resets on rebuild is a fine answer** — say which those are, so
  the next reader does not "fix" a deliberate reset.

- **Acceptance:** a rebuild that omits a field is either impossible or fails to compile; every
  field-by-field status rebuild is found and converted or named deliberate; the count is
  reported; and **a test covers the frequency-change path 11.116 found**, because that one was
  discovered by accident rather than by anything watching.

**Stop line — what this task did NOT do.** The `Stack` shared-anchor sweep is **done as a

**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Adding fixtures is easy. **Measuring how far the fixtures are from

**Depends on:** 11.43, which found it. **Absorbs task 11.47's Discovered Scope entry on

**MERGED 2026-09-01 — this task now also carries task 11.111, whose entry stands below

layer. **This task is the *fixture* more forgiving than reality** — every publish fixture

cases the deliverable is already written as **a rule and a count, not a mass edit.** One
window, one commit, two counts.

**The finding, in one sentence: every publish fixture in this repository publishes a project
with no tag.** That is why the whole end-to-end suite stayed green for a month **while every
real first publish refused a row.** 11.43 added one case with a tag; **the general shape is

> **This is now a class with instances on both sides of the project.** The screenshot fixture
> was more forgiving than reality three times over — short names, too few bearings, no live
> caution — and the test fixtures are simpler than any project a person would publish. **In
> both places the instrument was honest and the input was not.**

**So the deliverable is a measurement, not more fixtures.** How far is a test project from a
field project? Tags, bearings, members, observations, tag versions, span of time, length of
names. **Put numbers on both sides and report the gap.** Adding cases without that leaves
nobody able to say whether the next one is covered.

**Then close what the numbers show, in the order the numbers justify** — not in the order the
files happen to sit. **And absorb 11.47's self-stamped-fixture entry**, which is the same

- **A fixture that is deliberately minimal is a fine answer** — a unit test of one rule does not

- **The one to get right first is publish**, because that is where the cost has already been

- **Acceptance:** the gap between a test project and a plausible field project is stated as

  those are the ones that were passing for the wrong reason.

### Task 11.119 — Which controls in this project have never once been executed?
**Status:** **Done, 2026-09-01. The survey is `CLAUDE_DOCS/UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md`, and it
carries task 11.77's instrument half.** Nothing was fixed. Three populations, counted
separately: **26 instruments** — 3 watched to detect by an external harness (and only 1 of
those 3 is green on the runner today), 4 with an internal negative control, **2 carrying a
detection proof nothing ever runs**, 8 watched to abort only; **~22 app controls and 1 server
control with zero coverage**, plus 12 container/entrypoint/platform controls verdicted NEVER
RUN and 5 UNKNOWN; **29 remedies**, 17 never followed, 4 followed-and-failed, **5 falsified**.
The method is coverage plus caller-sweeps plus symbol grep — run history was used only to date
items, never to find them — and the document says where the derivation stops. The two largest
single findings: **nine of the app's ten permission-refusal messages have never once been
rendered**, and **the sign-in screen tells a person to check their email when no email sender
exists in this codebase.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The searching is mechanical. **Designing a search that is genuinely
different from the ones already done is the task**, and a sweep that re-finds what 11.88 found
would be wasted.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Proposed by task 11.79, which is the third instance.**

**MERGED 2026-09-01 — this task now also carries task 11.77, whose entry stands below
unchanged and must be read in full before starting.** They are one question asked of three
populations. **11.77 asks which *instruments* in `scripts/` have ever been watched
detecting** — as opposed to merely aborting, which is a different property and has been
read as though it were the same one. **This task asks which *controls* in the app and the
server have ever executed at all, and which *remedies* have ever been followed by somebody
they did not already work for.** All three are "what in this project has never been
exercised", and running them in two windows means reading the same tree twice to answer
one question. **Both halves forbid fixing anything.** Keep the three populations separate
in the report — instruments, controls, remedies — with a verdict per item and a count per
population. **A merged list with one number has lost all three.**

**The class: a control that was correct when written, and was silently falsified by a later
task.**

- **Task 11.79.** The audit purge demoted itself to the `tritrack_app` role. **Task 10.83 had
  revoked that role's right to delete audit rows — deliberately, so a compromised server cannot
  erase the record of its own compromise.** The purge would have failed on a developer's laptop,
  let alone a server. **`ensureServerAppRole`'s own comment said a purge would need "its own,
  narrower-scoped credential", and nobody read it back.**
- **Task 11.98.** A screen told removed members to wait for an invitation, weeks after
  invitations were deleted — **with a comment two files away saying that wording had become
  false.**
- **Task 11.80's predecessor.** A documented remedy that could not run in the shipped container.

> **The common factor is not the code. It is that the falsified thing was never run.** Every one
> of these was found by somebody eventually executing it, months later, by accident or because a
> task finally reached it. **A control nobody exercises cannot tell you it has stopped being
> true.**

**So the question is not "is this control correct?" — it is "has this control ever run?"** and
that is a different search from any this project has done.

**And task 11.80 added a second question of the same shape, which this survey should ask
alongside the first: has this remedy ever been followed by somebody it did not already work
for?**

> **That is a distinct class from the wrong-cause one, and worse in a specific way.** A message
> naming the **wrong** cause sends somebody to the wrong place and they come back. **A message
> naming the right cause and prescribing a remedy that cannot fix the commonest case is
> followed, fails, and costs the reader their trust in the diagnosis** — after which the next
> correct message is not believed either.
>
> 11.80's instance: the backup failure told the operator to do something that **worked only for
> people it already worked for.** It had never once been followed by anybody it did not help,
> **which is why it survived.**

**A remedy nobody has followed is in the same position as a control nobody has run**, so
enumerate both.

**Make it different, deliberately.** Task 11.88 answered this for **gate instruments** and
produced a list of two. **This is the same question asked of the app and the server**, and if
the method reduces to re-running 11.88's search it has been scoped wrongly.

- **Start mechanically: what has zero coverage?** Then narrow to what matters — **a control is
  something that refuses, deletes, expires, purges, revokes, bounds or validates.** A helper
  with no coverage is untested; a *control* with no coverage is a claim nobody has checked.
- **Include the things tests cannot reach**: scheduled jobs, CLI entrypoints, container
  healthchecks, anything invoked by an operator rather than by code. **The purge was exactly
  this — a program nothing called.**
- **Added 2026-09-02, from task 11.89's own closing caveat: record not only *whether* a thing
  has run but *where*.** 11.89 verified its live instrument against a locally-built server
  image on Michael's Mac and said plainly it had never run on a GitHub runner — **the first
  place anything in this project behaves differently**, as task 11.69 found twice. So the
  verdict for an item is not binary. **"Run, but only ever on one machine, by one person, by
  hand" is a third state**, and it is the state most of this project's instruments are
  probably in. It is also the cheapest one to change, which is why it belongs in the report's
  ranking rather than in a footnote.
- **Report the list, and for each: has it ever executed, anywhere, on any machine?** *"No"* is
  the finding. **Do not fix them** — the list is the deliverable, and fixing found instances
  inside a survey is how a survey stops halfway.

- **Acceptance:** a written list of controls with no evidence of ever having been executed, with
  what each one claims and where; the method is stated and is demonstrably not 11.88's; and the
  report names **which of them would be cheap to exercise and which need a machine somebody
  does not have** — so the follow-up can be scheduled instead of admired.

### Task 11.120 — The Offline Data Map has two steps of a four-step chain, and finding out why is the task
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04.** The screen now uses the project extent when there is no fix, and
**the 250× slowdown was re-measured and was never this provider.** Task 11.103 attributed it to
`currentProjectProvider`; the cause was its own `estimateTileCount` finding, which it fixed in the
same commit. Measured three ways on 2026-09-04: watch in, today's tile counter — the suite runs in
**1 second**; watch *removed*, 11.103's old tile counter restored — **one test takes 4 minutes 18
seconds**. So the watch contributes nothing measurable, and there is no on-device finding to file:
`currentProject` is `keepAlive` and costs **9–21 ms once per app launch** (dominated by the
database open every screen pays for anyway) and **8.8 microseconds per rebuild**, on a macOS host
with a real on-disk database — recorded and bounded in
`test/features/more/current_project_watch_cost_test.dart`, which prints both numbers every run.
**No task number is owed for an expensive provider, because it is not one.** 11.146's half landed
too: the *Offline Data* screen's region rows now say when an elevation area has files on disk that
cannot be read, and what to do about it. **Nobody has looked at either change on a phone.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Wiring one provider is trivial. **Explaining why wiring it made a
test suite 250 times slower is the work**, and task 11.103 was right that this is the valuable
half.
**Depends on:** 11.103, which tried it and backed it out.

**The symptom.** The Offline Data Map has **steps 1 and 4 of the fallback chain only** — the
device's position, and the honest empty state. **It ignores the project extent**, so with no
GPS fix it opens on the whole planet and somebody has to pan to their study area before drawing
a download region. **It no longer opens on the Atlantic**, which is what 11.103 was for.

**The investigation, which is why this is Opus and not a five-line fix.** 11.103 wired
`currentProjectProvider` into that screen and **backed it out: the screen's own suite went from
under a second to over three minutes per test, with an in-memory database.**

> **That is not a test problem until it is proved to be one.** **If watching that provider is
> expensive under the test clock, it may be expensive on a phone** — and **other screens watch
> it.** A 250× cost that only shows up when something watches is the shape of a provider doing
> work on every rebuild, and the app's own map, record and log screens are all downstream of
> the same question.

- **Measure before fixing.** What does that provider do on each watch, how often does it
  rebuild, and what is the cost on a device rather than under `flutter test`? **If the answer
  is that it is cheap in production and pathological only under the test clock, say so and the
  fix is trivial.** If it is not, **stop and report** — that is a different and larger finding
  than a missing map step, and it should not be fixed inside this task.
- **Then wire the extent step in**, whichever way the measurement allows.

- **Acceptance:** the Offline Data Map uses the project extent when there is no fix; **the 250×
  slowdown is explained**, with a stated cost on-device rather than only under test; and if the
  provider turns out to be expensive in production, that is filed as its own finding with a task
  number rather than absorbed here.

> **What landed, 2026-09-04.** The screen takes **steps 1, 3 and 4** — a device fix, then the
> project extent, then the whole-planet framing. **Step 2 (the last day's recordings) was
> deliberately left out and the reason is written into the code**: this screen is choosing an area
> to *cover*, and the project extent is that area by definition, where the Main Map is showing
> somebody their data and "where you were working last" is the better answer there. Reaching step 2
> would also pull four recording repositories into a screen that has never read one.
> Placement is no longer decided on the first build alone — the project arrives from a database, so
> the first build always sees `loading` — and **a camera the person has already panned is never
> taken back from them.**

#### Merged in 2026-09-04 — task 11.146, because it lands on this same screen

**A terrain tile is refused and nobody is ever told.** Task 11.143 gave the store real health
states and **silently re-fetches an unusable tile — and if the person is offline at that moment it
silently stays a hole.** 11.143 declined to add a signal mid-task because where it belongs is a
design call. **CORRECTED 2026-09-04 by task 11.120: this screen has no region list.** The Offline Data Map
has coverage polygons on a map, a legend and job progress cards. **The screen with one row per
downloaded area is `ManageOfflineMapsScreen` ("Offline Data"), and that is where the sentence
went.** Task 11.135's survey settled it: the *live tile* signal belongs where somebody is
downloading on purpose, and this is a fact about **stored** data whose remedy needs a connection,
so it belongs on the screen somebody reads before going out. **The prediction was the planning
session's and it was wrong** — quoted here so it is findable as the error.

- **`tileHealth` already returns `absent` / `unusable` / `incomplete` / `complete`.** The states
  are named — **do not invent a second vocabulary.** See `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`,
  *A DEM Tile's Presence Is a Record, Not a File*.
- **Check task 11.135 first.** It surveyed five screens that say nothing when tiles do not arrive;
  **its answer should not be re-derived.**
- **Do not duplicate task 11.142's caveat.** That one says a *viewshed* was computed over
  incomplete terrain. This would be about the *stored data*. **If that distinction cannot be put in
  one sentence a field biologist would act on differently, say so and recommend not adding it** —
  that is a legitimate outcome and this entry means it.
- **Say what a person can do.** Per the standing rule that a check must name what is wrong,
  *"some terrain is damaged"* with no action is worse than silence. **Re-downloading needs a
  connection; say so when there is not one.**
- **The full original entry is task 11.146**, kept in this document and marked merged.

> **Order matters within this task: settle the extent/fallback chain first.** The signal's home is
> the region list, and this task may change what that list is. **Do not design the signal against a
> screen you are about to alter.**
