### Task 11.121 — The capability guard checks two shapes out of six, and the wrong two are missing
**Status:** Done, 2026-09-01. `scripts/verify_merged_manifest_capabilities.sh` now checks
`android:exported="true"` on every element that can carry it (by real XML parsing, not a
regex or an element-name list), plus `<queries>` entries separately, alongside the existing
`<uses-permission>`/`<uses-feature>` checks. The stop condition was checked first: today's
built APK exports exactly two components, `MainActivity` (required for launch, already the
recorded K-3 trust boundary from task 10.77) and AndroidX's `ProfileInstallReceiver`
(already recorded, permission-guarded) — nothing unrecorded. Both new checks were watched
going red with an injected exported receiver and an injected `<queries>` entry, then
reverted. `CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md` records the `<queries>` decision (kept in the guard, as a
disclosure rather than an attack surface) and the exported-components sweep result.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium.
**Depends on:** 11.76, which built the guard and named its own limit.

**The finding.** `scripts/verify_merged_manifest_capabilities.sh` checks `<uses-permission>`
and `<uses-feature>` — **the two shapes task 11.66's worked example happened to use.**
`CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md`'s second-pass table records four more **by hand**: `<queries>`,
`<service>`, `<activity>`, an exported `<receiver>`, and `<uses-library>`. **A plugin adding one
of those merges into the built APK and nothing in CI says so.**

**11.76 asked whether this is worth closing, and said the design question — *which elements are
capability-relevant?* — is a real one rather than a small addition. It is, and the answer
narrows the task rather than widening it.**

> **The six shapes are not equal, and only one property makes any of them matter:
> `android:exported`.** A `<uses-library>` is inert. **An exported `<activity>`, `<service>` or
> `<receiver>` is a component any other app on the phone can invoke** — an attack surface that
> arrived without anybody deciding to add one, on a device holding collar locations.
>
> **So the criterion is not "which of the six elements?" It is "did anything become reachable
> from outside this app?"** That is one question, it is checkable, and it is the one the
> capability matrix exists to answer.

- **Check for exported components across every element that can carry the attribute**, rather
  than enumerating element names. **An element list is a hand-maintained list**, which is the
  defect this guard was built to end.
- **`<queries>` deserves a separate sentence:** it is not an attack surface but it *is* a
  disclosure — it declares what other apps this one can see. **Decide whether it belongs in the
  matrix at all**, and record the answer.
- **Watch it go red**, as 11.76 did with its own check, by adding an exported component to a
  test manifest.

**And if this finds an exported component that is already in the built APK today, stop and say
so before fixing anything** — that would be an unrecorded trust boundary rather than a gap in a
guard, and it belongs in `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md` before it belongs in a diff.

- **Acceptance:** the guard fails on any newly exported component regardless of element type;
  the `<queries>` decision is recorded; the check is watched going red; and **anything already
  exported in today's APK is reported rather than quietly accepted.**

### Task 11.122 — The sentence telling you not to try is the branch reached when nobody knows why
**Status:** **Partial — items 1 and 2 Done 2026-09-01 (commit aa2ded4); item 3 not started.**
Items 1 and 2 are what task 11.89 depends on, so **11.89 is unblocked.** Item 3 — an issue
code on the wire — stopped at the sizing, on this task's own instruction to ship 1 and 2 and
say so: it needs a client schema migration (a new column on `Sync_Held_Rows`, a version bump
in the shared package), a change to the push response envelope, and five server-side outcome
sites, which is a protocol-and-migration change rather than the improvement-on-top the entry
describes. **See the Discovered Scope entry below for what it would take.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Item 1 is small and the rule for it is already written. Item 2
is a decision about what the app says when it does not know why, and **the wrong answer to
that question is what is on the screen today.**
**Depends on:** 11.84, which measured the behaviour and found the copy. **Blocks 11.89.**

**Two findings, one story, which is why they are one task and not two.** Somebody pastes a
name carrying a control character or a bidirectional override. **Nothing stops them:**
`identity_validation.dart`'s `validateRequiredName` checks only that the field is non-empty
— no length bound, and no use of the shared `RowValidator.isWellFormedPersonName` the server
enforces. Both the identity setup screen and the profile screen use it. The name saves. One
sync later the server refuses the `Users` row; **the row is held once and never retried, and
11.84 measured that and it is right.** What is wrong is what the person then reads.
`held_row_details.dart`'s `HeldRowReason.rejected` branch says *"That is a fault in the app
or a version mismatch, not something wrong with what you recorded"* and *"nothing you can do
in the app will change the answer."* **Both sentences are false for this case** — it is
something about what they recorded, and editing the name in Profile fixes it and re-offers
the row automatically, measured. **This is task 11.54's defect class: copy describing a
mechanism the code does not have.**

**1. Check the name where it is typed, using the rule that already exists.** Point
`validateRequiredName` at the shared declaration rather than restating it — one change
covers both screens. **The bound stays enforced at the boundary**; this is a courtesy to the
person, not a security control, and nothing about the server's refusal changes.
- **The screen must let somebody correct a name that is already stored and has become
  invalid.** Task 11.89 widens the rule and makes that case real. **A profile screen that
  refuses to submit because of a value it loaded is a screen nobody can get out of** — and
  the only way out of this one is the very field it is refusing.

**2. The `rejected` branch must stop asserting a cause it cannot know.** Name the real
defect before choosing a fix. It is **not** that `rejected` lacks a second reason. It is
that **the branch reached when the client has no information states a cause as fact.** The
push response carries an outcome with no issue detail, so the client genuinely cannot tell
"your value is malformed" from "app or version mismatch" — and today's copy resolves that
uncertainty by picking one and asserting it.

> **Fix the default before fixing the case.** Whatever else this task does, the branch
> reached when the client does not know why must say only what is known: the server refused
> this record, here is where to look, here is how to ask. **It must never say there is
> nothing you can do**, because that is the one sentence that is unrecoverable when it is
> wrong — the person stops trying, and a person who stops trying files no report.

That is the class fix, it is cheap, and **it holds for refusal reasons nobody has invented
yet** — which is the test of whether a fix is aimed at the class or the instance.

**3. Then, and only once item 2 has landed, put an issue code on the wire** so the name case
gets the true sentence and the remedy rather than the honest shrug. **Two constraints if you
do.** The code must be derived from the same shared declaration that produced the refusal
rather than typed at the throw site — *a structure keyed on a string somebody writes is a
hand-maintained list*, and this project has that rule from task 11.88. And **an unrecognised
code must fall to item 2's honest default**, never to today's.

- **Acceptance:** a malformed name cannot be saved from either screen, and a name already
  stored and now invalid can still be corrected; the `rejected` fallback claims no cause it
  cannot know and never tells anybody that nothing can be done; if an issue code ships, the
  unknown-code path is tested and lands on the honest default; and the false sentences are
  gone from `held_row_details.dart` rather than reworded around.

### Task 11.124 — Which part of the record was refused, and the migration tests that will govern saying so
**Status:** **DONE 2026-09-02.** All three suites green: app 2029, server 838 against a real
Postgres, shared package 336.

**One thing the brief got wrong about the mechanism, and the judgment call made instead.**
The brief said the client must store the code via *"a new column on `Sync_Held_Rows`, a
`latestSchemaVersion` bump, and a migration step."* **`Sync_Held_Rows` is a client-only
table** — it is not in `tableSpecs`, it does not move with `latestSchemaVersion`, and it is
created by `SyncHeldRowStore.ensureTable` on every open rather than by a numbered migration.
Bumping the shared constant would announce a change to the *synced* schema, which is
negotiated with the server on every request, when nothing about the data contract had moved.
**So the two new columns are added in place inside `ensureTable`**, following
`UnknownColumnStore.ensureTable`'s precedent from task 10.76 — additive rather than 10.76's
drop, because a held row is the memory that field data has not reached the server and the
missing value here is only an explanation. `test/data/sync/held_row_issue_code_test.dart` is
the populated-database upgrade test the acceptance asks for: same obligation, different
mechanism. **`latestSchemaVersion` is unchanged at 11.**

**11.82's half found nothing, and that is the result.** The v8 test now stops at v8 and stays
green; the v7 test had the identical defect (`from: 6, to: latestSchemaVersion`) and was fixed
with it, also still green. So neither, once corrected, was hiding anything. The new
`test/data/schema_v9_migration_test.dart` covers the `Tag_Versions` table, its index and
`Observations.tag_version_id` on a populated v8 database, and passes.

**The database re-open question is answered: harness-only, nothing real can reach it.** The
app opens its database exactly once per process, from a `keepAlive` provider; the only other
open in the codebase (`PreMigrationBackup`'s version probe) closes before the real one; and
**nothing in `lib/` deletes the database file** — there is no in-app restore, and every
filesystem delete in the app targets map tiles, DEM tiles, keychain entries, or old
pre-migration snapshots under `pre_migration_backups/`. About eight minutes.

**Was:** Not started. **Below the line. Nothing is broken while it waits** — task 11.122
put an honest default in place, so today a person whose record is refused reads a sentence
that claims no cause and offers steps rather than one telling them to stop.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The wire change is mechanical. **What is not: a refusal code
that must be derived rather than typed, a disclosure bound that must not be widened, and a
client schema migration arriving in a repository whose migration tests do not test what
their names say.**
**Depends on:** 11.122, which shipped items 1 and 2 and **measured what item 3 costs rather
than guessing.**

#### Do this before anything else: remove the pattern that makes adding a field dangerous

**Added 2026-09-02 from task 11.96's sweep, and the ordering is the argument.** `SyncSchedule`
(`lib/data/sync/sync_schedule.dart`, 5 fields) **hand-rebuilds itself in five methods** —
`recordAttempt`, `recordSuccess`, `recordFailure`, `withFrequency`, `resumed` — exactly the way
`SyncStatus` did before 11.96/11.117 replaced it with `copyWith`. **Third instance of the class,
same subsystem.**

> **This task adds a field to the sync layer.** A hand-written rebuild is precisely the thing that
> makes adding a field dangerous: every argument is supplied, every one is valid, **and the
> compiler cannot tell you that one call site forgot the new one.** For `SyncStatus` the silent
> default meant *healthy*. **Give `SyncSchedule` a `copyWith` first, then add the field.**

**And a behaviour change from 11.96 is signed off here, 2026-09-02, because it touches the same
object.** `setFrequency`'s old rebuild silently reset `running`/`progress` to false/null on every
call, which the neighbouring `dismissStaleness` rebuild never did; `copyWith` now carries both
through. **Verified by the planning session rather than accepted on description:** `setFrequency`
writes the store and rebuilds the status and **does not cancel a running round**, so the round
really is still going and the old reset was the bar making a false statement about the app's own
state. **Correct as shipped.** The reopen trigger would be `setFrequency` ever gaining the power
to cancel a round — at which point `running: false` becomes true again and this must be revisited.

**MERGED 2026-09-01 — this task carries task 11.82, whose entry stands below unchanged and
must be read in full before starting.** The reason is not thematic. **This task adds a
migration**, and 11.82 is the task that makes the migration tests test what they name: the
v8 test currently upgrades all the way to the latest version rather than stopping at v8, so
it passes for a reason other than the one it claims, and **there is no populated-database
upgrade test for v9 at all.** Adding a v10 migration under that discipline means the new
migration ships with an upgrade test that is honest about what it covers. **Do 11.82's half
first** — a correct instrument before the thing it must measure — and say in the report
whether fixing the v8 test found anything once it stopped where it says it stops.

**The finding, and 11.122 measured every part of this rather than estimating it.** The push
response (`SyncPushResponse` in `packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/sync_protocol.dart`) carries
`outcomes` — a row key mapped to a bare outcome string — **and nothing else**, so the client
genuinely cannot tell "your value is malformed" from "app or version mismatch". The server
sets `SyncRowOutcome.invalid` at **five separate sites** in
`server/lib/src/sync/sync_service.dart`, none of which currently carries the `RowIssue` list
that explains the refusal. `RowIssue` has no code field. And the client must **store** the
code, which is a new column on `Sync_Held_Rows`, a `latestSchemaVersion` bump, and a
migration step.

**What it buys:** *"the first name has a character the server will not store"* instead of
*"the server refused this and did not say why."*

**Three constraints, and each of them is the kind that gets lost in the middle of a protocol
change:**

- **The code must be derived from the `ColumnSpec` bound that produced the refusal, not
  typed at the throw site.** That means adding a code to `TextShape`/`TextBound` and
  threading it out of `RowValidator`. **A code chosen by hand at five call sites is a
  hand-maintained list** — task 11.88's rule, and the reason this is Opus.
- **An unrecognised code must fall back to the honest default task 11.122 shipped**, which
  means the two named constants in `held_row_details.dart` **stay reachable rather than
  being replaced.** Test that path with a code the client has never seen. The whole value of
  11.122 is that the default is correct for reasons nobody has invented yet; a task that
  deletes it to make room for the specific case has undone it.
- **The detail may ride only on the `invalid` outcome.** The `unauthorized` outcome stays
  deliberately opaque — security model §4.13 — and **a code attached to it would reopen the
  existence oracle.** This is a security bound, not a design preference.

- **Acceptance:** the v8 upgrade test stops at v8 and a populated-database v9 test exists,
  both before the new migration lands; the refusal code is derived from the column's declared
  bound and no code is written by hand at an outcome site; an unknown code is tested and
  reaches 11.122's default; `unauthorized` carries no detail and a test says so; and the
  schema bump ships with its own populated-database upgrade test rather than relying on the
  ones this task just repaired.

trigger is restated as something that can actually happen** — decide which, and say why. **A
trigger nobody can pull is decoration**, which is the rule task 11.50's deferral already rests
on.

#### 5. The secret-rotation procedure, which nobody has followed

`server/README.md:222` gives four steps. **Step 2 is "update `.env`", and on an
already-initialised Postgres volume that plausibly does not change the database's password** —
it changes what the server presents, after which the server cannot connect. Steps 1 and 4 give
no SQL, unlike the session-revocation block immediately below them. **11.119 flagged this as
uncertainty rather than asserting it, which was right.** Run it against a throwaway stack with
an existing volume. **If the procedure is wrong, stop and report** — a documented remedy that
breaks the server is a worse finding than a missing one, and it is 11.80's class exactly.


#### 6. Michael's five answers, 2026-09-02 — three verdicts, one contradiction, one new finding

He answered the survey's five UNKNOWN questions. **Record the verdicts in
`UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md`, and treat the last two as work rather than as answers.**

- **`scripts/restore_db.sh` — never run by hand. Verdict: NEVER RUN.**
- **`scripts/audit_retention_status.sh` — "not that I can remember". Verdict: NEVER RUN**, which
  agrees with the survey's own finding that it has no caller anywhere.
- **The three backup values in the VM's `.env` — "I don't think so".**
- **`scripts/server_up.sh` — not used.** He starts the stack with
  `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev-lan.yml up --build -d`.

**(a) A NEW FINDING, and it is 11.80's class again: the script that exists to make starting the
stack correct cannot express the only configuration anybody actually starts.** `server_up.sh`
runs a bare `docker compose up "$@"` — **it carries no `-f` files of its own and offers no way
to add them**, so running it would silently drop `docker-compose.dev-lan.yml`, which is what
turns the file-based magic-link sender on and is the whole reason the two-device walkthrough
works. **So the remedy for task 11.70's ownership problem is unusable by the one person running
this stack**, and nothing says so: the script's own header explains at length why a raw
`docker compose up` is wrong, and then hands back something that cannot be used instead.
**Decide and implement one of: the script accepts or composes the extra files; `COMPOSE_FILE`
is documented as the supported way (verify it, do not assume Compose reads it from `.env`); or
the header says plainly that a multi-file stack must export `TRITRACK_BACKUP_UID/GID` by hand
and how.** **Whichever, watch the backup-scheduler come up owning the right user afterwards** —
that is the property, not the flag.

**(b) A contradiction that must not be resolved by guessing, and the likely answer is a
finding.** He also reports the newest archive in `backups/` is named for **31 August** — but
says the three backup values are probably not filled in. **Both cannot be true of a working
daily schedule.** Task 11.78's own comms record that the first successful backup that server
ever took was on 2026-08-31, the day that task ran. **Today is 2 September. A newest archive
two days old is not evidence backups work; on a daily schedule it is the symptom that they
stopped** — and per the survey's own item 4, **nothing in this project reads a container's
health, so nobody was ever going to be told.**
**Settle it on the VM rather than by reasoning:** `scripts/backup_status.sh` for the sentence,
`docker compose ps` for the colour — they run the same program and cannot disagree. **Report
which it is.** If the scheduler has been failing since 31 August, that is a real finding about
the beta host and it stops this task rather than being fixed inside a batch.

- **Acceptance:** item 1 is answered with the instrument's real output and the record is
  corrected wherever it carries the false cause; each item attempted is reported as done, or
  as not done with a reason; **no item is reported as done on the strength of reading a file**;
  anything that turns out to be a real finding stops rather than being fixed inside a
  batch; **Michael's four verdicts are written into `UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md`**; and **the
  backup contradiction is settled by running something on the VM, not by reasoning about
  it.**
