### Task 11.207 — Climb and descent on the profile, and the first thing in this app that recalculates as you walk
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-09.** The climb and descent are sampled at the DEM's own ground spacing —
derived from `ElevationGrid.cellSizeDegrees`, ~73 m at the fixture's latitude, never the fixed 41
points — and summed by accumulating same-direction change past a named 10 m threshold whose reason is
SRTM's 10 m relative vertical accuracy. **The brief's "≈38 m/px at z12" is the *source* tiles'
resolution and not the grid's**: the stored DEM is ~90 m (`kDemCellSizeMeters`), which is what
deriving from the grid gives and what "never coarser than the DEM" means here. **No cap** — measured
first: 274 samples and about 1 ms for a 20 km line, 1,215 samples and about 5 ms for an 89 km one
(`test/features/map/terrain_profile_cost_test.dart`). `_ElevationProfilePanel` was generalised into
`lib/features/map/widgets/elevation_profile_panel.dart` and now serves both callers;
`_NavigationBanner` is gone and navigation is a collapsed panel on the bottom edge carrying target,
distance, bearing, climb, descent and Stop. Following a fix is contained to `resumed` — the
subscription is dropped on any other lifecycle state — with re-sampling gated on
`max(10 m, the fix's accuracy)` and suppressed entirely while collapsed after the first sample.
**No background location and no background work.** Ten tests across
`terrain_profile_test.dart`, `terrain_profile_cost_test.dart` and
`elevation_profile_panel_test.dart`; **the lifecycle and totals assertions were watched red under six
deliberate sabotages**, and one of them changed the test: with the app paused the rendered text does
not move *whether or not the fix was taken*, so the containment is asserted on the subscription
(`hasListener` on the fixture's own stream) rather than on the screen. The map's clear band was
re-measured and **went up** — 512 at the default text size against 438 before — because the banner
left the top-left column for the bottom edge, where furniture already sits. **Below the line.**
Michael, 2026-09-09: put total ascent and descent beside
the distance and bearing above the elevation graph, and give the Navigate screen the same panel with
the grey bar, updating as the user moves.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Neither half is intricate. **The judgement is in one number that will
read as a fact and one behaviour that has never existed in this app.**
**Depends on:** nothing.

#### 1. The ascent number is a measurement, and the sampling is where it goes wrong

**Michael's answer to what it is for: "how hard is this walk."** So it is the sum of every climb and
every descent along the line, not the net change.

**The defect to avoid is under-reporting, and the current code walks straight into it.**
`_ElevationChart` samples the line at **a fixed 41 points whatever its length**. On a 200-metre line
that is a reading every 5 metres; **on a 20-kilometre line it is one every 500 metres**, and every
gully between two samples does not exist as far as a sum is concerned. **A long walk would report a
fraction of its real climb, in a box, next to a distance that is exact.**

> **The opposite worry is small here and saying so keeps somebody from over-engineering it.**
> `ElevationGrid.elevationAt` is **bilinear**, so the surface between DEM posts is smooth rather than
> jittery — over-sampling it does not manufacture ascent the way over-sampling a GPS track does. **The
> rule is therefore one-sided: the number's sampling must never be coarser than the DEM's own
> spacing.** The chart may sample as finely as it likes for a smooth line.

- **Sample the number at the DEM's ground spacing.** The store is z12 terrarium — the source says
  **≈38 m per pixel at the equator, finer with latitude.** Derive the step from the grid rather than
  typing 30.
- **Ignore runs smaller than a stated threshold, by accumulating same-direction change and only
  committing a run once it exceeds it.** Not by discarding individual steps — that is the version
  that quietly loses a real slow climb. **Name the threshold as a constant with its reason beside
  it**; the reason is the vertical accuracy of the source data, not a number that looked nice.
- **Do not add a sample cap on speculation.** At DEM spacing a 20 km line is a few hundred samples.
  **Measure the real cost at a realistic worst case** — the largest project extent this app supports —
  **and add a cap only if the measurement asks for one.** If one is added, the panel says when it is
  in force; a silently capped total is the defect this item exists to prevent.
- **The same two points must always give the same answer**, whatever the panel's height, the chart's
  width, or how it was opened. **Assert that.**

**Where it goes:** the profile panel's header row, which currently reads `⟷ 1.24 km · 072°`. An up
arrow and a down arrow beside it. **That row is also the collapsed state**, so it is the one row that
has to hold everything and it is already tight — `Flexible`/ellipsis, like every other narrow row on
these screens.

#### 2. The Navigate screen gets the same panel, and the banner disappears into it

**Michael chose to fold the existing banner in.** Collapsed, the grey bar reads the target, the
distance and the bearing, and carries the **Stop** button. Pulled up, the graph with climb and
descent. `_NavigationBanner` goes.

**Generalise the existing panel; do not write a second one.** `_ElevationProfilePanel` already has
exactly the collapse-to-a-handle behaviour being asked for, including the snap. **Two copies of this
graph would drift within a month**, and the ascent number would then be right in one of them.

#### 3. The recalculation rule, and it is the part to get right

**This is the first thing in this app that recomputes because a person moved.** Everything else waits
for a tap.

**Michael's constraint, and it is the whole containment: recalculate only while the app is in the
foreground with the screen on.** He described the real workflow — look, decide, pocket the phone,
walk, check once or twice. **So there is no background work of any kind, and no background-location
permission is introduced.** Say that plainly in the code, because the next person to touch this will
be tempted.

- **Subscribe to position updates only while the lifecycle state is `resumed`; drop the subscription
  otherwise.**
- **Recompute when the person has moved more than `max(10 m, the fix's own reported accuracy)`.** A
  flat 10 m re-draws forever on a phone standing still, because that is roughly what GPS noise is.
- **Collapsed still updates distance and bearing; it does not recompute the profile.** Those numbers
  are arithmetic on two coordinates and cost nothing, **and they are exactly what Michael said people
  check** — the graph is the expensive half and the half nobody is looking at while it is shut.
- **Outside downloaded terrain, say so and keep navigating.** The graph is unavailable; the distance
  and bearing are not. **This will happen more often here than on the measure tool**, because a person
  can walk out of a downloaded region.

#### 4. What to assert, because two of these are easy to fake

- **A synthetic DEM with a known answer** — a ramp up then down — and the ascent and descent asserted
  **exactly**. A test that only checks the number is positive is not a test of this.
- **The same line at two different panel heights gives the same totals.**
- **The lifecycle rule needs a positive control in the same test**: assert that position updates *are*
  taken while resumed **and** are not while paused. **The "not while paused" half alone passes if the
  widget never built at all**, which is the standing rule about assertions made by absence.

- **Acceptance:** the number's sampling is derived from the DEM and never coarser than it; the
  threshold is a named constant with its reason; no cap is added without a measurement, and any cap is
  visible; the panel is generalised rather than duplicated and `_NavigationBanner` is gone; no
  background location or background work is introduced; the collapsed bar updates the cheap numbers
  only; the synthetic-DEM totals are exact; the lifecycle test carries its positive control.



### Task 11.208 — A threshold Michael overruled, and two ways the suite cries wolf
**Status:** Done, 2026-09-09. **Below the line.** Three small things out of task 11.207's two reports.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** Item 1 is one constant and a paragraph that must be rewritten rather
than edited. **Items 2 and 3 are both about the suite that gates every commit.**
**Depends on:** 11.207.

#### 1. The climb threshold drops to 5 m, and the reason in the file has to change with it

**Michael's call, 2026-09-09, having read what it costs.** `kTerrainReliefThresholdMeters` goes from
10.0 to **5.0**.

**Do not just change the number.** The doc comment above it currently derives 10 from **SRTM's
specified relative vertical accuracy — 10 m at 90% confidence** — and says a run smaller than that
cannot be told apart from the source's own error. **That reasoning does not support 5, and leaving it
in place would make the file claim a derivation it no longer has.**

**Rewrite it to say what is now true:** the number is **a field judgement made against that
specification, not derived from it.** Michael walks country with rolling eight-metre knolls that the
cautious number reported as flat, and he chose to accept some of the source's noise as counted climb
in exchange for seeing them. **Say both halves** — what it now catches and what it now adds — so the
next person can move it again with the same information.

> **This is the good version of a number changing.** The old value had a citation; the new one has a
> reason. **What would have been wrong is a number with neither**, and the way that happens is
> somebody editing the digit and leaving the paragraph.

#### 2. A test with 75% of its budget spent, on real wall-clock time, in the suite that gates commits

`test/core/net/request_deadline_test.dart`'s *"a slow but moving answer is never interrupted"* refused
one of task 11.207's commits and then passed three times in a row. **The cause is visible in the test
rather than guessed:** it feeds a chunk every **30 ms against a 40 ms inactivity deadline** — **75% of
the budget** — on real wall-clock time, **so a machine busy running the other 283 test files can slip
past it.**

> **Task 11.204's rule applies exactly: that is a reproducible cause, not a shrug.** And task 11.207
> did the right thing twice over — **it did not use the escape hatch, and it did not fix somebody
> else's file on the way past.**

**Give it margin or give it a fake clock.** A fake clock is the better answer if it is cheap here,
because margin only moves the failure to a busier machine. **Whichever is chosen, say why**, and
**state the new ratio of chunk interval to deadline as a number.**

**Why this is worth doing at all, and it is not tidiness.** The pre-commit suite gates every commit.
**Three tasks in a row used the escape hatch in early September because a red nobody trusted was
standing**, and this is the shape of red that produces that.

#### 3. A guard that refuses correctly and names the wrong file

`test/routing/shell_provider_chain_test.dart` went red on its own self-check because `map_screen.dart`
briefly held an **adjacent-string-literal concatenation inside a `${...}` interpolation**. Its string
blanker mis-tracks that, the brace-depth declaration finder loses where declarations begin, and **the
check refuses rather than deriving nonsense — which is the right behaviour.**

**The defect is the message, not the refusal.** It cost ten minutes because **it named the wrong
file**, and the next person to hit it will go and stare at the provider they just added.

- **Fix the message first and treat that as the deliverable:** say what construct was found, in which
  file, at which line, and that the check has abstained rather than failed.
- **Hardening the blanker is optional and secondary.** If it is cheap, do it; if it is not, say so.
  **A safe refusal that misdirects is a tax on somebody who did nothing wrong**, and the tax is paid
  in the message.

#### 4. Not a task: the colour count stands at three, and the threshold is five

Task 11.207's profile trace was `ColorScheme.primary` at both call sites — **the brand green, matching
nothing on the map, on a panel whose one subject is a line drawn above it in another colour.** That is
**the third defect of the "a colour that arrived by default rather than by decision" class found by a
person looking**, after the Position screen's tag label and the six `ColorScheme` fallbacks.

**No instrument yet, and the reason is task 11.199's own written threshold: the fifth report is when
you build it.** **Recording the count here so the next one is counted rather than merely fixed**, and
recording what the instrument would have to do, so the question is not re-derived from scratch: a grep
is useless because `primary` is used legitimately everywhere, so it would have to **render against a
sentinel theme and assert that nothing takes the sentinel except where it is meant to.**

- **Acceptance:** the threshold is 5.0 **and its paragraph is rewritten rather than edited**; the
  timing test's new ratio is stated as a number with the choice explained; the guard's message names
  the construct, the file and the line, and says it abstained; the colour count is recorded.



### Task 11.209 — Getting a position out of this app without retyping it
**Status:** Done. Michael, 2026-09-09: *"What I want to avoid is having to
manually type lat/lons into other apps on my phone."*
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** Mostly plumbing. **The two things to get right are a dependency
decision and four record types that do not all mean the same thing.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Half of it already exists in the wrong place.**

#### 1. Do not build a second copy of a format this app already has

**`lib/data/sharing/observation_share.dart` already encodes an observation into TriTrack's own
pasteable format**, `TT1:`-prefixed, currently at payload v4, **and `log_screen.dart` already offers it
as a per-row Copy.** The paste screen parses exactly that.

> **So "Copy for TriTrack" on the map card is a second call site, not a second format.** If this task
> writes its own encoder the two will diverge, and the failure will be somebody's pasted bearing
> refused on a colleague's phone in the field. **Reuse the encoder; do not re-encode.**

#### 2. The menu, and it varies by record type because the record types are not alike

**Michael's shape, agreed 2026-09-09:** a share icon on the selection card opening

- **Copy coordinates** — in the project's own format, via `CoordinateFormatter.format`. **Decimal
  degrees, degrees-minutes-seconds and UTM are all already supported; do not invent a precision or a
  fourth format.** This is the plain answer to what he actually asked for.
- **Copy for TriTrack** — the existing encoder. **Only where the encoder supports that record.**
- **Share…** — the platform's own share sheet, offering the text and **a GPX file**.
- **Open in Maps.**

**`_MapSelection` is a `sealed class` with four variants** — observation, estimate, truth point, free
point — **so a `switch` over it is exhaustive and the compiler will refuse an unanswered case.** **Use
that.** A fifth selection type added in a year then cannot ship without somebody deciding what sharing
means for it. **That is the difference between fixing the class and fixing the instance, and here it
is free.**

- **A free-tapped point is not a record**: coordinates, share and maps, **no TriTrack copy** — there is
  no observation to encode.
- **A bearing is not a point, and Michael has accepted the limitation in writing.** Its maps pin is
  **the observation's own position, which is where the observer stood**, and the label says so.
  **Mapping apps do not draw bearings; that is a known limitation and is not to be worked around.**
- **A position estimate's uncertainty does not survive a map pin.** Also accepted. **The plain text
  and the GPX carry it; the pin cannot.** Say so in the code rather than leaving it to be rediscovered.

**Maps handoff is in the list but not at the top of it**, because it is the only entry that does
nothing without a signal, and this is a field app.

#### 3. The dependency, and §3.8 wants a sentence not a version

**`url_launcher` is already a dependency**, so *Open in Maps* needs nothing new. **The native share
sheet does** — `share_plus` or equivalent.

**§3.8 says every dependency is pinned *and reviewed*, and the review is the sentence.** Write it
beside the pin: what it is for, what it costs, and what the app does if it is ever dropped. **A
dependency added without that line is the shape task 11.175 spent itself on.**

- **Platform behaviour, stated rather than assumed:** on Android a `geo:` URI opens a chooser —
  **which is how a point reaches Gaia or Avenza without a second menu item** — and on iOS the Apple
  Maps URL is the right target. **Handle "nothing on this phone answers that scheme" rather than
  failing silently.**
- **The GPX file is written to a cache directory and named for the record**, not left in a place that
  accumulates.

#### 4. What to assert, because "the share sheet opened" is not a test

- **The exact string produced for each of the four selection types**, in each of the three coordinate
  formats. That is the deliverable and it is fully assertable without a share sheet.
- **The GPX parses back.** A file Gaia refuses is worse than no file, and *"it was written"* is not
  evidence that it is valid. **Parse it and compare the point to the record it came from.**
- **The TriTrack payload from the map card is byte-identical to the one `log_screen.dart` produces**
  for the same observation. **That is the check that stops the two diverging**, and it is the one that
  matters most.

#### 5. Two things not to disturb

- **The selection card's header row is inside the map's space budget.** Put the icon **in that row
  beside the close button, not in a new row**, and re-run the budget test rather than assuming.
- **The share strings are user-visible copy** — the content lane collects them, per the standing
  arrangement.

- **Acceptance:** one encoder, with a test proving both call sites agree byte-for-byte; the menu
  switches over the sealed type with no default case; a free point offers no TriTrack copy; a
  bearing's pin is labelled as the observer's position; the dependency carries its review sentence;
  the GPX parses back; the budget test is re-run; the new sentences are listed for the content lane.



### Task 11.210 — A wait that gives up quietly, and two reds with a measured rate
**Status:** Done, 2026-09-09. `elevation_profile_panel_test.dart`'s `pumpUntil` now throws a
`TestFailure` naming the condition and the budget when it times out; all 15 call sites updated.
The other two waiters (`map_screen_test.dart`'s `ComputationFailed` poll, `magic_link_reader.dart`'s)
were judged safe and left unchanged — see comms entry for the reasoning and the measured rates.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** Item 1 is small and provable by reading. **Item 2 is a measurement and
must not be answered with a hypothesis.**
**Depends on:** 11.209, which reported both.

#### 1. "Does not reproduce" and "reproduces one time in twelve" are different claims

Task 11.209 reported two failures in a 2585-test single-process run as *"do not reproduce"*, and gave
the numbers that contradict the word: `elevation_profile_panel_test.dart`'s *"collapsed, it updates
the distance but not the profile"* passed **11 of 12** across two rounds of repeats.

> **It reproduced. Once in twelve.** The word matters because *"does not reproduce"* closes a question
> and *"one in twelve"* opens one with a rate attached. **The report is the reason the correction is
> possible** — it gave the count rather than the impression, which is exactly what `CLAUDE.md` asks
> for, and this entry is a refinement of the wording rather than a complaint about the work.

#### 2. A defect that is true whatever the flake turns out to be

`pumpUntil` in that test file:

```
while (!until() && DateTime.now().isBefore(deadline)) { … }
await tester.pump();
```

**When the ten-second budget runs out, the loop simply ends and the function returns.** It does not
throw, does not warn, and reports nothing. **A caller cannot tell "the condition became true" from
"I gave up waiting for it."**

> **That is this project's founding defect, in a helper used at 15 call sites in one file: a check
> that cannot distinguish success from its own failure.** And it is worse under exactly the
> circumstances being investigated — **the budget is real wall-clock time, so a machine busy running
> the other 2584 tests is the machine most likely to exhaust it** and least likely to say so. Task
> 11.208 has just moved another test off the real clock for the same reason.

**Fix the class: the wait fails loudly when its condition never came true, naming the condition and
how long it waited.** **The correct pattern already exists in this repository, twice** — derived, not
remembered:

- **`map_with_no_position_test.dart` polls the same way and then asserts**, with the reason *"the map
  never built"*. **Its timeout cannot pass for success.**
- **`pumpInAppShell` in `test/support/app_shell_harness.dart` throws a `TestFailure`** naming the
  screen and the budget.

**Two more waiters were found by the same search and are not yet judged** —
`map_screen_test.dart`'s wait for `ComputationFailed`, and `magic_link_reader.dart`'s. **Check both

### Task 11.214 — The database is in the iPhone's backup, and the flag that excludes it does not survive
**Status:** **CANCELLED 2026-09-10 by Michael's decision. Do not run `/11-214`.** He confirmed that
**iOS already lets a person switch off backup for one app in the phone's own settings**, and Google
began rolling out the same per-app control in June 2026. **So the rare project that needs its
coordinates off Apple's and Google's servers already has the switch, and this app does not need to
build one** — no Apple-specific code, no TriTrack setting, nothing new to maintain and nothing that
can silently stop working. **The replacement is task 11.215 and one paragraph in the guide.**
**Was PAUSED 2026-09-10, and the planning session was wrong to write it as a fix.** He asked the question this entry never did: **is turning cloud backup off actually the right
trade for a field app?** A phone lost in a canyon is far likelier than a stolen cloud account, and the
records at risk are the same set either way — **the ones not yet on his server.**

> **What was measured on 2026-09-10, both from the vendors' own documentation.**
> **Apple: iCloud Backup is *not* end-to-end encrypted by default** — *"the keys to your backups are
> secured in Apple data centres"* — so Apple can read it and can be compelled to produce it. **Advanced
> Data Protection makes the whole backup end-to-end encrypted**, but it is a **per-person setting each
> field tech would have to turn on themselves**, and **it cannot be set by an app**. *(Apple also
> withdrew it for UK users in 2025 after a government demand, so its availability is not guaranteed
> everywhere.)*
> **Google: unclear, and the wording is doing work.** *"**Some** of your data is end-to-end encrypted
> with your device's screen lock"*, with photos and carrier media named as exceptions. **Google does
> not say an app's data file is covered**, so it cannot be claimed that Google is unable to read it.
> **The planning session guessed the opposite an hour earlier and was wrong** — turning Android's
> backup off did buy something real.

**So the decision is genuinely balanced and it is Michael's.** Leave backup on everywhere and accept
that Apple and probably Google can read it; or leave it off everywhere and lose the safety net for
unsynced records. **Task 10.79 has already taken the second option on Android without him being
asked**, which is the thing to put right first, whichever way he goes.

**Was:** Not started. **Below the line, and it is the open half of a finding that reads as closed.**
Task 10.79 shut the same door on Android; **iOS and macOS are still open, and always were.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The Swift is short. **What makes it Opus is that getting it wrong is
silent, and this app has no custom platform channel to copy from.**
**Depends on:** 10.79, which found it.

#### 1. What it is, in one paragraph

`getApplicationSupportDirectory()` is included in iCloud and Finder backups by default. **The database
and its two sidecar files go with it.** If somebody's iCloud account is ever compromised, **every
animal location they have recorded is in what was taken.** This is not a regression — it is how the
app has always behaved, and task 10.79 is the first thing to write it down.

**Set `NSURLIsExcludedFromBackupKey` on the database file and both sidecars.**

#### 2. Three things that make this harder than fifteen lines of Swift

**A. The flag does not survive the file being recreated.** A fresh install, a restore, or a migration
that rebuilds the database produces a *new file*, and **a resource value set on the old one means
nothing.** **Set it on every launch, not once**, and say so in the code — *"once at first run"* is the
defect this class is famous for.

**B. A flag that reads back is not a backup that excluded it.** **Read the value back and assert it**
— that is a real check and it costs nothing. **But state plainly, in the code and in the report, that
it proves the call succeeded and nothing more.** Whether the backup actually left the file out is a
different claim and **only Michael's hardware can make it.**

> **These are two different sentences and this project has been bitten by collapsing them.** *"We set
> the flag"* and *"the file is not in the backup"* are not the same statement, and a green check on
> the first must not be written as though it were the second.

**C. This app has no custom platform channel at all.** Task 11.30 removed the last one, and task
11.66 confirmed the absence. **So this reintroduces a mechanism the app deliberately shed** — worth a
sentence rather than a shrug. **Check whether a maintained package does this before writing native
code**, and choose either way **with the trade-off written down**: a dependency for one API call
carries §3.8's review sentence, and so does new native code carry the cost of being the only such code
in the repository.

#### 3. Verification is a person, so write the row that tells them

**`flutter test` cannot check this.** So **add a row to `RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md`'s hardware section**:
back the device up, restore to a scratch device or inspect the backup, and confirm the database is not
in it. **A trigger nobody is told to pull is not a trigger** — that is why B1 and B2 exist in that
document and this belongs beside them.

#### 4. L-10 keeps one identity and gets an honest title

**Task 10.79 asked whether the iOS half should get a finding number of its own. It should not.**
`TriTrack_Security_Model.md` already carries it as *"closed on Android and open on iOS"*, and
**splitting one exposure across two identifiers means two closures to remember and a half-open finding
in each.**

**But its title is the Android mechanism** — *"`android:allowBackup` is absent and therefore true"* —
**so a reader scanning titles sees a platform they have already fixed and moves on.** **Retitle L-10
to name the exposure rather than the Android switch**, and make sure **nowhere it appears can be read
as closed while either platform is open.**

- **Acceptance:** the flag is set on the database and both sidecars **on every launch**; it is read
  back and asserted; **the report says a set flag is not a proof of exclusion**; the package-or-native
  choice carries its written trade-off; a hardware row exists in the release checklist; L-10 is
  retitled and reads as open.



### Task 11.215 — Put Android's backup back, and write the decision down as a decision
**Status:** **Done, 2026-09-10.** **Michael's call, 2026-09-10**, after the planning session brought
him a fix instead of a trade-off.
**Model:** **Sonnet, low.** One line reverted, one document status changed. **The care goes into the
document, not the code.**
**Depends on:** 10.79, which turned it off without asking.

#### 1. Turn Android's automatic backup back on

Task 10.79 set `android:allowBackup="false"` and `android:fullBackupContent="false"` in the manifest.
**Take both back out**, leaving the comment history intact so the reversal is legible rather than
looking like the finding was never there.

**Why, in Michael's words and reasoning:** a phone lost in a canyon is far likelier than a stolen
cloud account, **and the records at risk are the same set either way — the ones not yet on his
server.** For essentially every project the redundancy is worth more than the exposure. **The app is
for field teams working days without signal, and it should behave like it.**

#### 2. Say so in the security model, and say it as an accepted risk rather than a closed one

**L-10 is not closed and it is not open. It is accepted, deliberately, with a reason and a remedy** —
which is the third state this project's documents already use elsewhere and the one that must not be
collapsed into either neighbour.

- **Retitle it to name the exposure rather than the Android switch**, as task 11.214 would have. A
  reader scanning titles must not see a platform and move on.
- **State the decision, dated, with the reasoning above** — not "we decided not to fix it", but *why*,
  in terms of what a field team loses either way.
- **Name the remedy that exists**: on iPhone, and on Android where the June 2026 rollout has reached,
  **a person can switch off backup for this app alone in the phone's own settings.** That is what
  serves the rare project working with a species that cannot afford a leak.
- **Update the poachers row** in the risk table. It currently says L-10 *"copies the whole database to
  a cloud account by platform default"* as an open degradation. **It is now an accepted one with a
  user-side control**, and the row should say that rather than continuing to read as unmanaged.

> **Why the wording matters more than the code here.** The whole of this decision lives in a document.
> **If it reads as "nobody got round to it", the next security review reopens it and somebody turns
> the backup off again** — which is exactly what happened this time, to a finding that had never been
> weighed against what it costs.

#### 3. Keep what 10.79 got right, and retire what is now unnecessary

- **The warning for phones with no passcode stays.** It is built, it is cheap, and **the entire
  argument for trusting a phone at all rests on it being locked.**
- **Delete `.claude/commands/11-214-*.md`.** That work is cancelled and a runnable-looking command
  for it is a trap.

- **Acceptance:** Android's backup is on again and the manifest says why in a comment; L-10 is
  retitled, dated and written as accepted with its reasoning and the user-side remedy; the poachers
  row no longer reads as unmanaged; the passcode warning is untouched; 11.214's command file is gone.

- **§14.10 — "Every §2 actor and §3 surface — current verdict"**

### Task 11.218 — Three things task 11.34 found while measuring, all worth doing whatever is decided
**Status:** Done, 2026-09-10. **Below the line.** **None of these depends on the copy-on-add decision** —
two are live defects a person can hit today and one is a document that is factually wrong.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** Item 1 is a document. Items 2 and 3 are small, and **item 2 carries a
stop order** because its size has not been measured.
**Depends on:** 11.34, which found all three.

#### 1. The security model protects a flow that does not work, and names a route that does not exist

**§5.9(a) keeps the orphan-tag write path open in order to protect the "adopt an unlinked tag" flow.
Task 11.34 measured that flow: it cannot happen.** An unlinked tag is **never offered by any push and
never returned by any pull**, because both sides narrow the tag table to the identifiers a project's
own rows name — and an unlinked tag belongs to no project.

**Finding F4 is wrong in the same area, and more plainly.** It says tag identifiers travel in share
payloads. **They do not** — a share payload carries a frequency, a pulse rate and a name, and **no
identifier at all.**

**Correct both.** This is needed whether or not copy-on-add is ever built.

#### 2. The app offers a thing the server has refused since August, and says so unhelpfully

**A person with two projects on one phone can open *"Link existing tag"*, choose a tag already used by
their other project, and watch it appear to work.** It is then **refused forever on the next sync**,
with a message saying the server would not say why.

> **Michael can hit this today.** Nothing is lost — the record stays on the device — **so it is a
> wasted afternoon rather than lost data.** The server has refused this since task 11.3; the app has
> simply never agreed with it.

**Copy-on-add would remove it by construction, and copy-on-add is at least one decision and one large
task away.** So fix it now, cheaply: **stop offering what will be refused.**

**Measure the fix's size before committing to it.** If the honest fix is small — narrowing what that
dialog offers — do it. **If it turns out to reach further than that, stop and report**, because the
structural fix is already designed and waiting.

#### 3. The paste screen matches against every tag on the device

A pasted bearing is matched against **the whole device's tag list rather than the active project's**,
so an imported record can name another project's tag and be held. **One provider changes.**
**Independent of everything else and worth doing either way.**

- **Acceptance:** §5.9(a) and F4 both corrected with the measurement that disproves them; the link
  dialog no longer offers a tag the server will refuse, **or the task stopped and said why**; the paste
  screen matches within the active project; **no production behaviour is changed beyond these three.**

**Done, 2026-09-10, commit pending.** All three landed; item 2's fix was small, as hoped, and did not
reach the stop order. §5.9(a) and finding F4 corrected in place (struck through, not deleted, per this
project's convention) citing task 11.34's §1.5 measurement. The link dialog now excludes any tag with a
`Project_Tags` row for a different project (`ProjectTagRepository.tagIdsClaimedByOtherProjects`, one new
method, mirroring the server's `_tagIsClaimedElsewhere` exactly — any row, active or removed, since a
link deactivates but is never tombstoned). The paste screen now matches against
`projectActiveTagsProvider(activeProjectId)` instead of the device-wide `localTagsProvider`, which was
deleted (no remaining callers). Full suite green (2,832 passed, 15 pre-existing skips, 0 failures); the
website copy-drift check passed (`dart run website/tools/check_app_quotes.dart`) since two user-visible
strings changed (the link dialog's empty-state message, and the class doc comment).

project has ever spent — plus a migration on two databases and the archive reader.

#### The specification is `CLAUDE_DOCS/TAG_COPY_ON_ADD_DESIGN.md`. Do not re-derive it.

**Read §2 through §4 in full.** Both decisions it left open are now taken and recorded at the top of
that file: **Design B**, and **the lineage identifier rather than a pointer.** **Everything below is
what the design document does not cover — ordering, and the ways this can go wrong quietly.**

#### 1. Count before you migrate, and print what you found

**§3.1 first, on whatever database is about to be touched**: tags in total, linked to exactly one
project, to two or more, to none. **Print all four.**

> **A migration that forks rows must say how many it forked, in its own output, or nobody can tell a
> clean run from a run that did nothing.** That is this project's founding defect applied to a
> migration, and a migration is the worst possible place to meet it.

**Michael ran it on his Mac on 2026-09-10 and the answer is `1|5`** — **five tags, each in exactly

> assumption it inherited from a five-row database.

**Two things that make the refusal safe rather than optimistic.** The server has refused two projects

than writing a fresh one-off guard, and carry a positive control that fires in the same run** — an
assertion that only ever passes is the shape this project refuses.

#### 3. Say what the size is before spending it, and stop at a seam rather than half-doing it

**§1.6 gives an outer bound of 101 files.** If this cannot be one coherent commit — **and a
half-migrated tree is worse than an unmigrated one** — **name the seam, stop there, and report.** The

**The design document lists what becomes wrong the day this lands.** All of it, in this task:

#### Why this exists at all, and it is worth writing down

**The pre-commit suite is `flutter test`. That is the client.** The server integration tests need a
Postgres, and the gate instruments need a running server, so neither can run inside a hook — they
run in CI. Task 11.219 changed **the wire format between the two**, and every check that could have
seen it was on the other side of a push that had not happened yet.

> **A change to the contract between two programs is invisible to a suite that only runs one of
> them.** 11.219's own pre-commit run was green and honest; it was answering a narrower question
> than the one that mattered. This is not a failure of 11.219's care — it is a gap in where the
> checks live, and it is now named.

**Both suites can be run locally.** `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` brings up a throwaway
Postgres and runs the server suite; `scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh` brings the stack up and runs every
wire-speaking instrument. **Neither costs a GitHub Actions minute**, and Michael has a hard budget
until 1 October. **See item 3, which is not optional.**

#### 1. `USE_FINGERPRINT` — this one belongs to task 10.79, not to 11.219

The Platform Build workflow **built the APK successfully** (567 s). What failed afterwards is the
guard `scripts/verify_merged_manifest_capabilities.sh`:

> `FAIL: the merged manifest declares permission "USE_FINGERPRINT" and CLAUDE_DOCS/CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md has no row mentioning it.`

**The guard is right and the app is fine.** Task 10.79 added `local_auth: ^3.0.2` for the device-lock
presence check, and wrote a `local_auth_android` row in the matrix's second-pass table naming
**`USE_BIOMETRIC`** — derived from the plugin's documentation, and **carrying its own caveat, in
writing: *"Not yet verified against a built APK."*** The plugin also declares the older
`USE_FINGERPRINT`, for Android below API 28. **The first real build did exactly what that caveat
said it would do**, which is the pleasant version of this: a row that admitted what it had not
checked, checked.

- **Extend 10.79's existing `local_auth_android` row** to name both permissions and say why there are
  two. **Do not add a second row for the same plugin** — one plugin, one row, is what the table's
  shape means.
- **Read the permission's real attributes off the merged manifest, not off the plugin's
  documentation** — in particular whether it carries a `maxSdkVersion`, which is the whole reason a
  legacy permission is still declared. **The mistake being corrected is trusting the docs; do not
  repeat it three lines lower.**
- **This is 10.79's, and say so in the commit message.** 11.219's own command file carried the rule:
  *if it belongs to an earlier commit, say whose it is rather than fixing it inside this one.*
- **The row's caveat is only removed for what this build actually proved.** The guard reads the
  manifest and asks whether the matrix mentions each thing it finds; **it never asks the reverse.**
  So this build proves the manifest *contains* `USE_FINGERPRINT` and that nothing else in it is
  unrecorded. **It proves nothing about the `share_plus`, `url_launcher_android` or
  `package_info_plus` rows' contents** — those carry the same caveat and it stays until something
  checks that direction. **Leave them alone and do not quietly upgrade them.**

##### The part that is not mechanical, and it is most of the work

Several of these assertions were written about **an operation that no longer exists.** A contributor

### Task 11.221 — A button the server refuses, sixty dead lines, and two guards
**Status:** Done 2026-09-10. All five items landed; item 3's premise was false (round8 has carried
the guard since its first commit — see Discovered Scope) and item 5 had a consequence the entry did
not name (the instrument self-test step ran only on `schedule` or the button — see Discovered
Scope). Server suite 982/982 in Docker and the gate (23 instruments, 155 round8 checks) both green
locally. **Item 1 is above the line**; the other three are cleanups that are cheap
now and get more expensive as they age. **All four came out of task 11.220 and none of them is
11.220's to have fixed** — three are production server or app code outside a test-repair task, and
the fourth is an instrument it could not confirm without a run it did not need.
**Model:** **Opus, medium. One window; the four items touch different files and none depends on
another.**
**Depends on:** 11.219 and 11.220. **Michael took item 1's decision on 2026-09-10.**

#### 1. Project Setup offers "Add back" to a contributor and the server refuses it

**The app and the server disagree, and the app is the one that is wrong.** On a removed tag,
`_ProjectTagRow` renders an **"Add back"** button whose `onPressed` is gated on `mayWrite` —
contributor-level — and `TagRepository.restoreToProject` runs **no `assertMayEdit`** at all.
`RowAuthorizer._authorizeTagLifecycle` reserves every change to an existing tag for an owner, and
clearing a tombstone is a change. **So a contributor presses the button, the row comes back on their
phone, and the push is refused.**

> **This is the shape task 11.218 closed for a different operation, open again here.** An app that
> offers what the server refuses teaches a person the app is broken, and it does it after they have
> already acted.

**Michael's decision, 2026-09-10: owner-only stands, and the button greys with a reason.** The rule
is *contributors add new collars; owners change existing ones.* A contributor who needs a removed
collar back creates a new record for it, and `NearDuplicateTags` tells them it resembles one the
project already has.

- **`restoreToProject` gets `assertMayEdit`**, exactly as `removeFromProject` beside it has. **The
  local check is the point** — a refusal that only happens at the server is a refusal a person meets
  minutes later, offline, with no explanation.
- **Gate the button on `isOwner`, not `mayWrite`**, matching the "Remove from project" control four
  lines above it that already does.
- **The reason belongs in `tagsSectionDisabledReason`, not on the row.** Task 11.138 put it there
  once under the section rather than once per tag, deliberately — do not undo that. **That string is
  also stale on its own account:** it says *"You can link and add tags here"* and there is no such
  thing as linking a tag since 11.219. **Rewrite the whole sentence, do not append to it.**
- **`restoreToProject`'s doc comment still states the old rule in so many words** — *"Contributor-
  level, not owner-only, and the asymmetry is the decision (task 11.12)"*. **It is now the opposite.
  Rewrite it, name 11.219 as what moved it and Michael's decision as what settled it**, and say what
  the asymmetry is now: create versus change, not add versus remove.
- **Watch it red.** A test that a contributor's `restoreToProject` throws, and a widget test that the
  button is disabled for a contributor and enabled for an owner. **Both watched failing first**, or
  they are claims.
- **`PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md`'s T3 row already records this as a device/server disagreement with a ✗
  and points here.** Turn the ✗ back into a ✓ **in the same commit**, or the matrix starts lying in
  the other direction.

#### 2. Sixty lines of tag re-delivery in the server that cannot execute

`SyncService.applyPush` collects `newlyLinked` tag ids inside a branch guarded by
`item.table.name == Tables.projectTags`, and `_redeliverNewlyLinked` re-stamps their `server_seq` so
a teammate whose cursor is already past a tag still receives it. **`item.table` comes from a loop
over `syncTables`, and `Project_Tags` is not in `syncTables`, so the branch cannot run.**

**Unnecessary, not broken.** A tag is created *inside* a project now, so it has never been below a
reader's cursor while unreachable — the situation the machinery existed for cannot arise.

- **Delete the branch, `newlyLinked` and `_redeliverNewlyLinked`.**
- **`refreshServerSeqFor` is live and stays.** `JoinService` calls it twice for the
  `Users`/`User_Emails` re-stamp — the same mechanism for people. **Read those two call sites before
  touching anything**, because the two things share a helper and only one of them is dead.
- **Say in the commit message why the property no longer needs code**, not just that the code is
  unreachable. Unreachable is why it can go; *a tag is reachable from the moment it exists* is why
  nothing has to replace it.
- **`member_authorization_test.dart` records the deletion of the two tests that covered this and
  points at the plan.** Update that note to point at this task's commit instead of at a pending item.

#### 3. The last instrument whose duplicate description silently eats a verdict

`CLAUDE.md`'s task-11.88 rule: a structure keyed by a string somebody types must make a duplicate a
hard error. **`verify_round8_server_surface.py` is the last `attack()` implementation without that
guard.** Task 11.220 added it to two others **and it found a live defect on its first run** — eight
probes reporting seven verdicts, because two malformed ids differed only past a 24-character
truncation.

- **Add the same guard, and its first run is the answer.** If it finds a collision, that collision is
  the finding and fixing it is part of this item.
- **Fix a collision by labelling the case, not by lengthening the truncation.** 11.220's fix is the
  precedent: a longer prefix is the same defect with a larger constant in front of it.

#### 4. A push with two rows for one primary key answers `applied: 1` and one `invalid`

Measured 2026-09-10, and it **predates 11.219**. Two `Tags` rows sharing `(tag_id, project_id)` in
one push answer `{"applied": 1, "outcomes": {"Tags/<id>/<project>": "invalid"}}`. The first row
lands; Postgres refuses the second on the primary key; **the outcome map is keyed by the row
reference, which both rows share, so the second verdict overwrites the first.** The caller is told
`invalid` for a key one of whose rows landed, and `applied: 1` contradicts the only outcome in the
map. **A client cannot tell which of its two rows to retry.**

**Not reachable from this app** — the local database holds the same primary key, so our client cannot
build such a push. **That is why it is item 4 and not item 1**, and it is not a reason to leave a
response that contradicts itself.

- **The fix is per-row, in this project's grain.** Task 10.46 spent itself removing "one bad row
  fails the whole push", so **do not answer this with a whole-push refusal.** Detect the duplicate
  key **before applying**, mark **every** row sharing it `invalid`, and apply none of them —
  `applied` and the outcome map then agree, and the client is told plainly which key to retry with
  one row.
- **The refusal must disclose nothing.** It is decided from the push's own contents, so it cannot
  depend on server state — **say that in the code comment**, because the next reader will wonder,
  and §4.13 is the reason they will.
- **Watched red**, with the count asserted: two rows in, `applied: 0`, one outcome, `invalid`.
- **`verify_11_9_team_surface.py` has carried this as a `note()` since before 11.219.** Promote it to
  an `attack()` once the behaviour is defined, so the answer is measured every gate run rather than
  observed.

#### 5. Stop the nightly gate run until the Actions quota resets — Michael's decision, 2026-09-10

**`gate-instruments.yml` runs at 04:00 UTC every night**, on days nobody touches the repository. Its
own workflow file calls it *"the twenty-minute Docker run"*. **Michael has roughly 150 GitHub Actions
minutes until the quota resets on 1 October — about twenty-one nights.** At the workflow's own
estimate the nightly alone spends his whole remaining balance in a week, having been asked no
question anybody was waiting on.

> **This is not a judgement that the nightly is worthless.** It exists for a real reason, written in
> the file: an instrument can rot without anybody touching it — a base image moving under it, a
> dependency, a Docker Compose behaviour change. **That reason does not stop being true; it stops
> being worth twenty minutes a night during three weeks in which the same instruments are being run
> on a Mac before every push.**

- **Comment out the `schedule:` block. Do not delete it.** A deleted schedule is indistinguishable
  from one that was never there — this project's oldest rule — and the whole point is that it comes
  back.
- **Write the reopen trigger beside it, in the file: 1 October 2026, when the quota resets.** Not
  "when convenient". `TASK_COMMS.md`'s "waiting on Michael" section carries the same date, and a
  reminder is set for that day.
- **The push and `workflow_dispatch` triggers stay.** A change under `scripts/`, `server/` or
  `packages/` still runs the instruments, and Michael can still press the button. **What is being
  removed is the run that asks nothing.**
- **One written reason elsewhere goes stale the moment you do this, and it must move with it.**
  `server/test/security/shipped_defaults_test.dart`'s failure message argues that its check matters
  because the Docker run in `gate-instruments.yml` *"is nightly and path-filtered"*. **Half of that
  sentence stops being true.** Its argument gets *stronger*, not weaker — with the nightly off, a
  commit that deletes a `run_instrument` line while touching nothing under `scripts/` has even less
  chance of being caught. **Rewrite the sentence to say that, and date it.** A test whose stated
  reason has been quietly falsified is the class this project has paid for four times.

- **Acceptance:** a contributor's put-back refused on the device with a rewritten reason string, the
  button gated on `isOwner`, both tests watched red, and the T3 row's ✗ turned back into a ✓;
  the dead re-delivery machinery gone with `refreshServerSeqFor` untouched; the duplicate-name guard
  in the last instrument with whatever its first run found; the duplicate-key push answering
  `applied: 0` with every affected row `invalid`, watched red, and its `note()` promoted to an
  `attack()`; the nightly schedule commented out rather than deleted, its reopen date written beside
  it, and `shipped_defaults_test.dart`'s falsified sentence rewritten and dated.



### Task 11.222 — The migration that will meet real data has never met any
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-11** — the beta-server count, its one open item, came back. **It disagreed
with this entry's own premise: the server is on schema 11, not 13**, and one collar is linked to no
project, which the refusal this task built stops on. **Both are task 11.227.** The two defects this
task found in the v14 migration — that it could not run against any v13 database at all, and that its
"refusal" silently placed a shared collar rather than refusing — are fixed and were watched failing
first. Its oracle for the v7/v8/v9 groups is task 11.226; its "does a server with data exist"
question is answered by the census and folded into 11.227.
**Superseded status line below.**
**Status (as written):** Partial — 2026-09-11. Code and tests done and green (15 tests in the migration file, server
suite green in Docker); the beta-server count is the open item and only Michael can run it. **Two
defects found in the migration itself and fixed in the same commit: it could not run on any v13
database at all (dropped `Tags`' key while `Project_Tags` still referenced it), and its "refusal" of
a two-project tag was a `LIMIT 1` that guessed.** See the comms entry.
**Above the line, and it is the only item on this list with somebody's field
season behind it.** `server/test/schema/postgres_migration_upgrade_test.dart` exists to prove a
migration leaves existing rows untouched **against a populated database**. It covers v7, v8 and v9.
**It has no group for v14 — the tag re-key, the largest schema change this project has made, and the
one that will run against Michael's beta server.**
**Model:** **Opus, high. Run alone, fresh window.** The obstacle is that the file's own technique has
run out, so this is a test-harness design problem before it is a test.
**Depends on:** 11.219, which wrote the migration, and 11.220, which found the gap.

#### What is actually at risk

**The v14 migration is deliberately written to abort rather than guess.** If it meets a tag that
belongs to two projects it raises a `NOT NULL` violation instead of placing the tag somewhere. That
was the right call — task 11.219 wrote it that way on purpose, and Michael's Mac measured `1|5`, five
tags each in one project, so the abort path is an explicit refusal rather than dead code.

> **`1|5` is one device.** It is not a statement about the beta server, which holds a team's real
> season, and it is not a statement about a phone. **A migration whose failure mode is "abort partway
> through somebody's only copy" should have met a populated database before it meets that one.**

**And the harmless direction is untested too.** Nobody has confirmed that a v13 database full of
bearings, sessions, estimates and truth points comes out of v14 with every one of those rows
unchanged and every foreign key still resolving. That is the whole reason this file exists.

#### The obstacle, and it is the interesting part

**The file bootstraps the current schema and strips off later *additions* to reach an older shape.**
That worked while every migration was additive. **v14 is not additive — it re-keys `Tags`** — so
stripping backwards cannot produce a v13 shape, and task 11.220 found the technique already failing
at the edge: the **v9** group needed a `UNIQUE (tag_id)` constraint added in `setUp` just to keep
running (SQLSTATE 42830, watched failing first; the reasoning is in a comment there).

**A v13→v14 group has to reconstruct a v13-shaped `Tags` and a whole `Project_Tags` table from a v14
bootstrap.** That is a different technique, not a longer `setUp`.

- **Decide the technique first and write down why**, before writing the group. The two obvious
  candidates are **reconstruct backwards** (keep bootstrapping current and hand-build the old shape)
  and **replay forwards** (a committed v13 schema snapshot the migrations run over). **Replay
  forwards is what most projects end up with and it is not automatically right here** — a snapshot is
  a hand-maintained copy of something that already exists, which is a shape this project has been
  bitten by repeatedly. **Whichever is chosen, the argument goes in the file**, because the *next*
  non-additive migration will read it.
- **If the technique that wins means the v7/v8/v9 groups should change too, say so and stop.** Do
  not rewrite them inside this task. **A test file that measures nothing while it is being rebuilt is
  the worst state it can be in**, and the existing groups are green today.

#### What the v14 group must actually prove

- **The populated case.** A v13 database holding at least one project with tags, `Tag_Versions`,
  bearings, a triangulation session, an estimate, an exclusion and a truth point. After the
  migration: **every row still there, every value unchanged except the keys the migration is
  supposed to move, and every foreign key resolving.** Count the rows before and after and **assert
  the counts**, because a migration that silently drops a table is exactly the failure this file is
  for.
- **The refusal.** A v13 database with **one tag in two projects**, which the local schema permits
  and the app offered until task 11.218 closed it. **The migration must abort, the database must be
  left as it was, and the error must name the tag.** An abort that leaves a half-migrated database
  is worse than either outcome — **assert the state afterwards, not just the exception.**
- **The empty case.** A v13 database with a project and no tags at all. Cheap, and it is the case a
  new beta tester's device is in.
- **Watch each one red.** Break the migration's project-scoping in a scratch copy and confirm the
  populated group fails; remove the abort and confirm the refusal group fails. **A migration test
  that has never failed is a claim about a migration.**

#### After it is green, and this is the payment for the whole task

**Michael's beta server should be counted before it is migrated**, with the same query task 11.219
ran on the Mac — tags in total, in exactly one project, in two or more, in none. **Write the exact
command into `CLAUDE_DOCS/TASK_COMMS.md`'s "waiting on Michael" section, with the address of the
machine to run it on**, which is a thing this project has got wrong before by naming a file and not a
computer. **If the answer is not "every tag in exactly one project", this task's refusal group is no
longer a hypothetical and the migration needs a decision before it runs anywhere.**

- **Acceptance:** the technique chosen with its reasoning written in the file; a v13→v14 group
  covering populated, refusing and empty, each watched red; row counts asserted rather than spot
  checks; the aborting case verified to leave the database unchanged; the beta-server count written
  into `TASK_COMMS.md` with the machine named; and **if the technique implies rewriting the v7/v8/v9
  groups, that is reported and not done here.**



### Task 11.223 — The one record designed to survive a dead database does not survive the deployment
**Status:** Done 2026-09-11. `docker-compose.tls.yml`'s `server.volumes: !override` now lists
`tritrack_server_state:/var/lib/tritrack` alongside the two certificate mounts, with a comment saying
why all three have to be listed together. The guard in `shipped_defaults_test.dart` now runs `docker
compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.tls.yml config` (with placeholder values for every
required `.env` variable, since `config` only renders the merged YAML and never reads what they name)
and asserts the volume against the **merged** output — long-form (`type: volume`, `source:`, `target:`),
which is how `docker compose config` renders every mount regardless of which short/long syntax either
file writes. Watched failing with the fix reverted, confirmed passing with it restored. **The sweep
found the same defect twice more, in the two development-only overlays, and left both unfixed per
this task's brief — see Discovered Scope.**
**Model:** **Sonnet.** The fix is one line. **The guard is the task.**
**Depends on:** 11.129, which built the thing this restores.

#### What is wrong

**`docker-compose.yml`'s `server` service mounts a named volume, `tritrack_server_state`, at
`/var/lib/tritrack`.** Task 11.129 put it there on 2026-09-02 for a stated reason: a sign-in answers
`202 sent` whether a link went out or not, the compensating visibility is the audit log, the audit
log is a Postgres table — **so when Postgres is gone the person is told "sent", no link arrives, and
the audit write fails too.** The degradation record is what survives that, and this volume is what
makes it survive a restart.

**`docker-compose.tls.yml` — the production deployment — declares `volumes: !override` on the same
service.** `!override` replaces the list rather than merging it, so the two origin-certificate mounts
are the *entire* list and **`tritrack_server_state` is not mounted at all.** The record lands in the
container's writable layer and dies with the next `docker compose up --build`.

**Neither file is wrong on its own terms, and the order says why.** The `!override` was written on or
before 2026-08-19 (task 10.74), where it is correct and deliberate — the file's own comment explains
that an untagged empty list would leave the base `ports:` concatenated in, which is the whole point of
the override. **The volume it now discards did not exist for another two weeks.** Task 11.129 added
`tritrack_server_state` to the base file and had no reason to look at a TLS overlay.
**Correct-when-written, then silently falsified by a change one file over.**

#### The guard is green and the property is false, which is the part that matters

`server/test/security/shipped_defaults_test.dart` has a test named *"a named volume covers the
directory the record is written to"*, whose stated reason is *"without this the record lives in the
container layer and dies with the container."* **That is exactly the defect, described exactly, by a
test that passes** — because `compose` in that file is `docker-compose.yml` alone, and the shipped
deployment is `docker-compose.yml` **plus** `docker-compose.tls.yml`.

> **A check that reads a different artefact from the one that ships cannot fail when the shipped one
> is wrong.** This project has a name for the class and a rule against it, and here it is in its own
> test suite.

#### What to do

1. **Add `- tritrack_server_state:/var/lib/tritrack` to the TLS overlay's `server.volumes` list**,
   beside the two certificate mounts. **Keep the `!override`** — it is load-bearing for `ports:` and
   correct here too; what was missing is one line inside it. **Say in a comment why all three entries
   have to be listed together**, so the next person adding a mount to the base file finds the
   sentence before the defect.
2. **Make the guard read what ships.** The test must assert the property against **the merged
   configuration**, not against the base file. `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f
   docker-compose.tls.yml config` prints it, and that is a subprocess this suite can run — the same
   move `broken_control_trigger_test.dart` makes when it reads a workflow rather than trusting a
   list. **If a subprocess is not acceptable in that suite, parse both files and apply the
   `!override` rule explicitly, and say which you chose and why.**
3. **Watch it red.** Remove the line added in step 1 and confirm the guard fails. **It has passed
   through the entire life of this defect; a green that has never been earned is a claim.**
4. **Then sweep the same question once, because the answer is cheap and this is the only visit.**
   `!override` appears in more than one place across the overlays. **For every `!override` in every
   compose overlay, list what the base file declares at that key and what the overlay discards**, and
   report the table. **Do not fix anything else you find** — report it, and the finding decides
   whether it is a task. The sweep is what turns one instance into knowing there is not a second.

#### The sweep — every `!override` in every overlay, done 2026-09-11

| File | Service | Key | Base file declares | Overlay discards it for | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `docker-compose.tls.yml` | `server` | `volumes` | `tritrack_server_state:/var/lib/tritrack` | two certificate mounts | **Was the defect. Fixed by this task.** |
| `docker-compose.tls.yml` | `server` | `ports` | `${SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}:${SERVER_PORT:-8080}:8080` | nothing (`[]`) | Deliberate and documented — no host port at all once the proxy is the only way in. Correct. |
| `docker-compose.server-test.yml` | `postgres` | `ports` | nothing (base declares no `ports:` on `postgres`) | nothing | Nothing to discard; tagged pre-emptively per its own comment. Correct. |
| `docker-compose.server-test.yml` | `server` | `ports` | `${SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}:${SERVER_PORT:-8080}:8080` | replaced with a hardcoded loopback test port | Deliberate and documented. Correct. |
| `docker-compose.e2e.yml` | `server` | `ports` | `${SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}:${SERVER_PORT:-8080}:8080` | replaced with a hardcoded loopback port | Deliberate and documented. Correct. |
| `docker-compose.e2e.yml` | `server` | `volumes` | `tritrack_server_state:/var/lib/tritrack` | one bind mount for the magic-link directory | **Same defect as the TLS file, confirmed by rendering `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.e2e.yml config`: `tritrack_server_state` is absent from the merged output.** The comment beside it says "the base `server` service declares no `volumes:` today" — true when task 10.47 wrote it, false since task 11.129. **Not fixed — reported, per this task's brief.** |
| `docker-compose.dev-lan.yml` | `server` | `volumes` | `tritrack_server_state:/var/lib/tritrack` | one bind mount for the magic-link directory | **Same defect, same stale comment, confirmed the same way.** **Not fixed — reported.** |

**Two of seven `!override` sites discard the durability volume undetected, in the two development-only
overlays (e2e and dev-lan) rather than the production one.** Lower stakes than the TLS file — these
stacks are ephemeral test/dev runs, not the deployment holding a field season — but the record is
still silently non-durable on either one, and both comments assert something that stopped being true
two weeks before either file was touched again. **Recorded in Discovered Scope rather than fixed here**,
since this task's brief was the TLS file and the guard, not a second and third fix found by the sweep.

- **Acceptance:** the volume present in the merged configuration; the guard reading the merged
  configuration rather than the base file, and watched failing without the fix; **every `!override`
  in every overlay listed with what it discards**, reported and not fixed.

"link an existing tag to this project" for weeks, and **task 11.218 closed exactly that trap.** His
phone holds two instances of it, both created before 11.218 landed.

#### 1. Build §3.3, as written

**Read §3.3 in full and implement it.** Ordering by `Project_Tags.created_at` ascending; the first
link's project keeps the original `tag_id`; every later project gets a fresh `tag_id` with the same
`lineage_id` and `copied_at` set to that link's `created_at`; the version chain is copied per forked
project; that project's `Observations`, `Estimated_Positions`, `Triangulation_Sessions` and
`Actual_Tag_Locations` re-point, and each `tag_version_id` moves to the forked version with the same
`effective_from`.

**Two things §3.3 does not settle and this task must.**

- **What happens when `created_at` ties, or is null.** The ordering decides which project keeps the
  original id, and a tie makes that non-deterministic — which is the one property §3.3 chose the
  ordering for. **Pick a stable tiebreak, state it in the code, and test it.**
- **Whether `Non_Detections` really is left alone.** §3.3 says yes and gives the reason. **Confirm
  the reason still holds against `assertSealedColumnsFeedNoReachability` rather than against the
  design document**, and if it does, **write the consequence into the security model's §5.9(b) as
  §3.3 instructs**: a forked project's non-detections keep naming the original collar's id, a
  dangling reference that was already permitted to be one.

#### 2. This is mechanical, and saying so is what makes it safe to run unattended

**A bearing belongs to exactly one project.** So after the fork, each project's records follow that
project's own copy of the collar, and nothing is mixed, merged or averaged across projects.
**`lineage_id` keeps the two copies tied together**, which is what it was added for.

> **The question 11.219 refused to answer on nobody's behalf — *which project keeps the original
> id* — has no scientific content.** It decides a UUID, not a record. What would have had scientific
> content is guessing *whose bearings belong to which collar*, and that is not a guess: the row's own
> project answers it. **Say this in the migration's comment**, because the next reader will meet the
> refusal's wording first and needs to know what changed.

#### 3. The migration must report what it forked, in its own output

Same rule as the census: **a migration that moves rows and prints nothing cannot be told from one
that did nothing.** After the fork, print: how many tags were forked, how many new tag rows were
created, how many version rows copied, and how many records re-pointed, per table. **A run that forks
nothing prints zeroes rather than nothing.**

#### 4. Test against a database that reproduces Michael's, before it runs on Michael's

- **A fixture with the exact shape:** six tags, four single-project, two each shared between two
  projects, with bearings, a session, an estimate, a truth point and a version chain in *both*
  projects of each shared tag. **Numbers asserted before and after** — no row lost, no row
  duplicated except the ones the fork creates, every foreign key resolving.
- **The property that matters, asserted directly:** every observation that named tag X in project B
  now names project B's copy, **and still carries the same frequency, pulse rate and effective
  version**. A fork that re-points a bearing at a collar reading something different has changed the
  scientific record.
- **Watch it red.** Break the re-pointing so project B's bearings keep the original id, and confirm
  the test fails. **The refusal path must also keep a test** — it should still fire for a case this
  fork genuinely cannot handle, if any exists; if none does, say so and delete it rather than leaving
  a branch nothing can reach.

#### 5. Then it runs on the phone, and the phone is the acceptance

**Michael installs the build and opens the app.** Expected: it starts; **six collars become eight
rows** (four untouched, two forked into two each); every bearing, session, estimate and truth point
still resolves; the Log and the map show what they showed before. **The migration's own output goes
in the report**, read off the device log the same way this task's census was.

- **Acceptance:** §3.3 implemented including the version chain and the re-pointing; the tiebreak

  the fork's counts printed; the fixture reproducing Michael's shape passing with counts asserted and
  watched red; **and the app opening on Michael's iPhone with all eight tag rows and every record
