### Task 11.294 — A test from tasks 11.289/11.290 fails four runs in five and blocks every commit

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-20. **Before:** 5 red in 5 full-suite runs (`scripts/repeat_suite.sh 5`,
176–248 s each), 0 red in 5 runs alone. **After:** 0 red in 4 full runs (`repeat_suite.sh 4`,
162–191 s) plus one further full run the hook itself made, 0 red in 3 alone. **The cause, named:**
`ProjectsScreen.build` watches `undeliveredProjectDeletionsProvider` (task 11.290's fold-in), a
database-reading provider this test never pre-resolved, so its first build began on the fake clock
from `pumpWidget`. Every sqflite statement outside a transaction creates a 10-second lock-warning
`Timer` in the caller's zone and cancels it once the statement holds the lock. The build advanced
one statement per microtask flush; when the sqflite isolate's reply was slow enough that the build
was still unfinished as the test's last real-clock block ended (the poll for the push), the
end-of-block flush issued the build's next statement behind the delivery round's real-clock
statements, the round could not release the lock before the binding's pending-timer check, and the
test failed. **Measured, not argued:** a temporary print at the poll's exit across 11 runs was
`AsyncLoading` in every red run and `AsyncData` in every green one. The full suite's seven parallel
test processes stretch the isolate's reply latency; six CPU-burning loops did not (4 of 4 green), so
it is I/O scheduling, not CPU. **Same cause class as 11.290's harness gotcha, different symptom:**
there the stranded continuations were waited on and the test hung; here nothing waited, the build
ran to wherever it got, and what remained was sqflite's warning timer. **The app does not do this** —
see the comms entry: the timer is sqflite's own deadlock diagnostic on every call in every app, real
on a phone and cancelled in microseconds; the provider holds no lock past a single statement, opens
no transaction, and only reads (plus two idempotent `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`). The pre-commit
hook now keeps its JSON stream on a red and prints the path; a second, deterministic red found on the
way (a `path:NN` citation in `TASK_COMMS.md` from task 11.287's entry, committed through the escape
hatch) was rewritten. Command file deleted in the closing commit.
**Was:** Not started. **Above the line, and it is the most urgent thing in this plan** — it
refuses Michael's commits today and the only way past it is the escape hatch, which is a control
being switched off routinely rather than exceptionally.
**Found by task 11.287, 2026-09-20**, which had to commit through
`TRITRACK_PRECOMMIT_RED_IS_PREEXISTING=1` and did the work to prove the red was not its own.
**Model:** **Opus** — a load-dependent failure is where a plausible fix is most likely to be wrong
and to look right.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### What fails, and the measurement that makes it a defect rather than a flake

`test/features/more/projects_screen_test.dart` — *"deleting a published project (task 11.289) offers
the tombstone to the server at once, from the list"* — failed in **4 of 5 full-suite runs** and **0
of 3 runs alone**, on a commit that changes no file under `lib/`, `test/` or `packages/`. **So the
four red runs are runs of the tree at `57f6de7`**, not of task 11.287's work. The exception:

> *A Timer is still pending even after the widget tree was disposed*

— a 10-second sqflite lock timer created on the fake clock, reached by
`undeliveredProjectDeletions` → `findUndeliveredProjectChanges` → `SyncEngine.wouldOffer` →
`SyncRowReceiptStore.ensureTable`.

**A provider still running when the test's tree is torn down**, from tasks 11.289 and 11.290, and
**exactly the shape those tests' own comments say they were written to avoid.**

#### Two things to hold apart, because fixing the wrong one hides the other

- **The test's teardown** — the timer outlives the tree. This is what goes red.
- **Whether the app does the same thing.** `undeliveredProjectDeletions` runs on every app open and
  every foreground. **A provider that keeps a lock timer alive past the widget that asked for it is
  not obviously harmless in a real app**, and the fake clock is what makes it *visible*, not what
  makes it *happen*. **Answer this second question in writing even if the answer is "harmless, and
  here is why."** Task 11.290 already recorded a related harness gotcha in Discovered Scope; read it
  before concluding this is the same thing, and say whether it is.

**The load dependence is the evidence, not the nuisance.** Four in five under a full suite, zero in
three alone, means something about concurrent execution decides it. **Do not accept a fix that makes
the test pass without naming what the ordering was.** A green run is what this failure already
produces one time in five.

#### One instrument fix, in the same task because it is what you will want while doing this

`scripts/pre_commit_suite.sh` deletes its JSON stream on exit (`trap 'rm -f "$stream"'`), **so the
exception text of a red is gone by the time anybody reads the refusal** — diagnosing this one cost
a second full run just to see it. **Keep the stream on a red.** Defect vocabulary 84; it costs
nothing and it is the difference between one run and two every time the hook refuses.

- **Acceptance:** the cause is **named in terms of what runs concurrently**, not just fixed;
  **watched red first** — run the full suite enough times to establish a rate before the fix and
  after, and report both rates rather than a single green run; the app-behavior question above is
  answered in writing; the pre-commit stream survives a red and the report says how it was checked;
  `flutter test` green locally across **at least three full runs**, **no CI until 1 October**.
  **Report the run counts. One green run does not distinguish a fix from the one-in-five.**

### Task 11.293 — A sign-in link the relay refused is recorded as sent

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-21, commit eb8e13c. Two rows, not one: the existing `sent` row is
untouched, and `EmailSender.sendMagicLink` gained an `onOutcome` callback that `SmtpEmailSender`
calls from its own detached future. **Corrected 2026-09-21 by task 11.298: this entry said
"strictly after the HTTP response has gone out", and that was a timing fact rather than a structural
one** — on the sender's own address-refusal path the callback fired synchronously, and a relay with
its port closed would have beaten the response on the ordinary path too. It is structurally true
now: every delivery starts in a microtask, and the route holds the failure row until its own `sent`
row is written. **The sentence is left visible rather than rewritten away**, because a claim about
ordering that was true in every test anybody ran is the kind a later reader should see corrected.
`auth_routes.dart` uses it to write a second `linkRequested outcome=undelivered` row **only when
delivery fails** — no confirmation row on success, since a refusal was the one thing invisible
today and doubling the log on the common case buys nothing. Watched red first (new route-level
tests failed against the pre-fix `lib/`, one file failing to compile for want of the parameter);
server suite green locally against real Postgres, 1111 tests, 0 failures. See the report in
`TASK_COMMS.md`.
**Was:** Not started. **Above the line** — it is the one place a real deployment's mail failure
would be visible, and today it is not.
**Found by task 11.287, 2026-09-20.**
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** task 11.287, which built the sender. **Fresh window.**

#### The gap

`auth_routes.dart` records `linkRequested outcome=sent` **before the relay has answered.** So a link
the relay refused reads as `sent` in the audit table, and the only trace of the failure is a
`NOT DELIVERED` line in the container log. **That route's own comment says operational visibility
comes from the audit log** — for the SMTP path that sentence is now false, and a comment that has
gone false is worse than one that was never written.

The person who asked for the link sees the same `202` either way. **That is correct and must not
change** — it is the account-enumeration defense (§4.5). This task is about what the *operator* can
see, not what the caller can.

#### What makes it small, and the one thing that makes it not trivial

One hook and one new outcome string. **The thing to get right is that the send is deliberately
detached** — it runs on a future the request does not await, which is what stops the response timing
varying with the relay (§7.6, closed by 11.287). **So the audit row cannot be written by the request
handler**, and a design that awaits the send to record its outcome would re-open the finding 11.287
just closed. Write the second row from the detached path.

**Decide and state whether a refused delivery is one row or two** — `sent` then `undelivered`, or a
single row written late. Two rows keep the request's own record honest about what it knew at the
time; one row is tidier and loses that. **Either is defensible; say which and why.**

- **Acceptance:** a refused delivery is visible in the audit log with an outcome distinct from a
  successful one; **the HTTP response is byte-identical and identically timed on both paths**, with
  a test asserting it — this is the control 11.287 closed and this task is the most likely thing to
  re-open it; the one-row-or-two decision stated in the entry and the code; `auth_routes.dart`'s
  comment about operational visibility is true again; **watched red first**; the redacted-recipient
  and never-the-token rules from 11.287 hold in the new row too; server tests green locally, **no CI
  until 1 October**.

### Task 11.302 — An owner who deletes a project by mistake cannot undo it from any device

**Status:** **Done — 2026-09-27**, commits `8723868` and `f2cb37b`. Michael's second device look
(phone owner, Mac member, fresh throwaway) confirmed all of it: the Mac's *Your requests* card said
the project had been deleted, the phone restored it, and the Mac got it back **with the "is back in
your projects" sentence**. The first look's two defects (the member not told; the card still saying
"you're in") are fixed. The look also produced task 11.313. **Above the line.** **Michael decided
this on 2026-09-21**, asked directly: a project deleted from the app should be restorable from the
app.
**Found by task 11.292, 2026-09-21**, which built the screen this belongs on and asked the question
rather than assuming.
**Model:** **Opus** — it is a write that un-does a delete, and the §4.28 route it lands on is one
day old.
**Depends on:** task 11.292 — **its device look must be reported first**, because this builds on a
section nobody has yet seen work. *(Reported 2026-09-22; 11.292 is `Done`.)*

#### What was built and decided (2026-09-24)

- **The route: an action on the existing `POST /projects/<id>/deletion`, not a new route.** Same
  owner acting on the same project's deletion, same standing in the answer, and a new route would
  be a new surface to inventory and attack for one verb. `ProjectDeletionAction.restore` in the
  shared package. §4.21.2's row for the route now argues it, and **a new check refuses the code
  until it does**: `permissions_matrix_membership_test.dart` requires that row to name every value
  of the enum (a new action adds no route, so the route-level derivation could not see one) —
  watched red on `restore` before the row was amended. §4.28.1's "what this does not build"
  paragraph is replaced by the four decisions below; the registry of derived sections says what
  the new check does and does not read.
- **Who may restore is the listing's population, from the listing's own query text.**
  `ProjectDirectoryService.isDeletedBy` and `listDeletedFor` are both built from one SQL fragment
  (`_deletedByCaller`), and the server test reads what each caller may do off the listing's own
  answer for them (`expectRestoreFollowsListing`): the owner who deleted it may; a co-owner who did
  not, a contributor, a stranger, an owner demoted after deleting and a tombstone with no audit
  name are refused with the same `403 forbidden` and the tombstone is checked to still stand.
  Watched red by letting any owner restore.
- **Decision 3 — owner-only, and narrower: the owner who deleted it.** Widening restore to
  co-owners means widening the *listing* to co-owners too (nobody can restore what no screen
  shows), which moves §4.28.1 off its strongest footing. No report of a co-owner needing it exists;
  the deleting owner can restore from any device. **Reopen trigger, in §4.28.1:** the first report
  of a co-owner who needed to undo a colleague's delete buys widening both, as one decision.
- **Decision 1 — unconditional while the tombstone stands.** A tombstone keeps every record, so
  time does not make restoring less correct, and a restore window would be a second clock beside
  the destruction one. Restoring **withdraws any scheduled destruction in the same transaction**,
  and the confirmation dialog says so when one is scheduled. Once destroyed, the restore is refused
  like a fictional id and **the app asks pull** (which names a destroyed id under §4.13's existing
  exception) and says *"… was already deleted from the server, so there is nothing there to
  restore."* The route itself does not name it — the exception is not widened.
- **A race closed on the way: the sweep re-reads the schedule under a lock**
  (`ProjectDestructionService.destroyIfStillDue`). `destroyDue` read its list once and then
  destroyed; an owner's *cancel* committing in between was destroyed anyway — **pre-existing since
  task 11.290**, and a restore near the deadline makes it likelier. A two-connection test holds a
  real uncommitted cancel while the sweep runs; red without the re-read.
- **The server's write** (`SyncService.restoreTombstonedProject`): `deleted_at` cleared, **revision
  + 1** (so the restored row beats every tombstone a phone holds under the shared merge rule
  whatever the clocks say — a test with a phone clock a day fast went red without the bump, and the
  first version of that test did *not*, because its clocks were friendly), the restorer's name,
  and **a fresh `server_seq`** (red without it: the row sits below every member's cursor). Through
  the same `_update` every push uses. A second restore changes nothing and writes no audit row, so
  a retry after a lost answer reads as done. New audit event `project_restored`.
- **Decision 2 and what every device does — asserted, not described**
  (`restored_project_arrival_test.dart`). A device holding a **settled** tombstone — linked, not
  waiting to send it, not refused — asks `/projects/mine` on each foreground and after *Sync now*;
  a project listed live again gets one ordinary round, which pulls the restored row and pushes
  anything unsent. Reported only if the row actually landed. **The owner's phone** gets it back and
  is told it restored it; **a member's phone** gets it back with every record and is told, by
  name, who restored it (*"Robin Owner had deleted it and has restored it on the server, with
  everything in it."*) — through the app's messenger, because a project reappearing unexplained
  reads exactly like the fault that hid it; **a phone holding an unsent bearing** sends it on the
  same trip. Not brought back: a deletion not yet delivered (the Projects list's undo owns it), a
  refused one, an unlinked copy, a project the server has not restored. A device holding no
  settled tombstone asks no server. Each exclusion watched red by removing it; the refused-deletion
  one passed at first because the merge protects that tombstone anyway, so its test now asserts
  the device does not even ask.
- **The screen:** *Restore* is a button on each row of *Deleted from your devices, still on the
  server*, beside the ⋮, behind a confirmation that says every member gets it back. Five widget
  tests in the app shell: the request sent, the scheduled-deletion wording, the destroyed case, the
  not-the-owner case, and an older server (a `400`, said as a possibility).
- **`server/README.md`**: a bare `UPDATE "Projects" SET deleted_at = NULL` — the route back this
  entry named in *The gap* — **is not a working restore for any phone that already holds the
  project**: it leaves the revision and `server_seq` where the tombstone put them. The README now
  says so and points at the app.
- **Michael's first device look, 2026-09-24, found two defects; both fixed the same day.**
  (1) **The member was not told.** The Mac got TestProject07 back with its bearing and no sentence:
  it still had the project *open* (a tombstone arriving by sync hides a project but does not close
  it), and the restore arrived through a route that did not speak — most likely the Projects list's
  pull-to-refresh, which runs *Sync now*, which ran the fetch and discarded its answer. The
  announcement had been put on one of three routes. **It now comes from `ProjectMerger` itself**
  (`ProjectRestoration`, beside `DataArrival`): any server page that takes a `Projects` row from
  deleted to live is announced after commit, and `app.dart` listens and speaks for restores by
  another account. Tests for the open-project round and for the already-open app with
  pull-to-refresh, both red without the merge-level announcement. (2) **The join-requests card
  said *"It's on this device and syncing — open it from your projects list"* above a list that no
  longer held the project.** The arrival was recorded once and never re-asked (task 11.83's card).
  `JoinRequestWatcher` now re-reads the row on every data arrival, and the card says the project
  has been deleted and will come back by itself if restored. A first attempt had the card watch the
  project list directly, and it **hung the existing card tests** by reading the database from a
  widget's fake clock (defect vocabulary entry 12). Moved to the watcher.

#### The gap

Since task 11.289 an owner's plain *Delete* reaches the server as a tombstone. Nothing on any
device can clear it. **The only route back is `UPDATE "Projects" SET deleted_at = NULL` over
`psql`** — which means a mis-tap is recoverable only by the one person who can open a database, and
only if he still has the project id.

Task 11.292 put those projects on a screen. **The records were never deleted** — that is what
"tombstone" means here — so restoring is clearing a mark, not reconstructing anything.

#### Where it goes, and the one thing that makes it more than a button

*Projects → Join a project → **Deleted from your devices, still on the server*** — the section
11.292 built, beside *Delete from server…*. The same three conditions already decide who sees a
row (an open owner membership, a tombstoned row, and the caller sent the tombstone), **so the
population that can restore is already derived and already tested.**

**The hard part is what happens on the devices that already believe it is gone.** The owner's own
phone deleted its local copy; other members' phones stopped seeing the project when the tombstone
synced. **Restoring on the server does not put it back on anybody's device by itself**, and a
restore that silently leaves every member without the project is a restore in name only. **Decide
and state what each device does on its next sync**, including the phone that still holds local
records it never pushed.

#### Three things to settle in writing rather than in code

1. **Does a restore need a grace window, or is it unconditional while the tombstone stands?** Once
   the destruction sweep has run there is nothing to restore — say so in the UI rather than letting
   a person find out by tapping.
2. **What does a member see?** They lost the project without being told. **They are the population
   least able to tell a restore from a fault**, and the §4.28.1 route deliberately does not list
   them. Whatever they see on the next sync, decide it here.
3. **Is restoring an owner-only act?** It should follow the delete it undoes, and the delete is
   owner-only — but **say it rather than inherit it**, because the route's author clause ("the
   caller sent the tombstone") is narrower than owner, and a co-owner watching a colleague's
   mistake is exactly who would want this.

#### The route

`§4.28.1` is one day old and its field table is derived by a test. **Restoring is a write, and that
section describes a read** — so decide whether this is a new route or an action on the existing
deletion route, and **amend §4.28 or §4.21.2 accordingly rather than shipping an undocumented
route.** Task 11.290's `POST /projects/<id>/deletion` already takes an `action` and nothing else;
that shape exists and may fit.

- **Acceptance:** an owner can restore a tombstoned project from the section 11.292 built, and
  **the same test population that gates the listing gates the restore**, derived not re-stated; what
  every device does on its next sync — the owner's, a member's, one holding unpushed local records —
  is **decided in writing and asserted by a test**, not left to be discovered; the
  already-destroyed case is refused with a sentence a person can act on; the route is documented in
  the security model under whichever section it belongs to, with a derivation test that refuses the
  code until it is; **watched red first**; **a device look is in the acceptance and the report asks
  Michael for it by name** — this undoes a destructive act and no test stands in for that;
  `flutter test` and the server suite green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.337 — Localization improvements found while checking the ellipse (later; not before Michael asks)

**Status:** **Below the line. Recorded 2026-10-07 so nothing found is lost; not to be briefed until Michael asks**
(`CLAUDE.md` standing decision 5). Each item is a published method with its source, or is marked as TriTrack's own.

1. **System testing: a measured bearing precision and bias** (White & Garrott 1990, ch. 5, and ch. 4 Eq. 4.4). Test
   bearings to a transmitter at a known spot give the project's bearing standard deviation (and any compass bias); κ comes
   from that, the same for every fix, and the chi-square ellipse is then correct by its own assumptions. LOAS also takes a
   user-entered standard deviation. The biggest real-world gain: it also finds bias, which no per-fix statistic can.
2. **The goodness-of-fit test for bounce** (White & Garrott 1990, pp. 68–69): with a known standard deviation and three or
   more bearings, Σ((θᵢ − μᵢ)/s)² against chi-square with n − 2 degrees of freedom flags a fix whose bearings disagree more
   than the system allows. A caution, not a correction.
3. **A maximum ellipse size** set per study (White & Garrott 1990, p. 72), beyond which an estimate is flagged unreliable.
4. **The Andrews robust estimator** (Lenth 1981; White & Garrott's recommendation, pp. 70–71, for areas with reflected
   signals): its field coverage was 78% against the maximum-likelihood estimator's 41% in Garrott et al. (1986)'s data
   (Table 4.1).
5. **An F-based ellipse when κ comes from the fix** (LOAS manual, 1/1/2005, p. 11, "F" and "Adjusted F", no formula given).
   Task 11.334 measured 2·F(2, n−2): 86–92%; and F × n/(n−2), **TriTrack's own inference** of what "Adjusted F" means: 92–96%
   everywhere. Ship only with an exact citation.
6. **Store κ, the scale used and the caution codes with each saved estimate** (11.323's and 11.334's Discovered Scope), so
   a methods section can report what the app showed. A minor schema change.
7. **The solver's weak spots** (11.336's Discovered Scope): in the simulation it stopped at its starting point in 1.2% of
   fixes (all four printed were 3-bearing) and says "Solver did not fully converge". Measure which fixes and whether a
   better starting point finds Lenth's maximum. **Not a new method** (the estimate it seeks is the same maximum-likelihood
   point), but it changes the solver, so it waits with the rest.
8. **Michael's proposal (2026-10-09, `Claude outputs/My thoughts on ellipse error regions for Claude.docx`): a computed 95%
   region with a κ for each bearing.** Compute the likelihood on a grid, store the 95% region as a polygon (10+ points) beside
   the ellipse, and allow a κ per bearing, taken from the swept range (people sweep the range they are 95% confident holds
   the signal, read as a von Mises 95% interval). Sources the planning session found: per-bearing κ in the likelihood (White &
   Garrott 1990, p. 68); the likelihood-ratio region (the hill's 5% outline in the theory page's step 5) is standard
   statistics, and the ellipse approximates it. **New and needing validation:** the sweep-to-κ mapping, checked against
   bearings to a transmitter at a known spot. **Michael, 2026-10-10: hold until the current list is done; then the planning
   session writes a design proposal (method, sources, sweep-to-κ, a simulation against today's ellipse) for his decision.**
   Reopens standing decision 5 only with his say-so.

### Task 11.331 — A deployment day is the field site's day, wherever the person looking at it is

**Status:** **Partial — built 2026-10-10, commits `d2cb477` and `a305ff2`; held at Michael's one-device check.** All seven
items built, each behavior watched red where a test can see it. Schema v20 (minor). Library `timezone` 0.11.1 (tz database 2025c)
and boundary data timezone-boundary-builder 2026d, simplified to 100 m: **3,984,822 bytes in the app** (ceiling 15 MB); §3.8 names
both and the alternatives, for the planning session's review. Night on `d2cb477`: 25 passed, 1 skipped by design; the UTC and Auckland
suites were red on one stale test (it expected the phone's midnight), corrected in `a305ff2` and green in all three zones through
the night's runner; the quote check's red lines are the 9 left by earlier tasks, none new. One deviation from item 5, named in
`TASK_COMMS.md` and Discovered Scope. **Above the line (before the beta). After 11.324; `/w-35` waits for it.**
**Model:** Opus, high. **Decided by Michael, 2026-10-06**, after the planning session weighed plain dates
and advised against them: **do not switch deployment dates to plain dates; give each project a field-site
time zone.** Now `CLAUDE.md` standing decision 4.

**Why.** A deployment's attached and removed days are stored as midnight on the entering phone's clock,
and the zone is not saved. So a day reads as the day before on any phone west of where it was entered;
the form's "today" is the phone's, not the field's (Michael entering an Arizona deployment from London
at 11 pm gets tomorrow); `deployments.csv` carries a UTC moment that turns into the wrong day for anything
entered east of UTC (a New Zealand season reads a day early); and the server, which runs on UTC, can only
guess whether a value is a bare day or a real swap time (`deployment_interlock.dart`'s notes, tasks 11.264
and 11.266: about one hand-picked swap time in 24 reads wrong). **Why not plain dates** (recorded so
nobody reopens it): matching a bearing to a collar still needs to know whose midnight; old values cannot
be converted without guessing their zone; it rewrites the overlap rules and the wire format wholesale; and
it still starts the form on the phone's "today". Bearings, non-detections, true locations, sessions and
estimates already store local time and offset; they are not part of this task.

1. **The project has a time zone** (an IANA name, for example `America/Phoenix`).
   - **Default: the zone at the centre of the project's area** (its bounding box), **always the centre's
     own zone, never the nearest land** (Michael, 2026-10-06: an ocean study site may be far from any
     land). Coastal waters belong to the neighbouring country's zone in the boundary data; beyond them,
     use the sea zone for that longitude (the `Etc/GMT±N` zones, whose sign is inverted: `Etc/GMT+7` is
     UTC−7). Show a sea zone in plain words ("UTC−7, sea time zone, no daylight saving"), never its raw
     name. If the project has no area yet, the creator's phone's zone; when an
     area is set later and its zone differs, suggest the new one.
   - **The creator confirms it at creation**, shown in plain words (for example "Arizona time, no daylight
     saving — chosen from the centre of your project area"), and can change it there. Why this matters
     near home: the Navajo Nation keeps daylight saving inside Arizona, so a centre on one side of that
     line is an hour different from the other.
   - **It works offline.** The zone boundaries and rules ship with the app; report how much size that adds,
     and name the data's source and update path.
2. **Each deployment row records the zone its days were written in** (the project's zone at that moment).
   A bare day is midnight in that zone. Every screen, the form's default "today", the overlap rules and
   the export read days in that zone. Exact same-day swap times stay exact moments.
3. **The project's zone can be changed later** by whoever can edit project settings (follow
   `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md`; add the row if it is missing). **The confirmation says what happens:** days
   already recorded stay the same days; new entries and "today" use the new zone. **No existing row is
   rewritten**, because each row knows its own zone; that is what makes the change safe with phones offline
   holding older rows. Say in the report what a change does to bearing matching at the edge of a day for
   rows written under the old zone (expected: the boundary moves by the zones' difference, usually an hour).
4. **The server stops guessing.** Its bare-day-or-time test uses the row's zone, replacing the UTC

check is `docker logs "$CONTAINER" 2>&1 | grep -qi "starttls required"` under `pipefail`. **The planning
session's leading suspect:** `grep -q` exits at its first match, the next write from `docker logs` gets

is left to write, which is why it is intermittent. `nightly_check.sh`'s `start_awake` already met the same
shape in 11.325. A quick count finds **28 `| grep -q` pipelines in `scripts/` and `server/`, in 6 files
that set `pipefail`**. A check that can read "found" as "missing" is a broken instrument: it trains
everyone to rerun reds.

1. **Make it fail on demand, or show it cannot.** For example, a long log with the match early, under
   `pipefail`. If the suspect is wrong, find the real cause before changing anything.
2. **Fix the class, not the one line.** Every `| grep -q` (and `| head`, or anything else that stops reading
   early) in a script that sets `pipefail` gets a shape that cannot misread: capture first, then match, or
   `grep -c`/`grep … >/dev/null`, whichever reads plainest. List each one changed.
3. **A guard** that fails if the shape comes back in a `pipefail` script, watched red first.
4. **The two anonymous Docker volumes each night leaves on the VM** (11.328's Discovered Scope): find the
   drill that creates them and have it remove its own. Never touch named volumes.
5. Add the instance to `CLAUDE_DOCS/DEFECT_VOCABULARY.md` if an entry fits, or a new entry if none does.

### Task 11.320 — The app explains too much, in too many words

**Status:** **Done — 2026-09-30.** Michael's phone check passed ("all looks good"). Commits `6184384` to
`5272a67` (11 commits, one per screen group; full suite green at each). 241 sentences rewritten,
9,184 words to 6,132; every sentence of about 25 words or more in the app was rewritten or kept on
purpose. One shared (i) button, `lib/widgets/info_button.dart`. `check_app_quotes` has 13 red
lines, all guide quotes this task's copy made stale, each named in `TASK_COMMS.md` for `/w-33`.
**Above the line.**
**Michael, 2026-09-30:** many explanations in the app are *"very verbose"*. *"Longer isn't better.
Efficient clarity is better. Longer is only better if it is clearer."* Where a long explanation is
really needed, it should sit behind an **(i)** button.
**Model:** **Opus, high.** This is a writing task more than a coding one.
**Depends on:** task 11.319. **Run before `/w-32` and `/w-33`**, since they photograph and quote
this text. **Fresh window, on the Mac. It may take more than one session:** commit per screen, and
if the session runs long, stop at a screen boundary and close `Partial` with the list of screens
left. The same command resumes from that list.

#### How to work

1. **Inventory first.** List every user-visible sentence in `lib/`, meaning explanations, notices,
   errors, empty states and dialog bodies, not button labels. Record its screen and its word count.
   Sort longest first. Put the inventory in the report, not in a new document.
2. **Rewrite, screen by screen, longest first.** The rules:
   - **Say what the person needs to know or do, first.** Cut history, internal reasons and
     anything the person cannot act on.
   - **On screen: one or two short sentences.** If the full explanation is genuinely needed (a
     destructive act, a legal or safety point, a state nobody would guess), keep a one-line summary
     on screen and put the rest behind an **(i)** button.
   - **Plain words.** No internal terms (cursor, tombstone, payload, row). One idea per sentence.
   - **An error says what happened and what to do next.**
   - **Keep every fact that decides what a person does.** Shorter must not become vaguer.
3. **One shared (i) widget.** There is none today; several screens hand-roll an info icon. Build
   one, reuse it everywhere, and make it reachable by screen readers and at every text size.
4. **Wording that a test pins for a reason stays pinned.** Some tests exist to forbid a word (for
   example "permanent" in the deletion dialog) or to require a fact. Read why before changing the
   test; if the test protects a promise, keep the promise in the new wording.

#### Acceptance

- The report opens with a **before/after table** for every changed sentence (screen, old word
  count, new word count, new text), so Michael can scan it in one pass.
- The clipped-text sweep stays clean at every size. `flutter test` green. **Do not run

- **`check_app_quotes` will go red where the guide quotes old wording.** That is expected. List

### Task 11.316 — Every server rebuild needs pub.dev, because the Dockerfile copies the source first

**Status:** **Done — 2026-09-29**, commits `2279836` and `dbff1c9`. Michael's VM run at `03425e1`: gate 25 of 25, the 11.85 drill clean, all five variants built (they all failed at `dart pub get` on 2026-09-27), real server back up and syncing. **Above the line**, and small.
**Found by task 11.312, 2026-09-27** (Discovered Scope, "Every broken-control drill variant needs
pub.dev to build"). **The planning session chose both of its fixes, 2026-09-28.**
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window. Fixes on the Mac; closes `Partial` with VM steps, one per
step.**

`server/Dockerfile` copies `server/` before it runs `dart pub get`, so any edit to the server throws
away the downloaded packages and the next build must reach pub.dev. That broke Michael's own server
rebuild on 2026-09-21, and it broke all five drill variants on 2026-09-27, about half an hour of
waiting each time the VM's container network was down.

1. **Download packages before copying the source.** Copy only the `pubspec.yaml` and
   `pubspec.lock` files the server needs (its own, and `packages/tritrack_sync`'s, which it uses by
   path), run `dart pub get`, then copy the source. Read the Dockerfile first for anything else that
   needs a path package present at `pub get` time. **This changes how the shipped image is built**,
   so show the built server still starts and passes the gate. **Watched:** build, edit one line
   under `server/lib`, build again; the second build must show the package step as cached.
2. **The drill stops at the first variant that cannot build for lack of network**, instead of
   trying all five. Its message names the one-line check (`ip -4 addr show docker0`; no `inet`
   line means restart Docker, per `server/README.md`). **Watched red** with a build that has no
   network, e.g. `--network none`; say how you simulated it.

- **Acceptance:** both watched as described; **Do not run `dart format`**; no CI until 1 October;
  the report ends with the VM steps, one per step: real server stopped first, gate, drill stack up,
  the 11.85 drill, stack down, real server started, app syncs.

### Task 11.315 — Taking a bearing cannot show where it crosses the others

**Status:** **Done — 2026-09-29**, commit `15c941c`. Michael's field test passed ("the new feature is great"); his two follow-ups and the answers to this task's two questions are task 11.317. Every acceptance test was watched red first by breaking the code on purpose; the full suite is green (3755 passed). **Above the line.**
**Found by Michael in the field, 2026-09-27**: on a trail, after each bearing he opened the map to
see how it crossed his earlier ones. **Every decision below is his (2026-09-28)** unless marked as the
planning session's.
**Model:** **Opus, high.** The map, the compass and GPS all live at once, on screens that are
already large.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window. Built and tested on the Mac; closes `Partial`, held at
Michael's field test on a phone.**

#### What to build

A map for taking a range bearing, so the person sees the wedge they are sweeping cross the day's
earlier bearings **while they sweep**.

1. **Getting there.** A **Take on map** button beside today's range capture on the Record screen.
   Range capture starts in two places today (`observation_logging_screen.dart` and
   `bearing_entry_sheet.dart`); read which one a person uses while taking a bearing, and put the
   button there, or in both if both are live. **The existing compass capture is unchanged. Preview
   is unchanged**; it keeps showing only the bearing being recorded. **Range sweep only**; the
   single-point capture stays where it is (planning session's call; say so if the code makes that
   awkward).
2. **What the map shows.**
   - **The person's position**: the record draft's position, the same one Preview uses, including
     a manual adjustment made there.
   - **Today's earlier bearings on the same tag**, each as a center line plus a faint wedge.
     "Today" is the device's local date. Say exactly how "same tag" is decided, and prove that
     other tags and yesterday's bearings are left out.
   - **The wedge being swept, live and brighter.**
   - **Every line and wedge reaches the edge of the screen, and is redrawn on every pan, zoom and
     rotation.** Cap it at the map's existing 40 km ceiling (`_maxBearingRangeMeters`, Michael's
     field report of reception range): past that, a line is not information. That cap is the
     planning session's call. Reuse the map's geometry (`geo_math.dart`, `bearingWedgePoints`,
     `BearingWedgeCache`); **do not write a second one.**
   - **True north throughout.** The compass reads magnetic; convert with the declination the same
     way Preview does (override, else the WMM model). Earlier bearings drawn the way the Map tab
     draws them.
3. **Two orientations, one button.** **North up** (the map stays still; the wedge turns) and
   **facing up** (the map turns so the direction the phone points is always up). Starts north up
   the first time and remembers the choice on this device. Not synced; it is a view preference.
   Facing up is **smoothed**, so compass wobble does not shake the map. When the compass reports
   interference or no heading, facing up says so and stops turning rather than spinning.
4. **Moving the map.** Pan and zoom work **before and after** the sweep. **While the button is
   held, the map ignores touches**, so a brushed thumb cannot move it mid-bearing. A **back to me**
   button puts the position back in view. In facing up, panning away pauses the turning until back
   to me is tapped, so the map does not fight the finger.
5. **Taking it.** The same hold-and-release button as today. After release: **Confirm** puts the
   bearing into the record form, and the person still reviews and taps Save (no second save
   path). **Retake** clears the sweep and stays on the map. **Cancel** goes back with the form
   unchanged.
6. **Where it appears.** Phones with a compass only; hidden where there is none (the Mac), using
   the app's existing check. **Without downloaded map tiles** the lines still draw, over a blank
   background, with the scale bar.

#### Acceptance

- Tests, each watched red first where a test can see it: the edge extension after pan, zoom and
  rotation; the same-tag, today-only filter; Confirm fills the form and Cancel leaves it unchanged;
  touches ignored during the hold; the orientation remembered; the button hidden without a compass.

#### 1. `verify_11_49_server_reads` — flags an approved field as an attack

*"ATTACKS THAT SUCCEEDED AND ARE NOT REGISTERED: a field beyond the four §4.28 names — extra
['destroy_at']."* `destroy_at` was **deliberately added** to `/projects/mine` by task 11.290 on
2026-09-20 and §4.28 was amended to five fields. The Dart field-set test derives from §4.28; **this
probe hard-codes "four"**. It is task 11.297's class exactly — a count carried by hand into a second
place. **Derive it from §4.28's table**, the way `project_directory_field_set_test.dart` does.

#### 2. `audit_retention_status` — a time bomb in test data went off on 2026-09-21

*"project_join_requests: oldest of decided join requests is 34d old — PAST ITS 30-day window.
RETENTION HAS STOPPED BEING APPLIED."* On a database created minutes earlier. The cause is in
`verify_11_49_server_reads.py`: it seeds 225 decided join requests with **`decided_at =
'2026-08-20 01:00:00+00'`**, a fixed date. Written in late August they were a few days old; on
2026-09-23 they are 34 days old, past the 30-day window plus its 48-hour grace — **which it crossed
on 2026-09-21.** `audit_retention_status` runs later against the same database and reports them.

**Fix the fixture — dates relative to now — and then sweep for the class.** **Six gate scripts
carry fixed `2026-08-` dates** (a grep, not a census of what each date means — read them): any of
them sitting under a time-relative rule is the same bomb on a longer fuse. **Say how many were
genuinely time-dependent.**

#### 3. `backup_restore_drill` — the check that a bad restore never wipes live data is not running

Step 7e fails: *"refused, but not at the decrypt verification"* — the truncated archive is refused
by the **sidecar-versus-signature** check instead: *"the .schema sidecar says major '5' and the
signature says major '2'."* The drill's own forging helper is the cause: `sign_archive()` defaults
**`major="${2:-2}"`**, written before the schema reached major 5, so every damaged archive it forges
is signed as major 2 while the sidecar copied from the real archive says 5.

**Real backup and full restore both passed in the same run** — steps 4 through 7 — so this is not
a broken backup. **But the case the drill exists for is currently untested**: G-3, that a restore
from a truncated archive is stopped at decryption **before the live database is dropped.** The
drill's own comment names this exact failure — *"A drill whose cases all short-circuit at the newest
check is a drill that only tests the newest check."* **Derive the major from the schema constant**,
not a default.

*"the server port is published to loopback only — published on ['0.0.0.0']"* and *"the LAN address
192.168.0.136 does NOT reach it — answered 200 — this is B3 live."* **The shipped default is still
loopback.** The VM's `.env` line 1 is ` SERVER_PUBLISH_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` — deliberately, so the phone

itself resolves them" resolves them **with that `.env` present.** It is testing this machine, not
what ships. **Render the shipped defaults with an isolated environment** so no operator setting
reaches the check, and **state what the LAN section tests** — the stack it controls, or whatever
happens to answer.

(**That `.env` line starts with a space.** Compose tolerates it; a grep anchored at `^` did not find
it. Note it and move on — it is a formatting quirk, not a defect.)

`scripts/gate_smoke_test.sh` brings up its own server on port 8080. **On a machine already serving

already allocated`** and a generic *"could not bring the stack up."* On a CI runner this never
happens, which is why nobody noticed — defect-vocabulary entry 110 exactly. **Check the port before

#### 6. The broken-control drills attack whatever is on port 8080 — a safety guard, and the most important item here

`scripts/verify_round8_broken_control.py` runs its **healthy phase against `http://localhost:8080`
without checking what is there**, expecting the throwaway `tritrack-gate` stack. **On a machine that

### Task 11.309 — Generated files drift from their sources and nothing notices

**Status:** Done, 2026-09-22, commit `c6f585a` (sweep), commit `9851733` (guard).
**Above the line** — it is small, and it is the second sweep in two days.
**Found twice: by task 11.305 (2026-09-21) and again by task 11.307 (2026-09-22)**, each of which
reverted the drift rather than carry it, and each of which had to notice it by hand.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### The pattern, which is the point — the sweep is not

A task edits a doc comment on a source file and does not run `build_runner`, so the `.g.dart`
beside it keeps the old text. Nothing fails. The next task to run the generator finds a diff it did
not make, and has to decide whether to carry somebody else's change or revert it. **Both tasks that
met this chose to revert and say so, which is right** — and both spent attention on it.

**Two are stale on `main` right now**, from task 11.256's doc comments: the app-context provider and
the download manager. Task 11.306 swept three others two days ago **in its own commit**, which is
the shape to repeat.

#### The fix is a guard, and the sweep is its first red

**Run the generator and fail if it changes anything tracked.** That is the whole check. It makes the
drift impossible to introduce silently instead of making somebody notice it later, and the two
current files are what it catches on its first run.

**Derive the cost before choosing where it lives.** `build_runner` is not free, and this project has
a pre-commit suite that already runs a full `flutter test`. **Time it**, and say in the report
whether it belongs in the pre-commit hook, in a CI workflow (dormant until 1 October), or as a
`scripts/` command the hook calls only when a file under `lib/` changed. **A guard nobody can afford
to run is a guard that gets disabled.**

#### One thing to be careful about

**Generated output can differ between machines or SDK versions.** If it does, a guard that fails on
any diff fails for the wrong reason and will be switched off within a week. **Check whether the
output is stable** — regenerate twice, and on a second machine if one is to hand — and if it is not,
say so and narrow the check to what is stable rather than shipping a flaky one.

- **Acceptance:** the two stale files are swept **in their own commit**, separate from the guard;
  the guard runs the generator and fails on any tracked change, **watched red first** on exactly
  those two before they are swept; its cost is **measured and reported**, and where it runs is
  argued from that number; the stability question is answered by regenerating rather than assumed;
  if the guard cannot be made non-flaky, **it is not shipped** and the report says why; `flutter
  test` green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.308 — A failed build looks like progress, and nothing says which commit is serving

**Status:** Done, 2026-09-21, commit `19f94e6`. **Above the line** — it is the operator's side of
task 11.307, it hit Michael twice, and it is the layer that made the other one expensive.
**Found 2026-09-22 by Michael**, who noticed the failure himself after it had already cost an
evening: *"There was an issue in the build. This happened before but I missed it."*
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.** Adjacent to 11.307; either order.

#### What happened, and why missing it was reasonable

`dart pub get` inside the Docker build could not reach pub.dev, hung for **372 seconds**, and
failed. `scripts/server_up.sh` has `set -euo pipefail` and exited non-zero **correctly**. But the
last thing on screen was:

```
[+] up 0/5
 ⠙ Image tritrack-server              Building                                       374.0s
```

**A spinner and the word "Building" is what success looks like mid-flight.** The error was above it,
already scrolled past. And **the previous server kept running**, so every subsequent check —
the app connecting, the database answering, the sync working — said everything was fine.

**The script's own ending makes this worse in a way worth naming.** It closes with two genuinely
good paragraphs about backup freshness and the scheduler's uid, printed **after** the compose
command. On a failed build those never print, and on a successful one they are what a person reads
— so the screen's most reassuring text is furthest from the thing that failed.

#### The fix is not "check the exit code" — the script already does

**The gap is that a person cannot tell, afterwards, which commit is serving.** That is the question
tonight needed and could not answer without four database queries and a `curl`.

**So: after a successful start, print what is actually running** — the commit the running server
image was built from, asked of the container rather than assumed from the working tree, in the same
place the backup and uid lines are printed. Those two paragraphs exist because this project already
decided that a script which starts a server should say **what it actually started**, measured rather
than inherited. This is the same rule applied to the thing the script is named for.

**And on a failure, say what is still serving.** A non-zero exit that leaves the old server running
should say so in one sentence, because the state after a failed rebuild is not "nothing happened" —
it is "the previous version is still answering", which is the fact that misled everybody.

#### Two things to derive rather than take from here

- **How the running container can name its build.** A label, a build arg, an embedded constant — it
  is a decision, and the honest one survives a rebuild from a dirty tree. **Say what a dirty tree
  prints.**
- **Whether `--build` failing is distinguishable from the image being up to date.** Both end with
  no new image. The report should say which of those the operator saw, or that the script cannot
  tell them apart.

#### The noise problem, because it is the same evening's second false signal

Every restart prints `ERROR: role "tritrack_app" already exists` and `ERROR: tuple concurrently
updated` from Postgres. **Both are harmless** — the roles persist in the volume, and the second is
the catalog race task 10.89 documented. **Both say ERROR, in red, on a healthy start.** So this
stack showed alarming text for a healthy state and calm text for a broken one, in the same session.
**Decide whether these can be quieted or must be explained** — quieting a real error to remove noise
would be the worse defect, so if the answer is "explain", the explanation goes where somebody
staring at the log will meet it, not in a document.

- **Acceptance:** a successful start prints the commit actually serving, **asked of the running
  container**, with the dirty-tree case stated; a failed start says in one sentence that the previous
  version is still answering; the `--build`-failed versus already-current question is answered or
  declared undecidable; the Postgres startup noise is either quieted **with a reason it is safe** or
  explained where a person reading the log will see it; **watched red first** — break the build on
  purpose and read what the script says; the DNS failure that started this (`daemon.json` resolvers
  on a Parallels VM) is written into `server/README.md` beside the other operator notes, because it
  has now cost this project two evenings; **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.307 — A server too old to answer looks exactly like a feature that does not work

**Status:** Done, 2026-09-22, commit `b66b365`. The app cannot know the server's build (established
by reading the handshake — see the comms entry), so the sentence names both causes and claims
neither; it lives in `SyncTransportException`'s remedy table as reason `route_not_offered`, and
the join screen, the Projects list and the sync bar all read it from there. Task 11.290's own
one-cause sentence is deleted.
**Above the line** — it cost the project time the day it was predicted, and
it is the shape a collaborator meets first.
**Found 2026-09-22 by Michael and the planning session**, doing task 11.292's device look. **Task
11.292's own report predicted it in writing** — *"until the beta server is rebuilt, the app's new
section reads a `404` from the old build and simply stays absent — it will not say anything is
wrong"* — and the very next person to touch the feature lost four database queries to it anyway.
**A risk written down in a comms entry is not a control.**
**Model:** **Opus** — it is a decision about what the app may conclude from a `404`, and the wrong
answer makes a real outage read as an old server.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### What happened, in order, because the order is the finding

Michael deleted a published throwaway project and the join screen's *Deleted from your devices,
still on the server* section never appeared. We then established, one query at a time, that the
tombstone had reached the server, that it carried his user id in `last_modified_by`, and that his
owner membership was open with no `end_date` and no `deleted_at` — **every condition the listing
requires.** Only then did we ask whether the route existed: `curl` answered **404**. The running
server predated task 11.292.

**Everything looked correct because everything was correct.** The app was current, the database was
in exactly the right state, and the screen had nothing to render because the server does not answer
that question yet — **and said so to nobody.**

#### The decision this task has to make, and it is not "show an error on 404"

A `404` from a route the app knows about has **two** causes and the app cannot tell them apart from
the status code alone: *this server is older than this app*, and *something is wrong with this
server or the path to it*. **Deciding it is always the first would turn a real outage into a
reassuring sentence**, which is this project's own wrong-cause class.

**So find out what the app can already know.** `schemaMajorVersion` exists and sync already has
vocabulary for a version mismatch on both sides — read how the sync round establishes it, and
answer whether the join screen can reach the same fact rather than inventing a second mechanism.
**If the app can know the server's version, a `404` on a known route is a version statement and can
be said plainly. If it cannot, say so** — and then the honest sentence names both possibilities,
the way task 11.306's does, rather than guessing.

#### Scope, because this is a class and not one screen

**Derive which routes the app calls that a server may not have**, rather than fixing the one we met.
The join screen's deleted-projects listing is today's instance; `/projects/<id>/deletion` (task
11.290) has the same property, and anything added later will too. **Report the list you derived and
the command you derived it with.**

#### One thing that is already right and must stay that way

**The section being absent rather than broken is correct behavior for an old server** — the app
should not show a control that cannot work. This task is about saying why it is absent, not about
showing it anyway.

- **Acceptance:** the routes at risk are **derived and reported with the derivation**, not taken
  from this entry; the app's ability to know the server's version is established by reading the sync
  handshake, and the answer is stated either way; whatever is shown **does not claim an old server
  when it cannot tell** — if both causes remain possible, the sentence names both; **no control
  appears that cannot work**; **watched red first**; the sentence is read aloud in the report;
  `check_app_quotes` green and the content lane told if any quoted string moved; `flutter test` and
  the server suite green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.306 — The access-refused sentence guesses a cause that is wrong for half the people who see it

**Depends on:** task 11.305, done. **Fresh window.**

#### The sentence, and the two people who now read it

Task 11.305 made a `403` with **no membership row at all** read as *access refused* rather than

- **No causal guess.** The device genuinely cannot tell, and 11.305's own sentence already says why.
- **Both remedies**, in the order of likelihood: ask an owner; and if this is not your project, open

- **The reassurance stays.** *Nothing on this device has been changed or lost* is the most important

### Task 11.305 — A second account's first sync unlinks the first account's project and tells them they left it

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-21, commit `66e7a1f`. (B) built: one derivation of "have I left
this project" — `ProjectMembershipRepository.hasDeparted`, a closed row and no open one — read by
`SyncController.build`, by both of `_run`'s paths, and by `departedProjectIds`; a `403` with no row
at all now reads *access refused*. Started from the "Finding 3" red as the entry asked; the fix was
also watched red three more ways by sabotaging `hasDeparted` back to the wide reading. Sign-out
untouched; its guard green. `flutter test` 3645 passed / 16 skipped and the server suite 1150
passed, both locally — no CI until 1 October. **Two things the entry's own wording got wrong are
corrected below**, and the (C) question is answered: **later, not less likely.**
**For the planning session:** resolved in `CLAUDE_DOCS/TASK_COMMS.md`.

#### What (B) leaves — corrected against the code, 2026-09-21

The entry says the device goes on asking and being refused *"once per foreground"*. **It is once
per app launch, not per foreground**, and this is the code rather than the entry: a `403` is
terminal (`SyncTransportException.isTerminal`), so the first refusal sets `stoppedReason` on the
schedule and `shouldAttemptAt` answers no from then on — but `stoppedReason` lives only in memory
(`_persistedSchedule` reads the frequency and the last attempt, nothing else), so the controller's
next rebuild (a relaunch, a project switch, a sign-in) forgets the stop and the next due foreground
tries once more. Manual *Sync now* is never gated. So the cost carried, per launch with the other
account's project still open: one refused pull, one audit-log denial under the second person's id,
and an amber *"The server is refusing access to this project. Tap to check."* on the map icon until
they open a different project. **And one thing the entry did not name:** that refusal is written
into the *first* person's project's remembered-failure slot, so when they sign back in their bar
reads *Access refused … not retried since* for exactly one round — sign-in clears the last-attempt
stamp, the round runs at once and succeeds, and the record is forgotten. The mirror of 11.304's
Finding 1, in the other direction, and now pinned by the third leg of the measured group.

**Original entry, kept as written:** **Above the line.** Nothing is lost and nothing is disclosed — **what
crosses the account boundary is bookkeeping and a false sentence**, not data — but a person is told
something untrue about a project they were never on, and another person's device quietly stops
syncing.
**Found by task 11.304, 2026-09-21**, by the measurement its brief demanded rather than by a
reading. **The brief predicted the fix would be small and said to stop and report if anything
crossed. Something crossed.**
**Model:** **Opus** — it changes a rule task 11.54 designed, and the two readings it reconciles are
each correct in their own place.
**Depends on:** task 11.304, done. **Fresh window.**

#### What happens, measured

Alex signs out; Sam signs in on the same device. Alex's project is still linked, with Alex's cursor.
Sam's first automatic round pushes nothing — task 11.237's gate finds Sam no membership row and
offers nothing — and pulls Alex's project under Sam's token, which the server refuses.

**The refusal is then read wrongly.** `classifySyncFailure` turns that `403` into `membershipEnded`
whenever the signed-in person holds no *open* membership row, and Sam holds **no row at all**.
`SyncController.build` asks the same question differently — `_weHaveLeft` requires a row that exists
*and is closed* — but `_run`'s wider answer is the one that acts. So it clears Alex's sync state and
tells Sam *"You're no longer on this project, so it has stopped syncing."*

**Alex, signing back in, finds the project silently not syncing** — the status bar is hidden for a
merely-unlinked project — and relinking it from *Join a project* re-pulls the whole thing from zero.

#### The decision, made: **(B)**

11.304 costed two and recommended the second. **I agree, and the reason is which path pays.**

- **(A) Clear the bookkeeping on sign-out.** Closes the one route — only publish and join set the
  linked flag, so this is the only way a linked project meets a person with no row. **And it
  charges every *same-person* sign-out a full re-pull of every project on the device**, plus a
  relink each. On a phone on cellular in the field that is the expensive path, and the same person
  signing back in is the overwhelming majority of sign-outs. **It makes the common case pay for the
  rare one.**
- **(B) Fix the reading.** One derivation of *have I left this project*, shared by `build` and
  `_run`, so a `403` with **no row at all** is *access refused* and not *you left*. Costs nothing on
  the common path. **This is a defect on its own terms** — two places deriving the same question
  differently, and the wider one acting — and worth fixing even if the account case never arose.

**What (B) leaves, stated rather than discovered later:** a device holding another account's linked
projects goes on asking about them and being refused, once per foreground, until that person opens
a different project. That is a nuisance on the status bar and **an audit-log denial per foreground
under the second person's id on the server.** Bounded and visible; not silent.

#### (C), named because the next person will reach for it

**The linked flag and the cursors are device-global; identity is per-account.** The shape that makes
this class impossible is scoping sync bookkeeping by account, so a second person's device simply has
none of the first person's. **That is not this task** — it is a schema change and a migration for a
case with one known route — but **say in the report whether (B) makes (C) less likely to ever be
needed or merely later**, because a fix that removes the symptom and leaves the mismatch is how this
kind of thing comes back wearing a different name.

- **Acceptance:** one derivation of "have I left this project", used by both call sites, with the
  no-row-at-all case reading as *access refused*; **`sign_out_leaves_sync_state_test.dart`'s
  "Finding 3" guard pins today's wrong behavior, so the fix starts from a red** — start there and
  say you saw it; the sentence Sam sees is checked by reading it as a person, not by asserting a
  code; **no change to sign-out**, and the guard that holds that stays green; the per-foreground
  refusal (B) leaves is stated in the entry with its audit-log cost; the (C) question is answered in
  writing; `flutter test` and the server suite green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.304 — Three comments say signing out clears every project's cursor; nothing does

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-21, commit `b35356c`. `flutter test` green locally, full suite —
no CI until 1 October. Measured first, as the entry asked, and **the measurement found a defect
this entry did not predict** — see "What was measured" below and this phase's Discovered Scope.
The documentation half is complete: the comments say what the code does and a test fails if they
drift. **The defect is filed, not fixed**, because the entry says a crossing stops this being a
documentation task and the fix is a rule change for the planning session to scope.
**For the planning session:** resolved in `CLAUDE_DOCS/TASK_COMMS.md`.
**Above the line** — it is a false statement in three places about what
happens to somebody's data when they sign out, and it was believed by a task this week.
**Found by task 11.299, 2026-09-21**, which wrote down a sign-out-then-re-join route around the
stale-device refusal **on the strength of the comment**, then read `signOut` and found the route
does not exist. **That is the cost already paid**; the next reader pays it again.
**Model:** **Opus** — the decision is about what a sign-out means, and it touches two accounts on
one device.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### What was measured (2026-09-21)

**Three things, each as a test that stays.**

1. **Sign-out.** `test/core/providers/sign_out_leaves_sync_state_test.dart`, first group: a
   device with two published projects, cursors 42 and 7, a last-success stamp and a remembered
   failure, signs out through the real `CurrentSession.signOut`. The only request made is
   `/auth/sign-out`; every per-project key in `SyncStateStore` is byte-for-byte what it was.
   **Watched red** by temporarily making `signOut` clear one project — the guard names the key.
2. **A different account signs in on the same device.** Same file, second group. Alex signs out;
   Sam signs in (the adopter gives Sam their own `Users` row and touches none of Alex's records);
   the open project is still Alex's, still linked, with Alex's cursor. Sam's first round —
   **automatic, on the first foreground, because sign-in makes a round due at once** — sends **no
   push**: task 11.237's gate (`SyncEngine.offersNothingFor`) finds no membership row for Sam and
   withholds every row, so nothing Alex recorded is offered under Sam's name and the bar counts
   nothing as waiting. It sends **one pull, for Alex's project, from cursor 42, under Sam's token**,
   and the server refuses it. **Nothing is disclosed and nothing is offered.** The server-side half
   is a new test in `server/test/integration/member_authorization_test.dart`'s "cross-project
   isolation" group, run against a real Postgres: a pull carrying a cursor another account earned,
   from that account's device id, is refused identically to a fictional project and records no
   `sync_cursors` row for the refused caller. **Watched red** by querying the row the server *does*
   record (Bob's own).
3. **The same person signs back in.** Third group. Alex's next round pulls Q from 7 and P from 42
   — the incremental path. **Had sign-out cleared, both would be 0**: every project over the air
   again, on a phone in the field.

**And the defect, found by the second measurement.** The refused pull is not read as "access
refused". `classifySyncFailure` turns a `403` into `membershipEnded` whenever the signed-in person
holds no **open** membership row — and Sam holds no row at all. `SyncController.build` asks the
narrower question (`_weHaveLeft`: a row exists *and is closed*); `_run` asks the wider one, and
`_run`'s answer is the one that acts: `_unlinkIfWeAlreadyLeft` runs `SyncStateStore.clear` on
Alex's project. So Sam's first automatic round **unlinks Alex's open project, erases the cursor Alex
earned, and tells Sam *"You're no longer on this project, so it has stopped syncing"*** — about a
project Sam was never on. When Alex signs back in, P is silently not syncing: the bar is hidden for
a merely-unlinked project, and relinking it from "Join a project" re-pulls it from zero. **What
crosses the account boundary is Alex's bookkeeping, undone by Sam's session, with a false message
to Sam.** The test pins this as today's behavior, named as the defect, so the fix starts from red.
Filed in Discovered Scope; not fixed here, per this entry's own instruction.

#### The decision, with its cost

**Sign-out keeps every project's sync bookkeeping; the comments now say so.** Eight copies of the
false claim were corrected, not three — the brief's count came from the phrasings it had seen, and a
census by subject (`grep -i "sign.out\|signing out"` over `lib/`, `test/`, `server/`, read whole)
found six in `lib/` and two in test comments. Each now says what `clear` is for (a device that has
learned it is off the project — four callers, all named in `clear`'s doc) and that sign-out is not
among them; the ones at the mechanism (`signOut`, `clear`) name the test that holds it.

**Why not clear.** The common sign-out is the same person signing back in, and the measurement
shows what they keep: an incremental pull instead of the whole project. Clearing would also leave
every project **unlinked** after every sign-out, and an unlinked project's bar is hidden — the
person would have to notice nothing was syncing and relink each project from "Join a project".
That is the expensive path *and* the quiet one — and it is paid on **every** sign-out to spare
the rare one.

**What clearing would buy, said honestly.** Only publish and join ever set the linked flag, so
the leftover-after-sign-out route is today the *only* way a linked project meets a signed-in
person with no membership row. Clearing on sign-out would therefore close the defect's one route:
the second person's device would hold no linked project and make no round. **Two ways to close
the finding, then, and they are not the same size:** (A) clear on sign-out — closes the route,
charges every same-person sign-out a hidden bar, a relink per project and a full re-pull; or (B)
fix the reading of the refusal — one answer to "have I left this project", shared by `build` and
`_run`, so a `403` with no row at all is *access refused* — which costs nothing on the common
path and leaves the different-account device asking and being refused each foreground (a
nuisance on that person's bar, and an audit-log denial per foreground under their id on the
server) until they open another project. **This task recommends (B)** and did not build it,
because the entry said to stop and say so; the filed task is where that choice is made.

**The cost carried meanwhile.** A second account signing in on a device whose open project
belongs to the first account will unlink that project on its first foreground and erase its
cursor. Nothing is lost — the records are on the device and the project is one "Join" away — but
the first person is not told, and the second is told something false. Michael's devices are all
his own; the case needs a shared field device with two accounts.

#### The finding

`signOut` clears the session store and nothing else. **No caller of `SyncStateStore.clear` runs on
sign-out, and none ever has.** Three doc comments say every project's cursor and linked flag are
cleared. They are wrong, and they have been wrong since they were written.

#### This is a decision before it is a fix, and the task must not guess which way

**Make sign-out do what the comments say, or make the comments say what sign-out does.** Both are
defensible and they are not the same size.

- **Clearing on sign-out** is the safer-sounding option and it is not free: every project on the
  device would re-pull from zero on the next sign-in, which on a phone in the field is the
  expensive path, and it discards bookkeeping that is correct for the account that is still the
  same account in the overwhelming majority of sign-outs.
- **Correcting the comments** is honest and leaves the real question unasked.

**The question that decides it, and the task answers it with a measurement rather than an
argument:** what happens today when a person signs out and a *different* account signs in on the
same device? The cursors and linked flags of the first account's projects are still there. **Find
out what that device then does** — whether it offers rows, whether it pulls from a position the
new account never earned, whether anything is disclosed across the account boundary. **That
measurement decides the task.** If nothing crosses, the comments are the defect and the fix is
small. If something crosses, this stops being a documentation task.

#### The class, named because it is the third this week

A comment describing behavior nobody implemented is a claim, and **a task read it and acted on it
four days ago.** It is the same family as the dated measurement in `pending_departure.dart`
(task 11.301) and the "purge already works" brief (task 11.291): **prose about mechanism, believed
because it was specific.**

- **Acceptance:** the two-account measurement is run **first** and reported, whichever way it comes
  out; the decision is stated in writing with its cost, not implied by the diff; whatever is chosen,
  **the three comments and the code agree at the end**, and a test fails if they drift — a comment
  that has gone false is what this task exists to stop recurring; if clearing is chosen, the
  re-pull cost is stated in the entry; **watched red first**; `flutter test` green locally, **no CI
  until 1 October**.

### Task 11.303 — Four different refusals share one headline, and two of them are wrong

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-21. `flutter test` green locally, full suite — no CI until 1 October.
`check_app_quotes` green, no quoted string moved. **For the planning session:** resolved in
`CLAUDE_DOCS/TASK_COMMS.md` — the count was five, not four.
**Found by task 11.299, 2026-09-21.**
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### What was derived (2026-09-21)

**Five codes reach `SyncHealth.versionRefused`, not four.** `classifySyncFailure` checks
`error.userMessage != null` ahead of the `403` split, so `project_destroyed` — whose sentence says
the project was deleted, nothing about the app — lands in `SyncFailureCause.refusedWithRemedy` the
same way `cursor_too_old` and `rate_limited` do. Verified with a test that runs every code in
`knownSyncRefusals` (minus the join-only codes, which no sync round ever answers with — see
`joinRefusalCodes`, added to `project_join.dart` so that boundary is checked rather than assumed)
through the real classifier and asserts the resulting set.

The five: `schema_version_mismatch`, `protocol_version_mismatch`, `cursor_too_old`, `rate_limited`,
`project_destroyed`.

#### What changed

`SyncTransportException` gained `userHeadline`, declared beside `userMessage` in one shared
`_remedy` record per code — a code cannot pick up a sentence without a headline of its own, and
`sync_transport_refusal_test.dart` derives the five and fails if one is missing. A version skew's
headline still depends on direction (`Update needed` only when *this app* is behind; `Server needs
an update` the other way; `Version mismatch` when neither number crossed); the other four are fixed
per cause: `Too many attempts`, `Offline too long to sync`, `Project deleted`.

`SyncStatus` gained `lastErrorHeadline`, written alongside `lastErrorMessage` everywhere that field
already was. The Sync Status screen's `_headline()` now reads it for `SyncHealth.versionRefused`
instead of a fixed string, falling back to the new `syncRefusalHeadline(code)` — reusing the same
declaration — for the one case with no live headline: a device that restarted since its last
attempt, which only has `RememberedSyncFailure.stoppedReason` (a bare code, no version numbers) to
go on. `rate_limited` is a 429, not one of `isTerminal`'s statuses, so it is the one cause in the
family that cannot even reach that fallback — checked directly in a test.

#### The rate-limited case, read aloud

Headline: **"Too many attempts."** Sentence beneath it: **"Too many attempts. Wait a few minutes
and try again."** Nothing about updating the app.

#### The finding

The Sync Status screen heads every refusal that carries a sentence with **"Update needed"** — the
two version codes, `cursor_too_old`, and `rate_limited`. One headline, four causes, and **the
headline is true of two of them.** A person who has simply asked too often in fifteen minutes is
told their app is out of date; a person whose device has been away two years is told the same.

**The map icon uses the sentence rather than the headline and is right**, which is the shape of the
fix already present in the codebase.

#### Precedent, and it decides the approach

**Same shape as tasks 11.104 and 11.113: a cause of its own rather than a branch inside the
headline.** Read both before designing. A `switch` that picks a headline string is the version of
this that looks fixed and re-rots the moment a fifth code is added — **the headline should come
from the same place the sentence does**, so a new code cannot acquire a wrong headline by default.

#### One thing to check rather than assume

**Enumerate the refusal codes from the code, not from this entry.** Four are named here because
11.299 named four; that number came from a reading, not a derivation, and this plan's own history
says a count in a brief is an assertion about the code. **Derive it, and say what you found.**

- **Acceptance:** the codes are **derived** and the count reported against this entry's four; each
