### Task 11.301 — A departure the server has already made moot is retried forever

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-21, commit `ceeb35c`. `flutter test` green locally, full suite —
no CI until 1 October. Reproduced first, as the entry asked, and the reproduction found a bigger
and different cause than the entry described — see below. **For the planning session:** resolved
in `CLAUDE_DOCS/TASK_COMMS.md`.
**Found by task 11.292, 2026-09-21, by reading the flush rather than by reproducing it.**
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### What reproducing it actually found (2026-09-21)

The entry's mechanism — a self-departure's push refused whole-request `403` because the owner had
already removed the person, never recognized as settled — **is real, but it was not reachable**,
because of a second, older defect the reproduction exposed first: **`SyncEngine._push`'s task 11.237
gate (`offersNothingFor`) silences a self-departure's own row before it can ever be offered.**

`MembershipController.leaveProject` and `pending_departure.dart`'s foreground flush both close the
caller's own `Project_Memberships` row *locally* before ever trying to push it. Task 11.237 made
`_push` return nothing at all whenever this device's own membership standing on a project reads
`notAMember` — which is exactly what closing your own row produces. So **every self-departure's own
delivery push — not only the "already removed" case — was silently offering zero rows and never
reaching the server**, confirmed by a standalone probe: seeding an ordinary (nobody-removed) closed
departure row and calling `SyncEngine.run` directly, with `transport.pushCalls` staying `0`
throughout. Task 11.237 shipped 2026-09-13, after `pending_departure.dart`'s own "measured on
2026-08-29 against the real server" note; nothing since has exercised a departure delivery through a
transport double that could show the row actually going out, so the regression went unnoticed for a
week. This is the same shape defect vocabulary entry 104 names — a new state (11.237's snapshot
standing) exposed a defect in an existing ladder (11.57's departure delivery) that predated it.

**Both bugs together produced the entry's exact symptom** — the flush loops on every foreground and
the project never unlinks — but by two different routes: a device whose owner never removed it loops
because push offers nothing and no receipt is ever possible; a device whose owner *did* remove it
first would, once the first bug is fixed, finally reach the server and meet the entry's described
`403` — which the flush still would not have recognized as settled.

#### Both fixes, narrowly scoped

1. **`SyncEngine._push` (`lib/data/sync/sync_engine.dart`)** — when `offersNothingFor` is true, it
   now asks a new `_collectOwnDeparture` for exactly the caller's own not-yet-confirmed self-departure
   row(s) on `Project_Memberships` (the same definition `findUndeliveredDepartures` uses) and offers
   only those, through the same response handling (`_pushRows`, factored out of `_push` so both paths
   share one implementation) — receipts, held rows and conflicts all work exactly as they do for an
   ordinary push. Every other row of a snapshot or a colleague's archive stays withheld;
   `snapshot_project_push_test.dart`'s existing assertions ("a snapshot puts nothing on the wire",
   "a member whose row is closed is withheld too") are unchanged and still green, because neither
   fixture gives the pushing device's own user id a departure row to be exempt for.
2. **`SyncController.deliverPendingDepartures` (`lib/core/providers/sync_provider.dart`)** — now
   catches the push's `SyncTransportException` and, when
   `pending_departure.dart`'s new `departureSettledByRefusal` (`error.statusCode == 403`) says so,
   treats the departure as settled the same way a confirming receipt would: `store.clear`, unlink,
   stop asking. Narrowly named and doc-commented as true only for a self-departure's own whole-request
   `403` — not generalized to any other write, and specifically not to
   `deliverPendingProjectChanges`'s deletion-`403` handling one method away, which stays the opposite
   rule on purpose (task 11.290's "Deleted here, not yet on the server").

Without fix 1, fix 2 alone is unreachable dead code for the entry's own reproduction steps — the push
never throws at all, so the `403` branch never runs. Both are required to close the observed symptom.

- **Acceptance, checked against what actually shipped:** the reproduction was run (via
  `FakeSyncTransport`, per this project's "a test suite that needs a server is forbidden" invariant,
  rather than two physical devices) and reported above, including that it found a different mechanism
  than the entry named; a self-departure refused with `403` settles — pending change clears, project
  unlinks, flush stops asking (`test/core/providers/departure_refused_settles_test.dart`, first test);
  **watched red first**: both fixes were reverted locally and the test failed for the reason predicted
  each time (push count 0 with only fix 1 reverted; project still linked after a `403` with only fix 2
  reverted); the narrowness is written at the code, in both `_collectOwnDeparture`'s and
  `departureSettledByRefusal`'s doc comments, each naming the deletion case explicitly; no other
  refusal shape changes behavior (a second test asserts an unreachable server leaves the departure
  pending); `flutter test` green locally, full suite, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.300 — The container-count guard skips the one phrasing it cannot check

**Status:** Done. **For the planning session:** resolved in `CLAUDE_DOCS/TASK_COMMS.md`.
**Found by the planning session 2026-09-21**, while checking task 11.291's carry of six → seven by
running the guard's own pattern by hand over the tracked tree.
**Model:** **Sonnet, small.**
**Depends on:** task 11.297, done. **Fresh window, short.**

#### The hole

`container_count_test.dart` matches the count phrase with an optional *"the other"* prefix and then
**filters those matches out** — the comment says so in as many words: *skip "the other N
containers"*. So `TriTrack-server-architecture.html`'s *"The other six containers"* is unchecked.

**It is correct today**, which is why nobody noticed: postgres is reached by the other six of
seven. **It is a hand-maintained number that the guard deliberately looks away from**, and the next
service added makes it wrong with nothing to say so — which is the entire defect 11.297 was built to
abolish, surviving inside 11.297.

#### Why it was skipped, and why that reasoning does not hold

The prefix was recognized so a relative count would not be mistaken for a total and fail. **That is
the right diagnosis and the wrong remedy.** A relative count is not uncheckable; it is checkable
against a different number. `the other N` must equal the derived count **minus one**, and a sentence
naming a different relation than "all but this one" should not be written as *the other N* at all.

#### The second instance, found 2026-09-21, which is the argument

**`CONTAINER_COUNT.md`'s own carve-out paragraph quoted that sentence's number and had gone stale
by one** — in the file that defines the rule, in a file the scan excludes by design. So the skipped
phrasing had already rotted a copy of itself inside the instrument, within two days of the
instrument being built, and only a by-hand read found it. The paragraph now describes the phrase
instead of reproducing it (entry 48's discipline), which fixes that copy and **does nothing for the
one in the HTML**, which is this task.

#### One question to answer rather than assume

**Is "the other N" always "all but the one this row is about"?** It is in the one occurrence that
exists. **Derive whether that holds for every occurrence rather than assuming the single instance
generalizes** — and if a second shape turns up, say so and decide rather than widening the rule to
fit it quietly.

- **Acceptance:** `the other N` is checked against the derivation minus one instead of being
  skipped; **watched red first** by moving that number; the comment saying it is skipped is replaced
  by one saying what it is checked against; the "always all but one" question is answered from the
  occurrences rather than from this entry; `CONTAINER_COUNT.md` says what the guard now covers, since
  its job is to be readable by somebody who has not read the test; `flutter test` green locally.

any server can refuse a device under the new clock: **August 2028.** Nothing is at risk before then
and the entry says so rather than letting urgency be inferred from the subject matter.

last clause promises.

**The planning session's position on the receipt-store observation, 2026-09-21, recorded rather
than decided.** Task 11.299 found that task 10.11's reason for never building the recovery flow —
*"the device cannot tell records made while away from stale copies of purged records"* — was
written on 2026-08-05, and that **task 10.33 gave every device a per-row receipt store eight days
later**. A row with no receipt was made while away and can resurrect nothing; a receipt older than
the row's version is an edit to something the server once held, which is the one dangerous class; a
matching receipt is not offered at all. **That is the "which is which" the decision said nobody
could answer.** It is untested, undesigned, and a receipt says *had* rather than *still has*, so it
is a lead and not a design. **I am not costing the flow on it today and I am saying so rather than
leaving the entry to imply it has been considered**: the honest judgement needs the receipt store
read properly, the trip-wire carries the date, and doing it now would be a guess wearing an
estimate's clothes. **The instruction, attached to the trip-wire's reader:** when
`scripts/tombstone_retention_status.sh` first says a sweep will refuse somebody, re-read 10.11's
premise against the receipt store **before** sizing the flow — the answer may be much smaller than
10.11 believed.
**Model:** **Opus** — the decision is what the app owes a person whose records it will not take.
**Depends on:** task 11.291, done. **Fresh window.**

#### The sentence, and the clause

A device refused for staleness is told: *"…Nothing on this device has been changed or lost — its
records need to be reconciled before it can sync again."*

**The first two sentences are true and were defended by 11.291.** The last clause names
*reconciling* as a step, and **there is no such step.** **Corrected 2026-09-21 by task 11.299,
which derived this instead of inheriting it: only export exists.** The two paragraphs below said
re-joining gives the device the server's copy — **it does not.** Joining a project the device
already holds *relinks the copy already there*, and the sync round that follows pushes first,
which is the request being refused; even with nothing to push, the pull runs from the cursor the
device still holds rather than from zero and is refused identically. **The refusal holds on every
route from a device that holds the project**, which is the right outcome and was found by looking
for the way around it and failing. I took "re-join to take the server's copy" from task 11.291's
report and repeated it twice without opening `ProjectJoiner`. The original wording follows so the
correction has something to correct.

What the entry said: what exists is export, and re-joining the
project to take the server's copy. What does not exist — task 10.11's deliberately unbuilt recovery
flow — is any way to get the bearings recorded while away onto the server **without also offering
the stale copies of purged records**, which is the resurrection the refusal exists to prevent.

**So the copy is not a lie about a mechanism; it is a promise of an act.** That is a smaller fault
than a false mechanism and a real one: a person in the field reading it will look for a button.

#### The two answers, and they are not equally sized

1. **Change the clause to what a person can do today** — export. **(Written as "export, and
   re-join to take the server's copy"; the re-join half was false and task 11.299 derived that

   a wrong fact should show that it did.)** The original wording: export, and re-join to take the server's

2. **Build 10.11's recovery flow.** Large, and the reason it was never built is that the honest
   version has to distinguish *records made while away* from *stale copies of records the server
   purged*, on a device whose whole problem is that it cannot tell which is which.

**Do 1 now and decide 2 on its own evidence.** Do not let the copy fix stand in for the flow, and
do not hold the copy fix hostage to it. **Say in the report which of the two the task did.**

### Task 11.292 — A project an owner deleted but never destroyed can be reached from nowhere

**Status:** **Done — 2026-09-22, on Michael's device look**, commit `4b5c100`. All four steps
confirmed on a real phone against a server rebuilt from `main`: the *Deleted from your devices,
still on the server* section listed his throwaway with the date; *Delete from server… → Delete
immediately…* showed the backups wording with no "permanent"; *Remove now* emptied the row and the
section with it. **The date rendering is a pass worth recording rather than waving through** — the
server stamped `2026-09-22T04:31Z` and the phone showed *21 September*, which is correct in
Arizona (UTC-7) and is a raw instant crossing the UTC boundary and landing right, in a project that
has had a raw-instant picker bug in a UTC-negative zone before (task 11.269).
**The look cost four database queries before it reached the feature at all**, because the server
had silently failed to rebuild — see task 11.307 and task 11.308.
**Found by task 11.290, 2026-09-20.**
**Model:** **Opus** — it is a §4.28 disclosure decision before it is a screen.
**Depends on:** task 11.290, done. **Fresh window.**

#### What was built and decided (2026-09-21)

- **The operator command first**, in `server/README.md` and below, run against a throwaway stack
  before any code (the proof is described under *The operator path* below).
- **The decision: a second route, not a sixth field — Security Model §4.28.1.** Both versions are
  stated there and the sixth field is refused for reasons about the section rather than the code:
  every existing reader of `/projects/mine` would have received rows it was never written to see,
  on a row-level condition the field table has no column for. **The general "show me deleted
  projects" listing is refused in writing**, with the reason: it is a question about the server's
  history, fails both of §4.28's footings, and is the shape §4.13's reopen trigger names.
- **`GET /projects/deleted/mine`** (`project_directory_service.dart` → `listDeletedFor`): the
  tombstones the caller sent, on projects the server records them as **owner** of. Three clauses,
  each with a test that goes red without it — the co-owner-who-did-not-delete case for the
  author clause, the owner-demoted-after-deleting case for the role clause (a contributor can never
  have sent a `Projects` tombstone, so that clause is load-bearing only for somebody the deletion
  routes would now refuse). Four fields, `no-store`, the same `LIMIT` and the same rate-limit
  bucket as `/projects/mine`. No identifier on the route at all.
- **Every row is actionable through routes that already existed.** `ProjectAuthorizer.resolve`
  never reads `Projects.deleted_at`, so `_requireOwner` admits an owner to a tombstoned project's
  `/deletion` routes — read off the resolver, then **measured**: schedule shows `destroy_at` on the
  listing; *delete now* empties it and retires the id.
- **§4.13 for a tombstoned id, measured for the first time.** Task 11.290 measured a *destroyed*
  id; a *tombstoned* one had never been. A stranger asking the deletion routes or pull about a
  tombstoned project gets `403 forbidden`, byte-for-byte the fictional answer (no named refusal).
- **The app**: the join screen gained a section, *Deleted from your devices, still on the server*,
  under the joinable rows — absent when empty and when the server is older than the route (a
  `404` is treated as "not offered", any other failure is said in the section without losing the
  join list). Each row says *"You deleted it on <date>. Its records are still held on the server."*,
  the countdown when scheduled, and ⋮ → *Delete from server…* / *Cancel scheduled deletion*
  through the same dialogs and the same `ProjectDeletionNotices` as the joinable rows. **No Join
  and no Restore** — see the second decision below.
- **Derivation kept honest**: `project_directory_field_set_test.dart` now reads both of §4.28's
  field tables and ties each to its route by the paragraph above it, so the two cannot be
  swapped; §4.28.1 is registered as derived; §4.21.2 and `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` M11 carry the
  route. All three planning documents were edited under the brief's own instruction ("both amend
  §4.28") and the derivation tests' refusal.

#### The refused departure: decided — that section, but not until an undo exists; not built here

Task 11.289's open half asked where a refused *departure* is shown, narrowed by 11.290 to *the
Projects list's "Deleted here, not yet on the server" section, or nowhere*. **Counted from the
mechanism before deciding.** A departure is one row — the person's own `Project_Memberships` row
with `end_date` set — and the server admits a self-departure past the role gate and the ownership
rule (`isSelfDeparture`, task 11.28). The **only** per-row refusal it can still draw is
`lastOwnerRemoval`: the app refuses to let the last owner leave, so this needs two devices to
disagree about who owns the project (a co-owner demoted or removed on the server after this
device last pulled). The other outcome — a whole-request `403 forbidden` because the owner had
already removed them — is not a refused departure at all: the person is off the project, which is
what they asked for (see Discovered Scope for what that case does cost). **Reports to date: zero;
reachable causes: one.**

**The decision: that section is the right place, and a row there without an UNDO would be a trap,
so it is not built until the undo exists.** The section works for deletions because UNDO
(`restoreById`) is the way forward; for a departure the way forward is *undo leaving* — put
`end_date` back on the person's own membership row — and **no such write exists anywhere in the
app** (`grep -rn "undoLeave\|rejoin" lib` on 2026-09-21 finds only prose). A sentence saying *"the
server has not accepted your leaving; you are still on the project for everybody else"* with no
control beside it is exactly the shape `CLAUDE.md` calls a refusal with no way forward. Meanwhile
the refusal is not silent while the person keeps their copy: a departed project stays linked and
openable from the Projects list until the server confirms the departure, and its Sync Status
screen lists the held membership row. **It becomes silent the moment they delete their copy**,
which is the trap 11.57 described. **Trip-wire:** the first report of a person who left a project
and is still listed as a member by its owner buys the undo-leave write and the row in that
section together, as one task; until then this stays a recorded decision, not a note.

#### The gap between two tasks that were built a day apart

Task 11.289 made a phone's project deletion reach the server, where it arrives as a **tombstone**:
the `Projects` row is marked deleted and every record in it stays. Task 11.290 built **destruction**,
which removes them. **The two do not meet.** `/projects/mine` excludes tombstoned projects and the
join screen lists what the server offers, so **a project in that state appears on no screen on any
device, including its owner's**, and the only way to destroy it is an operator `INSERT` into
`project_destruction` over `psql`.

#### The operator path, written down because it is the honest reach today

Scheduling a destruction for a project no screen can name is one row in `project_destruction` keyed
on the project id with a `destroy_at` in the past, followed by the sweep. **Michael did exactly this
for four projects on 2026-09-20 and it worked.** Put the command in this entry and in
`server/README.md` beside the other operator commands, **so the next person does not derive it under
pressure on a server they care about.**

**Written and proven by task 11.292, 2026-09-21, before any code.** The full text with its
reasoning is `server/README.md` → *"A project an owner deleted but never destroyed — the operator
path"*. Run against a throwaway stack (its own compose project, `-p tritrack-11292-proof`, so no
real database was touched): a seeded tombstoned project with one animal and one membership was
listed by step 1, scheduled by step 2, and step 3 printed *"Destroyed 1 project whose date had
passed (3 rows)"*; step 1 re-run returned no rows and `project_destruction.executed_at` named it.
The three steps, `docker compose` from the deployment directory:

```bash
# 1. See what is flagged deleted, and who deleted it.
docker compose exec postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" \
  -c "SELECT project_id, project_name, owner_user_id, last_modified_by, deleted_at \
        FROM \"Projects\" WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL ORDER BY deleted_at;"'

# 2. Schedule one, by id. now() means the next sweep; now() + interval '30 days' gives the grace.
docker compose exec -T postgres sh -c 'psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB" -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1' <<'SQL'
INSERT INTO project_destruction (project_id, scheduled_by, destroy_at)
VALUES ('<project_id from step 1>', 'operator', now())
ON CONFLICT (project_id) DO NOTHING;
SQL

# 3. Run the sweep now rather than waiting for its hourly wake.
docker compose run --rm project-destruction --once
```

#### Why this is a disclosure decision and not a screen

Listing tombstoned projects means either a sixth field on `/projects/mine` or a second route, and
both amend security model §4.28 — whose rule is that every field on that route is defended one at a
time, on one of two footings (the caller's own fact, or a fact about a project the caller already
holds). **The defensible version is narrow:** projects the server records *this caller* as owner of,
whose tombstone this caller's own device sent. **The version to refuse is a general "show me deleted
projects" listing**, which is a question about the server's history rather than about the caller's
own projects, and §4.13's reopen trigger names that shape directly. **This task is the most likely
thing in the plan to trip that trigger; read it before designing the route.**

#### The open half of an older entry belongs here

Task 11.289's Discovered Scope entry asked where a refusal about a project you cannot open should be
shown. **Task 11.290 answered it for deletions** — the Projects list's "Deleted here, not yet on the
server" section. **A refused *departure* has the identical shape and no surface**, and the answer is
now constrained rather than open: that same section, or nowhere. **Settle it here** instead of
leaving it for a third task to rediscover.

- **Acceptance:** the operator command is written into this entry and `server/README.md` **before
  any code is written**, and run against a throwaway project to prove it; the §4.28 decision is made
  **in writing**, with the narrow and the general versions both stated and the general one refused
  with its reason; whatever is built is **owner-only** and holds the existing shape — no route
  answers a destroyed or tombstoned id differently from a fictional one to a caller who does not
  already hold that id; the refused-departure surface is decided and either built or **recorded as
  declined with a reason**; **watched red first**; server and Flutter suites green locally, **no CI
  until 1 October**.

### Task 11.291 — Nothing runs the purge, so every retention floor on every server is zero

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-21, commit `72064a7`. The sweep runs as the `tombstone-retention`
compose service; the first-run policy is decided and written into the service's header (below,
and in `server/README.md`); command file deleted in the closing commit. Server suite green
locally (1141 tests, including 7 new); `flutter test` carries one pre-existing red the planning
session introduced in `CLAUDE.md` (see Discovered Scope). **No CI until 1 October.**
**Found by task 11.290, 2026-09-20**, while reusing `TombstoneRetentionService.purgeableTables` for
project destruction: `grep -rn "\.purge(" server/lib server/bin` finds the audit sweep and nothing
else. **Re-run by this task first, 2026-09-21: two hits, both `AuditRetentionService.purge()` in
`bin/audit_retention.dart`. Confirmed — nothing called the tombstone purge.**

#### What was built and decided (2026-09-21)

- **The first-run policy: a tombstone's age is the server's clock, never the device's.** `purge()`
  aged a row by `deleted_at`, the phone's stamp, stored as text and written by whatever clock the
  phone had. It now ages by `received_at`, the one `TIMESTAMPTZ` on a synced row that is the
  server's own reading of when it accepted the delete. **So the first sweep on any server purges
  only deletes that server has itself held for the whole window, and can refuse only a device that
  has not synced that project in the whole window** — which is the policy 10.11 wrote down and the
  old clock did not deliver. The brief's two options were "floor at now minus the window" and
  "floor at now"; this is the first option on the correct clock, and on Michael's seven-week-old
  server it behaves like the second: **the first sweep there purges nothing and refuses nobody**,
  and the first purge that can happen lands in **August 2028** at the earliest. Cost: a record
  deleted on a phone years before the server existed and uploaded at publish is kept 24 months
  from its upload, not its deletion — kilobytes. What the old clock would have cost on that same
  server: every such upload purgeable on the first sweep, and any phone with its clock set years
  back able to make a fresh deletion purgeable at once. Written into the service's library
  comment, `docker-compose.yml`, `server/README.md` and `.env.example`; **watched red first** —
  a tombstone held six years by the server with a month-old device stamp was kept, and a
  tombstone stamped 2020 by the device and received today was purged, both under the old rule.
- **The population the old design would have refused, counted from the mechanism rather than
  guessed.** The purge is held back by every device that synced the project inside the window,
  read from `sync_cursors` — and until this task the only writer of that table was `/sync/ack`,
  which the app sends only after a page that *moved*. So a project's publisher (a push, then pulls
  that return nothing) and any device on a quiet project had **no row at all**, were invisible to
  the holdback, and would have been refused on their next push the first time anything in their
  project was purged — with the sentence *"offline too long"* shown to a phone that had synced
  every week. **The pull route now records the cursor a device pulls from** (the same committed
  position an ack carries, through the same monotonic `acknowledge`, recorded after the guard and
  never on the removed-member disclosure page). Widened scope, declared: it is what makes the
  policy's own sentence — *a device that keeps syncing can never be stranded* — true. Watched red:
  the publisher had no row after a quiet pull.
- **The refusal, over the wire, by name, keeping its records.** A device below the floor pushing
  its live copy of a purged record plus a new bearing gets `409 cursor_too_old` with two integers
  and nothing else; neither row is written; its recorded position is byte-identical before and
  after; an incremental pull from its old position is refused the same way; a full re-pull from
  zero is answered. Watched red with the push guard removed: the push answered `200` and the
  deleted record came back.
- **The shape is the existing one, three times now.** `bin/tombstone_retention.dart` is
  `bin/project_destruction.dart` one table over: `--once`, `--schedule`, `--check`; runs as
  `tritrack_app` for the reason that file gives (it deletes from every synced table and cannot
  touch the audit log); one transaction per sweep so a project's tombstones and its floor go
  together; the loop stays up while failing. `--check` measures **how long the oldest purgeable
  tombstone has been past the window** and prints what the next sweep would purge and **how many
  devices it would refuse** — the number an operator reads before the first `docker compose up`.
  `scripts/tombstone_retention_status.sh` runs the same program, starts only Postgres, and is in
  the gate; `scripts/operator_status.sh` names it as a question it does not ask;
  `tombstone_retention_schedule_test.dart` pins the wiring the way the other two are pinned.
  **Consolidation with 11.290's sweep did not fall out for free and was not done**: three ~250-line
  loop files now share a shape by copy (Discovered Scope).
- **The container count moved from six to seven**, and 11.297's guard caught it on the first
  `flutter test`; the three Live documents, the diagram and the Record declaration were carried
  to seven in this task, and the diagram was rendered and looked at.

#### The refusal sentence, quoted, and defended in two-thirds

`StaleCursorException`'s own text — *"device cursor 12 is below project proj-a's purge floor
900"* — reaches no person: the route turns it into `409 cursor_too_old` and the app's
client-authored copy is what a person reads:

> *This device has been offline too long to sync this project safely. Records deleted while it was
> away can no longer be identified, so syncing now could bring them back. Nothing on this device
> has been changed or lost — its records need to be reconciled before it can sync again.*

**The first two sentences are now true by construction** — after this task the only device that
can be refused is one that has not pulled the project in 24 months (or never on this server), so
"offline too long" is the cause, not a guess. **The last clause names a step the app does not
offer.** "Reconciled" is honest about not knowing and promises no mechanism, which is why it is
defended rather than rewritten here; but a person reading it has nowhere to go. See Discovered
Scope for what the way back actually is today.
**Model:** **Opus** — the first-run policy is a judgement about other people's devices, and the
wrong one locks a field team out of its own sync.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### What is missing, stated precisely

`TombstoneRetentionService` exists. `purge()` exists. `StaleCursorException` exists and is tested.
**Nothing calls `purge()`.** The guard is real; the sweep it guards is not wired to anything. **Task
11.290's brief said "the purge already works" and the planning session wrote that sentence** — see
the defect vocabulary, entry 27. What works is the refusal a purge *would* make necessary.

So today, on every server: rows carrying `deleted_at` accumulate without bound, every purge floor is
zero, and **`StaleCursorException` has never fired in production, which means its first firing will
be a surprise to whoever meets it.**

#### The first run is the whole task

Wiring a sweep is an afternoon's work. **Running it the first time against a database holding two
years of history refuses every device whose cursor predates the new floor** — and on Michael's
server that population is not hypothetical: old phones, the Mac, anything that has been away. A
refused device is not broken, but the person holding it sees a sync that will not complete and has
no way to know why.

**Decide the policy before wiring the sweep, and write it into the plan entry and the service's own
doc comment:**

- Does the first floor start at **now minus the retention window**, or at **now** — with the window
  biting only for deletions made after the sweep is switched on? The second costs one retention
  period of unpurged rows and refuses nobody. **State the choice and its cost; do not let the
  default fall out of the implementation.**
- What does a refused device tell the person holding it? **Read `StaleCursorException`'s message as
  a person would** before concluding it is adequate, and quote it in the report.
- Is there a way back for a refused device that does not cost its local records?

#### The shape already exists, twice, and a third one would be the defect

`bin/audit_retention.dart` is one sweep and `bin/project_destruction.dart` is another — both compose
services with healthchecks that measure how far behind they have fallen, and both have a `scripts/`
status command. **Do not invent a third shape.** Task 11.290's entry argues the two sweeps could
share one; **that consolidation is not this task** unless it falls out for free, and if it does, say
so in the report rather than doing it quietly.

- **Acceptance:** the first-run policy is **decided and written down**, with the refusal a wrong
  choice would cause named in the same sentence; the sweep runs on a timer in a compose service of
  the existing shape, with a healthcheck reporting how overdue it is and a `scripts/` status command
  to match the other two; **watched red first** on a test that ages a deletion past the floor and
  asserts the row is gone; a second test asserts a device whose cursor predates the floor is refused
  **by name** and **keeps its local records**; the `StaleCursorException` message is quoted in the
  report and either defended or rewritten; server suite green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.
  **Michael runs nothing on his own server until the report says what the first sweep there would
  refuse.**

### Task 11.290 — An owner can destroy a project, on a schedule everybody can see

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-20, commits `1cc4497` and `852b696`; device look completed by Michael
the same day: schedule, countdown, cancel and *delete immediately* confirmed on the first look;
the let-it-run step found the row not updating on a phone that did not have the project open
(fixed in `852b696` — the list now asks the server about a project that left the listing) and
was confirmed on the second look with the grace period at zero and the sweep run by hand. Command
file deleted in the closing commit. **Above the line.** Unblocked by task 11.289, which landed 2026-09-20.
**Designed with Michael 2026-09-20**, most of it by him.

#### What was built (2026-09-20)

- **The server owns the clock.** `project_destruction_service.dart`: one server-only row per
  scheduled deletion (`scheduled_at`, `destroy_at`, `executed_at`), the date set from the server's
  clock plus `TRITRACK_PROJECT_DELETION_GRACE_DAYS` (blank → `TRITRACK_BACKUP_KEEP`, 30). Routes
  `GET`/`POST /projects/<id>/deletion`, owner-only through `_requireOwner`; the body carries an
  action (`schedule` / `immediate` / `cancel`) and nothing else. `bin/project_destruction.dart`
  is `bin/audit_retention.dart` one table over — a compiled `--schedule` loop in a new
  `project-destruction` compose service, and a `--check` healthcheck that measures how far past
  its date the most overdue deletion is. **Watched failing first**: the service test with the
  sweep stubbed out (the project outlived its date), and the resurrection guard with the check
  removed (the owner's re-push answered `200` and the project came back).
- **Every member sees it.** `GET /projects/mine` carries `destroy_at` (§4.28's fifth field, the
  security model amended). The app keeps what it last heard per project (`ProjectDeletionNotice`,
  in `SyncStateStore`), asks the server when the Projects list opens, on pull-to-refresh, and on
  foreground when it already holds a countdown. The row is tinted and says the days left and the
  date; the owner's menu offers *Delete from server…* / *Cancel scheduled deletion*, everybody
  else's shows them greyed with the reason; *Export records* is on the row for everybody.
- **"Delete now" is behind a second confirmation** whose words are *"removed from the server now,
  and out of the server's backups within N days"*, with N from the server
  (`backup_retention_days` on the standing) — never "permanently", and a test asserts the word is
  absent.
- **A destroyed id is retired.** `/sync/push`, `/sync/pull` and `/sync/ack` answer it `403
  project_destroyed` (§4.13's written exception, with the reasoning and a reopen trigger). A device
  offline across the deletion keeps every record, is told the cause on its next round in its own
  words, and is unlinked so nothing keeps offering rows to a refusal. Michael's decision; a test
  counts the bearings before and after.
- **Task 11.289's open question, folded in.** A project deleted here whose tombstone the server has
  not accepted — by a whole-request `403`, or by the per-row `unauthorized` that lands in the
  held-row store, which is the common case — appears in a *"Deleted here, not yet on the server"*
  section at the foot of the Projects list, says which of the two it is, and offers UNDO.
- **A project absent from this device is reached** from the join screen: an owner's row there has
  ⋮ → *Delete from server…*, using the same dialogs, without downloading the project first. That
  is where Michael's seven old-phone projects are.
- **From the device look (2026-09-20):** the dialog's buttons are *Schedule delete* and *Delete
  immediately…* — Michael found "Cancel / Delete now / Schedule" unclear. And a phone that did
  not have the destroyed project open never learned it was gone, because only that project's own
  sync round had ever asked the server about it; the Projects list now asks directly (one pull of
  one row) about any project it is counting down that has left the server's listing, and the
  server's named refusal settles it. Watched red first.
- **Found on the way:** `TombstoneRetentionService.purge()` is scheduled by nothing (Discovered
  Scope); `join_project_screen.dart`'s `_reload` was `setState(() => _available = _load())`, an
  arrow closure returning a `Future`, which asserts in a debug build and was silent in release
  (fixed here).
**Model:** **Opus** — it decides what a promise about deleted data may say.
**Depends on:** 11.289, Done. **Fresh window.**

#### The need is governance, not volume

A bearing is a few numbers; the terrain tiles that take space live on phones. **What a researcher
needs is to say “that project is gone” and have it be true** — a permit condition, a landowner
agreement, a collaborator who withdraws consent. *“It is flagged deleted and hidden”* does not
answer that.

#### The design, as Michael specified it

1. **The owner schedules a project for deletion.** A deliberate action, not a checkbox on the
   ordinary delete.
2. **The project stays in the list, highlighted, showing the days remaining.**
3. **The owner can cancel** from that row, any time before the clock runs out.
4. **“Delete immediately”** is offered when scheduling, behind an extra confirmation.
5. **When the clock runs out the project and its records are destroyed.**

#### Four corrections to that design, agreed 2026-09-20

- **The server owns the clock and executes the deletion on its own timer.** Not *“on next sync”*: an
  owner who schedules a deletion and leaves for a field season must not end up with a project that
  quietly never dies, and **a device with a wrong clock must not be able to shorten or extend
  somebody's grace period.** The shape already exists here — the audit-retention container deletes
  expired rows on a schedule, unattended.
- **Every member sees the countdown, not only the owner.** A contributor's bearings are about to be
  destroyed and they are that person's season. **They cannot cancel; they can export**, and the
  grace period is long enough to.
- **“Delete immediately” may not say “permanently.”** Backups keep 30 archives by default, so the
  project is recoverable from a dump for about a month whatever the live server does. **The honest
  sentence is “removed from the server now, and out of the backups within 30 days.”**
- **A device offline across the deletion keeps its records locally, with an explanation, so the
  person can export and archive them.** **Michael's decision.** Nothing is silently dropped.

#### The grace period, and the one number that makes it honest

**Default it to the backup retention window** (`TRITRACK_BACKUP_KEEP`, 30 archives). A shorter period
would promise a speed the backups do not deliver. **Configuration, so an institution with different
rules can set it.**

#### Out of scope, decided

**The audit log is not part of “gone.”** Michael, 2026-09-20. Sign-in events keep a year and
data-access 180 days, and both reference the project; they stay.

#### Two things to fold in rather than file separately

- **Task 11.289 asked for this.** If the server refuses an owner's deletion (ownership differs;
  build skew), it is held on a project no screen can open — **the person believes it is gone and it
  is live for the team.** That task's own recommendation: **a row in this task's list saying “the
  server has not accepted this deletion”** is the obvious home. Do that rather than a retry.
- **A project that is not on this device cannot be reached at all.** Found 2026-09-20 when Michael
  tried to delete two projects from his Mac and deleted a different one instead: **the Projects list
  shows what this device holds, not what the server holds.** A project created on a device he no
  longer has is invisible and undeletable from every device he does have. **Seven such rows sit on
  his server now.** Whatever this task builds should reach them — or say plainly that it does not,
  and what does.

#### Reuse rather than reinvent

- **`ProjectStanding`** (`MemberStanding` / `NotAMemberStanding` / `UnknownStanding`, built by task
  11.237) already models a project on a device the server will not answer for. **A scheduled or
  destroyed project is likely a case in that family**, not a new mechanism — and 11.237 left *“an
  imported project cannot be removed from the list”* open, which wants solving with this.
- **The purge exists** (`tombstone_retention_service.dart`), per project, with a floor, and a device
  behind a purge is **refused** rather than allowed to push records back (`StaleCursorException`).
  **The resurrection problem is already solved.**
- **Deleting sets `deleted_at` on the row itself** — record and mark are one row, so removing it
  removes the data. There is no separate marker object to reason about.

- **Acceptance:** an owner can schedule a destruction and cancel it; the countdown and its day count
  are visible **to every member**, with export reachable from there; the server executes on its own
  timer with no device involved, **watched failing first** with the clock advanced; “delete
  immediately” exists behind a second confirmation and **its wording does not claim more than the
  backups allow**; a device offline across the deletion keeps its records and says why; a refused
  deletion is visible in the list; **what this reaches and does not reach for a project absent from
  the current device, stated in writing**; **a device look in the acceptance, asked for by name** —
  this destroys data and no test stands in for it; `flutter test` and
  `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.289 — Deleting a project destroys the only scope that could have pushed the deletion

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-20, commit `bfc7631`; device look reported by Michael the same day.
Code, tests and documents landed first with `flutter test` and `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`
green locally (counts in the comms entry); the task was then held at the device look the acceptance
names, and Michael confirmed both halves on his phone: a published project deleted with signal
reached the server as a tombstone, and one deleted in airplane mode reached it once the network
came back. Task 11.290 is unblocked. **Above the line.**

#### What was built (2026-09-20)

- **The sibling of task 11.57's departure recovery, for the project's own row.**
  `lib/data/sync/pending_project_change.dart` derives every change to a `Projects` row — a
  tombstone, an undo of one, a rename from the list — on a **linked** project that the next push
  for that project would offer, and `SyncController.deliverPendingProjectChanges` runs one engine
  round for each such project until the server confirms it. Called from `app.dart` on cold launch
  and every foreground (the durable path — a phone that deleted a project out of signal gets it back
  there), from `syncNow` (Michael's exact steps were the manual button), and as an immediate attempt
  after Delete and after UNDO on the Projects list. **The ordinary round's per-project scope is
  unchanged.** What the flush costs is written in the file's header: a `Projects` scan and one
  indexed probe per linked project per foreground, no network unless something is stranded.
- **Derived, not copied.** The derivation does not decide which `Projects` rows a device may offer;
  it asks the new `SyncEngine.wouldOffer`, which is the push's own `_pendingClause` with the held-row
  suppression and the snapshot gate applied to one row. A departed member's (11.54) or snapshot
  holder's (11.238) local delete therefore comes back "not offered" for the reason `offer_rules.dart`
  states, and the derivation names neither case.
- **Watched red first.** `test/core/providers/deleted_project_tombstone_test.dart`: delete the open
  project, tap "Sync now" (with no project open, and with a different project open) — the tombstone
  did not reach the fake server until `syncNow` was wired. The offline case is asserted in full:
  delete with the transport dead, the flush fails and leaves the row pending and the project linked,
  the transport comes back, the next flush delivers it, and the launch after that offers nothing.
  `projects_screen_test.dart` gained the screen-level half: the real Delete control offers the
  tombstone at once when there is signal.
- **The server side, which Michael's measurement never reached because the push never happened.**
  `publish_and_join_test.dart` now pushes an owner's `Projects` tombstone weeks after the fact:
  `deleted_at` is stored, the outcome is `updated`, and `/projects/mine` no longer lists it. A
  contributor's tombstone for the owner's project is refused `unauthorized`.
- **A stale sentence corrected in `mutation_authorization.dart`.** Both exemptions defended themselves
  with *"a device never offers a `Projects` row to the server at all"* — true when written, false
  since task 11.57 let an owner's own row through (which is how a rename, or this tombstone, reaches
  the server). The exemptions were never unsafe; the reason is narrower and is now the one written.
  Task 11.238's entry below carries the same sentence and is left as history.
- **Michael's nine stranded rows are repairable from the app, automatically**, for every project he
  deleted *on this phone*: the rows are still there (soft-deleted, his `last_modified_by`, his
  `owner_user_id`, still linked — only leaving a project unlinks it, not signing out), and no receipt
  matches their post-deletion `updated_at`, so the first launch of this build with signal delivers
  each one. What it cannot repair is a project deleted on a device he no longer has, or one the
  server refuses; those are an operator `UPDATE` on the VM, and the comms entry says how to tell.

**Found by Michael 2026-09-20**, with a controlled test he proposed himself after his server showed
nine live projects and zero deleted ones.
**Model:** **Opus** — it is a sync-scope decision, not a bug fix, and the obvious repair is wrong.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### Measured, not inferred

Michael published a project named `ZZ-DELETE-TEST`, confirmed it arrived on the server, deleted it
on the phone, selected a different project, synced, and queried again. **`deleted_at` was still
empty.** His phone said *“no project selected”* at the moment of deletion.

**The mechanism, read in `lib/core/providers/sync_provider.dart`:** a sync round begins

```dart
final projectId = await ref.read(activeProjectIdProvider.future);
if (projectId == null) return;
```

— **sync is scoped to the active project and does nothing at all when there is none.** And
`projects_screen.dart`'s `_deleteProject` sets the active project to null when the project it just
deleted was the active one.

**So the project row is the only row in this app whose deletion destroys the scope that would have
pushed it.** Deleting a collar, an animal or a bearing is safe: the project stays selected and the
tombstone rides out on the next round. Deleting the project strands its own tombstone, permanently,
and **selecting another project does not help** — that round pushes that project's rows.

#### What this costs a person, stated plainly

- **A project you delete stays on the server, live.** Any new device you sign in on pulls it back.
- **On a shared project it is worse than clutter.** An owner who deletes a project believes it is
  gone for the team. **It is not.** Every teammate keeps it, and the owner has no way to know.
- **Michael's own server has nine live projects and zero tombstones**, which is what a month of this
  looks like.

#### The obvious fix is wrong, and that is why this is Opus

**“Push the tombstone at delete time, before clearing the active project”** fails the case this app is
built for: **a person deleting a project in the field, with no signal.** The push cannot happen, and
the tombstone is stranded exactly as before — **with the added harm that it now looks handled.**

**So the constraint, not the design:** a project's deletion is pending work that must survive until
the server has acknowledged it, the same as any other unsent row, and it must survive a device that
is offline for a week. **How sync's scope changes to carry it is the task's to decide and to argue.**

- **Do not widen sync to “all projects” without saying what that costs.** The per-project scope is
  load-bearing elsewhere and was chosen; check why before changing it.
- **Read task 11.237's neighbour first.** An imported project cannot be removed from the list at all,
  which is the same family of problem approached from the other side.
- **Say what happens to the nine rows already stranded on Michael's server** — whether they are
  repairable from the app, or whether that is a one-time operator cleanup. **Either answer is fine;
  silence is not.**

- **Acceptance:** a project deleted on a device reaches the server as a tombstone, **including when
  the device is offline at the moment of deletion and syncs days later**, watched failing first; what
  the per-project scope change costs, stated in writing; the already-stranded rows addressed one way
  or the other; **a device look in the acceptance, asked for by name** — this is a deletion crossing
  to a server and no test can stand in for it; `flutter test` and
  `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.288 — The Tag Library's delete counts copies in projects that no longer exist

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-20. **The delete is built and works; the wrong number is fixed.** Code and
tests for the delete landed 2026-09-19 (commit `3aec9a8`). **Michael's device look on 2026-09-20 confirmed all
four controls** and found a fifth thing the acceptance never thought to ask about: the confirmation
told him a project still held a copy of a tag that had never been in a project. **Above the line —
it is a false statement shown to a person in the moment they are deciding to delete something.**
The reproduction confirmed the predicted cause, and both counts are now corrected at the query —
see the resolution below.
**Michael, 2026-09-19**, while building a 50-tag library: *“In the tag library, there doesn't appear
to be a way to delete a tag. I should be able to select a single tag or select multiple, or select
all and trash them.”* **That request is satisfied.** The title of this task changed on 2026-09-21 to
name what is left; the original is the sentence above.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### Confirmed on the device 2026-09-20 — four things that are done and need no repeat

Long-press enters a selection mode; *Select all* selects and deselects again; delete runs; **undo
restores.** Michael ran all four. The confirmation's copy-stays sentence exists, and the
`entryCount` color consequence is documented at the call site. **Only the count is open.**

#### What he saw, and why his own fix is the wrong one

He deleted a library entry created for the test and never added to any project. The dialog said:

> *“You can undo this from the confirmation that follows. This collar is still in use by a project
> on this device — deleting it from your library does not touch that copy.”*

**His reading was that the sentence should be hedged** — *“If this collar is still in use…”* — and
it is worth writing down why that is the wrong fix, because it is the tempting one. **The app is not
guessing.** `_confirmDelete` in `tag_database_screen.dart` composes that sentence only when the
count comes back above zero and leaves it out entirely at zero. **So the sentence is not an
overstatement of something uncertain; it is a faithful report of a wrong number.** Hedging would
leave the number wrong, make the app sound unsure about something it can know exactly, and move the
defect to a place no test is looking.

#### The number, and the likeliest reason it is wrong

`libraryCopyCount` counts rows in `Tags` carrying this lineage where **the tag's** `deleted_at` is
null. **It never asks whether the project those rows belong to still exists.** Deleting a project on
the device soft-deletes the `Projects` row and leaves its tags untouched — `projects_screen.dart`
calls `softDeleteById` on the project alone, with no cascade. So the tags of every project Michael
has deleted this month are still answering this count.

**That is a prediction and the task's first job is to settle it, not to assume it.** It fits what he
did and it fits the code, but **nobody has run the query against a device showing the symptom.**
Reproduce first: create a library entry, add it to a project, delete the project, then open the
delete confirmation for that entry. **If the sentence appears, this is the cause. If it does not,
the cause is something else and the rest of this entry is wrong** — say so and stop rather than
fixing what the entry told you to fix.

#### The same gap is already on a screen that has nothing to do with deleting

`otherProjectCopyCount` has the identical shape — same table, same missing question about the
project — and it is what `tag_form.dart` uses to tell somebody *“N of your projects use this
collar”* while they are editing one. **So the wrong number is already being shown outside this
dialog**, and a fix applied to the confirmation alone would leave it standing. **Fix the query, not
the caller.** Three call sites read these two counts; none of them should change.

#### What a deleted project's copies should count as, and it is a decision rather than an oversight

**The obvious answer — do not count a copy whose project is soft-deleted — is probably right and is
not automatic.** A project soft-deleted on this device may still be live on the server and live for
teammates; this device's `deleted_at` says only that *this person* deleted it *here*. What saves the
obvious answer is what the count is **for**: it feeds a disclosure about what editing or deleting a
collar on this device would reach, and an edit here reaches nothing in a project this device has
deleted. **So exclude it — and write the sentence that says why**, because the next person will meet
a case where “deleted here” and “gone” come apart and will need to know which one this query meant.
**§2.5 is unchanged and unaffected: stating a count is safe, naming the projects is not.**

- **Acceptance:** the reproduction above is run **first** and reported whichever way it comes out;
  **watched red first** on a test that creates a library entry, copies it into a project, deletes the
  project and asserts the count drops — failing before the fix; **both** `libraryCopyCount` and
  `otherProjectCopyCount` corrected **in the query rather than at any call site**, with the three
  call sites left alone; the reason a soft-deleted project's copies do not count **written at the
  query** in the terms above; **the confirmation's wording is not hedged and does not change**;
  `flutter test` green locally, **no CI until 1 October**. **No new device look is required** — the
  four controls are confirmed and this is a number a test can judge. Report the count before and
  after on a database built to carry the fault.

#### Resolved 2026-09-20

**The prediction held.** Reproduced in `test/data/tag_repository_test.dart`: a library entry copied
into a project, that project soft-deleted on the device, then `libraryCopyCount` and
`otherProjectCopyCount` both asked against the same fixture. **Both came back `1` before the fix and
`0` after** — the deleted project's copy stopped counting, in both queries, on the first run of the
new tests. Watched red first (both new tests failed against the unfixed query with `Expected: <0>,
Actual: <1>`), then fixed by joining `Tags` to `Projects` and requiring `Projects.deleted_at IS NULL`
in both queries — the fix is entirely in `TagLibraryRepository`, no call site changed. The reasoning
(a soft-deleted project here is not the same as a project that no longer exists elsewhere; this count
answers what an edit *on this device* would reach) is written at `otherProjectCopyCount`'s doc
comment, with `libraryCopyCount` pointing to it rather than repeating it. `flutter test` green
locally (3596 passed, 16 skipped, exit 0). Commit `3f66ba0`.

### Task 11.287 — In production the server sends no email, so nobody can sign in

**Status:** **Partial — built, tested and delivering against two local relays, 2026-09-20; the one
remaining step is a link reaching a real inbox through the relay NAU names.** Commit hash in the
`TASK_COMMS.md` entry. What was built: a relay-agnostic SMTP client in `server/lib/src/auth/smtp_email_sender.dart`
(STARTTLS required or implicit TLS, AUTH PLAIN/LOGIN, no provider named anywhere), configured by
seven `TRITRACK_SMTP_*` variables; **a production server now refuses to start with no relay
configured** — the silent `NullEmailSender` is no longer reachable under `TRITRACK_ENV=production`;
a startup probe that connects, negotiates TLS and authenticates, then reports on a `Sign-in email:`
log line; a fifth mode of the server binary, `--send-test-email <address>`, for the real-inbox check
on the NAU host where the image has no Dart SDK; `scripts/verify_smtp_delivery.sh`, which pushes that
command through Mailpit with STARTTLS required and authentication on, wrong password first. **Header
injection, the named risk: refused twice, at the HTTP boundary as before and again in the sender
before any socket opens** — the plan's own payload `a@b.com\r\nBcc: attacker@example.org` is a
test that asserts an empty relay transcript. A delivery failure lands in the container log with the
relay's reply (recipient redacted, token never) and the caller's `202` is byte-identical — **watched
failing first**: with the failure line silenced, ten tests go red; on a live server with the relay
stopped, the request answered `202` and the log said `NOT DELIVERED … Connection refused`. The
architecture SVG, its HTML and the deployment HTML no longer claim the server makes no outbound
request; the diagram now shows the relay. **Reported `Partial` deliberately** — a local catcher is
not an inbox, and the whole defect was delivery being absent while everything looked fine.
Previously: Not started. **Above the line, and it blocks the NAU deployment Michael is arranging.** **It is not blocked on NAU** — see “What NAU has to answer” below; the code is relay-agnostic and can be built and tested against a local relay now. It closes `Partial` until a link reaches a real inbox.
**Found 2026-09-19** while drafting the deployment sheet for NAU ITS.
**Model:** **Opus** — it touches auth, secrets and an outbound network path the security model has
opinions about.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

**`resolveEmailSender` returns `NullEmailSender` whenever `TRITRACK_ENV=production`**, and
`NullEmailSender.sendMagicLink` is an empty method with a comment saying so. The file sender is
refused under production on purpose — *“a development convenience that still works in production is
how prototypes ship with a hole in them”* — and **nothing was ever built to replace it.**

**So a production deployment today: accepts `POST /auth/magic-link`, answers `202`, writes the
token, and delivers nothing.** Sign-in is the first thing anybody does and it is the first thing
that fails. **The 202 is correct** — §4.5 requires an identical response whether or not delivery
worked, so the endpoint cannot tell anyone. **This is the account-enumeration defence working
exactly as designed and hiding a total outage behind it.**

**Nobody has filed this.** The plan mentions SMTP four times, always as a future condition on
somebody else's sentence — *“SMTP header injection the moment 10.14 adds a real sender”*, *“reopen
only if somebody builds SMTP”* — and **task 10.14 is `Done` without having built it.** This project
has a name for that shape: **a trigger nobody is looking for is not a trigger.** Four conditional
sentences across one document, and no entry owning the work.

#### What this task is

- **A real `EmailSender`**, chosen and configured from the environment the way the other two are.
  **The interface already exists and is already the right shape** — `sendMagicLink` takes the
  address, the URL and the expiry, and the contract already says *“implementations must not include
  any caller-supplied content in the message beyond the address itself — otherwise this becomes a
  message-delivery channel for whoever can hit the endpoint.”* **Honor that; it is the whole
  security surface of this feature.**
- **Header injection is the named risk and it is already written down.** Plan line 3334 records that
  `a@b.com\r\nBcc: attacker@example.org` has reached `EmailSender` and was harmless only because
  neither existing sender sends anything. **It stops being harmless in this task.** Whatever library
  is used must be checked for header-injection handling, and the check written down rather than
  assumed.
- **A delivery failure must reach the operator and must not reach the caller.** `FileEmailSender`
  already solved this shape: the HTTP response stays an identical 202 and the diagnosis goes to the
  container's stderr, **because on 2026-08-30 a root-owned directory meant no link was ever written
  and eleven gate instruments could only report the symptom.** Copy that, and watch it fail first.
- **Credentials are secrets and the architecture diagram currently says the server makes no
  outbound request at all.** **Both of those change**: `CLAUDE_DOCS/TriTrack-server-architecture.html`
  says *“the server sends no email and makes no outbound request at all”* and
  *“Outbound TCP 443 — the proxy renewing its certificate. Nothing else.”* **That will be false the
  day this lands**, and it is the sentence NAU's infosec review was given. **Correcting it is part
  of this task, not a follow-up.**

#### What NAU has to answer, and what it does not block — corrected 2026-09-19

**The planning session first wrote that this task could not be built until NAU answered. That was
wrong, and Michael caught it by asking what the sentence meant.**

**A generic SMTP sender does not care which relay it is pointed at.** Host, port, username,
password, TLS — the same client works against NAU's relay, a commercial sending service, or a local
test server. **So the code is not blocked and this task can run now.**

**What genuinely needs NAU is verification and shipping.** Without real credentials and a real
sending address, nobody can confirm a link lands in an inbox, and **that end-to-end check is the
entire point of the feature** — every part of this path answers an identical `202` whether or not
delivery worked, so a build that compiles and a build that delivers look the same from outside.

- **Run the task against a local test relay** (a throwaway SMTP catcher on the host) and get the
  behavior right: header injection, the operator-visible failure, the identical 202.
- **Leave the relay's host, credentials and sending address as configuration**, the way every other
  secret in this deployment already is. **Do not hard-code a provider.**
- **The task closes `Partial` until a link has reached a real inbox** through a real relay. **That
  is the part waiting on NAU**, and it is one configuration change plus one test, not a rewrite.

**The question for ITS, unchanged:** which relay, which sending address, and will NAU relay mail for
a research service? A `@nau.edu` sending address needs somebody at NAU to agree to it; the
alternative is a commercial sender, which works identically and means sign-in mail arrives from
something other than NAU. **That is a choice worth making deliberately rather than by default.**

- **Acceptance:** the sender is relay-agnostic and configured, with no provider hard-coded, and
  **delivers a link end to end against a local test relay**; header injection
  checked and the finding written down; a delivery failure reaches the operator's stderr and leaves
  the HTTP response an identical 202, **watched failing first**; the production path no longer
  resolves to `NullEmailSender`; **`TriTrack-server-architecture.html`'s two outbound-traffic claims
  corrected in the same commit**, and `SERVER_DEPLOYMENT_PRIMER.md` too if it repeats them;
  `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` and `flutter test` green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.
  **The task reports `Partial` and names the one remaining step** — a link reaching a real inbox
  through NAU's chosen relay — rather than claiming `Done` on a local catcher.

**The guide is a website. TriTrack is an offline-first field app.** A link solves “I am at my desk
and want to read about deployments.” **It does nothing for a crew in a canyon with no bars**, which is
exactly where somebody needs to know what *contested* means or why a record was refused.

of need — Sync Status carries the sentence, a held row carries its own remedy, the interlock names

a link is enough, and it should be weighed rather than assumed.

### Task 11.285 — The app has no disclaimer of any kind, and NAU has sent one

**Status:** **Blocked on Michael — do not write a command file or run this until the wording is
settled.** The text NAU sent is not yet the text that should ship, for the reason below.
**Michael brought it 2026-09-18**, from NAU's Associate Vice President for Research and Innovation,
who said *“please feel free to adapt as needed.”*
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium**, when it runs.

**Measured 2026-09-18: `lib/` and `website/content/` contain no disclaimer, no warranty language and
no limitation of liability anywhere.** Not a relocation — a gap.

#### Why the text as received is not the text to ship, and this is for Michael to put to NAU

**Every operative term in it is from a two-party patent license agreement**: *THE PARTIES*, *THIS
AGREEMENT*, *LICENSOR*, *LICENSEE*, *LICENSED PRODUCTS*, *PATENT RIGHTS*, *whether any patent will
issue*. The liability cap is *“the amounts paid by Licensee to Licensor under this Agreement during
the one year period preceding…”*

**A biologist who installs TriTrack has signed no agreement and paid nothing.** That cap evaluates to
zero for them — plausibly the intent, but stated as a reference to a document they have never seen.
And a warranty disclaimer about *whether a patent issues* and *whether the licensed technology
infringes* is a real concern between NAU and a commercial licensee and **says nothing about whether
the app works.**

**The open question, and it is Michael's to ask:** is this meant for end users, or for an agreement
with somebody licensing the technology? **They are different documents and this project may need
both.** The planning session is not a lawyer and this entry is not legal advice.

#### What this app's disclaimer has to say, which the received text does not

**The risk a field app carries is not patent validity.** It is that a **position estimate is an
estimate**, computed from bearings a person typed and from third-party elevation and map data, and
that somebody may make a navigation or safety decision from a map in the backcountry.

**A starting point for NAU counsel to rewrite — not final text, not drafted by a lawyer:**

> **TriTrack is research software, provided as-is.** Northern Arizona University makes no warranty
> of any kind, express or implied, including merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose.
>
> **Position estimates are estimates.** Bearings, computed positions and terrain visibility are
> calculated from data you enter and from third-party elevation and map data. They can be wrong.
> **Do not rely on TriTrack for navigation, for personal safety, or as the sole basis for any
> decision that matters.**
>
> **You are responsible for your own data.** Keep your own backups.
>
> To the fullest extent permitted by law, NAU is not liable for any damages arising from use of this
> software.

NAU's two paragraphs then sit underneath, **verbatim**, as the formal text.

#### Where it goes — this part is settled and is the planning session's call

**A disclosure behind a tap nobody takes is a check that fails into a place with no reader.** A
collapsed dropdown alone is exactly that shape. **The app already solves this**: the sync indicator
carries a color and a shape always, with the sentence one tap away.

- **App Info (`More → App Info`), always visible:** the short plain-English paragraphs. No dropdown.
- **One tap away:** the full formal text, **selectable**, exactly as counsel words it. That is where
  the dropdown belongs. `app_info_screen.dart` has no expanding section today — this is its first.
- **The website carries the same text**, as a sibling of `privacy.md`, so somebody can read it
  **before installing** and a beta crew's institution can find it. Content-lane task, after this one.
- **Not a first-run modal.** Small known beta crews, and a wall of capitals everybody dismisses is
  worse disclosure than a page they can find.

**One open question rather than a recommendation:** exported CSVs and backup files leave the app and
get emailed around. **Whether a line belongs in an export header is a real question and a cheap one**
— but it is NAU's call, not a design call, and it is not assumed here.

- **Acceptance (when unblocked):** the settled wording is in `app_info_screen.dart`, the summary
  always visible and the formal text one tap away and selectable; **a device look is in the
  acceptance** — this is a legal disclosure and nobody has seen it render; the website sibling page
  is a separate content task; `check_app_quotes` handled the approved way if the website quotes any
  of it; `flutter test` green locally.
