### Task 11.282 — Terrain tiles are fetched one at a time, and nobody has decided whether that is wrong

**Status:** Not started. **Below the line — do not run it now.** Nothing is broken.
**Filed 2026-09-18** so a question raised twice, in two comms entries, has one home and a trigger
instead of living in prose.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**

**The fact.** Every request in the map's terrain path is a plain sequential `await` — both the loop
over DEM tiles in `_ensureTerrainForRegion` and the loop over terrarium tiles inside
`DemTileFetcher.fetchTile`. Nothing runs two requests at once. After task 11.281 a cold-cache fill is
**143 requests, projected at 18–19 s** on the connection `/w-20` measured (125–133 ms mean). A handful
in flight would cut that to a few seconds.

**Why it is below the line and not above it.** Eighteen seconds of *“Downloading terrain… i/143”*,
with a progress count on screen, in country the phone has never seen before, **is tolerable**. It was
fifty before 11.281. Nobody has complained about either.

**And the three costs are real, which is why this was never folded into 11.281:**

- **Politeness to a public bucket.** `elevation-tiles-prod` is somebody else's free service and a
  field season is many devices.
- **Error handling multiplies.** One failure in a sequential loop is a retry; six failures at once,
  partway through a region, is a design question nobody has answered.
- **A phone radio may cost more battery kept busy in parallel than it saves in seconds**, which is
  the opposite of what a field app wants. **This is an assumption, not a measurement** — and it is
  the assumption that would have to be measured before the change could be called a win.

**The trigger, stated once so it can be watched:** **a field report that the map takes too long on
first use in new country**, or the readiness ceiling's headroom actually eroding (a larger seeded
viewshed, a slower network). Until one of those, the sequential loop is the cheaper answer and this
entry stays below the line.

**If it is ever run, it needs a measurement first, not a patch:** battery drawn over a cold-cache
fill, sequential versus a small concurrency limit, on a real phone on cellular. **A change that
trades battery for seconds in a field app has to know which way the trade went.**

### Task 11.281 — The map downloads 380 terrain tiles when 143 would do, on every cold cache

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-18. **Above the line.** **Measured by task `/w-20`, 2026-09-18.**

**What shipped.** `DemTileFetcher.fetchTile` takes an optional `TerrainTileCache` (a thin wrapper
around a `z/x/y`-keyed lookup, exported from `dem_tile_fetcher.dart`); when given, it is checked
before each terrarium-tile fetch and filled in as new ones arrive, instead of starting from an empty
map on every call. `_ensureTerrainForRegion` (`map_screen.dart`) now creates one `TerrainTileCache`
before its loop over the region's DEM tiles and passes it to every `fetchTile` call in that loop —
**scoped to one region fill**, discarded when the loop ends, per the brief's instruction not to build
a second persistent cache: `DemTileStore` already persists DEM tiles across region fills, and the
redundancy measured by `/w-20` was entirely inside one fill, at the terrarium layer beneath it.
**Discovered scope, applied rather than deferred:** `DownloadManager._runDem` (the Offline Data
Map's DEM download job) has the identical loop-over-DEM-tiles shape and was paying the identical
redundancy on every download job covering more than one DEM tile; since the fix is the same
`TerrainTileCache` with no new abstraction, it was given the same one-line treatment rather than
filed separately.

**Regression test**, `test/viewshed/dem_tile_fetcher_test.dart`, group "region fill (task 11.281)":
reproduces `_ensureTerrainForRegion`'s own bounds computation for the harness's seeded fixture
(`seedLat` 42.7008, `seedLon` -117.3612, 35 km range) without importing `map_screen.dart`, confirms
it yields the same **72 DEM tiles** `/w-20` measured, then asserts **143** terrarium-tile requests
with a shared `TerrainTileCache` and, in a sibling test, **380** without one — both numbers matched
exactly on the first run, so the "watch it red first" step is the second test rather than a
separate revert-and-rerun: it is the fix's own before-state, asserted permanently rather than
checked once and deleted.

**Wall-clock:** not re-measured against the real bucket. The distinct-request count (143 vs. 380)
is what the fix changes and what the test asserts; `/w-20`'s own per-request timing (125–133 ms
mean) was against the real AWS bucket, which this task's regression test deliberately does not
call (a `MockClient`, so CI and a laptop with no network both run it). Applying `/w-20`'s measured
mean to 143 requests instead of 380 implies roughly **18–19 s** instead of ~50–53 s on the same
connection — an arithmetic projection from `/w-20`'s numbers, not a new measurement, and flagged as
such. **If a precise new wall-clock figure is wanted for the F1 cross-reference, that needs a task
that hits the real bucket the way `/w-20` did**, which this task's brief explicitly separated from
the de-dup fix.

**180 s readiness ceiling:** untouched, as instructed. **No screenshot baseline regenerated.**

`flutter test`: full suite green (3524 passed / 16 skipped / 0 failed), including the new group.
Ran locally; **no CI until 1 October**, per the standing hold.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

**The measurement, taken against the real bucket rather than reasoned about.** Filling the map's
terrain for the seeded 35 km viewshed needs **72 DEM tiles**, and the code as written issues
**380 terrarium-tile HTTP requests** to fetch them — of which only **143 are distinct**. Adjacent
0.1° DEM tiles overlap in which z12 terrarium tiles cover them, and `DemTileFetcher.fetchTile`
**builds a brand-new empty lookup map on every call**, so nothing is shared across the 72 sequential
calls `_ensureTerrainForRegion` makes. `grep -rn "TerrainTile" lib/` finds only the fetcher and the
type — nothing else caches one by its coordinates.

**237 of 380 requests — 62.4% — are the same run downloading a file it already has.**

Two runs on an ordinary connection: **50.0 s and 52.9 s** of wall-clock for the 380 sequential
requests (mean 125–133 ms, median ~110 ms, p90 ~180 ms — a normal HTTPS round-trip, not a throttled
one). PNG decoding all 380 cost 2.3 s, noise by comparison. That is **44–47% of the 113.2 s / 113.5 s**
the screenshot harness measures for this screen.

**This is not harness debt.** The harness fetches from the same public bucket over the same code path
a phone does. **Every cold-cache map load in the field pays this**, and a field device pays it in
battery and cellular data as well as seconds.

- **The fix is a cache shared across one region fill**, keyed on the terrarium tile's own `z/x/y`,
  living where the 72 `fetchTile` calls can all see it instead of being reset by each one.
- **Do not build a second persistent cache without saying why `DemTileStore` is not enough.**
  DEM tiles already persist through `DemTileStore.saveTile`; the redundancy measured here is at the
  *terrarium* layer, inside one region fill. **Request-scoped is the minimal fix and probably the
  whole of it** — if you conclude otherwise, say so in writing before writing the code.
- **Watch it red first, and the instrument is obvious for once:** a test that counts terrarium-tile
  fetches for a known region and asserts **143, not 380**. That number is a fact about the geometry,
  so it is a regression test that will still mean something in a year.

**Explicitly not in scope, and the reason is a real trade-off rather than a scope fence.**
Both loops in this path are plain sequential `await`s — nothing runs two requests at once. 143
sequential requests at ~125 ms is still ~18 s that a handful in flight would cut to a few. **But
parallel requests are a judgement call, not a free win**: politeness to a public bucket, error
handling when several fail at once, and a phone radio that may cost *more* battery kept busy in
parallel than it saves in seconds. **The de-dup has no trade-off to weigh; parallelism has three.**
Recorded here as a question, not as work — and a task that fixes the de-dup and reports the new
wall-clock is exactly what would tell somebody whether the parallelism question is worth opening.

**One cross-reference, because a measurement taken next month could be misread.** Release checklist
**F1** asks Michael to measure what automatic sync costs in battery and cellular data on a real day
in the field. **Map terrain is not sync**, and 237 redundant tile downloads on a cold cache would sit
in the same day's data figure. **Fix this before F1 is measured**, or F1 measures two things and
attributes both to sync.

- **Acceptance:** a region fill issues 143 terrarium-tile requests where it issued 380, asserted by a
  test that counts them, **watched red first**; the cache's scope stated in writing, with why
  `DemTileStore` does not already cover it; the new cold-cache wall-clock reported so the parallelism
  question can be answered later from a number rather than an impression; **the 180 s readiness
  ceiling not touched** (task `/w-20` recommended against it and nothing here changes that);
  `flutter test` green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.280 — The Sync Status screen takes longer than twenty seconds to say “you're not on this project”

**Status:** Done — 2026-09-18, commit `a1d1ecb`. Not the timing question the brief posed: neither
"real slow-down" nor "always-slow path." A third thing, found by instrumenting the actual round
rather than guessing between the two offered. See below.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.**

#### What it actually was (2026-09-18)

**Neither fork in the brief was right, and the twenty-second ceiling was never the problem.** The
round that follows a membership closing never threw at all — with nothing new to push, `_push`
returns before calling the transport, so the 403-and-disclosure path in `sync_engine.dart` never
ran. The ordinary pull still carried the closed-membership disclosure, merged it into the local
`Project_Memberships` row, and the round reported success. But the very next screen build reads
`currentProjectProvider`, which calls `ProjectMembershipRepository.ensureOwnerMembership` — the
task 8.4/11.1 repair that backfills a missing owner row on a pre-8.4 database. That method's
"no open row" check could not tell *never had one* from *had one and it was just closed*, so it
silently inserted a **brand-new, open, local-only owner membership row** for the just-removed
creator — undoing the disclosure the pull had just delivered, on every screen navigation. The
readiness condition waited twenty seconds for a state the app had already made unreachable.

Confirmed by instrumenting the real code path (not a synthetic reproduction first — that one,
written before the harness was traced, did not reproduce, because it lacked the `currentProject`
read the real navigation always does): `git log`-clean, printed the classification at each step
against the actual `flutter drive` run, watched `_weHaveLeft` find a membership row with a random
new `membershipId` and today's `createdAt` where the closed `seed-membership-owner` row should
have been.

**Fix:** `ensureOwnerMembership` now checks whether the creator holds *any* row for the project —
open or closed — before inserting. Only a creator with no row at all (the true pre-8.4 backfill
case) gets one created. A closed row means they left or were removed, and the repair leaves it
alone.

**This is a real, person-facing defect beyond the screenshot harness**, not just a harness fixture
bug: any project *owner* who is removed (or who leaves) will have their own device silently restore
their membership the next time any screen reads the project — `currentProjectProvider`,
`projectByIdProvider` and `allProjectsProvider` all call this repair. `SyncFailureCause
.membershipEnded` was permanently unreachable for an owner, on every device, since whichever of
task 8.4/11.1 (the repair) and 11.54/11.60 (the disclosure) landed second — both predate this
session and neither date was re-derived, since the fix does not depend on when the conflict first
became live to be correct now.

**New regression test:** `test/core/providers/app_context_provider_test.dart`, *"does not resurrect
a creator whose own membership row was closed (task 11.280)"* — watched red against the unfixed
code (asserted the resurrection happens), green after the fix.

**Not touched:** contributors and viewers removed from a project are unaffected — this repair is
keyed to `Projects.owner_user_id` specifically, not to membership generally, so only a removed
*owner* of a project they personally created hits this path.

**`sync-removed` baseline:** confirmed on all three profiles (`iphone-6.1`, `iphone-6.9`,
`ipad-13`) — the round now classifies as `membershipEnded` immediately (readiness: "ready after
0.0s (ceiling 20s)"), and the captured image differs from what is already committed by under the
review threshold on two profiles (0.11%, 0.0014%) and not at all on the third — nothing needs
`--accept`.

**`flutter test`:** full suite green except one pre-existing, unrelated failure —
`command_file_staleness_test.dart` flags `.claude/commands/w-20-where-the-113-seconds-goes.md`
(filename names a task, description names none), committed by the planning session in `a991adc`,
before this task started. Not touched here; belongs to whoever owns that command file.

**The measurement, and it is not a flake.** The screenshot harness drives a membership ending and
waits for `SyncHealth.membershipEnded` to become visible on the Sync Status screen. It **threw on
every one of three profiles, in two separate runs**, one of them taken before `/w-13` made any edit:
*“still not ready after 20.0s”*. **Three profiles × two runs is a reproduction, not an
intermittency**, and `/w-13` was right to report it rather than raise the ceiling.

**What is already ruled out, so nobody re-derives it:**

- **Not a wording drift.** The string `"You're not on this project"` is still exactly what
  `sync_status_screen.dart` prints — `/w-13` checked the source, not its memory of it.
- **Not caused by `/w-13`.** It reproduced against a clean tree before any edit.
- **Not the harness's general readiness work.** Every other state on all three profiles settled.

**The question, and it forks two ways — answer which before fixing anything:**

1. **A real slow-down since 2026-09-09**, the last date this state photographed cleanly. A lot
   landed in between (11.243, 11.245, 11.248, 11.250, 11.251, 11.56). **If so it is a person-facing
   defect, not a test one**: the screen that tells somebody they have been removed from a project is
   taking more than twenty seconds to say so, and a person who has just lost access is exactly the
   person who will not wait.
2. **An always-slow path that no picture ever exercised until now.** Then the twenty seconds is the
   honest number and the harness's ceiling is what was wrong — **but say what the real time is**,
   measured, rather than raising a ceiling until it passes. This lane already has the rule: *a number
   raised until the pictures look right will be wrong again the next time the fixture grows.*

- **One picture is deliberately uncommitted and stays that way until this task closes.** `/w-13`
  reverted `sync-removed` on all three profiles rather than accept what the harness actually wrote —
  **which was a picture of `sync-records-held`'s screen, the round before**, under the name
  `sync-removed`. **Committing it would have published a mislabelled baseline**, which is the exact
  defect class that lane exists to catch. The three committed files are therefore older than the run.

- **Acceptance:** which of the two above it is, answered in writing with a measurement either way;
  if a slow-down, the cause named and fixed, **watched red first**; if inherent, the true time
  stated and the harness's ceiling set from it with the reasoning written beside the number; the
  `sync-removed` baseline photographs the state its name claims, on all three profiles;
  `flutter test` green locally, **no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.279 — The nullable instant column: six documents point at it and no task owns it

**Status:** Not started. **Below the line — do not run it now.** Nothing is broken and nothing is
waiting on it. **Filed 2026-09-18 by the planning session** so the fix that five separate decisions
have deferred *to* has one home, one number, and one trigger, instead of six prose mentions in three
documents.

**Why it exists as an entry rather than as work.** `deployment_interlock.dart`, design §4 and §4a,
and tasks 11.251, 11.263, 11.264 and 11.266 all reach the same place: `attached_date` and
`removed_date` are single instants with no offset, so *which day a person meant* is only recoverable
in the zone that wrote it. Every one of those decisions was correctly taken **not** to bundle the
column into itself. **But a fix nobody has filed is a fix nobody can find, and this project's own
rule is that a trigger nobody is looking for is not a trigger.** This entry is the looking.

**What it would be:** a nullable instant column beside each date (or a stored zone), so a date-only
value and a timed value are told apart by what the row says rather than by what the reader's clock
says. It touches the wire, the server schema and the shared interlock — **a schema major**, not a
line.

**The two costs it closes**, both currently accepted in writing and neither of them a defect today:

- **§4's display cost** — the same row renders the neighbouring date on a device in another zone.
- **The sentinel's reader-dependence** — a bare day is only *at* midnight in the zone that wrote it,
  which is why task 11.266 had to make the server stop reading the sentinel at all, and why doing so
  gave up catching a same-day bare-day pair pushed by a legacy device sharing the server's zone.

**The trigger, stated once so it can be watched:** **a project whose crew spans time zones.** Until
one exists, §9's wipe-and-rebuild remains the cheaper answer and this entry stays below the line.
**When one does exist, this is the task**, and the four producers enumerated in
`DeploymentInterlock`'s class comment are its acceptance list.

**Do not fold this into a task that merely touches deployment dates.** Five tasks have now declined
to, each for a good reason, and each of those reasons is still true.

### Task 11.276 — Three fixture files write a same-day bare-day handover the interlock has forbidden since 11.263

**Status:** Done, 2026-09-17, commit `4f35f06`.

**1. The production question, answered: `deploymentDateFor` is exact in production. This is a
fixture-only defect, not a field-data defect.** Every production writer of a deployment date routes
through `deploymentDateFor(...)` — checked by reading every call site in `lib/`
(`deployments_provider.dart`, `animal_detail_screen.dart`, `observation_logging_screen.dart`,
`deployment_linking.dart`, `deployment.dart`) and confirming each either calls it directly or passes
along a value that already came from it. The one exception, `deployment_linking.dart`'s
`LinkPlan.at(instant)`, is the deliberate same-day-swap case (task 11.251, design §4a) — it writes a
real confirmed instant on purpose, not a bare day, and is unaffected by this question.
`grep -rn "DateTime\.utc(" lib/ server/lib/ packages/*/lib/` (excluding generated files) finds five
literals, none of them a deployment date: `tag_version_repository.dart`'s `_comparisonStamp`,
`wmm.dart`'s two WMM year boundaries, and two `plausibleFloor` clock-skew constants (server and
`untrusted_import.dart`). The server itself never constructs a deployment date at all — `sync_service.dart`
only reads and relays the column a device already wrote; `postgres_schema.dart` only declares its
type. **Nil finding, stated as plainly as a positive one: no production path builds a deployment date
any way but `deploymentDateFor`, so the fixtures were writing a shape no device — and no server —
produces.**

**2. What the ten tests were actually exercising.** All ten built their fixtures with a raw
`DateTime.utc(y, m, d)` literal shared between one deployment's `removedDate` and the next's
`attachedDate`, believing (three of the comments say so explicitly) that this was the ordinary
"sequential, not overlapping" shape a real season has. **It never was, on any device.** A real device
never writes `DateTime.utc(y, m, d)` for a bare day — it writes `deploymentDateFor(DateTime.now())`,
which is local midnight. So every one of these ten tests has, since it was written, actually been
exercising **whichever of the interlock's two readings the test runner's own zone happened to give a
`DateTime.utc(...)` literal** — a bare day under `TZ=UTC` (where the literal genuinely sits at local
midnight) and a timed instant everywhere else (Arizona included), never the sequential-bare-days
shape the comments describe and none of the ten actually needed. Nine of the ten
(`individual_merge_test.dart`'s seven, `tag_repository_test.dart`'s one, and
`individuals_test.dart`'s "recolouring the animal" test) are not about date-boundary logic at all —
merge behaviour, palette accounting, colour propagation — and the touching literal was incidental
scaffolding. The tenth, `individuals_test.dart`'s "reassigning a collar to a second animal the same
day" test, is different: it is *deliberately* about a same-day tie on `MAX(attached_date)`, and that
tie has to survive intact — the fix for it could not simply move the day apart the way the other
nine could (see item 3).

**3. The fixtures, not the rule.** Nine of the ten pairs had their shared boundary rebuilt as two
distinct bare days one calendar day apart, each built through `deploymentDateFor` rather than a
second hand-written literal — `deploymentDateFor(DateTime.utc(2025, 6, 1))` reads as a genuine local
midnight in whatever zone the test runs, so the two ends can never collide regardless of `TZ`, closing
the class rather than one instance of it. The tenth pair could not move — the whole point is a tied
`attached_date` — so it was given a real time of day (`DateTime.utc(2026, 9, 14, 12, 0)` instead of
bare midnight), matching how a real same-day recapture is recorded since task 11.251 (a confirmed
instant, not a bare date) and keeping the tie on the literal value the `MAX()` comparison is about.

**4. Watched red first.** Stashed the three fixture edits, ran all three files under `TZ=UTC`,
confirmed the `OverlappingDeployment: This animal would be wearing two tags at once… (deployment
d-2025 overlaps on the animal)` throw (and the matching `d1` case in `tag_repository_test.dart`),
restored the fix. All three files pass under both `TZ=UTC` and `TZ=America/Phoenix` afterward.

**`flutter test` green under both zones — no CI until 1 October, so these are the only runs this
task has**: `TZ=America/Phoenix` (2:34 wall-clock) and `TZ=UTC` (2:13 wall-clock), both full suites,
both `+3499`/`+3496` passed with the pre-existing 16/19 skip counts task 11.275 already recorded (the
3-test difference is a pre-existing skip pattern, not something this task touched). No sweep of the
rest of the suite for further timezone-sensitivity, per this task's own scope fence — that is
11.278's job if wanted.

> **Task 11.278 is closed, not deferred — planning session, 2026-09-17.** `offline-suite.yml` runs
> the full Flutter suite on `ubuntu-latest`, which is UTC, so **CI would have caught both 11.276 and
> 11.277 on the push that introduced them**; it was switched off, not blind. From 1 October the UTC
> leg returns by itself and finds whatever is left, every push, for no extra minutes — a hand-run
> sweep this month would spend a window to learn something CI relearns continuously afterwards.
> **The one thing CI still will not see is a daylight-saving zone**, which neither Arizona nor UTC
> is, and that is now the third 1 October edit in `TASK_COMMS.md`'s "waiting on Michael" section
> rather than a task.

**For the planning session:** nothing new to add to the plan; task 11.278 (a further timezone sweep)
remains exactly as optional/undecided as task 11.275 left it.

**For Michael:** nothing to run. Test-fixture-only change; no app behaviour changed.

**Model:** Sonnet, medium. **Depends on:** nothing. Ran after 11.277 in the same window, as
directed.

**Original entry follows, superseded by the Status above.**

`main`'s `flutter test` is red under `TZ=UTC` right
now, and green only because every machine that has ever run it sits in America/Phoenix.
**Found by task 11.275, 2026-09-17.**

`test/data/individual_merge_test.dart` (7 tests), `test/data/tag_repository_test.dart` (1 test)
and `test/data/individuals_test.dart` (2 tests) each build two deployments on one animal whose
bare-day dates touch — e.g. one removed `DateTime.utc(2025, 6, 1)`, the next attached the same
instant. `deployment_interlock.dart`'s own class comment says plainly that a removal and an
attachment on the same bare day **overlap** and are refused, since task 11.263 withdrew the
one-day allowance. Run under `TZ=UTC` — the zone in which `DateTime.utc(...)` genuinely reads as
local midnight — the interlock refuses exactly what its own rule says it should, and ten tests
that assumed the link would succeed fail with `OverlappingDeployment`.

**Why nobody has seen this red before:** `deploymentDateFor` (in
`packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/deployment_interlock.dart`) computes "local midnight" with the
bare `DateTime(year, month, day)` constructor, which is only the same instant as a fixture's
`DateTime.utc(...)` value when the reading process's own zone is UTC. On every zone this project
has actually run the suite in (America/Phoenix, and — found by the same sweep — Australia/
Brisbane), that mismatch misclassifies the fixtures' bare days as timed instants, and the
resulting arithmetic happens not to overlap.

> **That paragraph originally ended “two independent bugs are cancelling to a false green”. The
> planning session amended it on 2026-09-17 and moved the amendment to the front, because the
> original wording named `deploymentDateFor` as the second bug and it may not be one.**
>
> **Item 1 below is this task's first move, and nothing under `test/` may be touched until it is
> answered in writing.** Editing the ten fixtures destroys the only evidence that the question was
> ever askable: a test made green before it is understood cannot be asked again. That is this
> project's own defect vocabulary — *a check that fails correctly into a place with no reader* —
> arriving one step earlier than usual, at the moment somebody decides what a failure meant.

- **1. Before any fixture is edited: is `deploymentDateFor` wrong in production, or only wrong
  about these fixtures?** Answer it in writing, either way, with what you read to answer it.

  **The planning session's reading, offered as a hypothesis to confirm or overturn — not as a
  conclusion to implement:** every production write of a deployment date goes through
  `deploymentDateFor(DateTime.now())`, which yields local midnight, and a grep of `lib/`,
  `server/lib/` and `packages/*/lib/` on 2026-09-17 found **no production code anywhere that
  builds a deployment date as `DateTime.utc(y, m, d)`** — the only such literals outside `test/`
  are `_comparisonStamp`, two WMM year boundaries and two `plausibleFloor` constants, none of them
  a deployment date. If that holds, `deploymentDateFor` is exact for every value a device writes,
  the fixtures are writing a shape no device produces, and the only cross-zone weakness is the one
  the class comment already documents at length and the plan already carries in Discovered Scope —
  in which case this is a fixture task and nothing more.

  **If it does not hold — if you find any production path that writes or compares a deployment
  date built some other way — stop, edit no fixture, and report it.** That would be a defect in
  field data, and it outranks this entire task.

- **2. Then say what the ten tests have actually been testing.** Under Arizona a fixture's
  `DateTime.utc(y, m, d)` is not local midnight, so `deploymentEndHasTime` reads it as a **time**.
  These ten tests have therefore been exercising **the server's reading of a deployment date, not
  a device's**, for as long as they have existed, while reading on the page as though they proved
  device behaviour. Name which of the two each one is meant to prove, and make the fixture say it
  out loud.

- **3. Fix the fixtures, not the rule.** The interlock is doing what task 11.263 and Michael's own
  words ask of it; a same-day bare-day handover is genuinely invalid data under the current
  design. Give each pair either a time on the boundary (as a real handover would record, per
  design §4a) or move the boundary off the shared day. **Build a bare day the way the app builds
  one — through `deploymentDateFor` — rather than with a second hand-written literal**, so this
  fixture family cannot drift from production's definition of a day a second time.

- **4. Watch each fix red first**, per this project's standing discipline — stash it, confirm the
  `OverlappingDeployment` throw, restore it.

**Acceptance:** **item 1 answered in writing, with its evidence, before any file under `test/` is

of the ten tests was actually exercising named; all three files' interlock-adjacent tests pass

### Task 11.277 — `test/data/fixtures.dart`'s `_localNow` is a different instant everywhere but Arizona

**Status:** Done, 2026-09-17, commit `18a16ed`. `_localNow` is now built as `_now.toLocal()` rather
than a second hand-written literal, so the two can never name different instants under any process
`TZ`. Watched red first under `TZ=UTC` against the unfixed constant — `map_screen_test.dart`'s
per-tag colouring test failed with the exact measured colours this entry already recorded
(expected `Color(0.9020, 0.6235, 0.0000)`, got `Color(0.6196, 0.6196, 0.6196)`) — then green after
the fix, under `TZ=UTC` and `TZ=Australia/Brisbane` both.

**The other six call sites, audited rather than assumed clear:**

- `startedAtLocal` (`TriangulationSession`, via `sampleSession`) — grep of `lib/` finds no
  production code that reads `startedAtLocal` in a moment comparison at all (only storage
  round-trip and one plain-text display). Not a reader of this class, not just unexercised.
- `Observation.timestampLocal` (default in `sampleObservation`) — **is** read in a moment
  comparison: `log_screen.dart`'s `_LogEntry.time` getter uses it, and that value feeds
  `admits()`, `_animalAttributionFor` and `_animalSortKey`, all of which call
  `DeploymentRepository.animalForObservationIn(..., at: e.time)` against deployments built from
  `_now`. **This is the same defect shape as the Map's, one screen over** — but every existing
  Log-screen test that seeds a deployment also passes an explicit `timestampUtc` to
  `sampleObservation`, so `timestampLocal` is derived from that override (`timestampUtc?.toLocal()
  ?? _localNow`), never from the bare `_localNow` default. **Not currently exercised, but it would
  have broken the moment a test used the defaults together** — the fix removes that landmine
  regardless of whether anything was standing on it yet.
- `sampleMinimalObservation`'s `timestampLocal` — used only by round-trip, foreign-key, sharing,
  CSV and backup-archive tests, none of which seed a deployment or ask an attribution question.
  Not exercised, and not near anything that would exercise it.
- `NonDetection.timestampLocal` (default in `sampleNonDetection`) — same reader as Observation's:
  `log_screen.dart`'s "no signal" legend swatch passes `nd.timestampLocal` into `_animalAttributionFor`, and `_LogEntry.time`
  reads it too. `log_screen_test.dart`'s only non-detection test seeds no deployment at all, so the
  comparison never runs. Not currently exercised.
- `sampleEstimatedPosition`'s `timestampLocal` — **the one already found broken**, via
  `map_screen.dart`'s `_visible`/`_tagColor`/`_attributionOf`, all called with `e.timestampLocal`
  against `data.deployments`.
- `ActualTagLocation.timestampLocal` (default in `sampleActualLocation`) — same reader family:
  `log_screen.dart`'s truth-point rows call `_animalAttributionFor(id, truth.timestampLocal, ...)`,

  truth-point tests seed no deployment. Not currently exercised.

**So: two of six other call sites (`Observation.timestampLocal`, `NonDetection.timestampLocal`, and
by the same reasoning `ActualTagLocation.timestampLocal` — three, not two) feed the same
`animalForObservationIn` comparison the Map's bug lived in, all through `log_screen.dart`, and none
of them happens to be exercised by an existing test with the fixture defaults left in place.** That
is a fact about today's test suite, not about the code path's safety — the fix at the source
(`_localNow = _now.toLocal()`) closes all three at once rather than leaving them as three more
landmines for the next test that omits `timestampUtc`.

**For the planning session:** worth a line in the Log screen's own documentation, or a comment on
`_LogEntry.time`, noting that its `timestampLocal` reads feed a cross-zone-sensitive comparison —
nothing enforces it today, and this task did not add a check, only a fixture fix. Consider whether

Also a real red under `TZ=UTC` and
`TZ=Australia/Brisbane`, found by the same sweep as 11.276 but a different, simpler cause.
**Found by task 11.275, 2026-09-17.**
**Model:** **Sonnet, low.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Run this one first, in the same window as task 11.276, and commit it
separately.** They touch different lines of the same file family and neither's fix depends on the
other's, but they need the same expensive three-zone verification runs, and a window holding two
unrelated reds cannot tell which fix cleared which. **Two windows both running `flutter test` on
one machine is the exact condition task 11.253 could not reproduce and would not rule out** — so
these two share a window rather than racing.

`test/data/fixtures.dart` line 23 declares `final _now = DateTime.utc(2026, 7, 16, 18, 30, 0);`
and line 24 `final _localNow = DateTime(2026, 7, 16, 11, 30, 0);` — the second built with the
**local**, not `.utc`, constructor. The two are meant to name the same real moment, 11:30 in
Arizona (UTC-7) being 18:30 UTC, and they do — **only when the test process's own zone happens to
be Arizona's.** Evaluated under `TZ=UTC`, `_localNow` becomes 11:30 UTC: seven hours before `_now`.
Under `TZ=Australia/Brisbane`, seventeen hours before.

**What this broke, found first:** `map_screen_test.dart`'s per-tag-coloring test builds an
`EstimatedPosition` timestamped `_localNow` and a `Deployment` attached at `_now`; `_localNow`
landing before `_now` makes `Deployment.coversMoment` correctly say the estimate falls before its
own deployment starts, so `MapScreen._tagColor` falls back to the neutral "no individual" grey
instead of the animal's colour. Measured: expected `Color(0.9020, 0.6235, 0.0000)`
(`TagColorPalette.colorForIndex(0)`, tag Alpha's own colour), got `Color(0.6196, 0.6196, 0.6196)`
(`TagColorPalette.noIndividual`).

**`_localNow` is used at six more call sites** (`startedAtLocal`, three more `timestampLocal`
defaults, per `grep -n "_localNow" test/data/fixtures.dart`) — this task's job is to say which of
those are exercised anywhere that compares a `_localNow`-derived value against a `_now`-derived
one the way the map test does, not to assume the one failure found is the only one.

- **Fix:** build `_localNow` from `_now` directly — `_now.toLocal()` — so the two can never drift
  apart regardless of which zone reads them, rather than picking a second zone-dependent literal.
- **Re-run task 11.275's three-zone sweep (or just `TZ=UTC` and `TZ=Australia/Brisbane` against
  this one file's dependents) after the fix**, watched red first against the unfixed constant.

**Acceptance:** `_localNow` cannot read as a different instant depending on process `TZ`; every
call site that compares it against a `_now`-derived value checked, not just the one that failed;
watched red first under `TZ=UTC`; `flutter test` green under Phoenix, UTC and Brisbane.

### Task 11.253 — The suite gave two different answers in two consecutive runs, and it is the only evidence anything has

**Status:** Done, 2026-09-15. **The full suite ran 10/10 clean — 3321 tests passed, 322 of 322 test
files reached, 15 skipped by tag, every run, byte-for-byte the same counts. Nothing recurred.**
`scripts/repeat_suite.sh` is now in the repo (pointed at from `README.md`) so the next person who
sees this can ask again without inventing the loop. Per this entry's own acceptance, ten clean runs
close the task.

> **Closed, but nothing was explained, and this entry should not read as though something was.**
> **Added by the planning session 2026-09-15.** Two failures happened. Ten quiet runs make them
> rarer than one in ten; they do not make them absent. **And those ten runs deliberately removed
> the one variable that separates the two conditions — on my advice.** 11.246's failures happened
> in a window that was also *committing*, which runs `scripts/pre_commit_suite.sh`, i.e. **a second
> full `flutter test`**, against a working tree the other window was editing. **11.253 ran on a
> clean, quiet tree**, because I told Michael to keep the machine quiet so the measurement would
> mean something. That is the right way to measure a suite and the wrong way to reproduce *this*.
>
> **A hypothesis, offered as one, and explicitly not a finding, because nothing has reproduced it.**
> Both observed failures have the shape that machine load and a busy `.git` produce, and neither has
> the shape a code defect produces:
> - **`no_committed_secrets_test.dart` failed in `setUpAll`**, which shells out to git and walks
>   every blob reachable from any ref. **A concurrent write to `.git` is exactly what breaks an
>   enumeration of it**, and this project has hit `.git/index.lock` contention between its two
>   windows repeatedly.
> - **`tag_edit_intent_dialog_test.dart` touches no file, no git and no real clock** — it is six
>   `pumpAndSettle()` calls, and `pumpAndSettle` fails on a **timeout**. That is what an overloaded
>   machine causes and what nothing in that widget could cause on its own.
>
> **One cause would explain both, and would explain why ten quiet runs passed.** **How to falsify
> it:** `scripts/repeat_suite.sh` while something else hammers the machine and writes to `.git` — a
> second suite, or a commit loop. **Nobody has run that, so this stops here.** It is a trigger, not
> a task: **if either test goes red again, find out what else was running before looking at the
> test.** **Above the line, and ahead of every feature task.** **With no CI until
1 October, a local `flutter test` is the entire evidential basis for every task shipped this month.**
A suite that cannot produce the same answer twice does not weaken one report; it weakens all of them.
**Reported by task 11.246, 2026-09-15**, honestly and in passing: one full run failed in
`test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart`'s setup; **an immediate re-run failed somewhere else
entirely**, `test/widgets/tag_edit_intent_dialog_test.dart`. Both passed standalone. Neither is in
anything 11.246 touched.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** The work is a protocol, not a puzzle — but it must be run, not
reasoned about.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Fresh window.** **Run it before the next feature task.**

#### The rule this is filed under says the opposite of what was done with it

`CLAUDE.md`: *"One observation is not a flake, and calling it one is a decision you have not
earned… A test that fails only in a full suite is a claim about the suite, not about the test… the
cost of shrugging is specific here: the pre-commit suite gates every commit, and a red nobody
trusts is how three tasks in a row came to use the escape hatch in September."*

**11.246 cited that rule as permission to file this and move on. The rule exists to forbid exactly
that**, and the task was otherwise careful, which is what makes it worth naming: **a rule that can
be read as its own opposite will be.** The entry is not a criticism of 11.246 — the finding is in
this plan because that task wrote it down rather than quietly re-running until green.

**And this is more evidence than the precedent had, not less.** Task 11.204 saw *one* test fail
once. **Here two different tests failed in two consecutive runs.** That is not one observation.

#### 1. Reproduce before theorising, with a stated number

**Task 11.205 is the precedent and the method: it ran the full suite ten times and reported that
11.204's flake did not recur.** Do that.

- **Run the full suite at least ten times.** Record, for each run, pass/fail and **which test
  failed** — not just a count.
- **Say the number you ran and the number that failed**, in the report. A protocol without its
  denominator is an anecdote.
- **If nothing recurs in ten runs, that is the finding and it closes this task** — recorded the way
  11.205 recorded it, not as "probably fine".
- **No hypothesis before a reproduction.** `CLAUDE.md`'s rule, and this project has paid for it.

#### 2. If it does recur, the question is about the suite

**A test that passes alone and fails in company is a claim about shared state**, not about that
test. The candidates this project has already met, offered as places to look and not as an answer:
a provider or binding left alive between test files, a temporary directory or file reused across
groups, a real-clock wait, an ordering dependency. **`no_committed_secrets_test.dart` failing in
its *setup* is a strong hint** — a setup failure is usually about the filesystem or the working
directory, which is shared state by definition.

- **Name the mechanism and show it**, the way 11.251 showed its wire measurement: make the failure
  happen on demand, then make it stop.
- **If the two failures have different causes, they are two findings.** Do not fold them because
  they arrived together.

#### 3. Whatever the outcome, leave the next person a way to ask

**There is no CI until 1 October and then there will be.** A repeat-the-suite-N-times invocation
that a person can run without inventing it — a script, or one line in `README.md` beside the other
test commands — is worth more than this task's own answer. **Say what you added.**

- **Acceptance:** the full suite run at least ten times, with the number and every failure named; a
  recurrence either reproduced on demand and fixed, or stated as not recurring in N runs with N
  given; **no hypothesis offered in place of a reproduction**; a documented way to repeat the
  measurement.

### Task 11.254 — Merging two animals is irreversible, owner-only on the phone, and unguarded on the server

**Status:** **Done 2026-09-15.** The acceptance's second branch — *"a written statement of why that is
impossible, with the alternative costed"* — is the one that applied, and it is in
`PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` §4.7 (IN4) and §8 entry 13. **The server has no twin because the product has
no rung**: every write a merge makes, and its exact end state, is reachable by a contributor through
`AnimalDetailScreen`'s own controls — withdraw a collar (DP3), attach it to the other animal (DP1),
put its attached date back (DP2), delete the emptied animal (IN3, which task 11.244 made
contributor-level nine days after 11.241 said no such control existed). The owner rung is on one
button. The three ways it could become a rung are product decisions and are Michael's; §8 entry 13
costs each, and the number is **zero contributors on any server today**. The cross-author loop is
derived from `tableMutationRules` (seven anyUser tables), with `Tags`/`Tag_Versions` read out of
`_authorizeTagLifecycle`'s source as the expected refusals — watched red twice. T3 settled: §2's
preamble was the stale text (written by the 11.23 sweep, falsified by 11.24 the same week, never
re-read) and it is replaced with the true state; §7's row was right. Server suite green locally in
Docker; `flutter test` green via the pre-commit hook. **No CI until 1 October — those local runs
are the only evidence this task has.**
**Above the line for Gate C, below 11.253 for running order.** Nobody else's
data is on the server yet, which is the only reason this is not urgent — **and Gate C's condition is
precisely "before anyone else's data is on it".**
**Found by task 11.246, 2026-09-15**, while writing `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` §4.7 — **not asked for
by its brief**, which is the sweep working.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Not because it is large, but because **the obvious fix does not work**
and the task's first job is to notice that.
**Depends on:** nothing.

#### What is true, read from the code on 2026-09-15

`IndividualMerge.merge` re-points every deployment of the absorbed animal to the kept one and then
soft-deletes the absorbed animal. It calls `assertMayEdit` **before the first write**, which is the
right shape — a merge a contributor cannot finish must not start. **That check is on the device.**

**On the server, `Tables.individuals` and `Tables.deployments` are both `MutationRule.anyUser`.**
So a contributor who edits their own database file, or crafts the equivalent push, can fold one
animal's entire history into another's — irreversibly — at the contributor rung.

#### 1. The trap: this is not a table rule, and raising the rule would break a deliberate decision

**Do not start by changing `tableMutationRules`.** Task 11.243 decided that linking a collar to an
animal is **contributor-level**, with reasoning Michael accepted — *"which collar went on which bird
is what the person holding the bird knows"* — and contributors legitimately create animals and
deployments. **Making either table owner-only would refuse the ordinary field workflow to fix an
attack.**

**The difficulty is real and it is the point of the task: a merge is an *operation*, and every
individual row it writes is legal.** Re-pointing a deployment is legal. Soft-deleting an animal is
legal. **The combination is the irreversible act, and the server sees rows.**

**There is a precedent in this codebase and it is where to start:** `RowAuthorizer`'s
`_authorizeTagLifecycle` / `changeTagRequiresOwner` is an operation-level check sitting on top of a
table rule, for exactly this kind of problem. **Read it before designing anything.**

**One shape worth weighing, offered and not decided:** the destructive half is the tombstone, not
the re-pointing. Deployments re-pointed without a deletion are recoverable by hand; an absorbed
animal is not. **If deleting an `Individuals` row can be held to a different rung than editing one,
most of this closes without touching the field workflow** — say whether `MutationRule` can express
that today, and what it would cost if it cannot.

#### 2. The cross-author loop, folded in rather than made its own task

11.246: the "shared tables" cross-author test in `server/test/authz/permissions_matrix_test.dart`
covers `Triangulation_Sessions`, `Estimated_Positions` and `Actual_Tag_Locations` **but not
`Individuals` or `Deployments`**, which carry the identical rule and arrived five weeks later.

- **Widen the loop**, and **derive its table list from the rules rather than writing four more
  fixtures by hand** if that is possible — a hand-maintained list is already wrong, and this one
  just proved it by being five weeks stale.

#### 3. A thing the document appears to say twice, differently — settle it, do not assume

`PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md`'s §4 preamble names **T3, removing a tag from a project**, as a live
instance of *"a device-layer check with no server twin"*. **§7's own T3 row says the opposite** —
owner-only on the server since task 11.24, naming `RowAuthorizer._authorizeTagLifecycle`, with all
three tick columns filled.

**One of those is wrong and this task should find out which, by reading the code rather than either
sentence.** **Delete the losing text.** `CLAUDE.md`'s rule about two defensible texts that disagree
applies inside one document as much as between two. **If it turns out they are describing different
halves of T3**, say so in the document, because as written they read as a contradiction.

- **Acceptance:** the merge gap closed at the server, **without raising either table's rung** and
  without refusing the contributor workflow 11.243 chose — or, if that proves impossible, a written
  statement of why, with the alternative costed; the refusal watched red; the cross-author loop
  covers `Individuals` and `Deployments`, with its table list derived if it can be; the T3
  contradiction settled and the losing text deleted; `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` green
  locally, **with no CI until 1 October**.

### Task 11.250 — A typed-wrong frequency has to be fixed twice, and the screen that would say so whispers it

**Status:** **Done 2026-09-14**, `flutter test` green (3277 passed). **Confirmed on Michael's phone
the same day** — *"I tested the result of the previous task and the updates to the frequency got
pushed to the projects' tags."* **That is the check this task actually needed**: every criterion
here was a widget or unit test, but the defect was found on a phone and a person seeing it fixed on
the same phone is the only evidence that the thing found is the thing repaired.
**It left `check_app_quotes` red on one line of `managing-your-tags.md`, named with its new
wording, and that is correct** — the content stream owns that page. See `/w-19`, and see
`CLAUDE.md` on why *"`check_app_quotes` green"* should never have been in this task's acceptance.
**Above the line** — it was wrong data on a field screen, and the person who
made the edit believed it took.
**Found by Michael on his phone, 2026-09-14**, testing 11.249: *"fixing a info about a tag in the
database doesn't propagate out the tag in the project — I updated a tag's frequency and it didn't
update in the tag shown for the animal it was attached to."*
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** One dialog, one repository method, and a decision already made below.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Do not run it in the same window as 11.245** — both edit `tag_form.dart`.

#### What is actually happening, measured rather than inferred

**This is not a refresh bug and it is not new.** Read on 2026-09-14:

- The Tag Database screen lists `Tag_Library` — this device's own equipment record, one row per
  transmitter, device-local, never synced (task 11.219).
- A project holds its **own copy** of that collar in `Tags`, joined to the library row by
  `lineage_id` and by nothing else.
- `TagLibraryRepository.update` writes the library row and stops. Its own doc comment says so:
  *"Editing a library entry reaches no project, by construction."*
- **And the reverse is also true and was not written down anywhere:** Project Setup's tag form calls
  `TagRepository.update` only. **An edit in either place reaches exactly one row.** A frequency typed
  wrong once has to be corrected once per project plus once in the library, and nothing counts them
  for you.
- The view layer is innocent. `refreshTagViews` invalidates every tag view on the device and the
  Animals screen reads `projectTagsProvider` live. **Michael's project copy was redrawn correctly —
  it still held the old frequency.**

#### The half of this that is a defect on its own terms

**The app already predicted this exact confusion and put the sentence where nobody reads it.**
`TagForm._copyProvenance` renders, on a library entry some project holds a copy of, the line:

> One of your projects uses this collar &nbsp;&nbsp;(i)

**That line is a description, not a warning.** The sentence that would have stopped the edit —
*"changes you make here will not reach that project — change the tag on the project itself for
that"* — is behind the information icon, and a person correcting a typo has no reason to tap it.

**This is the project's own recurring shape: a check that fails correctly into a place with no
reader.** It is worth naming as that in the fix, because the temptation will be to rewrite the
dialog behind the icon, which is already right.

#### 1. The visible half says the consequence

The always-visible line must carry the consequence, not the fact. Something of the shape *"Changes
here will not reach the 1 project using this collar"* — **his words, fewer of them, and still a
count and never a project's name** (§2.5: naming a project would disclose that a device holds a
project the person is only a viewer on). **Keep the information icon and its longer text as they
are.**

#### 2. There is one route that fixes it everywhere, and this task builds it

**Decided by the planning session 2026-09-14, and Michael can flip it before this runs.** The copy
exists so two projects can keep separate *histories* of one collar — that is what copy-on-add is
for. **It does not exist so that a typo has to be fixed N+1 times**, and asking a person to open
every project and retype the same number is how a dataset ends up with two frequencies for one
transmitter.

So: when a library edit changes anything and any project holds a copy, the form offers **one
action — apply this to the projects that use this collar** — and it is offered, never automatic.

- **It asks task 11.32's question once, and applies that answer to every copy.** Correcting a typo
  and recording a drift are both statements about the *physical transmitter*, so the answer is
  genuinely the same for every project holding it. **Do not ask it once per project.**
- **Each copy still writes its own `Tag_Versions` row**, in its own project's chain. Copy-on-add
  applied to history is exactly that (see `TagVersion.projectId`), and this task must not collapse
  the chains.
- **A project the person cannot write to must be refused, and counted, not skipped in silence.**
  The owner-only rule on a project's tag lives on `TagRepository.update` and it still applies; the
  result line has to say how many were updated and how many were refused, in that plain English.
  **A push that silently updated three of four is worse than one that updated none.**
- **Derive the columns from `tagColumnKinds`, not from a list written here.** Everything the library
  form can change is `measurementContext` (`frequency_mhz`, `pulse_rate`, `pulse_pattern`,
  `tag_name`, and the five pulse-mode columns) or `collarLife` (`status`, `notes`). Colour is not a
  tag column at all since schema v16 — it is the animal's.

> **The one sub-decision left open for Michael, and it is about `tag_name` only.** A project's copy
> may have been deliberately renamed, and pushing the library's name over it would destroy a choice
> somebody made. **Written as: the push carries every changed field, name included** — which is
> right once task 11.245 has made that field mean *Tag ID*, an equipment identifier rather than a
> per-project label. **If Michael would rather the name stay per-project, the push excludes
> `tag_name` and the line says so.** Do not decide this in the code; it is decided here or by him.

#### 3. The other direction gets a written decision, not silence

Editing a **project's** tag does not reach the library either, and no comment anywhere says that is
deliberate. **It is** — the library is one person's record of their own equipment, and a teammate's
project should not rewrite it. **Write that sentence on `TagRepository.update`**, beside the one
already on `TagLibraryRepository.update`. An undocumented asymmetry is how the next reader "fixes"
one of the two.

#### 4. What must not change

- **Copy-on-add stays.** Nothing here merges the library and a project's tags into one row.
- **No push on sync.** This is a local action on one device's own library, reaching that device's
  own projects. A teammate's copy changes when the project's row syncs, the ordinary way.
- **`lineage_id` still decides nothing about reachability** — it is `provenance`, and
  `assertSealedColumnsFeedNoReachability` enforces that. This task reads it to *find* the copies,
  which is a read on one device, not a rule about which rows travel. **Say so where the read
  happens**, or the next audit will file it.

- **Acceptance:** the always-visible line states the consequence, asserted on a library entry with
  a copy and absent without one; the push exists, asks correction-or-change once, writes a version
  row per project, **watched refusing a project the person may not write to and reporting the
  count**; the asymmetry sentence is on `TagRepository.update`; `check_app_quotes` green;
  `flutter test` green.

### Task 11.231 — The Erase tool still deletes a neighbour's tiles, and two rules disagree about "inside"
**Status:** Done — 2026-09-12. All three items fixed and tested; see `TASK_COMMS.md` for the
commit and the full test list. Nothing here needs a device — the acceptance is entirely
mechanical (set arithmetic and a lookup that refuses), so unlike the 11.229/11.230 family this
does not carry a "Michael must look" item.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** The hard thinking was done by 11.230; the pieces it built are meant
to be reused here.
**Depends on:** 11.230, which built `deleteRegion` and `sharedWithPhrase`.

#### 1. The Erase tool has the defect 11.230 just fixed one screen over

`_eraseSelection` on the Offline Data Map removes every tile and DEM file under a shape the person
drew, **with no check for saved areas**, and says only *"Removes downloaded map tiles and elevation
data whose coverage falls inside this selection. This can be re-downloaded later."*

**11.230 left it alone on purpose** — its brief was the per-area delete, and this is a different
contract: **the person chose the shape, not an area**, and erasing "everything under here" has a
real use the area delete does not, namely the pan-cache tiles no area owns.

**The decision, taken by the planning session 2026-09-12: make Erase subtract saved areas, the same
way `deleteRegion` now does.** Reasoning, so it can be argued with rather than guessed at:

- **The two failures are not symmetric.** Erasing too much costs a field download that needs a
  connection the person does not have where they need it. Erasing too little costs disk space, and
  is undone by deleting the area on purpose, offline, in two taps. **Prefer the recoverable side.**
- **One rule in both places is the simpler app.** Michael's standing principle is
  simplicity/readability over verbosity; *"deleting never touches what another area still needs"*
  is one sentence a person can hold, and two different rules for two buttons that look alike is
  exactly what nobody can hold.
- **It keeps the tool's real use.** Pan-cache tiles belong to no area and are still erased.

**So Erase must report honestly rather than silently do less.** After erasing, say what was kept
and why — *"kept 240 tiles that 'West block' and 'East block' still cover"* — using
`sharedWithPhrase`. **A tool that quietly frees less than the person expected is the same defect as
one that quietly deletes too much**; both leave the person with a wrong belief.

> **If Michael prefers the other option** — Erase keeps deleting everything and the confirmation
> names the areas it will damage — **that is a legitimate answer and this entry is where to say so.**
> It was not put to him as a question because it is reversible either way and he asked for fewer
> round trips; **it is recorded as a decision with its reasoning so that reversing it is cheap.**

#### 2. Elevation coverage and elevation erase disagree about "inside"

`DemTileStore.tilesIntersectingPolygon` — what an area is credited with and what the download
fetches — counts a 0.1° tile if it **touches** the polygon. `deleteTilesInPolygon`, which the Erase
tool uses, removes a tile only if its **centre** is inside.

**So drawing the exact outline of a saved elevation area and erasing it leaves the edge tiles and
the area reads Partial rather than gone.** The per-area delete is already consistent (it deletes the
intersecting set, less neighbours); **only the Erase tool has the mismatch.**

- **Make one rule the rule and say which**, in the code, beside both functions. **Touching is the
  one coverage already uses**, so it is the candidate — but state the consequence you are choosing:
  a touch rule erases slightly outside the drawn shape, which for an unowned tile is fine and for
  an owned one is now prevented by item 1 anyway.
- **Test the exact-outline case specifically** — draw an area's own polygon, erase it, and assert
  nothing of it remains. That is the case that reads as a bug to a person.

#### 3. `TileSources.byId` answers an unknown id with OpenStreetMap

**Found by a test passing for the wrong reason**, which is the most valuable way to find anything
here. 11.230's first fixture used `'osm'`; `byId` handed back OpenStreetMap, the delete went looking
under `tiles/osm_standard/` while the files sat under `tiles/osm/`, and **the neighbour "survived"
because nothing at all was deleted.**

**Today's exposure, measured:** the new delete does not go through `byId` (it uses the region's own
`sourceId` string), but **the download path `_runTiles` still does.** A source renamed or retired in
a later build would make every area recorded under the old id re-download under the new one, **while
its old files sit on disk forever — uncounted, and unfreeable except by "Delete all".**

- **Make `byId` refuse an unknown id** rather than substituting a default. **A lookup that cannot
  fail is a lookup that cannot be trusted**, and this one turned a test green by deleting nothing.
- **Decide what a manifest entry with a dead source id should say**, because refusing in `byId`
  moves the failure rather than removing it. A named, visible *"downloaded with a map source this
  version no longer has"* on the row, with delete still working (it uses the stored string), is the
  shape to aim at.

- **Acceptance:** Erase subtracts saved areas and **says what it kept and why**, with a test watched
  failing against today's behaviour; coverage and erase use one documented rule for "inside" and the
  exact-outline erase leaves nothing; `TileSources.byId` refuses an unknown id, **watched refusing**,
  and a manifest entry naming a dead source is visible rather than silently re-pointed; and the
  pan-cache tiles that belong to no area are still erasable, with a test saying so.
