### Task 11.230 — Deleting one downloaded map area damages its neighbours, and nothing identifies an area
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-13** — Michael tapped inside an area on "Manage on map" and deleted areas
successfully, which was the whole remaining acceptance. ~~Partial — 2026-09-12.~~ Everything below is built and green; **the one thing the suite
cannot prove is that a finger on the phone reaches the map's tap handler** (the tests call the
handler with a coordinate), so the tappable-areas acceptance waits on Michael opening "Manage on
map" and tapping an area. Both neighbour tests were watched red against the code as it stood —
the surviving tile area came back 16/20 and the surviving elevation area 3/4 — before the fix.
Details in `TASK_COMMS.md`.
**Raised by Michael 2026-09-12**, who predicted the
defect from first principles before anyone read the code: *"the selected area might have tiles that
extend beyond the area selection... this could cause a deletion of a large tile that overlaps with a
different existing map area that is still needed, right?"* **He was right, and the code is worse
than his description.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The delete is destructive, the correctness rule is a set operation over
two coordinate systems, and the honest size number falls out of the same computation.
**Depends on:** nothing.

#### What was measured, 2026-09-12

**Tiles live in one shared tree:** `<app support>/tiles/<sourceId>/<z>/<x>/<y>.png`
(`tile_cache.dart`). **An area is a polygon in a JSON manifest** (`offline_region.dart`,
`offline_region_store.dart`). **Nothing anywhere records which area a tile belongs to.**

**So the sharing is not limited to coarse tiles.** Any overlap between two areas shares **every**
tile in the overlap at **every** zoom, because there is exactly one file per (source, z, x, y). A
single low-zoom tile covering two distant areas is the extreme case, not the whole case.

**The per-area delete already exists and already does the damage.**
`manage_offline_maps_screen.dart` walks `GeoPolygon.tilesInPolygon` for the area's polygon and zoom
range and deletes every file it finds, **with no check for any other area.** Its own doc comment
says what follows: it *"reconciles (which downgrades any overlapping region to partial rather than
lying about coverage)."*

> **That comment is the defect stated as a feature.** Refusing to lie about coverage is right.
> **Silently making a neighbour incomplete, in a screen whose whole purpose is freeing space, is
> not** — and the confirmation says only *"Frees the storage it uses; it can be re-downloaded
> later"*, which mentions neither the neighbour nor the fact that re-downloading needs the network
> the user does not have in the field. **The remedy it offers is the one the app exists to avoid
> needing.**

**And the numbers on screen are already inflated.** Each area shows `sizeBytes` for its own
polygon, so **overlapping areas double-count the shared tiles.** The figures a person is given to
decide what to delete overstate what deleting would free.

#### 1. Delete only what no other area covers

**Michael's rule, and it is correct:** a tile survives if any *other* area still covers it.

- Compute the deleted area's tile set, subtract the union of every other area's tile set, delete the
  remainder. **Derive the other areas from the manifest at delete time** — not from a list written
  when the area was made, because areas are added and removed after that.
- **Tiles belonging to no area at all are fair to delete.** Panning the map writes into the same
  tree (`cached_tile_provider.dart`), so the cache holds tiles no area claims. They are
  re-downloadable and unowned. **Say this in the report** so the next reader does not mistake it for
  a bug.
- **After the delete, an overlapping area must still read complete**, because its tiles are still
  there. **That is the assertion that proves the fix** — build two overlapping areas, delete one,
  and watch the other stay whole. **Watch it red first**, against today's behaviour.
- **`Non_Detections` of this task: the DEM store has the same shape.**
  `DemTileStore().deleteTilesInPolygon(region.polygon)` deletes by polygon with no neighbour check
  either. **Same rule, same fix, same test.** Do not fix one and leave the other.

#### 2. Say what will actually be freed

The unique-tile computation from item 1 **is** the honest size. Use it twice:

- **The confirmation says how much this delete will really free** — not the area's own footprint.
- **The list's per-area size stops double-counting**, or says plainly that areas overlap. Decide
  which and say why; a number that is wrong in a predictable direction is worse than a number with
  a caveat.

#### 3. Let a person name an area, and show them something they can recognise

**`OfflineRegion.name` exists and is nullable**, and nothing sets it — so the list reads
*"Tile area"* and a bounding box, which is what prompted this. **Michael's answer, 2026-09-12:
let the user name the areas.**

- **Ask for a name when the area is drawn**, with a sensible default already filled in so a person
  in a hurry can accept it rather than face an empty box.
- **Existing unnamed areas must stay usable and be renameable** — a migration that drops them, or a
  list that hides them, is worse than the problem.

#### 4. The map screen becomes the manager

**On "Manage on map" (`offline_data_map_screen.dart`), the highlighted areas become tappable**, and
a tap opens a small sheet offering:

- **Update** — re-download the area's tiles. **Safe by construction: it overwrites and deletes
  nothing**, so it needs no neighbour logic. Say that in the code rather than leaving the next
  reader to work out whether it does.
- **Delete** — with the confirmation from item 2, naming the area and the real number.

**Overlapping areas mean a tap can land inside two of them.** Decide what happens — the smaller, a
chooser, the topmost — and **say why**; picking silently is how a person deletes the wrong one.

- **Acceptance:** deleting an area leaves every tile any other area covers, **proven by an
  overlapping-areas test watched failing against today's code**; the same for DEM areas; the
  confirmation states the real bytes freed and names the area; per-area sizes either stop
  double-counting or say they overlap; a person can name an area when drawing it and rename one
  later, with existing unnamed areas intact; areas are tappable on the manage-on-map screen with
  Update and Delete; and the two-areas-under-one-tap case is decided in writing.


### Task 11.228 — The same dropped volume in two more overlays, and a guard that only watches one
**Status:** Done, 2026-09-15. **Both overlays now mount the durable degradation-record volume, each
with a written reason in its own comment, and `server/test/security/shipped_defaults_test.dart` gained
a group that checks every discovered overlay against a hand-kept decision map rather than one named
file** — watched red separately for each of the three overlays that used to be silent, and for an
overlay with no recorded decision. `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` green locally, 1020 tests, all
61 suite files reached; **no CI until 1 October**, so that run is the only evidence.

#### What was decided and built (2026-09-15)

- **`docker-compose.e2e.yml`: mounted, not omitted.** Checked the throwaway-stack concern the brief
  raised — nothing in `test/e2e/` ever makes Postgres unreachable, so the record stays empty on every
  green run, and a red run is already kept up rather than torn down (`run_e2e_tests.sh`'s own task
  11.130 trap), which is the same durability this volume is for. A green run's `down -v` deletes it
  same as the Postgres volume, so nothing carries into the next clean run.
- **`docker-compose.dev-lan.yml`: mounted, matching production.** A developer's stack on a real
  network is production at lower stakes, per the brief's own framing; no argument for it to lose the
  record production keeps.
- **The guard now iterates every overlay it discovers by filename**, reusing `_composeFiles()`'s
  directory walk, and checks each against a `decisions` map with a reason per entry (including
  `docker-compose.server-test.yml`, which never touches `server.volumes:` and inherits the base
  mount undisturbed — recorded so an overlay that starts overriding that key without updating the map
  fails here rather than shipping silently degraded). **An overlay absent from the map fails the
  test for that overlay**, rather than passing by omission. Watched red four ways: each of
  `docker-compose.e2e.yml`, `docker-compose.dev-lan.yml` and `docker-compose.tls.yml` with its mount
  stripped, and `docker-compose.dev-lan.yml` removed from the decision map.
- **A fourth overlay is caught automatically**: the file-discovery loop, not a list, decides which
  overlays this group checks, so a new `docker-compose*.yml` is walked in and fails until somebody
  adds its verdict to `decisions` — which is the "how a fourth overlay gets caught" sentence the
  brief asked for, written into the guard's own doc comment.

**Original brief follows.**
**Model:** **Sonnet, low.** Two files, one guard, and one judgement per file.
**Depends on:** 11.223, which fixed the production overlay and built the merged-config guard.

#### What the sweep found

`docker-compose.e2e.yml` and `docker-compose.dev-lan.yml` each declare `volumes: !override` on the
`server` service, and each therefore discards `tritrack_server_state` — **the same defect 11.223 just
fixed in the TLS overlay, in two more files.** Both carry the same comment, *"the base server service
declares no volumes: today"*, which **was true when it was written** (task 10.74, on or before
2026-08-19) and has been false since task 11.129 mounted the volume on 2026-09-02.

> **This is the correct-when-written-then-silently-falsified shape, and the sweep is why we know
> there are exactly three instances rather than an unknown number.** 11.223's brief said *fix nothing
> else you find; the finding decides whether it is a task.* This is that decision.

#### 1. Decide per file whether the volume belongs, rather than assuming it does

**11.223's report says "the same one-line-plus-comment fix would close both." Do not inherit that.**
These two stacks are not the production one and the answer may differ:

- **`docker-compose.e2e.yml` is a throwaway stack.** A named volume that outlives a run can carry
  state from one end-to-end run into the next, which is the opposite of what an e2e stack wants.
  **Mounting it may be the wrong fix here**, and "no volume, deliberately" is a legitimate answer.
- **`docker-compose.dev-lan.yml` is a developer's stack on a real network.** A degradation record
  that dies on every `--build` is the same loss as production, just cheaper.

**Whichever way each goes, the outcome is written into the file as a comment saying why** — a mount
with its reason, or a deliberate omission with its reason. **A third file silently inheriting a
fourth person's assumption is how this defect got to three instances.**

#### 2. The guard must name which overlays it checks

11.223's guard renders the merged TLS configuration and asserts the volume. **It says nothing about
the other two overlays, so a regression in either is invisible to it — which is the same shape as
the original guard reading only the base file, one level up.**

- **Make the guard iterate the overlays** rather than naming one, and **assert the decided outcome
  for each** — present where step 1 said present, absent where step 1 said absent. An overlay whose
  outcome nobody decided should make the guard fail, not pass by omission.
- **Watch it red for each overlay separately.** A loop that asserts three things and is only ever
  watched failing on one of them is a loop that has been tested once.

#### 3. Say how a fourth overlay gets caught

`!override` is load-bearing where it is used and will be used again. **One sentence, in the guard or
beside it, saying what a new overlay must do to be covered** — and if the guard can discover overlays
by filename rather than by list, prefer that, because **a hand-maintained list is already wrong.**

- **Acceptance:** each of the two overlays has a decided, commented outcome; the guard checks every
  overlay rather than one, **watched failing separately for each**; an overlay with no decision fails
  the guard rather than passing; `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh` green locally — **CI is off
  until 1 October**, so that run is the only evidence.


### Task 11.184 — The last menu entry that hides instead of explaining, and one that looks like it does
**Status:** Done. **Neither is a §4.21.4 violation** — task 11.183
surveyed all nine screens and found no screen hiding project data from a member. **Both are
consistency, and one of them is the last survivor of a shape task 11.12 spent itself removing.**
**Model:** **Sonnet.** Two small changes. **The judgement is whether to make them at all**, and both
questions are stated below rather than assumed.
**Depends on:** 11.183, which found both. **Michael may veto either; neither changes what anybody can
read.**

#### 1. "Publish to server" is hidden from a non-owner; every other entry in that menu is not

`lib/features/more/screens/projects_screen.dart` **removes** the *Publish to server* entry for a
non-owner, while every other entry in the same menu is **shown greyed with its reason.**

> **It discloses nothing and it is still the odd one out.** Publishing is a write, and the entry's
> presence tells nobody anything about the project. **But task 11.12's rule is "explain, don't
> hide", and 11.99 and 11.137 applied it across this app** — an absent control teaches a person that
> the app is broken or that they missed something, where a greyed one with a reason teaches them who
> to ask.
- **The default answer is to grey it with a reason, for consistency with the four entries beside
  it** — this is applying a rule the project already made, not making a new one. **If there is a
  reason publishing is different, say it and leave it alone**; "an owner might not want a viewer to
  know publishing exists" is a real argument and should be written down if it is the one that wins.
- **It is one line either way. Do not let it become an afternoon.**

#### 2. A non-owner's project-setup fields cannot be selected, and nothing is being withheld

`enabled: false` on those fields makes the text legible but **not selectable**. **Every value is
also in the project list and in the tag CSV export**, so nothing is hidden — but *"I cannot copy
this text"* is the sort of difference somebody eventually reads as data being kept from them.

- **Decide, do not assume.** Read-only-but-selectable is the honest rendering of *you may see this
  and not change it*; disabled is the rendering of *this control is not for you*. **Say which one
  these fields are**, and if the answer is the first, use the widget that says so.
- **Check the same shape elsewhere before changing one screen.** If other read-only-for-a-role
  fields use `enabled: false`, **fix them together or say why this one is different** — one screen
  behaving unlike the rest is the defect being fixed here, not a style preference.

- **Acceptance:** the publish entry either explains itself or the reason it is different is written
  in the code; the project-setup fields' rendering is a stated decision rather than a default; any
  same-shape sites elsewhere are named with a verdict; and **any user-visible copy change is
  declared in the comms entry**, since the content lane is paused and collecting them.


### Task 11.179 — Four documents that can drift, closed with one instrument each
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-06.** Four instruments, three of them watched red under deliberate
sabotage and the fourth (the citation ratchet) watched red in both of its directions. **(1)** The
dead citations were **21** on the day, not 22 — the documents moved between 11.123's measurement and
this one — and every one named a deleted feature rather than a moved file: the cloud backup
(`3a9a2c8`), the per-address invitations (task 11.81), one command file deleted under the
delete-when-resolved rule, and two citations into pub packages that were never repository files at
all. **Fixing them found a live defect the citation was only the symptom of:** two rows of
`PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` still described cloud backup as a current capability eight days after the
code was deleted. `test/documentation/planning_document_citations_test.dart` now fails on a citation
naming a file that does not exist and holds a per-document ceiling that may fall and never rise; the
argument for why that number is allowed is in the file. **(2)**
`test/documentation/command_file_staleness_test.dart` reads each command's task id out of its
frontmatter, requires the filename to agree, and reads the status from this document — from
`WEBSITE_COMMS.md` for the website lane, because `WEBSITE_PLAN.md` has no status field. Watched red
against a resurrected `Done` task, a resurrected finished website task, and a command for a task with
no entry; `Deferred` and `Partial` pass. **(3)** The pending-decision sweep was **measured before
anything was proposed and the answer changed the design**: 19 phrasings return ~155 matches
repository-wide, 34 outside `CLAUDE_DOCS/`, and reading all 34 leaves **exactly one** live claim that
a decision is owed — `server/backup/freshness.sh`, which is *true*, because 11.80 stopped at that
decision. "Undecided" in this codebase is domain vocabulary for a join request. So the outcome is a
**coupling** rather than a sweep, in 11.183's shape: the sentence must be present while 11.80 is
outstanding and absent once it is not. **(4)** The Appendix decision index has **no code-side truth**
— nothing in `lib/` or `server/` can be read to check a cell — but it has a document-side one, and
that is where 11.159's measured gap lived. The four missing rows (§4.26–§4.29) were added and
`test/documentation/security_model_decision_index_test.dart` now requires every top-level §4
decision to have a row and every row to name a real section. **The appendix says in its own body
that only the first column is derived**, because a document with a checker teaches a reader that it
is checked. **Below the line.** These are the four bullets task
11.123 did not reach, carried here as one task because Claude Code asked for that and was right —
**they are all "a document says something the code or another document could contradict", and they
want the same shape of instrument.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Each check is small. **Two of them would be built green**, and
deciding what to do about that is the task.
**Depends on:** 11.123, which measured two of the four. **Do not re-measure what it already
measured** — the numbers are below.

#### 1. The `path:NN` citations — the decision, made, so the task implements rather than debates

**Measured by 11.123:** `CLAUDE_DOCS/*.md` carry **712** `path:NN` citations — 251 in
`DEVELOPMENT_PLAN.md`, 176 in `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md`, 158 in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`, 66 in
`UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md`, and 61 across the rest. **688 resolve to exactly one committed file, 22
name a file that no longer exists, 2 are an ambiguous basename, and none points past the end of its
file.**

**The planning session's decision, 2026-09-06, and the reasoning is on the record so it can be
disagreed with.**

- **Reject the "line number past the end of the file" check outright.** 11.123 measured it: it
  would go green today against all 712 and catch nothing. **That is the check-that-cannot-fail
  class**, and building one here would be worse than building nothing, because a document with a
  citation checker teaches a reader that the citations are checked.
- **Reject banning `path:NN` outright.** It means rewriting 712 citations for a benefit that is
  mostly in the ones written from now on.
- **Do build the two things that bite.** **(a)** A citation naming a file that does not exist is a
  failure — that is the 22, and it is a real defect found by a cheap check. Fix the 22 as part of
  this, and say for each whether the file moved or the claim died. **(b)** A **ratchet**: the number
  of `path:NN` citations per document may go down and never up. New citations name the line's
  content instead — the way `UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md`'s uid-70 and diagnostics entries were
  rewritten on 2026-09-06, both of which had rotted the same week.
- **The ratchet's baseline is a number in a file, which this project distrusts — so say why it is
  allowed here.** It is not a hand-kept *list*: the check recomputes the real count every run and
  compares. It can only be raised by somebody editing it on purpose, which is the point.
- **Which direction the ratchet moves is the whole of why it is safe, and task 11.180 measured the
  other kind — added by Claude Code 2026-09-06, at that task's instruction to write this where
  11.179 will meet it.** This ratchet only ever moves **down**, and only when somebody deliberately
  removes citations, so **forgetting to edit it can only ever produce a red that says "you added
  citations"** — never a silent pass. Compare `app_shell_harness_default_test.dart`'s per-file
  bare-pump counts, which move **up during ordinary work**: adding a test to a file that already has
  its exemption obliges an edit to a ledger in another directory, where no new decision is being
  made. **In that file's first four days, every one of the five edits to its list was such a bump,
  and the one time a task did not make it, `flutter test` was red on `main` for two commits.**
  **A ratchet that must be edited during normal work will eventually be edited without thought, or
  not at all.** So: **keep this one un-raisable by ordinary editing.** If a change ever makes new
  `path:NN` citations legitimate — a document that must quote line numbers — **that is the moment
  this stops being the safe kind of ratchet and needs re-arguing**, not the moment to bump the
  baseline. And the failure message should name **which document rose, by how many, and the
  alternative** (cite the line's content), so the person meeting it is not left guessing which of
  the two things they are supposed to do.

#### 2. The `.claude/commands` staleness check — **it would be built green, and that is the task**

**Measured by 11.123:** all 20 command files are for tasks whose `Status:` is `Not started` or
`Deferred`. **So the check passes on the day it is written.** It is still worth building — the
directory was **122 of 152 stale** in September, and the planning session's current habit of
deleting a command when it resolves that task's comms entry **is a habit, which is what this whole
task exists to replace.**

- **A check written green proves nothing until it has been watched red.** Sabotage it: resurrect a
  command file for a `Done` task and show the check fails. **`Deferred` and `Partial` are
  legitimately re-runnable and must still pass.**

#### 3. The pending-decision sweep

A document sentence saying a decision **is still owed** outlives the decision. `server/README.md`
carried one for four days after the decision was made, **on the same day it was built** (task
11.140). **Find the shape** — "to be decided", "still owed", "not yet chosen", whatever this
repository actually writes — **and say how many there are before proposing what to do about them.**
**Do not assume the phrasing;** grep tells you a token appears, not what it means.

#### 4. The security model's Appendix decision index

Same family: an index of decisions that can disagree with the decisions. **Say first whether it has
a code-side truth at all.** If it does not, the honest outcome is a marker saying so — **which is
exactly what 11.123 built for the rest of that document, and the pattern to copy is already there.**

- **Acceptance:** the 22 dead citations are fixed and each is explained; the ratchet exists and its
  baseline's legitimacy is argued in the file; the staleness check has been **watched red** against
  a resurrected command; the pending-decision shape is measured before anything is proposed; and the
  Appendix either gets an instrument or a marker saying why it cannot have one.


### Task 11.177 — The magnetic needle swings while the phone turns, and it should not move at all
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-06.** The hypothesis was confirmed before anything was changed: driving a
90° turn through the dial with today's call-site shape moved the "live" needle by up to **10.5°** in
the direction of the turn. The fix is the frame distinction rather than the subtraction — the dial
now has exactly one display quantity (the smoothed heading), `magneticBearingDeg` was renamed
`capturedMagneticBearingDeg` and is non-null **only** while a frozen capture is reviewed, and the
live needle is a literal `0.0` that no edit can turn back into a raw-versus-smoothed subtraction.
Two further sites had the same mixture and were fixed with it: the **true-north tick** and the
**navigation line** were placed off the raw true heading and drifted up to **20.5°** against the
smoothed ring mid-turn (invisible because both are supposed to move); they now take declination from
the raw pair and apply it to the smoothed heading. The **uncertainty wedge** inherited the needle's
frame and is fixed by the needle. Both **range sweeps** were already correct and are documented as
such. A third defect surfaced on the way: `_currentDisplayedDeg` fell back to a stored value on the
animation's final frame, so the ring never reached the sample it was easing toward and
`didUpdateWidget` returns early once the heading holds — a **permanent 7.5° residual** after a 90°
turn, now fixed by keying on the controller's status. Eight widget tests in
`test/features/compass/compass_dial_needle_test.dart`; **all four fixes were watched going red under
deliberate sabotage** and the smoothing is untouched. **Above the line. Michael reported it from the
app, 2026-09-06**, in the app's signature screen.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The suspected line is one subtraction. **What makes it Opus is that
the obvious fix — delete the smoothing — undoes a deliberate fix for a different complaint of
Michael's**, and the same expression is load-bearing for a case where the needle *should* move.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Related to 11.106**, which added the smoothing this interacts with.

**What Michael sees.** *"The red needle in the compass interface rotates in the direction of the
phone's rotation and then settles out. It should simply point in the phone's direction, so should
never move relative to the screen."* **He is right about the intent** — `compass_dial.dart`'s own
comment says the needle sits at *"0 when showing the live heading (so it sits exactly at top, like
a real compass)"*.

**What is certain, read from the code rather than inferred.** `compass_screen.dart` passes **the
same value** to two parameters: `magneticBearingDeg: reading.magneticHeadingDeg` and
`liveHeadingDeg: reading.magneticHeadingDeg`. Inside the dial they stop being the same number:

- `ringRotationDeg` is the **smoothed** copy — `liveHeadingDeg` eased toward each new sample over
  100 ms by `_CompassDialState` (task 11.106, added because Michael reported choppy ring motion on
  a Samsung phone).
- `magneticBearingDeg` is used **raw**.
- `needleRelativeDeg = shortestDifferenceDegrees(ringRotationDeg, magneticBearingDeg)` — which is
  **raw minus smoothed.**

> **The hypothesis this suggests, and it is a hypothesis until something confirms it.** While the
> phone turns, the smoothed copy lags the raw one, so that subtraction is non-zero and the needle
> swings; when the turn stops, the smoothing catches up and it returns to zero — *"settles out"*.
> The sign works out to the direction of rotation, which matches Michael's description. **It is a
> resemblance strong enough to test first and not strong enough to fix without testing** —
> `CLAUDE.md`'s rule about a cause inferred from a resemblance applies. **Reproduce it in a widget
> test before changing anything**: drive a sequence of headings through the dial and assert the
> live needle's angle stays at zero. If that test passes as the code stands, this diagnosis is
> wrong and the task should say so and start again.

- **Do not fix it by removing the smoothing.** It exists because Michael reported the ring's motion
  as visibly choppier on Android, and 11.106's own comment records that the underlying explanation
  **could not be confirmed on real Android hardware.** Removing it trades a bug he can see for a
  bug he already complained about.
- **The same expression is correct in the other case, and the fix must keep it.** In
  `bearing_entry_sheet.dart`, `magneticBearingDeg` is `lastCaptured?.magneticBearingDeg ??
  reading.magneticHeadingDeg` — **when a captured bearing is being reviewed it is a genuinely
  frozen value**, and then the needle *should* swing as the phone turns away from it. So the
  question is not "stop subtracting", it is **"which quantity is the needle relative to, and is the
  displayed heading the same quantity on both sides of the subtraction?"**
- **Sweep the rest of the dial for the same mixture, and give a verdict per site.** The uncertainty
  wedge is centred on `needleRelativeDeg` and inherits this exactly. `rangeSweepStartRelativeDeg`
  and `rangeSweepDeg` both use the smoothed heading and look self-consistent; `trueNorthRelativeDeg`
  and `navRelativeDeg` use `liveTrueHeadingDeg`, which is **not** smoothed at all — say whether
  those swing against a smoothed ring and whether that is visible. **Silence about a site is not a
  verdict.**
- **The class, so this is fixed once.** **A smoothed copy and a raw copy of the same quantity must
  never meet in one subtraction.** If the display works in smoothed values, everything drawn on it
  is relative to the smoothed heading; the raw value belongs only where a captured number is read.
  **Say in the code which of the dial's inputs are display quantities and which are data**, because
  that distinction is what got lost when the smoothing was added to a widget that already assumed
  its two inputs were identical.

- **Acceptance:** a widget test drives a turn and asserts the **live** needle does not move, and it
  was watched failing against today's code; the reviewed-capture needle still swings and has its own
  test; every other marker on the dial has a written verdict; the smoothing is still there; and the
  display-versus-data distinction is stated in the file.


### Task 11.178 — The tag database cannot be sorted, and forty tags is a list you scroll rather than read
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-06.** A `PopupMenuButton` (sort icon) in `TagDatabaseScreen`'s app bar
offers "Sort by frequency" / "Sort by name"; the choice persists via a new `keepAlive` riverpod
provider (`TagSortOrderSetting`, `lib/core/providers/tag_sort_provider.dart`, SharedPreferences-
backed like `ActiveProjectId`). `allTagsProvider` stayed a plain provider — the list is sorted in
Dart in the screen (`sortTags`), per the warning below. Name order uses a new `naturalCompare`
(`lib/core/utils/natural_sort.dart`) rather than a plain string sort, because a plain sort puts
`"Tag 10"` before `"Tag 2"` on this project's numeric-ish tag names; both are unit-tested
(`test/core/utils/natural_sort_test.dart`, plus a `sort order` group in
`tag_database_screen_test.dart`). Export follows the same sorted list the `ListView` renders, not
the provider's raw order. No ascending/descending choice — just the two named orders.
`project_setup_screen.dart`'s own `allTagsProvider` read is unchanged (still frequency order,
unsorted-by-name) — deliberately, since nobody asked for that screen's order to change and it
wasn't in scope. **Below the line — usability, not a defect.** Nothing is broken and no data
is at risk. **Michael asked for it on 2026-09-06** and it is cheap; it sits below the line only
because it does not gate a beta, and he can call for it whenever he likes.
**Model:** **Sonnet.** Small and self-contained. **One decision needs care** — see the warning about
the provider — and it is called out below rather than left to be discovered.
**Depends on:** nothing.

**What Michael asked for.** Sort the tag database by **frequency** or by **tag name**.

**Where it stands today.** `TagRepository.findAll` orders by `frequency_mhz, tag_name` and nothing
offers a choice; `TagDatabaseScreen` renders that order straight into a `ListView`. **So frequency
already is the default and the work is the choice, not the sorting.**

- **Sort the loaded list in Dart. Do not parameterise `allTagsProvider`.** That provider is named
  explicitly by `arrival_refresh.dart` and `tag_view_refresh.dart`, which enumerate what a sync
  round must refresh; **turning it into a family is a change to the sync-refresh machinery to get a
  sort order**, and task 11.154 built that enumeration carefully. A project's tag list is tens of
  rows, not thousands. **If you disagree after looking, say so before doing it.**
- **Four small decisions, each of which should be made rather than defaulted into.**
  **Where the control lives** — the app bar already carries export, import and a title, and the
  screen has a FAB. **Whether the choice persists** across a restart; a person who sorts by name
  once probably means it. **Whether ascending/descending is offered** or the two orders are simply
  *frequency* and *name*. **Whether the CSV export follows the on-screen order** — it currently
  exports `tagsAsync.value!`, so it follows whatever the provider gave; if the screen sorts and the
  export does not, they will silently disagree.
- **Scope is this screen.** `project_setup_screen.dart` also reads `allTagsProvider`. **Say whether
  it should follow the same order or keep its own, and do not change it silently.**
- **One thing to check rather than assume.** Tag names in this project are frequently *numeric-ish*
  (`"148.123"`, `"Tag 7"`, `"Tag 10"`). **A plain string sort puts `Tag 10` before `Tag 7`.** Say
  what the sort actually does with the names in the test data, and if it is wrong for real field
  names, fix it or record it as a known limit — **do not let it go unremarked.**

- **Acceptance:** the list can be ordered by frequency or by name; the four decisions are made in
  writing, not defaulted; the export/on-screen agreement is settled either way deliberately;
  `allTagsProvider` is still a plain provider or the reason it is not is argued; and the name-sort
  behaviour on realistic tag names is stated.


### Task 11.176 — A readiness probe that measured the wrong container, and named the wrong culprit
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-06.** h6 now asks Postgres directly, inside the Postgres container, and
builds the backup image explicitly so a build failure is reported as a build failure — watched
producing `the backup image would not build` with `age=1.3.1-r5` restored on purpose, where the old
code said `postgres never came up`. The class fix is `scripts/lib/wait_for.sh`: one readiness loop
that keeps every attempt's combined output and hands the last one back through `wait_for_evidence`,
so a loop that runs out says what it actually got. **Four of the seven scripts changed**
(`verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh`, `backup_restore_drill.sh`, `verify_source_identity.sh`,
`verify_ats_transport_security.sh`); **three were deliberately left** — `verify_i1_source_identity.sh`,
`verify_tls_termination.sh` and `verify_deployment_refusal_matrix.sh` already read the subject's own
log or container state and print it on every failure path, and each now carries a comment saying it
was looked at and why it was left. Both new failure paths were watched: the sabotaged build, and an
exhausted readiness loop, which printed psql's real error instead of a bare verdict; the occupied-port
sabotage on the ats responder printed *"the python process has already exited"* beside curl's own
message. h6 (7 checks), the restore drill (42 checks) and `verify_source_identity --report-only`
(7 checks) all pass clean afterwards.
**Above the line.** Nothing is red because of it. **It is here because it
already cost a diagnosis** — it is the reason the fourth gate failure had to be carried as a
hypothesis instead of read off the log.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The one-line instance is trivial. **The sweep is the task**, and the
judgement is which loops are honest already.
**Depends on:** 11.175, which found it. **Reported by Claude Code, 2026-09-06.**

**The instance.** `scripts/verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh:88-103` waits for Postgres by running
`psql` **inside the backup container** (`compose run --rm backup psql --host=postgres ...`). When
the backup *image* would not build, every one of the sixty attempts failed, and the script then
printed **`HARNESS ERROR postgres never came up`**. **Postgres was healthy the whole time.**

> **Two separable defects, and the second is the one that generalises.**
> **(a) The probe measured a compound.** Its success needs the backup image to build *and* the
> network to work *and* Postgres to be up; its failure message names one of the three.
> **(b) The loop threw away the evidence sixty times.** Every attempt is `>/dev/null 2>&1`, so
> the `ERROR: unable to select packages` that would have named the real cause was discarded on
> every pass, including the last one.

- **Fix (b) as a class, because it is cheap and it is where the value is.** A readiness loop's
  **final attempt must surface what it actually got.** Poll quietly; when the loop runs out, run
  once more with output shown, or keep the last attempt's stderr and print it with the failure.
  **A harness that knows why it failed and does not say is worse than one that never knew.**
- **Sweep the readiness loops in `scripts/` and report on each, rather than assuming this one is
  the only one.** Seven scripts have such loops (`backup_restore_drill.sh`,
  `verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh`, `verify_i1_source_identity.sh`, `verify_tls_termination.sh`,
  `verify_source_identity.sh`, `verify_ats_transport_security.sh`,
  `verify_deployment_refusal_matrix.sh`). **Several already look honest** — they poll the subject
  directly over the network or read the service's own logs, and `verify_i1` and `verify_tls` even
  distinguish *refused to start* from *not up yet*, which is the behaviour to copy. **Say which
  ones you changed and which you left alone and why.** A sweep that touches everything it looked
  at is a sweep that was not really looking.
- **Fix (a) where it is real, and do not manufacture it where it is not.** h6's probe should ask
  Postgres directly. **Do not "fix" a loop whose probe genuinely is its subject.**
- **A failure message must name what was measured, not what was expected to fail.** If a probe
  cannot separate three causes, it says so — *"could not reach postgres through the backup
  container; the cause may be the database, the network or the image"* is honest, and would have
  saved this diagnosis.
- **Watch it fail.** Break the backup image build on purpose and show that h6 now names the build
  error rather than Postgres. **A harness change nobody watched fail is a harness change nobody
  checked.**

- **Acceptance:** h6 probes Postgres directly; every readiness loop's last attempt surfaces its
  real error; every loop in the seven scripts is accounted for as changed or deliberately left;
  and the deliberately-broken build was watched producing the right message.


### Task 11.137 — Thirteen taps that can do nothing at all, and seven reasons hidden where a finger cannot reach
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-02.** All thirteen sites (plus a fourteenth the sweep's table missed —
`truth_point_edit_dialog.dart`'s *save*, the same shape as its delete three hundred lines away) go
through one mechanism, `runGuardedWrite` in `lib/core/errors/guarded_write.dart`. Refused and
failed are separate branches with separate sentences and separate snackbar keys; `refused:` is
`required` but nullable, so a site where no permission governs the action (share, CSV export, the
near-duplicate read, the publish pre-read) has to say so deliberately, and a refusal arriving
there anyway is reported through the honest `failed` sentence rather than asserting a permission
nobody checked. Both branches are rendered at 6.1-inch phone geometry in
`test/features/silent_write_failures_test.dart` and they fit. All eight tooltip-hidden disabled
reasons — seven menu entries in `log_screen.dart` and three buttons in `map_screen.dart`, which is
two more than the brief counted — are now on the control, via `reasonedMenuItem` /
`DisabledReasonNote` in `lib/widgets/disabled_reason.dart`, which is task 11.99's `_item` lifted
out of `projects_screen.dart` so there is one of it rather than three. **A ninth was found and
fixed on the way**: the Team tab's Distance sort chip, whose "no GPS fix" reason was also
tooltip-only, and whose fallback line only appears once somebody has *selected* distance and then
lost their fix. **Eleven further tooltip-as-reason sites are named in `TASK_COMMS.md` and were not
touched** — they are outside this task's table and each needs its own layout decision. **One
measured cost:** the map's bearing selection card grows from 153 to 205 logical pixels *while Edit
is refused* (a widget-test over-estimate; the reason wraps to three lines in a font about twice
Roboto's width). The permitted card is unchanged at 153 and keeps its old budget;
`selection_card_height_test.dart` now measures both. 2032 app tests pass.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Item 2 is mechanical and has a pattern to copy. **Item 1 is a shared
design applied thirteen times, and Claude Code asked specifically that it not be folded into
something unrelated** — that request is honoured; item 2 joins it only because it is the same
surface and touches the same files.
**Depends on:** 11.94, which measured both. **Related to 11.126**, which established that the nine
`on UnauthorizedMutation` handlers that *do* exist are all reachable — **these are the sites with
no handler at all.**

**One question, asked twice: what does a person see when an action does not happen?**

#### 1. Thirteen unguarded write handlers

**Thirteen UI-facing call sites in `lib/` await a provider's result with no `try`/`catch` at
all.** A refused delete, save, share, supersede, exclude or export **shows nothing** — no error,
no dialog, no stopped spinner. **It looks exactly like a tap that did not register.**

| File | Method |
|---|---|
| `log_screen.dart` | `shareLogEntry`, `deleteLogEntry`, `_writeMark` (supersede/exclude), `restoreToEstimates` |
| `observation_sharing_screen.dart` | `_createTag`, `_saveObservation` |
| `tag_database_screen.dart` | `_exportCsv` |
| `projects_screen.dart` | `_deleteProject`, `_confirmPublish` |
| `truth_point_edit_dialog.dart` | `confirmAndDeleteTruthPoint` |
| `observation_edit_dialog.dart` | `showEditObservationDialog` |
| `near_duplicate_tag_dialog.dart` | `confirmTagIsNotADuplicate` |
| `position_estimation_screen.dart` | `_deleteEstimate` |

> **This is not new and it is newly measured, which is the whole value of the sweep.** It was true
> before task 11.94; nobody had counted it. **A silent refusal is worse than a wrong message**,
> because a wrong message gets reported and a tap that does nothing gets repeated.

- **One shared pattern applied thirteen times, not thirteen edits.** *Claude Code asked for this
  explicitly and it is the right instinct* — thirteen bespoke `catch` blocks is thirteen future
  divergences, and this project already has the rule about hand-maintained repetition.
- **Reuse what exists rather than inventing a vocabulary.** Task 11.122's honest default and task
  11.124's refusal detail already decide **what a refusal says**; the nine
  `on UnauthorizedMutation` handlers 11.126 rendered already decide **how a refusal looks.** This
  task is about the sites that have neither, so **the answer should look like the ones that
  already work.**
- **Distinguish "refused" from "failed".** A permission refusal and a disk error are not the same
  sentence, and the pattern must not flatten them — that is the wrong-cause class this project
  keeps finding.
- **Render at least one of the thirteen in a test at real phone geometry**, per 11.126: a message
  that exists and does not fit is the defect that survived every previous sweep.

#### 2. Seven disabled reasons hidden in a tooltip a touchscreen never shows

`log_screen.dart`'s `PopupMenuItem`s — Edit, Delete, Supersede, Exclude, Restore observation, and
Edit/Delete truth point — plus **one Edit button in `map_screen.dart`** put their *disabled
reason* in a `Tooltip`, **while the item's own text label is perfectly visible.** So the person
sees a greyed-out row and no reason at all.

**This is the exact pattern `projects_screen.dart` was fixed away from by task 11.99**, whose
`_item` helper carries the doc comment *"Disabled with the reason on the item, not in a tooltip"*.
**The same defect surviving next door, in the file the fix was not applied to.**

- **Copy `projects_screen.dart`'s `_item` shape** — a second-line note on the item — rather than
  designing a third way of saying the same thing.
- **Task 11.101's sweep counted tooltips standing in for labels and found these separately**;
  this is the narrower defect of a tooltip standing in for a *reason*. **Say in the report whether
  any others of that shape exist**, since the sweep was looking for the other kind.

- **Acceptance:** every one of the thirteen sites reports something when the write is refused, by
  **one shared mechanism**; refused and failed are distinguishable; at least one is rendered at
  phone geometry in a test; the seven disabled reasons are on the item rather than in a tooltip,
  following 11.99's existing helper; and **any further tooltip-as-reason sites are named.**

### Task 11.139 — Every row on that panel is a fixed height, and somebody's phone is set to large text
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04.** Three screens measured across the twelve text sizes an iPhone can
actually be set to, in the app shell at 6.1-inch phone geometry with both banners live. **The
finding was real and worse than the entry expected: a viewer's Position panel struck the overflow
stripe at xLarge, one notch above the default** — and the *second* failure mode, text cut off with
no stripe and no ellipsis, started two notches up and was invisible to everything in the suite.
Floors before → after, measured in the test font (which is about twice Roboto's width, so every
number is a lower bound on a real phone): **Position, viewer: xLarge → xxxLarge clean, first stripe
AX1. Position, owner: xxLarge (silent clip) → AX2 clean, first stripe AX3. Record form, owner: AX1
(silent clip on SAVE OBSERVATION) → AX3 clean. Record form, viewer: AX1 → AX2 clean. Main Map:
never stripes and never clips at any size** — its clear band closes instead, holding its 96-pixel
floor through the whole ordinary slider (111 at xxxLarge) and losing it at AX1 (46). Every floor is
asserted in both directions by the three space-budget test files, so a regression fails and so does
an unrecorded improvement. **Stopped at:** the sizes on the ordinary Dynamic Type slider are clean
on all three screens; above them, what gives way between the panel and the map is a design decision
and is in Discovered Scope rather than guessed at. **The iPad question in this entry was also
settled and fixed** — see below. **Nobody has checked a floor against a real device**; that is
Michael's one action. **Below the line — raised 2026-09-03 and returned the same day, and the
reason is recorded rather than quietly reversed.** It was raised because `/w-09` made a larger
system text size the leading candidate for the Navigate row that overflowed on Michael's phone.
**Michael checked: his iPhone's text size is the default, and he has never changed it. So that is
the fifth cause named for that one event and the fifth to be wrong**, and this task loses the
urgency that raising it borrowed.

**It keeps its own merits, which never depended on that story:** nothing in the app or the
screenshot harness has ever been rendered at a text scale other than 1.0, a striped overflow is
the most alarming-looking failure Flutter produces, and the app is about to reach people who are
not Michael.

> **RAISED AGAIN 2026-09-03 — on new evidence and a different reason, which is stated so the two
> are not confused.** `/w-11` measured item 2 at five bearings, the number Michael says a real
> session holds: **the Position screen shows four of the five rows on a 6.9-inch iPhone and four
> of five on a 13-inch iPad** — and the screen says **`N=5` and `5 of 5 selected` directly above a
> list showing four.** That is not a stress fixture and it is not a text-scale hypothesis. **It is
> the ordinary case, on both devices, with the screen contradicting itself in the same glance** —
> and a person deciding which bearings to include before saving a position is the one reading it.

> **The one setting nobody has checked, and it is the next thing to ask rather than a sixth cause
> to assert: iOS Display Zoom.** Settings → Display & Brightness → Display Zoom (or *View*) has a
> **Larger Text / Zoomed** option that changes the device's **logical width in points** without
> changing its text scale — which is the one remaining way a stock iPhone reports fewer logical
> pixels across than a simulator at standard zoom. **This is a hypothesis. It goes in this entry
> and not in a comment**, per the rule `/w-09` established.

**TWO ADDITIONS 2026-09-03, both from `/w-09`.**

1. **The harness renders at text scale 1.0 and has no way to notice anything else.** So this
   task's measured floors are the **first** time any screen in this project is looked at the way a
   person with larger text sees it. **If a floor turns out to be below the default-plus-one-notch
   mark, that is not a hypothetical — it is very likely the thing that overflowed on Michael's
   device.** Say so plainly if you find it.
   **A screenshot profile at a larger text scale was deliberately not added by `/w-09`**, because
   a guide illustrated at 200% text is the wrong guide and where those images live is a decision.
   **Decide here whether the pictures are wanted, and if so ask the content lane for the profile
   rather than adding one.**
2. **The same class, one screen wider: on a 13-inch iPad the Position screen's bearings list shows
   the same four rows it shows on a phone.** The panel is a **fixed fraction of screen height**
   (the shape task 11.109 measured), so twice the vertical space buys no extra rows — somebody
   checking which bearings are selected before saving has to scroll a list that would fit whole on
   the screen they are holding. **`/w-09` did not establish whether four is a floor or a
   coincidence of its fixture, and filed it as a judgement rather than a defect.** **Measure it
   here.** **And measure it against five bearings, not eight: Michael's answer, 2026-09-03, is
   that a tracker rarely takes more than five to one tag.** That makes the finding stronger rather
   than weaker — **if the panel shows four rows, a realistic session does not fit on any device**,

**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Replacing fixed heights is mechanical. **Deciding how far to take it
is not** — text scaling touches every screen, and "all of it" is how a below-the-line task becomes
a month.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Named by 11.138**, which added one more instance and said so rather
than letting it pass as new.

**The finding.** The Position screen's save row is a **fixed-height box** and the sentence inside
it is sized against a number measured in the widget-test font. **At a large system text size that
sentence overflows and renders with the yellow-and-black stripe.** 11.138 was explicit that this
was already true of every other row on that panel — **the whole panel is built from fixed
heights** — so it added an instance of an existing condition rather than a new kind of problem.

> **Why it is worth a number even though nothing is broken today.** A field biologist reading a
> phone in bright sun, or anybody over about forty, is exactly the person who turns system text
> up. **The app is about to go to people who are not Michael**, and a striped overflow is the most
> alarming-looking failure Flutter produces — it reads as a crash to somebody who has never seen

- **A striped overflow is not the only failure.** A row that clips its text silently is worse,
  because nobody reports it. **Say which panels clip and which stripe.**

- **One cross-link added 2026-09-02, because this task can move a number another task is waiting

  whichever way it moves.

- **Acceptance:** a measured overflow floor per affected panel, stated as a text scale; a ranking

  reported.**

**What was answered, 2026-09-04.**

- **The clear-band figure this entry asks for: unchanged at 101 logical pixels** with both shell
  banners live, against the floor of 96. Every height function this task wrote returns exactly the

### Task 11.140 — One command that answers every question an operator has to remember to ask
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-02.** `scripts/operator_status.sh` asks all three questions in one
report. Each section ends in exactly one of `OK`, `PROBLEM` or `COULD NOT CHECK`, and the exit
status carries the same three-way distinction (0 / 1 / 2). Every input was made to fail in
`server/test/security/operator_status_test.dart` (27 tests, real script, stubbed compose):
an unreadable backup directory, a backup check that will not run, a backup check that hangs,
a missing degradation record, an unparseable one, a server container that will not answer, and
a database that is down — none of them prints as good news. **Verified on a real stack, not
only stubbed:** run against a completely stopped stack it answered questions 1 and 2 (backup 17
days old; six audit writes lost) and reported question 3 unanswerable, and the rate-limit SQL
was run against a throwaway Postgres with seeded rows. The boundary — **it does not push,
nothing tells anybody** — is printed in the command's own output and in `server/README.md`.
**ABOVE THE LINE — it closes a decision three tasks have been waiting on
since 2026-08-30, and it is the last one before the beta that is nobody's to make but Michael's.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Collecting three existing answers is easy. **Deciding what the
command must never claim is not** — every one of its inputs has a way of being unable to answer,
and a health summary that reports "fine" when it could not check is the defect this project has
spent itself removing.
**Depends on:** 11.78, 11.129, 11.130 — **all three raised it and all three correctly declined to
invent a channel.**

**Michael's decision, 2026-09-02: one operator health command.** Asked where a warning should go
when something stops, he chose a single command over accepting three separate polls, over building
an email sender, and over surfacing it to a project owner in the app.

> **The reasoning behind the choice, so a later task does not re-open it.** The three commands
> already exist — `backup_status.sh`, `--degradation-report`, `docker compose ps` — **and the
> record is that nobody remembers to run three things.** One command needs no mail sender, no
> credentials and no new authenticated route; **it collapses three things somebody has to remember
> into one they might actually run**, and it gives any future push notification exactly one place
> to read from. **What it does not do is push.** Nothing tells anybody. That limit is accepted and
> must be stated in the command's own output rather than left for a person to discover.

**The three questions it must answer, and they are already answered separately today:**

1. **Is there a recent backup?** `scripts/backup_status.sh` — the newest archive's age against
   `TRITRACK_BACKUP_MAX_AGE_HOURS`, its provenance, and where it is (task 11.78, and it already
   says nothing copies an archive off the host).
2. **Was anything refused because the database was unreachable?** `--degradation-report`
   (task 11.129) — **and it works while the database is down, which is the point of it.**
3. **Is the sign-in rate limit tripping?** The `rate_limit_tripped` audit rows (task 11.130).
   **Michael settled the limit's size on 2026-09-02 — three per address per fifteen minutes,
   "that sounds about right" — so this reports, it does not tune.**

**What decides whether this command is worth having:**

- **Every input has a way of being unable to answer, and each must say so distinctly.** The
  backup age cannot be read if the directory is unreadable — **task 11.125 measured exactly that
  and found the container reporting *freshness unknown* while the host-side script said *50 hours
  old*, same program, different identity.** The rate-limit count needs the database, which is the
  thing question 2 exists because it goes away. **A summary that folds "I could not check" into
  "nothing to report" is worse than the three commands it replaces**, because it converts three
  honest silences into one confident lie.
- **Say what it does not cover.** It is a snapshot of three things; it is not a monitor and it is
  not everything. **Name the boundary in the output.**
- **It must run when the database is down**, because that is when two of the three questions
  matter most. `--degradation-report` already does; the composite must not lose that property by
  connecting to the database first.
- **Where it lives is a real choice with a precedent: the diagnostics console is loopback-plus-token
  gated and off by default (§4.10).** A server-side command run by whoever is on the host needs no
  such gate. **Prefer the command; say why if you choose otherwise.**
- **Then update the standing list.** `TASK_COMMS.md`'s "Open — waiting on Michael" item 6 is the
  decision this closes, and tasks 11.129 and 11.130 both point at it. **Close them by name.**

- **Acceptance:** one command answers all three questions; **each unanswerable input is reported
  as unanswerable rather than as healthy**, tested by making each one fail; it runs with the
  database down; its boundary is stated in its own output; and the three tasks waiting on this
  decision are closed by name with what was built.

### Task 11.141 — The status command does not say which machine it is talking about
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-03.** `scripts/operator_status.sh` now prints a header — host, compose
project, and the backup directory's host path — before question 1, derived each run from
`hostname` and `docker compose config --format json` (never a hand-typed label). Re-run locally,
it read: `Host: MacBook-Pro-5.local`, `Compose project: tritrack`, `Backup directory:
/Users/mws22/Developer/tritrack/backups` — **confirming task 11.140's two findings (an 18-day-old
backup and six lost audit writes) were about that machine's own local stack, not the beta server,
exactly as suspected and now provable.** 3 new tests in
`server/test/security/operator_status_test.dart` (33 total) assert the header appears before any
verdict, that two different stacks (stubbed `docker compose config`) produce visibly different
headers, and that an unanswerable config says `COULD NOT BE DETERMINED` rather than guessing.
**Model:** Sonnet, medium.
**Depends on:** 11.140, which built the command.

Original finding, kept for context:
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** Naming the subject is easy. **Deciding what identifies a deployment
— and getting it from something that cannot lie — is the part worth thinking about.**
**Depends on:** 11.140, which built the command.

**The finding.** `scripts/operator_status.sh` prints backup ages, lost audit writes and
rate-limit counts, and **names neither the host, the compose project, nor the directory it read.**
So a run on Michael's Mac against a throwaway stack is **textually indistinguishable** from a run
on the Ubuntu beta server.

> **This is not hypothetical.** Its first real output reported **a 17-day-old backup** and **six
> lost audit writes at about 01:17 UTC** — alarming statements about a beta server, and **both
> most likely about a local test stack.** The report said so honestly (*"I believe that was my own
> test stack… but I cannot prove it from here"*), **and it could not prove it because the command
> does not say.**

- **Name the deployment in the output, at the top, before any verdict.** At minimum: the host, the
  compose project the answers came from, and the backup directory that was read. **A person
  reading a pasted output should be able to tell which machine it came from without asking.**
- **Take the identity from the thing being measured, not from the shell.** A hostname printed by
  the script says where the *script* ran; **the compose project and the container's view of the
  backup directory say where the *answers* came from**, and 11.125 already measured a case where
  those two disagreed — the host-side script said *50 hours old* while the container said
  *freshness unknown*, same program, different identity. **When they can differ, print both.**
- **Do not invent a deployment name in a config file.** A hand-typed label is a hand-maintained
  list and will be copied to the second machine unchanged, which is exactly the failure being
  fixed.

- **Acceptance:** the output names the host, the compose project and the backup directory before
  any verdict; the identity is derived rather than configured; **a run against two different
  stacks produces two visibly different outputs**, tested; and the two findings 11.140 reported to
  Michael are re-run under the corrected command and re-stated with their subject named.

### Task 11.142 — Two spinners that never stop, and a viewshed that may be made of half the terrain

> **CORRECTION 2026-09-03, and it is the seventh cause named wrongly on this project in a week.**
> **The Members screen does not spin forever on a device with no server.** Both providers fail
> immediately with `not_configured`, and under the app's own `appRetryPolicy` — 1.6 seconds — the

> see:** `retry_policy_applied_test.dart` scans `lib/` for `ProviderScope(`.
>
> **`/w-11` saw a real thing and attributed it to the app; this entry repeated the attribution as
> fact.** The rule for exactly this was written the day before — *a report is evidence about what
> its author saw; a task entry is an instruction about what is there* — and this is its second
> live test and second failure at the entry.
>
> **What the task still shipped is right and stays:** the two sections now have honest empty-state
> sentences rather than nothing, and **on the "server did not answer" path they genuinely can spin
> forever**, which is the one case where the brief's words were true — see task 11.61.
> **The published `project-members.png` remains wrong** until the content lane re-takes it.
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-03 — except the guide picture, which this session cannot take.**
Item A: both Members sections now say why they are empty, and *no server configured*, *not signed
in*, *this build will not use the saved address* and *the server did not answer* are four different
sentences instead of one. **The brief's stated cause was wrong and is corrected in the entry
below** — the spinners do not spin forever in the shipped app; they spin forever in the screenshot
harness, whose provider container omits `appRetryPolicy`. Item B: **established — it can happen**,
by a route the code comment described incorrectly, and a viewshed drawn from part of the terrain
now says so on screen. `test/viewshed/partial_terrain_viewshed_test.dart` and
`test/features/more/members_without_a_server_test.dart` are the measurements. **Left undone: the
picture.** Re-taking it needs `integration_test/screenshots/regenerate.sh`, which drives a
simulator and writes into `website/` — the content lane's instrument and the one directory a code
task never edits. See `TASK_COMMS.md`.

**Original entry below.**

**Status:** Not started. **ABOVE THE LINE for item A** — it is what a first-time user sees on the
app's default configuration, and it has been in the published guide picture since that picture was
first taken.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Item A is small once decided. **Item B has to be established before
it can be fixed**, and `/w-11` was explicit that it read the code and did not see it happen.
**Depends on:** `/w-11`, which found both — item A because a readiness check finally asked *"is
anything still loading?"* and got **yes, for twenty seconds.**

**One question, asked twice: what does the app show when something did not finish?**

#### A. The Members screen spins forever on a device with no server

On a device with **no server configured**, the project Members screen shows a **"Join code"**
heading and a **"Waiting to join"** heading with **a spinner under each that never stops.** Both
need the server; with none configured nothing ever resolves and **nothing on screen says why.**

> **A device with no server is the app's default, fully supported state — task 10.2 built that
> seam deliberately.** So this is not an edge case: **it is what somebody sees the first time they
> open the app.** And the committed `project-members.png` has had both spinners in it, on both
> device profiles, since it was first taken. **Nobody noticed for weeks because nothing was
> wrong by any assertion anybody had written.**

- **Those two sections should say why they are empty**, not spin. The vocabulary already exists —
  task 11.122's honest default, and 11.137's shared refusal helper — **so this should look like
  the sentences that already work, not a new one.**
- **Distinguish "no server configured" from "the server did not answer."** The first is a
  settings state with an action attached; the second is task 11.135's territory. **Flattening them
  is the wrong-cause class.**
- **Re-take the guide picture afterwards**, and say in the report that the published one was
  wrong. `/w-10` will otherwise photograph it again.

#### B. A viewshed drawn from whatever terrain arrived

`_ensureTerrainForRegion` stops on the first failed fetch and **the caller composes anyway**, so a
partial download can produce a viewshed drawn from part of the terrain **with nothing on screen
distinguishing it from a complete one.**

> **`/w-11` flagged this as uncertain and it must stay uncertain until measured.** It read the
> code and did not observe it. **Establish whether it can happen before designing anything** — and
> if it cannot, that is the result.

- **It matters beyond the app, which is why it is here rather than in a note.** The screenshot
  harness cannot see it either: `/w-11`'s readiness condition can tell *an overlay was drawn* from
  *none was*, and **cannot tell *drawn from all 72 tiles* from *drawn from 30*.** So a published
  picture could show a viewshed that is wrong about the terrain and no instrument would object.
- **If it can happen, the fix is to say so, not to hide the overlay.** A viewshed computed from
  partial terrain is still useful to somebody who knows that is what it is; **one presented as
  complete is a claim about where an animal could be heard from.**

- **Acceptance:** on a device with no server, neither Members section spins — each says why it is
  empty, and "not configured" reads differently from "did not answer"; the guide picture is
  re-taken; **item B is established one way or the other before any code changes**; and if a
  partial viewshed can be drawn, it says so on screen.

### Task 11.143 — A tile that arrived half-written is kept forever and never asked for again
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-03.** Completeness is now a record written beside each tile after the
file is closed (`DemTileRecord`: byte count, cell count, filled-cell count, attempt count), and
`hasTile` asks that record rather than asking whether a file exists. A truncated tile is refused
everywhere it could be read — `loadTile`, `elevationAt`, `composeForBounds` — and goes back on the
fetch list. **Watched failing:** six of the fifteen checks in
`test/viewshed/half_written_tile_test.dart` go red when `tileHealth` is reverted to the old
existence rule. **Tiles already on devices: treated as unknown and validated from their own bytes**
(parse them, count the filled cells, write a record from what is actually there) — no network, so a
whole tile settles offline and a truncated one is caught anyway; reasoning in `tileHealth`'s doc
comment. **Empty and partial are named separately:** an all-noData grid is refused by `saveTile`
outright, a partial one is served but re-fetched up to `kDemTileMaxFetchAttempts` (3). **In-place
corruption that does not change the file's length is explicitly out of scope** and said so in
`DemTileRecord`'s doc comment. **The `/w-10` candidate was not reproduced**; the readout was fixed
anyway — the count now means "how many are done", so it never reaches its own denominator and stops.
**Below the line by frequency, above it by consequence** — a momentary
network blip becomes a permanent hole in the terrain a viewshed is computed from.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Detecting a truncated tile is the easy half. **Deciding what counts as
complete, and what to do with the ones already on devices, is not.**
**Depends on:** 11.142, which closed the all-empty case and said plainly it had closed only that.

**The finding.** A terrain tile that arrived **partly** is still written to the store and **never
requested again.** The download path treats "a file exists" as "the tile is here", so a blip during
a fetch is indistinguishable from a completed one **forever after**.

> **Task 11.142 made a viewshed say when it was computed over terrain with gaps.** That is the
> symptom made honest. **This is the cause**, and it is worse than the symptom because it is
> permanent: the app will never notice, never retry, and go on computing over the hole every time
> anybody asks.

- **Decide what "complete" means and store it, rather than inferring it from the file.** A byte
  count, a checksum, or a marker written only after a successful close — **the choice matters less
  than that the answer is recorded rather than deduced.** Inferring completeness from existence is
  the thing being fixed; do not replace it with a subtler inference.
- **Say what happens to the tiles already on Michael's devices.** They were written under the old
  rule and carry no evidence either way. **"Treat pre-existing tiles as unknown and re-fetch on
  next use" and "leave them" are both defensible — pick one and write down why**, per this
  project's rule about what a widened rule does to rows already in the field.
- **A partial tile is not the only shape.** Say whether a tile can also be written *empty* or
  *corrupt* and whether the same marker covers those, or explicitly does not.
- **Added 2026-09-03 from `/w-10`, as a candidate rather than a fact: the terrain fetch reached
  *72 of 72* and then never finished**, on both device profiles in the same run, past a
  three-minute ceiling, with no viewshed ever drawn — **while two runs earlier the same screen
  was ready in under a second.** `/w-10` did not establish the cause and said so; it may be the
  DEM source rate-limiting a machine that had run the harness eight times in two hours, and **it
  may be this task's class.** Check it while you are here.
  > **And keep the shape even if the cause turns out to be elsewhere: the count reaching its
  > total is not the same as the fetch completing, and nothing on that screen distinguishes
  > them.** A progress readout that has arrived at its own denominator and stopped is the most
  > confusing possible state to leave somebody in — it looks finished and is not.
- **Watch it fail:** truncate a tile mid-write and confirm the store refuses it rather than
  serving it.

- **Acceptance:** completeness is recorded rather than inferred; a truncated tile is not served;
  the decision about tiles already on devices is stated with its reason; and the check is watched
  refusing a deliberately truncated tile.

### Task 11.144 — A finished sync round writes to a screen while that screen is building
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-03.** **The cause is a provider deriving from a provider, not a
side effect in `build`** — so task 11.95's remedy (defer the write to a post-frame callback)
did not apply and was not used. The Position screen's `_tagObserversProvider` watched its
`_directionalObservationsProvider`; a sync round marks the second stale, the screen's `build`
recomputes it there, that notifies the first, which invalidates itself, and invalidating a
provider sends the surrounding `ProviderScope` a `setState` — above the widget being built.
The two providers are now one, so there is nothing downstream to notify.
**Demonstrated on a simulator, not asserted:** with the fix, sixteen rounds run from all five
tabs (clean, offline, recovered on each) plus a dropped-on-arrival round raise no assertion,
and the capture run reaches 29 of 29 states with no screen throwing; before it, the first
round to move the bar tripped it, with a stack ending at
`ConsumerStatefulElement.watch → _EstimationContentState.build`.
**The other four branches were checked and the count is four of five** — `/map`, `/record`,
`/position` and `/more` each watch a provider some other provider also watches; `/compass`
does not. **None of them is a live instance**, because the providers concerned
(`currentUserProvider`, `serverConfigProvider`, `mayWriteProjectDataProvider`) are not what a
sync round moves. See `TASK_COMMS.md` for the list and the recommendation.
**Not reproducible under `flutter test`:** four attempts against the unfixed code came back
green, because the automated binding's scheduler always flushes before `build`. The guard is
therefore a source check, `position_estimation_provider_chain_test.dart`, confirmed red
against the old shape. **(Task 11.145 moved and widened it: it is
`test/routing/shell_provider_chain_test.dart` now, covering all five branches.)** **ABOVE THE LINE.** Invisible on a phone and **blocking four pictures the
guide's most-read failure section needs** — and a widget writing during its own build is a real
ordering fault whether or not a release build checks for it.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Finding the offending write is mechanical. **Deciding where the work
belongs instead is not**, and this is the second screen with the same defect.
**Depends on:** `/w-10`, which measured it. **Blocks `/w-12`.**

**The finding, measured over eight runs on 2026-09-03 in three different orderings.** Whenever a
sync round changes what the sync bar says — **a clean round, a failed one, or one that drops an
incoming record** — a debug build reports *"setState() or markNeedsBuild() called during build"*
and the screenshot run stops there. **It is not a timeout:** one run carried an explicit
thirty-minute ceiling and stopped at 4m11s, at the round rather than at a clock.

**The first `package:tritrack` frame is `_EstimationContentState.build`**, in
`lib/features/position_estimation/screens/position_estimation_screen.dart`.

> **And there is nowhere in the app to stand while a round completes.** That screen is in the
> widget tree **whichever tab is showing**, because `StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack` keeps every
> visited branch mounted. So this is not "a screen you can navigate away from" — **it fires on any
> completed round, from anywhere in the app.**

- **This is task 11.95's class on a different screen.** Read what that task did before designing
  anything; if the same remedy applies, apply it rather than inventing a second one.
- **The states themselves are fine and that is established, not assumed.** The run printed
  `healthy`, `offline` and `recordsMissing: 0 pending, 0 held, 1 dropped` — **task 11.97's seam
  works exactly as advertised, and only the photographing fails.** Do not go looking for a defect
  in the sync bar.
- **Say whether any other screen kept mounted by that shell has the same shape.** `indexedStack`
  means every visited branch is live; **the question is not "does this screen do it" but "how many
  of them do".**
- **Watch it go green:** the measurement already exists — `/w-12` will photograph the four states
  the moment this lands, and `/w-10` left the scaffolding in place for exactly that.

- **Acceptance:** a completed sync round raises no framework assertion in a debug build, from any
  tab; the other branches kept mounted by the shell are checked and the count reported; **and the
  four sync-bar states are photographable**, demonstrated rather than asserted.

**Written decision, planning session, 2026-09-04 — SUPERSEDED THE SAME DAY, and both halves
are kept because the reasoning still holds. Michael's instruction is that findings become tasks,
so the four chains are now task 11.145, below the line. The recorded fact and its reopen trigger
stay where they are; the task points at them rather than repeating them.** The decision as it
was written: **the four other provider chains do not get a task of their own.** Task 11.144's report found the same *shape* on four of the shell's five
branches: `/map`, `/record`, `/position` and `/more` each `ref.watch` a provider that some other
provider also watches (`currentUserProvider`, `mayWriteProjectDataProvider`, `serverConfigProvider`);
`/compass` watches none. **None is a live instance**, because a sync round does not move any of
those three, and the report was careful to say it was claiming *unexercised*, not *safe*.
**Opening a fifth task to fix four things that cannot currently fire would be scope arriving
faster than it is closed**, which is the thing this project is currently trying not to do. **What
they get instead is a recorded standing fact**, in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` under *What
`flutter test` Cannot See*, naming all three providers and the condition that would make them
live: **the day a sync round starts moving any of them.** **The reopen trigger is that sentence**,
and it is written where somebody adding a provider to a sync round will be looking. If that
happens, this becomes a task and not before.
