### Task 11.146 — A terrain tile is refused and nobody is ever told
**Status:** **MERGED INTO 11.120 on 2026-09-04, and DONE there the same day.** The signal went on
the **Offline Data** screen's region rows (`ManageOfflineMapsScreen`) — the screen that actually
has a region list; the Offline Data Map has coverage polygons and job cards, not rows. Only
`unusable` is counted: `absent` is what "Partial" on the same row already says, and `incomplete` is
usable elevation the store will top up. **Do not run this command; it is deleted.**
Both tasks land on the Offline Data Map's region list, and Michael's standing instruction is to merge
where merging is honest. **Designing one screen twice in two windows is the thing that instruction
exists to prevent.** The whole of this entry's substance is carried into 11.120's, including the
instruction that recommending *against* the signal is a legitimate outcome.

**The entry below is kept rather than deleted, because 11.120's brief points at it.**
**Original status:** **Below the line.** Nothing is wrong today — the person is not misled,
because task 11.142 makes the *viewshed* say it was computed over incomplete terrain.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** The mechanism exists and the states are already named. **This is a
placement decision plus copy, not a design.**
**Depends on:** 11.143, Done, which built the health states, and 11.142, Done, which owns the
viewshed's caveat. **Read both before choosing where this goes.**

**The finding, from 11.143's report.** The store now knows a tile is unusable and **silently
re-fetches it. If the person is offline at that moment it silently stays a hole.** A corrupt tile
on disk is a distinct fact from a viewshed computed over gaps, **and the app currently never says
it.** 11.143 did not add a signal because deciding where it belongs is a design call it declined
to make mid-task — which is the rule working.

- **`tileHealth` already returns `absent` / `unusable` / `incomplete` / `complete`.** The states
  are named; **do not invent a second vocabulary for them.**
- **The likely home is the Offline Data Map's region list**, where a person can act — but check
  task 11.135's five screens first, because it did this survey once and its answer should not be
  re-derived.
- **Say what a person can do about it**, per this project's rule that a check must name what is
  wrong. "Some terrain is damaged" with no action is worse than silence, because it worries
  somebody who then has no move. **Re-downloading needs a connection; say so when there isn't one.**
- **Do not duplicate 11.142's caveat.** If the viewshed already says it was computed over
  incomplete terrain, this signal is about the *stored data*, not the *result* — and if that
  distinction cannot be made clear in a sentence, **say so and recommend not adding it**, which is
  a legitimate outcome.

- **Acceptance:** a person who has a refused tile can find that out and knows what to do; the
  wording is checked against 11.142's so the two do not say the same thing twice; and the choice of
  screen names the survey it came from.


### Task 11.147 — At accessibility text sizes the Position screen cannot have both the bearings and the map
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04.** The lower panel scrolls as one above the ordinary text-size
slider and the map keeps its floor; the controls row wraps instead of running off the edge; and
the ladder tests were changed with the remedy so that they assert what is *reachable*, not merely
that nothing burst.

**What landed.** The panel's own minimum — its furniture plus one bearing row — no longer pushes
past the map's floor, and where it would have, the whole panel becomes one scrolling column
instead of a clamped frame. The controls row's sort menu, "All" and "None" are a bounded `Wrap`,
so they take a second line rather than the 36-to-137 pixels off the right-hand edge 11.139
measured; the cautions button, which was the one thing in the header row that could not narrow,
is `Flexible` with an ellipsis. At the default text size **nothing moved**: the panel's furniture
still sums to 151.5 and the clear band is still 101.

**Task 11.109's rule is amended in both places it lives** — the boxed note at the top of its own
entry above, and rule 1 of the SPACE BUDGET in `position_estimation_screen.dart`.

**The ladder is now clean for both roles through AX4** (it was AX2 for an owner and xxxLarge for
a viewer). It stripes at AX5, and that is left deliberately: the body available to the map and
panel together is **nothing at all** at that size, so removing the stripe would delete the one
true signal on the screen without making it usable.

**Three findings, all in Discovered Scope.** The largest is that the app shell leaves this screen
**143 logical pixels of body at AX3 and 2.5 at AX4** — the split was where it showed, not what
caused it. The second is that the map's clear band is enforced against a reserved constant while
the overlays inside it are text that grows, so the band is already under its floor at xLarge. The
third is that the Record screen's stripe at the top two sizes is untouched by this remedy and
**resembles** the shell finding without anybody having measured it.

**Every number is measured in the test font, about twice Roboto's width, so all of it is a lower
bound. Nobody has looked at a device.**
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The horizontal half is small. **The vertical half is a choice between
two floors that were each established with a written reason, and picking one means overriding the
other in a named set of conditions** — that is a design decision, not a layout fix.
**Depends on:** 11.139, Done, which measured all of this and deliberately did not choose. **Also
read 11.109 and 11.110**, which set the two floors now in conflict.

**The finding, measured by 11.139 across the whole iOS text-size ladder — do not re-derive it.**
At the five Larger Accessibility Sizes, the Position panel's furniture plus **one** bearing row no
longer fits above the map's own 96-pixel floor on a 6.1-inch phone. **A viewer overflows from AX1,
an owner from AX3.** The panel is clamped and shows the stripe.

> **Two real rules contradict each other here and both have reasons on record.** Task 11.109's —
> *the subject cannot be dragged away* — and task 11.110's clear band. **Neither is wrong; they are
> jointly unsatisfiable on that screen at those text sizes.** Say which one yields, in which
> conditions, and write the reason beside the rule it overrides.

- **DECISION — Michael, 2026-09-04: the lower panel scrolls as one. The map keeps its floor.**
  Of the three 11.139 offered, this is the only one that loses no capability: the map still clears
  the height it needs to show a ray crossing, and every bearing stays reachable — a person scrolls
  to reach it instead of not having it. **Letting the map shrink was rejected because the floor
  exists precisely for the screen whose job is judging a position estimate**, and telling somebody
  their accessibility setting is unsupported was rejected because the people who turn those sizes
  on are the people who need them.
  **So task 11.109's rule is the one that yields, and it yields narrowly: only above the ordinary
  text-size slider, and only for the panel's scroll behaviour — not for the map's floor.**
  **Amend 11.109's rule where it lives** — its plan entry and its doc comment — to say it is
  overridden, in exactly those conditions, and why. **A rule still stated absolutely while the code
  has stopped honouring it is this project's most-repeated defect**, and this task must not create
  a fresh instance of it while fixing one.
  > **Scrolling is not a licence to stop measuring.** A scrollable panel cannot show the overflow
  > stripe, which is the same shape as the Main Map finding above it: **the thing that used to fail
  > loudly now cannot.** So the ladder tests must assert what is *reachable and legible* at each
  > size, not merely that nothing overflowed. **A green run that only proves nothing burst is a
  > check that cannot tell success from its own blindness.**
- **Second item, folded in from 11.139's report because it is the same panel at the same text
  sizes:** the controls row holding the selected count, the sort menu, "All" and "None"
  **overflows horizontally by 36 to 137 pixels at AX3 and above.** It needs to wrap or shed a
  control. **This is a different fix from the vertical work and it sits above 11.139's declared
  stopping line** — it was left, not missed.
- **The Record screen still shows the stripe at the top two sizes.** In scope if the chosen remedy
  reaches it; **say so explicitly if it does not**, rather than leaving a reader to infer it.
- **Every number 11.139 produced is a lower bound**, for the reason now recorded in
  `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md` under *Which Way the Test Font Errs*. **Do not treat the
  harness's floors as the phone's** in either direction.
- **Watch it fail:** the 45 existing cases across the ladder already fail in both directions.
  Extend them; do not start a second instrument beside them.

- **Acceptance:** the chosen remedy is implemented; the overridden floor's own documentation says
  it is overridden and where; the controls row no longer overflows at any size on the ladder; the

### Task 11.148 — The map's clear band is enforced against a constant, and the thing inside it is text
**Status:** Done, 2026-09-04. The reservation for the bottom readout column is measured rather than
predicted (`MapBottomReadoutColumn.heightFor`), and the clear band now holds at exactly its 96-pixel
floor from the default through **AX1** — a stop beyond the ordinary slider the task asked for. Two
things moved that a reader should not mistake for damage: the band at the default text size went
**101 → 96**, because the old constant over-reserved by five pixels and the panel keeps the
difference; and the map's floor stops being satisfiable at **AX2 rather than AX3**, because the floor
got honest about how tall the column is there. See the comms entry.
**Ranked above 11.149 deliberately, and the reason is the population.**
This is already broken **one notch above the default text size** — a setting a great many people
use and Michael's own phone is one tap from — while 11.149 bites at AX3, which almost nobody sets.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The fix is four lines. **Not making it the same mistake in a new place
is the work**, and there is a named trap below.
**Depends on:** 11.147, Done, which measured it. **Read 11.110, whose rule this narrows.**

**The finding, measured by 11.147 — do not take it again.** `_minMapHeight` reserves a flat
**94 pixels** for the bottom readout column. That column is a scale bar, a coordinate readout and
**a wrapping attribution credit.** The clear band comes out at **101 at the default, 93 at xLarge —
already under its own 96 floor at the first notch up — then 67, 62, and 13 at AX1**, while the
map's height stays at 246 the whole way.

> **A constant is a prediction, and this one is a prediction about text.** It is the identical shape
> to task 11.138's hard-coded `52`, which was correct at exactly one text size. **The rule already
> exists in `CLAUDE.md`: do not predict a wrapping sentence, ask the widget how tall it will be.**

- **Ask the column its height**, the way `DisabledReasonNote.heightFor` does. That is the remedy and
  it is not open for redesign.
- **The named trap, from 11.147's report: scaling 94 by the text scaler is wrong.** It
  **under-reserves at AX1**, because the credit does not grow smoothly — it gains a whole line.
  **A multiplier is still a prediction.** Anybody reaching for `94 * textScaler` has reproduced the
  defect in a form that looks like the fix.
- **Task 11.110's rule is already amended in place** to say it governs the default text size only —
  `position_estimation_screen.dart` line ~150, verified 2026-09-04. **Narrow it further only if this
  task changes what is true**, and do not restate it in a second location.
- **Watch it fail:** the clear band assertion goes red at xLarge against the current constant. It
  should, today.

- **Acceptance:** the reserve is measured rather than predicted; the clear band holds across the
  ordinary slider; no multiplier stands in for a measurement; and the failing case was watched.

### Task 11.149 — From AX3 the app shell has taken the screen, and no screen's layout can fix that
**Status:** **Done, 2026-09-05.** **The shedding decision is made in one place and every tab
inherits it:** `AppShellBody` in `lib/widgets/shell_banner.dart` holds the shell's banners to a
quarter of the space between the status bar and the navigation bar; over that bound a banner shows
as many whole lines as it is given and ellipsises the rest, and below one line it stands down
entirely; banners yield in the order they are listed in `TabShell`, which is the only place that
order is written; the navigation bar never sheds. **The body left to a screen went from 239 logical
pixels at AX3, 169 at AX4 and 56 at AX5 to 519, 545 and 533**, and nothing moves at all below
xxxLarge. **The mechanism was the finding as much as the size was:** the shell was a plain `Column`,
which hands a non-flex child unbounded height, so no banner could find out how much room the shell
had — the bound is now enforced by a small render object that lays each banner into what the budget
has left. **The Record screen was measured rather than inferred and the answer was the shell:** its
scrolling form was handed a viewport of **zero** from AX4 (AX3 for a viewer) and its pinned SAVE bar
alone overflowed the body by up to 509 pixels; it is now clean for an owner at every stop on the
ladder and for a viewer through AX4, with nothing on that screen changed. Four recorded ceilings
rose with no screen changing: the Main Map's clear band xxxLarge → AX1, the Position map's floor
AX1 → AX2, its clear band AX1 → AX2, its reachability AX3 → the whole ladder. **The
`_defaultPanelFraction` fallback is now `_panelFractionWhenNothingFits`**, a stated decision with
the reasoning and what a person sees at AX3, AX4 and AX5 written beside it — including that the
screen is non-monotonic in text size, which is why the whole-row record is now a set rather than a
threshold. **The Offline Data Map's AX5 exception is closed rather than named:** its coverage
legend was 632 pixels against a 555-pixel map area and **striped the screen by 101 pixels**, so its
rows are one line each with the rest ellipsised — the same rule as the shell's — and the 96-pixel
clear band now holds at every text size. New file `test/routing/app_shell_space_budget_test.dart`,
watched red against the old shell (banners took 623 of 679 pixels at AX5). 2263 tests pass. See the
comms entry.
**Superseded text follows.** **Below the line by population — these are the five Larger Accessibility
Sizes, off by default and reached through a second settings screen — and above it by kind: this is
the app shell, so it is every screen at once rather than one.**
**Model:** **Opus, high.** Nothing here is a layout bug to find. **It is a decision about what the
shell may keep when there is not room for all of it**, taken once for the whole app, and a wrong
answer is visible on every tab.
**Depends on:** 11.147, Done, which measured it and correctly refused to solve it from inside one
screen.

**The finding, measured on a 6.1-inch phone with both shell banners live.** The body left for a
screen's own content is **518 logical pixels at the default, 394 at AX1, 143 at AX3, 2.5 at AX4 and
nothing at AX5.** The Position map's floor alone is 246.

> **So from AX3 no split of any kind satisfies anything.** The shell's two banners, its navigation
> bar and the tag selector have taken the screen before the screen gets any of it. **This is why
> the Position screen still stripes at AX5, and 11.147 was right to leave it** — hiding the stripe
> there would have deleted the last honest signal on a screen it could not make usable.

- **Decide what the shell sheds, in what order, and say it once.** Banners that collapse to a line,
  a navigation bar that loses its labels, a tag selector that moves — **the choice matters less than

- **The Record screen is in scope, as a question rather than an assumption.** 11.147 reported it
  clean through AX3 for somebody who can record and AX2 for a viewer, striping above, and said

  that settles it already exists: **print the body height at each stop, as 11.147 added to the

- **Use the instrument that exists.** `collectLayoutOverflows` in `test/support/text_scale_probe.dart`
  now **names the widget that overflowed**, not just the direction and distance — 11.147 taught it to
  read the framework's `creator:` chain. **Point this task at that rather than adding a fresh
  one-off**, which is what the last three text-size tasks each did.
- **Added 2026-09-04 from 11.148's report — this is where a person at AX2 actually loses the map.**
  Once the map's floor is unmeetable, `_defaultPanelFraction` hands the panel **60% of the body**,

### Task 11.150 — The committed-secret scan is green in CI because there is almost nothing there to scan
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04.** **The brief's premise was right and is now measured, not inferred:**
`actions/checkout@v4` defaults to `fetch-depth: 1`, and a faithful local reproduction of that
checkout gives **1 commit and 1,047 distinct blobs** against the full clone's **652 commits and
4,744 blobs** — 3.8% of the content by bytes. The old guard, `greaterThan(100)`, passed on that.
**The frightening question is answered separately and first: the history is clean.** The full scan
ran over all 652 commits and read 4,246 blobs (the other 498 are over the 512 KB bound no detector
in that file has ever looked past) — no historical `.env`, no key or certificate file, no age
private key, and the only six PEM matches in the entire history are six revisions of the scanner
file itself. **Confirmed twice**, by the Dart test and by an independent shell pass over every
blob. **The runtime was fixed without narrowing the scope:** the scan now asks git only for blobs
the detectors would actually read and processes them in bounded chunks, so nothing that was
scanned stopped being scanned — **over twelve minutes down to about five seconds.** Caching and a
schedule were both rejected as unnecessary once that held; see `TASK_COMMS.md` for what each gives
up. The vacuity guard is now a group asserting the **scope** — the clone is not shallow, the walk
reached every commit and a parentless one, every requested blob came back — and **was watched
going red in a real shallow clone.** `offline-suite.yml` sets `fetch-depth: 0`. §4.6's gate row,
§3.6's row and §8.7 now say what established the claim and on what date.
**Superseded text follows.** **RAISED ABOVE THE LINE 2026-09-04, and the title changed with it** — this
was filed as "it has started running out of time" and the timeout turns out to be the smaller half.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The repair is small. **Establishing what has and has not actually been
scanned since 2026-08-?? is the task**, and it is the half that cannot be skipped.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by 11.147's full-suite run; the cause found by the planning session
2026-09-04 after Michael reported every CI action green.**

**The two facts that do not fit together.** `test/security/no_committed_secrets_test.dart` **timed
out after twelve minutes in its `setUpAll`** locally on 2026-09-04. **Every GitHub action was green
on the same code**, with `offline-suite.yml` budgeting about five minutes for the entire suite.

**The reason, read from the files rather than guessed:**

- `offline-suite.yml` line 32 is a bare **`- uses: actions/checkout@v4`** with **no `fetch-depth`.**
- The test's history pass is **`git rev-list --objects --all`** (line 178), which is exactly what
  task 10.58 widened it to and the whole value of the check.
- Its own guard against scanning nothing is **`expect(historicalBlobs.length, greaterThan(100))`.**

> **So in CI the "whole history" is one commit, and the guard written to catch precisely this
> passes anyway, because a single tip tree holds far more than a hundred blobs.** The check is
> green in five minutes because there is almost nothing there to scan. **This is the project's
> oldest rule — a check that cannot distinguish success from its own failure — inside the guard
> that exists to enforce it.**

**And it reaches a claim of record.** `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`'s gate table, §4.6, reads
*"holds — full git history clean (§7.4)"*. **§7.4 is the *manual* `git log --all -p` review that
task 10.58's test was built to replace.** The manual review stopped being run each round; the
automated replacement has been running against one commit. **Neither half is dishonest and the
claim may still be true — but nothing has established it since 10.58, and two mechanisms have each
been assuming the other covered it.** **Checked and clear: the NAU letter makes no claim about
this**, so nothing has been asserted to a reviewer.

- **Confirm the checkout depth rather than taking this entry's word for it.** `actions/checkout@v4`
  defaulting to `fetch-depth: 1` is the premise of everything above. **The decisive measurement is
  cheap: print `historicalBlobs.length` in CI and locally and compare the two numbers.** If they
  are close, this entry is wrong and the timeout is the whole story — **say so.**
- **Answer the underlying question separately and first, because it does not need this task.**
  Whether anything is actually in the history is settled by running that one test on its own,
  where it is not competing with 2117 others. **Do that, report the verdict, and keep it out of
  the plumbing work** — "is there a secret" and "is the check wired correctly" are two questions
  and only one of them is frightening.
- **Fix the guard, not just the depth.** A threshold that only rules out *zero* does not rule out
  vacuity. **Whatever the scan's scope is meant to be, the guard should fail when the scope is not
  that** — a count of reachable commits, or an assertion that a known old blob is present.
  **Deriving it beats picking a bigger number.**
- **Then, and only then, the runtime.** With real history the setup exceeded twelve minutes and
  that will grow monotonically. **Do not narrow the scope to make it fit** — the all-history pass
  is task 10.58's whole finding. Cache, incrementalise, or move it to a schedule, **and say what
  each gives up.** A scheduled job proven by a push has not proven its schedule.
- **Update §4.6's gate row to say what actually established it and when.** A row citing a manual
  review nobody has run, beside an automated check that has not been running either, **is a status
  document asserting a cause nobody re-derived** — the rule this project wrote after
  `UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md` misdirected two readers for two days.

- **Acceptance:** the blob counts in CI and locally are reported side by side; the history is
  scanned in full at least once and the verdict stated; the vacuity guard fails when the scope is
  wrong, watched doing so; the check finishes inside its budget with its scope intact; and §4.6's
  gate row says what established it and on what date.


### Task 11.151 — A tag linked to a project does not appear until the app is restarted
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04.** Cause established by measurement, not inherited: the three
providers that hold a project's tag views (`projectTagLinksProvider`, `projectActiveTagsProvider`,
`allTagsProvider`) were one-shot reads that only refreshed when a writer named them, and **every
write site picked its own subset by hand — no two picked the same one and not one picked all
three.** Nine writes link a tag to a project (eight user routes and a sync pull): five left the
project's own tag list stale until a restart, six left the Record screen's tag wheel stale, and
three left the Tag Database screen stale. **Michael's route — the Tag Database screen's "Link to
project" dropdown — named none of them.** All eight user routes now call one function,
`refreshTagViews` in `lib/core/providers/tag_view_refresh.dart`. **The
provider-derives-from-provider candidate (11.144/11.145) was ruled out** — see `TASK_COMMS.md`.
**The tidier-looking fix was tried first and rejected on evidence:** having the three providers
`ref.watch(recordingsRevisionProvider)` deadlocked `tag_database_screen_test.dart` (11 s green →
never finishes), because a bump landing during a provider's own build orphans its `Future` — the
trap `app_context_provider.dart` already documents on `currentUser`, which announces on
`DataArrival` when it auto-creates a user. **The sync-arrival case is therefore NOT fixed** and is
recorded in Discovered Scope alongside the membership and project-detail gaps. **Above the line, and it is the only user-visible functional defect
currently in the queue** — everything else open is layout, instruments, or below-the-line.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Making one list refresh is trivial. **Finding out how many other lists
have the same gap, and fixing the class rather than the instance, is the task.**
**Depends on:** nothing. **Found by Michael on his own device, 2026-09-03, reported 2026-09-04.**

**The finding, in his words.** *"If I link a tag up with an existing project, I have to restart the
app for it to show up in the project."*

> **What this costs a person.** They link a collar to the project they are about to go out with,
> the project still shows the old list, and there is nothing on screen saying to restart. **The
> most likely reading is that the link did not work**, so they do it again — and the state they
> end up in is not one anybody designed.

- **Establish the cause before choosing a remedy, and do not inherit either of the two obvious
  candidates.** This project has been wrong twice in a row by naming a defect's class from a
  resembling symptom. **Two candidates, both hypotheses:** the display provider is never
  invalidated because the write path bumps no revision the list watches (the shape
  `recordingsRevisionProvider` exists to solve elsewhere); or it is the provider-derives-from-
  provider family of tasks 11.144 and 11.145. **Measure which. Say in the report what ruled the
  other one out.**
- **Then ask how many others there are, because a link is not the only write of this shape.**
  Unlinking a tag, renaming one, adding or removing a member, a project's own details — **enumerate
  the writes that change what a list shows and say which of them refresh and which do not.** A
  hand-checked list of two is this project's most-repeated defect; **derive the set if you can, and
  if you cannot, say what your enumeration cannot see.**
- **Michael did not say where he linked it from.** There may be more than one route to linking a
  tag. **Check every route rather than the one you find first**, and say how many there were.
- **Watch it fail:** the test links a tag with the project screen already open and asserts the list
  changes without a restart. It must go red against the code as it stands today.

- **Acceptance:** a linked tag appears without restarting; the cause is established rather than
  assumed, with the rejected candidate named; the other writes of the same shape are enumerated and
  their state stated; and the failing case was watched.

**CORRECTED BY TASK 11.153, 2026-09-04 — one decision this task made deliberately was wrong, and it
is quoted here so it is findable as the error.** 11.151 reasoned that `refreshTagViews(projectId:
null)` should mean *"only the global tag list"*, because a rename touches no link. **But
`projectActiveTags` returns whole `Tag` rows, and the Tag Database edit dialog offers no project
when editing an existing tag** — so **every rename, retune and recolour there left the Record
screen's tag wheel offering the old name until the app was restarted.** `null` now means every
project. **The reasoning was sound about links and wrong about rows**, which is why it survived
being written down.


### Task 11.152 — A bearing row spends its width on a full name
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04 — commit `8417847`.** Bearing rows now render first initial and
surname (`observerShortName` in `position_estimation_screen.dart`); the full name is unchanged
everywhere else — the stored `Observation`/`User` rows, CSV/R export, sync, and the map marker's
long-press tooltip all still carry it, and the row itself carries it too, in a `Tooltip` wrapping
the shortened title so the collision case (two observers sharing an initial and surname) has a
full-name disambiguator one long-press away. **Collision is accepted, not resolved** — documented
at `observerShortName`'s definition, matching the existing initials badge, which already collapses
harder (two letters, no surname) on the same input. Sort-by-member still sorts by full name;
shortening only changed what is drawn.

**Space recovered, measured with `TextPainter` at the row's actual font (11px, weight 700) in the
`flutter_test` fallback font — noted because that font is roughly twice Roboto's width, so real
device savings are smaller than these, not larger:** at the default text scale, "Alice Vega" → "A.
Vega" saves 33px and "Val Reed" → "V. Reed" saves 11px (a short first name saves less, since only
the surname's characters were ever going to repeat). At AX1 (28/17 ≈ 1.65x) the same pair save
54px and 18px. All 34 of `position_screen_space_budget_test.dart`'s existing cases still pass
unchanged — the panel's declared furniture heights didn't move, so this measurement is additive
context, not a fix to the panel's existing floor.

Three tests in `position_estimation_screen_test.dart` asserted the row's visible text was the full
name; updated to assert the shortened form is what's drawn and that a `Tooltip` carries the full
name. Full suite 2196 passed, 15 skipped, 0 failures (was 2158 at task 11.153, three tasks and
several new tests ago); `flutter analyze` clean.

**Original status: Not started. Below the line. Nothing was broken** — this was density on the
panel that has the least room to spare.
**Model:** **Sonnet, medium.** The change is small and the only judgement in it is already made.
**Depends on:** nothing. **Raised by Michael from his own device, 2026-09-04.**

**The finding, in his words.** The bearings list on the Position screen shows who took each bearing,
and *"that is likely not needed or could be reduced to first initial. last name."*

**Michael's answer, taken as the decision: shorten it, do not remove it.** A bearing's author matters
the moment a team shares observations — the same reason truth points record who found them — but a
full name on every row is paying panel width for something a reader needs only to tell two people
apart. **Render it as first initial and surname.**

> **This is the panel tasks 11.139, 11.147, 11.148 and 11.149 have all been fighting for room on.
> This is the first change that gives room back rather than dividing it.**

- **Shorten the rendering, not the record.** The stored observation keeps the full identity; only
  the row is abbreviated. **Anything that exports, syncs or is read in R is untouched** — and say so
  in the report, because "we shortened the names" will read as a data change to somebody skimming.
- **Do not undo task 11.144's fix by accident.** It merged two providers so the observers arrive in
  the same round trip as the bearings, which is why the list no longer flashes raw user ids before
  the names appear. **That fix is about *when* the name arrives and stays needed whatever the name
  looks like.** Do not conclude the merge was pointless because the name got shorter.
- **Two people can share an initial and a surname.** Say what the row does then — a fuller form, a
  second initial, or nothing at all is a defensible answer. **Pick one and write down why**, rather
  than leaving it to whichever the data happens not to contain today.
- **Check the width claim rather than assuming it.** The ladder tests measure this panel at every
  text size; **report what the change actually buys**, in pixels, at the default and at AX1.

- **Acceptance:** rows show first initial and surname; the stored and exported identity is unchanged
  and the report says so; the collision case is decided in writing; and the space recovered is
  measured rather than asserted.


### Task 11.153 — Everything that arrives by syncing refreshes nothing until the app is restarted
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04 — commit `4d9a9ca`.** A membership change, a tag link or a project
rename that arrives on a sync pull now reaches the screens without a restart. `ArrivalRefresh`
(`lib/core/providers/arrival_refresh.dart`) listens to `DataArrival` — where the merger already
announces, so every inbound route is covered by construction — and invalidates one named list of
project views and one of tag views.

**The deadlock was established, not inherited, and the brief's own description of it was
incomplete in a way that mattered.** Invalidating a mid-build provider has three different
outcomes and only one is loud: a `keepAlive` provider **hangs silently and nothing throws**
(measured on `currentProjectProvider`); an `autoDispose` one **throws** *"disposed during loading
state"*; and one a widget is watching **recovers on the rebuild** — which is why the whole class is
invisible to any test that pumps a screen. **Deferring to a later event-loop turn was measured to
make no difference at all** (`Timer.run`: identical hang), so the remedy is to wait until the
providers have settled and re-run then. `arrival_refresh_test.dart` has a case that times out at
four seconds with the guard removed and returns immediately with it.

**Cost, measured, and the brief's premise was wrong.** *"Including every bearing saved"* does not
happen: saving a bearing calls `recordingsRevisionProvider.bump()` directly and never reaches
`DataArrival`. The seven announce sites are a merged sync page, a first-run or recovered user row,
sign-in identity adoption, an unknown-column promotion, a tag CSV import, a profile edit and a
pasted share — **so the frequency is per sync round that actually changed rows, not per write.** One
whole refresh on a five-project, five-member device with forty collars: **median 15.4 ms** (13.5–19.8
over 20 runs). **The four gating providers are 1.5 ms of that**; the project lists are 4.0 ms and the
tag views 8.1 ms. A paginated pull announces per page, so a fresh join of forty pages costs about
0.6 s of refresh spread across a much longer download.

**No change widens anybody's permissions**, and this was checked rather than asserted: every
provider touched re-reads the same local membership rows it read before, no write path changed, and
`BaseRepository.assertRoleMayWrite` and the server's `RowAuthorizer` still decide every write. What
changed is only *when* a screen finds out what this device already believed.

**Two live defects were found on the way and both are fixed here, and neither is about syncing.**
See Discovered Scope. Full suite 2158 passed, 15 skipped, 0 failures; `flutter analyze` clean;
suite runtime 1:15 against a 1:14 baseline on the same machine, with 14 more tests.

**Original brief below.** **This is the team half of task 11.151**, and it is worse
than the half that was fixed, because the person it fails is not the person who did anything.
**Model:** **Opus, high.** The remedy is one idiom. **It is one idiom that has already been
measured deadlocking the app**, and four of the providers concerned gate controls rather than fill
lists, so the blast radius is the work.
**Depends on:** 11.151, Done, which fixed all eight local routes and deliberately left this one.

**The finding.** A tag link, a membership change or a project rename that arrives on a **sync pull**
refreshes nothing. 11.151 closed the eight routes where *you* are the one who acted; **this is every
route where somebody else acted and it reached you.**

> **What it costs a person, and it is not a cosmetic list.** An owner promotes you to contributor on
> their device. Your device syncs. **The Record screen still refuses your bearing and the Members
> screen still shows your old role, until you close and reopen the app** — with nothing on screen
> saying so. The same holds for a teammate publishing a collar you need, and for a project renamed
> elsewhere. **The beta is a real team; this is the failure mode of a real team.**

**THE TRAP, MEASURED BY 11.151 — read this before choosing a remedy.**

**The obvious fix deadlocks the app.** Having these providers `ref.watch(recordingsRevisionProvider)`
— which `DataArrival` already bumps from inside the sync merger — means **a bump can land during a
provider's own build, which orphans that provider's in-flight `Future` so it never completes.**
This is not theoretical and not test-only: `currentUserProvider` announces when it auto-creates a
user, **so it is reachable on a first run.** 11.151 measured it turning `tag_database_screen_test.dart`
from eleven seconds green into a run that never finishes.

> **A safe shape is a listener that invalidates from *outside* any build.** That is a direction, not
> a design — **establish it works here rather than inheriting it**, and say what you measured.

- **The six providers are named and they are not all the same kind.** `projectMembershipsProvider`,
  `projectOwnersProvider`, `isProjectOwnerProvider`, `myProjectRoleProvider`,
  `mayWriteProjectDataProvider`, `allProjectsProvider`. **Four of those gate controls rather than
  fill a list**, and re-running a permission provider on every announcement — including every
  bearing saved — is a cost nobody has measured. **Measure it. A permission check that runs on every
  write is a different program from one that runs on a screen opening.**
- **There is already a correct local shape to copy, and copying it is the point.**
  `membership_provider.dart`'s `_afterMembershipChange` is a single named function every local
  membership write calls, and it invalidates all six. **The sync merger simply never calls it** — it
  announces on `DataArrival` instead. **The fix may be as small as making the announcement reach
  that function safely**, which is exactly the shape 11.151 built for tags in `refreshTagViews`.
- **Do not let a permission provider refreshing become a permission *changing*.** A role arriving by
  sync is data from another device; **this task makes the screen honest about what it already
  believes, it does not widen what anybody may do.** If any change here alters who may write, stop
  and say so — that is §4's territory and not this task's.
- **Watch it fail:** a membership change delivered by a sync pull, with the Members screen already
  open, must change what that screen says without a restart. **It must go red today.**

- **Acceptance:** what arrives by syncing is visible without a restart; the deadlock shape is
  established as avoided rather than assumed, with the measurement; the cost of re-running the four
  gating providers is measured and stated; no change widens anybody's permissions; and the failing
  case was watched.


### Task 11.154 — The lists that say what to refresh are hand-kept, and one of them had a hole for three weeks
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04 — commit `a7813f0`.** Both halves landed and all four guards were watched going red.
The two refresh lists are now *enumerable* — `visitProjectViewProviders` and `visitTagViewProviders`
take a visitor, so a test reads the list itself rather than a copy — and
`test/core/providers/refresh_lists_test.dart` derives each listed provider's transitive read-set at
run time from a `ProviderObserver` and fails if anything it reads is neither refreshed nor on a
declared, reasoned exception list. **Dropping `projectRoleForUserProvider` reproduces 11.153's exact
finding from scratch** (7 tests red, naming the provider). Each of the 15 entries also has a
behavioural case — a database change its value must reflect after a refresh — checked against the
enumerated list in both directions, so **a leaf entry no other provider reads also cannot be dropped
silently**. Part two is an assertion now: every family on either list is `autoDispose`, watched red
by flipping one to `keepAlive`. The app-wide audit is
`test/documentation/invalidation_sites_test.dart`: **37 by-name invalidations across 21 files, each
declared with a verdict**, undeclared sites and stale declarations both red. **No second instance of
the 11.153 hole was found.** One candidate — sign-in adopting a server identity rewrites the user
column of every synced table while `auth_provider.dart` invalidates only `currentUser` — was
implemented as a fix and then **reverted, because `ServerIdentityAdopter` already announces through
`DataArrival` after its transaction** (task 11.45's sixth inbound path). Two standing facts added to
`TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`, including what neither instrument can see. 2196 app tests pass.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** The audit is mechanical. **Deciding what a derived guard can actually
assert — and saying honestly what it still cannot see — is the work.**
**Depends on:** 11.153, Done, which found both halves and audited only the two lists it owned.

**Two findings from 11.153, merged here because they are the same object: the refresh lists and the
guard that watches them.**

**Part one — a hand-kept invalidation list can be complete and still wrong.**
`_afterMembershipChange` invalidated `myProjectRole` but not `projectRoleForUser`, **which is the
single line `myProjectRole` consists of.** Invalidating a provider does not re-run the providers it
reads (measured, riverpod 3.3.2, now a standing fact in `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`). So **an
owner changing somebody's role watched the members list update and the "Your role" card beside it
not, from the same tap.** Live since task 11.12.

> **11.153 audited the two lists it owned and said so.** The question it left is the one that
> matters: **does any other hand-kept invalidation list in this app have the same hole?**
> A hand-maintained mirror of something the code already knows is this project's most-repeated
> defect — tasks 11.14, 11.21, 11.23 and 11.45 were all the same shape.

- **Enumerate every place that invalidates providers by name**, and for each, follow what those
  providers read. **Derive the transitive set if you can.** If you cannot, **invert it**: list what
  is deliberately not invalidated, with a reason, so an unrecognised case fails — the two shapes
  `CLAUDE.md`'s guard rule allows.
- **Watch it fail:** removing one entry from a list must turn something red. Today it does not.

**Part two — the deadlock guard cannot see families, and is safe only by accident.**
`ArrivalRefresh` holds a refresh back while any provider on its list is mid-build. **Riverpod 3.3.2
exports no way to enumerate a family's live instances, so families cannot be checked.** That is
tolerable today **only because every family on these lists is `autoDispose`, which throws rather
than hanging** — the loud outcome. `ArrivalRefresh` states this limit in its own doc comment, which
is correct and is not a guard.

> **The next person to add a `keepAlive` family to a refresh list re-opens the silent hang, and
> nothing will notice.** That is a screen that never finishes opening, with nothing thrown.

- **The cheap remedy is available and should be taken unless it is shown not to work: assert that
  every family on these lists is `autoDispose`.** The live instances cannot be enumerated; **the
  providers on the list can.** That converts *safe by accident* into *safe by assertion*, and turns
  the hazard into a red test at the moment somebody adds the wrong kind.
- **If that cannot be expressed against riverpod 3.3.2, say so with what you tried**, and record the
  accepted risk where the person adding a provider will meet it — **not only in a doc comment on the
  class they are not editing.**
- **Watch it fail:** add a `keepAlive` family to a refresh list and confirm the new guard goes red.

**Do not widen this into a refactor.** Both halves are about making existing lists honest. **The
cost of a whole refresh is already measured — 15.4 ms median — and is recorded**, so no part of this
task needs to argue from performance.

- **Acceptance:** every by-name invalidation list is enumerated and its transitive gap closed or
  declared; a guard fails when an entry is removed; families on refresh lists are asserted
  `autoDispose` or the failure to do so is documented where somebody adding one will read it; and
  both guards were watched going red.


### Task 11.155 — Eight more checkouts that have never said what they were given
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04.** All eight examined with a stated verdict; **no job needed a
deeper clone, and one that already had one did not need it either.** Three corrections to the
brief, all measured rather than reasoned:

1. **`broken-control-check` was not bare.** It has carried `fetch-depth: 0` since the first CI
   commit (`6ee8186`), with a comment saying a shallow clone "cannot create" a `git worktree`.
   **That is false** — measured: `git clone --depth 1` of this repository, then
   `git worktree add --detach <dir> HEAD`, succeeds and produces a complete tree, which is all
   three `verify_*_broken_control.py` scripts ask of git. The full clone was removed. So the real
   count of bare checkouts was **seven**, not eight.
2. **Clone depth was the wrong axis for every one of the seven.** None of the jobs reads git
   history. What two of them *were* silently narrowed by is the test runner's own exit code.
3. **The two real findings, both measured on 2026-09-04.** `flutter test test/network --tags
   network` **without `--run-skipped` skips every test and exits 0** — so the weekly tile-credit
   job would go green having asked no provider anything, if that one flag were ever dropped. And
   `dart test` **exits 0 when every test it loaded was skipped, and when it loaded only some of
   the files it should have** — demonstrated live: a run of 2 of `server/test`'s 55 files exits 0.
   (Loading *nothing* is loud — an empty package exits 79 — which is the opposite of what an
   earlier draft of this work asserted before it was measured.)

**The remedy is `scripts/assert_suite_scope.py`**, wired into `run_server_tests_docker.sh` and
`tile-credit-freshness.yml`. It reads a `package:test` JSON report and asserts that the set of
suites the run loaded equals the set of `*_test.dart` on disk under the given directory, in both
directions; that at least one test ran; and, with `--no-skips`, that nothing was skipped. **Not one
of its expectations is a number a person chose** — all are derived from the filesystem. It prints
the counts on every run, green or red. Both assertions were watched going red under the environment
that was previously accepting them: the all-skipped network run (`flutter test` exit 0, checker exit
1) and the 2-of-55 server run (`dart test` exit 0, checker exit 1 naming the 53).

Verified green afterwards: the full server suite in Docker, 55/55 suites and 888 tests, and the live
tile-credit run, 4 tests against three providers. `flutter test test/documentation test/security`
passes, 285 tests.

**Written reasons for the five jobs that got no new assertion** are in each workflow beside its
checkout step — `gate-instruments`, `build-check` (Android and Apple), and `website`
(drift-check and publish). The short form: every one of them reads only the tree at HEAD, and every
environment dependency they do have (Docker, the network, the Android SDK/Xcode, the deploy secret,
the Hugo download) already fails the job outright rather than narrowing it, with the vacuity guards
`verify_merged_manifest_capabilities.sh` and `check_app_quotes.dart` already in place. **Above the line, and bounded** — eight workflow files and the scripts they
call. It is above the line because the last unchecked one of these was green and wrong for weeks.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Reading eight short YAML files is mechanical. **Working out what each
job silently assumes about its environment is not**, and that is the whole task.
**Depends on:** 11.150, Done, which fixed the ninth and deliberately did not audit these.

**The finding, in 11.150's own words: it fixed `offline-suite.yml` because that is the only workflow
running the secret scan, and it did not audit the rest.** *"That is an unchecked assumption, not a
clean bill of health."*

**The eight bare `actions/checkout@v4` steps**, none carrying `fetch-depth`: `gate-instruments`,
`broken-control-check`, `server-suite`, `build-check` (×2), `website` (×2), `tile-credit-freshness`.

> **Depth is the instance, not the class.** `actions/checkout@v4` with no `fetch-depth` is a
> one-commit clone, and a one-commit clone is silent — the job runs, passes, and reports nothing
> about what it was not given. **The class is anything a developer's machine has that a runner does
> not:** full history, submodules, LFS objects, a warm cache, network access. **Ask each job what it
> reads from its environment, not just how deep its clone is.**

- **Do not add `fetch-depth: 0` to all eight and call it done.** A full clone on a job that does not
  need one costs time on every push for nothing. **The deliverable is knowing which jobs need what**
  — say for each of the eight what it reads, and whether a shallow checkout narrows it.
- **The gate instruments are the ones to look at hardest.** `gate-instruments` and
  `broken-control-check` exist to detect things; **an instrument narrowed by its environment is
  exactly the defect 11.150 found**, and `CLAUDE_DOCS/UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md` already carries that
  as a fourth verdict — *executed constantly, by the right mechanism, against almost none of its
  subject.*
- **Where a job does depend on something the runner may not give it, make it say so in its log.**
  11.150's remedy is the pattern: the scan now prints the commit and blob counts it actually
  reached, every run, **so the number is where a person will see it change.** Copy that rather than
  inventing a threshold — the worked example is the group `the history scan reached the whole
  history` in `no_committed_secrets_test.dart`.
- **Watch it fail:** for every job you change, the new assertion must go red under the environment
  it was previously accepting. **A job you decide needs nothing gets a written reason, not silence.**

- **Acceptance:** all eight are examined and each has a stated verdict — needs full history, needs
  something else the runner may withhold, or needs nothing and why; every job that depends on its
  environment asserts and logs what it got; each new assertion was watched going red; and no full
  clone was added to a job that does not need one.


### Task 11.156 — The offline suite reports PASS on an exit code, and a run that reached a tenth of the tests is textually a pass
**Status:** **Done 2026-09-04 — commit `9eec98d`.** `scripts/run_offline_suite.sh` now writes a
JSON report and hands it to `scripts/assert_suite_scope.py --test-dir test --declared-skips
test/declared_skips.json`. Every run states *"250 suite(s) loaded of 250 `*_test.dart` on disk;
2196 test(s) ran, 15 skipped; 2 declared skip rule(s), 0 undeclared skip(s), 0 stale rule(s)"*.
**Watched failing three ways:** `flutter test test/localization` prints "All tests passed!", exits
0 — the exit code the old script called PASS — and the check now reddens naming 243 missed files;
dropping the network rule from the declaration reddens naming the undeclared skip; adding a rule
for a test that is not skipped reddens naming the stale rule. **Skips are the declared set, not a
count**, per the planning session's answer. **Reporter cost measured, and it is not material:**
two pairs of full runs, reporter off then on, gave 111.3 s -> 106.4 s and 81.7 s -> 84.8 s — faster
in one pair, slower in the other, against a 29.6 s spread between two reporter-free runs of the
same command. The overhead is below what this machine can resolve; that is the honest claim, not
that it is zero.
**Above the line. This is the gate that runs on every push**, it is the
largest suite in the project, and it has the hole task 11.155 just closed in two smaller jobs.
**Model:** **Opus, medium.** Wiring the reporter is small. **The skip decision below is not**, and
getting it wrong reproduces the defect being fixed.
**Depends on:** 11.155, Done, which built `scripts/assert_suite_scope.py` and proved the shape on
`server-suite` and `tile-credit-freshness`.

**The finding.** `scripts/run_offline_suite.sh` runs a bare `flutter test` and echoes **PASS** on
its exit code. **A run that loaded a tenth of `test/` and passed everything it loaded exits zero**,
and the script says PASS. Nothing anywhere states how many test files were reached.

> **This is the same shape as task 11.150's, one layer up.** That one was a check green over one
> commit because the *checkout* narrowed it. This is a suite green over an unknown fraction because
> the *invocation* narrowed it. **`UNEXERCISED_CONTROLS.md` now carries the generalisation: "has it
> run against what it claims to cover?" is a question about the invocation, not only the checkout.**

- **The mechanism already exists and must not be reinvented.** `--file-reporter=json:` plus
  `scripts/assert_suite_scope.py --test-dir test`, exactly as 11.155 wired the other two.
- **THE DECISION 11.155 DECLINED TO MAKE, and the planning session's answer — take it unless you can
  show it is wrong.** The offline suite has a standing count of legitimate skips. **Do not assert
  that count.** Asserting a number a person chose is precisely the trap task 11.150 named, and
  `greaterThan(100)` is what it looks like a month later. **Assert the *set* instead:** a declared
  list of skipped tests, each with a reason, so **a new skip that nobody declared fails the run**
  and a skip that stops being needed fails it too. That is `CLAUDE.md`'s fail-closed-with-reasons
  shape — the second of the two the guard rule allows — and it is available here because the skips
  are nameable. **Log the count beside it; assert the set.**
- **Measure the cost before shipping it, because nobody has.** 11.155 flagged this as uncertainty
  rather than hiding it: **the JSON reporter's overhead on a 2,158-test run is unmeasured.** Time it
  with and without and report both numbers. **If it is material, say so** — a slower gate on every
  push is a real cost and this task is not entitled to spend it silently.
- **Watch it fail:** run the suite restricted to one directory and confirm the assertion goes red
  and **names the files it missed.** A red that does not say what was skipped is half a check.

- **Acceptance:** the offline suite states the suites loaded against the `*_test.dart` files on
  disk, every run; a narrowed run goes red and names what it missed, watched; skips are asserted as
  a declared set rather than a count, or the reason that is impossible is written down; and the
  reporter's cost is measured and reported either way.


### Task 11.29 — An owner of one project must not silently re-tune another project's tag
**Status:** **CANCELLED 2026-08-22. Do not run `/11-29`.**

**Michael reversed the decision on 2026-08-22, and the reversal is right.** Tag
frequencies drift — a VHF transmitter does not hold its nominal frequency for its
whole life — so forbidding edits forbids recording reality. This task solved the
wrong problem.

**What replaces it is not a different rule; it is the removal of the question.**
Tasks 11.32 and 11.34 together mean no two projects share a tag, so no project can
re-tune another's. The frequency a bearing was taken at is recorded on the bearing,
and a tag added to a project is copied into it.

**Kept below rather than deleted, because one thing it found survives the
cancellation:** any message about a tag must never reveal that another project
exists. That constraint moves to task 11.34.
**Model:** **Opus** — medium effort. The disclosure trap in the refusal message is
the part that needs care.
**Depends on:** 11.23, 11.26.

**Michael decided this on 2026-08-22: no, an owner should not be able to do this.**

Today an owner of one project may rename, re-tune or retire a tag that another
project is also using, and that project is never told. **What that costs a
biologist:** bearings recorded against "collar 148.520" quietly come to mean
something different from what they meant when they were taken, in somebody else's
dataset, with no record that anything changed. That is a research-integrity
problem, not a convenience one.

**The rule: refuse the edit unless the caller owns every project using the tag.**
Enforce it at the server, not only on the screen — task 11.26 exists because a
screen-only rule is not a rule.

- **The refusal message is a disclosure question, so get it right.** It must not
  name the other project, or its owner, or anything about it. Someone with no
  access to project B must not learn that project B exists by trying to rename a
  tag. "Another project is using this tag" is the whole of what may be said.
- **Name the consequence rather than discovering it later: a tag two projects
  share becomes effectively frozen** — neither owner can correct even a typo. That
  is the price of the decision and it is the right price, but it must be written
  down and it must be what the user is told, not a bare error. Say in the report
  how a typo in a shared tag's name is meant to be fixed; if the answer is "ask
  the other owner," that is fine, but somebody has to be able to find out who to
  ask, and per the point above the app cannot tell them.
- ~~Do **not** solve this by copying the tag into the project. That creates exactly
  the duplicates Phase 12 exists to merge.~~ **REVERSED by Michael's decision of 2026-08-22
  and designed by task 11.34: copying into the project is exactly the answer.** The bullet is
  struck rather than deleted because it is the reasoning that was overturned, and a reader who
  greps for it should find the reversal rather than nothing.

> **Phase 12's deferral was re-taken on 2026-09-10 and it stands — with a different reason and a
> trigger.** It had been deferred partly on the argument that duplicates would be rare, **which rested
> on a sentence task 11.34 measured as false**: adding a tag to a project is contributor-level, not
> owner-only, so no role check holds duplicates down.
>
> **The new reason is better than the old one.** Merging two tags is a change to somebody's recorded
> data, and **nobody has yet seen how often duplicates actually happen or what they look like.**
> Building a merge tool on a guess about its own input is how it ends up merging the wrong things.
> **The beta is the measurement** — the engineering scope is unchanged either way (within-project
> merges only), so nothing is lost by waiting and a real answer is gained.
>
> **The trigger, so this is not indefinite: the first beta project that reports duplicate tags as a
> nuisance brings the phase forward.** Michael can overrule this scheduling call at any time.
- **Acceptance:** the edit is refused at the server when another project uses the
  tag; permitted when the caller owns them all; the refusal discloses nothing
  about the other project, demonstrated by a test; the frozen-shared-tag
  consequence is documented.

### Task 11.30 — Remove the cloud backup, and narrow what an export carries
**Status:** **Done 2026-08-29 — commit `3a9a2c8`.** **Confirmed on hardware by Michael,
2026-08-30: the iOS and Android apps both build.** That closes the one risk this task
left open — it removed platform channels and their Xcode and Gradle references, and a
stale project-file reference is exactly what passes analysis and fails a device build.
**Michael also accepted the narrower archive in writing on 2026-08-30**; the reasoning is
at `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.15.2 and the question is closed. All three parts landed: the
automatic cloud backup is removed from the code and the interface (settings model,
provider, scheduler, service, iOS and Android platform channels, UI section, the
"not backed up" banner, and the Xcode/Gradle references that would have broken the
build); the archive no longer carries `User_Emails`, and both CSVs no longer carry
`altitude_agl`; and task 10.97's bounds walk is complete (NaN refused on every
numeric column, a declared `TextBound` on every text column derived from
`tableSpecs`, and `SyncRowOutcome.fromDb` raising a catchable exception).
Inventory item 4 is retired in `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md`; §4.15 and §4.15.1 are
closed as **overtaken** in the security model, and the acceptance for the width
that legitimately remains is written up as **§4.15.2**. Tasks 10.84 and 10.85 can
be marked closed. 1524 app tests and 273 shared-package tests pass; the two
`no_committed_secrets_test` failures are pre-existing on a clean tree and unrelated.

**One conflict to record, because the resolution was a judgement call.** This
command's own text (merged 2026-08-22 from task 11.31) says *"Do NOT do this yet:
removing the feature"* and to leave the task open with step 2 outstanding. **The
plan entry below, dated 2026-08-30, reverses exactly that** and explains why —
there are no users yet, so no one's only off-device copy is at risk. The plan is
newer and is authoritative for what to build, and the command told me to read this
entry, so the feature was removed. **If that reversal was not intended, this is the
commit to revert.**

**Re-scoped by Michael's decision of 2026-08-30, and the scope
grew rather than shrank — read this before the older text below.**

**The decision: remove the automatic cloud backup entirely. Not default-off — gone.**
Server sync replaces it. **The CSV and project export stay untouched** — a project owner
wanting raw spreadsheets at the end of a season is a real need and a different feature,
and Michael has accepted its disclosure risk in writing as understood and necessary.

**Why removing it now is safe, and why that stops being true soon — this is the whole
of the sequencing 11.31 insisted on.** 11.31's spec refused to remove the feature before
a server was deployed, because *"until then, that cloud copy is some users' only
off-device copy of their data."* **There are no users yet.** Michael is the only person
holding a project, and the server sync he has been testing all week works in both
directions. **So the removal is free today and would risk somebody's only backup the day
after a beta ships.** Do it now.

**What this decision deletes, which is more than a feature:**

- **Trust-boundary inventory item 4** — "linked cloud backup folder (third party can
  write)" — stops existing. **A surface removed is worth more than a surface hardened**,
  and this is the largest single reduction available to this project.
- **Task 10.84 (archive encryption with client key custody) loses its subject.** Its
  whole premise is §4.15.1's dated acceptance of *the cloud-backup archive* shipping
  unencrypted. No cloud-backup archive, no acceptance to renew, and **no key-custody
  design with no undo to get right.**
- **Task 10.85 (the linked cloud folder is a write surface) loses its subject** for the
  same reason.
- **A scheduled background write of every animal coordinate to a third-party cloud
  disappears** — which was on by default, decided when this app was single-user, and
  never re-decided when project sharing arrived.

**What it does NOT delete, and this must be stated so nobody assumes it did.** The
archive **codec** stays: importing a project `.zip` and restoring a backup still exist,
and findings K-1 and J-1 are about that codec, not about the delivery channel. Inventory
items 2 and 3 are unaffected and remain Hardened. **The removal takes away a way in, not
the parser behind it.**

**A third item, added 2026-08-30, and it is squarely this task's subject: the export
carries a column that is always zero and looks like a measurement.** `altitude_agl` — the
receiver's height above ground — exists on `Observations` and `Non_Detections`, is
exported in the CSV as `altitude_agl_m`, and **nothing in the app can set it.** The model
defaults it to `0` and the viewshed quietly substitutes 1.5 m for a held antenna. So
every exported row carries a zero in a column a person post-processing would reasonably
read as a recorded height.

**This is not the aerial question** — Michael ruled aerial tracking out of the beta on
2026-08-30, and rightly. **It is this task's own question asked of a different column:**
an export should not present a value nobody supplied as though somebody measured it.
**Decide and do the smallest honest thing** — leave it out of the export until it can be
set, or export it as empty rather than `0`, or make it settable if that turns out to be
trivial. **Do not build the aerial workflow here.** Say which you chose and why.

> **Loop closed 2026-09-12.** 11.30 chose to leave the column out, which was right, and
> wrote that it *"returns the day a person can set it."* **Task 11.67 landed that day**:
> `altitude_agl_m` is back in both CSV exports, set from the Record screen's *At altitude*

> in 11.30's reasoning is revised; its precondition simply ended.

  acceptance is closed as **overtaken**, not renewed and not lapsed in silence.

**Michael decided on 2026-08-30 that macOS cloud backup is out of scope** — moot once
the feature is gone, and recorded so the earlier instruction to explain it on screen is
not carried out on a feature that no longer exists.

**The older scope below still applies to the export half.** **Worth more than its
position suggests, noted 2026-08-30:**
it carries task 11.31's step 1 — **turning the cloud backup off by default** — and that
default is still **on**. Until it runs, every project's whole archive, every animal
coordinate included, is copied unencrypted to the user's cloud folder without anybody
choosing it. **That is the cheapest single reduction in exposure available**, it needs
no server and no key design, and it makes task 10.84's question smaller.

**Michael decided on 2026-08-30: macOS cloud backup is out of scope for the beta, and
the screen must say so.** The `cloud_backup` channel exists on iOS and Android and
`macos/Runner/AppDelegate.swift` registers nothing, so the app currently **offers a
feature the platform cannot perform**. Found by task 11.40. It belongs here because this
task already owns what leaves the device and the backup feature's own retirement.
**Say it plainly on the screen rather than disabling a control with no explanation** —
an offer that silently does nothing is the class this phase has closed four times.
**Model:** Sonnet
**Depends on:** 11.23.

Exporting a project is not gated by role at any layer, and **the security model is
right that it cannot be** — a member who can read the data can copy it, and 11.20
already accepted a narrower version of the same thing. That is not the finding.

**The finding is that the export is wider than the screen.** It includes every
named person's **prior email addresses** — data no member ever sees in the app and
which nobody has reasoned about. The security model's wording, "data they are
authorized to see," does not cover it, because they were never authorized to see
it; it simply came along.

**Carries task 10.97 as of 2026-08-29** — read its entry, which stands unchanged and
is the larger half. It carries findings M-1 (`NaN` escapes every numeric bound on
every path, because NaN is unordered rather than out of range), L-7 and N-7 (no text
column has any length bound — a 5 MiB tag name is stored and delivered to every
device, measured live), and L-8 (an unknown outcome string throws an `Error` rather
than an `Exception`, breaking every deployed client's push the first time the server
adds a sixth outcome).

**Why they are one task and not two: both are a single walk of `tableSpecs` asking a
question per column.** 10.97 asks *what bounds this value*; this task asks *may this
value leave the device*. Same derivation, same drift guard, same file. Split, the
schema gets walked twice and the guard written twice — and the second walk is where a
column gets missed. **Do the walk once and record both answers per column.** Choose
each bound deliberately, as 10.97's caveat requires: a tag name and a free-text note
want different limits, and an identifier-shaped column wants a shape and not a length.

- **Narrow the payload to what the app shows.** Prior addresses are the known
  instance; check for siblings while you are in there — superseded identity
  values, soft-deleted rows, audit columns — and say what you found either way.
- **Then write the acceptance for what remains**, with a reason, so the width
  question has an answer and not just the gating question.
- This covers the project `.zip` and the spreadsheet export. The scheduled cloud
  backup carries the same payload and is being retired — see task 11.31 — but
  **do not make this fix depend on that retirement**, because the `.zip` a person
  emails to a colleague is the path that matters most and it is not going away.
- **Acceptance:** an export contains no personal data the app does not display;
  the remaining width is accepted in writing with a reason.

### Task 11.31 — Retire the unencrypted cloud backup
**Status:** **MERGED into task 11.30 (2026-08-22). Do not run `/11-31`; run `/11-30`.**
Both are about what leaves the device. The spec below still applies in full,
including the instruction to do step 1 only and leave the task open if no server
is deployed, and 11.30 carries it.
**Model:** Sonnet — medium effort. The sequencing matters more than the code.
**Depends on:** a deployed server. **Do not remove the feature before then.**

**Michael decided this on 2026-08-22: the automatic backup to the user's own cloud
storage is redundant once the server is live, and should be retired. The export
stays** — a project owner wanting raw spreadsheets at the end of a season for
analysis is a real need and a different feature.

This closes the single most-argued accepted risk on the project: project data,
including every animal coordinate, copied unencrypted to iCloud or Google Drive,
**on by default**, a decision made when the app was single-user and never re-made
when project sharing arrived.

**The sequencing is the whole task, and getting it wrong loses somebody's field
season.** Until a server is actually deployed and reachable, that cloud copy is
some users' only off-device copy of their data. So:

1. **Now, and independent of any server:** change the default to off, and make the
   on-switch state plainly what it copies and where.
2. **Only once the server is deployed and a restore from it has been drilled:**
   remove the feature, and migrate anyone who had it on — they must not simply
   stop having backups.
3. Leave the export path untouched.

- **Acceptance:** the default is off; no user silently loses their only backup;
  the security model's acceptance entry for this risk is closed rather than
  edited, with the date and the reason; the NAU letter's question about this
  default is updated to describe the decision instead of asking for one.

  erases the cursor they earned, and shows *"You're no longer on this project, so it has stopped
  syncing"* to somebody who was never on it; the first person, signing back in, finds the project
  silently not syncing — the bar is hidden for a merely-unlinked project — and relinking it from

  today's behavior** by `sign_out_leaves_sync_state_test.dart`'s second group ("Finding 3"), so

- **[Found by task 11.292, 2026-09-21, while counting how a departure can be refused. Read from
  the code, not reproduced; nothing built.] A departure that meets a whole-request `403 forbidden`
  is retried on every foreground, forever, and the device never unlinks.** `deliverPendingDepartures`
  runs a round per undelivered departure and reads the outcome from the row receipt; when the
  owner had already removed the person, the push draws `403 forbidden` before any row is looked at,
  no receipt is ever written, and the project stays linked with the departure pending — one refused
  request per foreground, for as long as the copy is kept (and *after* it is deleted, because
  `findUndeliveredDepartures` deliberately includes tombstoned projects). The person is off the
  project, which is what they wanted; the cost is the wasted request and a project that reads as
  linked on their device. **The ordinary round already handles this for the *active* project**
  (`classifySyncFailure` reads a `403` against a closed local membership as `membershipEnded` and
  `_unlinkIfWeAlreadyLeft` clears the link); the departure flush bypasses that classification
  and reads only the receipt, and a project somebody has left is by definition rarely the active
  one. The fix shape: the flush treats a `403 forbidden` on a departure round the way the round
  does. Small; file it if the request-per-foreground bothers anybody.

- **[Found by task 11.298, 2026-09-21. Fixed here; recorded because it corrects a claim in this
  entry and in task 11.293's.] Task 11.293's "the callback fires strictly after the response has gone
  out" was a timing fact, not a structural one, and a relay with its port closed beats it too.**
  The sender's address refusal fired the callback synchronously inside the request; measured live,
  the `undelivered` row preceded the `sent` row by 2 ms. A connection refused on a closed port is
  sub-millisecond and would have done the same on the relay path. The route now waits for its own row
  before writing the failure row (a `Completer`, completed in a `finally`), and the sender starts every
  delivery in a microtask. **Not a §4.5 oracle** — the timing keyed on syntax the caller chose, and
  the boundary now refuses that syntax first. 11.293's test needed one `await` added: the second row
  is one microtask later than it was, by construction.

- **[Found by task 11.287, 2026-09-20. Not built; the audit row's shape is the planning session's.]
  A sign-in link the relay refused is recorded as `sent` in the audit log.** Delivery is
  asynchronous because §4.5 requires it — `sendMagicLink` returns before a socket opens, so the
  response cannot vary with the relay — and `auth_routes.dart` writes its `linkRequested` row with
  `outcome: sent` before the relay has said anything. The development file sender could fail
  synchronously into `internal_error`; the SMTP sender cannot, by design. So today a refused
  delivery exists in exactly one place: the container log (`docker compose logs server | grep "NOT
  DELIVERED"`), which nobody at NAU will be tailing. **What would close it:** an `onFailure`
  callback on `SmtpEmailSender`, wired in `bin/server.dart` to write a second audit row
  (`linkRequested`, a new outcome `delivery_failed`, the normalized address) through the audit
  connection that already exists there. One hook and one outcome string; not built because the
  brief named stderr and adding an audit outcome is a §4.7 vocabulary change. **Ask the planning
  session whether the audit log is meant to be where an operator sees this** — `auth_routes.dart`'s
  own comment says operational visibility comes from the audit log, and for the SMTP path that
  sentence is now false.

- **[Found by task 11.287, 2026-09-20. Doc drift in the security model, for the planning session.]
  Three places the model is now wrong or silent.** (1) The §7.6 row and the §11 findings-table row
  saying `EmailSender.sendMagicLink` returning `void` is *"a latent timing oracle the moment an SMTP
  sender exists … fix before an SMTP sender exists, not after"*: the SMTP sender exists, the
  signature is unchanged, and it is not an oracle — the send runs on a detached future and the
  method returns before the connection is attempted (a test asserts the relay's transcript is empty
  when `sendMagicLink` returns). `void` was always the fire-and-forget the model asks for; a
  `Future<void>` would have been the hazard. Close both rows. (2) §4.6's secret inventory names
  "the SMTP credentials" as a future item; `TRITRACK_SMTP_PASSWORD` is now real, is placeholder-
  checked, never printed, and is matched by the committed-secrets test's existing `SMTP_PASSWORD`
  pattern. (3) §4.19.4 asks the outbound question of every format the app writes; the server now
  writes one — a mail message — and its row is: *the receiving system is a mail relay and a mail
  client; the only caller-influenced bytes are the recipient address in one header, refused unless
  it is one `@` between plain ASCII; the body is fixed text and a server-generated URL.*

- **[Found by task 11.289, 2026-09-20. Not built; needs a decision.] A project tombstone the server
  refuses is held on a project no screen can open.** If the server answers the owner's `Projects`
  tombstone with anything but accepted — `unauthorized` because ownership on the server differs from
  the phone's, `invalid` on a build skew — the round records it in the held-row store keyed by the
  deleted project, exactly as for any refused row. But the held-row list is on the sync status screen
  of the **open** project, and a deleted project is never open, so nothing surfaces it and the flush
  correctly stops re-offering it (a held row is not pending). The person believes the project is
  gone; it is live for the team; nothing says so. The same shape already exists for a refused
  *departure* (task 11.57 recovered the unsent case, not the refused one). **Not built here** because
  the honest fix is a surface, not a retry — where does a refusal about a project you cannot open get
  shown? — and that is a screen decision. Ask the planning session whether the Projects list, the
  More tab dot, or the sync screen's "all projects" view is the place, and whether a held departure
  should join it.
  **Half built by task 11.290 (2026-09-20, commits `1cc4497` and `852b696`); marked by the planning
  session 2026-09-21.** The Projects list gained a "Deleted here, not yet on the server" section at
  its foot, with UNDO, covering **both** routes a refusal takes — the whole-request `403` and the
  per-row `unauthorized` this entry named as the common one. **So the screen question this entry
  asked is answered: the Projects list is the place**, not the More tab dot and not the sync
  screen's all-projects view. **What is still not built is the last clause** — a refused *departure*
  has the identical shape and no surface — and its answer is now constrained rather than open: that
  same section, or nowhere. Carried into task 11.292 rather than left here.
  **Decided by task 11.292 and endorsed by the planning session 2026-09-21: that section, but not
  until an undo-leave write exists — and it does not.** The reasoning is counted rather than
  asserted. The server admits a self-departure past every gate but one, so the only per-row refusal
  a departure can draw is `lastOwnerRemoval`, which needs two devices disagreeing about who owns the
  project; a whole-request `403` because the owner already removed the person is **not** a refused
  departure — they are simply off the project. **One reachable cause, zero reports.** The deletions
  section works because UNDO is the way forward; for a departure the way forward is *undo leaving*,
  and no such write exists anywhere in `lib/`. **A row saying "the server did not accept your
  leaving" with nothing beside it is a refusal with no way forward**, which is worse than the
  silence it replaces. The trip-wire in 11.292's entry closes this: the first report of somebody
  who left and is still listed as a member buys the undo-leave write and the row **together, as one
  task**.
