- **[Found by task 11.263, 2026-09-16. Fixed in the same commit; recorded because it was live since
  task 11.243 and nothing had ever tested it.] The server refused the ordinary same-day swap on every
  sync.** `SyncService.applyPush` decides every row against the *stored* rows and writes afterwards.
  A swap is two rows in one page — the old deployment closed at 14:32 and the new one opened at
  14:32, written in one transaction on the device — and the new row was checked against the old row
  *still open in the store*: an unbounded overlap, refused as `invalid`, held on the device. Every
  synced swap since the server started enforcing the interlock (2026-09-14) left its new deployment
  held. Nothing in `server/test` had ever pushed a swap; the first test that did
  (`server/test/integration/deployment_interlock_test.dart`) went red on it. **Fixed by checking each
  `Deployments` row against the store *as the earlier rows in the page leave it*** — the device
  pushes in `updated_at` order, which is the order it made each change true, so the server now sees
  what the device's own transaction saw. Order therefore matters and is asserted both ways. **For
  Michael:** any deployment his phone holds as "the server would not take this" from a swap before
  this build should go through on the next retry; the count of such rows is on his phone, not here.

- **[Found by task 11.263, 2026-09-16. Fixed in the same commit, in the shared package.] The
  interlock refused a tombstone.** `conflictFor` skipped a *stored* tombstone and never asked whether
  the *candidate* was one, so the server refused a withdrawal whenever the row being withdrawn
  overlapped something — which is exactly when a person needs to withdraw it. A withdrawn link cannot
  create an overlap; it now conflicts with nothing in either position. The device never asked this of
  a tombstone (its unlink goes straight to the soft delete), so only the server was affected.

- **[Found by task 11.263, 2026-09-16. A decision for Michael, with the number it needs.] "Day only"
  on a same-day removal that does not overlap *yet* leaves the collar unlinkable for the rest of the
  day, and nothing on the other animal's screen says why.** The brief withholds *Day only* exactly
  where it would overlap, and that is what was built. But a removal recorded today as a bare day
  covers the whole of today, so a link of that collar to any animal later today overlaps it and is
  refused — and the picker, which asks the write's own arithmetic, hides the collar rather than offer
  a refusal. The person who took tag 2 off Kea with *Day only* at 09:00 goes to Marie at 14:00 and
  tag 2 is not in the list. The way in is Kea's screen → *Edit removed date* → today → *Set a time*,
  and the dialog's sentence hints at it (*"useful if another collar went on the same day"*), but the
  picker itself is silent. **The number:** this is Michael's own tag-2 flow of 2026-09-15, which
  drove task 11.251; it is not a corner. **Two remedies, either is one line:** withhold *Day only* for
  *today* altogether (a time defaulted to now is a tap, and a timed removal is never wrong where a
  bare day was right — the case the design keeps *Day only* for is a *past* day), or keep it and add
  copy where the collar is hidden. The first is the smaller change and the one the design's own
  sentence — *"a same-day handover requires a time"* — already argues for. Pinned as it stands in
  `animals_screen_test.dart` ("a collar taken off Kea today as a BARE DAY is not offered") so the
  consequence is visible rather than discovered.

- **[Found by task 11.263, 2026-09-16. A risk Michael is now carrying, priced.] The server reads the
  bare-day sentinel in *its* zone, and the shipped container's zone is UTC.** The interlock now has to
  tell a bare day from a time, and does it the way `Deployment.coversMoment` always has — a bare day
  sits at *local* midnight. On the phone that wrote the row that is exact. On the server a day
  written at Arizona midnight is 07:00 UTC and reads as a time. Two consequences, both written on
  `DeploymentInterlock`: a bare day reads *narrower* there, so a same-day pair of bare days pushed by
  a device that does not enforce the rule is let through (the device with this build refuses it
  first, so this is about a build without it); and a *timed* value that happens to land on UTC
  midnight — a swap picked by hand at exactly 17:00 in Arizona, one minute in 1 440, or accepted as
  offered at 17:00:00, one second in 86 400 — reads *wider* there and would be refused on push
  though the device accepted it. This is design §4's cross-zone reopen trigger with the server as a
  second reader; the nullable instant column or a stored zone closes both, and the trigger's own
  wording should now say the server is a reader. Nothing else changes: every overlap that does not
  turn on the sentinel — two open collars, a collar on two animals for a week, a back-dated link —
  is exact on both sides.

- **[Found by task 11.242, 2026-09-13. Fixed in the same commit; recorded because it was live for
  three days and nothing noticed.] Every backup of the beta server since major 3 shipped was labelled
  "schema major 2".** `server/backup/backup.sh` mapped the database's schema version to a major with a
  hand-typed threshold chain that stopped at 2 (task 10.35's bump); `server/backup/restore.sh` refused
  anything above `SCHEMA_MAX=2`; and `scripts/backup_restore_drill.sh` asserted "2" in three places
  — so the drill passed against a v14 server *because* backup.sh had the same stale copy. The label
  is in the cleartext sidecar **and in the signed trusted comment** that restore.sh decides on. What
  it cost: nothing yet — a wrong-in-the-compatible-direction label restores fine — but had backup.sh
  alone been corrected, restore.sh would have refused the server's own backups. Now: the major
  history is data (`schemaMajorFirstMinor` in `schema_constants.dart`), all three scripts are at 4
  (the drill reads the constant rather than typing it), and a new group in
  `server/test/security/shipped_defaults_test.dart` parses backup.sh's chain and restore.sh's bound
  against the map — watched going red against the committed scripts. **Not coupled:** restore.sh's
  `SCHEMA_MIN=1` mirrors the app's private `_lowestMigratableMajor`, which the server suite cannot
  import; the test only checks it is ≤ the current major. Both are 1 and neither has ever moved.

- **[Found by task 11.242, 2026-09-13. Decision for the planning session; no code today.] Major 4 is
  spent and free until a second device installs — should `Tags.color_hex` be dropped from the wire
  while it is?** 11.240 kept the column, nullable and written null, because *dropping* a wire column
  is a major bump and v16 was scoped additive. The major has now moved anyway. Dropping it inside
  major 4 would remove a column that `TagColumnKind.retired` exists only to explain; keeping it costs
  a few bytes a row forever and one kind in an enum. **But it is not free under the new check.** The
  freeze for major 4 was taken at v16 with the column present, so a v17 that drops it goes red —
  correctly: a device on major 4 keeps showing and re-sending it — and the honest answer is a
  major 5. The alternative, re-freezing major 4 with the column gone (`--refreeze`), is exactly the
  *"nobody is on that build yet"* argument this task exists to stop leaning on. **Recommend leaving
  the column where it is.** Recorded so the question is answered rather than re-asked.
  **DECIDED 2026-09-13 by the planning session: leave it, and the reasoning above is the decision.**
  The argument that settles it is the last one: **`--refreeze` is the "nobody is on that build yet"
  reasoning wearing a flag**, and this task exists because that reasoning was load-bearing and wrong.
  **A column costing a few bytes a row is not a reason to spend the mechanism built to stop us
  spending majors casually.** If a later task wants it gone, it is a major 5 with its own
  justification — **which is exactly the price the freeze was built to charge.**

- **[Found by task 11.242, 2026-09-13. Trip-wire, no code.] `RowValidator`'s closed enum sets are
  the one tightening the freeze cannot see.** `status`, `role`, `sex`, `coordinate_format` and the
  rest are checked against sets written into the validator's own `switch`, not into `ColumnSpec`, so
  a value removed from one of those enums is a tightened rule with no test on it. This class stands
  at zero instances. **The first removal of an enum value buys moving the sets onto the column
  declaration and adding them to the freeze**, not a note.
  **CONFIRMED 2026-09-13 by the planning session: a trip-wire, not a task, and the trigger is
  written where it will fire** — the first task that removes an enum value. **The count is what makes
  this the right call:** zero instances, and a guard built now would assert a shape nobody has yet
  broken. **This is the same ranking `/11-233` and `/11-236` were given** — rank before guarding —
  and it is worth noticing that the answer differs by population, not by taste: the freeze was built
  because a shared column had *already* changed shape, and this one has not.

- **[Found by task 11.237, 2026-09-13. Read, not measured on a phone; needs a task number.] A
  person holding a read-only snapshot cannot delete it.** `Projects` is `MutationRule.owner`, and
  the only exemption is `MutationExemption.departedMember` — somebody who *was* on the project. The
  snapshot holder never was, so the projects list offers them neither Leave (nothing to leave) nor
  Delete (not an owner, not departed). The copy sits in their list until they join or reinstall.
  **Not built in 11.237** because it is a second exemption on a rule whose one exemption says
  *"adding a second should be as uncomfortable as this one was"*, and because the argument that made
  the first safe — a `Projects` row is never offered to the server — applies here identically and
  deserves to be written down as the reason rather than inherited. One small task: an exemption
  verified the same way (no open row for the actor, and — the new half — no closed one either), and
  the Delete item enabled for a snapshot with its own note.

- **[Found by task 11.237, 2026-09-13. Decision for the planning session, no code needed today.]
  `ImportCase.adopt` — a member importing a project this device has never held — lands the project

  (the standing says member, every write goes) and *not syncing* (nothing marks it linked, so
  `SyncController` reports `notLinked`). The honest way for that person to sync is the one that
  already exists — Projects → Join a project lists it, or pull-to-refresh after approval — and

- **[Found by task 11.237, 2026-09-13. Fixed in that task; recorded because it moved a rule.]
  `ProjectMembershipRepository.insert` no longer runs the general role gradient after its
  authority check.** The gradient reads the acting user off the row's `last_modified_by`, which on
  every other table is a sound stand-in; on a membership grant the row is written *by* the owner
  *about* the member and the audit column may name either, so the row cannot say who is acting and
  `MembershipInsertAuthority` has already re-derived the permission from the person who can. With
  11.237's refusal it would have refused the very row that makes somebody a member. The authority is
  the whole of that gate now, written directly with the same abort-on-conflict.

- **[Found by task 11.235, 2026-09-12. Measured, then avoided; recorded because nothing enforces it.]
  `currentProjectProvider` must not touch the database when there is no active project, and about
  every widget test that pumps a screen without a project depends on that without saying so.** The
  first version of this task's fix issued `currentProject`'s repair-input watches before its first
  `await`, which starts the membership repository — and so opens the database — even on the
  no-project path. **In the full suite that hung `observation_sharing_screen_test.dart` for ten
  minutes per test**: five early tests in the file pumped the screen bare, each started a database
  open inside `testWidgets`' fake clock where its completion can never run, and sqflite's factory
  lock (held by the first open) then made the sixth test's real `runAsync` open wait forever. One
  file, because each test file is its own isolate. **The boundary is real and load-bearing** — the
  header comment of `tag_database_screen_test.dart` names it in passing — **and it is prose.** The
  fix here keeps the old order in `currentProject`, and the guard test couples that order to the
  provider's `keepAlive` annotation. **Whether "a provider that must not open the database on its
  empty path" deserves its own check is the planning session's call**; the cost of not having one
  was one twenty-minute suite run and a diagnosis, this time.

- **[Found by task 11.235, 2026-09-12. MEASURED, live today, not yet seen on a phone. Needs a task
  number.] The Sync Status screen's "Try again" button on a refused record fails the same way the +
  button did.** `heldRowRetryProvider` (`sync_held_rows_provider.dart`) is auto-disposing; the
  screen reads it bare with `ref.read(heldRowRetryProvider)(projectId, row)` and the closure it
  returns uses the provider's `ref` **after** the database write that releases the row. A probe
  calling it exactly the way the screen does threw *"Cannot use the Ref of heldRowRetryProvider
  after it has been disposed"* after the release. **What a person sees:** the spinner on "Try again"
  stops, the record still shows as refused, and no sync starts — the release *did* happen in the
  database, so the record is pushed at the next scheduled sync round rather than now, and the list
  catches up then. Nothing is lost; the button lies about doing nothing. The exception is
  unhandled, so nothing is said. **Same fix shape as 11.235:** issue the `ref.read`s before the
  first `await`, or make the action a method on a keep-alive notifier; and the tap's failure has to
  say so. Not fixed here — the brief said report, do not fix, and it is a different screen.

- **[Found by task 11.235, 2026-09-12. Count, ranked, no action taken — for the planning session to
  decide whether a guard is worth its false positives.] The auto-dispose-plus-`ref`-after-`await`
  shape, derived across `lib/` rather than counted by grep.** The brief's 117 `await ref.*` lines
  across 17 files re-derived as **115 across 15 files** and, more usefully, is the wrong unit — a
  line reading `await ref.watch(x.future)` is the *safe* form (the `ref` call happens before its own
  `await`). What was measured instead: Riverpod disposes a bare-read auto-dispose provider **one
  microtask after the read returns**; a `ref.*` after **one** `await` of an already-resolved future
  still runs, after **two** it throws, and after any real gap (database, timer, network) it throws.
  So the derivation counts `ref.*` uses, in the provider body or in a `Ref`-taking helper it calls,
  by how many `await`s stand before them. **Population: 39 auto-disposing providers in 17 files**
  (31 functional, 8 class notifiers, 0 legacy). **Body shape present (≥1 await before a `ref` use):
  11.** **Dangerous body shape (≥2 awaits, or a real gap): 4** — `ownedProjectIds`,
  `departedProjectIds`, `syncHeldRowDetails`, `heldRowRetry`. **Of those, reached by a bare
  `ref.read(...)` with no listener holding them alive: 1** — `heldRowRetry`, the entry above. The
  other three are only ever `ref.watch`ed from a widget's `build`, so they are alive while on
  screen; their failure mode is an unhandled-exception log line if the screen is left or the
  provider invalidated mid-build, not a broken control. **Three more are one added `await` from
  the dangerous shape *and* are read bare today:** `mayWriteProjectData` (the tag database's
  project menu and the Record screen's "Add new tag"), `strandedRecordCount` (the leave/delete
  warning on Projects), and `serverHttpClient` (sign-in). They work now; the instrument that
  found them is `scratchpad`-only and was checked against the pre-fix file, which it flags, and
  against `isProjectLinked`, a synchronous arrow function it first flagged wrongly and now does
  not. **Recommendation:** one task, below the line, that fixes `heldRowRetry` and decides whether
  the three one-away providers get the same `_ownerRepairInputs` treatment; a repository-wide
  guard is not recommended yet — it would fire on the seven safe-today providers and teach people
  to ignore it.

- **[Found by task 11.220, 2026-09-10. Measured against a running server. **DECIDED by Michael

  asymmetry to **create versus change**: `RowAuthorizer._authorizeTagLifecycle` lets a contributor

  cannot un-retire it — they create a second tag for the same animal, which is the duplicate task

  `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md`'s T2 row needs its reactivation half struck through and dated per this

- **[Found by task 11.220, 2026-09-10. Measured — the branch is unreachable. **NOW TASK 11.221
  ITEM 2.**]
  About sixty lines of tag re-delivery machinery in the server are dead, and their comments still

  guarded by `item.table.name == Tables.projectTags`, and `_redeliverNewlyLinked` re-stamps those
  tags' `server_seq` so a teammate whose cursor is already past them still receives them. **`item.table`

  broken: a tag is created *inside* a project now, so it is reachable from the moment it has a

- **[Found by task 11.220, 2026-09-10. This is the one with real data behind it. **NOW TASK 11.222,

  `server/test/schema/postgres_migration_upgrade_test.dart` has no group for schema v14, which is the

  That file exists to prove a migration run *against a populated database* leaves existing rows

- **[Found by task 11.220, 2026-09-10. Exercised on a fixture with a known answer. **NOW TASK 11.221

- **[Found by task 11.220, 2026-09-10. Measured, and it predates 11.219. **SETTLED 2026-09-10: it
  does need a task, and it is 11.221 item 4.** 11.220's report and this entry disagreed — the report
  filed it as needing no task, this entry as probably needing one, and leaving both standing is the
  thing this project treats as a defect in its own records. The deciding argument is not
  reachability, which is nil from our own client, but that the response contradicts itself and there
  is a per-row fix in the grain task 10.46 established.] A
  push carrying two rows for one primary key gets one outcome, and the response contradicts
  itself.** Measured on 2026-09-10: a push of two `Tags` rows with the same `(tag_id, project_id)`
  answers `{"applied": 1, "outcomes": {"Tags/<id>/<project>": "invalid"}}`. The first row inserts and
  the second is refused by Postgres on the primary key — but the outcome map is keyed by the row
  reference, which both rows share, so the second call overwrites the first's verdict. **The caller
  is told `invalid` for a key one of whose rows landed, and `applied: 1` disagrees with the only
  outcome in the map.** This is `CLAUDE.md`'s duplicate-key rule one layer out from the instruments —
  the key here is derived from the row rather than typed by a person, so a duplicate is a client
  defect rather than an author's, but the response is unreadable either way and a client cannot tell
  which of its two rows it should retry. `verify_11_9_team_surface.py` has recorded this as a
  `note()` since before 11.219 (*"two rows with one primary key in one push"*), so it has been
  visible and unowned. **11.220 left it alone and recorded the measurement in a comment in
  `member_authorization_test.dart` beside the test that provoked it**, rather than asserting the
  behaviour and thereby blessing it.

- **[Found by task 11.34, 2026-09-09. Measured by reading the code, not reproduced against a
  running server. NEEDS A TASK.] The app offers linking a tag to a second project, and the server
  has refused exactly that since task 11.3 — for the same person, on their own two projects.**
  `RowAuthorizer._tagIsClaimedElsewhere` compares against the project named in the sync envelope,
  with no exception for a caller who owns both, so a tag referenced by project A can never be linked
  into project B. The "Link existing tag" dialog on Project Setup offers **every tag on the device**
  anyway. The link is written locally, appears to work, and is refused forever on the next sync —
  and **the held-row screen cannot explain this one**: its tag branch asks whether the record's tag
  has been added to *this* project, and for the link row itself the local answer is yes, so the
  person gets the honest fallback *"the server would not take this record and did not say why"* and
  a "Try again" that can never succeed. **This is the shape task 11.43 was opened for — a client
  offering rows the server is bound to deny — and it is the last instance of it in the tag path.**
  Copy-on-add (task 11.34's design) removes it by construction; **if that design is not built soon,
  this wants its own task**, because it is reachable by Michael with two projects on one phone.

- **[Found by task 11.34, 2026-09-09. Measured by reading the code, not reproduced. NEEDS A TASK.]
  The shared-bearing paste screen can attach an imported record to a tag belonging to a different
  project.** Its parse step walks `localTagsProvider` — every tag on the device — and stops at the
  first tag whose frequency and name match the pasted payload. If that tag belongs to another
  project, saving writes an `Observations` row into the current project naming a tag that project
  does not reach, which the server refuses and holds. The held-row screen *does* explain this one
  correctly, so the cost is a wasted save and a wait rather than a mystery. **The fix is one
  provider: match against the active project's tags, not the device's.** Small, independent of the
  copy-on-add design, and worth doing whether or not that design is built.

- **[Found by task 11.34, 2026-09-09. Measured by reading the code, not reproduced. NEEDS A
  DECISION, then possibly a task.] Importing a colleague's archive can rewrite a row in your own
  tag log.** `ProjectMerger` scopes every incoming row to the archive's manifest project — except
  that the check is skipped for tables with no project column, which is exactly `Users`,
  `User_Emails` and `Tags`. So an incoming `Tags` row whose identifier this device already holds is
  merged into the local row by last-write-wins, whatever project of yours that tag belongs to.
  Identifiers are random UUIDs, so this needs both devices to genuinely be talking about the same
  tag row — **which is precisely what happens when two people worked from one shared tag.** This is
  **cancelled task 11.29's problem on the import path**, and copy-on-add removes it by construction.
  It is listed as a decision rather than a defect because the merge is doing what the merge is for;
  what is missing is that a tag has no project to be scoped to.

- **[Found by task 11.34, 2026-09-09. Measured. A PLAN CORRECTION, and Phase 12 depends on it.]
  "Adding a tag to a project is owner-only" is false, and both task 11.34's entry and Phase 12's
  scoping paragraph say it.** Adding is **contributor-level on all three layers and deliberately**
  — `ProjectTagRepository`'s own comment settles it (*"Deactivating is owner-only; activating is
  not… additive, unblocking, contributor-level, same as creating a tag"*, task 11.12, decision
  2026-08-21), the server's `Project_Tags` branch defers to the ordinary role gradient, and
  `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` §7 row T2 says in as many words that the owner-only note *"was about T3,
  not T2."* What **is** owner-only is *removing* a tag from a project, enforced since task 11.24.
  **What actually holds within-project duplicates down is the near-duplicate warning, whose buttons
  are "Go back" and "Create anyway" and which refuses nothing on purpose.** This does not weaken the
  claim that copy-on-add makes Phase 12 *smaller* — that rests on cross-project duplicates ceasing
  to matter, which is untouched. It weakens the claim that the remaining duplicates will be **rare**,
  and that was the argument for deferring Phase 12 past the beta. **The planning session should
  strike the sentence from Phase 12 and re-take the deferral decision.**

- **[Found by task 11.34, 2026-09-09. Measured on both sides of the wire. A SECURITY-MODEL
  CORRECTION, needed whatever happens to copy-on-add.] The orphan-tag flow that §5.9(a) of
  `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` keeps a write path open to protect does not work today, in either
  direction.**
  §5.9(a) says an unlinked tag *"still has to replicate between one person's phone and their
  laptop."* It cannot. The client narrows every global table by `_globalReachClause`, which requires
  the tag id to appear in a project-scoped row of the project being synced, so an unlinked tag is
  never queued for any push; and pull narrows `Tags` to `ProjectReachability`'s tag set, computed
  the same way, so no pull can return one. Sync is per-project on both sides and an unlinked tag
  belongs to no project. **This is the recorded-failure-reason-nobody-re-derived class turned on the
  project's own records**, and it matters twice: the residual is being kept open for nothing, and it
  is what makes task 11.34's device-local tag library free. **Also measured: finding F4's stated
  route — *"Tag ids travel in Phase 6 share payloads"* — is false.** The share payload carries a tag
  *key* (frequency, pulse rate, name) and no identifier, deliberately and with a comment saying so,
  and the tag CSV export has no identifier column either. The only shipped artefact carrying tag
  identifiers is the project backup archive, and an archive only collects tags its own project
  references, which makes them claimed rather than orphaned.

- **[Found by 11.200, 2026-09-08, NOT fixed — six of them, one worth a number on its own.] Six more
  `ColorScheme` members are read in `lib/` and never passed by `app_theme.dart`, so Flutter is
  substituting a colour nobody chose.** 11.200 defined `onSurfaceVariant` and built the guard that
  derives the rest; **its first run is the first honest count of this class**, and the list lives in
  `_knownFallbacks` in `test/core/theme/color_scheme_tokens_defined_test.dart` with each member's
  actual fallback beside it. **The one that is a defect rather than a smell is `outlineVariant`**,
  which falls through `onBackground` to `onSurface`: the Position screen's dimmed observer badge
  draws the circle in `outlineVariant` and the initials on it in `onSurfaceVariant`, and before this
  task **those were the same colour — 1.00:1, an observer's initials completely invisible whenever
  their bearing is excluded from the estimate.** Defining `onSurfaceVariant` lifted it to 3.26:1
  light and 2.46:1 dark, which is visible and still not right; **the circle wants a real
  `outlineVariant`.** That is also the one place `CLAUDE.md`'s *a row out of the estimate keeps its
  dimming and gives its colour up* rule is being enforced by an accident. **The other five are
  cosmetic and can travel together:** `errorContainer`/`onErrorContainer` (four banners drawing in
  full-strength bounce red where Material 3 means a pale tint),
  `secondaryContainer`/`onSecondaryContainer` (one notice), and `surfaceContainerHighest` (three
  sites, which fall back to `surface` and want `surface` anyway — listed so it is a verdict rather
  than an oversight). **Defining `errorContainer` restyles every red banner in the app at once, so
  it wants the same treatment 11.200 got: one change, then a device look.**

- **[Found by 11.200, 2026-09-08, NOT fixed — it is the screenshot harness, not the app.] Two of the
  three screenshot profiles produce 20–47% drift on screens nothing touched, and the third does
  not.** On identical code, `ipad-13` moved every screen by 0.12–1.10% — exactly what a text-colour
  change looks like — while `iphone-6.1` reported `truth-point-edit` at 37.14% and `iphone-6.9`
  reported `map` 44.38%, `joined-sync-indicator` 46.80%, `truth-point-panel` 38.27%,
  `bearing-selected` 38.32%, `bearing-dragged` 37.39% and `position` 22.15%. **Reading the diffs
  says what they are and it is not a colour:** `truth-point-edit` is the whole page ghosted about 60
  device pixels down (the keyboard-inset artefact `/w-12` already found on `ipad-13`), and `map` is
  the **viewshed overlay present in one capture and absent from the other** — `/w-11`'s
  a-widget-existing-is-not-a-widget-drawn class, on a readiness condition that evidently still
  passes before the overlay has decoded. **The cost is that a real regression on any of those seven
  screens is currently unreportable**, because the number it would produce is smaller than the
  noise. **The iPad profile is the evidence that this is the harness**: same commit, same change, no
  outliers.

- **[Found by 11.175, 2026-09-06, NOT fixed — it is a different script's message and wants its own
  number.] A gate instrument reports "postgres never came up" for a failure that has nothing to do
  with postgres.** `verify_h6_archive_forgery.sh` waits for the database by running `psql` through
  `docker compose run ... backup psql` — that is, **inside the backup container**. So when the
  backup image cannot build, every probe fails and line 103 declares
  `HARNESS ERROR postgres never came up`, while postgres itself is healthy. **That is exactly the
  wrong-cause class this project keeps finding, in an instrument rather than in app copy**, and it
  cost real time here: it was the reason the fourth failure could not be diagnosed from the CI log
  and had to be carried as a hypothesis. **The fix is not to make the message vaguer** — it is to
  let the probe say what it could not do (reach postgres *from the backup container*), and ideally
  to distinguish "the client container would not build" from "the database did not answer", which
  are two different repairs by two different people. Low cost, and it pays off the next time the
  build breaks on somebody else's schedule.

- **[Found by 11.149, 2026-09-05, NOT fixed — it is one screen's pinned bar rather than the shell,
  and it wants its own number.] A viewer still gets an overflow stripe on the Record screen at
  AX5.** The shell now guarantees every screen **533 logical pixels** at that text size (it was
  56), and for somebody who can record the Record form is clean at every stop on the ladder. **A
  viewer is not**: their pinned action bar carries the sentence saying why they cannot save, and at
  AX5 the bar alone wants 565 pixels, so the scrolling form is squeezed to a **zero-height
  viewport** and the column overflows by 32 — the yellow-and-black stripe, which reads as a crash
  to somebody who has never seen one. **It affects only that role and only that one setting.** The
  shape of the fix is that screen's rule 3 ("the pinned bar is one short line and one button; it
  does not grow"), which the viewer's sentence quietly breaks — either the sentence moves into the
  scrolling form for a viewer, or the pinned bar gets a measured maximum and the sentence yields
  inside it. Measured and recorded per stop in `record_screen_space_budget_test.dart`, whose
  `cleanThrough` now says AX5 for an owner and AX4 for a viewer.

- **[Found by 11.149, 2026-09-05. Needs a decision, and it may want a sweep task.] A space budget
  written for a child of a `Column` is not enforced, and nothing says so.** A `Column` hands every
  non-flex child **unbounded height**, so a widget inside one cannot find out how much room it has
  and any rule of the form "this furniture gets at most X" is silently inoperative. **This is not a
  hypothesis: the first version of 11.149's own bound was written that way and measured doing
  nothing** — the collapse that appeared to be working was an accidental `TextOverflow.ellipsis`
  forcing every banner to one line, including at the default text size, where nobody had asked for
  it. Two live instances were found and fixed by that task (the app shell's banner column, and the
  Offline Data Map's top row, where the coverage legend grew to 632 logical pixels and striped the
  screen). **The general form is worth a sweep**: anywhere in `lib/` that a comment claims a piece
  of furniture is bounded, check whether the widget is a non-flex child of a `Column` — if it is,
  the bound is a sentence rather than a constraint. `AppShellBody` in `lib/widgets/shell_banner.dart`
  is the worked example of enforcing one; it lays each child into what the budget has left, in
  priority order, with a small render object.

- **[Found by 11.145, 2026-09-04, NOT fixed — it is a different defect from the four chains that
  task was about, and it wants its own number.] Changing your name on the Profile screen and then
  changing tab writes above the screen that is building.** Measured on an iPhone 17 Pro Max
  simulator (iOS 26.5), `integration_test`, debug build, reproduced on three separate runs and on
  the same two transitions each time (`/compass` → `/position`, `/more` → `/map`):
  `container.invalidate(currentUserProvider)` followed within ~300 ms by a tab switch raises
  *"setState() or markNeedsBuild() called during build."* **A Profile save does exactly that
  invalidation, and so do identity setup and sign-in.** In a debug build the framework stops on
  it; in a release build it runs anyway, which is how it has gone unnoticed.
  **It is not the shape task 11.144 fixed and it is not the four chains 11.145 was written about.**
  No `package:tritrack` frame appears in the stack at all. The entry point is
  `ConsumerStatefulElement._updateTickerMode ← _TickerModeState.didChangeDependencies ←
  StatefulElement.performRebuild` — **`TickerMode` toggling is what
  `StatefulShellRoute.indexedStack` does when you change tab** — and from there three nested
  `ProviderElement.flush` levels walk the ancestor chain `mayWriteProjectData → myProjectRole →
  currentUser`, whose rebuild notifies `myProjectRole`'s own `Ref.watch` listener, which calls
  `Ref._invalidateSelf → scheduleProviderRefresh →
  _UncontrolledProviderScopeState.scheduleRefresh → setState`. **So the widget does not have to
  watch the stale provider directly; watching anything descended from it is enough**, which is
  strictly wider than the shape the source guard models and is why 11.145 did not try to widen the
  guard to cover it — a check that flagged every screen watching anything derived would flag every
  screen.
  **What was measured and what was not.** `DataArrival.announce()` followed immediately by a tab
  switch raised nothing, on any of the five transitions, even though task 11.153's `ArrivalRefresh`
  does invalidate `mayWriteProjectDataProvider` on arrival — its settle-first guard appears to be
  doing real work, and that is a measurement on one device, not a proof. Nothing was measured about
  what a user actually sees in a release build; the honest claim is an ordering fault that a debug
  build refuses and a release build performs.
  **How to reproduce, in about ten minutes:** an `integration_test` file that calls `bootApp` and
  `goTo` from `integration_test/screenshots/harness.dart`, installs a `FlutterError.onError` that
  records the message, then for each pair of adjacent routes settles, calls
  `container.invalidate(currentUserProvider)`, and navigates to the next route within ~300 ms. The
  probe was **deliberately not committed** — an instrument nobody runs rots, and this one
  demonstrates an open defect rather than guarding a closed one.
  **Suggested shape of the fix, offered as a starting point rather than a conclusion:** the
  invalidation sites are already enumerated in `test/documentation/invalidation_sites_test.dart`,
  and `ArrivalRefresh` already owns the "do not invalidate while something is mid-build" idea for
  the sync path. The obvious question for whoever takes this is whether the same holding pattern
  belongs on `currentUserProvider`'s three invalidation sites, or whether the right place is one
  layer down in how the shell's branches are kept mounted.

- **[Found by 11.155, 2026-09-04, NOT fixed — it is outside that task's eight-checkout scope and
  wants its own number.] The offline suite has the same silent-scope hole the server suite had, and
  it is the biggest suite in the project.** `scripts/run_offline_suite.sh` runs a bare
  `flutter test` and reports PASS on its exit code. Measured the same day: `dart test` and
  `flutter test` **exit 0 when every test they loaded was skipped, and when they loaded only some
  of the files they should have** — so a run that reached a tenth of `test/` is textually a pass.
  The suite has ~2,158 tests across `test/` and a standing count of legitimate skips, so it needs
  the same treatment `server-suite` just got — `--file-reporter=json:` plus
  `scripts/assert_suite_scope.py --test-dir test`, with skips permitted but counted and printed —
  and one judgement call the tool cannot make: **whether the number of skipped tests should also be
  asserted against something, or only logged.** Logging it is the honest minimum; asserting a
  skip *count* would be a number somebody chose, which is the trap 11.150 named. **Ask the planning
  session for a task number.**

- **[Found and FIXED by 11.153, 2026-09-04. Recorded because it is not what the task was for and it
  had been live since task 11.12.] Invalidating a provider does not re-run the providers it reads,
  so changing somebody's role updated the members list and not the "Your role" card beside it.**
  `myProjectRole` is one line — it returns `projectRoleForUser` — and `_afterMembershipChange`
  invalidated the first and not the second, so it rebuilt against the cached old role and reported
  it. **This is a purely local write, nothing to do with syncing: the owner is sitting in front of
  the screen, taps to change a role, and half the screen updates.** Measured on riverpod 3.3.2 and
  fixed by putting `projectRoleForUserProvider` on the shared list;
  `project_view_refresh_test.dart` goes red without it. **The general rule is now a standing fact in
  `TriTrack_Technical_Context.md`** — a refresh list must name every provider in the chain, not the
  one the screen happens to read.

- **[Found and FIXED by 11.153, 2026-09-04. Same reason for recording: it corrects a deliberate
  decision of task 11.151.] Renaming a collar left the Record screen's tag wheel offering the old
  name until the app was restarted.** 11.151 defined `refreshTagViews(projectId: null)` as *"the
  write only touched the global tag database — a rename, a recolour, a retirement — and no link
  changed"* and invalidated only the global list on that argument. **The argument does not hold:
  `projectActiveTags` hands back whole `Tag` rows**, so the name, the frequency and the colour a
  project's tag wheel shows change every time the tag does. And it is not a corner — **the Tag
  Database screen's edit dialog offers no project when editing an existing tag, so that route passes
  null on every rename, retune and recolour.** Colour is the map's legend key (Phase 4.4), so a
  stale one is a wrong legend rather than a cosmetic lag. Null now means *every project*;
  `tag_view_refresh_test.dart` goes red under the old semantics.

- **[Found by 11.153, 2026-09-04. Needs a decision, not necessarily a task.] A refresh list can be
  guarded against mid-build invalidation only for the providers that are not families**, because
  riverpod 3.3.2 exports no way to enumerate a family's live instances. `ArrivalRefresh` states this
  limit in its own doc comment. It is tolerable today because every family on the two lists is
  `autoDispose`, which fails loudly rather than hanging — **but that is a property of the current
  providers, not a proof, and the day somebody adds a `keepAlive` family to one of these lists the
  silent-hang case is back with nothing to catch it.** Worth a note in whatever governs adding
  providers to a refresh list, or a guard test that fails when a `keepAlive` family appears on one.

- **[Found by 11.147, 2026-09-04. Needs a task, and it is bigger than any one screen.] At
  accessibility text sizes the app shell leaves its screens almost no room, and the Position
  screen's split was only the place it showed.** 11.147 measured the body left to the Position
  screen's map and panel *together*, on a 6.1-inch phone with both shell banners live: **518
  logical pixels at the default text size, 394 at AX1, 143 at AX3, 2.5 at AX4 and nothing at
  AX5.** The map's own floor is 246, so from AX3 onward the whole body is smaller than one half of
  it needs and **no split of any kind satisfies either floor** — this is not a thing task 11.147's
  remedy could have fixed, and it is why the Position screen still paints an overflow stripe at
  AX5 (`_PositionEstimationBody`'s column, over by 132 pixels). What is eating it is not the
  screen: it is the shell's two conditional banners, its navigation bar and the tag selector,
  each of which grows with the text and none of which has a budget. **The bands are sentences,
  and a sentence gains a whole line at a width nobody predicts** (task 11.139's rule), so this
  gets worse faster than linearly. Every number is measured in the test font, about twice
  Roboto's width, so **a real phone has at least this much body and probably a good deal more —
  and nobody has looked at one.** Two things a task here should decide: whether a banner that is
  taller than a fraction of the screen becomes a tap-to-read line instead, and whether the
  navigation bar's labels drop at accessibility sizes as iOS's own do.

- **[Found by 11.147, 2026-09-04. Needs a task.] The Position map's clear band is enforced against
  a reserved constant while the overlays inside it are text that grows.** Task 11.110's rule says
  the clear band is a floor, and `_minMapHeight` reserves 246 pixels for the map on the strength
  of the top control row being 56 and the bottom readout column being 94. The bottom column is a
  scale bar, a coordinate readout and a wrapping attribution credit — **all text**. Measured with
  both shell banners live, the clear band is **101 logical pixels at the default, 93 at xLarge —
  already under the 96 floor at the first notch up — 67 at xxLarge, 62 at xxxLarge and 13 at
  AX1**, with the map's height unchanged at 246 throughout. Nothing was added to the map to cause
  it. **The fix is to stop predicting the readout column's height and ask it**, the way
  `DisabledReasonNote.heightFor` does for the save row (task 11.139); the trap to avoid is
  scaling 94 by the text scaler, which under-reserves at AX1 because the credit gains a line.
  The rule is amended in place in `position_estimation_screen.dart` to say it governs the default
  text size only, per this project's rule about a rule stated absolutely while the code has
  stopped honouring it.

- **[Found by 11.147, 2026-09-04. Recorded, not obviously a task.] The Record screen's stripe at
  the top two text sizes is untouched by 11.147's remedy and is very likely the same shell
  collapse above.** 11.147 changed only the Position screen's panel/map split and its controls
  row, so the Record screen's ladder is exactly where 11.139 left it: clean through **AX3 for
  somebody who can record and AX2 for a viewer**, striping above. **That is stated as a fact
  rather than a diagnosis** — the resemblance to the shell finding is a hypothesis and nobody has
  measured the Record screen's body height. The measurement that would settle it is the one
  11.147 added to the Position ladder: print map + form height at each stop and see whether the
  body has collapsed the same way.

- **[Found by 11.139, 2026-09-04. Needs a decision from Michael before it can be a task.] Above the
  ordinary text-size slider, the Position screen has to choose between the bearings list and the
  map, and nobody has ever chosen.** At the five Larger Accessibility Sizes the panel's furniture
  plus one bearing row no longer fits above the map's own 96-pixel floor, so the panel is clamped
  and overflows — a viewer from AX1, an owner from AX3. **Both floors are real rules with reasons
  written down** (task 11.109's "the subject cannot be dragged away", task 11.110's clear band), and
  at those text sizes they contradict each other on a 6.1-inch phone. The options are: let the map
  go below its floor, let the panel scroll as a whole, or say plainly that this screen needs a
  larger device at accessibility text sizes. **11.139 deliberately did not pick one** — it is a
  design call, not a mechanical one — and it wrote the measurement down instead.

- **[Found by 11.139, 2026-09-04. Small, needs a task.] Two horizontal overflows in the Position
  panel's controls row at AX3 and above.** The row holding "N of N selected", the sort menu, "All"
  and "None" runs off the right-hand edge by 36 to 137 pixels once the labels get big enough. It is
  a different fix from the vertical work 11.139 did — the row needs to wrap or shed a control, not
  grow — and it sits above the stopping line that task declared.

- **[Found by 11.139, 2026-09-04. No task; recorded so nobody re-derives it.] The Main Map fails at
  large text in a third way that neither "stripes" nor "clips" describes.** Nothing on that screen
  is in a box that can overflow — every overlay simply covers more map as its labels grow — so the
  suite would report it perfectly healthy at every text size while **the band of map with nothing
  drawn over it falls from 229 logical pixels to 46 at AX1 and to 0 at AX4.** It is asserted now,
  as a floor that holds through the ordinary slider and is recorded as lost above it. **The general
  lesson is the one worth keeping: a screen whose furniture floats over its subject cannot report
  its own crowding through any framework error, so the only instrument that works there is a
  measured band.**

- **[Found by 11.142, 2026-09-03. Needs a task.] A terrain tile that arrived *partly* filled is
  saved and never asked for again, so a momentary blip becomes a permanent hole in the elevation
  data.** `DemTileFetcher.fetchTile` builds one 0.1° elevation tile out of about four public
  terrain images and, by design, leaves the cells it could not fetch empty rather than failing the
  whole tile. Task 11.142 stopped the *worst* case — a tile where nothing at all arrived is no
  longer written to disk — because saving that one turns a single offline attempt into coverage
  the download loop believes in forever. **The partial case is still saved**, and the only question
  the loop ever asks is `hasTile`, which cannot tell a complete tile from a three-quarters-full
  one. What it costs a person: a viewshed permanently missing a wedge of terrain, with the app
  correctly saying it is incomplete and no way offered to fix it. **The fix needs a record of how
  full a tile is** — a sidecar, a filename, or a coverage column — plus a re-fetch when a tile is
  wanted and is known to be short. **Deliberately not done in 11.142**, which was asked to
  establish whether the defect exists and say so on screen, not to redesign the tile store.

- **[Found by 11.142, 2026-09-03. Belongs to the content lane, not to `lib/`.] The screenshot
  harness runs a retry policy the app does not, which is why the published Members picture shows
  two spinners.** `bootApp` in `integration_test/screenshots/harness.dart` builds its
  `ProviderContainer` with no `retry:`, so every provider in the photographed app runs Riverpod's
  default — ten attempts over 38.2 seconds — while the shipped app runs `appRetryPolicy` and gives
  up after 1.6. A provider that fails immediately therefore spins for most of a minute in the
  harness and for under two seconds on a phone. **Two consequences.** The one-line fix is
  `retry: appRetryPolicy` on that container. And `readiness.dart`'s comment on `project-members`
  states a cause that was never true — *"their providers never resolve"* — which is the
  wrong-cause class turned on the project's own records, the thing `CLAUDE.md` warns about twice.
  **Not edited by task 11.142**, which is a code task and does not touch the content lane's files.

- **[Found by 11.142, 2026-09-03. Scope note, no new task.] `retry_policy_applied_test.dart`
  cannot see the file that got this wrong.** It scans `lib/` for `ProviderScope(`; the harness
  above is an `UncontrolledProviderScope` fed by a raw container, in `integration_test/`. Its own
  doc comment already says it says nothing about containers built in tests, and that exemption is
  right for an ordinary widget test — **but the screenshot harness is not measuring a unit, it is
  photographing the app, and a photograph taken under a different retry policy is a photograph of
  a different app.** Widening the guard would put a content-lane file into the code lane's red,
  which is task 11.118's lesson, so the honest home for this is whatever task fixes the harness.

- **[Found by 11.138, 2026-09-02. CLOSED the same day by Michael's answer — no task follows.] The
  only way to get elevation data into the app is to draw an area on a map, and the second route
  the interface advertised did not exist.** Manage Offline Maps carried a permanently greyed
  `Import DEM file (.asc) — unavailable` button whose reason lived in a tooltip a phone never
  opens. Task 11.138 established the reason rather than rewording it, and it was worse than the
  source comment claimed: that comment described re-wiring `DemRepository` against the tiled
  store, **and `DemRepository` does not exist** — it was deleted in `886d7ce` when elevation moved
  to `DemTileStore`'s 0.1° lattice. The button was not awaiting a rewire; it was awaiting a
  rewrite of something already gone, and its TODO pointed readers at a class that had not existed
  for months. **The button is removed**, replaced with a line saying where elevation actually
  comes from (draw the area on the Offline Data Map, tick elevation).
  **Michael answered the open question on 2026-09-02: he never needs to load an elevation file
  from disk.** So there is no unwritten feature behind this control and no follow-up task — the
  removal is the whole answer, and this entry is closed rather than pending.
  **The reusable lesson is the TODO, not the DEM.** A comment naming the class that will fix
  something is a reference to code it does not own, and a deletion does not go back and correct
  it — this is the same shape as `CLAUDE.md`'s rule about a harness patching a line it does not
  own, and about a status document repeating a failure reason nobody re-derived. **Before
  repeating a TODO's stated plan, check that the thing it names still exists.**
- **[Found by 11.138, 2026-09-02.] The capture buttons are greyed with no reason during the
  seconds before the compass produces its first heading.** `POINT` and `RANGE` are disabled when
  `liveHeadingDeg` is null even on a device that *has* a compass, and the visible line under them
  covers only the no-compass-at-all case. **Deliberately not fixed by 11.138**: the state is
  momentary, so a line that appears and vanishes a second later is its own defect, and choosing
  between "wait a beat before showing it" and "say nothing" is a judgement about a screen nobody
  in the execution environment can watch. Worth a look on hardware first — it may be too fast to
  see.
- **[Found by 11.138, 2026-09-02. Needs a device, not a task.] What the tag list's new "view
  only" label costs per row is between nothing and 20 logical pixels, and the harness cannot
  narrow it.** A tag row nobody may edit now says so in words on its subtitle instead of showing
  a bare padlock. Measured at 6.1-inch phone geometry it adds one subtitle line — 20 pixels —
  but per task 11.133 the test font is about twice Roboto's width, and this subtitle is wrapping
  in the harness at a length that fits one line on a phone. **Two words shorter did not help**
  ("locked" measured the same 20), which is the tell that the harness, not the label, is at the
  wrap boundary. Per task 11.87's rule this needs one look at a real phone with a long tag list,
  not another round of test output.

- **[Found by 11.133, 2026-09-02. TASK 11.134 item 2, given 2026-09-02.] The satellite basemap's credit is a hard-coded
  copy of a string Esri publishes and changes, and it was already wrong.** The app named
  **Maxar**; the service's own metadata (`.../World_Imagery/MapServer?f=pjson`, queried
  2026-09-02) names **Vantor** — Maxar was renamed. Task 11.133 corrected the value and left the
  mechanism, because changing it is a network call on a screen that has none. **This is the
  correct-when-written-then-silently-falsified class in its purest form:** Esri's own
  instructions say to read `copyrightText` from the service and to "frequently verify names as
  data source providers can change", and a `const` string cannot do either. It also has teeth
  that most copy drift does not — showing the credit is a licence condition, so a stale credit is
  a breach rather than a typo, and **nothing in the app or the suite would ever say so.** Two
  shapes are worth pricing against each other: fetch `copyrightText` at runtime and fall back to
  the constant when offline (correct, but adds a network dependency to the map's credit), or keep
  the constant and add a check that fetches the metadata and fails when the two disagree
  (cheaper, catches it on a schedule rather than in the field, and cannot break the app). **The
  same question applies to OpenStreetMap and OpenTopoMap** — both publish their required strings
  on pages that can change — so this is one task about a mechanism, not three about strings.
- **[Found by 11.133 via its licence research, 2026-09-02. TASK 11.134 item 1, given 2026-09-02 and placed first — and it can stop the
  map working with no error the app can explain.] The OpenStreetMap tile usage policy requires a
  distinct, stable `User-Agent` naming the app, and says traffic using a library default
  (`okhttp/x.y`, `Java/1.8`, and similar) **will be blocked.** Nothing in this repository was
  found setting one for tile requests; the tiles are fetched by `flutter_map`'s own client.
  **Uncertain and not verified:** I did not confirm what `flutter_map` actually sends, and the
  policy page was read as part of the attribution research rather than tested against. The
  failure mode is what makes it worth a task anyway — a block arrives as tiles that stop loading,
  which the app currently reports as nothing at all, on the one screen a field tech spends the
  day on, and possibly only after the app has been in use long enough to be noticed. **A task
  should first find out what is being sent** (that is the cheap half) before deciding what to do
  about it.
- **[Found by 11.133, 2026-09-02. DECIDED 2026-09-02 by the planning session: add it. Carried
  as task 11.134 item 3.] Whether "Powered by Esri" is owed at all.** **The decision is to satisfy
  it rather than answer it.** 11.133 could not settle from Esri's published pages whether direct
  raster tile access triggers the requirement, and **the cost of being wrong is asymmetric**: the
  text is four words, Esri's terms allow it to live behind a menu or button, and App Info and the
  credit's ⓘ are both already exactly that. **A question that costs more to answer than to
  satisfy should be satisfied.** Recorded as a decision rather than a finding so nobody re-opens
  the research.
  **The original finding follows.** Esri states it as a separate requirement from data
  attribution, covering use of their "APIs, SDKs, open source libraries, services, or data".
  This app fetches raster tiles from an Esri service directly through `flutter_map`, and nothing
  read on 2026-09-02 settles whether that triggers it. **It is probably cheaper to satisfy than
  to answer:** the same page allows the text to live "in a window that is accessible from a menu
  or button", and App Info and the credit's ⓘ are both exactly that — so adding the line there
  costs one string and closes the question either way.
- **[Found by 11.128, 2026-09-02. HALF-FIXED — the other half needs the planning session, and
  it is one line.] `test/documentation/dev_stack_host_prerequisites_test.dart` has been RED on
  `main` since task 11.125's commit.** Two offenders. The first was real and is fixed here:
  **`scripts/server_up.sh` did not source `scripts/lib/host_user.sh`.** 11.125 taught that
  script to accept `-f`, which is exactly what made it able to bring up
  `docker-compose.dev-lan.yml` — the overlay that turns the file-based magic-link sender on —
  and that overlay falls back to `0:0` when `TRITRACK_DEV_UID`/`GID` are unset. **On the beta
  Linux host that means the development server runs as root and every sign-in link it writes is
  `root:root 0600`, unreadable by the person who asked for it, while `/auth/magic-link` answers
  `202` either way (§4.5).** Same ownership fault 11.125 existed to stop, one directory over,
  introduced by the fix. The second offender is
  `.claude/commands/11-125-the-red-is-not-what-the-record-says.md` (since deleted, under the delete-the-command-when-its-comms-entry-resolves rule), which quotes a raw
  `docker compose -f … -f docker-compose.dev-lan.yml up --build -d` line in prose while
  describing the defect. **Claude Code did not touch it — `.claude/commands/` is the planning
  session's to stage** — so the guard is still red. **Recommended fix: correct that one line in
  place rather than widening the guard's skip set.** `CLAUDE_DOCS/` is skipped as a historical
  record; a slash-command file is not the same thing, because a command file is an instruction
  somebody runs, and blinding the guard to that directory would blind it to every future command
  that tells a person to bring a stack up by hand.

- **[Found by 11.128, 2026-09-02. NOT FIXED — needs a task, and it is the reason `/ready`
  earns its keep.] When the database goes away underneath a running server, the operational
  visibility §4.5 promises does not exist.** Measured: with the server up and Postgres stopped,
  `POST /auth/magic-link` answered **`202`** — correctly, because §4.5 requires a byte-identical
  response and `auth_routes.dart` swallows the internal failure on purpose. Its comment says
  *"operational visibility comes from the audit log below"* — **and the audit write fails too,
  because it needs the same database.** The server printed one `audit log write failed:
  PgException` line to stdout and that was the entire record. So in this state a person is told
  their sign-in link was sent, it never arrives, and **nothing anywhere holds a record of it**.
  Neither half is wrong on its own; the gap is that the compensating control is unavailable in
  exactly the failure it compensates for. `/ready` now names the state to an operator who asks,
  which is a mitigation and not a fix — nothing pushes.

- **[Found by 11.128, 2026-09-02. FIXED the same day, by 11.128, after Michael said to make
  the change.] The `server` service in `docker-compose.yml` had no `healthcheck:` at all**, so
  `docker compose ps` reported nothing about the one process anybody uses. It now runs
  `/app/bin/server --health-check` — a second mode of the same binary, because the runtime image
  is `debian:bookworm-slim` with no `curl` and the Dockerfile gives up the whole Dart SDK on a
  smaller-attack-surface argument. **Its verdict is `/health` and its message is `/ready`:** a
  server whose database is gone reports *healthy* on purpose, and its health log says in a
  sentence that sign-in is dead and which route to ask.

  **One thing this entry said before it was built was wrong, and measuring it is what caught
  it: a healthcheck does not make anything restart.** `restart: unless-stopped` reacts to the
  container *exiting*; Docker Engine's restart policies do not act on health at all — that is a
  Swarm/Kubernetes behaviour. Forced unhealthy on a real stack, the container sat at
  `Up (unhealthy)` with the same process id and a restart count of zero. So the honest claim is
  visibility, not recovery, and `server/README.md` says exactly that. **The original entry
  below-the-line reasoning — "so `restart: unless-stopped` cannot restart a process that is
  alive-but-wedged" — was an assumption about Docker that nobody had checked**, which is the
  same shape as the finding this task started from.

- **[Found by 11.76, 2026-09-01. NOT FIXED — TASK 11.121, given 2026-09-01, with the criterion narrowed to `android:exported`.]
  The new merged-manifest guard only checks `<uses-permission>` and `<uses-feature>`,
  which is what task 11.66's own worked example checked — it does not check every shape
  Gradle can merge in.** `CLAUDE_DOCS/CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md`'s "second pass" table records
  four more shapes task 11.66 found by hand and none of them are XML a
  `uses-permission`/`uses-feature` grep would ever match: `file_picker`'s `<queries>` entry,
  geolocator's `<service>` and `<activity>`, `androidx.profileinstaller`'s exported
  `<receiver>`, and `androidx.window`'s `<uses-library>`. A fifth plugin that adds a new
  exported component of one of those shapes would merge into the built APK silently, the
  same way the location permission and the sandbox entitlement did before task 11.40, and
  nothing in CI would say so. Recorded rather than fixed because generalizing the check to
  "every element the merged manifest can contain" is a real design question — which
  elements are capability-relevant is closer to `_isCapabilityPlistKey`'s judgement call
  for `Info.plist` than to a fixed list — and task 11.76's own scope was the two shapes it
  was asked to close.

- **[Found by 11.113, 2026-09-01. FIXED by task 11.114, 2026-09-01.] The sync bar's colour
  never changed just because sync had stopped happening.** "Synced 2 min ago" and "Synced 3 days ago"
  render in the same calm grey — the last-successful-sync time is only ever *printed*, and
  nothing compares it against now (verified across every use of `lastSuccessAt` in `lib/`).
  Only a *failed attempt* changes the bar, and **the app forgets the last failure when it
  restarts**, so a sync that failed at 9am shows a calm bar again after a restart at 10am.
  **What it costs a person:** a field tech whose sync broke on Monday sees a calm bar all
  week and finds out on Friday. This is how Michael came to see "Synced 21 hours ago"
  against a server the app had never contacted.
  **The design, decided with Michael on 2026-09-01:**
  1. **Threshold: 24 hours since the last successful sync**, flat, regardless of the
     frequency setting. The warning is about *where the data is*, not about whether the
     schedule is behaving — somebody on "only when I ask" still has records in exactly one
     place. A threshold that bends to the setting can be argued into silence.
  2. **Colour follows what is at risk, not the clock** (Michael's decision, of two offered).
     **Red, with the count, when records are waiting** — those exist on one device and
     nowhere else: *"Not synced in 3 days — 47 records are only on this phone."* **Amber
     when nothing is pending** and it is only stale incoming data: *"Not synced in 3 days.
     You may be missing teammates' records."* The bar already computes `pendingCount`, so
     this costs nothing. It also matches how the bar already uses the two colours —
     `rowsRefused` is red because a record exists in one place; `recordsMissing` is amber
     because nothing is lost.
  3. **Dismissable, re-arming at the next 04:00 local time** (Michael's decision; he chose
     4am over the 8am he first proposed and over a plain 24-hour timer, because *"likely
     before fieldwork begins in most situations"* — which puts the reminder ahead of the
     workday instead of into it). **No minimum-interval floor**, deliberately: the only way
     to get a same-day reappearance is to dismiss between midnight and 04:00, and the cost
     there is one extra tap, once. That is much cheaper than a warning returning mid-transect,
     which is what an 8am re-arm would have done to a crew leaving at 5am.
  4. **Dismissed means the alarm goes, not the bar.** It falls back to the ordinary grey
     "Synced 3 days ago" line rather than hiding. That line is what the bar was built for —
     the glance on the way out of a trailhead — and hiding it would make a dismissed device
     look identical to a healthy one.
  5. **The dismiss applies to staleness and to nothing else.** It must never be able to
     silence a held record, a rejected certificate, a refused address or an ended membership.
     Those are conditions with a remedy and somebody who has to act; **a dismissable one is a
     condition nobody ever fixes.** This is the acceptance criterion most worth a test.
  6. **Fold in the restart amnesia** above, or say why not. Staleness catches it at the
     24-hour mark but not before.
  **Point 6, decided by Claude Code rather than folded in:** the restart amnesia is **not**
  fixed here. Fixing it means persisting `SyncFailureCause` and `SyncSchedule`'s
  `consecutiveFailures`/`stoppedReason` durably per project — today `SyncController.build`
  reconstructs `SyncSchedule` from only `frequency` and `lastAttemptAt`, so a live
  `broken`/`certificateRejected` state genuinely resets to `healthy` on every restart or
  provider rebuild, not only in the >24h case this task closes. That is a second, separable
  persistence change with its own storage and migration surface, not a fold-in — **needs a
  task number.** Until it exists, a device that restarts within 24 hours of a real failure
  can show a calm bar for up to 24 hours; **staleness now bounds that window, where before
  it was unbounded.**
  **Why a dismiss at all, since it is the part that looks like a concession:** task 10.12's
  own reasoning is that an indicator people learn to ignore is worse than none. A crew in a
  valley for a week with a permanent red bar stops seeing the bar — including on the day it
  turns red for a held record. **The dismiss is what protects every other state the bar has.**
  **Where it goes:** `SyncStatus.health` in `sync_provider.dart` gains the state;
  `sync_status_banner.dart` and `sync_status_screen.dart` switch on it exhaustively already;
  the dismissal timestamp belongs in `syncStateStoreProvider` beside `frequency` and
  `lastAttemptAt`, which is device-wide and already `SharedPreferences`-backed.
  **One thing to measure, per task 11.109:** the bar gains a dismiss control, and a real
  touch target fights a 12pt strip. Say what the bar looks like afterwards.

- **[Found by 11.113, 2026-09-01. Given a task number (11.115), CLOSED 2026-09-02.] "My phone
  has no signal" and "the server is switched off" are one state, both reported as "Offline".**
  Task 11.115 investigated a device-connectivity check and closed the item as not reliably
  possible app-wide — iOS/macOS's `NWPathMonitor` cannot distinguish "no network" from "network
  up, nothing behind it" at all, so a check would answer confidently and wrongly on exactly the
  captive-portal case this matters for. Full reasoning in task 11.115's write-up and in
  `lib/data/sync/sync_failure.dart`.

- **[Found by 11.105, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — needs a task number.] A provider that fails
  makes the app wait 38 seconds before it can say anything.** Riverpod 3 retries a failed
  provider automatically — ten attempts, exponential backoff to a 6.4s ceiling, skipped only
  for an `Error` or a `ProviderException`. Anything that merely `implements Exception` gets
  the full run, and `p.future` stays pending throughout. **Measured: 38.2 seconds.** Nothing
  in the app sets `retry:` on its `ProviderScope`, so this is every awaited provider on every
  screen. Task 11.105 bounded the one site it touched with the 15-second timeout that was
  already there; **every other `await ref.read(x.future)` in `lib/` is unbounded** — a
  spinner that runs for most of a minute and then shows an error, which a person in the field
  reads as a hang. **The action:** decide whether the app sets its own `retry` policy (a
  one-line change at `ProviderScope`, and the right answer is probably "no retry for a
  refusal, retry for a network read"), or whether each awaiting call site gets a timeout.
  This is a decision, not a defect fix, which is why it is here rather than done.

- **[Found by 11.105, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — needs a task number. Same wrong-cause class as
  11.104, on the beta path.] A self-signed or untrusted certificate on the LAN server reports
  "this device could not tell why".** `server_config_screen.dart` catches `SocketException`
  and then `http.ClientException`, but `HandshakeException` is a `TlsException` and neither —
  `package:http` does not convert it — so a TLS failure falls to the catch-all and produces
  *"Sign-in did not finish, and this device could not tell why."* **This is the likely case,
  not the edge case:** task 10.49 committed a terminating reverse proxy and §4.1 requires
  https, so the first thing a beta tester meets on their own LAN server is a certificate the
  phone does not trust. **The action:** give `HandshakeException` its own sentence naming the
  certificate, ending in what to do about it. Found by task 11.105's sweep for the same shape
  at non-Riverpod boundaries; **not fixed there because it is a missing branch rather than a
  dead one**, and the task's remit was branches that cannot fire.

- **[Found by 11.105, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — needs a task number.] A failed identity read
  leaves the app on the splash screen forever, with no message.**
  `splash_screen.dart:59-63` does `Future.wait([delay, ref.read(currentUserProvider.future)])`
  with no `try`. `currentUserProvider` is keepAlive, so its error does arrive — after the 38
  seconds above — and then goes unhandled, `context.go` never runs, and the green splash
  screen stays up. **What it costs somebody:** the app appears to have frozen on launch, with
  nothing to read and nothing to tap, and the only recovery is force-quit and hope. **The
  action:** the splash needs a failure state that says the identity could not be read and
  offers something — retry, or continue to identity setup.

- **[Found by 11.105, 2026-08-31. FIXED 2026-08-31 in commit 41ba510, at Michael's decision.]
  Forty-six screens could show a person a raw exception — SQL statement and their own field
  data included.** Reported to Michael as three instances; the sweep found **sixty**
  `$e`-style interpolations of a caught error, of which 10 are `debugPrint` behind
  `kDebugMode` (legitimate), 4 chain a cause into a new exception in the data layer (not
  display), and **46 put the result on screen**. Michael chose to fix all 46 rather than
  grandfather any onto an allowlist. New: `describeFailure`
  (`lib/core/errors/failure_message.dart`) as the one place deciding what a person is told,
  with a stated three-point bar for which exception types may show their own message; the
  `LoadFailure` widget for the 29 `.when(error:)` branches, which were one situation rather
  than 29 judgements; and `test/documentation/raw_error_in_ui_test.dart` as the standing
  check. **Two things found during the work are worth more than the sweep:**
  - **The check was blind, and only caught its own blindness because a subagent reported a
    site it had left behind.** A fixed 600-character window on arrow bodies meant a `Text` in
    `server_config_screen.dart` had its `$e` past the window, so the check reported all clear
    on a file that still had the defect in it. It now balances brackets, and both shapes are
    verified red against a deliberately reintroduced defect.
  - **Task 11.105's own guard rejected new code written for this commit.** An
    `InvalidServerUrl` extractor was added to the authored-message list and was dead code,
    because `requireValidServerUrl` is called only from an autoDispose provider's build.
    Written by somebody who had just spent a day on that exact defect. The reasoning is kept
    in the file rather than silently dropped.

- **[Found by 11.105, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — needs a task number.] A viewshed that fails
  tells nobody anything.** `ComputationFailed(label, message)` is referenced in exactly one
  file — the one that declares it. The map's progress bar renders only
  `if (status is ComputationRunning)` (`map_screen.dart:883`), so on failure the bar simply
  vanishes. **What it costs somebody:** they tap Viewshed, watch a bar disappear, and have no
  way to tell whether it finished, failed, or never ran. The 46-site sweep wrote a real
  sentence into that state because it is what a renderer would use, but **nothing draws it.**
  **The action:** render the failed state, or delete it and say why it is not needed.

- **[Found by 11.105, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — small.] The viewshed has no control its
  failure message can point at.** `ViewshedConfig.maxRangeMeters` is hard-coded at 10 km and
  no screen changes it, so "try a smaller radius" — the obvious advice for a computation that

- **[Found by 11.100, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — small, needs a task number or a line in
  another one.]** **The navigation-target flag on the map is drawn about 13 pixels left of

  the box's *bottom* on the coordinate — right for a pin whose tip is at the bottom centre,

  a reader takes as the target, sits about half a box-width to the left. **What it costs
  somebody:** the flag is what you walk towards, and at survey zoom 13 pixels is tens of
  metres. **Not fixed here because 11.100's brief was explicit that item 1 ships alone if it
  grows**, and because the right fix is a judgment call — either `Alignment(-0.5, 1)`-style
  nudge, or swap the glyph for `Icons.place` and keep `topCenter`. Checked and **not** a

- **[Found by 11.100, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — belongs to the content lane, not to `lib/`.]**

- **[Found by 11.93, 2026-08-31. FIXED IN 11.93 — recorded because the class is wider than
  the instance, and the wider half is NOT fixed.]** **A caller could rewrite an identity
  column to their own name on an update.** `RowAuthorizer._authorizeNaming` asked "does this
  row name the caller?" before it asked the update rules, so writing *your own* name over
  somebody else's on an existing row passed. It was unreachable while every table naming an
  author also refused the write itself — you cannot rewrite the author of a row you may not
  touch — and 11.93 created the first table where both are true at once. Fixed for every
  table (the update rules now run first, and an identity column must be unchanged including
  nulls, so an edit can neither forge an attribution nor erase one). **What is not fixed:**
  `authorization_test.dart`'s task-11.24 group derives the tables it probes from
  `MutationRule.namesRowAuthor`, and since 11.93 that is no longer the same set as "tables
  that name a person". 11.93 added its own derived group for the new shape rather than
  widening theirs, because widening pulls in `Projects` and `Project_Memberships`, which
  are refused for different reasons and need their own cases. **Someone should decide
  whether the two groups become one derivation over `identityUserColumns`.**

- **[Found by 11.93, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — needs a task number.]** **Every repository's
  mutation rule is a hand-maintained second copy of `tableMutationRules`.** Each

  tests: flipping `Actual_Tag_Locations` to `MutationRule.author` in the shared rule table
  changed no client behaviour and turned no test red — the client kept using its own copy.
  This is the hand-maintained-mirror class task 10.66 made a standing criterion, and the
  fix is one test asserting `repository.rule == tableMutationRules[repository.table]` for
  every repository. 11.93 asserted it for the one table it was about; the other twelve are

- **[Found by 11.93, 2026-08-31. NOT FIXED — small, and it is a copy defect.]** **The
  truth-point precision helper text claimed a mechanism that is false half the time.** It
  read "This was prefilled from the device's reported GPS accuracy", which is true of a
  point recorded on a GPS fix, false of one recorded on a map pin (where the prefill is
