- **[Found by 11.92, 2026-08-31. Michael decided both halves the same day. NEEDS A TASK
  NUMBER — one task, because all of it is one schema migration.]** `Actual_Tag_Locations`
  is missing three columns, and the gap is not cosmetic.
  1. **`user_id` — who found it. Michael: "the truth point should be recorded with the
     user that logged it."** Today the only person-shaped column is
     `sync.last_modified_by`, which names whoever last edited the row. Consequences
     shipped in 11.92 that this reverses: the Log's observer filter hides every truth
     point, the Team tab's member sort puts them last, and edit/delete are gated on the
     project role alone (`truthPointEditVerdict`) because there is no author to compare
     against. **Michael settled the follow-on question on 2026-08-31: other contributors
     can edit.** So recording the author does *not* make editing author-only — the role
     gradient stays the rule and `truthPointEditVerdict` stays exactly as 11.92 shipped
     it. The column records **who found it**, which is a fact about the record, not a
     permission. **The task must not quietly tighten the gate while adding the column.**
  2. **An editable position. Michael: a user must be able to nudge the point on the map.**
     11.92 shipped edit-precision-and-kind only, on the reasoning that somebody who stood
     in the wrong place should re-record. **That reasoning is wrong for the case this
     feature exists for.** Michael's example: a collared lion tracked from a truck. Nobody
     walks into a pride to stand on the animal, so the recorded position is a place near
     it and the true point is metres away. Re-recording does not help — the person is
     still in the truck. **The record screen already supports this at creation time** (a
     manual map pin, `PositionSource.manualPin`, with the precision prefill deliberately
     suppressed because a pin's precision is not the phone's GPS accuracy); what is
     missing is the same picker on the edit path.
  3. **`position_source` — GPS fix or hand-placed pin.** Falls out of (2) and matters most
     there: `Observations` records it and this table does not, so a truth point cannot say
     whether its coordinate was measured at the collar or eyeballed across 200 m of
     savannah. The precision radius is currently the only thing carrying that distinction,
     and it carries it by convention rather than by record. **Once a position is editable
     this stops being a nicety** — a point that began as a GPS fix and was later nudged by
     hand is a different claim from either, and nothing would say so.
  - **Sequencing note for whoever writes the task:** the app is at schema v10 and all three
    columns are additive, so this is one v11 migration plus the backfill question for rows
    already written (a truth point recorded before v11 has no author and no source, and
    per this project's standing rule those read as *not recorded* rather than being filled
    in from `last_modified_by`). Task 11.16's rule applies: test it as an upgrade of a
    populated database, not a fresh build.

- **[Found by 11.88, 2026-08-31 — RESOLVED 2026-08-31, same day. Kept as the record.]**
  Once 11.88 fixed the compose-project mismatch and the wrong JSON field (see task 11.88's
  own entry), `verify_11_49_server_reads.py`'s "Entry 28" timing check reached a real
  server in CI for the first time and reported exactly the signal
  `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.13 ("The clock is a channel too") already documents from
  three earlier manual Linux measurements: a stable sign (9/9, ~24–70 µs) on the
  forbidden-versus-fictional pair while the null pair genuinely flipped. **Not a new
  leak** — the same residual task 11.72 already found and measured, simply never
  baselined because §4.13 recorded it as "accepted... subject to Michael's review," not
  yet final. **Michael answered directly, the same day: "i'm fine with someone learning
  the size of the team that way."** §4.13 now records that decision. **The first fix
  tried — a BASELINE entry mirroring R-2's shape — was wrong and was reverted the same
  day**: R-2 is a deterministic finding (always ADMITTED until someone closes it); this
  timing signal is genuinely probabilistic (it sits at this host's noise floor, so the
  sign is only *sometimes* stable), and a BASELINE entry only handles "still open" versus
  "now closed" — it does not have a mode for "may or may not trigger, both are fine."
  Baselining it just inverted the failure condition: the check went from failing when the
  sign happened to be stable to failing when it happened not to be, watched live on the
  very next run. **Converted to a `note()` instead** — an observation, not a pass/fail
  gate — matching the file's own long-standing comment above this probe ("Keep it, and do
  not treat it as the measurement"); the actual, magnitude-bounded enforcement is
  `server/test/security/authorization_timing_test.dart`, in the ordinary server suite on
  every commit. `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`'s own `Cg` check measures the same underlying
  phenomenon but was not baselined here — its one observed failure that day matched task
  11.90's separate, already-scheduled defect (a guard that tests sign, not magnitude,
  under machine load) rather than this genuine small residual, and blanket-accepting `Cg`
  now risks hiding a future load-driven false positive or a real regression that 11.90's
  fix is meant to catch. **Revisit once 11.90 lands**: that is the right point to decide
  whether `Cg` also needs a baseline entry citing this same acceptance.

- **[Found by 11.88, 2026-08-31 — RESOLVED 2026-08-31 by task 11.91 (`0c77ce4`). A name
  collision in `verify_11_49_server_reads.py` silently discards a genuine attack
  result.]** Confirmed
  live: the "shape" broken-control variant's patch (task 11.49's own VARIANTS) removes the
  session-listing bound and injects a `source_address` field into that response, and the
  reads instrument correctly detects the `source_address` field flip **only when nothing
  overwrites its verdict** — but `attack()` stores results in a plain dict keyed by the
  literal description string, and this script calls `attack()` with the *exact same*
  string for unrelated checks on different routes: `"raising the bound with a limit in
  the query string"` is used by the sessions route (line 930), the `/projects/mine`
  directory (line 1655), **and** `join-requests/mine` (line 1905); `"the response carrying
  anything shaped like a source address"` is used by the sessions route (line 792) **and**
  a separate disclosure-surface route (line 1597). Whichever call runs last in the file
  wins, silently overwriting an earlier, genuinely-flipped ADMITTED with a later,
  unrelated, correctly-refused result. This is why the "shape" variant showed 2 of 9
  required attacks staying BLIND in CI on 2026-08-31 even though the server's behaviour
  had genuinely changed — the instrument's own bookkeeping hid it, not the server. **A
  mechanical scan for repeated `attack()` name strings in this file found two more
  candidates not yet confirmed to collide in practice: `"listing with {label}"` and
  `"the response carrying {label}"`** — both f-string templates whose `label` values were
  not checked for overlap across call sites. This is the same class the project's own
  `gate_c_adversarial_baseline.json` comments already warn about for baseline lookups
  ("`Cd` names three distinct checks... a baseline keyed on it could absorb a genuinely new
  failure under an existing entry's identity") — here it is the same shape one level
  earlier, in the RESULTS dict itself rather than a baseline file, and it is data loss
  rather than a lookup ambiguity. **Fix the class**: every `attack()`/`control()`/
  `discriminator()` name in this file needs to be unique (or namespaced by route), and the
  two unconfirmed candidates need checking, not just the two confirmed ones. This has never
  shown up before because this is the first time `verify_11_49_broken_control.py` ever
  reached a real server in CI (see task 11.88, and its sibling entry above).
  **Resolution (task 11.91):** registration of a duplicate name is now a hard `SystemExit`
  naming both call sites. All five real collisions (the two named here, one of the two
  "unconfirmed" candidates, plus a third-route collision `Cd`-shaped one the plan did not
  know about) are namespaced by route; `"listing with {label}"` was established not to
  collide and left alone. `verify_11_49_server_reads.py`'s healthy sweep and all three
  variants of `verify_11_49_broken_control.py` were re-run live — the "shape" variant now
  flips all 9 of 9 required attacks, including these two. See task 11.91's own entry for
  the full disposition of what this invalidated.

- **[Found by 11.85 (round 9), 2026-08-31 — NEEDS A TASK. Finding R-3.] The
  adversarial pass can report a blocking finding when the machine is busy.**
  `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`'s `Cg` timing check **failed inside the full gate
  run** — `real-minus-fictional +0.125ms, positive in 7/7 trials` — and then
  **held on three consecutive re-runs on the same host with nothing else
  running**: +0.030 ms (4/7), -0.036 ms (2/7), +0.028 ms (5/7). Sign flips,
  magnitude at the noise floor. Task 11.72 measured the genuine residual at
  **+5.0 µs**; 125 µs is twenty-five times that, and the failing run was
  concurrent with seventeen other instruments on a laptop.
  **The mechanism, so this is a fix and not a re-run.** `Cg` has a drift guard:
  if the fictional-versus-fictional null has a *stable* sign (0/7 or 7/7) it
  reports INCONCLUSIVE, because a host whose drift dominates cannot resolve the
  effect. On the failing run the null was 5/7, so the guard stayed quiet while a
  load-driven bias pushed both comparisons positive. **The guard tests the null's
  sign and not its magnitude.** The repair is to compare the between-pair
  difference against the null *distribution* — already collected every run, and
  currently used only for its sign — rather than against zero.
  **Why it matters even though it fails safe.** It produces a false blocker, not
  a missed one, so nothing is left undefended — but §6's criterion 4 says the
  adversarial pass must match its baseline *exactly*, and a check that goes red
  under load quietly turns that into "on a quiet machine". A blocker nobody can
  reproduce is how a gate stops being believed. Registered as R-3 in
  `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §22.4.1.

- **[Found by 11.85 (round 9), 2026-08-31 — NEEDS A TASK. Finding R-1.] A stranger
  asking to join can choose what the second line of the owner's approval tile says.**
  `RowValidator.isWellFormedPersonName` refuses two character classes — C0/C1
  controls, and the bidirectional overrides, marks and isolates — and **neither
  contains `U+2028 LINE SEPARATOR` or `U+2029 PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR`**, which Flutter's
  text engine treats as hard line breaks. So a claimed name may carry a line break,
  and the owner's pending tile renders a second line the requester wrote — an
  address-shaped one, if they like. Confirmed live (16 name attacks, 14 refused,
  these two accepted) and **measured on screen**:
  `test/features/more/join_request_name_rendering_test.dart` reads the break offset
  off the tile's own render object and finds it exactly where the requester put it.
  **Below §4's bar and scheduled rather than accepted**, because what was measured
  is narrower than what the control's own comment claims to prevent: the tile's
  **title is the server-authenticated email address and is untouched**, the claim is
  still prefixed "Says they are", and six requester-chosen lines grow the tile
  rather than clipping its own text. The owner is still looking at the real address
  when they tap Approve.
  **Why this is not a one-line fix somebody should just make.** The regex is the
  *shared* declaration `Users.first_name` and `Users.last_name` carry, added by task
  11.81 for exactly this reason. Widening it is a question about **rows that already
  exist**: a `Users` row already holding one of these characters would start failing
  validation on the sync path. That is the same consequence 11.81's own Discovered
  Scope entry above records for the original rule, and it is a planning decision,
  not a round's. Registered as R-1 in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §22.4; the
  instruments baseline it, so the day it is fixed they go red and say so.

- **[Found by 11.81, 2026-08-31 — done inside 11.81, recorded because it changed a
  synced column's validation] A person's name had no shape rule at all, and the
  brief assumed it did.** Task 11.81's spec said the requester's claimed name must
  carry *"exactly the bounds `Users.first_name` already has — length, control
  characters, and bidirectional-override characters"*. **`Users.first_name` had one
  of those three**: `TextBound.name`, a length cap of 200. No control-character rule
  and no bidirectional rule existed anywhere in this codebase, for names or for
  anything else. Rather than invent a second set for the new route, the task
  centralised: `TextShape.personName` was added, `Users.first_name` and
  `Users.last_name` now carry it, and the join-request route calls the same
  `RowValidator.isWellFormedPersonName`. **The consequence to know about: a `Users`
  row whose name contains a control character or a bidi override is now refused on
  the sync path where it was previously accepted.** No honest name contains either,
  and no such row is known to exist, but it is a validation change on a synced
  column and it is recorded here rather than left to be discovered.

- **[Found by 11.74, 2026-08-30 — needs a task, and it belongs to whoever builds
  11.74's design] Four user-visible sentences and one design argument become false
  the moment the join code ships, and they are the exact defect class task 11.54
  exists to prevent.** They are listed with file and line in
  `JOIN_CODE_AND_APPROVAL_DESIGN.md` §3: the join screen's *"only work for the email
  address they were sent to"*, the issued-code panel's *"only works for the address
  above, expires in 14 days, and can be used once"*, the Leave dialog's *"you will
  need a new invitation to rejoin"*, and the departed-member delete warning's *"if
  you are ever invited back"*. The fifth is not user-facing but is worse: the header
  of `packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/invite_code.dart` argues that 8 characters is
  enough **because** a guessed code cannot be used by anyone but the invited address.
  Under a shared code that argument is simply false, and it is the argument the code
  length rests on. **Whoever builds this replaces the argument, not just the
  sentence.**

- **[Found by 11.74, 2026-08-30 — needs a task number, small] The client has no
  populated-upgrade test for schema v9, and the v8 one is not pinned.** Task 11.16
  established that migrations are tested as upgrades of populated databases, and
  there is a file per version from v2 to v8 — but no `schema_v9_migration_test.dart`
  exists, so the `Tag_Versions` migration that task 11.32 shipped has never been run
  against a populated database in a test. Separately,
  `test/data/schema_v8_migration_test.dart` upgrades `from: 7, to: latestSchemaVersion`
  rather than `to: 8`, so it silently absorbs every later migration and will absorb
  the next one too. **The v8 file is therefore not testing what its name says**, and
  the gap it leaves is exactly the one the missing v9 file would have filled. Neither
  is caused by 11.74 and 11.74 changes no schema; found while pricing the migration
  work and recorded so it is not lost.

- **[Found by 11.74, 2026-08-30 — a consequence of 11.74's design, for the planning
  session to weigh] Finding Q-1 gets heavier under the join-code design.** The project
  router writes no audit rows at all; that was accepted below the bar while the router
  only issued invitations. Under the new design the same router is where **memberships
  are granted** — approval, rejection, re-admission and code rotation all live there.
  An owner-granted membership with no audit record is a different proposition from an
  invitation with none. **Not filed as a defect, because Q-1 is already accepted in
  writing; filed as a reason to revisit the acceptance when 11.74 is built.**

- **[Found by 11.72, 2026-08-30 — a sweep result, and it needs no task] The
  rest of the refusal paths were read for the same defect, and none of them has
  it.** Task 10.66's standing rule is to fix the class rather than the
  instance, so after narrowing the project-access read I read every other place
  the server refuses somebody, asking whether the *amount of work* differs
  between the two answers it must not distinguish. **This is reading, not
  measuring — say so.** What it found:
  - **Asking for a magic link is clean, and better designed than the thing I
    fixed.** It runs the same three statements whether or not the address has
    an account, because it never consults `auth_accounts` at all — the account
    is created when the link is opened, not when it is asked for. So the
    unauthenticated route where enumeration would actually matter (email
    addresses are guessable; project ids are not) does not have this defect.
    **One residual, and I did not measure it:** the "one live link per address"
    update touches one row or none according to whether that address asked for
    a link in the last fifteen minutes, so in principle it says *"somebody is
    signing in as this person right now."* One row is a fraction of what was
    measurable here, and a prober's own request creates the row that its next
    request would see, so the probe poisons itself. Recorded, not scheduled.
  - **Redeeming a link, and redeeming an invitation, both return early on a bad
    code and so cost several statements less than a good one.** That is a real
    timing difference and it is not a leak: a good code *also succeeds*, so the
    outcome already tells the caller what the clock would. Left alone
    deliberately — this is what the rule means by two answers that must be
    indistinguishable, and these two need not be.
  - **The closed-membership disclosure contributes nothing**, measured rather
    than read: it returns no rows for every caller the exemption is not for,
    which is what it was designed to do.

- **[Found by 11.72, 2026-08-30 — NEEDS A TASK NUMBER] The offline suite is
  red on the GitHub runner, in a second widget-test file, and the cause is
  printed in the log.** Three of the last ten offline runs went red:
  `map_screen_test.dart`'s live tag-colour test on `5f49f1d`, and then
  `test/features/position_estimation/screens/position_estimation_screen_test.dart`'s
  "member sort orders the bearing list by observer name" on **both** `4705d6a`
  and `04a4903` — **and green again on `27c23ab` with nothing about it
  changed**, which is the coin-flip said out loud. **The decisive fact: `4705d6a` changed four documentation
  files and no client code at all**, so nothing introduced this — the suite
  simply started losing that coin flip. **Task 11.69 fixed one race in the map
  screen and said in so many words that it could not prove there was only one.
  This is the second one.** The new failure
  names its cause 59 times in the log: `MissingPluginException (No
  implementation found for method getApplicationSupportDirectory on channel
  plugins.flutter.io/path_provider)`. **In plain terms: something running in
  the background during that test reaches for a real device folder, and there
  is no device** — the test then fails on the pile of exceptions rather than on
  its own assertion. It is order- and timing-dependent, which is why it is
  intermittent and why a developer's Mac does not see it. **What the task would
  be:** find what calls `getApplicationSupportDirectory` during a widget test —
  the likely candidates are a provider that opens the database or a scheduler
  started by a screen's `initState` — and either stub the channel for the whole
  suite or stop the work starting at all. **Do it as the class, not the two
  instances:** if a plugin channel can be reached from a widget test, every
  screen test is a coin flip, and this suite is the thing standing between a
  regression and a beta. Not fixed by 11.72, which is server-side and touched
  no client code.

- **[Found by 11.41's follow-on, FIXED 2026-08-27 in `6119b1c`, but ONE PART
  NEEDS A TASK] A pull discarded records and reported a clean sync.**
  `SyncEngine._pull` threw away `ProjectMerger`'s report. The merger correctly
  refuses a row whose values this build's `RowValidator` does not recognise,
  and a row scoped to another project — and the engine then counted the row in
  `SyncRunReport.pulled` (which counted rows *on the wire*, while its own doc
  comment claimed "rows merged into the local database"), wrote a receipt for
  it, acked the cursor past it, and reported success. **A colleague's bearing
  could disappear between the wire and the database with nothing said anywhere
  and no way to ask.** That is finding D-3's asset — an irreplaceable field
  record present in one place and reported as being in two — reached from the
  **inbound** direction, where there was no instrument of any kind. The
  likeliest trigger is a build skew between a phone and a laptop, which is the
  normal state during development. Fixed: the report now carries
  `storedFromServer` and `droppedOnArrival` separately, `SyncHealth` gains
  `recordsMissing`, and the banner and status screen say so.
  **What still needs a task: the record of a drop is not durable.** A held row
  leaves a `Sync_Held_Rows` entry that survives a restart; a dropped one leaves
  nothing, so `droppedOnArrivalCount` resets on restart and on the next clean
  round. The outbound side learned this lesson at task 10.28 and the inbound
  side has not. **What the task would be:** a client-only store for rows
  refused on arrival, keyed the same way `Sync_Held_Rows` is, so the count
  survives and so the status screen can name the records rather than count
  them — and a decision about whether the cursor should ack past a row this
  device refused at all.
  **CLOSED by task 11.44 (2026-08-28) — the durability half.** `Sync_Dropped_Rows`
  is built to `SyncHeldRowStore`'s exact shape, the count survives a restart and a
  later clean round, the status screen names the record and the validator's own
  reason, and `_reconcileDrops` clears an entry when a corrected version of the
  record arrives on a later pull. **The second half was not decided, and is the
  item immediately below.**

- **[Raised by 11.41's brief, answered by nobody, NEEDS A DECISION FROM MICHAEL]
  Your device acks the sync cursor past a record it refused, so the only way that
  record ever arrives is somebody editing it again.** Task 11.44's brief asked for
  "a decision about whether the cursor should ack past a row this device refused at
  all," and what 11.44 built answers it by implication rather than by decision: the
  pull acks past the drop, and `_reconcileDrops` clears an entry only when the
  record changes again wherever it was written and arrives at a later `server_seq`.
  There is no "fetch everything again" action, and 11.44 was right to delete the
  status card's claim that updating the app and syncing again would bring it in —
  that sentence was false. **What it means in the field:** a teammate's bearing
  this build refused — the likeliest cause being a version skew between a phone and
  a laptop, which is the normal state during development — is on their device and
  on the server and permanently not on yours, and "did I get everything?" now has
  the honest answer "no, and there is no way to ask for it again." **The options
  are: accept it in writing** — the drop is durable, named and visible, which is a
  large improvement on silence, and a re-fetch is a new mechanism on the most
  safety-critical path in the app — **or task a bounded re-fetch**, replaying from
  a `server_seq` stored per drop rather than from zero, which is the shape that
  does not become "download the project again." Not decided here because what a
  field season needs from "did I get everything" is Michael's question rather than
  this session's.
  **DECIDED 2026-08-29 — Michael chose to accept it for the beta, with a written
  trigger, and scheduled the fix as deferred task 11.50 rather than leaving the
  question open.** The reasoning is the one this project already used for the
  viewer-restore dialog: the harm is bounded and *visible* — the record is named,
  the reason is named, and the notice survives a restart — while the fix is new
  machinery on the most safety-critical path in the app, and how often it fires in
  real use is unmeasured. The trigger that converts 11.50 from deferred to
  scheduled is written into 11.50 itself.


- **[Found by 11.41's follow-on, FIXED 2026-08-27 in `6119b1c`, but the guard
  NEEDS A TASK] Data arriving from anywhere but a screen was invisible until
  the app restarted.** `recordingsRevisionProvider`'s own docstring says it
  exists *"so a mutation made on one screen shows up immediately elsewhere,
  without waiting for an app restart to re-run that provider"* — and every one
  of its callers was a local UI edit. All five paths by which observation data
  arrives from **outside this device** — a sync pull, joining a project,
  redeeming an invite, restoring a backup, pasting a shared observation —
  announced nothing. `_mapDataProvider` and `historyDataProvider` are plain
  (non-`autoDispose`) family providers on tabs that live for the life of the
  process, so their cached result survived until the app was quit. **This is
  what Michael actually saw**: a Mac that synced, reported success, and showed
  no sign of the iPhone's bearings. All five now announce, and
  `test/core/providers/data_arrival_announced_test.dart` fails if one stops.
  **The hand-written list this left behind is CLOSED by task 11.45
  (2026-08-28).** The announcement moved into the writers (`DataArrival`, a
  plain callback list so `lib/data` still depends on neither Flutter nor
  Riverpod), and the guard now derives the set of files that write displayed
  data from the code. Doing so found six write paths the list of five never
  named — `ServerIdentityAdopter` (sign-in rewrites `user_id` across every
  table and hard-deletes the superseded `Users` rows), `UnknownColumnStore`'s
  promote, `ProfileEditor`, first-run/tombstone-recovery user creation,
  project-setup tag linking, and the tag created to receive a pasted share —
  all fixed in the same commit.

- **[Found by 11.41, NEEDS A TASK] Publish uploads a wider set of `Users` rows
  than the server will accept.** `ProjectPublisher` uploads exactly
  `ProjectExporter.collect`, and the exporter gathers reachable `Users` rows
  using `SyncTable.userColumns` — which **includes `last_modified_by`**. The
  server's `ProjectReachability` deliberately excludes that column (an audit
  column any caller may set is not a reachability edge; see its own note), so a
  `Users` row reachable only because somebody's name is in a `last_modified_by`
  somewhere is uploaded by publish and refused by the server. That is a live
  route to a held row on every first publish of a project that has ever had two
  people touch it. **The exporter is not wrong for its own purpose** — an
  archive that dropped that `Users` row would carry a dangling reference — so
  the fix is a decision about the *publish payload*, not about the exporter, and
  it needs its own task rather than a quiet change. Task 11.41's hold
  reconciliation stops such a hold being *permanent*, and its screen work makes
  it explain itself, but the row is still offered and still refused every time.
  **CLOSED by task 11.43 (2026-08-28).** The payload is now built from a stated
  rule — a device offers every row of the project except the records the server
  keeps for itself, who somebody is and what they may do — derived from each
  table's declared `MutationRule` rather than from a list of tables, so a
  fourteenth table is classified by definition. Both the publisher and the
  ordinary push read that one rule, so every record already stuck on a device
  resolves on the next sync with no migration and no button.

- **[Found by 11.41, NEEDS A TASK] The e2e suite had never signed in two

  subject of task 11.24's rule. That is why a defect visible the moment two

  **CLOSED, both halves.** The run: task 11.43 (2026-08-28) executed
  `two_people_one_project_e2e_test.dart` against a live server — its third group is

  the file count with `test/e2e/suite_coverage_test.dart`, which derives the

  each route to be exercised, and **requires some test in the suite to sign two

- **[Found by 11.41, NO TASK NEEDED — recorded because it is the same class as
  the finding] User-facing copy with no reader.**
  `HeldRowReason.explanation` was a user-visible sentence on an enum. It was
  reworded at task 10.34 and again at 11.24, each time trying to make one
  paragraph cover three unrelated causes, and by the time 11.41 replaced the
  screen that rendered it, **nothing in `lib/` read it at all** — only three
  tests did, which is a mirror asserting against itself. It is deleted. The
  general shape is task 11.17's ("hand-maintained mirrors must fail when they
  drift"), one layer down: a string a person is meant to read, kept alive by
  tests rather than by a reader.

- **[Found by 11.35, NEEDS A TASK] The device list has a route and no screen.**
  `GET /auth/sessions` returns the caller's own devices and **nothing in the app
  calls it**, so "sign out the phone I lost and leave my laptop alone" is now
  *possible* and still not *offered* — Server Connection still shows only SIGN
  OUT EVERYWHERE. This was 11.35's scope boundary, not an oversight: its
  acceptance is written entirely about the route, and 11.28's finding named the
  missing read as the blocker. **What the task would be:** a small list on the
  Server Connection screen, one row per device showing the last-used time and
  marking the one in your hand, with a revoke control per row calling the
  existing `/auth/sessions/revoke-device`; a confirmation that says plainly what
  happens when the row you picked *is* this device; and the honest empty/error
  states for a server that cannot be reached. **The one design question worth
  deciding before building it:** a device id is a UUID, and a list of five UUIDs
  is not a list a person can pick their lost phone out of. The last-used time is
  what actually distinguishes them, so the row should lead with that — or the
  schema gains a device label, which is a server change and a new piece of
  caller-supplied data, and 11.35 deliberately did not invent one.

- **[Found and fixed by 11.35, no task needed — recorded because it is the same
  class three times] Three guards were hand-written lists that a new thing would
  have been silently exempt from.** All three were found by adding one new thing
  and watching what did *not* fail. (a) `RateLimiter.evictExpired` computed the
  longest rate-limit window from four of the five policy fields — task 11.2's
  per-user invite bucket was never added, and it was harmless only because
  another rule happens to share its window. Now derived from a single
  `allRules` getter. (b) `shipped_defaults_test.dart` enumerated compose files
  by filename in two places, so a fifth compose file would have been exempt from
  both the publish-address rule and the trusted-proxy rule. Now enumerated from
  the directory, with a floor assertion so a wrong working directory fails
  loudly instead of passing vacuously. (c) The same test decided whether a file
  "declares `ports:`" with a raw substring match, so a file whose header
  *explains* that it deliberately declares no ports was judged to declare some.
  Now matched against non-comment lines. None of these was a hole; all three
  were instruments that would have stopped measuring without saying so, which is
  what task 10.66's standing criterion exists for.

- **[Found by 11.35, ONLY MICHAEL CAN RUN IT] The two-device walkthrough is
  written and unexecuted.** `README.md` §4 now describes, step by step, how to
  sign two accounts in on two real devices against one LAN server, and **no step
  of it has been run.** It cannot be run from here: it needs the Ubuntu 24.04
  ARM64 VM under Parallels with native Docker, two physical devices on the same
  network, and a debug build installed on the phone. The parts that are measured
  rather than assumed are the compose rendering (checked with `docker compose
  config` — the overlay leaves `ports:` and the publish address entirely to
  `.env`) and the file sender's behaviour (existing tests). The parts that are
  reasoned from the code and **not** demonstrated are: that the LAN stack starts
  at all with `TRITRACK_TRUSTED_PROXIES=peer-verified`, that the magic-link file
  is readable and pasteable from a phone, and that the app on a debug build
  accepts the VM's `http://` address. **If any step is wrong, the fix belongs in
  the README rather than in a report** — that is what the acceptance criterion
  "no step that is not written down" means.

- **[Found by 11.28, CLOSED by 11.35 on 2026-08-23 — the read exists; the
  screen does not, see the next item] Per-device sign-out cannot be offered
  because nothing lists a person's own sessions.** `POST
  /auth/sessions/revoke-device` exists and is correct, and it needs the lost
  device's `device_id`. A device knows its own id and nothing else — there is no
  route that returns the caller's sessions, and the only device listing on the
  server is behind the diagnostics console, which is off by default,
  loopback-only, and has no notion of a person. **In plain terms: the app can
  offer "sign me out of everything", but not "sign out the phone I lost and
  leave my laptop alone."** Task 11.28 shipped the first and said so on the
  screen rather than implying the second exists.
  **What the task would be:** an authenticated `GET /auth/sessions` returning
  the caller's own rows (`device_id`, created, last seen, expires, and which one
  is this device), never a token hash, with `WHERE user_id = <session>`; a
  capped result; the field-bounds and rate-limit treatment task 10.56 made
  standard for every route; and a small device list on the Server Connection
  screen with a revoke control per row. It is small, but it is a **new
  authenticated read surface**, not wiring, which is why 11.28 did not
  improvise it. Security Model §4.3 has been corrected to say the per-device
  granularity is unreachable and why.

- **[Found by 11.28, NEEDS A DECISION FROM MICHAEL — small, and it may be
  nothing] A person leaving states their own departure date, and nothing bounds
  it.** The departure exception permits any timestamp in `end_date`, so somebody
  could record that they left a project earlier than they did. Nothing in the
  app reads `end_date` as anything but "is this stint open" (any non-null value
  is equally closed), so it grants no access and takes none away; what it could
  do is make the members screen's "joined X to Y" line say something false, in a
  record a permit report or a publication might quote. It is also detectable —
  the server stamps `received_at` on the row when it actually arrived. **The
  options are: accept it (a person's own stint dates are theirs to state, and
  an owner could already set any date), or bound it (refuse an `end_date`
  outside a window around the server's clock).** Not fixed in 11.28 because a
  clock bound on one column of one table is a new mechanism, and this project's
  own history says new mechanisms are where findings come from.

- **[Found by 11.28, worth knowing rather than fixing] The whole server suite
  now runs on this machine.** Docker is present and working here, unlike when
  task 11.32 ran, so `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f
  docker-compose.server-test.yml up -d postgres` plus `dart test` in `server/`
  executes every Postgres-backed group. Baseline before this task: 658 tests
  green. After: 682. The app suite went from 1196 to 1258. **Nothing was skipped
  for want of a database**, which has not been true for several tasks.
  **One caution learned the hard way:** running the two suites *concurrently*
  produces spurious failures — three different tests failed across two
  concurrent runs and every one of them passed alone. The Flutter suite, the
  Dart suite and Postgres-in-Docker contend badly enough to blow past
  `setUpAll` and network timeouts. Run them one after the other. And do not
  read a piped `dart test … | tail` as a pass: the exit code belongs to `tail`,
  so the "All tests passed" line is the only honest signal.

- **[Found by 11.32, NEEDS TO BE RUN — not a defect, an unverified control]

  **RUN AND GREEN, 2026-08-22, by task 11.24** — `scripts/run_server_tests_docker.sh`

- **[Found by 11.24, NEEDS A DECISION FROM MICHAEL — nobody can fix this at the
  server] The app says only a project owner may publish a project, and no
  server-side check can enforce it.** Reproduced live: a contributor holding a
  copy of somebody else's *unpublished* project — which is what a project-file
  import or a restored archive leaves behind — published it under their own name
  and became its sole owner on the server. The genuine owner's next attempt on
  that project id drew `403 forbidden`, and will forever: a project id is the
  primary key of every row that belongs to it and this app has no way to re-key
  a project. **The server cannot close this**, and that is the finding rather
  than an excuse — for a project it has never seen, every row of the first push
  is self-asserted, memberships included, so there is no evidence that tells the
  real owner from somebody holding a copy. A check here would be one that cannot
  fail, which is the shape §4's B4 warns about. Bounded by having to already
  hold the project (ids are v4 UUIDs, not guessable). **Michael's call:** accept
  it in writing, or task something that changes the shape — the only real
  options are letting a project be re-keyed, or having the server refuse a first
  publish whose `Projects` row it has seen before under another owner, which it
  cannot have. `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §19.4; `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` row
  P1.

- **[Found by 11.24, NEEDS A TASK] The "waiting to sync" list has no cap, and
  this task made it much easier to fill.** `SyncHeldRowStore.held()` takes no
  limit and `sync_status_screen.dart` renders one card per held row. Refusals
  used to be rare; a project archive import can now produce thousands at once,
  and the screen would be perfectly truthful and completely unreadable. **This
  is the third instance of the shape task 10.87 recorded** for the consent
  dialog and the conflict queue, and 10.87's brief does not cover it. It should
  either join that task or get its own. Nothing is lost either way — this is a
  legibility defect, not a data one.

- **[Found by 11.24, KNOWN AND ACCEPTED IN WRITING] `Tags.last_modified_by` is
  still forgeable on insert.** A contributor can create a tag stamped with a
  teammate's name (measured live: `inserted`). It is left open deliberately:
  binding the audit column on insert for shared tables would refuse the first
  publish of a project whose tags a colleague created, and a held `Tags` row
  cascades — every observation referencing it becomes a foreign global reference
  and is refused too. What the forgery buys is that only the named person may
  later maintain that tag *while no project references it*, which is a nuisance
  and a self-inflicted lockout for the forger, not a false scientific record.
  The update path is closed. `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §19.6.

- **[Found by 11.32, KNOWN AND ACCEPTED IN WRITING] A contributor can append a
  spurious tag version, and the next bearing anybody records on that tag will
  cite it.** Appending is contributor-level on purpose: it is additive and
  forward-only (it never changes what an already-recorded bearing reads), it
  leaves the `Tags` row alone so the discrepancy shows in the tag list, and the
  extra version is visible in the tag's history. Requiring an owner would refuse
  a contributor's own new tag's first version — *intermittently*, because a sync
  batch limit can split the `Tags` row and its first version across two pushes,
  leaving the second permanently held, and a tag with no version gives every
  bearing on it a null measurement context forever and silently. Recorded in
  `PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` §7 beside rows T8a/T8b. **Revisit it there if it is
  revisited at all.**

- **[Found by 11.32, NEEDS A DECISION FROM MICHAEL] Three other tables name a

- **[Found by 11.32, ALREADY DONE — recorded so it is not rediscovered] The

- **[Found by 11.9, NEEDS A TASK AND A DECISION — this is the one item from the
  review that should not simply be accepted] A contributor can put a teammate's
  name on an observation, or on an exclusion mark, that the teammate never
  made.** Reproduced live against a real team: a contributor in a project pushes
  an `Observations` row whose `user_id` is the **owner's**, the server answers
  `inserted`, and the owner's next pull delivers a bearing they never took,
  under their name. The same works for `Observation_Exclusions` — a mark that
  retires somebody's bearing from the analysis, credited to a colleague who did
  not make that judgement. Registered as **N-1**, `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`
  §18.3, and re-measured on every run of
  `scripts/verify_11_9_team_surface.py`, which carries it in a baseline that
  goes **red if it ever starts being refused** so the register cannot quietly
  become a lie.
  **Why it does not block:** the actor must already be a contributor the owner
  invited, nothing is destroyed (the original rows are untouched, and
  re-attributing a *stored* row is refused), the fabricated row is visible in
  the Team log with the name on it, and it is removable — by the named author,
  or by an owner using the exclude control task 11.7 built.
  **Why it still needs deciding rather than accepting:** the mechanism is
  §4.17's clause 2 — "this project already reaches them" — which §4.17 itself
  says had *no reachable instance* in Phase 10 and would be reopened by "task
  11.2's invitation record". **What actually reopened it is not an invitation
  record**; it is `Project_Memberships.user_id` landing inside
  `ProjectReachability`, so every teammate vouches for being named as a side
  effect of being a teammate. Nothing was written down when that took effect,
  and Phase 11 shipped two features (the Team log, observer provenance in
  position estimation) whose whole purpose is provenance — this is the one input
  that makes both of them say something false.
  **Ask the planning session to schedule a task for N-1 and to make the design
  call it needs**, which is not a patch: either (a) narrow clause 2 from "does
  this project reach the named person" to a real provenance record — a
  different query, not a tightening of this one — or (b) keep clause 2 for
  `anyUser` rows and drop it for `author`/`authorOrOwner` rows, so shared
  project vocabulary still replicates but **a record that names an author must
  name the caller**. Option (b) costs a legitimate first publish of a
  colleague's imported observations, which is exactly the trade §4.17 already
  accepted for Phase 10 and which `SyncHeldRowStore` already makes payable. The
  full argument, including why this is B4 in letter and not B1/B2/B3, is at
  §18.3.
  **Scheduled as task 11.24 (2026-08-21), and the planning session's lean is
  (b), stated so it can be argued with rather than inherited:** (a) invents a new
  provenance mechanism, and nine rounds say new mechanisms are where findings come
  from, whereas (b) reuses a trade §4.17 already accepted and a hold path already
  built. **That lean is an opinion from a plan document, so 11.24's first step is
  to measure its cost rather than adopt it** — count the paths that legitimately
  construct an author-naming row with a non-caller author, and if that number is
  large, (b) is not cheap and the lean is wrong. A server-stamped "delivered by"
  value is considered there as a companion, not an alternative, with the explicit
  caution that visibility is the weakest link in this finding's
  not-blocking argument and not the strongest.

- **[Found by 11.9, a scheduling correction to task 10.97, not a new task]

- **[Found by 11.9, fixed here, no task needed] The gate harness's own

  the next stack to want port 8080 failed to bind — which is exactly what cost
  the eighth gate a false reading. **Fixed as the class, per task 10.66's
  standing rule:** there is now one EXIT handler that does both things, the
  self-test sets a flag instead of installing a trap, and the handler's comment
  says why a future cleanup is a line inside it rather than another `trap`.
  Recorded as N-8 in `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §18.4. **Worth noting for the
  phase's sake:** 10.108 fixed M-12 where it was reported and did not sweep for
  the same defect elsewhere in the same file, which is the pattern 10.66 exists
  to stop.

- **[Found by 11.21, belongs to 11.9's inventory, not a new task]

- **[Found by 11.19, needs a task] The picked-`.zip` restore has the same gap

- **[Found by 11.20, minor, needs a decision not a task yet] A viewer restoring
  a backup is asked which merge strategy to use, and only then told they may not
  restore at all.** The merge strategy dialog comes before `ProjectMerger.merge`
  is called, and the refusal comes out of the merger — so the user answers a
  question that turns out not to have mattered. It is cosmetic and it is
  recorded with a warning attached, because the obvious fix is the one 11.19 and
  11.20 were both told not to make: resolving the role in the screen as well
  would put a **second** answer to "may this person write here" on an import
  path, which is how §4.19's original rule became unreachable. If it is worth
  fixing, the shape that does not duplicate the rule is a preflight on the
  merger itself (one implementation, called twice), not a query in the widget.
  **Decided 2026-08-21: accepted for the beta, not scheduled.** Who reaches it
  is a viewer restoring a backup — a rare role performing a rare action — and
  what it costs them is one dialog of confusion before a clear refusal. What a
  fix costs is a change to the restore path, which is the most safety-critical
  client path in the app and three findings deep (J-1, K-1, this one), on a
  feature whose failure mode is losing a field season. That trade is wrong at
  this point in the schedule. **If the beta team hits it and says so, build the
  preflight** — and build it the way 11.20 described, one implementation called
  twice, never a second answer in the widget.

- **The backfill claim in 8.4 was true, and was also two bugs waiting for this
  task.** Verified against the code and then against a database rather than the
  entry: an owner membership *is* written on creation
  (`project_setup_screen.dart` `_save()`) and *is* backfilled on load for
  pre-existing projects (`_ensureOwnerMembership`, reached from
  `currentProject`/`projectById`/`allProjects`), and
  `app_context_provider_test.dart` proved both before this task ran. But the
  condition it used — *does `project.ownerUserId` hold any open membership* —
  has two wrong answers the moment ownership can move, and only one of them is
  benign. A creator who transferred a project away and closed their own owner
  stint holds no open membership, so **the next project load would have
  silently re-granted them ownership and undone the transfer**; and a creator
  demoted to contributor holds one, so a project whose only owner had left
  would *not* have been repaired. Fixed to ask about the project's owners
  rather than one user's row, with a test for each direction. Worth noting for
  the phase's own sake: the entry's claim was accurate and still could not be
  relied on, because what changed was not whether the rows existed but what
  question was being asked of them.
- **Server-side fixtures have no membership rows at all**, and 488 pre-11.1
  server tests pass unchanged because `resolveProjectOwners` falls back to
  `Projects.owner_user_id` when the membership table names no open owner. That
  fallback is load-bearing for more than old fixtures: the server authorizes
  every row of a push *before* writing any of them, so during a first publish
  the batch's own `Projects` row is not yet stored when its
  `Project_Memberships` row is judged. Both cases resolve through the same
  null-vs-empty distinction (`permittedByOwners`), documented in
  `TriTrack_Security_Model.md` §4.12.
- **`MutationRule.permits` now throws for the ownership rules.** Chosen over
  leaving the old single-value comparison working, because a call site still
  asking the old question is a place ownership transfer would silently not
  apply — and there is no way to find those by reading. It found both UI call
  sites immediately.
- **Client-layer inserts are unauthorized, which is fine everywhere except
  granting ownership.** `BaseRepository._authorize` runs against a stored row,
  so it says nothing about an insert — a deliberate Phase 8 property, and
  harmless for tables where an insert is new field data. It is not harmless for
  `Project_Memberships`, where inserting a row *is* the grant.
  `grantOwner` therefore checks the actor itself. **The general property is
  unchanged and is a real seam:** any future operation that confers privilege
  by inserting a row must do its own check, because the rule table will not.
  The server refuses these either way (`RowAuthorizer` judges the incoming row
  on an insert), so this is the client agreeing with the server rather than a
  boundary of its own. Worth a look in 11.2, which adds the invite-redemption
  insert path.
- **Ownership is now an asynchronous question in the UI**, where 8.3's was a
  column comparison already in hand. Both owner-gated screens render a spinner
  until it resolves rather than showing a provisional answer and correcting it
  — a flicker between "you may edit this" and "you may not" is a worse lie than
  a moment's wait. `ownedProjectIdsProvider` answers for a whole list in one
  lookup so an N-row screen does not open N ownership questions.
- **For 11.2:** ownership transfer exists at the repository layer
  (`grantOwner`, `endMembership`) with no screen driving it. That is deliberate
  — 11.2's owner dashboard is where the interaction belongs, and building a
  one-off transfer UI here would be the duplication 11.6 was deferred for. The
  dashboard should surface `LastOwnerRemoval.message` as written; it is a
  user-facing explanation, not a developer error.
- **For 11.9's inventory:** the last-owner guard is a *claimed control*, so it
  is a §4 B4 candidate and belongs on the trust-boundary list. Its within-push
  bookkeeping (`_ownershipsRemovedThisPush`) is the part most likely to be
  wrong under adversarial batching — it is tested for the two-in-one-push case
  but not for interleavings across concurrent transactions, where the real
  serialization guarantee comes from the surrounding sync transaction rather
  than from the authorizer.


#### From task 11.23 (2026-08-22) — the permissions matrix sweep

Every item below is a cell `CLAUDE_DOCS/PERMISSIONS_MATRIX.md` §8 could not close,
carrying the disposition §8 assigns it. **11.23 changed no behaviour.**

- **[CLOSED by task 11.219, 2026-09-10, by deleting the thing it was about]**
  *(original entry below)* Copy-on-add retired `Project_Tags` and with it the
  whole idea of a tag *link* that could be deactivated: a project's tag is a
  row in that project now, removing it is an ordinary soft delete of that row,
  and the server authorizes it the way it authorizes every other project row.
  `ProjectTagRepository` and its `assertMayUnlink` no longer exist, which is
  why the citation below no longer names a file — **the claim died with the
  code it described** rather than moving.
  **[NEEDS A TASK — a device-only permission with no server twin, which §4.23
  says is a finding rather than a design property] Only an owner may remove a
  tag from a project, and the server has never been told.**
  `ProjectTagRepository.assertMayUnlink`, in the deleted
  `lib/data/repositories/project_tag_repository.dart`,
  refused a contributor who tried to deactivate a project's tag link. Nothing in
  `RowAuthorizer` knows the rule exists: a `Project_Tags` row whose `status` is
  set to `inactive` passes `_authorizeRole` (a contributor has write rights),
  passes `MutationRule.anyUser`, never reaches `_authorizeGrantingInsert` (that
  is inserts only), and short-circuits out of `_authorizeTagReferences` because
  the project already reaches the tag. Verified by reading the authorizer end to
  end and grepping it for `status`/`inactive`/`unlink`: **no branch exists.**
  This is exactly §4.23's own point 2 — *"a client-side check that fails open
  where there is no server-side twin **is** a finding"* — and it is the shape
  tasks 11.19 and 11.20 were created to close on two other paths. The fix has a
  template already in the file: `_authorizeExclusionKind` is the same shape (a
  branch keyed on one table and one column value, with its own `DenialReason`).
  **Consequence in plain terms:** a contributor whose device pushes the row
  directly can take a tag out of the project for the whole team, which is a
  subtractive change to shared configuration the role gradient reserves for
  owners.

- **[CLOSED by task 11.28, 2026-08-23 — Michael chose the self-service option
  on 2026-08-22, and it is built and tested]** *(original entry below)*
  **[NEEDS A DECISION FROM MICHAEL, THEN A TASK] A viewer or contributor cannot
  leave a project.** There is no control, no server route, and
  `Project_Memberships` is `MutationRule.projectOwner`, so only an owner may
  write a membership row — including the row that is about you. Confirmed by
  grepping `lib/`, `server/` and `packages/` for any leave path: none exists,
  and the security model has no section about it either. A device that bypasses
  the UI is refused twice: `UnauthorizedMutation` on the device, which no screen
  catches, and `ruleDenied` on the server, after which the row is held and
  re-offered forever, leaving that device permanently divergent on it.
  **The three options are in the matrix's §8 entry 3**, and the choice is
  Michael's: leave it (a person asks an owner to remove them), add a
  self-service leave with a narrow server rule permitting a person to end their
  own stint and nothing else, or add it with owner confirmation.

- **[NEEDS A TASK — widen 11.24 before it is implemented, not after]
  `Non_Detections` is N-1's third table, and 11.24 as written would close two of
  three.** N-1 is registered against `Observations` and `Observation_Exclusions`.
  `Non_Detections.user_id` is governed by the same `MutationRule.author`, is in
  the same `SyncTable.userColumns`, reaches the same permitting line
  (`row_authorizer.dart:844`), and is rendered as the observer in the Log tab

  contributor can file "I listened at this place and time and heard nothing"

- **[NEEDS A TASK — and it changes 11.24's chosen design, so it must be read
  before 11.24 starts] Task 11.18's "withdrawn by" name is forgeable through the

- **[NEEDS A TASK — a comment claims a control that does not exist]
  Removing somebody from a project does not end their sign-in sessions, and
  `auth_routes.dart:509` says it does.** That comment states that "task 11.2's
  member removal calls `AuthService.revokeAllSessionsForUser` server-side,
  inside the flow that already established the caller is an owner." **There is
  no such call** — grepping the server for callers of that function returns only
  the person's own "sign out everywhere" route — and there could not be one,
  because member removal is an `end_date` on a synced row, not a request to the
  server, so there is no server-side flow to hang it on.
  **The removal itself still works**, and that is worth stating plainly so this
  is not read as worse than it is: project access is re-resolved from membership
  rows on every request, so a removed person is refused on their next sync
  whether or not their session survives. What is broken is the *record* — and a
  comment asserting a control that is not there is the failure shape this
  project has paid for more than once. Either wire the revocation up or correct
  the comment and §4.3.

- **[HALF CLOSED by task 11.28, 2026-08-23 — "sign out everywhere" is now on
  the Server Connection screen; per-device revocation is still unreachable and
  has its own entry in Phase 11's Discovered Scope, because it needs a route
  that lists your own sessions]** *(original entry below)*
  **[NEEDS A TASK, low urgency] "Sign out everywhere" and "I lost my phone"
  cannot be reached from the app.** `POST /auth/sessions/revoke-all` and
  `POST /auth/sessions/revoke-device` exist, are correctly self-service-only

- **[NEEDS A DECISION FROM MICHAEL — a research-practice question before it is a
  code one] An owner of one project can rename, re-tune or retire a tag another
  project is also using, and that project is never told.** Tags are global and
  multi-project by design; `TagRepository.assertMayEdit` and the server's
  reachable-tag branch both permit an owner of *any* project the tag belongs to.
  The other project's stored bearings then mean something different from what
  they meant when they were taken, with no notification and no record. The code
  documents the behaviour; the security model does not — its tag table is
  written per-project, as though a tag had one project. **Options in the
  matrix's §8 entry 7:** accept it (shared equipment behaves this way), notify
  the other projects, or refuse unless the caller owns every project using the
  tag.

- **[NEEDS A TASK OR AN ACCEPTED-RISK ENTRY] Export is ungated at every layer —
  which §5.2 defends — but it exports more than the exporter can see.**
  `ProjectExporter.collect` gathers every referenced person's **prior email
  addresses** (`project_exporter.dart:56`), so a viewer's `.zip` carries
  teammates' address history. The *gating* question is settled by §5.2 and §5.7
  and I am not reopening it. The *width* question is separate, is not covered by
  §5.2's "data they are authorized to see" wording, and nothing in the security
  model addresses it. Aggravated by the cloud auto-backup path, which does the
  same export **on a schedule** with nobody deciding each time.

- **[NEEDS A DECISION — probably small, but it reads as an oversight]
  Recovered tag locations can be received but never recorded.**
  `Actual_Tag_Locations` has a schema, a mutation rule, a repository with
  `insert` and `update`, and a map layer that draws its points — and the only
  use of that repository anywhere in `lib/` is a read at `map_screen.dart:2762`.
  No control creates one. Either this is an unfinished feature that needs a
  task, or the table exists only to carry values from elsewhere and should say
  so, because an uncalled `insert` reads as a bug to the next person.

  exists to prevent] The last-write-wins tiebreak is a value the device chooses
  for itself.** When two edits carry the same revision and timestamp, the higher
  `origin_device_id` wins, and that identifier is a random value the device
  mints and stores in plain text. A device that picks a high one wins every
  future tie deliberately. This sits in the security model's §6 discovered-scope
  list as *"Probably acceptable; the point is to record the acceptance
  explicitly rather than leave it unexamined"* — **with no task number, which is
  precisely the shape 10.72's sweep was meant to eliminate.** Either accept it
  in writing or give it a task.

  is immediate by a narrower mechanism that was already built:** the server

  narrow concurrency residual. Needs a task number.** Redemption refuses a
  second open row for a (project, user) pair, and `grantOwner` promotes rather
  than inserting — so every path this codebase has is covered. What is not
  covered is two *different* codes for the same pair redeemed concurrently:
  both transactions read no open row, both insert. The structural fix is a
  unique partial index on `(project_id, user_id) WHERE end_date IS NULL AND
  deleted_at IS NULL`, which belongs on both the client and the server and is

- **[Found by task 11.229, 2026-09-12. Measured on the widget, not the phone.] `TagEditDialog`'s
  "Link to project" dropdown (the *Add tag* path only) silently clips its own selected-item text —

  (unlinked)" is given 24 of the 48 logical pixels its own text needs at that width, so half the
  word is cut off with no ellipsis and no sign anything is missing — the failure this project's
  `clippedTexts` instrument exists to catch, because a `RenderFlex` overflow at least paints a
  stripe. This is `DropdownButtonFormField`'s own fixed menu-item height, unrelated to anything
  task 11.229 changed (the dropdown was not touched), and it does not get worse with a longer
  project name, only with a longer *unlinked* label — so it is live on every device today, not a
  hypothetical. **Needs a task**: give the dropdown an item height that respects the ambient text
  style, the way `position_estimation_screen.dart`'s `TextScaler`-based row heights already do
  elsewhere in this app.
  **Corrected by task 11.232, 2026-09-12, which re-measured this in the phone's font (Roboto,
  loaded from the SDK cache) before repeating it.** Three of the sentences above are the test
  font's, not a phone's. At the default size on a 6.1-inch phone the label is 117 px wide in a
  237 px box — **it fits, and nothing is cut off.** It wraps, and is then half-shown, from **AX3
  (2.35×)** up, and a project name goes the same way from AX4; that is the real defect and it is
  fixed (`isDense: false`, `tag_form.dart`). The cause was not "a fixed menu-item height" either:
  `DropdownButtonFormField` defaults to dense, and a dense `DropdownButton` boxes its selected
  item at exactly **one scaled line** of its text style — it *does* scale with the ambient text,
  and cuts whatever wraps past the first line. The `position_estimation_screen.dart` precedent was
  not the right tool — the box already scaled; it needed to follow its content. **The reusable
  error is the one `CLAUDE.md`'s widget-test-font rule already names**: a clip measured in the
  ~1.6×-wide test font was reported as live at that size on every phone.

- **[Found by task 11.229, 2026-09-12. Reproduced three times, on both `Edit tag` and `Read-only`,
  ruling out the dropdown above.] Opening "Tag details" on a tag with more than the default two
  pulse modes, at the OS's xxxLarge accessibility text size (1.35×) or larger, does not overflow or
  clip — it never finishes laying out at all.** In this task's own test harness that showed up as
  the test's ten-minute timeout with the CPU otherwise idle — the same dead-clock shape `CLAUDE.md`
  already names for an unresolved real `await`, here from a layout pass that apparently never
  settles rather than a wait. **On a real phone with Larger Accessibility Sizes on, this reads as
  the app freezing** the moment somebody opens a tag's details — worse than the clipping above, and
  it is not scoped to `tag_form.dart` alone to say so: nothing in this task narrowed the cause
  further than "somewhere in the pulse-mode editor's `Row`s, past three rows, at extreme text
  scale." Confirmed clean through xxLarge (1.24×); AX1 and above (task 11.229's test suite stops at
  xxLarge for exactly this reason, so `flutter test` does not itself hang). **Needs its own task,
  with room to bisect which widget is looping** — this is more urgent than the dropdown finding
  above, because it is a freeze rather than a cosmetic clip, and Michael's users are exactly the
  kind of fieldworker likely to have larger text turned on outdoors.
  **Corrected by task 11.232, 2026-09-12: there was no freeze, and the app never hung.** The
  dialog laid out in 86 ms at xxxLarge, on the first probe. The idle ten minutes were the test
  harness: 11.229's `expect` used `reason: '... $verdict'`, a verdict with a stripe in it renders
  as *"STRIPED: A RenderFlex overflowed by 3.4 pixels…"*, and `collectLayoutOverflows` decided what
  an overflow was by whether the error text contained `overflowed by` — so when that `expect`
  failed, the harness swallowed its own `TestFailure` as if it were a stripe, the binding asserted
  inside its uncaught-error path, and the test could never complete. Reproduced both ways on the
  same dialog at the same scale, the only difference being whether the `reason` quoted the stripe:
  one fails at once, the other waits ten minutes. Fixed by classifying on the act (a
  `FlutterError` from the rendering library), held by `test/support/text_scale_probe_test.dart`,
  watched red against the old code. **What the stripe was**: the pulse-modes header `Row` — a
  `Row` gives a non-flexible child no width bound, so as text grew only the title could give way;
  on a phone that squeezed *"Pulse modes"* to 19.7 px at AX5 (letters in a column), and in the
  wider test font it went on to a striped overflow from xxxLarge (3.4 px) to AX5 (255 px). Fixed
  with a `Wrap`, plus a declared shim for a Flutter defect (`SegmentedButton` throws when
  dry-laid-out, which a `Wrap` inside an `AlertDialog` does), with the shim's reopen trigger
  mechanised as a test. **Three things this entry got wrong at once, and all three are in
  `CLAUDE.md` already**: "the CPU was idle" was stated and not asked what it meant (a looping
  layout burns CPU; an idle hang is an unfinished wait); a cause was named from a resemblance
  ("the dead-clock shape") without a measurement beside it; and the instrument's own failure was
  never one of the hypotheses — the hang was called the app's because the harness was not on the
  list of suspects. The sentence that was right is the one the fix came from: *"a hunt whose
  instrument also hangs tells you nothing twice."*
- **[Found by task 11.302, 2026-09-24. Planning-session instrument; not edited by this task.]

- **[Found by task 11.302, 2026-09-24. Not built; needs a decision.] A member's project disappears

- **[Found by task 11.302, 2026-09-24. Not built; trip-wire.] There is no operator command to
  restore a tombstone the app cannot reach** — an account nobody can sign in as any more, or a

- **[Found by task 11.313, 2026-09-27. Not built; needs a decision.] A tombstoned project's own
  writes are authorized exactly like a live one's.** Item 3 needed the true answer to "what happens
  to a member's unsent records when their project is deleted" before writing the copy — the answer
  is that nothing is lost, because nothing anywhere checks a project's own `Projects.deleted_at`
  before authorizing or collecting a push of a row scoped to it. `SyncEngine`'s push selection
  (`_pendingClause`) filters only by the scope column and the snapshot gate (`offersNothingFor`,
  true only for a non-member), never by the project's own tombstone; the server's push route
  (`sync_routes.dart`) refuses only a **destroyed** project (`wasDestroyed`), never a merely
  **deleted** one, and `ProjectAuthorizer.resolve` reads a caller's role straight off
  `Project_Memberships` without ever reading `Projects.deleted_at`. So a device that has not yet
  learned the project is gone — behind on signal, or the tombstone is one page ahead of it in the
  same pull — can keep writing new rows into it after the owner deleted it, and the server accepts
  every one. That is good news for the copy in item 3 and a live question on its own: **should a
  push to a project the server already has tombstoned be accepted?** Ask the planning session to
  decide, and to say which of the destroyed-project check's three call sites (`sync_routes.dart`)
  is the right shape to copy if the answer is no.
  **[Resolved 2026-09-27 by the planning session: keep accepting.]** Written into Security Model
  §4.28.1 as decision 5, with its reason and reopen trigger.
- **[Found by task 11.312, 2026-09-27. Not built; needs a decision.] Every broken-control drill
  variant needs pub.dev to build, and the gate's own stack does not.** `server/Dockerfile` runs
  `COPY server server` *before* `RUN dart pub get`. So any edit under `server/` throws away the
  dependency layer, and a drill variant exists precisely to edit a file under `server/`. The gate
  builds unedited source and reuses the cached layer. On 2026-09-27 the VM's Docker build could
  not reach pub.dev: the gate went 25 of 25, and all five 11.85 variants failed at `dart pub get`
  with a socket error, each after about 370 seconds. That is roughly half an hour spent proving
  nothing. The same five had built in task 11.311's run, so the network, not the code, changed.
  **Two separate fixes, for the planning session to choose from:** (a) copy the two
  `pubspec.yaml`/`pubspec.lock` pairs and run `dart pub get` before copying the source. That is
  the standard layer order, and it makes a variant reuse the gate's downloaded packages. It
  changes the shipped image's build, so it is not a drill-only change. (b) Have the drill stop
  after the first variant that fails to build on a network error, instead of waiting on all five.
  Neither is done; this task's brief does not reach the Dockerfile.
  **The cause on the VM, 2026-09-28: this was the containers' network, for the third time** (twice
  on 2026-09-23, see `RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` D5 and `server/README.md`). `sudo systemctl restart
  docker` fixed it again, and the drill then built all five variants and passed. **Measured before
  the restart, and they count against UFW being the cause:**
  - `docker0`, the default container network, had **no IPv4 address**. Docker's own forwarding
    rule for it (`DOCKER-FORWARD -i docker0 -j ACCEPT`) and its outbound address translation for
    172.17.0.0/16 were both still in place.
  - A container asked for a raw connection got `No route to host`. It was not left timing out.
  - `dmesg` held no `[UFW BLOCK]` line from any 172.17 address.
  - A temporary `ufw route allow from 172.16.0.0/12` changed nothing, and it has been removed.
  - Putting the address back by hand (`ip addr add 172.17.0.1/16 dev docker0`) did not restore
    traffic either. Only the restart did.
  - NetworkManager does not manage `docker0`, and apt's history shows no Docker or iptables update.

  So the thing that fails is `docker0` losing its address. What removes it is still unknown. Ask the
  planning session to re-word D5 and the README, which still name UFW as the prime suspect. **The
  diagnostic that settles this fastest is `ip -4 addr show docker0`**: no `inet` line means this
  fault, and the restart fixes it. With three occurrences in five days, option (b) is worth more
  than it looked: each occurrence cost this drill about half an hour.
  **[Resolved 2026-09-28 by the planning session: both, as task 11.316.]** D5 and the README now
  name `docker0` losing its address and the one-line check, not UFW.
- **[Found by task 11.315, 2026-09-28. Not built; needs a decision.] The Record screen's RANGE
  button loses the sweep if the thumb slides while holding it.** RANGE is a tap recognizer, and
  Flutter's tap recognizer gives up after 18 logical pixels of movement (about 3 mm) and reports a
  cancel, which `_onRangeRelease(null)` turns into "no bearing". **Measured in a widget test, not
  on a phone:** a hold that slid 10 pixels recorded its bearing; one that slid 30 pixels recorded
  nothing, and nothing on screen says why. A person turning on the spot with a thumb on the button
  is exactly the case that slides. *Take on map*'s hold button reads raw pointer events instead,
  so it ends only when that finger lifts, and a test pins it. 11.315's brief said to leave the
  existing capture unchanged, so RANGE is untouched. **Ask Michael whether RANGE has ever dropped a
  sweep in the field;** if yes, the fix is small: RANGE moves to the same raw-pointer hold.
  **[Resolved 2026-09-29: Michael, "fix it". Task 11.317 item 3.]**

- **[Found by task 11.58, 2026-09-29. Not built; a decision about the recovery plan.] A restore
  that copies the whole disk brings the old database identifier back, and nothing inside the
  database can tell.** Task 11.58's identifier survives a VM snapshot rolled back, a volume
  restored by a host, or any copy below Postgres, because it comes back with everything else.
  Devices then keep their bookmarks and receipts from *after* the snapshot, which is the exact
  failure 11.58 closed for `backup.sh`/`restore.sh` restores. **The server runs in a VM on one
  laptop**, so a snapshot rollback is a plausible recovery step, and task 11.80's undecided
  backup destination may make it more so. **A second detector exists and was not built:** the
  server knows the highest `server_seq` it has ever issued, so a pull whose cursor is above it is
  a bookmark from a timeline this database never had, and could be answered as a changed
  database. **It only catches devices that sync before the restored server overtakes their
  bookmark**, so it narrows the gap rather than closing it. **Ask the planning session** whether
  VM snapshots are part of the recovery plan; if they are, this wants its own task, or the
  recovery procedure should say to rotate the identifier by hand (`DELETE FROM
  server_database_identity;` then restart the server) after any snapshot rollback.
  **[Decided 2026-09-29 by the planning session: the procedure, not the second detector.]**
  `RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` D6 says to rotate the name after any snapshot rollback or disk-level
  restore, and to ask ITS whether the NAU host is snapshotted. The detector stays unbuilt unless
  snapshots turn out to be routine.
- **[Found by task 11.58, 2026-09-29. Not built; recorded because the path is new.] A device that
  resets over a replaced database pulls from zero, and a pull from zero is exempt from the
  tombstone-retention guard.** The exemption is right for an empty device. A device that meets a
  replaced database is not empty: if it also holds a record that was deleted on the server more
  than the 24-month retention window ago, and purged, it never learns of the deletion, and once
  its re-pull has moved it above the purge floor, its push offers the record back as new. **Needs
  both a replaced database and a device away for two years**, so it is not worth a task today.
  Written down so that the next change to either the retention guard or the reset reads it.
  **[Accepted 2026-09-29 by the planning session: recorded, no task.]**
- **[Found by task 11.58, 2026-09-29.] The protection starts at the first sync after both the
  server and the app carry it.** A linked project with no identifier stored adopts whatever
  answers, because it has nothing to compare with. So **a server restored or rebuilt before its
  devices have updated and synced once is still invisible to them.** Pinned by the `LIMIT, pinned`
  test in `test/data/sync/stale_cursor_new_server_test.dart`. **Ask the planning session to put a
  line on `RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md`**: before restoring or rebuilding a server real devices have
  synced against, make sure the server and every device have run a build with task 11.58 and
  synced at least once. The plan entry for 11.58 said it was already on that checklist; it was
  not (`grep 11.58 CLAUDE_DOCS/RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` finds nothing).
  **[Resolved 2026-09-29: `RELEASE_CHECKLIST.md` D6.]**
- **[Found by task 11.319, 2026-09-30. A test-harness defect, worked around and not fixed.] The map

  80% with 8 and 84% with 10**, nearly the same at 5°, 10° and 15° of bearing scatter. With the *true* κ the same ellipse covers

- **[Found by task 11.334, 2026-10-07. A decision for Michael, with its number.] The F-scaled ellipse misses its target; F ×
  n/(n−2) meets it everywhere.** Same simulation, seed and layouts as 11.323 (its chi-square column reproduces exactly), 2,000
  runs per cell. Coverage at a nominal 95%, chi-square / F / F × n/(n−2):
  3 bearings 39.5–43.0% / 90.3–91.0% / 93.7–94.4%; 4: 55.0–59.9% / 86.0–90.0% / 92.0–94.3%; 6: 72.1–75.8% / 88.4–90.2% /
  93.3–94.5%; 10: 82.6–85.6% / 89.8–92.3% / 92.8–95.7% (full table in 11.334's `TASK_COMMS.md` entry). **Why F alone falls
  short:** the F region is exact when the scatter is estimated as the residual sum of squares over n − 2, and the app's κ (Lenth's
  Eq. 2.10 and Fisher's approximation alike, which the paper's page 150 confirms) averages over n, so it is too large by about
  n/(n−2). **Not cited:** LOAS's manual (1/1/2005, p. 10 [p. 11, corrected by `/w-36`]) calls its preferred ellipse "Adjusted F … an unbiased estimator" and
  gives no formula; Lenth's paper says nothing on confidence regions. A possible exact source is White & Garrott (1990), which
  the LOAS manual cites; not available to this session. **Ask Michael to choose:** (a) ship F × n/(n−2) on the strength of the
  derivation and this measurement, named as TriTrack's own; (b) find and cite a definition first (White & Garrott); or (c) ship
  plain F, accepting 86–92%. Then re-brief 11.334 (or a new number) with that scale, keeping the simulation as acceptance. **[2026-10-07: Michael chose none of these: standard methods only (`CLAUDE.md` standing decision 5). White & Garrott (1990) read: they use κ from a system-tested standard deviation with chi-square. Caution and figures: task 11.336; the scales and the rest: task 11.337, later.]**
