- **[Found by 11.130 (2026-09-02), NOT FIXED — needs a task number. THE PRODUCT FINDING, and
  the more important half of that task.] Somebody who asks for three sign-in links in a quarter
  of an hour is told "sent" and gets nothing, and the only record is in a log nobody reads.**
  §4.4 allows three magic-link requests per address per fifteen minutes; the fourth is answered
  with the **identical `202`** and no email, because a `429` keyed on an address would tell the
  caller that somebody else recently asked for links for it (§4.5). **That is the design working,
  and it is still a person at a trailhead who cannot sign in.** Three requests is what impatience
  looks like — tap resend, switch to the laptop, tap resend again — and the app cannot be told
  why (task 11.119 settled that it cannot). **Do not redesign the response; the uniform `202` is
  load-bearing.** Two questions were put to Michael; **he answered the first on 2026-09-02 and
  the second is still open.**
  - **(a) Is three per fifteen minutes the right size for a person rather than for an attacker?**
    **Settled: yes** — Michael's words were *"that sounds about right."* **So the number is not
    the lever, and a task must not spend itself re-tuning it.** Nobody has measured it against a
    real sign-in attempt and it is now not going to be; that is a deliberate decision rather than
    an omission, and it is recorded here so the next task does not re-open it as one.
  - **(b) Does anything tell an operator the limit is tripping? Still open, and it is now the
    whole of the remaining work.** The row is written to `auth_audit_log` and **nothing surfaces
    it** — this is task 11.129's neighbourhood. **With (a) settled, the person-facing problem does
    not go away: they are still told "sent" and still receive nothing, and §4.5 plus task 11.119
    mean the app cannot be told why.** So the only place the situation can become visible to
    anybody is the operator's side. **Ask the planning session for a task covering (b) alone.**

- **[Found by 11.130 (2026-09-02), NOT FIXED — record, do not chase until it recurs.]
  `_isStale` in `test/e2e/support/magic_link_reader.dart` allows no clock grace, on a premise
  that holds on Linux and is unproven on Docker Desktop.** Its doc comment justifies the absence
  of a grace window with "the server writes the timestamp inside a container sharing this host's
  kernel clock, so there is no skew to absorb." **On Docker Desktop the daemon runs inside its own
  virtual machine with its own clock** — the same shape of platform difference task 11.69 was
  bitten by, where a bind mount passes ownership through on Linux and is remapped on Docker
  Desktop and nothing said so. A container clock even a few milliseconds behind this process's
  would make a fresh link look older than the request that asked for it and fail a **random
  minority** of sign-ins, which is exactly the shape of the six failures. **Measured 2026-09-02:
  the container read slightly ahead of the host, so it does not reproduce and 11.130 does not
  assert it.** The comment now says where the premise holds, and the timeout report prints both
  instants, **so the next occurrence is answered by reading the failure rather than by opening a
  task.** A task is worth asking for **only if a red run shows a negative gap** — the fix would
  then be a bounded skew allowance or a request instant taken from the server, never a longer
  wait.

- **[Found by 11.96 (2026-09-02), FIXED by 11.124, 2026-09-02 — `SyncSchedule.copyWith` with the
  same `_unset` sentinel `SyncStatus` uses; all five rebuild methods now go through it, and a
  test group asserts each carries every field] `SyncSchedule` (5 fields:
  `frequency`, `lastAttemptAt`, `lastSuccessAt`, `consecutiveFailures`, `stoppedReason`,
  `lib/data/sync/sync_schedule.dart`) has the same shape 11.96/11.117 fixed for `SyncStatus`, one
  size down.** Five methods — `recordAttempt`, `recordSuccess`, `recordFailure`, `withFrequency`,
  `resumed` — each hand-rebuild a new `SyncSchedule` by re-typing all five field names off the
  existing instance instead of through a `copyWith`, so a sixth field added later could be silently
  dropped from any one of the five. **Not fixed here**: 11.96's swept `lib/core/providers/*.dart`
  specifically (where every other status class already had a `copyWith`) and this file sits outside
  that directory; five fields is a smaller surface than `SyncStatus`'s fifteen, so the same mistake
  is easier to catch by eye today, but the mechanism that makes it unrepresentable is the same
  one-line fix. **Ask the planning session for a task applying `copyWith` to `SyncSchedule` the way
  11.96 did for `SyncStatus`.**

- **[Found by 11.134 (2026-09-02), NOT FIXED — needs a task number.] Five of the six map surfaces
  still say nothing when tiles stop arriving.** The counting is class-wide — every live tile in the
  app goes through one `CachedTileProvider`, and `TileFetchHealth.failing` is a listenable any
  screen can read without a second counter. **Only the Main Map presents it**, because that is the
  screen a field technician spends the day on and because each of the other five (Position
  Estimation's map half, the Record screen's two previews, the project extent picker, the Offline
  Data Map) has its own space budget that adding a band would spend without anybody measuring it.
  **The Offline Data Map is the one that matters most of the five**: it is the screen somebody uses
  to download tiles deliberately, so it is where "the provider is refusing us" would be most useful
  and where its absence is most misleading — a region download that fails every tile currently
  reports only a count. **Ask the planning session for a task that decides, per surface, whether
  the band goes on, and measures the screen with it up.**

- **[Found by 11.134 (2026-09-02), ACCEPTED, not a defect — recorded so it is not re-derived.] The
  tile `User-Agent` names a website this app ships separately from.** It is
  `TriTrack (edu.nau.tritrack; +<the project site>)`, and the OpenStreetMap policy asks for a way
  to reach somebody. **If that site ever moves, every already-installed build keeps sending the old
  address** — the same shape as the rule about a client hard-coding a fact about a server. It was
  accepted rather than avoided because the alternative is no contact at all, and because the
  durable half of the string is the bundle identifier: a tile operator can identify the app from
  that whether or not the address resolves. **The choice for Michael, if he wants a different one:
  an email address instead of a URL** — more durable, but it goes out in the clear on every tile
  request to three third parties, which is why one was not chosen for him.

- **[Found by 11.134 (2026-09-02), FIXED in the same commit — one line, no task needed.] The Main
  Map's space budget test printed the literal text `$clear` instead of the number it measured.**
  A `\$` in an interpolated string in `map_screen_space_budget_test.dart`'s newest case. It only
  ever runs on failure, so nobody had seen it — **and it is the same class as the instruments that
  print a name instead of a finding**: the one line that would explain a red was there and did not
  say anything.


- **[Found by 11.126 (2026-09-02), FIXED in the same commit] Three horizontal overflows on two
  screens that had only ever been rendered 800 logical pixels wide.** Task 11.126's nine renders
  are the first time either screen was pumped at 6.1-inch phone geometry, and all three showed up
  in the first run: the tag edit dialog's "Date put on" row **over by 139 pixels**, its "Link to
  project" dropdown **over by 5.3**, and the observation-sharing screen's two button rows **over
  by 63 and 64** — which means "Paste from clipboard" has been cut off on every phone since it was
  written. **None of the three is a new regression and none was caused by this task**; each was
  live and invisible because the tests around them set an 800×1600 surface for an unrelated reason
  (a dialog that overflowed *vertically* at 800×600) and never went back. Fixed with `Expanded`,
  `isExpanded: true`, and two `Wrap`s, each watched failing at phone width first. **The general
  form is task 11.110's, one layer out: a test surface chosen to make one thing fit is a claim
  about width as well as height, and nobody re-examines it.**

- **[Found by 11.126 (2026-09-02), NOT FIXED — TASK 11.132, given 2026-09-02. Small, and it is on a screen
  a person opens whenever they edit a project.] Project Setup is titled "New Project" while it is
  editing an existing project.** `project_setup_screen.dart:106` builds the `AppBar` title from
  `_loadedProject`, and `_loadedProject` is assigned at `:112` **inside the body's `data` branch,
  during the same build** — so the title is computed before the assignment every time, and nothing
  schedules another build afterwards. **It is not a one-frame flicker; it is the title for the
  whole visit.** Measured while task 11.126 was driving the screen's tag controls: the settled
  screen rendered the tags section for a loaded project *and* the title "New Project". The fix is
  to take the title from the async value the build already has rather than from mutable state
  written mid-build — one line and a test, but it is a change to how that screen carries its
  loaded project and it deserves its own entry rather than a drive-by. **The class is worth naming
  because it is invisible by construction: state mutated during `build` cannot affect anything
  built earlier in that same `build`, and no test asserts a screen's title.**

- **[Found by 11.126 (2026-09-02), NOT A DEFECT and NOT MEASURABLE — recorded so nobody spends
  the hour again] One of task 11.118's marginal overlaps can never be measured by a widget test
  on that screen.** The centred measure-result card against the right-anchored legend needs
  **exactly one** measure point on the map — and under the fake clock `flutter_map` holds a tap
  until another pointer event arrives, **so taps land in pairs and the reachable states are zero
  or two, never one.** The pair is structurally moot now (that card lives inside the measured
  column), **but nobody watched it fail**, and that distinction matters on this project: it is
  *unmeasured by construction*, not *measured and clear*. **If it ever needs a verdict it needs a
  different instrument than a widget test** — an integration test with a real clock, or a unit
  test on the layout arithmetic alone.

- **[Found by 11.126 (2026-09-02), NOT A DEFECT — recorded because it looks like one] The tag
  database's create-tag pre-check and its write ask about two different projects.**
  `mayCreateTagProvider` asks whether the person may write to the **active** project (and answers
  yes unconditionally when none is active, since an unlinked tag has no project scope to refuse
  against). The create dialog then offers **every project on the device** in its "Link to project"
  dropdown, and `TagRepository.insert` asks about **whichever one was picked**. So a viewer with
  no active project is correctly offered the button and correctly refused at Save. **That is the
  two-layer design working, not a hole** — the write is the authority and it refused — and task
  11.126 now renders the sentence they read. It is recorded here only so the next reader who
  notices the mismatch does not re-derive it as a finding: *the pre-check is advisory and is
  allowed to be more permissive than the write; it must never be less.*


- **[Found by 11.118 (2026-09-02), CLOSED by 11.126 item B, 2026-09-02 — three of the four
  reproduced at phone geometry and are fixed by measurement rather than constants; the fourth did
  not reproduce (50 pixels of clearance) and was deliberately left alone with a guard test; both
  marginal ones are resolved. See task 11.126's entry for the measurements, and for the one
  marginal pair no widget test on that screen can drive at all.] Four `Stack`s in `lib/` have two
  children that can paint on top of each other, and one of them covers the only control that
  starts a recording.** Task 11.111's grep, run: **11 `Stack`s, 9 with two or more children
  sharing or overlapping an anchor — 4 accidental, 2 marginal, 5 deliberate.** The four:
  **(1)** `lib/features/map/screens/map_screen.dart:989` — `_SelectionInfoPanel`
  (`left:12, right:12, bottom:12`) is declared after the bottom band (`:835`, scale bar,
  coordinate readout, map credit) **and after the record FAB (`:979`, `right:20, bottom:20`)**,
  so selecting a bearing paints over all three. The bottom band carries `right: 76` with a
  comment saying it is there to clear the FAB; **nothing clears the selection panel**, and what
  a person loses is the button they press to record.
  **Michael checked (1) on the device, 2026-09-02, and downgraded it: real, and not harmful.**
  Selecting a bearing does cover the `+` record button on the lower right — **but the Record
  entry in the bottom navigation is still available, and tapping out of the selection brings the
  `+` back.** So the control is never actually lost. **Fix it anyway** — it is a few pixels of
  clearance and the band beside it shows exactly how — **but it is not urgent, and no report
  should describe it as a control a person cannot reach.** *This is what a reading of the source
  was worth before anybody opened the app: the overlap was real and the consequence was not.*
  **(2)** `map_screen.dart:879` and `:1040` — the elevation profile panel and the computation
  progress bar share `left:0, right:0, bottom:0` exactly. Their conditions
  (`_measurePoints.length == 2`, `status is ComputationRunning`) are **not** mutually exclusive:
  a solve can run while two measure points are down.
  **(3)** `lib/features/more/screens/offline_data_map_screen.dart:223` vs `:230` — the selection
  readout lifts itself by a hard-coded `140` when any job is active, which is sized for
  **exactly one**; the job cards stack at `12 + i*84`, so a second job reaches it and a third
  sits on it.
  **(4)** `offline_data_map_screen.dart:195` vs `:221` — the coverage legend (`left:12, top:12`,
  intrinsically sized) and the button column (`right:12, top:12`) share the top band with no
  width constraint on either, which is the defect the map screen already fixed by giving its
  left band `right: 76`.
  The two marginal ones are `map_screen.dart:867`/`:860` (a centred result card that can reach
  under a right-anchored legend on a phone) and
  `lib/features/position_estimation/screens/position_estimation_screen.dart:1072`/`:1084` (two
  identical `bottom:60` anchors whose conditions *are* exclusive today — duplicated code one
  edit away from a collision). The five deliberate ones are the map's two `map-top-band`
  branches, its banner/north-arrow pair (already fixed once, with the comment recording it),
  the fanned colour swatches, the compass dial's co-centred painters, and four `IgnorePointer`
  overlays. **Worth a task.** Say plainly what it is not: **this is a reading of the source, not
  a measurement.** None of the four was reproduced by a test, and 11.118 deliberately did not
  fix them, because a layout fix nobody has looked at on a phone is how the last three of these
  arrived. The natural instrument already exists — `test/support/app_shell_harness.dart` renders
  a screen at real phone geometry, and `clearBandHeight` measures what is left uncovered.

- **[Found by 11.118 (2026-09-02), FIXED in the same commit] A check that reads "every file in
  the repository" was reading generated output no commit contains, and it went red on a stale
  copy of a file that had already been fixed.**
  `test/documentation/dev_stack_host_prerequisites_test.dart` walked `Directory.current` past a
  hand-written skip list, so it also read `.agents/` — a **git-ignored mirror of
  `.claude/commands/` that the Claude Code harness generates and never refreshes.** Its copy of
  task 11.125's command file still quoted the raw `docker compose` bring-up line that the
  **tracked** original had since been rewritten to *describe* rather than quote — and that
  original says in so many words that it describes the line **because this very check fails a
  file carrying a runnable one.** So the tracked file was right, the generated copy was behind,
  and the check could not tell them apart: `flutter test` was red on Michael's machine for a
  file he could not fix by editing the repository, and green in CI where `.agents/` does not
  exist. **The corpus is now asked of git** —
  `git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard`, which is exactly the set a commit could
  contain: tracked files **plus** untracked-and-not-ignored ones, so a script written five
  minutes ago is still constrained while build and tool output is not. It refuses an empty
  corpus rather than passing vacuously on one. Watched to fail on a probe file, and watched to
  stop failing when it was removed. **The general form is worth remembering:** a check whose
  corpus is "the working directory" measures whatever happens to be lying in it, and on this
  project two windows and a harness all write there.

- **[Found by 11.84 (2026-09-01), FIXED by 11.122 item 2, 2026-09-01 — the false sentences are gone;
  the `rejected` branch now names no cause and offers steps, and `held_row_details_test.dart`
  reads the copy] A refused name is
  explained to the person as an app bug they can do nothing about — and it is neither.**
  Task 11.84 measured what happens when the server refuses a `Users` row for a malformed
  name: the row is held, reported, and never retried, which is right. **What the person
  then reads is wrong.** `held_row_details.dart`'s `HeldRowReason.rejected` branch says
  *"That is a fault in the app or a version mismatch, not something wrong with what you
  recorded"* and *"nothing you can do in the app will change the answer."* For a name
  refusal both sentences are false: it **is** something about what was recorded, and
  editing the name in Profile fixes it and re-offers the row automatically — measured.
  **This is the same defect class as task 11.54's** (copy describing a mechanism the code
  does not have). The cause is that `rejected` is one bucket for two unrelated things,
  and the client cannot tell them apart because the push response carries an outcome
  with no issue detail — so the fix is either a second reason or an issue code on the
  wire, which is a decision rather than a wording change. **Nobody has hit this**: it
  needs the second finding below to be reachable at all.
- **[Found by 11.84 (2026-09-01), FIXED by 11.122 item 1, 2026-09-01 — `validateRequiredName`
  now asks `RowValidator.isWellFormedPersonName` and `TextBound.personName.maxLength`, and both
  screens have a test] Nothing stops a name the
  server will refuse from being typed in the first place.** `identity_validation.dart`'s `validateRequiredName` checks only that the field
  is non-empty — no length bound, and no use of `RowValidator.isWellFormedPersonName`.
  Both the identity setup screen and the profile screen use it. So a pasted name carrying
  a control character or a bidirectional override is accepted, saved, pushed, refused by
  the server, and then explained with the wrong sentence. **The bound is enforced only at
  the boundary**, which is correct for security and wrong for the person: they find out
  one sync later, on a different screen, in words that tell them not to try. **Fixing
  this one first makes the one above much rarer, and it is the smaller change** — the
  rule is already written and shared.
- **[Found by 11.119 (2026-09-01), CLOSED FOR NOW by Michael's decision, 2026-09-01, commit
  `2719e89`. Kept as a conditional, not a task.] The sign-in screen no longer promises an email,
  and specific copy about how a code reaches somebody is only possible if the server learns to
  say.** Michael chose, of three options, to change the screen rather than build a mail sender
  or restrict the beta to people he hands a code to. **The literal instruction could not be
  met:** the app cannot say how the code reaches somebody, because `/auth/magic-link` answers
  the identical `202` whether the code was emailed, written to a file or discarded — §4.5
  requires it to. So the copy is honest about not knowing and names an action instead, and a
  narrow checked vocabulary (`test/documentation/sign_in_delivery_vocabulary_test.dart`, beside
  11.98's) keeps the promise from coming back. **If specific copy is ever wanted it is a real
  task and not a small one:** the server would have to report its delivery method on the
  sign-in response, which touches `auth_routes.dart` (watched by the broken-control workflow)
  and needs a disclosure decision — telling an unauthenticated caller that a deployment has no
  mail sender is a property of the deployment rather than of any account, **believed below the
  §4.13 bar but not verdicted.** **Reopen only if somebody builds SMTP.**
- **[Found by 11.122 (2026-09-01), DONE by 11.124, 2026-09-02 — the wire now carries a
  `RowIssueCode` and the offending column's name, `invalid` only] Telling somebody *which*
  part of their record the server refused is a protocol-and-migration change, not a wording
  one.** Task 11.122 shipped items 1 and 2 and stopped at item 3 on the task's own
  instruction. **What item 3 actually costs, measured rather than guessed:** the push
  response (`SyncPushResponse` in `packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/sync_protocol.dart`)
  carries `outcomes` — a row key to a bare outcome string — and nothing else, so a code
  needs a **new field on the wire**; the server sets `SyncRowOutcome.invalid` at **five
  separate sites** in `server/lib/src/sync/sync_service.dart`, none of which currently
  carries the `RowIssue` list that explains the refusal; `RowIssue` has no code field, and
  this task's constraint is that a code must be **derived from the `ColumnSpec` bound that
  produced the refusal** rather than typed at the throw site (task 11.88's rule), which
  means adding a code to `TextShape`/`TextBound` and threading it out of `RowValidator`;
  and the client must **store** the code, which is a new column on `Sync_Held_Rows` and
  therefore a `latestSchemaVersion` bump plus a migration step, under the upgrade-test
  discipline tasks 11.16 and 11.82 established. **The honest default is already in place, so
  nothing is broken while this waits** — a person whose name is refused now reads a sentence
  that claims no cause and offers steps, rather than one telling them to stop. What item 3
  buys is the *true* sentence instead of the honest shrug. **Two constraints carry forward
  unchanged:** an unrecognised code must fall back to the honest default (which means the
  fallback constants must stay reachable, not be replaced), and the code must not widen what
  a refusal discloses — the `unauthorized` outcome stays opaque per security model §4.13;
  only `invalid`, which is about the row the client itself sent, can carry detail.
- **[Found by 11.84 (2026-09-01), FIXED 2026-09-01 by the planning session — and it was
  worse than reported] The security model still lists the deleted redeem route.** `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`'s route table
  carries a row for `POST /projects/invites/redeem` explaining its lack of a `project_id`
  parameter. The route is gone as of 11.84. **Claude Code did not edit it** — it is the
  planning session's document and this is a one-line correction, not a judgment call.
  **What the planning session found when it went to make that one-line correction:
  §4.21.2 is stale in both directions at once.** It also still gives verdicts to the three
  owner-side invitation routes, deleted by 11.81 — four dead rows, not one — and it has
  **no row at all for any of the ten join-settings, join-code, join-request and
  re-admission routes that replaced them**, three of which are grants. The four dead rows
  are deleted and the gap is now stated in the document. **The ten were deliberately not
  hand-written in** — that is task **11.123**, which extends 11.84's own route enumerator
  to the second document that claims to list every route and is checked by nothing.

- **[Found by 11.103 (2026-09-01), FIXED IN 11.103, NO TASK NEEDED — recorded because of what
  it says about the class] Asking how many map tiles a box contains built the list to count
  it, and the app stopped responding.** `OfflineTileDownloader.estimateTileCount` was
  `SlippyMap.tilesForBounds(...).length` — it allocated one object per tile in order to
  measure how many there were. The Offline Data Map's **"New selection"** seeds a box covering
  60% of whatever is on screen, so a person who pinches out to find themselves and then taps it
  asks for every tile on the visible planet at zooms 12–16: hundreds of millions of objects, on
  the UI thread, with no progress and no way back. **This was live before task 11.103** — it
  needed only a wide zoom, which anybody can reach by pinching — and it is fixed here (one
  multiplication per zoom level; `offline_tile_downloader_test.dart` now bounds the call at one
  second and prints the count it measured). **How it was found is the part worth keeping:** it
  surfaced only because 11.103 changed that screen's *default* zoom to world scale, and the
  screen's own test suite went from under a second to over four minutes per test. Nothing
  failed. **A suite that gets 250× slower and still passes is reporting a defect in the only
  language it has**, and the standing habit should be to chase that rather than wait it out.

- **[Found by 11.103 (2026-09-01), NEEDS A TASK NUMBER — small] The Offline Data Map does not
  consult the project extent, only GPS.** Task 11.103 gave every map the same fallback chain
  (device fix → most recent recordings → project extent → an honest whole-planet view), and
  this screen implements the first and last steps only. Wiring `currentProjectProvider` into
  it was tried and **backed out**: that screen has never touched a repository, and the watch
  took its own suite from under a second to over three minutes per test even with an in-memory
  database. The defect this task existed to close is shut either way — with no fix the screen
  now shows the whole planet rather than a spot in the Gulf of Guinea. What is left is a
  *nicety*: somebody downloading tiles for their study area has to pan there first. Suggested
  scope: give this screen the project's extent through something cheaper than the full project
  repository (the four bbox numbers, read once), and find out why watching that provider is
  expensive under the test clock — **the second half is the more valuable one**, because if it
  is expensive in a test it may be expensive on a phone.

- **[Found by 11.109 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK NUMBER] The same accretion is now underway on
  the map layer of this screen, and nothing measures it.** Task 11.109 fixed the panel and left
  the map alone, but the Position map carries **eight** pieces of permanent overlay furniture: a
  three-way basemap toggle, a north arrow, a measure button, a legend button, a

  `position_screen_space_budget_test.dart` to assert a minimum area of unobstructed map, and

- **[Found by 11.109 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK NUMBER] No other screen has a space budget
  either, and the Main Map is the one most likely to have the same defect.** The defect 11.109
  fixed was invisible to every existing test because each one asks whether a control is present
  and correct, and none asks whether the screen still works with all of them at once. That is
  true of every screen in this app. The Main Map is the immediate candidate: it has a
  `DraggableScrollableSheet` with its own accumulated contents, and it is the screen this
  project has furnished most often. Suggested scope: generalise the harness in
  `position_screen_space_budget_test.dart` — pump the screen inside the real app shell at

- **[Found by 11.104 (2026-08-31), TASK 11.105 NEEDS RE-BRIEFING] The mechanism
  behind the dead typed catches is not `ProviderException` at every site, and at
  the site 11.104 fixed it is not `ProviderException` at all.** Task 11.105's
  entry says Riverpod 3 *wraps* a provider's error in `ProviderException`, so a
  typed `catch` cannot match. Measured on 2026-08-31 against the real providers:
  `await ref.read(serverHttpClientProvider.future)`, which is the exact call
  `SyncController._engine` and `CurrentSession._requireClient` make, does not
  deliver a `ProviderException` **or** the original `InvalidServerUrl`. It
  delivers `StateError: "The provider serverHttpClientProvider was disposed
  during loading state, yet no value could be emitted."` The provider is
  autoDispose and `ref.read(...future)` holds no listener across the await, so
  the element is torn down mid-build and **the original error is destroyed, not
  wrapped.** A shared unwrap of `ProviderException` would therefore fix nothing
  at this site. **The action:** re-scope 11.105 to cover both mechanisms — the
  `ProviderException` wrap *and* the autoDispose/`ref.read` teardown — and note
  that for the second one the durable fix is not a better `catch` at all. It is
  what 11.104 did: read the condition as a value from a keepAlive provider that
  cannot throw. An error that has to survive a provider boundary to reach a
  person is an error that does not reach them.

- **[Found by 11.104 (2026-08-31), FIXED IN 11.104 — recorded because it is a
  shape, not an incident] The Server URL field's placeholder proposed the exact
  address a release build refuses.** `hintText` was `http://192.168.1.42:8080`
  in every build — the LAN shape `README.md` §4 ends in. A field that suggests
  an example and then rejects it is the wrong-cause class one layer further out.
  It now follows the build mode. Worth a sweep at some point for other hints and
  examples that a release build's own rules disagree with.

- **[Found by 11.104 (2026-08-31), FIXED IN 11.104] The URL field was stricter
  than the thing it guards.** `validateServerUrl` used `Uri.isAbsolute`, which is
  false whenever a fragment is present, so the field refused
  `http://192.168.1.42:8080/#top` — an address `ServerConfig` would have accepted
  and flattened without complaint. `normalizeServerBaseUrl` already carried a
  comment saying `isAbsolute` was wrong for exactly this reason, and the
  validator twenty lines away still used it. **The same fact was known and fixed
  in one of two places** — the shape task 11.98 established a checked vocabulary
  for.

- **[Found by 11.104 (2026-08-31), FIXED IN 11.104] A security check keyed on a
  typed-in count.** `release_mode_transport_test.dart` asserted
  `'= !kDebugMode'.allMatches(source).length == 2`. Splitting one function into
  two turned it red with no control changed, and the only thing that would make
  it green again is editing the number — which is the failure mode the rule
  against hand-maintained lists exists to prevent. It now derives every
  `releaseMode` default from the source and requires each to be `!kDebugMode`,
  however many there are.

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK — BETA-BLOCKING] A release build
  with a plain-`http://` LAN server reports "Offline" and blames the network,
  and the message that names the real cause is never shown to anybody.** This
  is the largest thing the Android walkthrough found and it is **not
  Android-specific** — it is `!kDebugMode`, so an iOS release build does the
  same. `requireValidServerUrl` (`lib/core/providers/server_config_provider.dart:240`)
  correctly refuses `http://` in a release build and throws `InvalidServerUrl`
  carrying an excellent sentence: *"This build requires https:// — a plain
  http:// connection would expose your sign-in and your observations to anyone
  on the network."* **Nothing in the app catches `InvalidServerUrl`** —
  grepped, there is not one `catch` for it. Measured on a device: the sync bar
  says **"Offline — last synced 5 min ago"**, the Server Connection screen says
  **"Could not read your signed-in devices — nothing answered at that
  address"**, and the header still says *"Server configured"*. Three places
  tell the person their network or their server is broken. The network was
  fine, the server answered `/health` throughout, and map tiles kept loading.
  **Why it is beta-blocking:** the beta build *is* a release build, and
  `README.md` §4's whole LAN procedure ends in an `http://` address. The
  settings field's own validator does show the right message while you type,
  so the trap is a URL that reached storage any other way — a debug build, a
  restore, a device handed over configured. That is exactly the gap task 10.48
  built `requireValidServerUrl` for. **The action:** a task that carries
  `InvalidServerUrl`'s message to the sync bar, the sync-status screen and the
  server screen, so a refusal by *this build* never reads as a refusal by the
  network. Consider also whether §4 should tell a beta tester to run a debug
  build, or whether the LAN prototype needs TLS before the beta.

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK — the class behind the entry
  above] An error thrown inside a Riverpod provider does not arrive at the
  screen written to explain it.** Riverpod 3 wraps it. Its own doc says so:
  *"Using an asynchronous provider, you awaited `FutureProvider.future`, and
  the provider was in error state"* → the caller gets a `ProviderException`
  holding the original (the `riverpod` package's own `lib/src/common/stack_trace.dart`, version 3.3.2 — pub cache, not a file in this repository).
  So every `e is SomeTypedException` test at a `.future` await site is **dead
  code**, and this would have worked under Riverpod 2 — it is a migration
  casualty, not a coding mistake. **Two confirmed live instances, both
  reproduced on a device:**
  1. `lib/features/more/screens/project_setup_screen.dart:408` — deny location
     permission twice (Android 11+ then makes it permanent) and tap *Use
     current location*. The app says **"Could not get a GPS fix. Try again
     outdoors or with a clear sky view."** It has the right sentence —
     *"Location permission denied — enable it in Settings"* — and cannot reach
     it. A person who has just refused a dialog is told to go outside, forever.
     `logcat` also shows an unhandled Dart exception on every denial.
  2. The `InvalidServerUrl` entry above.
  **The action:** a task that fixes the *class* — unwrap `ProviderException`
  once, in one shared helper, and route every `.future`-await catch site
  through it — then sweeps `lib/` for every `is <Typed>Exception` downstream of
  a provider await and proves each one can still fire. Not one-site patches:
  this is the standing "fix the class, not the instance" criterion, and the two
  instances found here were found by walking two unrelated screens.

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK] Every first publish refuses one
  record, then raises a red alarm telling the person to report a bug that
  clears itself.** Reproduced on a fresh device: publishing a new project with
  one locally-created tag and one bearing puts `Projects`, `Tags`,
  `Project_Tags`, `Observations`, `Users` and `Project_Memberships` on the
  server and **refuses the `Tag_Versions` row**
  (`sync_traffic_log`: `rows_pushed=1, rows_applied=0, rows_rejected=1`). The
  app shows a red banner *"1 record isn't on the server"* and a card saying the
  refusal *"is not a case the app expects"* and *"this is worth reporting"*.
  **About four minutes later a routine sync accepted it silently** (push #8,
  `rows_applied=1`), so the alarm is real, alarming, and transient.
  **Cause, pinned:** `ProjectPublisher` sends **one table per HTTP request**
  (`lib/data/sync/project_publisher.dart:192-205`) and `Tables.all` orders
  `tagVersions` **before** `projectTags`
  (`packages/tritrack_sync/lib/src/schema_constants.dart:83-84`).
  `Tag_Versions` is a global table reached through `Project_Tags`, so
  `server/lib/src/authz/row_authorizer.dart:1899` denies it: the tag was not
  established earlier *in this push* (each request builds a fresh authorizer)
  and the project does not yet reach it (the `Project_Tags` row arrives in the
  *next* request). The server comment two blocks up at :1861 names this exact
  split-across-pushes hazard for the role rung and mitigates it there — and the
  reachability escape below has the same weakness with no mitigation.
  **Why no test caught it:** every server test pushes the tables together in
  one request (`server/test/integration/member_authorization_test.dart:2298`
  says so in its own comment), and the client-side test that claims this
  ("produces no refused record — the headline",
  `test/data/sync/project_publisher_test.dart:276`) uses a fake transport that
  models no reachability rule at all. **Task 11.43 is marked Done and its
  acceptance is not met on real hardware.** **The action:** a task to reorder
  `syncTables` so `projectTags` precedes `tagVersions` (FK-safe — the only
  reference is `Tag_Versions.tag_id → Tags`, which stays first), or make the
  publisher send dependency-linked tables in one request; **and** a test that
  replays the publisher's real request sequence against the real server rather
  than a fake. **This also fires release-checklist item F2's trigger and task
  11.50's deferral trigger** — somebody has now seen a refused record. The
  planning session should decide whether 11.50 stays deferred given the cause
  is understood and local.

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK] The capability enumeration
  reads the manifests a person wrote, not the one Android enforces.**
  `test/platform/capability_matrix_test.dart` parses only
  `android/app/src/{main,debug,profile}/AndroidManifest.xml`. Gradle merges
  every plugin's library manifest in before packaging, and the merged result
  contains components nobody in this repository typed: geolocator's
  `GeolocatorLocationService` with `foregroundServiceType="location"`,
  `GoogleApiActivity` and the Play-services version marker, file_picker's
  `GET_CONTENT */*` package-visibility query, AndroidX's
  `DYNAMIC_RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED_PERMISSION`, and an **implied required**
  `uses-feature android.hardware.location`. None of it is wrong today and all
  of it is now written down in `CLAUDE_DOCS/CAPABILITY_MATRIX.md` — but it
  arrived without anybody choosing it, which is the same shape as the missing
  location permission task 11.40 found, one level up. **The action:** a task
  that makes the guard read the *built* merged manifest (or `aapt2 dump
  badging` on the APK) and fail when a component appears with no row — so the
  next plugin upgrade that adds a permission cannot land silently. Note the
  guard would then need a build, so it belongs in the build-check workflow
  rather than the offline suite.

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK — decide before the beta ships]
  The Android release build is signed with the debug keystore.** Verified on
  the artifact, not just in the Gradle file: `apksigner verify --print-certs`
  on `app-release.apk` reports `CN=Android Debug`.
  `android/app/build.gradle.kts:31-34` says so and carries a `TODO`. Two
  consequences for a beta: **an APK rebuilt on a different machine has a
  different signature**, so testers get *"App not installed"* and must
  uninstall first — **which destroys every local observation on that device**,
  since the database lives in the app's private storage. And Google Play will
  not accept a debug-signed upload at all. The APK is also a 73.4 MB universal
  build (three ABIs); `--split-per-abi` or an app bundle would cut it to about
  a third. **The action:** a task that creates a real upload keystore, wires
  `key.properties` (already gitignored), documents where the key lives and who
  holds it, and decides APK-per-ABI versus bundle. **This is a decision only
  Michael can make** — where the signing key is kept is not a code question.

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK] The Android back gesture never
  leaves the app.** Pressed three times from the root Map tab, the activity
  stays resumed and nothing at all happens. On Android, back from an app's
  home screen is how you leave it; a screen that swallows it reads as a freeze,
  and this is the single most-used control on the platform. (Back is correct
  everywhere else: it dismisses the keyboard without popping, pops a pushed
  screen, and is correctly refused by the identity gate's
  `PopScope(canPop: false)`.) **The action:** a small task to decide and
  implement root-tab back behaviour — the Android convention is either "exit"
  or "return to the first tab, then exit", usually with a *press back again to
  exit* confirmation so a stray swipe cannot lose a draft.

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK] On the map, two of the three
  basemap options are drawn as bare text on top of the map.** `SegmentedToggle`
  gives the selected segment a filled background and leaves the other two
  transparent (`lib/features/map/screens/map_screen.dart:764-786`). Over a
  page that is fine; over a basemap the words *Street* and *Satellite* collide
  with street names and terrain and are close to unreadable — worst on the
  satellite and terrain layers this app is built around. Almost certainly the
  same on iOS; **not verified there**. **The action:** give the control an
  opaque or scrimmed background wherever it sits over a map. Same task can pick
  up two smaller things seen on the same walk: a stray rounded-box outline
  drawn between the position line and *"Draft autosaves"* on the record screen
  (`observation_logging_screen.dart` around :455-470, widget not identified),
  and the *"Try again"* action on a held-record card being green text on a red
  fill, which is hard to see and is the only way to act on that card.

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), SMALL, NEEDS A TASK] The server-URL field has

  `validateServerUrl` (`lib/core/providers/server_config_provider.dart:199-202`)

- **[Found by 11.66 (2026-08-31), SMALL] Two things worth writing down that are

- **[Found by 11.33 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK] Nothing exports a ground-truth
  point, so the column added to make exports survive a rename has nothing to
  travel in.** Task 11.33 records `tag_version_id` on every truth point for

  `Actual_Tag_Locations` at all — truth points are in no CSV and no archive
  the export path produces. A biologist who records a season of truth points

- **[Found by 11.33 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK] A truth point can be entered
  and drawn, and then never looked at, corrected or removed.** The map draws

- **[Found by 11.33 (2026-08-31), A DECISION FOR MICHAEL, THEN A TASK] Which
  kinds of truth point an accuracy statistic counts.** 11.33 deliberately
  computes nothing. When something does, the default it should ship with is
  **animal and collar together only**, because that is the only kind that
  validates the triangulation of a live collared animal; a collar-only point
  may be where the collar was shed days earlier, and scoring an estimate
  against it reports the app as wrong when it was right. The other two kinds
  should be available to include deliberately, with the screen saying which
  kinds a figure counted. Recorded here so the choice is made once, in the
  open, rather than assumed inside whichever task first computes a number.

- **[Found by 11.86 (2026-08-31), NEEDS A TASK] `backup_restore_drill` has
  never once passed on the real GitHub Actions runner since the check that
  fails it was added, and this is unrelated to the four invitation-route
  failures in the same run.** It fails at the drill's own step 0 — "The
  shipped compose file decides who the backup container is", added by task
  11.70 — which asks the backup container its own `id -u`/`id -g` and compares
  that against the invoking user's. **Evidence it predates this push**: the
  identical failure, at the identical step, appears on every CI run back to
  and including the very first run after task 11.70's commit landed
  (2026-08-30); it never went green on CI even once. **Evidence it is not the
  invite-404 defect**: no invitation, membership, or team route appears
  anywhere in this check's code path — it never speaks the sync wire at all.
  **Evidence pointing toward the actual mechanism rather than the CI
  environment generally**: the identical drill, run locally against Docker
  Desktop on a Mac, passes cleanly at step 0 and end to end (39/39 checks) —
  but the drill's own comments already document that Docker Desktop's
  file-sharing layer hides exactly this class of bug, so a local pass does not
  clear the Linux case the check exists to catch.

  **What I could not establish, and why:** the exact uid/gid the GitHub
  Actions runner's backup container actually reports. `fail()` writes that
  detail to a per-instrument log file `gate_smoke_test.sh` keeps only in a
  `mktemp` directory on the runner and never uploads; the workflow's own
  console output prints just the last five lines of that file on failure, and
  in every failing run those five lines are the teardown banner ("Tearing
  down… removed throwaway key and drill volumes"), not the `fail()` line
  naming the actual and expected values — the finding is in the log and never
  reaches anyone who only reads the workflow's console. That is worth its own
  small fix (keep the `fail()` line in the tail, or upload the instrument logs
  as an artifact on failure) independent of what step 0 turns out to mean.

  **Recommendation, not a diagnosis:** this reads more like task 11.70's fix
  for the backup container's operating user not actually holding on a real
  Linux host — the platform the check and the fix were both written for —
  than like a broken instrument, but I have not confirmed that with the actual
  mismatched uid values and did not modify the pipeline or the backup
  mechanism to chase it, per this task's instruction not to guess at a fix for
  anything backup-related. Ask the planning session to open a task that (a)
  captures the instrument's full log on a failing CI run (artifact upload, or
  print the `fail()` line instead of a fixed tail) and (b) resolves step 0
  against the real value it finds.

- **[CLOSED by task 11.79, 2026-09-01 — this became task 11.79 and is done.
  A third fact, worse than either of these two, was found while closing it: the
  sweep demoted itself to `tritrack_app`, which task 10.83 had revoked `DELETE`
  on both audit tables from, so it would have failed on a laptop as well.]
  Nothing runs the audit-log purge either, and the command the documentation
  gave cannot run on a deployed server.** Two separate facts, both live.

  **First: it is unscheduled, exactly as backups were.** `AuditRetentionService.
  purge()` is the mechanism and nothing calls it, so the retention windows in
  `server/README.md` — one year for sign-in events, 180 days for sync traffic —
  describe an intention rather than what is on disk. Both tables grow forever on
  a deployed server, and §4.7's own "Violated by:" list names "retention that
  quietly grows without bound".

  **What it costs a person, and why it is not beta-blocking the way 11.78 was.**
  A backup that never runs loses data nobody can get back. A purge that never
  runs *keeps* data: researcher email addresses and device identifiers
  accumulating years past the window that justified holding them, so every future
  breach of that database discloses more than the design said it could. That is a
  liability that grows with time, not a loss. It should be fixed before the
  database holds more than one project's people.

  **Second, and more concrete: the documented command has never been runnable on
  a real deployment.** `server/README.md` said to run
  `dart run bin/purge_audit_logs.dart`, "e.g. a daily cron inside the container".
  `server/Dockerfile` AOT-compiles only `bin/server.dart` and its runtime stage is
  a bare `debian:bookworm-slim` with **no Dart SDK and no source**, so that
  command fails on any deployed server. It works only on a developer's machine
  with the SDK and the repository. The README now says so; nothing is fixed.

  **The fix has a template now.** 11.78's shape applies almost unchanged: compile
  the purge entrypoint into the server image, schedule it the way
  `backup-scheduler` is scheduled, and — the part that matters — **measure the
  age of the oldest surviving row rather than whether a timer exists**, which is
  a `SELECT MIN(occurred_at)` on each table. Roughly a day's work.

- **[CLOSED by task 11.78, 2026-08-30 — this became task 11.78 and is done.]
  Nothing schedules a backup, and nothing notices that none has happened.** 11.70
  closed the case where the backup fails and says the wrong thing. It did not
  touch the case where the backup is simply never run: `server/README.md` says
  "schedule it the same way as the audit purge — a daily cron", which is a
  documented step a human performs and nothing checks — the same class 11.70's
  own decision rejected for the ownership fix. **What it costs a person:** the
  identical harm, arrived at differently. They believe they have encrypted
  backups; the newest archive is from the week they set the server up. The
  server knows when the last archive was written and says so to nobody. Worth
  scoping before beta: the smallest honest version is the diagnostics console
  (or the sync screen) naming the age of the newest archive, so "no backup since
  March" is visible rather than inferable.

- **[Found by 11.70 (2026-08-30), NOT FIXED — a claim in a document, planning
  session's call]** `TriTrack_Security_Model.md`'s C-4 evidence rows and §4.9
  describe the backup drill as it stood before 11.69 put `--user` in it. Those
  rows are now *more* true than they were between 11.69 and 11.70 — the drill
  measures the shipped procedure again, and Gate C entry 16's evidence is
  stronger than the record says. **Nothing there is false and no verdict
  moves**, so this is a record-keeping item, not a finding. Mentioned because

- **[Found by 11.69 (2026-08-30), second pass, NOT FIXED — needs its own task]
  A caller can tell which projects exist on the server by timing the refusal.**
  Somebody who is signed in but holds no membership on a project asks for it. The
  server refuses, and the refusal for a project that **really exists** is
  consistently a little slower than for one that does not — measured at **+0.052,
  +0.061 and +0.049 milliseconds** on three separate CI runs, the sign positive in
  **9 of 9 trials every time**, with the instrument's own null pair (two fictional
  ids, whose true difference is exactly zero) flipping sign each run, which is what
  rules out drift. The bodies are byte-identical; only the clock differs.
  **What it costs a person:** the project existence oracle that findings C-2 and D-1
  closed by making every refusal say the same thing is open again through the one
  channel none of that work covered. Somebody who once had access — a removed
  collaborator — can sweep ids and learn which ones are real projects on that server.
  **Why nobody saw it in four gates:** on a Mac the measurement is drift-dominated
  and the check reports mixed signs or INCONCLUSIVE; on a clean Linux runner, 54
  microseconds is resolvable. **The beta server is a Linux machine.** This is the
  exact thing the workflows were built to catch, on their first honest run.
  Found by `verify_11_49_server_reads.py` probe 7 (entry 28) and, once, by
  `gate_c_adversarial_pass.py`'s Cg check on `/sync/pull` — **two different routes,
  so it is unlikely to be one handler's accident.** **Nothing was baselined and no
  threshold was widened**, so the gate instruments workflow is red in about four runs
  of five until this is answered; that is deliberate. **Action: ask the planning
  session to open a task for it. It carries a decision — whether ~54 microseconds on
  a LAN deployment is inside `SECURITY_SCOPE_AND_EXIT.md`'s bar or is accepted in
  writing — and that decision is not Claude Code's to make.** Uncertainty worth
  stating: what actually costs the extra time was not investigated, and it may be as
  ordinary as one extra index probe.

- **[Found by 11.69 (2026-08-30), second pass, ANSWERED — no task needed] The
  five-line tail question has an answer that is not "upload the logs".** The entry
  below asks whether a redacted log upload is worth designing. Two days of runs say
  it is not the thing to fix: the tail failed twice, and both times the missing
  information was **one line the instrument already held and did not print** — the
  owner of the link directory, and the milliseconds behind a check name. Both are
  now printed, and neither is redactable material. **The tail is sufficient exactly
  when an instrument's last words are a finding rather than a name**, which is a
  standing obligation on instruments rather than a change to CI. **Action: ask the
  planning session to close the log-upload question with that answer, or to say why
  it disagrees.**

- **[Found by 11.69 (2026-08-30), NOT FIXED] The shipped backup job cannot write
  its archive on a Linux server.** The backup container runs as its own `postgres`
  user (uid 70) rather than root, deliberately. On Linux a bind mount passes host
  ownership through unchanged, so the `backups/` directory `server/README.md` tells
  an operator to create — owned by them — is one the container cannot create a file
  in, and the mode-600 signing key it tells them to generate is one the container
  cannot read. `backup.sh` then reports `pg_dump | age pipeline failed; no archive
  written`, **which names the wrong cause**, and an operator would reasonably read
  it as a database problem. On macOS with Docker Desktop none of it happens, which
  is why it survived four gates: the file-sharing layer presents host files to
  whichever user the container runs as. **What it costs a person: they set up
  encrypted backups, see one error they cannot interpret, and either give up or
  believe they have backups they do not have.** Task 11.69 fixed the two drill
  scripts (they now pass `--user`) so the instruments run on Linux, and wrote the
  trap and a `chown` workaround into `server/README.md` — **but the real fix is a
  custody decision, not a script change**: either the compose file declares a user
  for the backup service, or the documented procedure gains a `chown` step, or the
  image stops running as `postgres`. Each has a different consequence for who can
  read the signing key on a shared machine. **Action: ask the planning session to
  add a task for this and to decide which of the three shapes it wants; it is a
  §4.9 custody question, not a permissions bug.** Note the second cost: the drill
  passing is no longer evidence that a real deployment's backup can write.

- **[Found by 11.69 (2026-08-30), NOT FIXED] When a gate instrument fails in CI,
  only five lines of its log survive.** `gate_smoke_test.sh` writes each
  instrument's full output to a `mktemp` directory on the runner and prints
  `tail -n 5`. That directory dies with the runner, so the two backup failures
  above had to be diagnosed by reading the scripts and reasoning about uid
  semantics rather than by reading what actually happened — which is exactly the
  kind of inference this project keeps paying for. **The obvious fix is blocked by
  a real constraint, which is why this is a decision and not a chore:** those logs
  can contain live session tokens, and §4.7's never-log rule names the CI artifact
  specifically as the reason. **Action: ask the planning session whether a redacted
  upload is worth designing, or whether the five-line tail plus a re-run with
  `workflow_dispatch` is the accepted answer. Either is defensible; leaving it
  unstated is not.**

- **[Found by 11.40 (2026-08-29), DECLARED but NOT VERIFIED] Location on Android
  has never worked, and file access on macOS has never worked.** Both are the same
  class as 11.38's keychain failure and both were live for months. Android declared
  no location permission at all while `gps_provider.dart` requested one — Android
  denies an undeclared runtime permission **without showing a dialog**, so the app's
  own "location was denied" message appeared and a person read it as having refused.
  macOS declared the sandbox in all four entitlement files and never declared
  `com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-write`, so all six file-panel call
  sites (CSV export, CSV import, backup save, backup restore) get a panel and then
  no permission to touch what was picked. **11.40 added both declarations and a
  guard that fails if either is removed. Neither behaviour has been run**, because
  nobody has ever run this app on an Android device and the macOS export path has
  not been exercised since the entitlement landed. **Action: these are release
  checklist items H2 and H3 and they need Michael with a device; ask the planning
  session whether the Android half deserves its own task, since "has anyone ever run
  this on Android" is a larger question than one permission.**

- **[Found by 11.40 (2026-08-29)] `permission_handler` is a dead dependency with a
  latent permission surface.** Zero references in `lib/`, `packages/` or `test/`. At
  the pinned version its library manifest declares nothing and `ios/Podfile` sets no

  adds those macros it contributes a large permission set nobody chose. Not removed
  by 11.40 because removing a direct dependency needs a build on each platform to
  confirm, which this task could not run for iOS or Android. **Action: ask the
  planning session to schedule its removal, or to record a reason for keeping it.**

- **[Found by 11.40 (2026-08-29)] The macOS cloud-backup folder has no
  implementation.** iOS uses a security-scoped bookmark and Android a persistable

  `macos/Runner/AppDelegate.swift` registers no channel at all. Consistent with the

- **[Found by 11.40 / 11.52 (2026-08-29), DELIBERATELY NOT DONE] The
  source-identity verdict is described in several operator-facing files at once.**
  **This bullet used to name a total of seven and list six; task 11.212 removed the

  fictional null, pass/fail on sign stability, and INCONCLUSIVE rather than HELD
  when the null's own sign is unanimous. **This is a check that could not fail
  honestly**, which is the same class as a check that cannot fail at all.

- **[Found by 11.59 (2026-08-29), NEEDS A DECISION FROM MICHAEL, then possibly a
  task] The battery and data cost of automatic sync has still never been
  measured on hardware.**
  Task 10.8's numbers are reasoning and task 11.59 shipped that reasoning rather
  than measuring, deliberately: a measurement needs a phone in the field for a
  day against a real server, which is Michael's to run and not something a task
  can do from here. **What the reasoning says**, so a measurement has something
  to disagree with: at the default setting a device attempts at most four times
  an hour *while the app is open*, each attempt is one HTTPS round trip carrying

  to send and nothing to receive is a few kilobytes. **What is not known:** what
  that costs on a genuinely metered or satellite link over a working day.
  **The default itself is no longer in question** — Michael settled it on
  2026-08-29, after seeing automatic sync working on a running build: fifteen
  minutes stays, because *"other team data needs to be timely"*. What is left
  here is the cost, not the choice. **Action: a beta tester's device is the
  measurement.** If it turns out to matter, the remedy already exists and is on
  the screen — "Hourly" or "Only when I ask" — which is why this is not
  beta-blocking.

- **[Found by 11.36 (2026-08-29), NEEDS A TASK, BETA-BLOCKER CANDIDATE] The iOS app
  froze and had to be force-restarted after being signed out remotely — cause not
  established.** Michael revoked the iPhone's session from the Mac using the new
  device list on 2026-08-29. **The revocation itself worked**: after restarting, the
  iPhone was correctly signed out. But the iPhone's app stopped responding and needed
  a restart, which is the most severe symptom class this project has had reported.
  **The cause is not known and is not guessed at here.** What is known:
  - **No request this app makes to a server has a timeout.** Verified across
    `AuthClient` and `HttpSyncTransport`: not one call is wrapped in `.timeout(...)`,
    and neither client sets one (`createPlatformHttpClient` takes
    `CupertinoClient.defaultSessionConfiguration()` on iOS/macOS and a bare
    `http.Client()` elsewhere). So a stalled request leaves whichever control started
    it disabled — `_busy` stays true — for as long as the platform allows, which is
    60 seconds on iOS's request timer and **unbounded** on Android and Linux. That
    produces exactly the symptom class described. **It is a real defect either way and
    should get a task on its own merits**, whether or not it is this one.
  - **It is a plausible mechanism, not a diagnosis.** A revoked device should get a
    prompt `401`, not a stall, so the timeout gap does not by itself explain a freeze
    here. Task 11.36's own new screen is also on the suspect list and cannot be ruled
    out: it is what was open, and it re-reads the session list on every change to the
    stored session. Reading it found no rebuild loop, but "I could not find one" is
    not "there is none".
  - **Not reproduced.** One occurrence, on hardware, not repeated. **Action: ask the
    planning session for a task**, and it needs three facts from Michael that only he
    has — what screen the iPhone was on, whether it froze on its own or after a tap,
    and whether anything was spinning. **A timeout on every server request should be
    scoped as its own decision** rather than folded in: too short a limit breaks a
    large sync on a slow field link, so the number is a judgement about field
    conditions, not a default to pick.

- **[Found by 11.36 (2026-08-29), NEEDS A TASK] The e2e suite's magic-link reader
  reports a timeout as the per-address rate limit, which is a message naming the
  wrong cause.** Observed twice on 2026-08-29: fourteen and then three tests
  failed with *"the link ... was issued before this request and never refreshed
  within 0:00:10 — so the server accepted the request and wrote nothing, which is
  what the per-address rate limit looks like from the outside."* **That diagnosis
  is almost certainly wrong in these cases.** Every address involved was freshly
  minted by `randomEmail()` and the per-address bucket is three requests per
  fifteen minutes, so no address could have been near it. What actually fits is
  that the server's write to the bind-mounted directory took longer than the
  reader's ten-second timeout, and `waitForMagicLinkToken` reports *whatever it
  last saw* — a stale file from a previous run — as evidence of the rate limit.
  **What it costs:** the message sends whoever is debugging to restart the server
  to clear an in-process limiter that was never tripped, which is the same defect
  class as task 11.37 item 1 and this one is inside the test harness. **Not
  reproducible on demand, and that is stated rather than glossed:** four
  subsequent full runs were green, including two on a cold stack (`down -v` then
  `up --build`) and one immediately after a `restart`. **Action: ask the planning
  session for a task** to make the reader distinguish *"the file never changed"*
  from *"the limiter refused"* — it cannot tell them apart today, and a check that
  cannot distinguish two causes is the thing this project keeps paying for. It
  should probably also count its own requests per address, which is the one piece
  of evidence that would settle it.

- **[Found by 11.57 (2026-08-29), SCHEDULED as task 11.59 (2026-08-29), together
  with Michael's decision that the app should sync automatically and that the sync
  screen should offer a frequency control] Nothing in the app ever starts a sync on
  its own.**
  `SyncController.syncIfDue` exists, documents itself as *"an opportunistic
  attempt, e.g. on foreground"*, respects `SyncSchedule`, and **has no caller
  anywhere in `lib/`.** `syncNow` has three: the sync-status screen's button and
  pull-to-refresh, the held-row retry, and `_afterMembershipChange`. So a device
  syncs when somebody opens the Sync Status screen, retries a refused record, or
  changes a membership — and at no other time. There is no timer and no lifecycle
  hook; `app.dart`'s foreground observer runs the cloud backup and (as of this
  task) the stuck-departure recovery, and nothing else.
  **What that costs a person:** a field tech who records bearings all day and
  never opens Sync Status has nothing on the server, and the bar tells them so
  correctly — *"N records waiting to sync"* — which reads as "it is about to" when
  it means "it will not until you ask". **Static, not measured on hardware:** it
  is the absence of a call site, which is a strong fact about the source but says
  nothing about whether the omission was deliberate. **Action: ask the planning
  session for a task**, and it needs a decision from Michael first — automatic
  sync on foreground is a battery-and-data choice, not just wiring.

- **[Found by 11.57 (2026-08-29), SCHEDULED as task 11.60 (2026-08-29), CLOSED by
  task 11.60 (2026-08-29)] Somebody an owner removed cannot delete
  their local copy of the project without first pressing "Leave".**
  **Closed by the server-side arm Michael chose.** A pull from a device whose
  stint has ended is now answered with that person's own closed membership row
  and nothing else, so the device learns it was removed and the existing
  departed-member exemption is satisfied — no second deletion mechanism. Security
  Model §4.27, trust-boundary inventory entry 28 (Open until Gate C attacks it,
  task 11.49). The e2e matrix walk now asserts the new shape and says in its own
  comment why it changed. The description below is what was found, kept as
  written.
  Measured, and asserted in both halves by
  `test/e2e/membership_cycle_matrix_e2e_test.dart`. Task 11.54's
  `MutationExemption.departedMember` verifies against the *local* membership rows
  — no open stint, and a closed one — which holds for somebody who left and not
  for somebody who was removed, **because their device never learns it happened**:
  the pull that would carry the closed row is the request the server is now
  refusing. The route out exists (the Leave control is still offered, closing the
  stint locally, after which Delete appears) so this is a usability gap and not a
  second lockout — but nothing tells anybody to do it, and the app is meanwhile
  showing them an amber *"the server is refusing access to this project"*. **The
  fix is a decision, not an obvious edit:** either the app lets somebody delete a
  local copy of a project it cannot reach, or the server finds a way to hand a
  removed member their own closed row, which is a disclosure question.

- **[Found by 11.57 (2026-08-29), LOW — no caller today, but it will get one]

- **[Found by Michael on hardware 2026-08-29 after commit `a6bea69`, NEEDS A TASK
  NUMBER — the largest open item in this list] The whole membership cycle —
  add, invite, join, leave, remove, delete, re-invite, rejoin — has never been
  walked in more than one ordering, and two orderings produced four symptoms.**
  Full detail, including which parts are measured and which are hypotheses, is in
  `CLAUDE_DOCS/TASK_COMMS.md` under "Task 11.54 field report — 2026-08-29"; it is
  not copied here because it is long and the two copies would drift. In short:

  1. **A project left and deleted on a device cannot be rejoined on that device.**
     The invite code is correctly refused ("already a member" — the person really
     is one on the server), and `ProjectDirectoryClient.listAvailableToJoin`
     excludes the project because it counts a *tombstoned* local row as one the
     device already has. There is no route back. **Measured.** *This supersedes
     the "LOW / currently unreachable" entry below, which was wrong: it was
     reached the same day it was written.*
  2. **The "already a member" refusal advises "use Join a project instead"**,
     which is the one thing that does not work in state 1. Same defect shape as
     task 11.54's own subject: a surface naming a remedy the app cannot deliver.
  3. **A departure did not reach the owner's device at all** on a clean run
     against a freshly created project, though it did on 2026-08-29 against an
     older one. Not reproduced, and the candidates are in `TASK_COMMS`. The one
     ruled out by measurement is "the device never offers the row" —
     `offer_rules.dart` withholds only membership rows naming somebody else, and
     a departure names the caller in both governed columns.
  4. **Measured and true regardless of 3's cause: a departure that is not
     confirmed on the way out has no route out afterwards.**
     `MembershipController.leaveProject` leaves the project linked with the row
     pending, and `SyncController` only ever syncs the **active** project — which
     a deleted project never is. This deserves its own acceptance line whatever
     else the task finds.

  **The acceptance should be the matrix, not these four symptoms.** Each ordering
  is fine in isolation; it is the transitions that are not, which is why running
  two orderings once each found four things. Both directions of removal belong in
  it — the person leaving, and an owner removing them — because only the first has
  ever been walked.


- **[Found by 11.54 (2026-08-29), SCHEDULED as task 11.58 (2026-08-29)] A
  server-minted database identifier on the wire — the remaining half of task 11.51.** 11.54 reproduced
  the mechanism at the engine
  (`test/data/sync/stale_cursor_new_server_test.dart`, three passing cases) and
  did **not** fix it. A device pointed at a rebuilt or restored server reports a
  clean sync and delivers nothing, because its bookmark is keyed by project id
  alone and the new database's sequence starts at 1. **The reproduction also
  found a second carrier the original reading did not name, and it is worse than
  the cursor:** `SyncStateStore.clear` erases the cursor, the last-success stamp
  and the linked flag, but `SyncRowReceiptStore` is deliberately excluded on the
  stated grounds that "a receipt is a statement about what the server holds,
  which does not stop being true." **That reasoning does not survive the server
  changing underneath it** — it is a statement about *which* server holds it — so
  a receipt from the old database keeps a local row off the new server's push
  set, and unlike the cursor that does not self-heal as the new server catches
  up. **Action: ask the planning session for a task** covering (a) the server
  minting an identifier once when its schema is created and returning it on
  sync, (b) the client storing it beside the cursor and resetting **both the
  cursor and the receipts** when it does not match, (c) a sentence on the sync
  status screen naming what happened, and (d) a `SyncFailureCause` value for it,
  which 11.54 deliberately left out because nothing could produce one. The
  protocol change is additive and task 10.18's compatibility guarantee applies.
  **Not reproduced against a live rebuilt server** — the Docker stack was not
  brought up for this — and that gap should be written into the new task rather
  than assumed closed by the engine test.

  style plus iOS Dynamic Type, a deliberate choice to accept or change) or one
  does (which contradicts the code and is the more interesting finding).

- **[Found by 11.54, CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE AND FIXED (2026-08-29)] Leave,
  delete, get invited back — and the project came back invisible.** Michael ran
  it and it happened; this entry is kept rather than deleted because the
  mechanism is worth not rediscovering. Deleting writes a tombstone on the local
  `Projects` row and bumps its `revision`, and `MergeResolver.compare` reads
  **revision before timestamp** — so the local tombstone outranked the server's
  copy of the project, the pull correctly declined to overwrite a newer local
  row, and the tombstone survived every sync. Nothing errored; the sync reported
  success. Fixed in `ProjectJoiner.join`, which now withdraws a tombstone this
  device wrote before the grant: joining is the device's later, explicit
  statement that it wants the project here. `deleted_at` only — restoring
  through the repository would bump the revision again and lengthen the
  staleness. Covered by `test/data/sync/rejoin_after_delete_test.dart`, which
  asserts the mechanism as well as the symptom.
  **Residue, stated rather than hidden:** if the owner edited the project
  exactly once between the person leaving and rejoining, the rejoining device
  can show that project's name and extent one edit behind until the next owner
  edit. Content, never visibility, and self-correcting. Not worth a task on its
  own; worth knowing if somebody reports a stale project name after a rejoin.

- **[Found by 11.54 (2026-08-29) — SUPERSEDED THE SAME DAY; kept because being
  wrong here is the point] `ProjectDirectoryClient.listAvailableToJoin` counts a
  *tombstoned* local project as one this device already has**, so it is not
  offered in "Join a project". **This was filed as LOW and "nobody can currently
  reach it", and Michael reached it within hours** — it is the whole of symptom 1
  in the membership-cycle entry above, and it leaves a device permanently unable
  to rejoin a project it is a member of. The reasoning that made it look
  unreachable was that redeeming an invitation calls `ProjectJoiner.join`
  directly, which is true and irrelevant: the server correctly refuses a code to
  somebody who is *already* a member, so the code path is never reached and the
  listing is the only way back. **A prediction offered as a finding, which is the
  mistake this project has now recorded three times.**

- **[Superseded by the entry above — kept for the record] A departed member's
  local project delete is a soft delete, and nothing had established what
  happens if they rejoin afterwards.** 11.54 re-enabled the existing delete path for
  somebody who has left, which writes a tombstone on the local `Projects` row.
  That row is safe to write because `offer_rules.dart` classifies `Projects`
  among the tables a device never offers the server at all — so the tombstone
  cannot reach anybody else. **What was not established is the rejoin case:**
  the tombstone carries a newer `updated_at` than the server's copy, so a later
  `ProjectJoiner.join` may leave the rejoined project invisible on that device.
  It is written down rather than fixed because reaching it needs a live server
  and a rejoin, which this task could not run. **Action: ask the planning
  session to add it to whichever task next touches join, or give it its own.**
