- **From task 11.46 (2026-08-28): copy-on-add does NOT dissolve the rest of
  this, and the remainder must not be filed under task 11.34.** Task 11.46 was
  told to say so plainly either way, so: **measured, on two grounds, both
  evidence-backed.**

  1. **Copy-on-add governs `Tags` and nothing else.** The failure that was
     actually reproduced is `Triangulation_Sessions` → `Observations` — a
     session a colleague last edited, and the owner's own bearing naming it.
     No part of 11.34's design touches that table, or the four others whose
     rows carry a `last_modified_by` somebody else may have set.
  2. **Even for tags, copy-on-add governs the *add* path, not the *import*
     path** — and importing is how the projects in question come to exist.
     `ProjectMerger`'s insert branch preserves the file's own
     `last_modified_by` (`lib/data/sync/project_merger.dart:704-716`), and
     that is deliberate, asserted, and correct:
     `test/security/backup_restore_overwrite_test.dart:840-843` states the
     reason — *"an insert destroys nothing, so the file's own provenance
     survives it."* The audit column is only restated to the importer on the
     **update** half (`_patchFor`). So restoring a colleague's `.zip` puts
     colleague-stamped rows on this device on every table, whatever 11.34
     decides about tags.

  **What is left, now that the crash is fixed.** Nothing errors any more and
  nothing is lost: those rows and everything pointing at them are refused one
  at a time, held on the device, and each held record now names the record it
  is waiting on. But **they are held indefinitely**, because the person who
  would have to send them is not on the project and never will be. The only
  remedy the app offers is to open and edit each row by hand, which restamps
  it — fine for three rows, not for a season's archive, and nothing tells
  anyone that is the remedy.

  **Michael decided this on 2026-08-28: a restored record keeps the name of
  the person who made it.** Provenance wins over publishability. So the
  obvious fix — restamping an imported record as the importer so it can be
  published — is **off the table**, and the follow-up must not propose it.
  The current behaviour is therefore correct and unchanged; `_patchFor`'s
  restating on the *update* path is a different question (it protects an
  existing record from being overwritten, §4.19 rule 2) and was not part of
  this decision.

  **What that decision costs, stated so it is not discovered later.** A
  bearing, non-detection or supersede/exclude mark a colleague authored can
  **never** be published from your device — only from theirs. That is task
  11.24's deliberate trade (finding N-1), it is enforced over
  `MutationRule.namesRowAuthor` rather than a list, and
  `server/test/authz/authorization_test.dart` proves it holds even when the
  colleague is a **current member** of the project. If a colleague hands over
  an archive and moves on, their field records stay on that one device. Under
  this decision that is the accepted outcome, not a defect.

  **Action: ask the planning session for a follow-up task, and scope it to
  the audit column on shared-vocabulary tables — not to publishability in
  general.** The decision above settles the field-data half; what is left is
  narrower and much safer:

  - `Tags`, `Triangulation_Sessions`, `Project_Tags`, `Estimated_Positions`
    and `Actual_Tag_Locations` have **no author column at all**. Their only
    user column is `last_modified_by` — *"who last edited this shared
    vocabulary"*, not *"who recorded this observation"*. Refusing those is a
    much weaker claim than N-1's, and it is not what Michael's decision
    protects.
  - **And it is the expensive one.** A refused `Tags` row makes every bearing
    of *your own* that uses it a foreign global reference, so the audit column
    on somebody else's tag blocks **your** field data from reaching the
    server. That asymmetry — a weak claim with a heavy cost — is the whole
    case for the follow-up, and it is a different argument from the one task
    11.24 settled.

  **Became task 11.47, and closed by it on 2026-08-28.** The follow-up was
  scoped exactly as asked — to the audit column on shared-vocabulary tables,
  not to publishability in general — and the answer is that clause 2 is not
  asked of an audit name. The list of five was right about the instances and
  one short on the derivation: `Tag_Versions` is a sixth, and it inherited the
  answer by declaring its rule rather than by anybody noticing it.

- **From task 11.46 (2026-08-28): the client has no shared declaration of
  which column refers to which table, so it can only half-explain a held
  record.** The new "this record is waiting on that record" sentence finds the
  link by matching a held row's whole primary key against same-named columns,
  which is true of every reference in this schema except
  `Projects.owner_user_id` (already covered by the naming rules). The declared
  foreign-key graph exists only server-side, in
  `server/lib/src/schema/postgres_schema.dart`. **Small, and worth a task only
  if a third consumer needs it** — moving `foreignKeys` into
  `packages/tritrack_sync` would make the client's explanation derived rather
  than conventional, and is the same "one definition" move task 11.43 made for
  `vouchesForAForeignName`. The convention and its one exception are written
  down at the method that relies on them.

- **From task 11.47 (2026-08-28): §4.17's clause 2 is now unreachable, and that
  is recorded rather than tidied away.** Reaching it needs a rule that vouches
  for a foreign name *and* a column that is not the audit one; every table
  satisfying the first has `last_modified_by` as its only user column, so the
  audit exemption always takes it first. `RowAuthorizer._projectAlreadyNames`
  has exactly one call site and nothing now reaches it.
  **Deliberately kept, not deleted**, because it is the correct answer for a
  shape that does not exist yet — a shared-vocabulary table that also names
  somebody — and deleting it would mean rediscovering the rule the next time
  one is added. The tripwire is `mutation_rules_test.dart`'s "every relaxed
  table has no identity column for it to reach", which fires on that day.
  **Both the call site and Security Model §4.17 now say plainly that nothing
  rests on the clause today**, so it cannot be mistaken for live protection or
  cited as coverage. **No task recommended** — flagged so the next security
  gate reads it as an intentional dormant branch rather than a finding.

- **From task 11.47 (2026-08-28): the app-side suite could not have caught this
  change being made wrongly, and still cannot.** A sweep of `test/` and
  `integration_test/` found that **no app test — including the e2e suite —
  has ever pushed a row of any of the six shared-vocabulary tables carrying a
  `last_modified_by` naming somebody other than the pusher.** Every such row in
  every fixture is self-stamped, so an incorrect version of this change (one
  that had also exempted the audit column on `author` tables, breaking task
  11.24) would have gone green across the whole app suite. The server suite
  does cover it, end to end over HTTP, which is why this is a gap rather than a
  hole — the boundary is tested where the boundary is enforced.
  **Worth a small task**, and the natural home already exists:
  `test/e2e/two_people_one_project_e2e_test.dart` signs two distinct people in,
  so the owner seeding a `Tags` row stamped by the contributor plus their own
  bearing using it, and asserting `report.heldCount == 0`, would exercise the
  real client engine against the real server for the exact cascade this task
  fixed. Note that `test/e2e/suite_coverage_test.dart` measures *route*
  coverage, not authorization-cause coverage, so it will not flag the absence.
  **Re-scoped and largely closed by task 11.118 (2026-09-02), and the honest
  answer is "yes, in the place this entry named, but only against a real
  server."** Task 11.36 built exactly the fixture pair predicted —
  `tagLastEditedByAFormerColleague` / `bearingAuthoredByAColleague` in
  `test/e2e/support/e2e_harness.dart` — and
  `two_people_one_project_e2e_test.dart` pushes both **in one request**,
  asserting the tag's foreign edit stamp is `inserted` and the colleague's
  bearing is `unauthorized`. The stranger it stamps with is deliberately
  somebody the project can never reach, so §4.17 clause 2 cannot vouch and the
  11.47 relaxation is the only thing that can accept the row. **What remains
  open is narrower than the original finding, and should be stated rather than
  called done:** that file is `skip: e2eSkipReason`, so a plain `flutter test`
  still never pushes a foreign-stamped shared-vocabulary row. What runs by
  default is `suite_coverage_test.dart`'s **shape** check — it calls both
  fixtures and asserts, against `tableMutationRules`, that the row really does
  carry a foreign name in the audit column of a table whose rule permits one,
  and that no *identity* column does. **That is a guard on the fixture, not on
  the server.** So the boundary is tested where the boundary is enforced, and
  the app-side default suite has a fixture-shape guard standing in for it —
  which is the position the original entry called "a gap rather than a hole",
  and it is still exactly that. **No further task recommended**; closing it
  fully means running the e2e suite on every commit, which is task 11.40's
  open question and not this one's.

- **From task 11.43 (2026-08-28): a first publish can fail outright, with a
  database error, if the project uses a tag a colleague last edited.** Not
  introduced by 11.43 and not changed by it — recorded because measuring the
  publish payload is what made it visible. A `Tags` row is shared vocabulary, so
  §4.17's clause 2 governs it and the device rightly still offers it; but on a
  *first* publish the project on the server reaches nobody but its owner yet, so
  clause 2 cannot vouch and the tag is refused. The owner's own bearings then
  reference a `tag_id` the server does not hold, and `Observations.tag_id` is a
  real foreign key — so a later batch violates it and the whole request fails.
  `RowAuthorizer._replicableName`'s own comment claims clause 2 "is what keeps a
  first publish working when the project's tags were created by a colleague",
  and that claim looks false for the first publish specifically. **Worth a task**,
  and it should start by establishing whether the cascade is reachable rather
  than assuming it: the reward is either a fixed publish or a corrected comment.
  **Answered by task 11.46 on 2026-08-28, and this prediction was half right.**
  The tag *is* refused on a first publish and the comment *was* false — both
  corrected. But the cascade does **not** end in a database error along the tag
  path: `_authorizeTagReferences` refuses the dependent bearing before Postgres
  ever sees it, so the publish returns 200 with three refused rows and the
  project still lands. The dead request was real one table over, where no such
  check existed — see task 11.46 and Security Model §4.26. Left standing rather
  than rewritten, because a prediction that was worth acting on and turned out
  to be partly wrong is worth more as a record than as a deletion.
  What a person would see is a publish that fails with a database error and no
  explanation, on a project imported from a colleague's archive or built from
  their shared observations.

- **[Found by 11.108 (2026-09-01), NEEDS A TASK NUMBER] The same wrong-cause
  defect this task fixed for `HandshakeException` is still live on iOS and
  macOS, through a different exception shape.** `createPlatformHttpClient`
  (`lib/core/providers/server_http_client_provider.dart`) uses `CupertinoClient`
  on iOS/macOS instead of the `dart:io`-backed `IOClient` this task's fix
  targets. `cupertino_http`'s own source
  (`NSErrorClientException extends ClientException`,
  the `cupertino_http` package's own `cupertino_client.dart` — pub cache, not a file in this repository) shows a TLS/certificate failure on those two
  platforms arrives as a **`http.ClientException`**, not a `HandshakeException`
  — so it is caught by the existing `on http.ClientException` clause and
  reported as `_couldNotReach`: "Could not reach the server... check this
  device is on the same network... check the server is running." That is the
  same wrong cause this task exists to correct, on the two platforms this
  project's own sign-in work (task 11.38) treats as first-class. **Not fixed
  here** — it is a distinct exception type carrying an `NSError` with its own
  `NSURLErrorDomain` codes (**corrected 2026-09-01 against Apple's published constants, because
  this entry had them wrong: `-1201` bad date, `-1202` untrusted, `-1203` unknown root, `-1204`
  not yet valid** — more structured than the BoringSSL string-sniffing
  this task had to fall back to, so a proper fix could name causes more
  reliably on Apple platforms than this task managed on the others).
  **I could not test this against a real device or simulator** — this is
  static analysis of `cupertino_http`'s source, not an observed failure.
  Suggested scope: catch `NSErrorClientException` specifically ahead of the
  generic `http.ClientException` clause in `server_config_screen.dart`, and
  classify by `error.error.code` against `NSURLErrorDomain`'s certificate
  codes the same way this task classifies `HandshakeException`'s message.

  task.] A third copy of the signal-strength and bearing-quality words, disagreeing with the
  canonical one task 11.193 built.** `observation_edit_dialog.dart` (the "Edit observation" dialog
  reachable from the Log screen's menu) defines its own `signalStrengthLabel` —
  `'Moderate'` for `medium` and `'Very strong'` for `veryStrong` — instead of reading
  `observation_quality_display.dart`'s `'medium'`/`'very strong'`. Its bearing-quality `ChoiceChip`
  is worse: it shows `q.db`, the raw database token (`good`, `suspected_bounce`, underscore and
  all), the exact defect task 11.193 fixed on the Position screen. **Task 11.194 fixed the same
  defect where it had leaked into the Log row's own subtitle** (`_ObservationTile` was showing
  `o.bearingQuality!.db` too, reached through a different import than the edit dialog's) but left
  `observation_edit_dialog.dart` itself untouched — fixing it means deleting that file's local
  `signalStrengthLabel`/`_signalStrengthDisplayOrder` and repointing its two `ChoiceChip` rows at
  the canonical functions, which is a self-contained small task, not something to fold silently
  into a rename task about the Log row.

- **[Found by task 11.194, 2026-09-07. Needs Michael and a phone, not a task.] `V. strong` may sit
  close to the edge of its roller column on the Record screen.** Measured in `flutter_test`'s
  fallback font (about twice Roboto's width, task 11.133): the unbounded text is 146px against a
  122.7px column, so it ellipsizes in the test font. At half that width — the real-font estimate
  this project uses everywhere else — it would be about 73px against the same 122.7px, comfortably
  inside. **This could not be verified on a real device.** If the wheel ever shows a clipped
  "V. str…" instead of "V. strong" at the selected size, that is the thing to look for.
